items.text: משנת הפתיחה: בדיקת חמץ
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on the night of the 14th of Nisan, one searches for chametz by candlelight. Places where chametz is not brought in do not require searching, and the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding two rows in a wine cellar is introduced.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שבליל ארבעה עשר בניסן בודקים חמץ לאור הנר, ומפרטת מקומות הפטורים מבדיקה, וכן מחלוקת בין בית שמאי ובית הלל לגבי שתי שורות במרתף.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that on the night of the 14th of Nisan one searches for chametz by candlelight, and introduces the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding two rows in a wine cellar.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין בדיקת חמץ לאור הנר בליל ארבעה עשר, ומפרטת מקומות הפטורים מבדיקה, ומביאה את מחלוקת בית שמאי ובית הלל בשתי השורות במרתף.

items.text: מחלוקת בפירוש 'אור'
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on the meaning of "אור"
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what "אור" means in the Mishnah. Rav Huna says it means daybreak, and Rav Yehuda says it means night. The initial assumption is that each holds a literal interpretation.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה פירוש 'אור', ורב הונא אומר 'נגהי' (אור יום) ורב יהודה אומר 'לילי' (לילה), ומתחילה להבין את הדעות כפשוטן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'אור' (or) means in the Mishnah, and presents two interpretations: Rav Huna says it means 'נגהי' (daybreak) and Rav Yehuda says it means 'לילי' (night), with the initial assumption that each refers to the literal meaning.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה פירוש המילה 'אור' במשנה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna says 'אור' means daybreak (נגהי).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה פירוש המילה 'אור' במשנה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says 'אור' means night (לילי).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה פירוש המילה 'אור' במשנה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that each opinion is taken literally: Rav Huna means actual daybreak and Rav Yehuda means actual night.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה פירוש המילה 'אור' במשנה.

items.text: First objection from a biblical verse
items.text_en: First objection from a biblical verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the verse "the morning is light" (Genesis 44:3), which seems to show that "אור" means daytime. The Gemara deflects by noting the verse says "the morning is light" not "the light is morning", and cites Rav Yehuda's teaching about entering and exiting with good fortune.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the verse 'הבקר אור' (the morning is light), which seems to show that 'אור' means daytime, but resolves it by noting the verse reads 'הבקר אור' (the morning is light) not 'האור בקר', and cites Rav Yehuda's teaching about entering and exiting in good condition.
The Gemara deflects by noting the verse says 'הבקר אור' (the morning is light), not 'האור בקר' (the light is morning), so it means 'morning dawned', not that אור means daytime.
The Gemara supports this with Rav Yehuda's teaching in the name of Rav that one should always enter and exit with 'כי טוב' (good fortune), which uses the same idiom of 'morning is light'.

items.text: Second objection from another verse
items.text_en: Second objection from another verse
items.desc_en: Another objection is raised from the verse "and as the light of morning, the sun shines" (II Samuel 23:4). The Gemara deflects by explaining the verse means "like the light of morning in this world, akin to the sun's rising for the righteous in the world to come."

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection from the verse 'וכאור בקר יזרח שמש' (and like the light of morning the sun shines), which seems to indicate 'אור' is daytime, but resolves it by noting the verse says 'וכאור בקר' (like the light of morning) and interprets it as a metaphor for the world to come.

The Gemara deflects by noting the verse reads 'וּכְאוֹר בֹּקֶר' (like the light of morning), not 'אוֹר בֹּקֶר' (the light of morning), and explains it means 'like the light of morning in this world, akin to the sun's rising for the righteous in the world to come.'

items.text: קושיה מבראשית ופירושה
items.text_en: Third objection and resolution regarding creation
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from the verse "God called the light day" (Genesis 1:5). The Gemara first deflects by saying God called the light that was coming, but then challenges this with the parallel for darkness. It concludes that the verse means God designated light for daytime commandments and darkness for nighttime commandments.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה מפסוק 'ויקרא אלהים לאור יום', ודוחה שהכוונה לאור המאיר, ומסבירה שהקב"ה קרא לאור ולחושך למצוות היום והלילה.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from the verse 'וַיִּקְרָא אֱלֹהִים לָאוֹר יוֹם' (God called the light day), proving that 'אוֹר' (light) means daytime.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מפסוק 'ויקרא אלהים לאור יום' שמוכיח ש'אור' הוא יום.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deflects by saying the verse means God called the light that was coming (the dawn light) 'day'.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה שהכוונה לאור המאיר ובא, ופונה לקושיה על 'ולחושך קרא לילה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges this answer by applying the same logic to darkness, which would absurdly mean God called the coming darkness 'night' even though daytime continues until stars appear.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מפסוק 'ויקרא אלהים לאור יום' שמוכיח ש'אור' הוא יום.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the verse means God designated light for daytime commandments and darkness for nighttime commandments.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה שהכוונה לאור המאיר ובא, ופונה לקושיה על 'ולחושך קרא לילה'.

items.text: קושיה מתהילים ופירושה
items.text_en: Fourth objection from Psalms and its resolution
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from the verse "Praise Him, all stars of light" (Psalms 148:3), which seems to show "אור" means night. The Gemara deflects by explaining it means "shining stars," but then challenges that non-shining stars should also praise. It concludes that the verse teaches that starlight is also called light, relevant for one who vows to abstain from light.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה מפסוק 'הללוהו כל כוכבי אור' שמוכיח שאור הוא לילה, ודוחה שהכוונה לכוכבים המאירים, ומסיקה שהדבר נלמד לנודר מן האור.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from the verse 'Praise Him, all stars of light' (Psalms 148:3), which seems to show that 'אור' (light) refers to night.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מהפסוק 'הללוהו כל כוכבי אור' שאור משמעו לילה, שהרי הכוכבים נראים בלילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deflects by explaining that the verse means 'all shining stars,' not that 'אור' itself means night.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מהפסוק 'הללוהו כל כוכבי אור' שאור משמעו לילה, שהרי הכוכבים נראים בלילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if only shining stars praise, then non-shining stars should not praise, yet the verse 'Praise Him, all His hosts' includes them.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מהפסוק 'הללוהו כל כוכבי אור' שאור משמעו לילה, שהרי הכוכבים נראים בלילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the verse teaches that starlight is also called 'אור' (light), which is relevant for one who vows to abstain from light, as such a person is forbidden from starlight.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסיקה שהפסוק בא ללמד שאור הכוכבים נחשב אור, ולכן הנודר מן האור אסור באור הכוכבים.

items.text: קושיה מאיוב
items.text_en: Fifth objection from Job
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection from the verse "By light the murderer rises, he kills the poor and needy, and at night he is like a thief" (Job 24:14), which seems to contrast light with night, implying light is daytime.
items.desc: הגמרא מתחילה להקשות מפסוק באיוב שבו 'אור' משמעו יום, אך הקטע נקטע.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the verse 'לאור יקום רוצח יקוטל עני ואביון ובלילה יהי כגנב' (by light the murderer rises to kill the poor and needy, and at night he is like a thief), which seems to show 'אור' means daytime.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מפסוק באיוב שבו 'אור' משמעו יום, אך הקטע נקטע.

items.text: Reinterpretation of the verse from Iyov
items.text_en: Reinterpretation of the verse from Iyov
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'let the night be like a thief' does not prove that 'or' means day; rather, it is a metaphor for certainty versus uncertainty in the case of a pursuer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'let the night be like a thief' implies 'or' means day.
The Gemara answers that the verse is a metaphor for certainty versus uncertainty in the case of a pursuer, not a proof about the meaning of 'or'.

items.text: Challenge from Iyov's curse
items.text_en: Challenge from Iyov's curse
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised from Iyov's curse 'let him wait for light and there is none', implying 'or' is day. The Gemara explains it is a curse on his constellation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from Iyov's curse that 'he waits for light and there is none' implies 'or' means day.
The Gemara answers that Iyov was cursing his fate, not defining 'or' as day.

items.text: Challenge from David's statement
items.text_en: Challenge from David's statement
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised from David's statement 'night is light around me', implying 'or' is day. The Gemara explains it refers to the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from David's statement that 'night is light around me' implies 'or' means day.
The Gemara answers that David was speaking metaphorically about the World to Come and this world, not defining 'or' as day.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Yehuda's Mishnah
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Yehuda's Mishnah
items.desc_en: A Mishnah is cited where Rabbi Yehuda says 'they check on the night of the 14th and on the morning of the 14th', proving that 'or' means night. The Gemara concludes 'shma minah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from Rabbi Yehuda's statement that 'they check on the night of the fourteenth and on the fourteenth in the morning' — proving 'or' means night.
The Gemara concludes 'shma minah' — learn from it that 'or' means night.

items.text: Challenge from the dispute about work on the 14th
items.text_en: Challenge from the dispute about work on the 14th
items.desc_en: A Baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says work is forbidden from 'the time of light' and Rabbi Yehuda says from sunrise. This seems to show 'or' means day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says work is forbidden from 'the time of light' (אור), and Rabbi Yehuda says from sunrise.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's challenge to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's challenge to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov asks Rabbi Yehuda: where do we find a day partially forbidden for work? Rabbi Yehuda responds: the day itself proves, as it is partially permitted for eating chametz and partially forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov objects to Rabbi Yehuda: where do we find a day partly forbidden and partly permitted for work?
Rabbi Yehuda answers: the day itself proves it, since part is permitted for eating chametz and part is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara's inference and rejection
items.text_en: Gemara's inference and rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rabbi Yehuda's statement that 'or' in Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's statement means night, but rejects this, explaining that 'or' means dawn (the pillar of dawn).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: since Rabbi Yehuda says 'from sunrise', Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's 'אור' must mean night.
The Gemara answers: no, 'אור' here means the dawn column (daybreak).

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's counter-argument
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's counter-argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions: if 'or' means dawn, then Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's own position allows work at night, contradicting his challenge. He responds that for him, there is a distinction between day and night, citing a Tosefta about fasts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov interprets 'or' as dawn, then his own position permits work at night, contradicting his argument that no day is partially permitted and partially forbidden.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov responds that for him, the rabbis distinguish between day and night, citing a Tosefta about public fasts where he rules that eating is permitted until dawn.
The baraita records Rabbi Shimon's dissenting opinion that eating on a fast day is permitted until cockcrow, showing that the rabbis do distinguish between day and night.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's objection to Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's objection to Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov objects to Rabbi Yehuda: but for you, where do we find that the rabbis distinguish within the day itself?

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's response
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's response was valid, and explains that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov objected: you are comparing rabbinic prohibition of work to Torah prohibition of chametz.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi Yehuda's answer 'the day itself proves it' — is that a valid response?
The Gemara explains: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov responded that work is a rabbinic prohibition while chametz is a Torah prohibition, so the analogy fails.

items.text: Resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the hours of work prohibition are rabbinic, and the rabbis instituted a distance from the Torah prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the hours of work prohibition are rabbinic (דְּרַבָּנַן), not Torah-based.
The Gemara resolves further that the rabbis instituted a distance (הַרְחָקָה) from the Torah prohibition to create a buffer.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah about beacons
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah about beacons
items.desc_en: A Mishnah is cited that beacons are lit 'on the night of its intercalation', proving 'or' means night. The Gemara concludes 'shma minah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the practice of lighting bonfires for the new month: 'on the night of its intercalation' — proving 'אור' means night.
The Gemara asks: when are the beacons lit? The Mishnah answers: on the night of its intercalation (לְאוֹר עִבּוּרוֹ).
The Gemara concludes: this proves that 'אוֹר' means night (אוּרְתָּא), and the proof is conclusive (שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ).

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah about Temple service
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah about Temple service
items.desc_en: A Mishnah is cited that one who serves all night requires sanctification 'at light', implying 'or' is day. The Gemara dismisses this as 'or' is different (referring to morning).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from Rabbi's statement that one who sacrifices all night requires hand-and-foot sanctification 'at light' — implying 'אורה' means day.
The Gemara answers: 'אורה' (with a heh) is different from 'אור'.

items.text: Introduction of Mar Zutra's challenge
items.text_en: Introduction of Mar Zutra's challenge
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra raises another challenge, which will be addressed in the following text.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite an objection from Mar Zutra.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about miscarriage on the night of the 81st day
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about miscarriage on the night of the 81st day
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a woman miscarries on the night of the 81st day after childbirth. Beit Shammai exempt her from a sacrifice, while Beit Hillel obligate her.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a case: a woman who miscarries on the night of the 81st day, and the dispute between Beit Shammai (exempting) and Beit Hillel (obligating) regarding the sacrifice.

items.text: Gemara's question: What is the meaning of 'or'?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: What is the meaning of 'or'?
items.desc_en: Beit Hillel asks Beit Shammai why the night of the 81st day should differ from the day itself regarding the sacrifice. The Gemara infers from this that 'or' means 'night' (אורתא).

sub.text: Beit Hillel's question to Beit Shammai
sub.text_en: Beit Hillel's question to Beit Shammai
sub.desc_en: Beit Hillel asks Beit Shammai: why should the night of the 81st day differ from the day itself regarding the sacrifice, if they are equal in impurity?
The Gemara infers from Beit Hillel's phrasing that 'or' means 'night' (אורתא).

items.text: Proof from the laws of sacrifices: 'or' means night
items.text_en: Proof from the laws of sacrifices: 'or' means night
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that discusses the possibility of eating sacrifices on the night of the third day. The baraita concludes that 'or' means night, as it says 'on the day' and not at night. This supports the inference that 'or' is night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that raises a possibility: perhaps a sacrifice could be eaten on the night of the third day, based on a logical comparison (kal vachomer) from other sacrifices.
The baraita rejects the possibility by citing a verse that limits eating to daytime, not the night of the third day.
The baraita raises another possibility: perhaps leftover sacrifice should be burned immediately after the eating period ends, based on a logical comparison.
The baraita rejects this by citing a verse that specifies burning on the third day, not at night.
The Gemara concludes from the baraita's language that 'or' means night, confirming the earlier inference.

items.text: Proof from Yom Kippur prayers: 'or' means night
items.text_en: Proof from Yom Kippur prayers: 'or' means night
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about Yom Kippur where 'or' of Yom Kippur is the evening prayer, indicating that 'or' means night. Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel adds that one recites a full eighteen blessings due to Havdalah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about the Yom Kippur prayer schedule, where 'אור של יום הכיפורים' (the 'or' of Yom Kippur) refers to the evening prayer, showing that 'or' means night.
Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel adds that one recites a full eighteen blessings in the evening prayer because Havdalah must be included in the blessing 'חונן הדעת' (who graciously grants knowledge).
The Gemara concludes from this baraita that 'אור' (or) indeed means night, as the evening prayer is called 'אור של יום הכיפורים'.

items.text: Proof from the search for chametz: 'or' means night
items.text_en: Proof from the search for chametz: 'or' means night
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a teaching from the school of Shmuel that on the night of the 14th, one searches for chametz by the light of a candle. This confirms that 'or' means night.

sub.text: Gemara's citation from the school of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation from the school of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a teaching from the school of Shmuel (דְּבֵי שְׁמוּאֵל) that on the night of the 14th, one searches for chametz (חמץ) by candlelight (לאור הנר), proving that 'or' (אור) means night (אורתא).

items.text: Resolution: Regional differences in terminology
items.text_en: Resolution: Regional differences in terminology
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda do not dispute; rather, in Rav Huna's place they call night 'naghei' and in Rav Yehuda's place they call it 'leilei'. The Mishnah uses 'or' as a euphemism.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent dispute by explaining that both sages agree 'or' means 'night' universally, but each uses his local dialect — Rav Huna's region calls night 'naghei' and Rav Yehuda's calls it 'leilei'.

items.text: The principle of using clean language
items.text_en: The principle of using clean language
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah uses 'or' instead of 'night' because it is a euphemism, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that one should never utter a disgusting word. The Torah itself avoided saying 'unclean' directly. Additional proofs from Rabbi Yishmael's school and verses emphasize using clean language in Torah, rabbinic, and mundane matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the tanna of our Mishnah did not use the word 'לֵילֵי' (night) instead of 'אוֹר'.
The Gemara answers that the tanna employed a euphemism, in accordance with the principle of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that a person should never utter a crude thing, citing the Torah's avoidance of the word 'טְמֵאָה' (unclean) by using eight extra letters.
Rav Pappa adds that another verse uses nine extra letters to avoid saying 'טָמֵא' (impure).
Ravina argues that the verse actually adds ten letters due to the plene spelling of 'טָהוֹר'.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov cites a verse that uses sixteen extra letters to avoid saying 'טָמֵא'.

sub.text: Baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that one should always speak in clean language, citing verses that use 'רֶכֶב' (riding) for a זב (zav) and 'מוֹשָׁב' (sitting) for a woman, and supporting verses from Job.
The Gemara asks why the baraita needed the additional verses introduced by 'וְאוֹמֵר' (and it says).
The Gemara explains that the additional verses are needed to extend the principle of clean language from Torah to rabbinic matters and then to ordinary speech.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding 'riding' for women
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding 'riding' for women
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the claim that 'riding' (מרכב) is not used for women, citing verses where Rebecca and Moses' wife ride. It answers that in those cases, it is due to the fear of camels or it is a normal manner of travel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the claim that the Torah avoids the term 'מרכב' (riding) for women, citing verses where Rebecca and Moses' wife ride.

items.text: Gemara's defense of euphemistic language in the Torah
items.text_en: Gemara's defense of euphemistic language in the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the objection that the Torah uses the word 'riding' (רוכבת) for Avigail, which seems less euphemistic than 'sitting'. It explains that the context of nighttime fear or David's fear justifies the term, and alternatively, the fear of the mountain itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: the Torah uses the word 'riding' (רוכבת) for Avigail, which seems less euphemistic than 'sitting'.
The Gemara answers that the context of nighttime fear (ביעתותא דליליא) justifies the term 'riding' as a euphemism.
The Gemara offers an alternative: the fear of David (ביעתותא דדוד) justifies the term 'riding'.
The Gemara offers a second alternative: the fear of the mountain (ביעתותא דהר) justifies the term 'riding'.

items.text: Principle of concise language in Torah
items.text_en: Principle of concise language in Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara establishes a general principle: when two terms are equivalent, the Torah uses clean language; when matters are lengthy, it uses concise language. This is supported by Rav Huna's teaching in the name of Rabbi Meir that a teacher should always teach his student concisely.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: But in the Torah, is the word 'טָמֵא' (impure) not written?
The Gemara answers: Rather, wherever two terms are equivalent, the Torah speaks in clean language; wherever matters are lengthy, it speaks concisely.
The Gemara cites Rav Huna citing Rav in the name of Rabbi Meir: A person should always teach his student concisely.

items.text: Objection from 'riding' vs 'sitting'
items.text_en: Objection from 'riding' vs 'sitting'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that 'riding' and 'sitting' are equivalent, yet the Torah uses 'riding'. It resolves that the word is actually written as 'רוכבת' (with a vav), which is a euphemism.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: in every case where two terms are equivalent, does one not speak in a respectful term? Yet the Torah says 'רוֹכֶבֶת' (riding) and 'יוֹשֶׁבֶת' (sitting) which are equivalent, and it says 'רוֹכֶבֶת' (riding)!
The Gemara resolves: the word is actually written as 'רֹכֶבֶת' (with a vav), which is a euphemism for 'riding'.

items.text: Story of two students before Rav
items.text_en: Story of two students before Rav
items.desc_en: Two students sitting before Rav used crude metaphors ('something that stinks' and 'a kid that stinks') to describe a teaching. Rav refused to speak with the one who used the coarser term, demonstrating the importance of refined speech.

sub.desc_en: The first student describes the teaching as 'something that stinks' (דבר אחר מסנקן), using a crude metaphor.
The second student describes the teaching as 'a kid that stinks' (גדי מסנקן), a slightly less crude metaphor.
Rav refuses to speak with the first student who used the coarser term, demonstrating the importance of refined speech.

items.text: Story of two students before Hillel
items.text_en: Story of two students before Hillel
items.desc_en: Two students before Hillel (one being Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai) asked about the laws of harvesting olives and grapes with different phrasing. Hillel predicted that the one who used the more refined language would become a teacher, which came true.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story of two students sitting before Hillel, one of whom was Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai (or according to another version, before Rabbi and one was Rabbi Yochanan).
The first student asks why grapes are harvested in a state of טהרה (ritual purity) but olives are not harvested in טהרה.
The second student asks why grapes are harvested in טהרה but olives are harvested in טומאה (ritual impurity).
Hillel predicts that the student who used the more refined phrasing (the first one) will become a teacher in Israel.
The Gemara concludes that within a short time, that student indeed became a teacher in Israel.

items.text: Story of three priests and the defective animal
items.text_en: Story of three priests and the defective animal
items.desc_en: Three priests described the size of a piece of meat they received. One said 'like an olive', another 'like a bean', and the third 'like a lizard's tail'. The third was found to have a disqualifying blemish. The Gemara addresses the contradiction with the rule that we do not inspect animals from the altar upward, and resolves by emending the text or noting that the priest brought the defect upon himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story of three priests who each described the size of a piece of meat they received from the altar; the third was found to have a disqualifying blemish.
The Gemara objects: a baraita rules that we do not inspect animals from the altar upward, yet here the priests inspected the meat after it was on the altar.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by emending the text: either read 'שחץ (arrogance) of disqualification' instead of 'שמץ (blemish)', or note that the third priest brought the defect upon himself by his own words.

items.text: Story of the Arab who ate Passover sacrifices
items.text_en: Story of the Arab who ate Passover sacrifices
items.desc_en: An Arab ate Passover sacrifices in Jerusalem, claiming he was eating from the choicest parts. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira tricked him into asking for the tail (אליה), which is offered on the altar, exposing him as a non-Jew. He was killed, and the sages praised Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira for his wisdom.

sub.desc_en: An Arab (ארמי) goes up to Jerusalem and eats Passover sacrifices, claiming he is eating from the choicest parts despite the prohibitions against non-Jews and uncircumcised persons.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira (רבי יהודה בן בתירא) asks the Arab if they served him from the tail (אליה), and when he says no, instructs him to request it when he goes up.
The Arab follows the advice and asks for the tail, but the people of Jerusalem respond that the tail is offered on the altar, exposing his ignorance.
The people investigate, find the Arab is a non-Jew, kill him, and send praise to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira (רבי יהודה בן בתירא) for his wisdom in trapping him from afar.

items.text: Stories about euphemistic speech in reporting
items.text_en: Stories about euphemistic speech in reporting
items.desc_en: When Rav Kahana died, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Rav Idi reported it indirectly, quoting 'He who utters slander is a fool'. Similarly, Yochanan Chakoaka, when asked about wheat, answered about barley, and was rebuked for not using the proper euphemism for bad news.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a story: Rav Kahana fell ill, and the Sages sent Rabbi Yehoshua ben Rav Idi to check on him.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Rav Idi arrives, finds Rav Kahana dead, tears his garment, reverses the tear, and returns weeping.
The Sages ask Rabbi Yehoshua ben Rav Idi: 'Did he pass away?'

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Rav Idi's evasive answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Rav Idi's evasive answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Rav Idi replies: 'I am not saying;
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Rav Idi quotes the verse 'He who utters slander is a fool' (Proverbs 10:18) to avoid directly reporting the death.
The Gemara introduces a second story: Yochanan Chakoaka went to the villages, and upon his return, the villagers asked him about the wheat.
The villagers ask: 'Have the wheat become beautiful?'
Yochanan Chakoaka answers: 'Barley has become beautiful' — a euphemism for bad news.
The villagers rebuke him: 'Go tell the horses and donkeys,' citing the verse about barley and straw.
The Gemara asks: 'What should he have said?'
The Gemara suggests: 'Lentils have become beautiful' — a proper euphemism for bad news.

items.text: Anecdotes of Rav and halakhic derivations
items.text_en: Anecdotes of Rav and halakhic derivations
items.desc_en: Rav, upon arriving in Babylonia, is greeted by his uncle Rabbi Chiyya with a cryptic exchange about 'Ayvu' and 'Imma'. Rav then instructs his servant to remove his sandals and take his clothes to the bathhouse, from which three laws are inferred: a mourner is forbidden to wear sandals, a distant report of mourning is observed only one day, and part of the day is considered as the whole. Two more anecdotes follow: one about a man saying 'judge my case' indicating he is from Dan, and another about a man saying 'on the seashore I was raised' indicating he is from Zevulun.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Rav, upon arriving in Babylonia, is greeted by his uncle Rabbi Chiyya with a cryptic exchange about 'Ayvu' and 'Imma'.

Rav instructs his servant to remove his sandals and take his clothes to the bathhouse, from which the gemara infers three laws: a mourner is forbidden to wear sandals, a distant report of mourning is observed only one day, and part of the day is considered as the whole.
The gemara relates an anecdote about a man who says 'judge my case,' indicating he is from the tribe of Dan, as per the verse 'Dan shall judge his people.'
The gemara relates an anecdote about a man who says 'on the seashore I was raised,' indicating he is from Zevulun, as per the verse 'Zevulun shall dwell at the shore of the seas.'

items.text: Timing of bedikat chametz and the principle of zerizim
items.text_en: Timing of bedikat chametz and the principle of zerizim
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that since 'or' means night for everyone, and both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir agree that chametz is only forbidden from the sixth hour onward, the bedikah should be at the sixth hour. It then raises the objection that the zealous (zerizim) perform mitzvot early, so why not check in the morning? It cites the example of milah, where the entire day is valid but the zealous do it early, as Abraham rose early.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that since 'or' means night for everyone, and both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir agree that chametz is only forbidden from the sixth hour onward, the bedikah should be at the sixth hour.
The Gemara raises the objection that since the zealous (zerizim) perform mitzvot early, why not check in the morning?
The Gemara cites the example of milah, where the entire day is valid but the zealous do it early, as Abraham rose early.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and Abaye on the optimal time for bedikah
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and Abaye on the optimal time for bedikah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the bedikah is done at night because people are home and candlelight is good for searching. Abaye then rules that a Torah scholar should not begin his regular study session on the night of the 13th leading into the 14th, lest his study be prolonged and he neglect the mitzvah of bedikah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the bedikah is performed at night because people are home and candlelight is good for searching.
Abaye rules that a Torah scholar should not begin his regular study session on the night of the 13th leading into the 14th, lest his study be prolonged and he neglect the mitzvah of bedikah.

items.text: Who must check a rented house on the 14th?
items.text_en: Who must check a rented house on the 14th?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one rents a house to another on the 14th of Nisan, who is responsible for checking for chametz? Is it the landlord, since the prohibition is his, or the tenant, since the chametz is in his domain? It attempts to answer from a case about mezuzah, but Rav Mesharshiya distinguishes that mezuzah is an obligation of the resident. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak then cites a baraita: if the 14th began before the keys were handed over, the landlord checks; if after, the tenant checks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: if one rents a house on the 14th of Nisan, who must search for חמץ (leaven) — the landlord, since the חמץ is his, or the tenant, since the prohibition is in his domain?
The Gemara attempts to answer from a ברייתא (baraita) about מזוזה (mezuza), where the tenant must affix it, suggesting the tenant is responsible for mitzvot in the house.
Rav Mesharshiya rejects the proof, explaining that מזוזה (mezuza) is an obligation of the resident, not the owner, so the case is different.
The Gemara asks again: what is the ruling here regarding searching for חמץ (leaven)?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the dilemma by citing a ברייתא (baraita): if the 14th began before the keys were handed over, the landlord searches; if after, the tenant searches.

items.text: Presumption of being checked and who is trusted for biur chametz
items.text_en: Presumption of being checked and who is trusted for biur chametz
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a rented house has a presumption (chazakah) of being checked, relevant when the landlord is unavailable. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a baraita that everyone is trusted for biur chametz, even women, slaves, and minors, implying that the house is presumed checked.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak whether a house rented on the fourteenth has a presumption (חזקה) of being checked for חמץ (leaven), and clarifies the practical difference: when the landlord is unavailable, must the renter be troubled to search?

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers by citing a ברייתא (baraita) that everyone is trusted regarding ביעור חמץ (elimination of leaven), even women, slaves, and minors, implying that the house is presumed checked.

items.text: Initial challenge to the presumption of checking
items.text_en: Initial challenge to the presumption of checking
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that all are trusted to check for leaven is based on the presumption that the house has been checked, citing a baraita about a haver's produce being presumed tithed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's trust in all people to check for leaven is based on the presumption that the house has been checked, citing a baraita about a haver's produce being presumed tithed.

items.text: Rejection of the presumption argument
items.text_en: Rejection of the presumption argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the case of a haver's produce is different because the witnesses' statement has substance, whereas here the statement of those checking might not be reliable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the case of a haver's produce is different because the witnesses' statement has substance, whereas here the statement of those checking might not be reliable.

items.text: Textual challenge to the presumption
items.text_en: Textual challenge to the presumption
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if the Mishnah relied on a presumption of checking, it should have said 'all houses are presumed checked on the fourteenth,' not 'all are trusted.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if the Mishnah relied on a presumption of checking (חזקת בדוק), it should have said 'all houses are presumed checked on the fourteenth' rather than 'all are trusted.'

items.text: Inference from the alternative explanation
items.text_en: Inference from the alternative explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that if the Mishnah relies solely on the witnesses' statement, then without their statement there is no presumption, implying that the presumption of checking does not exist.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that if the Mishnah's ruling depends solely on the witnesses' statement (אמירה דהני), then without it there is no presumption of checking, implying that the presumption of checking (חזקת בדוק) does not exist.

items.text: Resolution: presumption exists but applies only to rabbinic law
items.text_en: Resolution: presumption exists but applies only to rabbinic law
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the presumption of checking does exist, but the Mishnah deals with a case where the house is known not to have been checked, and the witnesses are trusted because checking leaven is only rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the presumption of checking does exist, but the Mishnah deals with a case where the house is known not to have been checked, and the witnesses are trusted because checking leaven is only rabbinic.

items.text: Inquiry about a rented house found unchecked
items.text_en: Inquiry about a rented house found unchecked
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about a landlord who rents out a house presumed checked but it is found unchecked, and cites Abaye's distinction between places where the landlord checks for free or for payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a landlord who rents out a house presumed checked but found unchecked constitutes a mistaken transaction (מקח טעות).

Abaye distinguishes between places where the landlord checks for free (preferring to perform the מצוה (commandment) personally) and places where he checks for payment (preferring to fulfill it through his money), implying the transaction is not necessarily void.

items.text: Source for prohibiting leaven from the sixth hour
items.text_en: Source for prohibiting leaven from the sixth hour
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about eating times, and Abaye derives from two verses that the fourteenth of Nisan is included for removal of leaven, rejecting the possibility that it includes the nights of the fifteenth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah from elsewhere (Pesachim 2a) recording the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about the times for eating and burning leaven on the fourteenth of Nisan.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that leaven is prohibited from the sixth hour onward, a point agreed upon by all disputants in the Mishnah?
Abaye answers by citing two verses — 'seven days leaven shall not be found' and 'on the first day you shall remove leaven' — and resolves them to include the fourteenth of Nisan for removal.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the second verse comes to include the nights of the fifteenth for removal, teaching that the prohibition applies even at night, not just during the day.
The Gemara rejects the objection, stating that the inclusion of nights is not needed because the verse 'seven days' already implies both days and nights.

items.text: Gemara's initial argument from analogy
items.text_en: Gemara's initial argument from analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the prohibition of possessing leaven is linked to eating leaven, and eating leaven is linked to eating matzah, implying that leaven removal begins at the same time as the matzah obligation. It then questions whether this includes the night of the fourteenth, but rejects that because the verse says 'by day', and further limits it to daytime using the word 'akh'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by linking the prohibition of possessing leaven (השבתת שאור) to eating leaven (אכילת חמץ) and eating leaven to eating matzah (אכילת מצה), citing verses to establish the analogy.
The Gemara questions whether the analogy might include the night of the fourteenth for the removal of leaven.
The Gemara answers that the verse says 'by day' (ביום), excluding the night.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the removal should begin from morning (צפרא) of the fourteenth.
The Gemara answers that the word 'אך' (only) divides the day, indicating that removal begins from midday, not morning.

items.text: Beit Rabbi Yishmael's teaching about 'first'
items.text_en: Beit Rabbi Yishmael's teaching about 'first'
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the fourteenth is called 'first' in the verse, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'first' means from the beginning, citing a verse about Job.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the fourteenth is called 'first' in the verse, citing the verse 'בָּרִאשׁוֹן בְּאַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר יוֹם לַחֹדֶשׁ' (in the first [month], on the fourteenth day of the month).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'first' (רִאשׁוֹן) means 'from the beginning', citing the verse 'הָרִאשׁוֹן אָדָם תִּוָּלֵד' (the first man is born).

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding 'first' in Sukkot
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding 'first' in Sukkot
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if 'first' always means from the beginning, then the verse about the four species would also imply the first day of creation, not the festival. It resolves by noting that the context of Sukkot specifies 'seventh' and 'eighth' as festival days, so 'first' there refers to the festival. Similarly, the verse about leaven uses 'the first' to indicate the festival day, not the beginning of time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if 'first' always means from the beginning, then the verse about the four species on Sukkot would also imply the first day of creation, not the festival.
The Gemara resolves that the context of Sukkot specifies 'seventh' as the seventh day of the festival, so 'first' there refers to the festival day itself.
The Gemara objects that the verse about leaven also says 'the first day' and 'seven days', so 'first' should likewise refer to the festival day, not the eve.
The Gemara resolves that the definite article 'the' in 'the first' indicates the day before the festival, as otherwise the verse would have written 'first' without the article.
The Gemara objects that the same logic would apply to Sukkot, where 'the first' is written, and one might think it means from the beginning.
The Gemara resolves that the verse about Sukkot mentions 'the eighth day' as a festival day, so 'the first' there refers to the first day of the festival, not the beginning of time.

items.text: Further analysis of 'the first' and the three 'first's
items.text_en: Further analysis of 'the first' and the three 'first's
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the extra word 'the first' is needed, suggesting it excludes Chol HaMoed, but then argues that Chol HaMoed is already excluded by 'first' and 'eighth'. It concludes that the three instances of 'first' in the Torah are needed for the homiletical teaching of Beit Rabbi Yishmael, that in reward for three 'first's, Israel merited three 'first's: the destruction of Esau, the building of the Temple, and the name of the Messiah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the definite article 'the' in 'the first' is needed, since the exclusion of חולו של מועד (intermediate days) is already derived from the words 'first' and 'eighth'.

The Gemara explains that the definite article is necessary because otherwise one might think that the וָיו (conjunction 'and') in 'and on the eighth day' adds to the previous matter, implying that even חולו של מועד (intermediate days) are sacred; the article teaches that this is not so.

The Gemara objects that the Torah could have simply omitted both the וָיו (conjunction) and the הֵא (definite article), and further questions whether the phrase 'on the first day a sacred convocation' in the Passover context also means 'previous'.

The Gemara resolves that the three instances of 'first' in the Torah are needed for the homiletical teaching of בית רבי ישמעאל (Beit Rabbi Yishmael), that in reward for three 'first's, Israel merited three 'first's: the destruction of Esau, the building of the Temple, and the name of the Messiah.
Beit Rabbi Yishmael provides scriptural proof for each of the three 'first's: the firstborn Esau, the Temple as 'from the beginning', and the Messiah as 'a harbinger to Zion'.

items.text: Rava's alternative derivation from the Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Rava's alternative derivation from the Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: Rava derives the timing from the verse 'Do not slaughter the Paschal lamb while leaven is still extant', implying that leaven must be removed before the time of slaughter, which is the afternoon of the fourteenth. The Gemara clarifies that the verse refers to the time of slaughter, not each individual's slaughter.

sub.desc_en: Rava derives the timing of leaven removal from the verse 'Do not slaughter the Paschal lamb while leaven is still extant', implying that leaven must be removed before the time of slaughter.
The Gemara objects that the verse might refer to each individual's slaughter, not the general time of slaughter.
The Gemara resolves that the verse refers to the general time of slaughter, not each individual's slaughter.

items.text: Baraita with Tannaitic opinions on the derivation
items.text_en: Baraita with Tannaitic opinions on the derivation
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yishmael derives the timing from the Paschal lamb verse, Rabbi Akiva derives it from the juxtaposition of 'first' and 'no work', and Rabbi Yosei derives it from the word 'akh' which divides. The Gemara concludes with Rava's statement linking the removal of leaven to the eating of matzah.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports the derivation: the verse 'אך ביום הראשון תשביתו שאור מבתיכם' is interpreted by Rabbi Yishmael to mean the removal of leaven occurs on the eve of the festival, based on the juxtaposition with the Paschal lamb.

Rabbi Akiva states that no external derivation is needed, as the verse 'אך ביום הראשון תשביתו שאור מבתיכם' is juxtaposed with 'כל מלאכה לא תעשו', and we find that kindling is a primary labor (אב מלאכה), implying the removal occurs before the festival.

Rabbi Yosei argues that no external derivation is needed, as the word 'אך' divides the day, indicating the removal is on the eve of the festival; he adds that if it were on the festival itself, it would be forbidden because the removal of leaven is linked to the eating of חמץ (leaven) and the eating of חמץ is linked to the eating of מצה (unleavened bread), and Rava then speaks.

items.text: Three inferences from Rabbi Akiva's statement
items.text_en: Three inferences from Rabbi Akiva's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers three halakhot from Rabbi Akiva's earlier statement: that chametz removal is only by burning, that the prohibition of burning is separate from other prohibitions, and that we do not say 'since burning was permitted for need, it is also permitted without need'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers three halakhot from Rabbi Akiva's statement: chametz removal is only by burning, the prohibition of burning is separate, and we do not say 'since burning was permitted for need, it is also permitted without need'.

items.text: Baraita on the verses "lo yera'eh" and "lo yimatzei"
items.text_en: Baraita on the verses "lo yera'eh" and "lo yimatzei"
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verses: "lo yera'eh" teaches that you may see others' chametz, but "lo yimatzei" prohibits hiding or accepting deposits from a gentile. The baraita extends the prohibitions to a subdued gentile and to pits, and uses a גזירה שווה to apply the laws of both verses to each other.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'שִׁבְעַת יָמִים שְׂאֹר לֹא יִמָּצֵא' and asks why it is needed given the verse 'לֹא יֵרָאֶה לְךָ שְׂאֹר'.
The baraita explains that 'לֹא יֵרָאֶה לְךָ' permits seeing others' chametz, but 'לֹא יִמָּצֵא' prohibits hiding or accepting deposits from a gentile.
The baraita extends the prohibition to a subdued gentile living in the same courtyard, citing 'לֹא יִמָּצֵא בְּבָתֵּיכֶם'.
The baraita extends the prohibition to pits, cisterns, and caves, citing 'בְּכׇל גְּבֻלֶךָ'.
The baraita asks how to apply the laws of 'בַּל יֵרָאֶה' and 'בַּל יִמָּצֵא' to both houses and borders.
The baraita uses a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the repeated word 'שְׂאוֹר' to apply the full set of prohibitions from houses to borders.
The baraita concludes by applying the leniency of seeing others' chametz from borders to houses.

items.text: Abaye and Rava debate the baraita's structure
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava debate the baraita's structure
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that the baraita's statement about a subdued gentile is misplaced and should be reversed. Rava disagrees, maintaining that the baraita is correct as is and that the statement refers to the first part of the verse.

sub.desc_en: The baraita's statement is cited: for a gentile not subdued and not dwelling with you, the leniency applies; for a subdued gentile dwelling with you, the verse 'לֹא יִמָּצֵא' (it shall not be found) teaches a prohibition.
Abaye objects that the baraita's logic is backwards and argues that the order should be reversed.
Rava rejects the reversal and explains that the baraita is correct as is, applying the statement to the first clause about permission to see others' leaven.

items.text: Question on the baraita's logic
items.text_en: Question on the baraita's logic
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita uses a verse to permit something (seeing others' chametz) and then uses another verse to prohibit it (accepting deposits), when it could have simply derived the prohibition from the same verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita uses a verse to permit something (seeing others' chametz) and then uses another verse to prohibit it (accepting deposits), when it could have simply derived the prohibition from the same verse.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'לְךָ' (with you) appears twice, allowing one to be used for permission and the other for prohibition.

items.text: Contradiction in the baraita resolved by responsibility
items.text_en: Contradiction in the baraita resolved by responsibility
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes an apparent contradiction: the baraita first permits seeing others' chametz, then prohibits accepting deposits. It resolves this by distinguishing between accepting responsibility (prohibited) and not accepting responsibility (permitted).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction: the baraita first permits seeing others' chametz, then prohibits accepting deposits from a gentile.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between accepting responsibility (prohibited) and not accepting responsibility (permitted).

items.text: Rava's ruling and the dispute about דבר הגורם לממון
items.text_en: Rava's ruling and the dispute about דבר הגורם לממון
items.desc_en: Rava instructs the people of Mehoza to burn soldiers' chametz because they are responsible for it. The Gemara questions this based on the dispute whether דבר הגורם לממון is considered money, and answers that here the verse "lo yimatzei" applies, or alternatively that it is not considered money.

sub.desc_en: Rava instructs the people of Mehoza to remove the חמץ (leaven) of the gentile soldiers from their houses, because they bear responsibility for it and it is therefore considered theirs and forbidden.

The Gemara questions Rava's ruling: it works for the opinion that דבר הגורם לממון (an object that effects monetary loss) is considered like money, but what can be said for the opinion that it is not considered like money?
The Gemara answers that here it is different because the verse 'לֹא יִמָּצֵא' (it shall not be found) applies, prohibiting any leaven found in one's domain regardless of the monetary status.
An alternative version states that Rava's ruling works well for the opinion that דבר הגורם לממון is not considered like money, implying a different resolution for the opposing view.

items.text: Necessity of 'lo yimatzei' according to the view that chametz is like money
items.text_en: Necessity of 'lo yimatzei' according to the view that chametz is like money
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse 'lo yimatzei' is needed according to the view that chametz is considered like money (and thus not owned by the owner after Passover). It answers that one might think that since the chametz reverts to its owner after Passover, it is not in his possession, so the verse teaches that it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse 'lo yimatzei' is necessary according to the view that chametz is like money.

The Gemara answers that the verse is needed to counter a potential assumption that since chametz reverts to its owner after Passover, it is not in his possession, so the verse teaches that it is forbidden.

items.text: Animal of the arnona tax and firstborn status
items.text_en: Animal of the arnona tax and firstborn status
items.desc_en: Rava is asked whether an animal given as the arnona tax (a type of tax) is obligated in the law of firstborn. The question is divided into two cases: when the owner can redeem it with money (obligated) and when he cannot (exempt). A baraita is cited that seems to contradict Rava's ruling, but it is resolved by distinguishing the cases.

sub.desc_en: They asked Rava whether an animal given as a tax (arnona) is obligated in bekhor (firstborn offering), distinguishing between cases where the owner can redeem it with money and where he cannot.
Rava answered that the animal is exempt from bekhor.
An objection is raised from a baraita that states the animal is obligated in bekhor.
The resolution distinguishes that the baraita refers to a case where the owner can redeem the animal with money, so it is obligated.
The contradiction is resolved by distinguishing the cases: the baraita refers to a case where the owner can redeem the animal with money, while Rava's ruling applies where he cannot.

items.text: Alternative version: Rava's ruling on arnona animal and dough
items.text_en: Alternative version: Rava's ruling on arnona animal and dough
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rava ruled: the arnona animal is exempt from firstborn even if the owner can redeem it, while the arnona dough is obligated in challah even if he cannot redeem it. The reason is that an animal makes a sound (and thus the tax collector might claim it), whereas dough does not.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rava ruled: an arnona animal is exempt from bekhor even if redeemable, but arnona dough is obligated in challah even if not redeemable.
Rava explains the reason: an animal has a distinctive sound (making it noticeable as a gift), while dough does not.

items.text: Gentile's chametz in a Jew's courtyard
items.text_en: Gentile's chametz in a Jew's courtyard
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a gentile who enters a Jew's courtyard with his dough: if he just enters, the Jew is not obligated to remove it; if he deposits it, the Jew is obligated; if he designates a room for himself, the Jew is not obligated, based on the verse 'lo yimatzei'. Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi debate which clause the verse applies to.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents three cases of a gentile's dough in a Jew's courtyard: entering without deposit (no obligation), depositing (obligation), and designating a room (no obligation), citing the verse 'לֹא יִמָּצֵא'.
The Gemara asks which clause of the baraita the verse 'לֹא יִמָּצֵא' applies to.
Rav Pappa explains that the verse applies to the first clause: the depositor is obligated to remove the dough because of 'לֹא יִמָּצֵא'.
Rav Ashi argues that the verse applies to the last clause: the gentile who designates a room is exempt because he brings the dough into his own domain, as the verse says 'לֹא יִמָּצֵא בְּבָתֵּיכֶם'.

items.text: Does rental acquire ownership?
items.text_en: Does rental acquire ownership?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether rental of a room gives the gentile ownership, citing a mishnah that in places where renting is allowed, one may not rent a dwelling to a gentile because he might bring idolatry into it. If rental acquired ownership, then the gentile would be bringing it into his own house. The Gemara answers that the verse 'lo yimatzei' excludes a case where the chametz is not found in the Jew's possession.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether rental (שכירות) acquires ownership, citing a mishnah that prohibits renting a dwelling to a gentile because he would bring idolatry into it, implying that if rental acquired ownership, the gentile would be bringing it into his own house.

The Gemara answers that the verse 'לֹא יִמָּצֵא' (it shall not be found) excludes a case where the chametz is not found in the Jew's possession, so even if rental acquires ownership, the gentile's chametz is not the Jew's responsibility.

items.text: Finding chametz on Yom Tov and gentile's chametz
items.text_en: Finding chametz on Yom Tov and gentile's chametz
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that one who finds chametz in his house on Yom Tov should cover it with a vessel. Rava adds that if it is consecrated property, no covering is needed because people distance themselves from it. Similarly, for a gentile's chametz, one must make a partition of ten handbreadths as a reminder, but not for consecrated chametz.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that one who finds chametz in his house on Yom Tov should cover it with a vessel.
Rava adds that if the chametz is consecrated property, no covering is needed because people distance themselves from it.

items.text: Traveler and the thirty-day rule before Passover
items.text_en: Traveler and the thirty-day rule before Passover
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that a traveler who leaves within thirty days of Passover must remove chametz, but before thirty days he is not obligated. Abaye limits this to one who intends to return; Rava argues that if he intends to return, even from Rosh Hashanah he must remove it. Rava then applies his own reasoning to the case of one who makes his house a storehouse.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that a traveler leaving within thirty days of Passover must remove chametz, but before thirty days he is not obligated.
Abaye limits the obligation within thirty days to one who intends to return; if he does not intend to return, he is not obligated.
Rava argues that if the traveler intends to return, even from Rosh Hashanah he must remove chametz, and reinterprets the thirty-day rule as applying only when he does not intend to return.
Rava applies his own reasoning to the case of one who makes his house a storehouse: if he intends to clear it, even before thirty days he must remove chametz.

items.text: Reason for thirty days: laws of Passover are taught thirty days before
items.text_en: Reason for thirty days: laws of Passover are taught thirty days before
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the significance of thirty days: it is the period during which one asks and expounds the laws of Passover before the holiday, as taught in a baraita. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says two weeks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the significance of thirty days?
The Gemara answers with a baraita: they ask and expound the laws of Passover thirty days before Passover; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says two weeks.
The Gemara asks: what is the reasoning of the first Tanna (who requires thirty days)?

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's explanation for the order
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's explanation for the order
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that since the Torah was discussing Pesach, it continued with all matters of Pesach, including the second Pesach, even though Moses was standing in the first Pesach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that since Moses was standing in the first Pesach, he warned about the second Pesach, citing the verse about those who were impure.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that since the Torah was discussing Pesach, it continued with all matters of Pesach, including the second Pesach.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's proof from the beginning of the month
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's proof from the beginning of the month
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning: just as Moses stood at the beginning of the month and warned about Pesach, so too here the passage about the second Pesach follows the first because it is all one topic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the reasoning of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (רבן שמעון בן גמליאל)?

items.text: Challenge and alternative proof from Rabba bar Shimi
items.text_en: Challenge and alternative proof from Rabba bar Shimi
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's proof: how do we know Moses was at the beginning of the month? Perhaps he was on the fourth or fifth. Rabba bar Shimi offers a different proof from the verse in the second year, but the same challenge is raised.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's proof: how do we know Moses was standing at the beginning of the month? Perhaps he was on the fourth or fifth.

Rabba bar Shimi offers a different proof from the verse in the second year, citing the verse 'וַיְדַבֵּר ה׳ אֶל מֹשֶׁה בְמִדְבַּר סִינַי בַּשָּׁנָה הַשֵּׁנִית בַּחֹדֶשׁ הָרִאשׁוֹן' (And God spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the first month of the second year) and the verse 'וְיַעֲשׂוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת הַפָּסַח בְּמוֹעֲדוֹ' (And let the children of Israel perform the Pesaḥ at its appointed time).
The Gemara raises the same challenge against Rabba bar Shimi's proof: how do we know Moses was at the beginning of the month? Perhaps he was on the fourth or fifth.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution via a verbal analogy
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution via a verbal analogy
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the challenge by using a verbal analogy (גזירה שוה) between the word 'midbar' here and in the second month, proving that both were at the beginning of the month.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the challenge by using a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) between the word 'midbar' here and in the second month, proving that both were at the beginning of the month.

items.text: The principle that there is no chronological order in the Torah
items.text_en: The principle that there is no chronological order in the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote the first month's passage before the second month's, and Rav Menashya bar Tachlifa in the name of Rav answers that this teaches that there is no chronological order in the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote the first month's passage before the second month's, implying a chronological order.

sub.text: Rav Menashya bar Tachlifa in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Menashya bar Tachlifa in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Tachlifa answers in the name of Rav that this teaches there is no chronological order in the Torah.

items.text: Rav Pappa's distinction and the discussion on Klal u'Prat
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's distinction and the discussion on Klal u'Prat
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa limits the principle to two different topics, but within one topic order matters. The Gemara then discusses the implications for the hermeneutical rules of Klal u'Prat and Prat u'Chlal, and whether they apply when the general and specific are distant.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that the principle of no chronological order applies only to two separate topics, but within one topic order matters; otherwise, the hermeneutic rules of כלל ופרט (generalization and detail) would be undermined.
The Gemara adds that the same problem applies to the rule of פרט וכלל (detail followed by generalization), which would also be ambiguous without fixed order.

The Gemara objects that if order matters, the same difficulty should apply even to two separate topics, challenging the distinction; it notes that this works well for the opinion that distant general and specific clauses are not interpreted together, but what about the opinion that they are?

The Gemara resolves that even according to the opinion that distant general and specific clauses are interpreted together, this applies only within one topic; for two separate topics, the principle of no chronological order applies and they are not interpreted together.

items.text: The requirement to nullify chametz after searching
items.text_en: The requirement to nullify chametz after searching
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that one who searches for chametz must nullify it. The Gemara explores the reason: not because of crumbs (which are insignificant), but as a decree lest one find a nice loaf and become attached to it. Since after the time of prohibition one cannot nullify it, the nullification must be done earlier, but the Gemara questions why not nullify at four or five hours, and answers that since it is not yet the time of prohibition or removal, one might be negligent.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that one who searches for חמץ (leaven) must nullify it, and the Gemara questions whether the reason is because of crumbs, which are insignificant.

The Gemara objects that perhaps crumbs are significant because they are guarded in the house, and cites a ברייתא (baraita) about end-of-season figs and grapes to show that guarding for another purpose does not render insignificant items significant.
Rava explains that the nullification is a decree lest one find a nice loaf and become attached to it, and the Gemara questions why one cannot nullify it upon finding it.

The Gemara rejects this, explaining that one might find it only after the prohibition time when it is no longer in his possession to nullify, citing Rabbi Elazar's principle that two items (a pit in the public domain and חמץ (leaven) after the sixth hour) are treated as if in one's possession though they are not.
The Gemara asks why the nullification cannot be done at the fourth or fifth hour, and answers that since it is neither the time of prohibition nor removal, one might be negligent and not nullify it.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why not nullify at the sixth hour?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why not nullify at the sixth hour?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one cannot nullify chametz at the sixth hour, and answers that since the rabbinic prohibition is like a Torah prohibition, the chametz is not in one's domain to nullify.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one cannot nullify chametz at the sixth hour, given the rabbinic prohibition.

items.text: Support from Rav Giddel's statement
items.text_en: Support from Rav Giddel's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel quotes Rav that betrothal with wheat from the sixth hour onward is invalid, supporting the idea that after the prohibited time, the chametz is not in one's domain.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel cites Rav that betrothal with wheat from the sixth hour onward is invalid, supporting the principle that after the prohibited time the chametz is no longer in one's domain.

items.text: Objection from the baraita about nullification on Shabbat or Yom Tov
items.text_en: Objection from the baraita about nullification on Shabbat or Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: a baraita says one can nullify chametz in his heart even on Shabbat or Yom Tov, which is after the prohibited time, contradicting the previous answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: a baraita teaches that one can nullify chametz even on Shabbat or Yom Tov, which is after the prohibited time, contradicting the previous answer.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains that the baraita refers to a student sitting before his teacher who remembers dough that might become chametz, so he nullifies it before it becomes chametz, not after.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains that the baraita deals with a student sitting before his teacher who remembers dough that might become chametz, so he nullifies it before it becomes chametz.
The Gemara confirms that the baraita's wording 'was sitting in the study hall' supports this interpretation.

items.text: Rav's ruling on moldy bread
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on moldy bread
items.desc_en: Rav states that bread that has molded is permitted if matzah has increased (i.e., it is more likely matzah). The Gemara questions: if it is known to be chametz, what difference does the increase make?

sub.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna reports in Rav's name: a loaf that has molded is permitted if the matzah has increased (i.e., the proportion of matzah is greater).
The Gemara asks: how is this case to be understood?
The Gemara objects: if one knows it is definitely chametz, what difference does the increase of matzah make?

items.text: Alternative interpretation and analogy to coins
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation and analogy to coins
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the case is where we don't know if it is chametz or matzah, and questions why we follow the majority; it brings an analogy from coins found in Jerusalem during the festival, where we follow the later ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative scenario where we do not know if the item is chametz or matzah, and questions why we follow the majority.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah about coins found in Jerusalem, which are treated as maaser or chullin based on location.
The Mishnah continues: during the festival, coins are maaser; otherwise, they are chullin.
Rav Shmaya bar Zeira explains the reasoning: the earlier ones are gone, and these are the later ones, so we follow the majority.

items.text: Distinction: mold indicates chametz, but days of matzah explain
items.text_en: Distinction: mold indicates chametz, but days of matzah explain
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes: the mold itself indicates chametz, so why follow the majority? Rabbah clarifies: 'increased matzah' means many days of matzah passed, so daily fresh bread was placed on it, causing more mold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the case is different because the mold itself indicates the cause.
The Gemara asks: if the mold indicates the cause, what difference does it make if the matzah increased?
Rabbah explains: do not say that the matzah increased, but rather that many days of matzah passed over it.
The Gemara objects: if so, it is obvious!
The Gemara clarifies: it is necessary because the mold is abundant; one might think that since the mold is abundant, it is clearly genuine chametz, so it teaches us otherwise.
The Gemara explains: since many days of matzah passed over it, we say that each day fresh hot bread was placed on it, causing more mold.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda and resolutions
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda and resolutions
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects from a baraita where Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda follows the majority, not the later ones. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, Rav Zevid, and Rav Pappa offer different resolutions for that case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: do we really follow the later ones? It cites a baraita where Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda rules by majority, not by the later ones, and asks why.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves: the case involves coins where one doesn't know which were used last.
Rav Zevid resolves: the case involves separate piles of coins, so the later ones are not identifiable.
Rav Pappa resolves: the case involves coins found in a pit, so the later ones are unknown.

items.text: Blessing for bedikat chametz
items.text_en: Blessing for bedikat chametz
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that one who checks for chametz must recite a blessing. Rav Pappei and Rav Pappa dispute the wording: 'leba'er chametz' vs. 'al bi'ur chametz', with the Gemara noting that 'leba'er' implies future action.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda opens by stating that one who checks for chametz must recite a blessing.
The Gemara asks what blessing is recited.

sub.text: Rav Pappei's answer (in the name of Rava)
sub.text_en: Rav Pappei's answer (in the name of Rava)
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappei, citing Rava, answers that one says 'leba'er chametz' (to remove chametz).

sub.text: Rav Pappa's answer (in the name of Rava)
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's answer (in the name of Rava)
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa, also citing Rava, answers that one says 'al bi'ur chametz' (concerning the removal of chametz).
The Gemara clarifies that everyone agrees the phrase 'leba'er' (to remove) implies future action, resolving the dispute.

items.text: Dispute over the blessing formulation for chametz removal
items.text_en: Dispute over the blessing formulation for chametz removal
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding the blessing for removing chametz hinges on whether the phrase 'על ביעור חמץ' implies the action is already underway or yet to come.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between the two opinions is about the phrase 'על ביעור' (concerning removal): one holds it means 'at the start' and the other holds it means 'for the future'.

items.text: Challenges from blessings over circumcision and slaughter
items.text_en: Challenges from blessings over circumcision and slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises objections from the blessings over circumcision and slaughter, which use 'על', and the Gemara responds that these are special cases where the one performing the mitzvah is not the one acting.

items.text: Challenge from the blessing over lulav and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the blessing over lulav and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the blessing over lulav, which uses 'על', and explains that the blessing is said after taking it, so it is a case of 'over la'asiyatan' (blessing before the act) in a different sense.

items.text: Conclusion of the dispute and halakhic ruling
items.text_en: Conclusion of the dispute and halakhic ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the parallel case of sukkah and concludes that the halakha follows the formulation 'על ביעור חמץ'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the continuation of the baraita about the sukkah, which uses 'לישב בסוכה' (to sit in the sukkah), and concludes that the halacha follows the version 'על ביעור חמץ' (concerning removal of leaven).

items.text: Source for blessing before performing mitzvot
items.text_en: Source for blessing before performing mitzvot
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the principle that blessings are recited before performing mitzvot from a statement by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, and supports it with biblical verses showing that 'עובר' means preceding.

items.text: Exceptions to the rule: immersion and shofar
items.text_en: Exceptions to the rule: immersion and shofar
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses exceptions to the rule of blessing before the act, initially suggesting immersion and shofar, but then Rav Chisda limits it to immersion alone, supported by a baraita.

items.text: Source for searching chametz by candlelight
items.text_en: Source for searching chametz by candlelight
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the requirement to search for chametz by candlelight through a chain of scriptural analogies, and the Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael supports it with verses, addressing a potential objection about the scope of the search.

items.text: Baraita on prohibited light sources for searching
items.text_en: Baraita on prohibited light sources for searching
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that lists light sources not to be used for searching chametz, concluding that only candlelight is acceptable.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis taught in a baraita: one does not search by sunlight, moonlight, or torchlight, but only by candlelight.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Reason for candlelight
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Reason for candlelight
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that candlelight is suitable for searching chametz, and supports this with biblical verses.

items.text: Gemara's question: Sunlight vs. candlelight
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Sunlight vs. candlelight
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why sunlight is not used, noting that Rava said a courtyard needs no search (crows take chametz) and a portico is checked by its own light. It concludes the case is a skylight in a room, specifically its sides.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what circumstances the ruling about sunlight refers to, first suggesting a courtyard (which Rava said needs no search due to crows) and then a portico (which Rava said can be searched by its own light), rejecting both.
The Gemara answers that the case is a skylight in a room, and specifies that the area opposite the skylight is like a portico, but the sides require a lamp.

items.text: Torchlight vs. candlelight
items.text_en: Torchlight vs. candlelight
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a torch is not used, citing Rava's statements about torches. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and others explain that a candle can reach cracks, while a torch cannot; other distinctions are offered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a torch is not used for searching, citing Rava's statements that a torch is brighter than a lamp and is optimal for Havdalah.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that a candle can be inserted into holes and crevices, but a torch cannot.
Rav Zevid distinguishes: a lamp projects its light forward, while a torch projects its light backward.
Rav Pappa says that using a torch causes fear of fire, while a lamp does not.
Ravina explains that a lamp draws light consistently, while a torch's light fluctuates.

items.text: Tanna: Places exempt from search
items.text_en: Tanna: Places exempt from search
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that places where chametz is not normally brought need no search. The Gemara clarifies this includes various lofts, animal pens, and storerooms; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that a bed dividing the room requires search.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any place where chametz is not normally brought does not require searching.
