The Gemara asks what the inclusive phrase 'any place' comes to include.

The Gemara answers that it comes to include the list of places taught by the Sages: upper and lower holes, veranda roof, closet roof, cowshed, chicken coops, straw storehouse, wine and oil storages — all do not require searching.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that a bed that divides the room and separates requires searching.

items.text: Contradictions resolved: Holes and beds
items.text_en: Contradictions resolved: Holes and beds
items.desc_en: A baraita contradicts the Mishnah regarding holes between neighbors and beds. The Gemara resolves: holes differ by location (upper/lower vs. middle), and beds differ by height (raised vs. low).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that contradicts the Mishnah: regarding a hole between neighbors, each searches to where his hand reaches and nullifies the rest; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says a bed that divides the house with wood and stones underneath does not require searching.
The Gemara points out two contradictions: one between the two rulings about beds, and another between the two rulings about holes.

The Gemara resolves: the contradiction about holes is not difficult — one baraita refers to upper and lower holes, the other to middle holes; the contradiction about beds is also not difficult — one refers to a raised bed, the other to a low bed.

items.text: Wine and oil storerooms
items.text_en: Wine and oil storerooms
items.desc_en: A baraita states wine storerooms need search, oil does not. The Gemara explains the case is where one is uncertain if chametz entered; oil has a fixed eating time, wine does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the baraita that wine storerooms do not require searching, citing a contradictory baraita that wine storerooms require searching while oil storerooms do not.
The Gemara explains that the case here is one of uncertainty (מסתפק) whether chametz entered, and then raises a difficulty: if so, oil should also require searching.

The Gemara resolves the difficulty: oil has a fixed quantity for eating, so one does not need to enter the storeroom during the meal, whereas wine has no fixed quantity for drinking, so one might enter with bread.

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya: Beer storerooms in Babylonia
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya: Beer storerooms in Babylonia
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya taught that beer storerooms in Babylonia are like wine storerooms in Israel, in cases of uncertainty.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya teaches that beer storerooms in Babylonia are treated like wine storerooms in Israel, in cases of uncertainty.

items.text: Fish storage areas
items.text_en: Fish storage areas
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says fish storage needs no search, but a baratia says it does. The Gemara resolves: large fish need search, small fish do not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a fish storage does not require searching for leaven.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that requires searching in a fish storage.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the lenient ruling applies to large fish, the stringent one to small fish.

items.text: Salt and lime storage; reeds and dates
items.text_en: Salt and lime storage; reeds and dates
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna says salt and lime storage need search; Rav Pappa says reed and date storage need search.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna states that a salt storage and a lime storage require searching for leaven.
Rav Pappa adds that a wood storage and a date storage also require searching for leaven.

items.text: Danger of inserting hand into cracks
items.text_en: Danger of inserting hand into cracks
items.desc_en: A baraita exempts one from inserting a hand into cracks due to danger. The Gemara questions the danger (scorpion) and whether one would use the area; it explains the case is where the chametz fell and a dog can retrieve it. Rav Ashi adds concern about losing a needle.

sub.desc_en: A baraita exempts one from inserting a hand into holes and crevices for searching due to danger.
The Gemara asks what the danger is, suggesting it might be a scorpion.
The Gemara objects that if a scorpion were there, how would one have used the hole previously?
The Gemara answers that the case is where leaven fell into the hole.
The Gemara questions why a search is needed if leaven fell, citing the mishna that leaven under a rockslide is considered removed.
The Gemara distinguishes: there the rockslide prevents a dog from retrieving the leaven; here a dog can retrieve it.
The Gemara questions why there is concern for danger, citing Rabbi Elazar that those on a mitzva mission are not harmed.
Rav Ashi answers that the concern is lest one lose a needle and look for it, mixing personal interest with the mitzva.

items.text: Charity for ulterior motives
items.text_en: Charity for ulterior motives
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new topic: one who gives charity for a specific purpose (e.g., that his son live) is still considered a complete righteous person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a mitzva performed with a personal motive (e.g., charity for one's son's life or one's own share in the World-to-Come) is still considered a mitzva, citing a baraita that such a person is called a complete righteous person.

items.text: Challenge to the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Challenge to the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that one who searches for chametz is considered completely righteous, suggesting he might have looked after the chametz was already removed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah: How can one be called completely righteous after searching for chametz if he might have come later to inspect the spot where he already searched?

items.text: Rav Nachman's explanation and the principle of agents of a mitzvah
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's explanation and the principle of agents of a mitzvah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the Mishnah refers to danger from gentiles, citing a Tosefta about a shared wall. The Gemara questions the nature of the danger and invokes Rabbi Elazar's principle that agents of a mitzvah are not harmed, but distinguishes when danger is common.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the Mishnah's ruling is due to danger from gentiles, citing the Tosefta of Pleimo about a shared wall.
The Gemara questions what danger is meant, rejecting sorcery because the case of checking by candlelight at night involves awareness, unlike daytime use of a shared wall.
The Gemara objects with Rabbi Elazar's principle that agents of a mitzvah are not harmed, but distinguishes that where danger is common, the rule does not apply, citing Samuel's fear of Saul.

items.text: Question about students coming to the rabbi's house
items.text_en: Question about students coming to the rabbi's house
items.desc_en: Students ask Rav whether they may come early and return late to the rabbi's house, and Rav responds ambiguously.

sub.desc_en: Students ask Rav whether those who live in the field may come early and return late to the rabbi's house.
Rav responds that coming early is upon him and his neck, implying it is permitted.
Students ask Rav about returning late.
Rav responds that he does not know about returning late.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's statement and its support from a baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's statement and its support from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that agents of a mitzvah are not harmed on their way or on their return. The Gemara supports this with a baraita from Isi ben Yehuda, using a kal vachomer argument and a verse about returning safely.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Elazar's statement that agents of a mitzvah are not harmed on their way or on their return.
The Gemara asks: In accordance with whose opinion is this statement?
The Gemara cites a baraita where Isi ben Yehuda teaches that during the pilgrimage festivals, one's property is miraculously protected from harm.

The baraita applies a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if property that is prone to harm is protected, people who are not prone to harm are certainly protected, and a verse proves this applies also on the return journey.
The baraita concludes that the verse teaches one will find one's home in peace upon return.
The Gemara asks: Since protection applies even on the return, why does the verse need to specify protection on the way there?

The Gemara answers that the mention of going is needed for Rabbi Ami's teaching: only one who has land ascends for the festival, implying that the protection of the journey is linked to the mitzvah of pilgrimage.

items.text: Why certain fruits and hot springs are absent from Jerusalem
items.text_en: Why certain fruits and hot springs are absent from Jerusalem
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda and Rabbi Dostat bar Rabbi Yannai explain that Ginosar fruits and Tiberias hot springs are absent from Jerusalem to prevent pilgrims from having ulterior motives.

sub.text: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak asks why Ginosar fruits are absent from Jerusalem, answering that it prevents pilgrims from having an ulterior motive for their pilgrimage.
Rabbi Dostat bar Rabbi Yannai provides a parallel explanation: Tiberias hot springs are absent from Jerusalem for the same reason, to prevent pilgrims from coming for a non-religious purpose.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's ruling on a wine cellar
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's ruling on a wine cellar
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's statement about two rows in a wine cellar applies only where chametz is brought in, and that places where chametz is not brought in require no search.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the meaning of the term 'מרתף' (wine cellar) in the Mishnah?
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling applies only where chametz is brought in, and places where chametz is not brought in require no search.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Yochanan on the two rows
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Yochanan on the two rows
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda interprets the two rows as from floor to ceiling, while Rabbi Yochanan says it is one row shaped like a gamma. Both interpretations are supported by baraitot.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda interprets the two rows of the Mishnah as extending from the floor to the ceiling.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets the two rows as a single row shaped like the Greek letter gamma.
A baraita supports Rav Yehuda's interpretation, stating that the two rows extend from floor to ceiling.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation, describing the outer row facing the entrance and the upper row facing the ceiling.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on Beit Hillel's ruling
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on Beit Hillel's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel disagree on which rows Beit Hillel requires: Rav says the top row and the one below it, Shmuel says the top row and the one inside it. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Chiya taught like Rav, but all other Tannaim taught like Shmuel, and the halakha follows Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Beit Hillel requires checking two outer rows, which are the top ones.
Rav interprets Beit Hillel's ruling as requiring the top row and the one below it.
Shmuel interprets Beit Hillel's ruling as requiring the top row and the one inside it.
The Gemara asks what Rav's reasoning is, explaining that he focuses on the word 'חיצונות' (outer).
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah also says 'עליונות' (top), which seems to contradict Rav's focus on 'outer'.
The Gemara resolves that 'עליונות' excludes the very bottom rows, while 'חיצונות' defines the two rows as outer ones.
The Gemara asks what Shmuel's reasoning is, explaining that he focuses on the word 'עליונות' (top).
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah also says 'חיצונה' (outer), which seems to contradict Shmuel's focus on 'top'.
The Gemara resolves that 'חיצונה' excludes the innermost rows, while 'עליונות' defines the two rows as top ones.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Chiya taught like Rav, but all other Tannaim taught like Shmuel, and the halakha follows Shmuel.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one need not suspect that a weasel dragged leavened bread from house to house or place to place, because if so, there would be no end to the matter.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and challenge
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that if one sees a weasel take bread, one must suspect it and require a search. It challenges this from the ruling that gentile dwellings are presumed impure only after forty days, and that places accessible to weasels and pigs need no inspection.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction: the case of meat is different from bread, because a weasel does not leave leftovers of meat but does leave leftovers of bread.

items.text: Rava's objection and principle
items.text_en: Rava's objection and principle
items.desc_en: Rava objects: in the gentile dwelling case, there are multiple uncertainties, but here we have a definite taking, so uncertainty cannot override certainty.

items.text: First challenge from tithes and resolution
items.text_en: First challenge from tithes and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's principle from a case where a חבר died leaving produce presumed tithed, even though the produce was definitely obligated. It resolves that this is a case of certainty and certainty, because a חבר is presumed to tithe.

items.text: Alternative resolution via Rabbi Oshaya
items.text_en: Alternative resolution via Rabbi Oshaya
items.desc_en: An alternative answer: the produce might never have been obligated in tithes at all, as per Rabbi Oshaya who allows one to bring grain in its chaff to exempt it from tithes.

items.text: Second challenge from a stillborn fetus
items.text_en: Second challenge from a stillborn fetus
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another challenge to the principle that uncertainty does not override certainty, citing a case of a maidservant who miscarried into a pit.

items.text: Opening baraita
items.text_en: Opening baraita
items.desc_en: The baraita describes a case where a priest examined a miscarriage to determine the child's sex, and the Sages declared it pure because weasels and badgers are common there, implying they likely dragged it away.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a doubtful dragging can override the certainty of the miscarriage, then resolves by reinterpreting the baraita: the woman miscarried something resembling a fetus, making it a double doubt, and the priest's examination was to determine if it was a wind or a fetus, and if a fetus, its sex.

items.text: Alternative answer
items.text_en: Alternative answer
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: since weasels and badgers are common, it is certain they dragged it away at that time, even if they might have left some remains, so the case involves certainty versus certainty.

items.text: Contradiction from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Contradiction from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah states that one should hide leftover leaven to avoid needing rechecking, implying concern that a weasel might drag it, contradicting the earlier assumption that weasels are not a concern.

items.text: Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the 13th of Nisan, when bread is common and a weasel would not hide it, and the 14th, when bread is scarce and a weasel would hide it, explaining the Mishnah's concern.

items.text: Rava's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava objects that a weasel is not a prophet to know it is the 14th and hide the leaven, and instead explains that the Mishnah's instruction is to prevent the weasel from taking it in our presence, necessitating a recheck.

items.text: Supporting baraita for Rava
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rava
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rava's view, stating that one who wishes to eat leaven after checking should hide the remainder to prevent a weasel from taking it in his presence, requiring a recheck.

items.text: Rav Mari's decree and supporting cases
items.text_en: Rav Mari's decree and supporting cases
items.desc_en: Rav Mari explains that the Mishnah's instruction is a decree lest one leave ten pieces and find nine, leading to a discussion of similar cases of doubt: nine piles of matzah and one of leavened bread, nine stores selling kosher meat and one selling non-kosher, and two piles with two mice entering two houses, analogous to two baskets of terumah and non-sacred produce.

items.text: Gemara's question: Is uncertainty in chametz like uncertainty in terumah?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Is uncertainty in chametz like uncertainty in terumah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the principle of uncertainty in rabbinic terumah applies to chametz, which is a Torah prohibition. It notes that bedikat chametz itself is rabbinic, since biblically nullification suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the principle of doubt in rabbinic terumah applies to chametz, which is a Torah prohibition, and clarifies that bedikat chametz itself is rabbinic since biblically nullification suffices.

items.text: Case of one piece of chametz and two checked houses
items.text_en: Case of one piece of chametz and two checked houses
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a mouse takes chametz into one of two checked houses, and we don't know which. This is compared to the mishnah of 'two paths' (שני שבילין) regarding tumah, with a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi, and Rava or Rabbi Yochanan's explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case of one piece of chametz and two checked houses, comparing it to the mishnah of two paths (שני שבילין) regarding tumah.
The mishnah cites the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi regarding the status of the tahorot when two people walked on the two paths.

Rava or Rabbi Yochanan explains the dispute: when both come together, all agree they are impure; when one after another, all agree they are pure; the dispute is only when one asks about himself and his fellow, with Rabbi Yossi comparing it to 'together' and Rabbi Yehuda to 'one after another'.

items.text: Case of doubt whether the mouse entered at all
items.text_en: Case of doubt whether the mouse entered at all
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers a case where it is uncertain whether the mouse entered the house at all. This is compared to the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding a person who walked in a field during the rainy season and is unsure if he entered a field with tumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the case of uncertain entry as identical to the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding a person who walked in a field during the rainy season.

The baraita presents the case of a person entering a field during the rainy season with uncertainty about entering a contaminated field, where Rabbi Eliezer declares him pure and the Sages declare him impure.
Rabbi Eliezer states his principle: uncertainty about entry into a contaminated area renders one pure, but uncertainty about actual contact with impurity renders one impure.

items.text: Case of mouse entered but not found
items.text_en: Case of mouse entered but not found
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a case where the mouse entered but after searching, the chametz is not found. This is compared to the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about an item presumed to be impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of a mouse that entered but was not found after searching, and links it to the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding an item presumed to be impure.
Rabbi Meir states that anything presumed to be impure remains in its impurity until the impurity is known to be elsewhere.
The Sages argue that one must search until reaching bedrock or virgin soil, implying a more lenient position that the chametz is not presumed to be present.

items.text: Case of mouse entered and found
items.text_en: Case of mouse entered and found
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers a case where the mouse entered and the chametz was found. This is compared to the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel about a field where a grave was lost and then found.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the case where the mouse entered and the chametz was found is the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi rules that the found grave is the lost one, so the field is pure; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires checking the entire field.

items.text: Cases of discrepancy in counted pieces
items.text_en: Cases of discrepancy in counted pieces
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses cases where one left nine pieces and found ten, or left ten and found nine, comparing them to disputes between Rabbi and the Sages about mixtures of chullin and ma'aser sheni.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of leaving nine pieces and finding ten, stating it is a dispute between רבי (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) and the Sages.

A ברייתא (baraita) is cited: if one left a מנה (maneh) of מעשר שני (second tithe) and found two hundred, according to רבי (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) the pile is a mixture of חולין (non-sacred) and מעשר שני (second tithe).
The Sages rule that all the money is חולין (non-sacred), assuming the original was taken and replaced.

The Gemara introduces the reverse case: leaving ten and finding nine, equating it to the latter clause of the same ברייתא (baraita) where one left two hundred and found a מנה (maneh); according to רבי (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi), one מנה (maneh) remains and one is missing.
The Sages again rule that all is חולין (non-sacred), assuming the original was entirely taken and replaced.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Baraita about lost axe
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Baraita about lost axe
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a case where one left chametz in one corner and found it in another, linking it to a dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis about a lost axe in a house. The Rabbis deem the house impure, suspecting a impure person took it, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel deems it pure, suggesting it was lent or moved.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case of finding chametz in a different corner, linking it to a dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis.
A baraita is cited: a lost axe in a house renders the house impure, because one suspects a impure person took it.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel argues the house is pure, suggesting the axe was lent or moved to another corner and forgotten.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the wording of the Baraita, suggesting it is missing a clause. It rephrases the Baraita to include the case of finding the axe in a different corner, where the Rabbis still deem the house impure, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel deems it pure, attributing the movement to the owner himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Baraita's wording, asking 'Who mentioned a corner?' implying the Baraita is missing a clause.

The Gemara resolves that the Baraita is missing a clause and rephrases it to include the case of finding the axe in a different corner, where the Rabbis deem the house impure and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel deems it pure.

items.text: Rava's rulings on mouse and child with bread
items.text_en: Rava's rulings on mouse and child with bread
items.desc_en: Rava states that if a mouse enters with a loaf and one finds crumbs, one must search for chametz because mice do not normally crumble bread. Conversely, if a child enters with a loaf and one finds crumbs, no search is needed because children typically crumble bread.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if a mouse entered with a loaf and crumbs are found, one must search for chametz because mice do not normally crumble bread.
Rava rules that if a child entered with a loaf and crumbs are found, no search is needed because children typically crumble bread.

items.text: Rava's series of unresolved queries about mice and weasels
items.text_en: Rava's series of unresolved queries about mice and weasels
items.desc_en: Rava raises a series of questions about whether a mouse that enters with bread and a mouse that exits with bread are the same or different, and similar scenarios with a white mouse and black mouse, and a weasel. Each query is left unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a mouse entering with bread and a mouse exiting with bread are the same mouse or a different one.
Rava asks whether a white mouse entering and a black mouse exiting with bread are definitely different, or perhaps the white mouse dropped the bread and the black one picked it up.

Rava asks whether a mouse entering and a weasel exiting with bread are the same bread taken from the mouse, or a different bread, noting that if the weasel took it from the mouse, the mouse would be found in the weasel's mouth.

Rava asks whether a mouse entering with bread and a weasel exiting with both bread and mouse in its mouth is certainly the same mouse, or perhaps the mouse dropped the bread out of fear, and the weasel took it; the query remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rava's queries about bread in hard-to-reach places
items.text_en: Rava's queries about bread in hard-to-reach places
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether one must retrieve bread from a beam, a pit, or a snake's mouth for bedikat chametz, considering if it is accessible or likely to be eaten. These queries are also left unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a loaf on a beam requires a ladder to retrieve it for bedikat chametz, or if it is exempt because it is inaccessible.
Rava asks whether a loaf in a pit requires a ladder to retrieve it, considering whether one might descend for other needs and eat it.
Rava asks whether a loaf in a snake's mouth requires a professional to extract it, or if it is exempt due to danger.
The gemara leaves all three queries unresolved (תיקו), noting the distinction between burdening one's body versus one's money.

items.text: Mishnah: Times for bedikat chametz
items.text_en: Mishnah: Times for bedikat chametz
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says one must check on the night of the 14th, the morning of the 14th, and at the time of removal. The Sages say if one did not check at night, one may check on the 14th; if not then, during the festival; if not then, after the festival, and any leftover should be hidden discreetly.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that one must check for חמץ (leaven) at three times: the night of the 14th, the morning of the 14th, and at the time of removal.
The Sages rule that if one did not check at night, one may check on the 14th; if not then, during the festival; if not then, after the festival, and any leftover should be hidden discreetly.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: the three times correspond to three Torah verses about chametz. Rav Yosef challenges this, citing a Tosefta where Rabbi Yehuda says one who fails to check at these times may no longer check, implying the dispute is about whether checking is still possible. The Gemara concludes the dispute is about whether one may check after the prohibition begins, due to a decree lest one eat from it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Yehuda's position that one must check for חמץ (leaven) at three specific times.

sub.text: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna answer that the three times correspond to three Torah verses about חמץ (leaven): 'לֹא יֵרָאֶה לְךָ חָמֵץ', 'שִׁבְעַת יָמִים שְׂאֹר לֹא יִמָּצֵא', and 'אַךְ בַּיּוֹם הָרִאשׁוֹן תַּשְׁבִּיתוּ שְּׂאֹר'.

Rav Yosef objects by citing a Tosefta where Rabbi Yehuda says that one who fails to check at these three times may no longer check, implying the dispute is about whether checking is still possible after the times have passed.

Mar Zutra presents an alternative version of Rav Yosef's objection, where Rabbi Yehuda says one who fails to check at any one of the three times may no longer check, emphasizing the dispute is about the very possibility of checking later.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda also agrees that if one did not check at the prescribed times, he may still check later, so the dispute is not about the possibility of checking but about something else.

The Gemara concludes that the dispute is about whether one may check after the prohibition begins: Rabbi Yehuda forbids it due to a decree lest one eat from the חמץ (leaven), while the Sages do not decree.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yehuda's decree
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yehuda's decree
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda would decree lest one eat from the chametz, citing a Mishnah where after the Omer offering, the markets of Jerusalem are full of flour and roasted grain, implying no such decree existed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehuda's decree by citing a Mishnah that after the Omer offering, Jerusalem's markets are full of flour and roasted grain, implying no such decree existed.

items.text: Rava's distinction for new grain
items.text_en: Rava's distinction for new grain
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Yehuda permits handling new grain before the Omer because it is only permitted through plucking (kituf), which reminds the person not to eat it, unlike chametz which is fully permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishna presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir says those who harvest before the Omer act against the Sages' will, while Rabbi Yehuda says they act in accordance with the Sages' will.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda does not decree a prohibition against handling new grain lest one come to eat it, unlike his decree regarding chametz.

Rava answers that new grain is different because it is only permitted through plucking (קיטוף), an atypical manner, which reminds the person of the prohibition, unlike chametz which is fully permitted.

items.text: Abaye's challenge: grinding and sifting
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge: grinding and sifting
items.desc_en: Abaye questions Rava's distinction, noting that grinding and sifting are also done with new grain, but the Gemara answers that these are done by hand or with a sieve, not in the usual way.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava's distinction, asking what about grinding and sifting, which are done in a typical manner.
The Gemara answers that grinding is done with a hand mill and sifting on top of a sieve, both atypical, so there is no concern.

items.text: Abaye's second challenge: reaping in irrigated fields
items.text_en: Abaye's second challenge: reaping in irrigated fields
items.desc_en: Abaye raises a contradiction from a mishnah that permits reaping in irrigated fields but not stacking, which was explained as following Rabbi Yehuda, yet here there is no reminder.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava's answer by citing a mishnah that permits reaping in irrigated fields in a typical manner, which was established as following Rabbi Yehuda, yet there is no reminder to prevent eating.

items.text: Abaye's alternative distinction
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative distinction
items.desc_en: Abaye offers a new distinction: with new grain, one is mentally separated from it (badil mineih) because it is not yet permitted, but with chametz, one is not separated because it is permitted until the time.

sub.desc_en: Abaye offers a new distinction: with new grain, one is mentally separated from it (badil mineih) because it is not yet permitted, but with chametz, one is not separated because it is permitted until the time.

items.text: Rava's challenge: consistency of Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages
items.text_en: Rava's challenge: consistency of Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages
items.desc_en: Rava questions whether the contradiction between Rabbi Yehuda's rulings on new grain and chametz is resolved, and then addresses the Sages' own consistency, arguing that one who seeks to burn chametz would not eat from it.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges the consistency of both Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages, asking why the contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's rulings is considered difficult while the Sages' own contradiction is not.

Rava resolves both contradictions: Rabbi Yehuda's is resolved as previously stated, and the Sages' is resolved by noting that one who seeks out chametz to burn it would not eat from it, unlike one processing new grain.

items.text: Rav Ashi's rejected resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's rejected resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi suggests that the mishnah about new grain refers only to flour and parched grain (kemach ve'kali), but the Gemara rejects this because the earlier stages before parching remain problematic, and the difficulty from the mishnah about reaping in irrigated fields persists.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi proposes that the mishnah about new grain refers only to flour and parched grain (קֶמַח וְקָלִי), resolving the contradiction.
The Gemara rejects Rav Ashi's suggestion, noting that the stages before the grain becomes parched remain problematic.
The Gemara further rejects the possibility of resolving via atypical harvesting, citing the mishnah about reaping in irrigated fields, and concludes that Rav Ashi's statement is a mistake.

items.text: Testing Rabbi Yehuda's principle: oil near a lamp
items.text_en: Testing Rabbi Yehuda's principle: oil near a lamp
items.desc_en: The Gemara tests whether Rabbi Yehuda only decrees when one is not separated from the item, citing a baraita where he permits placing an eggshell of oil near a lamp on Shabbat, because the severity of Shabbat makes one careful.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehuda issues a decree even in cases where one does not distance himself from the prohibited item.
The Gemara cites a baraita that prohibits placing an eggshell filled with oil beside a lamp on Shabbat, even if it is an earthenware tube, due to concern one might use the oil.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda permits this, and explains that due to the stringency of Shabbat, one is careful and distances himself from the oil, so no decree is needed.

items.text: Contradiction in Shabbat rulings: tying a bucket rope
items.text_en: Contradiction in Shabbat rulings: tying a bucket rope
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between Rabbi Yehuda's leniency regarding oil and his stringency regarding tying a bucket rope, and resolves it by distinguishing between oil (which might be confused) and tying (where tying and looping are not confused), and by noting that Rabbi Yehuda considers looping itself a form of tying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the leniency regarding oil and the stringency regarding tying a bucket rope, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda prohibits tying a bow.
The Gemara explicitly states that there is a contradiction between Rabbi Yehuda's statements and between the Rabbis' statements.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction for the Rabbis: oil might be confused with other oil, but tying a bow is not confused with tying a knot.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction for Rabbi Yehuda: he does not decree against tying a bow due to tying a knot, but rather considers a bow itself a full-fledged knot.

items.text: Further contradiction: tying with a weaver's rope
items.text_en: Further contradiction: tying with a weaver's rope
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another contradiction regarding the Sages' rulings on tying a bucket with a weaver's rope, and resolves that the Sages decreed about weaver's rope because it might be confused with ordinary rope, whereas looping is not confused with tying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the Rabbis' rulings on tying a bucket with a sash versus a rope, and clarifies that the mishna refers to a weaver's rope, not an ordinary rope.
The Gemara resolves that the mishna speaks of a weaver's rope, which is not a permanent knot.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis decreed about weaver's rope because it might be confused with ordinary rope, but looping is not confused with tying.

items.text: Testing the principle with a firstborn animal
items.text_en: Testing the principle with a firstborn animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the idea that Rabbi Yehuda does not decree when one is separated, citing a baraita where he forbids bloodletting a firstborn animal even though one is separated from eating it, and explains that the concern is that a person in a hurry might cause a blemish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that Rabbi Yehuda does not decree when one is separated from the prohibited item, citing a baraita about a firstborn animal.
The baraita states that Rabbi Yehuda forbids bloodletting a firstborn animal even if it might die, despite the fact that one is separated from eating it.
The Gemara explains that in the case of the firstborn, since a person is agitated and anxious, he might cause a blemish, so Rabbi Yehuda decrees.

items.text: Gemara's objection to the previous answer regarding Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to the previous answer regarding Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the earlier resolution that Rabbi Yehuda's concern about a person being distraught over his money applies only where one is permitted to act in a place where no blemish is made, lest he come to do so where a blemish is made. The Rabbis argue that if one is not permitted at all, he is even more likely to come to do it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle: if you permit a person distraught over his money to act in a place that does not cause a blemish, he will come to act in a place that causes a blemish.
The Rabbis respond that if you do not permit him at all, he is all the more likely to come to perform the prohibited action.

items.text: Distinction between cases of animal grooming and chametz
items.text_en: Distinction between cases of animal grooming and chametz
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda indeed applies the principle that a person is distraught over his money, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda permits certain grooming on Yom Tov while forbidding others. The Gemara distinguishes: there, if one refrains the animal might die, so the concern applies; here, with chametz, it is only a matter of discomfort, so the concern does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda applies the principle that a person is distraught over his money, citing a mishna where Rabbi Yehuda permits scratching but not scraping on Yom Tov.
A baraita defines scraping and scratching, clarifying that scratching does not cause a wound.
The Gemara distinguishes: in the case of a firstborn where the animal might die, the concern applies; with chametz, where it is only discomfort, the concern does not apply.

items.text: Why Rabbi Yehuda decreed regarding chametz but not regarding grooming
items.text_en: Why Rabbi Yehuda decreed regarding chametz but not regarding grooming
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda decreed regarding chametz but not regarding grooming, and answers: bread might be confused with bread, but the two types of grooming (קידור and קרצוף) are not confused with each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) issued a decree regarding חמץ (leaven) but did not issue a decree regarding קרצוף (scratching an animal).
The Gemara answers that bread is interchanged with bread, whereas קידור (scraping) is not interchanged with קרצוף (scratching).

items.text: Mishnah: Times for eating and burning chametz
items.text_en: Mishnah: Times for eating and burning chametz
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir says one may eat chametz all of the fifth hour and must burn it at the beginning of the sixth; Rabbi Yehuda says one may eat all of the fourth, suspends during the fifth, and burns at the beginning of the sixth. Rabbi Yehuda adds a parable about two loaves of a thanksgiving offering. Rabban Gamliel says unconsecrated food may be eaten all of the fourth, terumah all of the fifth, and burning at the beginning of the sixth.

sub.desc_en: רבי מאיר (Rabbi Meir) states that one may eat חמץ (leaven) the entire fifth hour and must burn it at the beginning of the sixth hour.
רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) says one may eat the entire fourth hour, suspend eating during the fifth hour, and burn at the beginning of the sixth.

רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) adds the sign of the two disqualified תודה (thanks-offering) loaves on the איצטבא (bench): while both are placed, all eat; when one is removed, they suspend; when both are removed, all begin burning.
רבן גמליאל (Rabban Gamliel) says חולין (non-sacred food) may be eaten the entire fourth hour, תרומה (priestly portion) the entire fifth hour, and all is burned at the beginning of the sixth.

items.text: Gemara cites a baraita on testimony about the new moon and time estimation
items.text_en: Gemara cites a baraita on testimony about the new moon and time estimation
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita from elsewhere: if witnesses disagree on the day of the month (e.g., one says the second, another the third), their testimony stands because one knows the month is intercalated. If they disagree by two days, it is void. Rabbi Meir applies the same logic to hours: a one-hour discrepancy is valid, two hours void. Rabbi Yehuda says a two-hour discrepancy is valid, but a three-hour gap is void because the sun's position would be inconsistent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: if witnesses disagree on the day of the month (second vs. third), their testimony stands because one knows the month is intercalated.
The baraita states Rabbi Meir's position: a two-day or two-hour discrepancy invalidates testimony, but a one-hour discrepancy is valid.
The baraita states Rabbi Yehuda's position: a two-hour discrepancy is valid, but a three-hour gap is void because the sun's position would be inconsistent.

items.text: Abaye's explanation of the limits of human error in time estimation
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation of the limits of human error in time estimation
items.desc_en: Abaye explains: according to Rabbi Meir, a person errs by nothing at all—the discrepancy is due to one witness referring to the end of the second hour and the other to the beginning of the third. According to Rabbi Yehuda, a person errs by half an hour—the discrepancy is resolved by one witness referring to the end of the third hour and the other to the beginning of the fifth, with a half-hour error on each side.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by stating the general principle: according to Rabbi Meir a person does not err at all, while according to Rabbi Yehuda a person errs by half an hour.

Abaye explains Rabbi Meir's view: the incident occurred at the transition between the second and third hours, so one witness refers to the end of the second and the other to the beginning of the third, with no error.

Abaye explains Rabbi Yehuda's view: the incident occurred at the midpoint of the fourth hour; one witness errs half an hour earlier (end of third hour) and the other errs half an hour later (beginning of fifth hour), so their testimony is valid.

items.text: Alternative version of Abaye's explanation
items.text_en: Alternative version of Abaye's explanation
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Abaye said: according to Rabbi Meir, a person errs by a negligible amount; according to Rabbi Yehuda, a person errs by an hour and a negligible amount. The explanations are adjusted accordingly.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version introduces Abaye's statement that according to Rabbi Meir a person errs by a negligible amount, and according to Rabbi Yehuda a person errs by an hour and a negligible amount.
The alternative version explains that according to Rabbi Meir the incident occurred either at the end of the second hour or the beginning of the third, and one witness errs by a negligible amount.

The alternative version explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda the incident occurred either at the end of the third hour or the beginning of the fifth, and one witness errs by an hour and a negligible amount.

items.text: The contradiction in testimony
items.text_en: The contradiction in testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where one witness says the event occurred at three hours and another says at five hours, with a discrepancy of two hours minus a bit. This sets up the problem of how to reconcile such conflicting testimonies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where one witness says the event occurred at three hours and another at five hours, with a discrepancy of two hours minus a bit.

items.text: Rav Huna's objection and Rava's initial response
items.text_en: Rav Huna's objection and Rava's initial response
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehuda raises an objection: if we were to scrutinize the witnesses and find their testimony contradictory, we would not execute based on it. How then can we execute based on a doubtful discrepancy? He cites the verse that the court must save the accused. Rava responds by explaining that the discrepancy is not a contradiction but a common human error.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehuda's question to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda asks Rava: if we examine the witnesses and find their testimony contradictory, how can we execute based on such uncertainty, when the Torah commands both judgment and acquittal?

Rava answers that the discrepancy is not a contradiction but a common human error: according to Rabbi Meir, a person errs by two hours minus a bit, and according to Rabbi Yehuda, by three hours minus a bit.

Rava elaborates that according to Rabbi Yehuda, the error is three hours minus a bit, so the event occurred either at the beginning of three or the end of five, and each witness cut off three hours minus a bit.

items.text: Rava's explanation of human error
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of human error
items.desc_en: Rava explains that according to Rabbi Meir, people err by two hours minus a bit, so the testimony is consistent if one witness meant the beginning of the second hour and the other the end of the third. According to Rabbi Yehuda, people err by three hours minus a bit, so the testimony is consistent if one meant the beginning of the third hour and the other the end of the fifth.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that according to Rabbi Meir, people err by two hours minus a bit, so the testimony is consistent if one witness meant the beginning of the second hour and the other the end of the third.
Rava explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, people err by three hours minus a bit, so the testimony is consistent if one meant the beginning of the third hour and the other the end of the fifth.

items.text: Mishnah on court examinations
items.text_en: Mishnah on court examinations
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that describes the seven חקירות (investigations) a court conducts, and distinguishes between חקירות and בדיקות (cross-examinations). If a witness says 'I don't know' regarding a חקירה, their testimony is invalid; but regarding a בדיקה, it remains valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about the seven interrogations (חקירות) and the distinction between interrogations and examinations (בדיקות) in capital cases.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer on the distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer on the distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why חקירות are different from בדיקות. It answers that חקירות are testimony that cannot be refuted by showing the witnesses' error, whereas בדיקות can be refuted. This is because if a witness is ignorant of a חקירה, the testimony is inherently flawed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why חקירות (cross-examinations) are treated differently from בדיקות (investigations) regarding the effect of a witness's ignorance.
The Gemara answers that חקירות (cross-examinations) constitute testimony that cannot be refuted by showing the witnesses' error, so ignorance invalidates it.
The Gemara explains that בדיקות (investigations) are testimony that can be refuted by showing the witnesses' error, so ignorance does not invalidate it.

items.text: Applying the error principle to court examinations
items.text_en: Applying the error principle to court examinations
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: if people can err by such a large margin, then the חקירה of 'which hour' is also testimony that cannot be refuted, because the witnesses can claim they erred. The resolution is that we give them the entire range of possible error: for Rabbi Meir, from the beginning of the first hour to the end of the fifth; for Rabbi Yehuda, from the beginning of the first hour to the end of the sixth. We do not give more because people do not err between day and night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if people can err by such a large margin, then the interrogation of 'which hour' is also testimony that cannot be refuted, because the witnesses can claim they erred.
The Gemara answers that we give the witnesses the entire range of their possible error: for Rabbi Meir, from the beginning of the first hour to the end of the fifth.
The Gemara explains that by right we should give even more leeway at the beginning, but people do not err between day and night.
The Gemara states that for Rabbi Yehuda, we give the witnesses from the beginning of the first hour to the end of the sixth, and by right we should give even more leeway at the beginning.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's hours
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's hours
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that people do not err between day and night, and that the fifth hour is when the sun is in the east and the seventh when it is in the west, providing the astronomical basis for the Mishnah's times.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that people do not err between day and night, and explains the astronomical basis for the Mishnah's hours: at the fifth hour the sun is in the east and at the seventh in the west.

items.text: The Mishnah: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: The Mishnah: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Mishnah is quoted: Rabbi Meir says one may eat chametz the entire fifth hour and must burn it at the beginning of the sixth; Rabbi Yehuda says one may eat the entire fourth hour, suspend eating during the fifth, and burn at the beginning of the sixth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, presenting the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda regarding the times for eating and burning chametz on Passover eve.

items.text: Abaye's analysis of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Abaye's analysis of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Abaye analyzes the Mishnah according to his own understanding of human error: for Rabbi Meir, who holds people err not at all or only slightly, one could eat the entire sixth hour; for Rabbi Yehuda, who holds people err half an hour or an hour and a bit, one could eat until half of the sixth or the end of the fifth. He concludes that testimony about hours is given to the vigilant, but chametz is given to everyone.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that according to Rabbi Meir, who holds people err not at all or only slightly, one could eat the entire sixth hour.
Abaye explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds people err half an hour or an hour and a bit, one could eat until half of the sixth or the end of the fifth.
Abaye concludes that testimony about hours is given to the vigilant, but חמץ (leaven) is given to everyone, explaining the Mishnah's stricter times.

items.text: Rava's analysis for Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Rava's analysis for Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rava analyzes Rabbi Meir's position: since people err two hours minus a bit, one cannot eat from the beginning of the fifth hour. The Gemara objects that if so, one could eat during the sixth hour, but Rav Adda bar Ahava explains that the sixth hour is when the sun stands at its zenith (noon), so it is clearly distinguishable.

sub.desc_en: Rava argues that according to Rabbi Meir, who holds people err by two hours minus a bit, one cannot eat from the beginning of the fifth hour because at five the sun is in the east and at seven in the west, making the fifth hour ambiguous.
The Gemara objects that if the fifth hour is ambiguous, then the sixth hour should also be permissible to eat, since it is equally close to noon.
Rav Adda bar Ahava answers that the sixth hour is when the sun stands at its zenith (noon), so it is clearly distinguishable and therefore not subject to the same error.

items.text: Rava's analysis for Rabbi Yehuda and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Rava's analysis for Rabbi Yehuda and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Rava analyzes Rabbi Yehuda's position: since people err three hours minus a bit, one cannot eat from the beginning of the fourth hour, and certainly not during the fourth. The Gemara objects that if so, one could eat during the fifth hour. Abaye resolves this by reiterating that testimony is for the vigilant, but chametz is for everyone.

sub.desc_en: Rava analyzes Rabbi Yehuda's position: since people err three hours minus a bit, one cannot eat from the beginning of the fourth hour, and certainly not during the fourth.
The Gemara objects that if so, one could eat during the fifth hour.
Abaye resolves the objection by reiterating that testimony is for the vigilant, but chametz is for everyone.

items.text: Rava's own explanation for Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rava's own explanation for Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rava rejects Abaye's explanation and offers his own: Rabbi Yehuda holds that chametz can only be destroyed by burning, so the Sages gave him an extra hour (the fifth) to gather wood. Ravina objects that Rabbi Yehuda himself said that at the time of removal, any form of destruction suffices. Rava then offers a new reason: a decree due to a cloudy day (when one might mistake the time). Rav Papa explains that the fourth hour is the time of the meal for everyone, so no decree is needed.

sub.desc_en: Rava rejects Abaye's explanation and offers his own: Rabbi Yehuda holds that chametz can only be destroyed by burning (אֵין בִּעוּר חָמֵץ אֶלָּא שְׂרֵיפָה), so the Sages gave him an extra hour (the fifth) to gather wood.
Ravina objects by citing Rabbi Yehuda's own statement: at the time of removal (בִּשְׁעַת בִּעוּרוֹ), any form of destruction suffices (הַשְׁבָּתָתוֹ בְּכׇל דָּבָר), not only burning.

sub.text: Rava's new reason and Rav Papa's explanation
sub.text_en: Rava's new reason and Rav Papa's explanation
sub.desc_en: Rava offers a new reason: a decree due to a cloudy day (יוֹם הַמְעוּנָּן) when one might mistake the time; Rav Papa explains that the fourth hour is the time of the meal for everyone (זְמַן סְעוּדָה לַכֹּל), so no decree is needed for the fourth hour.

items.text: The hours of meals and the baraita
items.text_en: The hours of meals and the baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita lists the appropriate meal times for different groups: the first hour for gluttons, second for bandits, third for heirs, fourth for workers, fifth for Torah scholars, sixth for everyone. The Gemara notes a contradiction with Rav Papa's statement that the fourth hour is the meal time for everyone, and resolves it by reversing the order for the fifth and sixth hours. Abaye adds that this applies only if one has not eaten anything in the morning.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists the meal times for different groups, from the first hour for gluttons to the sixth hour for everyone.
The Gemara objects that Rav Papa said the fourth hour is the meal time for everyone, contradicting the baraita which assigns the fourth hour to workers.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reversing the order: the fourth hour is for everyone, the fifth for workers, and the sixth for Torah scholars.
Abaye adds that this schedule applies only if one has not eaten anything in the morning; otherwise, the timing is irrelevant.

items.text: Comparison to testimony and the dispute's scope
items.text_en: Comparison to testimony and the dispute's scope
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that the dispute about hours for chametz parallels a dispute about testimony. The Gemara clarifies that this is not a new tannaitic dispute but a reinterpretation of the earlier one. Rav Shimi bar Ashi adds that if witnesses disagree about whether an event occurred before or after sunrise, their testimony is void; the same applies if one says before sunrise and the other at sunrise, lest one think they agree.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that the dispute about hours for chametz parallels a dispute about testimony.
The Gemara objects that this is obvious, as it is the same dispute already mentioned.
The Gemara explains that Rav Ashi's statement teaches that the earlier reinterpretation is a valid reinterpretation, not a new tannaitic dispute.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi adds that the dispute about testimony applies only to hours, but if witnesses disagree about before or after sunrise, their testimony is void.
The Gemara objects that this too is obvious.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi clarifies that even if one says before sunrise and the other at sunrise, their testimony is void, lest one think they agree.

items.text: Explanation of the Mishnah's phrase 'within sunrise'
items.text_en: Explanation of the Mishnah's phrase 'within sunrise'
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's phrase 'within sunrise' means that the sun had not yet fully risen, but there was already a glow of light, and the Mishnah teaches that this is considered day for the purpose of eating chametz.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'within sunrise' means the sun had not fully risen but there was a glow, and this teaches that it is considered day for eating chametz.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rava's challenges
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rava's challenges
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda. Rava challenges this, suggesting it should follow Rabbi Meir (since a Mishnah is stated as a setam) or Rabban Gamliel (as a decisive authority). Rav Nachman rejects both: the Mishnah is not a setam because of the difficulty with the word 'mutar', and Rabban Gamliel is not a decisive authority but states his own reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states in the name of Rav that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Rava challenges Rav Nachman: why not rule like Rabbi Meir, since a Mishnah (משנה) is stated as a setam (סתם, anonymous ruling) in his favor?
Rav Nachman rejects the challenge: that Mishnah is not a true setam because the word 'מוּתָּר' (permitted) creates a difficulty, implying it is not an anonymous ruling.
The Gemara asks: why not rule like Rabban Gamliel, who is a decisive authority (מכריע) between the disputants?
Rav Nachman rejects this as well: Rabban Gamliel is not a decisive authority (מכריע) but merely states his own reasoning (טעם דנפשיה).

items.text: Alternative explanation: Rav follows a Tanna
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Rav follows a Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: Rav's ruling aligns with a specific Tanna, Rabbi Elazar ben Yehuda Ish Bartota, who stated in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua that on Erev Pesach that falls on Shabbat, one may leave only enough for two meals until the fourth hour.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: Rav's ruling aligns with a specific Tanna, Rabbi Elazar ben Yehuda of Bartota, who cited Rabbi Yehoshua.

items.text: Dispute about burning terumot and the ruling
items.text_en: Dispute about burning terumot and the ruling
items.desc_en: The Sages object to Rabbi Elazar's ruling, arguing that pure terumot should not be burned lest food be found for them. Rabbi Elazar responds that they already searched and found none. The Sages counter that perhaps there is food outside the wall. Rabbi Elazar then argues that according to their logic, even doubtful terumot should not be burned lest Elijah come and purify them. The Sages reply that Elijah does not come on Shabbat or Yom Tov eves due to the burden. Ultimately, they established the halacha like Rabbi Elazar.

sub.desc_en: The Sages object to Rabbi Elazar's ruling that pure terumot should be burned, arguing that food might be found for them.
Rabbi Elazar responds that they already searched and found no food.
The Sages counter that perhaps there is food outside the wall.
Rabbi Elazar argues that according to the Sages' logic, even doubtful terumot should not be burned lest Elijah come and purify them.
The Sages reply that Elijah does not come on Shabbat or Yom Tov eves due to the burden.
The Sages established the halacha (הלכה) like Rabbi Elazar ben Yehuda Ish Bartota, who spoke in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua.

items.text: Clarification: the ruling is for burning, not eating
items.text_en: Clarification: the ruling is for burning, not eating
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the established halacha applies even to eating, and Rav Pappa in the name of Rava clarifies that it applies only to burning, not to eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the ruling applies even to eating; Rav Pappa answers in the name of Rava that it applies only to removal (burning).

sub.text: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava clarifies that the ruling applies only to burning, not to eating.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi supporting Rav Nachman's view
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi supporting Rav Nachman's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, when asked about a sack of chametz that was leaking, told the owner to wait until the fifth hour and then sell it. The Gemara debates whether this sale was to non-Jews (supporting Rabbi Yehuda) or to Jews (supporting Rabbi Meir). Rav Yosef initially says it was to Jews, but Abaye objects due to suspicion. Ultimately, Rav Adda bar Matna reports that Rav Yosef explicitly said it was to non-Jews, supporting Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story to show that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi also supports Rav Nachman's view.
Ravin bar Rav Adda relates a story where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi told a man whose sack of chametz was leaking to wait until the fifth hour and then sell it in the market.
The Gemara asks whether the sale was to non-Jews, which would support Rabbi Yehuda's view.
Rav Yosef initially answers that the sale was to Jews, supporting Rabbi Meir's view.
Abaye objects: if the sale was to Jews, why didn't the owner just take the chametz for himself?
The Gemara answers that it was due to suspicion, citing a baraita about charity collectors not selling to themselves.
The baraita elaborates that charity collectors sell to others and not to themselves, based on the verse about being innocent before God and Israel.
Rav Adda bar Matna reports that Rav Yosef explicitly said the sale was to non-Jews, supporting Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Alternative explanation: Rabbi's ruling follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Rabbi's ruling follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef suggests that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's ruling follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says that a bailee may sell perishable deposits in court to prevent loss. Abaye objects, citing Rav Yohanan's statement that this applies only when the owner is absent, but here the owner was present.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef proposes that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's ruling aligns with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who permits a bailee to sell perishable deposits in court to prevent loss.
Abaye objects, citing Rav Yochanan's statement that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling applies only when the owner is absent, but here the owner was present.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if one can sell consecrated animals beyond their needs in court, certainly here where there is total loss, the loaves should be sold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if consecrated animals beyond their needs are sold in court, certainly here where there is total loss the loaves should be sold.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's correction of a Tanna
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's correction of a Tanna
items.desc_en: A Tanna recites a baraita before Rav Yehuda using the phrase 'on the bench,' but Rav Yehuda corrects him to 'on the roof of the bench,' implying the loaves were not meant for storage.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna recites a baraita before Rav Yehuda using the phrase 'על גַּב הָאִיצְטְבָא' (on the bench).
Rav Yehuda rejects the Tanna's wording, asking rhetorically whether the loaves were meant for storage, and instructs him to say 'על גַּג הָאִיצְטְבָא' (on the roof of the bench).

items.text: Description of the Temple Mount structure
items.text_en: Description of the Temple Mount structure
items.desc_en: Rachaba quotes Rabbi Yehuda that the Temple Mount had a double portico, and a baraita supports this, with Rabbi Yehuda calling it an 'istevonit'—a portico within a portico.

sub.desc_en: Rachaba quotes Rabbi Yehuda that the Temple Mount had a double portico, and a baraita supports this, with Rabbi Yehuda calling it an 'istevonit'—a portico within a portico.

items.text: Reason for the loaves being invalid
items.text_en: Reason for the loaves being invalid
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the loaves are invalid. Rabbi Chanina explains that because they were numerous, they became invalid due to staying overnight, citing a baraita that one does not bring a thanksgiving offering on Passover due to leaven. Rav Ada bar Ahava clarifies that we are dealing with the fourteenth of Nisan, and one does not bring sacrifices to the Temple when they will become invalid. The Gemara concludes that everyone brings them on the thirteenth, and due to their number, they become invalid by staying overnight.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the loaves placed as an indicator are called disqualified.
Rabbi Chanina answers that because the thanks-offerings were numerous, the loaves became invalid by being left overnight.
A baraita is cited that one does not bring a thanks-offering on Passover due to the leaven in it.
The Gemara objects that the baraita's reason is obvious.
Rav Ada bar Ahava clarifies that the baraita deals with the fourteenth of Nisan, and one does not bring sacrifices to a situation where they will become invalid.
The Gemara concludes that everyone brings the thanks-offerings on the thirteenth, and due to their number, the loaves become invalid by staying overnight.

items.text: Alternative opinion: loaves were valid but called invalid
items.text_en: Alternative opinion: loaves were valid but called invalid
items.desc_en: In the name of Rabbi Yannai, they said the loaves were actually valid, but called 'invalid' because the animal sacrifice was lost. The Gemara questions why they couldn't bring another animal, and answers with Rabba's principle: if the bread is lost, one brings other bread; if the thanksgiving offering is lost, one does not bring another, because the bread is dependent on the offering, not vice versa.

sub.text: In the name of Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: In the name of Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: In the name of רבי ינאי (Rabbi Yannai), they said the loaves were actually valid, but called 'invalid' because the animal sacrifice was not slaughtered over them.
The Gemara asks: And let them slaughter the offering over the loaves? It answers: The animal was lost.

The Gemara asks further: And let them bring another animal and slaughter it? It answers that the owner said 'this is a thanks-offering and these are its loaves,' in accordance with the opinion of רבה (Rabba).
רבה (Rabba) explains: If the bread is lost, one brings other bread; if the thanks-offering is lost, one does not bring another, because the bread is dependent on the offering, not vice versa.

items.text: Further analysis: blood was spilled
items.text_en: Further analysis: blood was spilled
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests redeeming the loaves for secular use, but instead posits that the animal was slaughtered and the blood spilled. It then aligns this with Rabbi's view that two permitting factors can elevate one without the other, citing a baraita about the lambs of Shavuot. The Gemara even considers Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's opinion, explaining that if the blood was received in a cup and spilled, he follows his father's view that blood ready to be sprinkled is considered as sprinkled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the loaves cannot be redeemed and taken out for secular use.
The Gemara answers that the animal was slaughtered and the blood was spilled, so the loaves cannot be redeemed.
The Gemara aligns this answer with Rabbi's view that two permitting factors can elevate one without the other.
A baraita is cited about the lambs of Shavuot, showing Rabbi's position that slaughter alone can sanctify the bread even without sprinkling.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon states that the bread is never sanctified unless both slaughter and sprinkling are performed for their own sake.
The Gemara explains that even according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, the case is where the blood was received in a cup and then spilled.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon follows his father Rabbi Shimon's view that blood ready to be sprinkled is considered as already sprinkled.

items.text: Final baraita: practical rules for the loaves
items.text_en: Final baraita: practical rules for the loaves
items.desc_en: A baraita in the name of Rabbi Elazar states the loaves were valid: while placed, everyone eats; if one is taken, they suspend; if both are taken, all begin to burn. Another baraita from Abba Shaul begins.

sub.text: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: A baraita in the name of Rabbi Elazar rules that the loaves were valid: while placed, everyone eats; if one is taken, they suspend; if both are taken, all begin to burn.
The gemara introduces a baraita from Abba Shaul, which continues the discussion.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and dispute about burning terumah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and dispute about burning terumah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the practice of burning terumah on Pesach using the analogy of two cows plowing on the Mount of Anointing. Rabbi Chanina reports that priests never refrained from burning meat impure with a secondary impurity together with meat impure with a primary impurity. Rabbi Akiva adds a similar case with oil. Rabbi Meir deduces that pure terumah may be burned with impure terumah on Pesach, but Rabbi Yosei disagrees. The Mishnah concludes with the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua about burning doubtful terumah with definite impure terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a description of the practice of two cows plowing on the Mount of Anointing as a signal for the people to burn their leaven on Passover eve.

רבי חנינא (Rabbi Chanina) the deputy High Priest reports that priests never refrained from burning meat impure with a secondary impurity together with meat impure with a primary impurity, even though it adds impurity.
רבי עקיבא (Rabbi Akiva) adds that priests never refrained from lighting oil disqualified by a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) in a lamp impure from a corpse, even though it adds impurity.
רבי מאיר (Rabbi Meir) deduces from these statements that one may burn pure תרומה (priestly portion) with impure תרומה on Passover.
רבי יוסי (Rabbi Yosei) objects that the inference is not analogous, as the earlier cases involve two impure items, not pure with impure.

The Mishnah concludes with the dispute between רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer) and רבי יהושע (Rabbi Yehoshua): they agree that pure and impure are burned separately, but disagree about doubtful (תלויה) and definitely impure תרומה — Rabbi Eliezer says each separately, Rabbi Yehoshua says both together.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on Rabbi Chanina's case
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on Rabbi Chanina's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Chanina's statement: if meat impure with a secondary impurity (a second-degree) is burned with meat impure with a primary impurity (also a second-degree after contact), both are second-degree, so how is impurity added?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Chanina's statement: if meat impure with a secondary impurity (a second-degree) is burned with meat impure with a primary impurity (also a second-degree after contact), both are second-degree, so how is impurity added?

items.text: Rav Yehuda's answer: dealing with a third-degree
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's answer: dealing with a third-degree
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that the case involves meat that is a third-degree impurity (a secondary derivative), and the opinion holds that a third-degree may be made into a second-degree, thus adding impurity.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda answers that the case involves meat with third-degree impurity (a secondary derivative), and the opinion holds that one may render a third-degree item into a second-degree, thereby adding impurity.

items.text: Objection: food cannot make food impure
items.text_en: Objection: food cannot make food impure
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a food cannot make another food impure, citing a verse that only the food itself becomes impure, not that it makes similar food impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a food cannot make another food impure, citing a verse that only the food itself becomes impure, not that it makes similar food impure.

items.text: Abaye and Rav Adda bar Ahava's resolutions
items.text_en: Abaye and Rav Adda bar Ahava's resolutions
items.desc_en: Abaye limits the rule to non-sacred food, but for terumah and sacred food, food can make food impure. Rav Adda bar Ahava (citing Rava) says the rule applies to non-sacred and terumah, but for sacred food it can make food impure, which resolves the difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the difficulty by limiting the rule that food does not transmit impurity to non-sacred food, but for תרומה (priestly portion) and קדשים (sacred food), food can make food impure.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava (citing Rava) offers a narrower resolution: the rule applies to non-sacred food and תרומה (priestly portion), but for קדשים (sacred food), food can make food impure, which also resolves the difficulty.

items.text: Ravina's challenge: the verse is absolute
items.text_en: Ravina's challenge: the verse is absolute
items.desc_en: Ravina (citing Rava) argues that the verse speaks fully, applying to all cases—non-sacred, terumah, and sacred—so food never makes food impure. This leaves the difficulty unresolved.

sub.text: Ravina in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Ravina in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Ravina (citing Rava) objects that the verse speaks fully, applying to all cases—non-sacred, terumah, and sacred—so food never makes food impure, leaving the difficulty unresolved.

items.text: Alternative answer: liquids are involved
items.text_en: Alternative answer: liquids are involved
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the case involves liquids with the meat, as liquids can transmit impurity. But the Mishnah's wording is problematic. The Gemara concludes that even though food cannot make food impure biblically, rabbinically it can, resolving the issue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case involves liquids with the meat, so the meat becomes impure through the liquids.
The Gemara objects that if liquids are essential, the Mishnah should have said 'with the meat and liquids'.
The Gemara resolves that although food cannot make food impure biblically, rabbinically it can, so the Mishnah's wording is acceptable.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Akiva's case and Rav Yehuda's explanation
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Akiva's case and Rav Yehuda's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines Rabbi Akiva's case: oil that is a third-degree is burned in a lamp that is a second-degree. It asks what is novel, as it seems the same principle as before. Rav Yehuda explains that the case involves a metal lamp, which the Torah treats differently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by analyzing Rabbi Akiva's case: oil disqualified by a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) is a third-degree impurity, and when lit in a lamp impure from a corpse, it becomes a second-degree impurity.
The Gemara questions what is novel in Rabbi Akiva's teaching, since it seems to repeat the same principle as Rabbi Ḥanina's case: that a third-degree may be made into a second-degree.
Rav Yehuda answers that the case involves a metal lamp, which the Torah treats with a unique halakhic status, thus distinguishing it from the previous case.

items.text: Opening statement: the principle that a sword is like a corpse
items.text_en: Opening statement: the principle that a sword is like a corpse
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that a sword (metal vessel) that touches a corpse becomes a primary source of impurity (אב הטומאה), and the Tanna holds that a third-degree impurity can be made into a first-degree impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that a sword (metal vessel) that touches a corpse becomes a primary source of impurity (אב הטומאה), and the Tanna holds that a third-degree impurity can be made into a first-degree impurity.

items.text: Question on Rabbi Yehuda's forced interpretation
items.text_en: Question on Rabbi Yehuda's forced interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehuda was forced to interpret the Mishnah as referring to a metal lamp; why not a clay lamp? And what does the Mishnah mean by 'added'—there it is impure and impure, here it is invalid and impure!

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda was forced to interpret the Mishnah as referring to a metal lamp, rather than a clay lamp.
The Gemara further questions the meaning of 'added' in the Mishnah, contrasting the case of a clay lamp (impure and impure) with the metal lamp (invalid and impure).

items.text: Rava's answer: the Mishnah's wording forced Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rava's answer: the Mishnah's wording forced Rabbi Yehuda
