sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah juxtaposes blood to water according to Hezekiah's view, and cites Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan, who derives from the verse that only blood poured like water (i.e., from a slaughtered animal) makes food susceptible to impurity, but blood of sacrifices (not poured like water) does not.

items.text: Objection from a limb from a living animal
items.text_en: Objection from a limb from a living animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: regarding a limb from a living animal, the Torah says 'לא תאכל הנפש עם הבשר', and a baraita teaches that one may not give it to a Noahide, but it is permitted to dogs. The Gemara answers that a limb from a living animal is different because it is juxtaposed to blood in the verse 'כי הדם הוא הנפש'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a limb from a living animal, citing the verse and a baraita of Rabbi Natan that prohibits giving it to a Noahide but permits it to dogs.
The Gemara answers that a limb from a living animal is different because it is juxtaposed to blood in the verse.

items.text: Hezekiah's derivation: blood from a living animal is forbidden
items.text_en: Hezekiah's derivation: blood from a living animal is forbidden
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what purpose the juxtaposition of a limb from a living animal to blood serves for Hezekiah. He would say that blood is juxtaposed to a limb from a living animal: just as a limb from a living animal is forbidden, so too blood from a living animal is forbidden, specifically blood of bloodletting that causes the soul to depart.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah juxtaposes an אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי (limb from a living animal) to blood according to Hezekiah, and answers that the juxtaposition teaches that just as a limb from a living animal is forbidden, so too blood from a living animal is forbidden, specifically blood of bloodletting (דַּם הַקָּזָה) through which the soul departs.
Hezekiah answers that the juxtaposition teaches that blood from a living animal is forbidden, specifically blood of bloodletting that causes the soul to depart.

items.text: Deriving prohibition of benefit from a stoned ox
items.text_en: Deriving prohibition of benefit from a stoned ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the stoned ox: the Torah says 'לא יאכל את בשרו'. A baraita teaches that this verse teaches that even if the ox is slaughtered after its verdict, it is forbidden. The Gemara asks about deriving prohibition of benefit, and cites Shimon ben Zoma who derives from 'ובעל השור נקי' that the owner is free from any benefit. The Gemara then argues that 'לא יאכל' might imply only eating, not benefit, so the extra verse is needed. Finally, it suggests that 'לא יאכל' actually implies both, and 'ובעל השור נקי' comes to teach about the hide.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of the stoned ox (שור הנסקל) and cites a baraita that the verse 'לא יאכל את בשרו' teaches that even if slaughtered after the verdict, the meat is forbidden.

The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that benefit (הנאה) from the ox is also forbidden, and cites Shimon ben Zoma who derives this from the verse 'ובעל השור נקי' — that the owner is 'clean' of any property rights.
The Gemara objects: the need for the extra verse 'ובעל השור נקי' implies that 'לא יאכל' alone would only forbid eating, not benefit.

The Gemara resolves: 'לא יאכל' indeed implies both eating and benefit, and 'ובעל השור נקי' comes to teach that even the hide is forbidden for benefit, which might otherwise have been permitted since the verse says 'בשרו' (its flesh).

items.text: Alternative derivation for the hide's benefit
items.text_en: Alternative derivation for the hide's benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how those Tannaim who use the verse 'ובעל השור נקי' for other drashot derive the prohibition of benefiting from the hide. They derive it from 'את בשרו' — including what is attached to the flesh. The other Tanna does not expound 'את'. A baraita about Shimon HaAmsoni (or Nechemya HaAmsoni) is cited, who used to expound every 'את' in the Torah until he reached 'את ה' אלהיך תירא' and stopped, but Rabbi Akiva expounded it to include Torah scholars.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Tannaim who use the verse 'ובעל השור נקי' for other drashot derive the prohibition of benefiting from the hide.
The Gemara answers that they derive the prohibition from 'את בשרו', which includes what is attached to the flesh (i.e., the hide).
The Gemara notes that the other Tanna does not expound the word 'את'.

A baraita is cited about Shimon HaAmsoni (or Nechemya HaAmsoni) who used to expound every 'את' in the Torah until he reached 'את ה' אלהיך תירא' and stopped, with Rabbi Akiva later expounding it to include Torah scholars, illustrating that some Tannaim do not expound 'את' in certain contexts.

items.text: Deriving prohibition of benefit from orlah
items.text_en: Deriving prohibition of benefit from orlah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses orlah: the Torah says 'ערלים לא יאכל'. A baraita teaches that this only prohibits eating, but from where do we know that one may not benefit from it, dye with it, or light a candle with it? The verse 'וערלתם ערלתו... ערלים לא יאכל' comes to include all these. The Gemara argues that without this, one might think 'לא יאכל' only prohibits eating, but actually it implies both, and the extra verse is needed because of the word 'לכם' which might suggest it is permitted for your benefit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of orlah (ערלה) and cites a baraita that the verse 'ערלים לא יאכל' only prohibits eating, and asks from where we derive that one may not benefit from it, dye with it, or light a candle with it.
The baraita answers that the verse 'וערלתם ערלתו... ערלים לא יאכל' comes to include all these prohibitions of benefit.
The Gemara objects that without the extra verse, one might think 'לא יאכל' only prohibits eating, not benefit.
The Gemara resolves that 'לא יאכל' actually implies both eating and benefit, but the extra verse is needed because of the word 'לכם' which might suggest it is permitted for your benefit.

items.text: Purpose of the word 'לכם' in orlah
items.text_en: Purpose of the word 'לכם' in orlah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: now that these verses are written, what is the purpose of 'לכם'? It is used for a teaching: 'לכם' includes a tree that is planted... (the segment is cut off).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: now that these verses are written, what is the purpose of the word 'לָכֶם'? It answers that it comes to include a tree that was planted (for orlah purposes), as taught in a baraita.
The Gemara answers: it is for the teaching of a baraita that 'לכם' includes a tree that is planted (for idolatry, also forbidden in benefit).

items.text: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda on "לָכֶם"
items.text_en: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda on "לָכֶם"
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma holds that "וּנְטַעְתֶּם" implies only an individual, so "לָכֶם" comes to include planting for the many. Rabbi Yehuda argues that "וּנְטַעְתֶּם" implies both individual and many, and "לָכֶם" is a repetition that comes to exclude.

sub.text: Mishnah citation (Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda)
sub.text_en: Mishnah citation (Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda)
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites the Tanna Kamma's view that 'לָכֶם' includes planting for the many, and Rabbi Yehuda's view that it excludes planting for the many.
The Gemara explains the Tanna Kamma's reasoning: 'וּנְטַעְתֶּם' implies only an individual, so 'לָכֶם' comes to include planting for the many.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: both 'וּנְטַעְתֶּם' and 'לָכֶם' imply both individual and many, making it a double inclusion that comes to exclude.

items.text: Challenge from Terumah and Rav Pappa's answer
items.text_en: Challenge from Terumah and Rav Pappa's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Terumah is forbidden to a non-priest, yet we may mix terumah into food for an Israelite (for benefit). Rav Pappa answers that the verse says "תְּרוּמַתְכֶם" — it is yours, permitting benefit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Terumah is forbidden to a non-priest, yet we may mix terumah into food for an Israelite (for benefit).
Rav Pappa answers that the verse says "תְּרוּמַתְכֶם" — it is yours, permitting benefit.
The Gemara objects: But the word "תְּרוּמַתְכֶם" refers to all Israel, not to an individual.

items.text: Challenge from Nazir and answers of Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Challenge from Nazir and answers of Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: A nazir is forbidden wine, yet we may mix wine into his food. Mar Zutra answers from "נִזְרוֹ" — his own. Rav Ashi adds that "קָדֹשׁ יִהְיֶה" teaches that only his growth is holy, not other items.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: a nazir is forbidden wine, yet we may mix wine into his food.
Mar Zutra answers that the verse 'נִזְרוֹ' teaches that only his own nazirite growth is holy, not other items.
Rav Ashi adds that 'קָדֹשׁ יִהְיֶה' teaches that only his growth is holy, not other items.
The Gemara rejects Rav Ashi's proof because the verse does not explicitly say 'and nothing else', and concludes that the correct explanation is Mar Zutra's.

items.text: Challenge from Chadash and Rav Shemaya's answer
items.text_en: Challenge from Chadash and Rav Shemaya's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: New grain (chadash) is forbidden until the Omer, yet we may harvest it for animal feed. Rav Shemaya answers from "קְצִירְכֶם" — your harvest is yours.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: New grain (chadash) is forbidden until the Omer, yet we may harvest it for animal feed.
Rav Shemaya answers that the verse uses 'קְצִירְכֶם' (your harvest) to permit the harvest for one's own use, while the other opinion holds it refers to all Israel.

items.text: Challenge from Sheratzim and the answer from "לָכֶם" and "יִהְיוּ"
items.text_en: Challenge from Sheratzim and the answer from "לָכֶם" and "יִהְיוּ"
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Creeping things are forbidden to eat, yet we may sell them to gentiles. The answer is from "לָכֶם" — they are yours. The Gemara then asks: if so, may one initially hunt them? The answer: "יִהְיוּ" teaches they must remain in their state.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: creeping things (שרצים) are forbidden to eat, yet a Mishnah permits selling them to gentiles, contradicting the principle that prohibitions cannot be circumvented.
The Gemara answers that the verse uses 'לָכֶם' (to you) to teach that the creeping things are yours to sell, distinguishing between eating and ownership.
The Gemara objects: if so, one might think it is permitted even לכתחילה (a-priori) to hunt creeping things for sale, which seems problematic.
The Gemara resolves that the verse uses 'יִהְיוּ' (they shall be) to teach that the creeping things must remain in their existing state, prohibiting active hunting for sale.

items.text: Chizkiya's alternative derivation from sheratzim
items.text_en: Chizkiya's alternative derivation from sheratzim
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for Chizkiya, who derives permission from "לֹא יֵאָכֵל", the word "לָכֶם" is unnecessary; he would say his reason comes from here as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Chizkiyah's view: why does the Torah need both 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל' and 'לָכֶם' to permit selling? It could have omitted the prohibition entirely.
Chizkiyah answers that his own reasoning is also derived from this verse.

items.text: Challenge from Chametz and the derivation from "לְךָ"
items.text_en: Challenge from Chametz and the derivation from "לְךָ"
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Chametz is forbidden in benefit on Pesach, yet Rabbi Yose HaGelili says one may benefit from it? The answer: "לְךָ" teaches that only your own chametz is forbidden, but others' is permitted. The Gemara then discusses the multiple "לְךָ" verses and their applications.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Chametz is forbidden in benefit on Pesach, yet Rabbi Yose HaGelili permits benefiting from it?
The Gemara answers: The verse 'וְלֹא יֵרָאֶה לְךָ שְׂאוֹר' teaches that only your own chametz is forbidden, but others' is permitted.
The Rabbis object: The verse only says 'to you' — you may not see your own, but you may see others' and God's.
The Gemara answers: There are two instances of 'לְךָ' written, allowing for multiple applications.
The Rabbis object: One 'לְךָ' applies to a conquered gentile, the other to an unconquered gentile.
The Gemara answers: There are three instances of 'לְךָ' written, covering all cases.
The Rabbis object: One 'לְךָ' applies to leaven (שאור), the other to chametz (חמץ).
The Gemara concludes: Both verses are necessary, each teaching a distinct law.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on "לְכׇל מְלָאכָה"
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on "לְכׇל מְלָאכָה"
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva dispute the meaning of "לְכׇל מְלָאכָה" regarding the red heifer. Rabbi Yose holds it permits work for Heaven but forbids ordinary work; Rabbi Akiva holds it purifies for ordinary work but defiles for Heavenly work. The Gemara explains each sage's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita: Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds that the phrase 'לְכׇל מְלָאכָה' (for every work) regarding the red heifer permits work for Heaven but forbids ordinary work.
Rabbi Akiva argues that the phrase teaches that the red heifer purifies for ordinary work but defiles for Heavenly work.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yose HaGelili does not need a verse for impurity and purity, while Rabbi Akiva does not need a verse for prohibition and permission; each sage's verse addresses the other's concern.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva on the meaning of 'do not eat'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva on the meaning of 'do not eat'
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva disagree on whether the phrase 'do not eat' implies both a prohibition of eating and a prohibition of benefit. Rabbi Yosei holds that it does, and the verse permitting neveilah only permits benefit, while Rabbi Akiva holds that 'do not eat' only prohibits eating, and the verse comes to teach about impurity and purity. The Gemara then rejects this and offers an alternative explanation: both agree that 'do not eat' implies both prohibitions, but they disagree about whether when neveilah was permitted, its forbidden fat and sciatic nerve were also permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva disagree on whether the phrase 'do not eat' implies both a prohibition of eating and a prohibition of benefit.

The Gemara rejects the initial suggestion and offers an alternative explanation: both agree that 'do not eat' implies both prohibitions, but they disagree about whether when neveilah was permitted, its forbidden fat and sciatic nerve were also permitted.

items.text: Challenge regarding the sciatic nerve for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
items.text_en: Challenge regarding the sciatic nerve for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's position: while we find that the Torah permitted benefit from forbidden fat, what about the sciatic nerve, which is also prohibited? Two answers are offered: either the sciatic nerve is indeed prohibited for benefit, or it is derived through a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument from forbidden fat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: we find that the Torah permitted benefit from forbidden fat, but what about the sciatic nerve — should we say it is prohibited?
First answer: indeed, the sciatic nerve is also prohibited for benefit.
Second answer: the sciatic nerve is permitted for benefit, derived through a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument from forbidden fat.

items.text: Refutation of the kal vachomer and defense of Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Refutation of the kal vachomer and defense of Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon, who prohibits benefit from the sciatic nerve, could refute the kal vachomer: forbidden fat was permitted in its general category regarding a non-domesticated animal, but the sciatic nerve was never permitted. The Gemara responds that the discussion is only about a domesticated animal, where forbidden fat was never permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon, who prohibits benefit from the sciatic nerve, could refute the kal vachomer from forbidden fat because forbidden fat was permitted in its general category regarding a non-domesticated animal (חיה), whereas the sciatic nerve was never permitted even there.
The Gemara answers that the discussion is only about a domesticated animal (בהמה), where forbidden fat was never permitted, so the kal vachomer stands.

items.text: Dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Avahu on deriving prohibition of benefit
items.text_en: Dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Avahu on deriving prohibition of benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: given that the verses were already addressed, what is the dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Avahu? It explains that they argue about leaven on Passover according to the Rabbis, and about an ox that is stoned according to all opinions. Chizkiya derives the prohibition from 'lo yei'achel', while Rabbi Avahu derives it from neveilah.

sub.text: Gemara's question about the dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Avahu
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about the dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Avahu
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: given that all the verses were cited and answered, what is the basis of the dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Avahu? It explains that Chizkiya derives the prohibition of benefit from 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל' (it shall not be eaten) and Rabbi Avahu from neveilah.

The Gemara explains that they argue about leaven on Passover according to the Rabbis, and about an ox that is stoned according to all opinions; Chizkiya derives the prohibition from 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל' (it shall not be eaten), while Rabbi Avahu derives it from neveilah (carcass).

items.text: Practical difference between Chizkiya and Rabbi Avahu
items.text_en: Practical difference between Chizkiya and Rabbi Avahu
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Chizkiya and Rabbi Avahu, since both agree that these items are forbidden for benefit. It answers that the difference concerns unconsecrated animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard: Chizkiya derives their exclusion from 'lo yei'achel' and 'oto', while Rabbi Avahu holds that 'oto' excludes these items, and unconsecrated animals slaughtered in the courtyard are not prohibited by Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Chizkiya and Rabbi Avahu, since both agree that these items are forbidden for benefit.
The Gemara answers that the difference concerns unconsecrated animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard: Chizkiya derives their exclusion from 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל' and 'אֹתוֹ'.
Rabbi Avahu holds that 'אֹתוֹ' excludes these items, and unconsecrated animals slaughtered in the courtyard are not prohibited by Torah law.

items.text: Statement of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and its analysis
items.text_en: Statement of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and its analysis
items.desc_en: A certain Sage cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who asks for a source that all Torah prohibitions are also forbidden for benefit, giving leaven on Passover and an ox that is stoned as examples. The Gemara questions why he does not derive this from 'lo yei'achel' or from neveilah, and explains that he holds like Rabbi Yehuda that words are interpreted literally. The Gemara then asks why he does not use Rabbi Yehuda's own derivation from 'to the dog you shall throw it', and concludes that he holds that unconsecrated animals slaughtered in the courtyard are prohibited by Torah law, deriving this from the verse about a sin-offering that is burned.

sub.text: A certain Sage citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: A certain Sage citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: A certain Sage sits before Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani and states in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: from where do we derive that all Torah prohibitions are forbidden for benefit, citing leaven on Passover and an ox that is stoned as examples.

The Gemara asks: why does Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi not derive the prohibition of benefit from the verse 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל' (it shall not be eaten), and answers that 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל' implies only a prohibition of eating, not benefit.

The Gemara asks: why does he not derive it from neveilah (carrion), and answers that he holds like Rabbi Yehuda that words are interpreted literally (דברים ככתבן), so neveilah's permission for benefit is limited to its literal context.

The Gemara asks: if he holds like Rabbi Yehuda, why does he not derive the prohibition from the same verse that Rabbi Yehuda uses, namely 'לַכֶּלֶב תַּשְׁלִיכוּן אֹתוֹ' (to the dog you shall throw it)?

The Gemara answers: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that unconsecrated animals slaughtered in the courtyard (חולין שנשחטו בעזרה) are prohibited by Torah law, and he derives this from the verse about a sin-offering that is burned, applying the extra phrase 'בָּאֵשׁ תִּשָּׂרֵף' (it shall be burned in fire) as a general principle for all Torah prohibitions.

items.text: First derivation from 'bakodesh ba'esh tisaref'
items.text_en: First derivation from 'bakodesh ba'esh tisaref'
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the phrase 'bakodesh ba'esh tisaref' teaches that all forbidden items are burned. However, it is rejected because Rabbi Shimon uses this verse to teach that a sin-offering is burned in the sacred area, and it also includes other invalid sacred items.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the phrase 'bakodesh ba'esh tisaref' is not needed for its literal context of eating, so it should be applied to teach that all forbidden items are burned.
The Gemara rejects the proposal, arguing that the verse only teaches that sacred items are burned, not all forbidden items.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon uses this verse to teach that a sin-offering is burned in the sacred area, and it also includes other invalid sacred items.

items.text: Rabbi Yonatan's derivation from 'lo ye'achel' regarding milu'im
items.text_en: Rabbi Yonatan's derivation from 'lo ye'achel' regarding milu'im
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan cites a verse from the milu'im (consecration offerings) where 'lo ye'achel' is superfluous, teaching that it applies to all forbidden items. The Gemara then questions whether this verse is needed for Rabbi Elazar's teaching that a 'kodesh' item that becomes invalid incurs a negative commandment for eating it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan cites the verse from the milu'im (consecration offerings) where 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל' is superfluous, teaching that it applies to all forbidden items and, if not needed for eating, to prohibition of benefit.
The Gemara objects that if the verse teaches about all forbidden items, it might imply they are all burned, but the verse 'וְשָׂרַפְתָּ אֶת הַנּוֹתָר' limits burning to leftover (נותר) only.
The Gemara questions whether this verse is needed for Rabbi Elazar's teaching that any 'קֹדֶשׁ' item that becomes invalid incurs a negative commandment for eating it.

items.text: Abaye's alternative derivation from the first verse
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative derivation from the first verse
items.desc_en: Abaye proposes reversing the derivation: the verse 'ba'esh tisaref' is primary, and 'lo te'achel' is superfluous, teaching about all forbidden items. However, the verse 'hanotar' limits burning to leftover offerings, not all forbidden items.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes reversing the derivation: the verse 'באש תשרף' (it shall be burned with fire) is primary, and 'לא תאכל' (do not eat) is superfluous, teaching about all forbidden items.
The gemara objects that if the verse teaches about all forbidden items, they would all require burning, but the verse 'הנותר' (the leftover) limits burning to leftover offerings.

items.text: Rav Pappa's objection to Abaye
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection to Abaye
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye, arguing that the verse 'lo te'achel' might be needed to establish a separate negative commandment for eating, since Rabbi Elazar's teaching does not include lashes for a general negative commandment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye, arguing that the verse 'לֹא תֵאָכֵל' might be needed to establish a separate negative commandment for eating, since Rabbi Elazar's teaching does not include lashes for a general negative commandment.

items.text: Rav Pappa's alternative derivation from 'v'habsar asher yiga'
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's alternative derivation from 'v'habsar asher yiga'
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites a verse about meat that touches something impure, where 'lo ye'achel' is superfluous because a kal vachomer from tithes already prohibits eating it. This verse then teaches about all forbidden items, but again the word 'hanotar' limits burning to leftovers.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa proposes a new derivation from the verse about meat that touches impurity, noting that the phrase 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל' is superfluous.

The gemara explains that the prohibition of eating impure sacred meat is already derived by a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from the tithe, making the verse's 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל' superfluous for its own case.
The gemara anticipates the objection that warnings cannot be derived from a kal vachomer, and counters that the verse is linked by a היקש (analogy) from the tithe passage.
The superfluous 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל' is applied to teach that all forbidden items in the Torah are prohibited for benefit (הנאה), not just for eating.
The gemara rejects the inference that all forbidden items must be burned, limiting the burning requirement to leftover sacred meat (נותר) by the word 'הַנּוֹתָר'.

items.text: Ravina's question about multiple negative commandments
items.text_en: Ravina's question about multiple negative commandments
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether the verse might instead teach that one violates two negative commandments (for eating and for benefit), citing Abaye's principle that eating a putita incurs four lashes and eating a ant incurs five.

items.text: Opening dispute on lashes for non-edible fat
items.text_en: Opening dispute on lashes for non-edible fat
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a dispute about whether one receives lashes for eating non-edible fat (like tail-fat) — Rav says yes (six lashes), Shmuel says no (since it's not eaten via normal benefit). The argument pivots on interpreting 'eating' broadly vs. narrowly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a dispute between Rav and Shmuel about whether one receives lashes for eating non-edible fat, with Rav saying yes (six lashes) and Shmuel saying no, based on the principle of interpreting verses to avoid multiple prohibitions.

items.text: Deriving inclusion of eimurim and non-edible items from verse
items.text_en: Deriving inclusion of eimurim and non-edible items from verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from Leviticus 7:19 that eimurim (sacrificial fats) are included in the prohibition of eating non-sacred meat, and from the same verse's end that non-edible items (wood, frankincense) are also forbidden when touched by impurity. This expands the scope of prohibitions beyond edible flesh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the beginning of the verse 'וְהַבָּשָׂר אֲשֶׁר יִגַּע בְּכׇל טָמֵא לֹא יֵאָכֵל' (And the flesh that touches any impure thing shall not be eaten) is needed, and answers that it comes to include wood and frankincense.

The Gemara asks why the end of the verse 'וְהַבָּשָׂר כׇּל טָהוֹר יֹאכַל בָּשָׂר' (And as for the flesh, every one that is pure may eat of it) is needed, and answers that it comes to include the sacrificial parts (אֵימוּרִין).
The Gemara objects that the inclusion of sacrificial parts (אֵימוּרִין) is already derived from a different source, a baraita citing Leviticus 7:20.

items.text: Distinction between impurity of body vs. flesh
items.text_en: Distinction between impurity of body vs. flesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a key difference: impurity of the body (tumat haguf) leads to karet, while impurity of flesh (tumat basar) leads only to a lav (lashes). This clarifies the severity levels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between impurity of the body (טומאת הגוף), which carries karet, and impurity of the flesh (טומאת בשר), which carries only lashes.

items.text: General principle: lashes only via normal benefit
items.text_en: General principle: lashes only via normal benefit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan establishes that all Torah prohibitions are lashed only when violated through the normal mode of benefit/consumption. This excludes cases like eating raw chelev (fat) or placing non-edible fat on a wound.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states the general principle that lashes for Torah prohibitions are only administered when the violation occurs through the normal mode of eating.
The Gemara asks what case is excluded by this principle.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi answers that the principle excludes one who eats raw chelev (forbidden fat), who is exempt from lashes.

An alternative version reports Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan with the principle that lashes are only given for violations through the normal mode of benefit, and Rav Shimi bar Ashi excludes one who places chelev of a stoned ox on a wound.

items.text: Supporting case: fat of stoned ox exempt
items.text_en: Supporting case: fat of stoned ox exempt
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avya citing Rav Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan adds that fat from a stoned ox placed on its wound is exempt from lashes, reinforcing the principle that prohibitions are only punishable via normal benefit paths.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Avya citing Rav Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Avya citing Rav Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avya citing Rav Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan adds that fat from a stoned ox placed on its wound is exempt from lashes, reinforcing the principle that prohibitions are only punishable via normal benefit paths.

items.text: Orlah exemption: only fruit via normal benefit
items.text_en: Orlah exemption: only fruit via normal benefit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites a Mishna that lashes for orlah (uncircumcised fruit) apply only to produce from olives/grapes eaten normally, not to figs/pomegranates/etc. This aligns with the principle of benefit-mode specificity.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites a Mishna that lashes for ערלה (uncircumcised fruit) apply only to olives and grapes, not to figs or pomegranates, and infers this is because they are not eaten דרך הנאתן (in their normal benefit mode).

items.text: Abaye's objection: non-edible benefit still lashed
items.text_en: Abaye's objection: non-edible benefit still lashed
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges: if the principle only exempts non-edible benefit, why are kilayim (forbidden mixtures) lashed even when consumed not via normal eating? He argues the real reason is that the prohibition text lacks an explicit 'eating' clause.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rabbi Zeira's proof: if the principle of eating דרך הנאתן (in the normal manner of benefit) were the reason for the exemption in orlah, then fruit itself would be exempt when eaten not in its normal way, but here the exemption is merely because the liquid is only זיעה (sweat/exudate), not the fruit itself.

items.text: Consensus: kilayim lashed even for unusual benefit
items.text_en: Consensus: kilayim lashed even for unusual benefit
items.desc_en: Abaye concludes that everyone agrees kilayim (grape-wheat mixtures) are lashed even when consumed not via normal eating, because the prohibition lacks an explicit 'eating' verb — thus the principle of 'only via normal benefit' does not apply.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the dispute by stating that all agree regarding kilayim of the vineyard (כלאי הכרם) that one is lashed even for non-standard benefit, because the prohibition lacks an explicit verb of eating.

items.text: Issi ben Yehuda's derivation: basar bechalav from holiness verses
items.text_en: Issi ben Yehuda's derivation: basar bechalav from holiness verses
items.desc_en: Issi ben Yehuda derives the prohibition of meat-in-milk from two 'holy people' verses (Exodus 22:30, Leviticus 11:44), using a gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) to equate the contexts. This shows the prohibition is not limited to eating.

sub.desc_en: Issi ben Yehuda introduces a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between two verses containing 'קדוש' to derive that meat-in-milk is forbidden.
The gemara asks: from where do we derive that the prohibition applies to benefit (הנאה) as well as eating?

Issi ben Yehuda answers with a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if orlah (ערלה), which never involved a transgression, is forbidden for benefit, then meat-in-milk, which involved a transgression, should certainly be forbidden for benefit.

items.text: Kal vachomer argument: orlah vs. meat-in-milk
items.text_en: Kal vachomer argument: orlah vs. meat-in-milk
items.desc_en: The Gemara extends the logic: if orlah (uncircumcised fruit) is forbidden in benefit despite no sin committed, then meat-in-milk (involving a sin) should certainly be forbidden in benefit. This reinforces that benefit prohibition applies beyond eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if orlah (uncircumcised fruit) is forbidden in benefit despite no sin being committed, then meat-in-milk, which involves a sin, should certainly be forbidden in benefit, thereby extending the prohibition beyond eating.

items.text: Gemara's initial comparison: meat and milk vs. orlah and chametz
items.text_en: Gemara's initial comparison: meat and milk vs. orlah and chametz
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive that meat and milk is permitted for benefit by comparing it to orlah (which never had a permitted time) and chametz on Pesach (which had a permitted time but is punished with karet). The argument is refuted by pointing out that chametz is punished with karet, unlike meat and milk, and then kilayim of the vineyard is introduced as a proof since it has no karet yet is forbidden for benefit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by comparing meat and milk to orlah (which never had a permitted time) and then to chametz on Pesach (which had a permitted time but is punished with karet), attempting to derive that meat and milk is permitted for benefit.

The Gemara rejects the comparison to chametz because chametz is punished with karet, unlike meat and milk, and then introduces kilayim of the vineyard as a proof since it has no karet yet is forbidden for benefit.

items.text: Objection to the comparison with kilayim
items.text_en: Objection to the comparison with kilayim
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if the comparison with kilayim is valid, one could counter that kilayim is unique because one is lashed even for deriving benefit in an unusual manner, unlike meat and milk where lashes only apply for normal benefit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the comparison with kilayim is valid, one could counter that kilayim is unique because one is lashed even for deriving benefit in an unusual manner, unlike meat and milk where lashes only apply for normal benefit.

items.text: Abaye's defense and explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's defense and explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye questions the premise of the objection: is eating explicitly written regarding meat and milk? He explains that the Torah did not write 'eating' in the prohibition itself to teach that one is lashed even for deriving benefit in an unusual manner, thus the objection is invalid.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges the objection by asking: is the word 'eating' actually written in the prohibition of meat and milk?

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the objector's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the objector's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the objector derived the requirement of normal benefit from the case of neveila (carcass).
Abaye resolves that the Torah deliberately omitted the word 'eating' from the prohibition of meat and milk to teach that one is lashed even for deriving benefit in an unusual manner.

items.text: Another objection: kilayim never had a permitted time
items.text_en: Another objection: kilayim never had a permitted time
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a further objection: kilayim of the vineyard never had a permitted time, unlike meat and milk. Rabbi Adda bar Ahavah answers that this teaches that kilayim's roots are forbidden from the start, since they had a permitted time before rooting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why one cannot object that kilayim of the vineyard never had a permitted time.
Rabbi Adda bar Ahavah answers that kilayim of the vineyard is fundamentally forbidden, but it had a permitted time before rooting.

items.text: Rav Shmaya's challenge and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Shmaya's challenge and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Shmaya challenges Rabbi Adda's statement with a mishnah about a perforated pot in a vineyard: it is forbidden only if the plant added 1/200th. Rava resolves by citing two verses: one for initially sown seeds (forbidden upon rooting) and one for seeds that grew on their own (forbidden only if they added 1/200th).

sub.desc_en: Rav Shmaya raises an objection from a mishnah: a perforated pot transferred into a vineyard is forbidden only if the plant added 1/200th, implying that the original seeds are not forbidden.
Rava resolves the objection by citing two verses: one for seeds sown initially (forbidden upon rooting) and one for seeds that grew on their own (forbidden only if they added 1/200th).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on healing with forbidden substances
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on healing with forbidden substances
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one may be healed by anything except asheirah (idolatrous trees). The Gemara questions whether this applies in a life-threatening situation or not. It concludes that even in danger, asheirah is forbidden, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer explains that the verses 'with all your soul' and 'with all your might' teach that one must give up life or money for God, but not violate idolatry.

sub.desc_en: רבי יעקב (Rabbi Yaakov) cites רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) who rules that one may heal with any substance except for wood of an אשרה (idolatrous tree).
The Gemara questions the circumstances: if there is danger, even אשרה (asheirah) should be permitted; if no danger, all prohibitions should be forbidden.
The Gemara answers that the case involves danger, yet even so, אשרה (asheirah) is forbidden, citing a supporting ברייתא (baraita).
רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer) explains that the verses 'בכל נפשך' (with all your soul) and 'בכל מאדך' (with all your might) teach that one must sacrifice life or money for God, but not violate idolatry.

items.text: Ravin's version: excluding idolatry and forbidden sexual relations
items.text_en: Ravin's version: excluding idolatry and forbidden sexual relations
items.desc_en: Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that one may be healed by anything except idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and murder.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan said one may be healed with all things except for idolatry and forbidden sexual relations.

items.text: Source for murder as a capital sin
items.text_en: Source for murder as a capital sin
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi derives from a verse that murder, like a betrothed young woman, is a sin for which one must be killed rather than transgress. The analogy works both ways: just as one may save the betrothed woman by killing the pursuer, so too one may save the victim by killing the pursuer; and just as the murderer must be killed rather than transgress, so too the betrothed woman must be killed rather than sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the topic of murder (שפיכות דמים) as a capital sin, referencing the previously established rule for idolatry.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi derives from a verse that murder is analogous to a betrothed young woman, establishing the rule of 'be killed rather than transgress'.

Rabbi concludes the analogy: just as a betrothed young woman may be saved by killing the pursuer, so too a murder victim may be saved; and just as a murderer must be killed rather than transgress, so too the betrothed woman must be killed rather than sin.

items.text: Logical basis for murder
items.text_en: Logical basis for murder
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the prohibition of murder is also derived from logic, as illustrated by the story of someone who came before Rava and was told by a local official to kill another or be killed. Rava ruled that one should let himself be killed rather than kill, reasoning that one's own blood is not redder than the other's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the prohibition of murder itself?
The Gemara answers that it is derived from logic (סברא).
The Gemara cites the story of a man who came before Rava, where Rava ruled that one must let himself be killed rather than kill, because one's own blood is not redder than the other's.

items.text: Mar bar Rav Ashi's encounter with orlah benefit
items.text_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi's encounter with orlah benefit
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi found Ravina applying a medicinal ointment from orlah to his daughter. He questioned whether the leniency for danger applies only in life-threatening situations, not here. Ravina responded that this particular fever is like a life-threatening situation, or alternatively, that he was not deriving benefit in the normal way.

sub.desc_en: The narrator describes Mar bar Rav Ashi finding Ravina applying an orlah ointment to his daughter.
Mar bar Rav Ashi challenges Ravina, arguing that the rabbinic leniency for forbidden benefit applies only in life-threatening situations, not here.
Ravina responds that this particular fever is comparable to a life-threatening situation, thus justifying the leniency.
An alternative version reports Ravina answering that he was not deriving benefit in the normal way (דרך הנאה), so the prohibition does not apply.

items.text: Dispute on involuntary benefit
items.text_en: Dispute on involuntary benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a dispute: regarding benefit that comes to a person against his will, Abaye says it is permitted, and Rava says it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding benefit that comes to a person against his will.

items.text: First version of the dispute's parameters
items.text_en: First version of the dispute's parameters
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the dispute: all agree that if it is possible to avoid the benefit and one intends it, it is forbidden; if impossible and unintentional, it is permitted. They disagree when it is possible but unintentional. According to Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids an unintended act, all agree it is forbidden; the dispute is according to Rabbi Shimon, who permits it. Abaye follows Rabbi Shimon, while Rava limits Rabbi Shimon's leniency to cases where it is impossible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes the three parameters of the dispute: all agree that when possible and intentional it is forbidden, when impossible and unintentional it is permitted, and the dispute is only over the case of possible but unintentional.

The Gemara resolves the dispute: according to Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids an unintended act, all agree it is forbidden; the dispute is according to Rabbi Shimon, who permits it. Abaye follows Rabbi Shimon's leniency, while Rava limits Rabbi Shimon's leniency to cases where it is impossible.

items.text: Second version of the dispute's parameters
items.text_en: Second version of the dispute's parameters
items.desc_en: An alternative version: all agree that if it is possible and unintentional, that is the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon. If impossible and unintentional, all permit. They disagree when it is impossible but intentional. According to Rabbi Shimon, who follows intent, all agree it is forbidden; the dispute is according to Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids regardless of intent when possible. Abaye follows Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The alternative version opens by stating that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon is over the case of possible and unintentional.
The alternative version states that all agree that impossible and unintentional is permitted.
The alternative version shifts to state that the dispute is over the case of impossible and intentional.
The alternative version explains that according to Rabbi Shimon, who follows intent, all agree that impossible and intentional is forbidden.
The alternative version shifts to state that the dispute is according to Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids possible actions regardless of intent.
The gemara concludes that Abaye follows Rabbi Yehuda's position in this alternative version.

items.text: Rava's distinction regarding Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Rava's distinction regarding Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Yehuda only equates an unintended action with an intended one for stringency, not for leniency. This sets up the debate about the permissibility of an inevitable but unintended action.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by stating that Rabbi Yehuda only equates an unintended action with an intended one for stringency (לחומרא), not for leniency (לקולא).

items.text: Abaye's proof from Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and Rava's rejection
items.text_en: Abaye's proof from Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and Rava's rejection
items.desc_en: Abaye brings a proof that an inevitable but intended action is permitted, citing Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai who sat in the shade of the Temple courtyard while teaching all day. Rava rejects this, arguing that the Temple courtyard is different because it was built for that purpose.

sub.desc_en: Abaye brings a baraita about Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai sitting in the shade of the Temple courtyard all day while teaching, arguing that this shows an inevitable but intended action is permitted.
Rava rejects the proof, arguing that the Temple courtyard is different because it was built for that purpose, so the shade is not considered an unintended benefit.

items.text: Rava's proof from the artisans in the Holy of Holies and its refutation
items.text_en: Rava's proof from the artisans in the Holy of Holies and its refutation
items.desc_en: Rava brings a proof that an inevitable but intended action is prohibited, citing the artisans who were lowered in boxes into the Holy of Holies to avoid gazing at it. The Gemara refutes this by noting that sound, sight, and smell have no laws of me'ilah, and the restriction was merely a stringency.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita about artisans lowered in boxes into the Holy of Holies to avoid gazing, arguing that an inevitable but intended action is prohibited.
The Gemara objects that sound, sight, and smell have no laws of me'ilah (מעילה), so the restriction was merely a stringency (מעלה) in the Holy of Holies.
The Gemara concludes that the restriction was only a stringency (מעלה) instituted in the Holy of Holies, not a general prohibition.

items.text: Alternative version of Rava's proof and its resolution
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rava's proof and its resolution
items.desc_en: An alternative version has Rava citing the same baraita about sound, sight, and smell to prove that me'ilah does not apply but prohibition does, implying that an inevitable but intended action is prohibited. The Gemara resolves that this applies only to those standing outside, not inside.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version has Rava citing the baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi that sound, sight, and smell are not subject to me'ilah, implying that prohibition still applies.
The Gemara asks whether this implies that for those standing inside, where the action is inevitable and intended, it is prohibited.
The Gemara rejects this and explains that the baraita refers only to those standing outside, not inside.

items.text: Discussion of me'ilah regarding smell and the resolution by Rav Pappa
items.text_en: Discussion of me'ilah regarding smell and the resolution by Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita that smell has no me'ilah, citing a conflicting source that one who smells the incense is liable for me'ilah. Rav Pappa resolves that sound and sight have no substance, and smell after the smoke has risen has no me'ilah because its mitzvah has been fulfilled.

sub.text: Bar Kappara via Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Bar Kappara via Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the statement of Bar Kappara that sound, sight, and smell have no liability for me'ilah (misuse of consecrated property).
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that one who smells the incense is liable for me'ilah, contradicting the claim that smell has no me'ilah.
Rav Pappa resolves that sound and sight have no substance, and smell after the smoke has risen has no me'ilah because its mitzvah has been fulfilled.

items.text: Challenge from Terumat HaDeshen and priestly garments, and resolution via two verses
items.text_en: Challenge from Terumat HaDeshen and priestly garments, and resolution via two verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Pappa's principle that once a mitzvah is fulfilled there is no me'ilah, citing Terumat HaDeshen (the removal of ashes) which still has me'ilah. It resolves that Terumat HaDeshen and priestly garments are two verses that come as one, and thus do not teach a general rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Pappa's principle that once a mitzvah is fulfilled there is no me'ilah, citing Terumat HaDeshen (the removal of ashes) which still has me'ilah.
The Gemara resolves that Terumat HaDeshen and priestly garments are two verses that come as one, and thus do not teach a general rule.
The Gemara elaborates that Terumat HaDeshen is as stated, and priestly garments are derived from the verse 'וְהִנִּיחָם שָׁם' (and he shall leave them there), teaching that they require burial.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Dosa's view and resolution via Eglah Arufah
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Dosa's view and resolution via Eglah Arufah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the resolution using two verses works for the Sages but not for Rabbi Dosa, who holds that priestly garments may be used by a common priest. It then resolves by citing Terumat HaDeshen and Eglah Arufah as two verses, with additional exclusions for those who hold that two verses do teach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous resolution works for the Sages but challenges: according to Rabbi Dosa, who holds that the priestly garments may be used by a common priest, what can be said?
The Gemara answers that the halakhot of תרומת הדשן (removal of ashes) and עגלה ערופה (heifer whose neck is broken) are two verses that come as one, and therefore do not teach a general principle.
The Gemara asks: this works for the one who holds that two verses do not teach, but for the one who holds that they do teach, what can be said?
The Gemara answers that two exclusionary phrases are written: 'ושמו' (and he shall put it) and 'הערופה' (which had its neck broken), limiting the rule to those cases.

items.text: Final proof from the heifer and its rejection
items.text_en: Final proof from the heifer and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from a baraita about a heifer that was made to nurse and tread, which is disqualified even though the action was inevitable. It rejects this because the verse 'which has not been worked with' implies disqualification in any case, and the same would apply to the first case as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a heifer that was made to nurse and tread, which is disqualified even though the action was inevitable, as a proof against Rava's position.
The Gemara infers that here, where the action is inevitable and intentional, the baraita rules the heifer disqualified, contradicting Rava's leniency.
The Gemara rejects the proof by noting that the verse 'which has not been worked with' implies disqualification in any case, making the heifer's case unique.
The Gemara objects that if the verse applies in all cases, then even the first case of the baraita (where the heifer was merely led in) should also be disqualified.

items.text: Analogy to a bird resting on a consecrated animal
items.text_en: Analogy to a bird resting on a consecrated animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares the case of a bird resting on a consecrated animal to the case of a male mounting it, and Rav Pappa explains the derivation from the word 'עָבַד' (worked) and 'עוּבַּד' (was worked) to require intentional benefit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an analogy: a bird resting on a consecrated animal does not disqualify it, but a male mounting it does, and asks for the reason.
Rav Pappa explains that if the verse read 'עָבַד' (worked) it would require direct action, but if it read 'עוּבַּד' (was worked) it would include even unintentional benefit.
Rav Pappa resolves that since the verse is written as 'עָבַד' but read as 'עוּבַּד', it requires a case analogous to direct work — one where the owner derives benefit (ניחותא).

items.text: Challenge from the law of a found garment
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of a found garment
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a found garment that may be spread for its own needs but not for one's own, and distinguishes it due to concerns of the evil eye or thieves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a found garment that may be spread for its own needs but not for one's own, to challenge the previous distinction.
The Gemara distinguishes the case of a found garment, explaining that it is different because it is well-known and thus subject to concerns of the evil eye or thieves.

items.text: Challenge from sellers of garments
items.text_en: Challenge from sellers of garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about garment sellers who may sell in their usual manner but not with intent to protect from sun or rain, and the modest ones hang them behind on a stick. This refutes the one who taught the first version of Rava's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about garment sellers who may sell in their usual manner, provided they do not intend to protect from sun or rain, and the modest ones hang the garments behind them on a stick.

The Gemara concludes that since one could act like the modest ones and avoid prohibited intent, the baraita refutes the version of Rava's statement that forbids any benefit from a prohibited object even without intent.

items.text: Baraita on an oven heated with orlah peels or kilayim vines
items.text_en: Baraita on an oven heated with orlah peels or kilayim vines
items.desc_en: The baraita states: An oven heated with orlah peels or kilayim of the vineyard — if new, it must be broken; if old, it must be cooled. If one baked bread in it, Rabbi says the bread is forbidden, and the Sages say it is permitted. If one cooked on coals, all agree it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating the rule for an oven heated with orlah peels or kilayim vines: a new oven must be broken, an old one must be cooled.
The baraita presents Rabbi's position that bread baked in such an oven is forbidden, while the Sages permit it.
The baraita concludes that if one cooked bread on coals (not directly on the oven walls), all agree it is permitted.

items.text: Reconciling the baraita with the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages
items.text_en: Reconciling the baraita with the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction in the baraita regarding new vs. old ovens, and resolves it by attributing the versions to Rabbi and the Sages, then to Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages, citing the mishna about leaven of hullin and teruma that fell into dough.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that both new and old ovens must be cooled, not dismantled.
The Gemara initially resolves the contradiction by attributing the baraita's version to Rabbi and the mishna's version to the Sages.
The Gemara objects: Rabbi only prohibits the bread due to the benefit of the wood, but does he hold that a mixture of permitted and forbidden causes (זה וזה גורם) is prohibited?
The Gemara offers a second resolution: the baraita reflects the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer, while the mishna reflects the Sages.
The Gemara asks: which Rabbi Eliezer is being referenced?
The Gemara cites the mishna about leaven of hullin and teruma that fell into dough, where Rabbi Eliezer rules that the last addition determines the status, while the Sages say it never prohibits.

items.text: Abaye's principle of 'zeh vazeh gorem asur'
items.text_en: Abaye's principle of 'zeh vazeh gorem asur'
items.desc_en: Abaye states that the Mishnah's leniency applies only if one removed the forbidden wood before adding permitted wood; otherwise, the combined factors render the bread forbidden, implying that 'zeh vazeh gorem' is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that the Mishnah's leniency applies only if one removed the forbidden wood first; otherwise, the bread is forbidden, implying that 'zeh vazeh gorem' (combined factors) is prohibited.

items.text: Challenge to Abaye's attribution to Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Challenge to Abaye's attribution to Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is indeed as Abaye claims; perhaps Rabbi Eliezer holds that the last added wood determines the status, so even without removal the bread is permitted, and only simultaneous addition is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning might be based on 'achar acharon ani ba' (I follow the last factor), not on Abaye's principle, so simultaneous addition would be permitted.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on asherah wood and extension to all prohibitions
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on asherah wood and extension to all prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer requires benefit from forbidden wood to be cast into the Dead Sea, and the Sages argue there is no redemption for idolatry. The Gemara then questions whether Rabbi Eliezer's stringency applies only to idolatry or to all Torah prohibitions, and resolves with a baraita that he indeed prohibits in all cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on asherah wood, citing the Mishnah that wood from an asherah is forbidden for benefit, and if used to heat an oven, the oven must be dismantled or cooled.

The Mishnah continues: if bread was baked in such an oven, it is forbidden; Rabbi Eliezer says the benefit should be cast into the Dead Sea, and the Sages respond that there is no redemption for idolatry.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer's stringent ruling applies only to idolatry, which is severe, or also to all other Torah prohibitions.
The Gemara resolves by citing an explicit baraita that Rabbi Eliezer indeed prohibits in all Torah prohibitions.

items.text: Abaye's analysis of 'zeh vazeh gorem' and dispute over vessels
items.text_en: Abaye's analysis of 'zeh vazeh gorem' and dispute over vessels
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that if one holds 'zeh vazeh gorem asur', Rabbi Eliezer's view applies to all cases; if one holds 'zeh vazeh gorem mutar', the bread is permitted but vessels like bowls are forbidden due to the wood's benefit. The Gemara then debates whether a pot is forbidden even according to the lenient view because it absorbed flavor before permitted wood was added.

sub.desc_en: Abaye presents two scenarios: if one holds 'זה וזה גורם אסור' (a product caused by both permitted and forbidden factors is forbidden), then Rabbi Eliezer's view applies universally; if one holds 'זה וזה גורם מותר' (it is permitted), then bread is permitted but vessels like bowls are forbidden due to the wood's benefit.

The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between the lenient and strict views applies specifically to a oven (תנור) and pot (קדירה): according to the strict view they are forbidden, according to the lenient view they are permitted.
Some say that even according to the lenient view, a pot (קדירה) is forbidden because it absorbed the forbidden flavor before the permitted wood was added.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on orlah and kilayim wood, and his textual emendation
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on orlah and kilayim wood, and his textual emendation
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that an oven heated with orlah or kilayim wood requires destruction or cooling, and a dispute between Rabbi and Sages about the bread is resolved by Shmuel reversing the baraita. Alternatively, Shmuel holds that the halakha follows Rabbi over a colleague but not over many, and he reversed the text to uphold the Sages' prohibition.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that an oven heated with orlah or kilayim wood requires destruction or cooling, and cites a dispute between Rabbi (permits the bread) and Sages (prohibit it).
The Gemara objects that a baraita teaches the opposite of Shmuel's version.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel reversed the baraita text.
Alternatively, Shmuel holds that the halakha follows Rabbi over a colleague but not over many, so he reversed the text to uphold the Sages' prohibition.

items.text: Dispute about coals and the status of bread
items.text_en: Dispute about coals and the status of bread
items.desc_en: When bread is baked over coals, all agree the bread is permitted. A dispute arises between two Amoraim: one says only smoldering coals are permitted, but glowing coals are forbidden; the other says even glowing coals are permitted. Rav Pappa explains that for Rabbi, the bread is forbidden only when the firebrand is directly opposite the bread.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states a general rule: when bread is baked over coals, all agree the bread is permitted.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda / Shmuel and Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi / Rabbi Yochanan (two Amoraim)
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda / Shmuel and Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi / Rabbi Yochanan (two Amoraim)
sub.desc_en: Two Amoraim dispute the scope of the rule: one says only smoldering coals (עוֹמְמוֹת) are permitted, but glowing coals (לוֹחֲשׁוֹת) are forbidden; the other says even glowing coals are permitted.

The gemara asks: according to the opinion that glowing coals are forbidden, the reason is clear (the coals still impart benefit to the bread); but according to the opinion that even glowing coals are permitted, how can Rabbi ever forbid bread due to benefit of the wood?
Rav Pappa answers: Rabbi forbids the bread only when the firebrand (אֲבוּקָה) is directly opposite the bread, so the coals' heat is not the sole cause.

items.text: Gemara's question about forbidden wood for the Rabbis
items.text_en: Gemara's question about forbidden wood for the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that the Rabbis permit an asherah fire even when the torch is opposite him, and asks what case of forbidden wood remains for them. Rav Ami bar Chama answers: with a branch (sharshifa).

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question about an oven fired with consecrated wood
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question about an oven fired with consecrated wood
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda: if an oven was fired with consecrated wood and bread was baked in it, what is the status of the bread for the Rabbis who permit in the first case? Rav Chisda answers the bread is forbidden. Rava objects: how can this be compared to orlah, which is nullified in 200, while consecrated items are not nullified even in 1000?

items.text: Rava's objection: the one who fired misappropriated
items.text_en: Rava's objection: the one who fired misappropriated
items.desc_en: Rava argues that the real difficulty is: the one who fired the oven misappropriated (ma'al) the consecrated wood, and wherever the one who fires misappropriates, the wood should go out to non-sacred status (chullin).

items.text: Rav Pappa's answer: dealing with peace-offering wood according to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's answer: dealing with peace-offering wood according to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that we are dealing with wood from peace-offerings (shelamim), according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that consecrated items misappropriated unintentionally become desacralized, but intentionally they do not. Since the one who fires does so intentionally, the wood does not go out to chullin.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about ash of consecrated items
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about ash of consecrated items
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: is it always the case that when the one who fires misappropriates, the wood goes out to chullin? But a baraita teaches that all items that are burned, their ash is permitted, except for asherah wood, and the ash of consecrated items is always forbidden.

items.text: Two answers: fire from itself or items requiring burial
items.text_en: Two answers: fire from itself or items requiring burial
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama answers: the case is where a fire spread on its own from consecrated wood, so no person misappropriated. Rav Shemaya answers: it deals with items that require burial (geniza), as taught: 'and he shall place it' gently, 'and he shall place it' entirely, 'and he shall place it' without scattering.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's argument that chametz requires burning and the Sages' refutations
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's argument that chametz requires burning and the Sages' refutations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Yehuda says there is no disposal of chametz except by burning. The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda argues from notar: if notar, which is not subject to 'bal yera'eh' and 'bal yimatzei', requires burning, then chametz, which is subject to these, certainly requires burning. The Sages refute: this is a lenient conclusion, as if one cannot find wood, he would sit idle, but the Torah says 'you shall remove leaven from your houses' by any means. Rabbi Yehuda then offers other analogies based on prohibition of eating and benefit, and then on karet punishment, but each is refuted by counterexamples (neveilah, the stoned ox, its fat).

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's alternative reasoning and the Sages' challenge
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's alternative reasoning and the Sages' challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda argues that chametz should be burned because it is subject to the prohibition of 'bal totiru' like notar. The Sages counter with the example of the asham talui and chatat ha'of that are also subject to 'bal totiru' but are buried, not burned. Rabbi Yehuda is silent.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda presents an alternative argument: just as notar (leftover sacrificial meat) is subject to the prohibition of 'בל תותירו' (do not leave over) and is burned, so too chametz, which is also subject to that prohibition, should be burned.

The Sages object by citing the asham talui (suspensive guilt-offering) and chatat ha'of (bird sin-offering) brought for a doubt, which are also subject to 'בל תותירו' yet are buried, not burned, undermining Rabbi Yehuda's analogy.
Rabbi Yehuda is silent, unable to respond to the Sages' objection.

items.text: Proverbs about the carpenter and the sieve
items.text_en: Proverbs about the carpenter and the sieve
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef, Abaye, and Rava each offer proverbs about a carpenter who errs and is punished by his own tools, illustrating that Rabbi Yehuda was refuted by his own logic.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a folk proverb: 'In the spoon that the carpenter made, the mustard will burn his palate,' illustrating that Rabbi Yehuda was refuted by his own logic.
Abaye offers another proverb: 'He who made the stocks shall sit in the stocks; he is repaid through his own handiwork,' reinforcing the same point.
Rava adds a third proverb: 'He who made the arrows shall be killed with his own arrows; he is repaid through his own handiwork,' further illustrating the same idea.

items.text: The dispute about crumbling vs. grinding chametz
items.text_en: The dispute about crumbling vs. grinding chametz
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the Mishnah's phrase 'mefarer ve-zoreh': does it mean crumbling and then scattering to the wind, and crumbling and then casting into the sea, or crumbling and scattering to the wind, but casting into the sea whole? A similar question is raised about avodah zarah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma about the Mishnah's phrase 'mefarer ve-zoreh': does it require crumbling before both scattering to the wind and casting into the sea, or only before scattering to the wind, while casting into the sea may be done whole?

The Gemara raises a parallel dilemma about a mishna regarding avodah zarah (idolatry), where Rabbi Yosei says 'shochek ve-zoreh' or 'matil la-yam': does it require grinding before both actions, or only before scattering to the wind, while casting into the sea may be done whole?

items.text: Rabba and Rav Yosef's opposing resolutions
items.text_en: Rabba and Rav Yosef's opposing resolutions
items.desc_en: Rabba argues that avodah zarah going to the Salt Sea does not require grinding, while chametz going to other rivers requires crumbling. Rav Yosef argues the opposite: avodah zarah, which does not dissolve, requires grinding, while chametz, which dissolves, does not require crumbling.

sub.desc_en: Rabba argues that idolatry, which goes to the Dead Sea (ים המלח), does not require grinding, while chametz, which goes to other rivers, requires crumbling.
Rav Yosef objects, arguing the opposite: idolatry, which does not dissolve, requires grinding, while chametz, which dissolves, does not require crumbling.

items.text: Supporting baraitot for both opinions
items.text_en: Supporting baraitot for both opinions
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabba: one who walks in the desert crumbles and scatters to the wind; on a ship, crumbles and casts into the sea. Another baraita supports Rav Yosef: one who walks in the desert grinds and scatters; on a ship, grinds and casts into the sea.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabba: one who walks in the desert crumbles and scatters to the wind; one who travels by ship crumbles and casts into the sea.
Another baraita supports Rav Yosef: one who walks in the desert grinds and scatters to the wind; one who travels by ship grinds and casts into the sea.

items.text: Reconciling the contradictions
items.text_en: Reconciling the contradictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent contradictions: grinding is required for the Salt Sea but not for other rivers (for Rabba); crumbling is required for wheat but not for bread (for Rav Yosef).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction: grinding (שחיקה) is difficult for Rabba, but explained by the difference between the Dead Sea and other rivers; crumbling (פירור) is difficult for Rav Yosef, but explained by the difference between wheat and bread.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction for Rabba: grinding is required for the Salt Sea (ים המלח) but not for other rivers.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction for Rav Yosef: crumbling is required for wheat (חיטי) but not for bread (נהמא).

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on gentile chametz
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on gentile chametz
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that chametz of a gentile that passed Pesach is permitted for benefit, while that of a Jew is forbidden. The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as not following Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon, or Rabbi Yosi HaGelili, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda holds that chametz before and after its time is a negative prohibition, and during its time is a negative prohibition and karet.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law: chametz of a gentile that passed Pesach is permitted for benefit, while that of a Jew is forbidden, citing the verse 'לֹא יֵרָאֶה לְךָ שְׂאוֹר' (no leaven shall be seen of yours).
The Gemara asks which Tanna authored the Mishnah, suggesting it is not Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon, or Rabbi Yosi HaGelili.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda holds that chametz before and after its time is a negative prohibition, and during its time is a negative prohibition and karet, explaining why the Mishnah does not follow him.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon's ruling and Rabbi Yose HaGlili's objection
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon's ruling and Rabbi Yose HaGlili's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that chametz before and after its time is not prohibited at all, but during its time it is subject to karet and a negative commandment. From the time it is forbidden for eating, it is also forbidden for benefit. Rabbi Yose HaGlili expresses amazement that chametz is forbidden for benefit all seven days.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon rules that chametz before and after its time is not prohibited at all, but during its time it is subject to karet and a negative commandment, and from the time it is forbidden for eating it is also forbidden for benefit.
Rabbi Yose HaGlili expresses amazement that chametz is forbidden for benefit all seven days.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's source and Rabbi Shimon's rebuttal
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's source and Rabbi Shimon's rebuttal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse 'לֹא תֹאכַל עָלָיו חָמֵץ' that one who eats chametz from the sixth hour onward violates a negative commandment. Rabbi Shimon objects, arguing that the verse is linked to eating matzah, so the prohibition only applies when there is a positive commandment to eat matzah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse 'לֹא תֹאכַל עָלָיו חָמֵץ' that one who eats chametz from the sixth hour onward violates a negative commandment.
Rabbi Shimon objects, arguing that the verse is linked to eating matzah, so the prohibition only applies when there is a positive commandment to eat matzah.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the biblical sources for Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the biblical sources for Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: three verses ('לֹא יֵאָכֵל חָמֵץ', 'וְכׇל מַחְמֶצֶת לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ', 'לֹא תֹאכַל עָלָיו חָמֵץ') correspond to before, after, and during the time. Rabbi Shimon uses one verse for during the time, and interprets the other verses for other laws: 'וְכׇל מַחְמֶצֶת' for chametz leavened by another substance, and 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל חָמֵץ' for the Passover of Egypt being only one day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning, noting that three verses are written.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda uses one verse for before the time, one for after the time, and one for during the time.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon uses one verse for during the time, and interprets the other verses for other laws: 'וְכׇל מַחְמֶצֶת' for chametz leavened by another substance, and 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל חָמֵץ' for the Passover of Egypt being only one day.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's and Rabbi Yose HaGlili's alternative derivations
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's and Rabbi Yose HaGlili's alternative derivations
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda derives the law of chametz leavened by another substance, answering that the Torah expressed it with the term 'מַחְמֶצֶת'. For Rabbi Yose HaGlili, the Gemara offers two possibilities: either from the juxtaposition of 'הַיּוֹם' or that he does not expound juxtapositions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda derives the prohibition of chametz leavened by another substance, given that he already used the verse 'לֹא תֹאכַל עָלָיו חָמֵץ' for the time of the korban pesach.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda derives it from the fact that the Torah expressed the prohibition using the term 'מַחְמֶצֶת' (leavened by another substance).
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yose HaGlili derives the law of chametz leavened by another substance.
The Gemara offers the first possibility: Rabbi Yose HaGlili derives it from the juxtaposition of the verse 'הַיּוֹם' (today) next to the prohibition.
The Gemara offers the second possibility: Rabbi Yose HaGlili does not expound juxtapositions (סְמוּכִין), so he must have another source.

items.text: Revisiting the dispute and further analysis of the verses
items.text_en: Revisiting the dispute and further analysis of the verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the exchange between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, questioning how Rabbi Yehuda responds to Rabbi Shimon's objection. Rabbi Yehuda explains that the verse 'לֹא תֹאכַל עָלָיו חָמֵץ' comes to establish matzah as an obligation even in this time. Rabbi Shimon derives this from 'בָּעֶרֶב תֹּאכְלוּ', while Rabbi Yehuda uses that verse for the impure or those on a distant journey. Rabbi Shimon argues that such cases do not need a verse, as they are no worse than an uncircumcised person or alien, who may eat matzah and maror.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara restates Rabbi Yehuda's position that the verse 'לֹא תֹאכַל עָלָיו חָמֵץ' teaches that one who eats chametz from the sixth hour onward violates a negative commandment.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon's objection to Rabbi Yehuda is valid.
Rabbi Yehuda explains that the verse 'לֹא תֹאכַל עָלָיו חָמֵץ' comes to establish matzah as an obligation even in this time (i.e., after the destruction of the Temple).
The Gemara asks from where Rabbi Shimon derives the obligation to eat matzah.
The Gemara states that Rabbi Shimon derives the obligation from the verse 'בָּעֶרֶב תֹּאכְלוּ' (in the evening you shall eat).
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda uses the verse 'בָּעֶרֶב תֹּאכְלוּ' for the impure person or one on a distant journey, teaching that they still eat matzah and maror.
Rabbi Shimon argues that the impure or distant traveler does not need a verse, as they are no worse than an uncircumcised person or alien, who may eat matzah and maror.
Rabbi Yehuda responds that the verse is written in this context and written in that context, implying a distinction between the cases.

items.text: Conclusion: Identifying the author of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion: Identifying the author of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to identify the author of the Mishnah, questioning whether it follows Rabbi Yehuda, who would include even chametz of a gentile, or Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna authored the Mishnah, doubting whether it aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, who would forbid even a gentile's חמץ (leaven), or with Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction between a Jew's and a gentile's chametz after Pesach, suggesting that according to Rabbi Yose HaGelili, even within the time it would be permitted for benefit.
