sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction, arguing that according to Rabbi Yose HaGelili, even a Jew's chametz after Pesach would be permitted for benefit.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's answer: Rabbi Yehuda and the derivation from seeing
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's answer: Rabbi Yehuda and the derivation from seeing
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who derives the prohibition of eating chametz from the prohibition of seeing it, allowing benefit from others' chametz. He also explains why the Mishnah mentions benefit rather than eating.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov asserts that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who derives the prohibition of eating chametz from the prohibition of seeing it via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), permitting benefit from others' chametz.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains why the Mishnah mentions benefit rather than eating: it pairs the gentile's permitted benefit with the Israelite's forbidden benefit, and likewise pairs the time frame.

items.text: Rava's answer: Rabbi Shimon and the penalty
items.text_en: Rava's answer: Rabbi Shimon and the penalty
items.desc_en: Rava argues that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who penalizes the Jew for violating 'bal yera'eh' and 'bal yimatzei', thus forbidding his chametz but not the gentile's.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the Mishnah always follows Rabbi Shimon, who penalizes the Jew for violating 'בל יראה' (bal yera'eh) and 'בל ימצא' (bal yimatzei).

items.text: Gemara's objection to Rav Acha bar Yaakov
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to Rav Acha bar Yaakov
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to Rav Acha bar Yaakov, the Mishnah should have cited the verse 'lo ye'achel chametz' rather than 'lo yera'eh'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to Rav Acha bar Yaakov, the Mishnah should have cited the verse 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל חָמֵץ' (chametz shall not be eaten) rather than 'לֹא יֵרָאֶה' (it shall not be seen).

items.text: Gemara's resolution: The Mishnah refers to the first clause
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: The Mishnah refers to the first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's citation of 'lo yera'eh' refers to the first clause about a gentile's chametz, not the second about a Jew's, and the derivation from seeing to eating applies there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's citation of 'lo yera'eh' refers to the first clause about a gentile's chametz, not the second about a Jew's, and the derivation from seeing to eating applies there.

items.text: Dispute between Rava and Rav Acha bar Yaakov on eating gentile's chametz
items.text_en: Dispute between Rava and Rav Acha bar Yaakov on eating gentile's chametz
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava and Rav Acha bar Yaakov disagree on whether one who eats a gentile's chametz after Pesach is lashed, based on whether Rabbi Yehuda derives eating from seeing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rava and Rav Acha bar Yaakov regarding whether one who eats a gentile's chametz after Pesach is lashed according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rava holds that one is lashed because Rabbi Yehuda does not derive the prohibition of eating chametz from the prohibition of seeing chametz.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov holds that one is not lashed because Rabbi Yehuda derives the prohibition of eating chametz from the prohibition of seeing chametz.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov retracts based on a baraita
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov retracts based on a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov retracts his position due to a baraita about eating consecrated chametz, where Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana compares Yom Kippur to Shabbat for liability without payment.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rav Acha bar Yaakov retracted his earlier position based on a baraita about eating consecrated chametz during the festival, where opinions differ on whether one has misappropriated (מעל) sacred property.
The gemara asks who is the anonymous 'יש אומרים' (some say) in the baraita.

Rabbi Yochanan identifies the 'יש אומרים' as Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana, who compares Yom Kippur to Shabbat: just as on Shabbat one is liable to capital punishment (חייב מיתה) and exempt from monetary payment, so too on Yom Kippur one is liable to capital punishment and exempt from payment.

items.text: Rav Yosef's alternative explanation of the baraita
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's alternative explanation of the baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains the dispute in the baraita as being about whether one may redeem consecrated items to feed dogs, with the lenient opinion allowing it and the strict one forbidding it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef introduces the dispute as being about whether one may redeem consecrated items to feed them to dogs.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's explanation of the lenient opinion
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's explanation of the lenient opinion
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the one who says 'he misappropriated' holds that one may redeem consecrated items to feed them to dogs.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's explanation of the strict opinion
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's explanation of the strict opinion
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the one who says 'he did not misappropriate' holds that one may not redeem consecrated items to feed them to dogs.
Rav Acha bar Rava teaches this baraita, providing a supporting tradition for the dispute.

items.text: First explanation of the dispute: whether a cause of money is like money
items.text_en: First explanation of the dispute: whether a cause of money is like money
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a version of Rav Yosef's teaching: everyone agrees that consecrated items are not redeemed to feed to dogs, and the dispute here is whether a cause of money is considered like money. One who says there is misuse holds that a cause of money is like money; one who says there is no misuse holds it is not like money.

sub.text: Gemara's presentation of Rav Yosef's teaching
sub.text_en: Gemara's presentation of Rav Yosef's teaching
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rav Yosef's version of the dispute, stating that all agree consecrated items are not redeemed to feed to dogs.
The Gemara frames the dispute as whether a cause of money (דבר הגורם לממון) is considered like money.
The Gemara explains that the one who says there is misuse holds that a cause of money is like money, while the one who says no misuse holds it is not like money.

items.text: Second explanation: dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Second explanation: dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov says everyone agrees a cause of money is like money, and the dispute here is between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon. The one who says no misuse follows Rabbi Yehuda, and the one who says misuse follows Rabbi Shimon. The Gemara notes that Rav Acha bar Yaakov had previously said Rabbi Yehuda derives leaven of eating from leaven of appearance, so he must have retracted that view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov asserts that everyone agrees a cause of money is like money, and the dispute here is between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara objects that Rav Acha bar Yaakov previously held Rabbi Yehuda derives leaven of eating from leaven of appearance, implying he must have retracted that view.

items.text: Third explanation: dispute between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Third explanation: dispute between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says everyone agrees that consecrated items are not redeemed and a cause of money is not like money, and the dispute here is between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and the Rabbis. The one who says misuse follows Rabbi Yosei, and the one who says no misuse follows the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the dispute in the earlier anonymous statement is between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and the Rabbis: the one who says misuse occurred follows Rabbi Yosei, and the one who says no misuse follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Rav's ruling on chametz mixtures
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on chametz mixtures
items.desc_en: Rav rules: chametz during its time (Pesach), whether mixed with its own kind or not, is forbidden. After its time, mixed with its own kind is forbidden, but not with a different kind. The Gemara clarifies this is about a minimal amount (mashehu), not about taste, and explains Rav's reasoning: he follows the principle that all Torah prohibitions are forbidden in a minimal amount when mixed with their own kind, but by taste when not. Rav decrees chametz during Pesach with a different kind is forbidden because of its own kind, and after Pesach with its own kind is forbidden like Rabbi Yehuda, but does not decree for after Pesach with a different kind.

sub.desc_en: Rav states his ruling on chametz mixtures: during Pesach, any mixture is forbidden; after Pesach, only a mixture with its own kind is forbidden.
The Gemara questions whether Rav's ruling is about taste (נותן טעם) and challenges that after Pesach with a different kind would then be forbidden.

The Gemara clarifies that Rav's ruling is about a minimal amount (משהו), consistent with Rav and Shmuel's principle that Torah prohibitions are forbidden in a minimal amount with their own kind, but by taste with a different kind.
The Gemara explains that Rav decrees chametz during Pesach with a different kind is forbidden because of its own kind, and after Pesach with its own kind is forbidden like Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara explains that Rav does not decree after Pesach with a different kind is forbidden because of its own kind, as such an extensive decree is not made.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on chametz mixtures
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on chametz mixtures
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules: chametz during Pesach, with its own kind is forbidden, but with a different kind is permitted. After Pesach, both with its own kind and a different kind are permitted. The Gemara explains: during Pesach with its own kind is forbidden because Shmuel follows the principle that all Torah prohibitions are forbidden in a minimal amount when mixed with their own kind, but he does not decree for a different kind. After Pesach, both are permitted like Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that chametz during Pesach mixed with its own kind is forbidden, but with a different kind is permitted.

The Gemara explains that Shmuel follows the principle that all Torah prohibitions are forbidden in a minimal amount when mixed with their own kind, but he does not decree a decree for a different kind.
The Gemara concludes that after Pesach, both mixtures are permitted, following Rabbi Shimon's view that chametz after Pesach is permitted.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on chametz mixtures
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on chametz mixtures
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules: chametz during Pesach, whether with its own kind or a different kind, is forbidden by taste. After Pesach, both with its own kind and a different kind are permitted. The Gemara explains: during Pesach, Rabbi Yochanan follows his principle with Reish Lakish that all Torah prohibitions are forbidden by taste whether with their own kind or not. After Pesach, both are permitted like Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states his ruling: chametz during Pesach, whether with its own kind or a different kind, is forbidden by taste; after Pesach, both are permitted.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling during Pesach follows his principle with Reish Lakish that all Torah prohibitions are forbidden by taste whether with their own kind or not, and after Pesach it follows Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Rava's ruling on chametz
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on chametz
items.desc_en: Rava states the halakha: during Pesach, chametz is forbidden in any amount whether in its own kind or not (like Rav); after Pesach, it is permitted (like Rabbi Shimon).

sub.desc_en: Rava states the halakha: during Pesach, chametz is forbidden in any amount whether in its own kind or not (like Rav); after Pesach, it is permitted (like Rabbi Shimon).

items.text: Gemara's challenge and Rava's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and Rava's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava's leniency after Pesach, citing his own statement that Rabbi Simon penalizes chametz because one violated 'bal yera'eh' and 'bal yimatzei'. Rava distinguishes: the penalty applies to chametz itself, but not when mixed in a mixture, consistent with his practice of selling chametz after Pesach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava's lenient ruling for after Pesach, citing Rava's own statement that Rabbi Shimon penalizes chametz because one violated 'bal yera'eh' and 'bal yimatzei'.
The Gemara resolves: Rava's penalty applies only to chametz in its own kind, not via a mixture, and this aligns with Rava's practice at Rav Nachman's house to sell chametz after Pesach.

items.text: Rav's ruling on Pesach pots
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on Pesach pots
items.desc_en: Rav rules that pots used for chametz on Pesach must be broken. The Gemara asks why not wait until after Pesach and use them with non-chametz food; it answers that this is a decree lest one use them with chametz.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that Pesach pots must be broken, and the Gemara explains the reason: a decree lest one come to cook in them with their own kind.
The Gemara asks why not wait until after פסח (Passover) and use the pots with non-חמץ (leaven) food.
The Gemara answers that this is a decree lest one use them with חמץ (leaven) itself.

items.text: Shmuel's lenient ruling
items.text_en: Shmuel's lenient ruling
items.desc_en: Shmuel disagrees: the pots need not be broken; one may wait until after Pesach and use them with either chametz or non-chametz.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that pots need not be broken but may be kept until after Pesach and used for cooking both in their own kind and not in their own kind.

items.text: Shmuel's consistent practice and the Gemara's question
items.text_en: Shmuel's consistent practice and the Gemara's question
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes Shmuel's consistency: he told wine merchants to sell their wine before Pesach or he would rule like Rabbi Shimon. The Gemara asks why he didn't just rule like Rabbi Shimon, and answers that his place was under Rav's authority.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Shmuel's ruling aligns with his practice of threatening to rule like Rabbi Shimon for those selling pots.
The Gemara asks why Shmuel did not simply rule like Rabbi Shimon, and answers that it was because he was in Rav's territory.
The Gemara answers that Shmuel could not rule like Rabbi Shimon because his place was under Rav's authority, where Rav's stricter ruling was followed.

items.text: Rava bar Ahilai's decree on an oven
items.text_en: Rava bar Ahilai's decree on an oven
items.desc_en: Rava bar Ahilai forbade eating bread from an oven plastered with chametz, even with salt, lest one come to eat it with a condiment (kutach) that contains chametz.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Ahilai forbids eating bread from an oven plastered with chametz even with salt, lest one come to eat it with kutaḥ (a dairy dip).

items.text: Supporting baraita on habitual transgression
items.text_en: Supporting baraita on habitual transgression
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one may not knead dough with milk, and if one did, the entire bread is forbidden because of habitual transgression. This parallels the concern about habit.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited as support: one may not knead dough with milk, and if one did, the entire bread is forbidden due to habit of sin; similarly here.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and refutation of Rava bar Ahilai
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and refutation of Rava bar Ahilai
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not smear an oven with tail-fat, and if one did, all bread is forbidden until the oven is heated. The Gemara declares this a refutation of Rava bar Ahilai.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not smear an oven with tail-fat, and if one did, all bread is forbidden until the oven is heated.
The Gemara infers that once the oven is heated, the bread is permitted, and declares this a refutation of Rava bar Ahilai.

items.text: Distinction between metal and earthenware ovens
items.text_en: Distinction between metal and earthenware ovens
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi why Rava bar Ahilai was refuted, given that Rav said earthenware pots must be broken. Rav Ashi distinguishes: the oven was metal, the pots are earthenware. Alternatively, both are earthenware but one is heated from inside, the other from outside.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi why Rav said earthenware pots must be broken, given that Rava bar Ahilai was refuted.
Rav Ashi distinguishes: the oven was metal, the pots are earthenware.
Alternatively, both are earthenware but one is heated from inside, the other from outside, and the oven cannot be heated from inside for fear it will crack.

items.text: Ruling on a glass vessel (bukhya)
items.text_en: Ruling on a glass vessel (bukhya)
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules that a glass vessel heated from outside is forbidden, but if filled with coals it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that a glass vessel (בוכיא) heated from outside is forbidden for Passover use, but if filled with coals it is permitted.

items.text: Kashering knives for Pesach
items.text_en: Kashering knives for Pesach
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi how to kasher knives for Pesach. Rav Ashi explains his method: new handles, blades in fire, then handles in boiling water. The halakha is that both handle and blade require boiling water in a primary vessel.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi how to kasher knives for Pesach.
Rav Ashi says he makes new knives, but Ravina objects that this is only possible for him.
Rav Ashi explains his method: new handles, blades in fire, then handles in boiling water.
The halakha is that both handle and blade require boiling water in a primary vessel.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on a wooden mixing bowl
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on a wooden mixing bowl
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua rules that a wooden mixing bowl is kashered by immersion in boiling water in a primary vessel, based on the principle that as it absorbs, so it expels.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua rules that a wooden mixing bowl is kashered by immersion in boiling water in a primary vessel, based on the principle that as it absorbs, so it expels.

items.text: Inquiry about clay vessels (kunya) and distinction from wine libation
items.text_en: Inquiry about clay vessels (kunya) and distinction from wine libation
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires about using clay vessels for Pesach: green ones are certainly forbidden, black and white are questionable, and smooth ones are also questionable. Amemar rules them forbidden because they absorb. A distinction is made regarding wine libation, where they are permitted, because wine is used cold while chametz is used hot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires of Amemar about using clay vessels (קוניא) for Pesach: green ones are certainly forbidden, black and white are questionable, and smooth ones are also questionable.
Amemar rules that these vessels are forbidden because they absorb, citing the Torah's principle that clay vessels never expel their absorbed contents.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Marimar's ruling on wine libation
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Marimar's ruling on wine libation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why are clay vessels permitted for יין נסך (wine libation) according to Marimar, while chametz is forbidden? It suggests the distinction might be that wine libation is only rabbinic while chametz is biblical.
The Gemara resolves: wine is used cold (צונן), so absorption is minimal and rabbinic leniency applies, while chametz is used hot (חמין), so absorption is severe and biblical prohibition applies.

items.text: Vessels used cold and the case of kneading bowls
items.text_en: Vessels used cold and the case of kneading bowls
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that vessels used cold for chametz may be used for matzah, except for a leavening vessel (beit se'or) because its leavening is strong. Rav Ashi adds that a haroset vessel is similar. Rava rules that kneading bowls in Machoza are like beit se'or because they are constantly used and left with dough.

items.text: Mishnah on a gentile's loan and dispute between Abaye and Rava
items.text_en: Mishnah on a gentile's loan and dispute between Abaye and Rava
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a gentile lent money to a Jew on his chametz, it is permitted after Pesach; if a Jew lent to a gentile, it is forbidden. The Gemara records a dispute: Abaye says the creditor collects retroactively, Rava says from the time of seizure. They agree that if the debtor consecrated or sold the property, the creditor can repossess it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: if a gentile lent to a Jew on his chametz, it is permitted after Pesach; if a Jew lent to a gentile, it is forbidden.
The Gemara records a dispute: Abaye says the creditor collects retroactively (למפרע), Rava says from the time of seizure (מכאן ולהבא).
The Gemara notes that both agree: if the debtor consecrated or sold the property, the creditor can repossess it.

items.text: Abaye and Rava dispute the nature of the creditor's lien
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava dispute the nature of the creditor's lien
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding whether a creditor who seizes collateral retroactively acquires it from the time of the loan (למפרע) or only from the time of seizure (מכאן ולהבא). Abaye argues retroactive, Rava argues prospective.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Abaye and Rava by citing the Mishnah's case of a creditor redeeming collateral and clarifying that the dispute applies when the creditor sold or consecrated the collateral.

Abaye argues that the creditor's lien is retroactive (למפרע), so when the debtor fails to pay, it retroactively reveals that the collateral was always in the creditor's domain, making the sale or consecration valid.
Rava argues that the creditor's lien is prospective (מכאן ולהבא), because the debtor could have paid and prevented the seizure, so the creditor only acquires the collateral at the moment of seizure.

items.text: Challenge to Rava from the case of Reuven's orphans
items.text_en: Challenge to Rava from the case of Reuven's orphans
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama's case challenges Rava: if Reuven sold a field to Shimon with surety, and Reuven's creditor seizes it, then Shimon pays off the creditor, the orphans cannot reclaim movables. Rava rules that a clever Shimon can give land to the orphans and then reclaim it. The Gemara argues this only fits Abaye's retroactive view, not Rava's prospective view. Rava deflects using Rabbi Natan's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's view by citing Rami bar Chama's case.
Rami bar Chama presents a case where Reuven sold a field to Shimon with surety, and after Reuven's death, his creditor seizes it, and Shimon pays off the creditor.
Rava rules that a clever Shimon can give land to the orphans and then reclaim it, citing Rav Nachman's principle that a creditor can repossess land that orphans collected for their father's debt.

The Gemara argues that this ruling only fits Abaye's retroactive view, not Rava's prospective view, because if the creditor's lien is prospective, the orphans' land should not be subject to the creditor's claim.

The Gemara deflects the objection by invoking Rabbi Natan's principle, which allows the creditor to collect from the orphans because Shimon's debt to the creditor is linked to the orphans' debt to Shimon.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah: gentile loan on chametz
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah: gentile loan on chametz
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a gentile lent to a Jew on chametz, the chametz is permitted after Pesach. This fits Abaye's retroactive view (the chametz was always the gentile's), but not Rava's prospective view. The Gemara resolves that the case is where the gentile took the chametz as a pledge (הרהנו אצלו), so it was never in the Jew's domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that if a gentile lent to a Jew on chametz, the chametz is permitted after Pesach, and argues that this fits Abaye's retroactive view but not Rava's prospective view.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's case is where the gentile took the chametz as a pledge (הרהנו אצלו), so it was never in the Jew's domain, thus even Rava's view is satisfied.

items.text: Attempt to align the dispute with Tannaic sources
items.text_en: Attempt to align the dispute with Tannaic sources
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to connect the Abaye/Rava dispute to a Tannaic dispute about a Jew lending to a gentile on chametz, but rejects it because the parallel would require the opposite ruling in the reverse case (gentile lending to Jew).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Abaye/Rava dispute about retroactive versus prospective collection aligns with a Tannaic dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Meir regarding a Jew lending to a gentile on chametz.

The Gemara rejects the alignment by pointing to the reverse case (gentile lending to Jew), where the expected opposite rulings do not match the Tannaic positions, proving the dispute is not about retroactive versus prospective collection.

items.text: Dispute about a gentile's acquisition of chametz collateral
items.text_en: Dispute about a gentile's acquisition of chametz collateral
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Meir concerns a case where the gentile took possession of the chametz as collateral. They argue over whether a creditor acquires the collateral, based on Rabbi Yitzchak's derivation from the verse 'and it shall be righteousness for you'. The Tanna Kamma holds that this applies only between Jews, not from a gentile, while Rabbi Meir argues a fortiori that a Jew does acquire from a gentile, but all agree that a gentile lending to a Jew does not acquire the chametz.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case the Mishnah's dispute is about, and answers that it involves a gentile who took chametz as collateral, and they argue over Rabbi Yitzchak's principle.
Rabbi Yitzchak derives from the verse 'וּלְךָ תִּהְיֶה צְדָקָה' (and it shall be righteousness for you) that a creditor acquires the collateral.
The Tanna Kamma holds that Rabbi Yitzchak's derivation applies only between Jews, so a Jew does not acquire collateral from a gentile.
Rabbi Meir argues a fortiori that a Jew does acquire from a gentile, but all agree that a gentile lending to a Jew does not acquire the chametz.

items.text: Resolution of the Mishnah's ruling via the 'from now' distinction
items.text_en: Resolution of the Mishnah's ruling via the 'from now' distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can permit chametz after Passover if the gentile does not acquire it. It resolves the contradiction by distinguishing whether the gentile said 'from now' (me'akhshav) at the time of the loan, which effects immediate acquisition, or not. A baraita about a gentile pawning bread with a Jew supports this distinction: if the gentile said 'I have transferred it to you', the Jew acquires it and it is prohibited after Passover; otherwise not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the Mishnah says chametz left as collateral with a gentile is permitted after Pesach, but you said a gentile does not acquire it from a Jew.
The Gemara resolves: the Mishnah's case is where the gentile said 'from now' (מעכשיו), acquiring the chametz, while the earlier case is where he did not say 'from now'.
A baraita is cited: if a gentile pawned bread with a Jew, the Jew does not violate chametz unless the gentile said 'I have given it to you' (מעכשיו), proving the distinction.
The Gemara concludes that the distinction between saying 'מעכשיו' (from now) and not saying it is indeed valid.

items.text: Baraita on chametz found in a shop with mixed workers
items.text_en: Baraita on chametz found in a shop with mixed workers
items.desc_en: A baraita rules that chametz found after Passover in a Jew's shop where gentile workers enter is forbidden, while chametz found in a gentile's shop where Jewish workers enter is permitted. This illustrates the principle that ownership is determined by the primary owner of the premises.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules: chametz found after Pesach in a Jew's shop with gentile workers is forbidden, while in a gentile's shop with Jewish workers it is permitted.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on chametz buried under rubble
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on chametz buried under rubble
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that chametz covered by a collapse is considered as if it were destroyed. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds a measure: if a dog cannot search it out. The Gemara adds that one must also nullify it in the heart, and the depth of a dog's search is three handbreadths. Rav Acha bar Yosef asks Rav Ashi whether this depth applies to the general rule of hiding items in the ground; Rav Ashi distinguishes: here it is due to smell, requiring three handbreadths, but there for concealment from sight, one handbreadth suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that chametz buried under a collapse is considered destroyed, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds the measure of a dog's inability to search it out.
Rav Chisda adds that one must also nullify the chametz in the heart, and a baraita specifies the depth of a dog's search as three handbreadths.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yosef's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef asks Rav Ashi whether the three-handbreadth depth applies to Samuel's rule that silver vessels require burial in the ground for safekeeping.
Rav Ashi distinguishes: here the three handbreadths are needed due to smell, but there for concealment from sight, one handbreadth suffices.
Rafram bar Papa specifies that for concealment from sight, a depth of one handbreadth is sufficient.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on eating terumah chametz
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on eating terumah chametz
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who eats terumah chametz on Passover pays the principal and an added fifth if unintentional, but is exempt from payment if intentional. The Gemara begins to cite a parallel Mishnah about eating terumah in general, setting up a comparison.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who eats terumah chametz on Passover pays the principal and an added fifth if unintentional, but is exempt from payment and the value of the wood if intentional.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of a parallel Mishnah
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of a parallel Mishnah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a parallel Mishnah about eating terumah in general, setting up a comparison with the Mishnah about terumah chametz.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who eats terumah, whether ritually impure or pure, pays the principal plus an additional fifth, and also pays a fifth of that fifth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who eats terumah, whether ritually impure or pure, pays the principal plus an additional fifth, and also pays a fifth of that fifth.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry: payment by measure or by value
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry: payment by measure or by value
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: when one pays for the terumah he ate, does he pay according to the volume he consumed or according to the monetary value at the time of eating? It first clarifies that if the item decreased in value, he pays according to the original value, as in the case of a robber. The real question is when the item increased in value: does he pay by volume (returning the same measure) or by value (paying the original price)?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: when one pays for the terumah he ate, does he pay by measure or by value? It first clarifies that if the item decreased in value, he pays according to the original value, as in the case of a robber.
The Gemara then asks the real question: if the item increased in value, does he pay by measure (returning the same volume) or by value (paying the original price)?

items.text: Rav Yosef's attempted proof from the beraita
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's attempted proof from the beraita
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef attempts to prove that payment is by volume from a beraita: one who ate dried figs and paid with dates is blessed. If payment were by volume, the blessing makes sense because he ate a measure worth one zuz and paid with a measure worth four. But if payment were by value, he only pays the value of what he ate, so why is he blessed?

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef attempts to prove that payment is by volume (לפי מדה) from a beraita: one who ate dried figs and paid with dates is blessed, which only makes sense if payment is by volume, not by value.

items.text: Abaye's rejection: payment by value, blessing for convenience
items.text_en: Abaye's rejection: payment by value, blessing for convenience
items.desc_en: Abaye rejects the proof, arguing that payment is always by value. The blessing is because he ate something that was not readily marketable and paid with something that is easily sold, so he benefits from the convenience.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rejects the proof from the baraita about dried figs and dates, asserting that payment is always by value (לפי דמים), and the blessing is because the eater consumed something not readily marketable and paid with something easily sold.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah of leavened terumah on Passover
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah of leavened terumah on Passover
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye from a Mishnah: one who eats leavened terumah on Passover pays principal and fifth. If payment is by value, how can this be, since leavened bread on Passover has no monetary value? The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yossi HaGelili, who permits benefit from leavened bread on Passover.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye from a Mishnah: one who eats leavened terumah on Passover pays principal and fifth; if payment is by value, how can this be, since leavened bread on Passover has no monetary value?
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yossi HaGelili, who permits benefit from leavened bread on Passover.

items.text: Further challenge: intentional eater exempt
items.text_en: Further challenge: intentional eater exempt
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges further: the Mishnah says that one who eats intentionally is exempt from payment and from the value of the wood. If it follows Rabbi Yossi HaGelili, why is he exempt? The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana, who treats Yom Kippur like Shabbat regarding payments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yossi HaGelili, why does it exempt the intentional eater from payment and the value of the wood?
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana, who treats Yom Kippur like Shabbat regarding payments, thus exempting the intentional eater.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Akiva vs. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Akiva vs. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a beraita: Rabbi Akiva exempts one who eats leavened terumah on Passover from payment, while Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri obligates. Rabbi Akiva argues there is no benefit from it, but Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri compares it to impure terumah, which is paid for despite no benefit. Rabbi Akiva distinguishes: impure terumah has benefit for heating, but this has no benefit at all, comparing it to impure terumah of berries and grapes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Akiva exempts one who eats leavened terumah on Passover from payment, while Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri obligates payment.
Rabbi Akiva objects to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's position, arguing that there is no benefit (הנאה) from eating leavened terumah on Passover.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri responds by comparing leavened terumah on Passover to impure terumah (תרומה טמאה) during the rest of the year, which also provides no benefit yet requires payment.
Rabbi Akiva rejects the comparison, distinguishing that impure terumah has benefit for heating (היתר הסקה), whereas leavened terumah on Passover has neither benefit for eating nor for heating.
Rabbi Akiva compares leavened terumah on Passover to impure terumah of berries and grapes (תרומת תותים וענבים), which also has no benefit for eating or heating.

items.text: Distinction: separating terumah that became leavened vs. separating leavened terumah
items.text_en: Distinction: separating terumah that became leavened vs. separating leavened terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute applies only when one separated terumah and it later became leavened. But if one separated leavened dough as terumah, all agree it is not sanctified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute by distinguishing between separating terumah that later became leavened (where the dispute applies) and separating already-leavened dough as terumah (where all agree it is not sanctified).

items.text: Another tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov vs. Rabbi Elazar Chasma
items.text_en: Another tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov vs. Rabbi Elazar Chasma
items.desc_en: Another beraita: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov exempts from payment, while Rabbi Elazar Chasma obligates. Their argument mirrors the previous one, but Rabbi Elazar Chasma adds that even this leavened terumah has benefit for heating, as the priest can feed it to his dog or use it as fuel under his pot.

sub.desc_en: The beraita opens by citing the verse 'וְנָתַן לַכֹּהֵן אֶת הַקֹּדֶשׁ' and interprets it as referring to something fit to be sacred, excluding one who eats leavened terumah on Passover, exempting him from payment — the view of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

Rabbi Elazar Chasma obligates payment, and when challenged by Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov about what benefit there is, he retorts by asking what benefit there is in eating impure terumah during the rest of the year, for which one still pays.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov objects that impure terumah has at least benefit for heating (הסקה), whereas leavened terumah on Passover has neither benefit for eating nor for heating.
Rabbi Elazar Chasma resolves that even this leavened terumah has benefit for heating, as the priest can feed it to his dog or use it as fuel under his pot.

items.text: Abaye's statement on the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.text_en: Abaye's statement on the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.desc_en: Abaye asserts that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri all agree that chametz on Pesach is forbidden for benefit, but they disagree on the method of payment: Rabbi Akiva says payment is according to value, while Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says it is according to measure.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri all agree that chametz on Pesach is forbidden for benefit, but they dispute the payment method: Rabbi Akiva says payment is according to value, while Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says it is according to measure.

items.text: Gemara's clarification and objection
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification and objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Abaye's statement is necessary, suggesting that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri might agree with Rabbi Akiva but holds like Rabbi Yosei HaGlili that chametz is permitted for benefit. The Gemara then objects that if so, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri should have responded to Rabbi Akiva as Rabbi Elazar Chasama responded to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Abaye's statement is necessary, suggesting that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri might agree with Rabbi Akiva on the payment principle but holds like Rabbi Yosei HaGlili that chametz is permitted for benefit.
The Gemara objects that if so, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri should have responded to Rabbi Akiva as Rabbi Elazar Chasama responded to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

items.text: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Abba Shaul on the payment for eating terumah
items.text_en: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Abba Shaul on the payment for eating terumah
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma holds that one who eats an olive's bulk of terumah pays principal and an added fifth, based on the verse 'and if a man eats holy things in error' and the principle that eating is defined as an olive's bulk. Abba Shaul argues that payment requires at least a perutah's worth, based on the word 'and he shall give' implying a significant amount. The Tanna Kamma explains that 'eat' excludes a damager, and 'give' is needed to exclude eating chametz terumah on Pesach.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the Tanna Kamma's position: one who eats an olive's bulk of terumah (תרומה) pays principal and an added fifth.
Abba Shaul argues that payment requires at least a perutah's worth (שוה פרוטה), not merely an olive's bulk.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Tanna Kamma's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Tanna Kamma's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Tanna Kamma's proof: the verse 'וְאִישׁ כִּי יֹאכַל קֹדֶשׁ בִּשְׁגָגָה' (and if a man eats holy things in error) implies that eating is defined as an olive's bulk (כזית).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Abba Shaul's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Abba Shaul's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Abba Shaul's proof: the verse 'וְנָתַן' (and he shall give) implies that giving cannot be less than a perutah's worth (שוה פרוטה).
The Gemara objects: but the other side (Abba Shaul) also has the word 'יֹאכַל' (eat) — the Tanna Kamma explains that this word comes to exclude a damager (מזיק), not to define the minimum measure.
The Gemara resolves for the Tanna Kamma: the word 'וְנָתַן' (and he shall give) is needed to exclude one who eats chametz terumah (תרומת חמץ) on Pesach, which is not fit to be holy.

items.text: Case of eating less than an olive's bulk of terumah
items.text_en: Case of eating less than an olive's bulk of terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a baraita stating that one who eats less than an olive's bulk of terumah pays principal but not the added fifth. It questions the scenario: if it is worth less than a perutah, why pay principal? If it is worth a perutah, why not pay the fifth? The answer is that it is worth a perutah, but since it is less than an olive's bulk, only principal is paid.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one who eats less than an olive's bulk of תרומה (priestly portion) pays the principal but not the added fifth.
The Gemara questions the scenario: if the terumah is worth less than a perutah, why pay principal? If it is worth a perutah, why not pay the fifth?
The Gemara answers that it is worth a perutah, but since it is less than an olive's bulk, only the principal is paid, not the fifth.

items.text: Rav Pappa's defense of Abba Shaul and refutation
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's defense of Abba Shaul and refutation
items.desc_en: The rabbis before Rav Pappa claim the baraita is not in accordance with Abba Shaul, who would require payment even without an olive's bulk if there is a perutah's worth. Rav Pappa argues that Abba Shaul requires both an olive's bulk and a perutah's worth. The Gemara refutes this by citing a mishnah where Abba Shaul only mentions a perutah's worth, and the Sages clarify that the perutah threshold applies only to me'ilah, not terumah, which requires an olive's bulk. The Gemara concludes that this is a refutation.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis before Rav Pappa claim that the baraita is not in accordance with Abba Shaul, who would require payment even without an olive's bulk if there is a perutah's worth.
Rav Pappa argues that Abba Shaul requires both an olive's bulk and a perutah's worth.
The Gemara refutes Rav Pappa by citing a mishnah where Abba Shaul only mentions a perutah's worth.
The Sages clarify that the perutah threshold applies only to me'ilah, not terumah, which requires an olive's bulk.
The Gemara concludes that this is a refutation of Rav Pappa's position.

items.text: Discussion on me'ilah and the exclusion of an intentional sinner
items.text_en: Discussion on me'ilah and the exclusion of an intentional sinner
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'and she sinned unintentionally' excludes an intentional sinner from me'ilah. The Gemara questions this with a logical argument: if other commandments with karet exempt the intentional sinner, then me'ilah, which has no karet, should certainly exempt. The baraita counters that me'ilah carries the death penalty, so a verse is needed. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes the baraita's shift from emphasizing karet to death. Rav Chiyya bar Avin explains that the argument is about death penalty for less than an olive's bulk, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak is praised for settling the matter, though Rabba and Rav Sheishet challenge this.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited to show that Rav Pappa retracted his position, teaching that the verse 'וְחָטְאָה בִּשְׁגָגָה' (and she sinned unintentionally) excludes an intentional sinner from me'ilah.
The Gemara raises a logical argument (קל וחומר): if other commandments that carry כרת (karet) exempt the intentional sinner, then me'ilah, which has no כרת, should certainly exempt.
The baraita rejects the argument, noting that other commandments lack the death penalty, while me'ilah carries it, so a verse is needed to exclude the intentional sinner.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rav Chiyya bar Avin why the baraita initially emphasized כרת (karet) but later shifted to emphasizing death.
Rav Chiyya bar Avin explains that the argument is about the death penalty applying even for less than an olive's bulk (פחות מכזית) in me'ilah, unlike other commandments.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak praises Rav Chiyya bar Avin for settling the matter, saying 'may your mind rest, for you have set my mind at rest.'
Rabba and Rav Sheishet challenge the praise, asking 'what rest?' and casting doubt on the premise of the argument.

items.text: Opening dispute: punishment for intentional me'ilah
items.text_en: Opening dispute: punishment for intentional me'ilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the mishnah's ruling that intentional me'ilah is punishable by death follows Rabbi's opinion, as taught in a baraita: Rabbi says death, Sages say a warning. Rabbi Abbahu explains that Rabbi derives this via a verbal analogy (gezeirah shavah) from terumah, where intentional consumption is also punishable by death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the mishnah's ruling that intentional me'ilah is punishable by death follows Rabbi's opinion, citing a baraita where Rabbi says death and the Sages say a warning.
Rabbi Abbahu explains that Rabbi derives the death penalty for intentional me'ilah via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from terumah, where intentional consumption is also punishable by death.

items.text: Inference from the gezeirah shavah: minimum measure
items.text_en: Inference from the gezeirah shavah: minimum measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the same analogy that just as terumah requires an olive's bulk (kezayit) for liability, so too me'ilah requires an olive's bulk.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the gezeirah shavah (גזירה שווה, verbal analogy) that just as terumah (תרומה, priestly portion) requires an olive's bulk (כזית) for liability, so too me'ilah (מעילה, misuse of sacred property) requires an olive's bulk.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges the inference: perhaps Rabbi holds like Abba Shaul, who requires a perutah's worth even without an olive's bulk. The Gemara notes that Rav Pappa himself said Abba Shaul requires both, so Rav Pappa must have retracted his challenge.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges the inference that Rabbi holds like the Rabbis, suggesting instead that Rabbi might hold like Abba Shaul, who requires a perutah's worth even without an olive's bulk.
The Gemara notes that Rav Pappa himself said Abba Shaul requires both an olive's bulk and a perutah's worth, so Rav Pappa must have retracted his challenge.

items.text: Mar bar Ravana's explanation of the mishnah's logic
items.text_en: Mar bar Ravana's explanation of the mishnah's logic
items.desc_en: Mar bar Ravana explains that the mishnah's distinction between me'ilah and other commandments is based on the principle of 'no intent required' (ein mitkavein): in other commandments, unintentional acts are exempt, but in me'ilah, even if one intended to benefit from non-sacred wool but benefited from sacred wool, he is liable.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ravana explains that the mishnah's distinction between me'ilah and other commandments is based on the principle of 'no intent required' (אין מתכוין): in other commandments, unintentional acts are exempt, but in me'ilah, even if one intended to benefit from non-sacred wool but benefited from sacred wool, he is liable.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a different explanation: the mishnah's distinction is based on the principle of 'no preoccupation' (ein mit'asek): in other commandments, if one is preoccupied with a different action, he is exempt, but in me'ilah, if one reached for a vessel and accidentally anointed his hand with sacred oil, he is liable.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative explanation: the mishnah's distinction is based on the principle of 'no preoccupation' (אין מתעסק), where in other commandments one is exempt if preoccupied, but in me'ilah one is liable even if accidentally anointed with sacred oil.

items.text: The case of separating terumah from leavened dough
items.text_en: The case of separating terumah from leavened dough
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the mishnah's ruling about separating terumah from leavened dough: if the dough became leavened after separation, the terumah is invalid; but if one separated leavened dough as terumah, all agree it is not sanctified. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives this from the verse 'titen lo' (give to him) — not to fire.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Mar's statement distinguishing between separating terumah from dough that became leavened (disputed) and separating leavened dough as terumah (universally invalid).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives the rule from the verse 'תִּתֵּן לוֹ' (give to him) — implying to the priest, not to fire, so leavened terumah destined for burning is not sanctified.

items.text: Challenge from Rav Huna bar Yehoshua and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from Rav Huna bar Yehoshua and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua challenges: if terumah from impure produce is valid when done unintentionally, why not apply 'lo le'oro'? The Gemara resolves: there it had a time of fitness (sha'at hakosher), here it did not. The case without a time of fitness is when the dough leavened while still attached to the ground; if it leavened after being detached, it is sanctified. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua confirms that this is the ruling in the study hall.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua challenges: if terumah from impure produce is valid when done unintentionally, why not apply the rule 'לוֹ (to him) and not to its fire' to invalidate it?
The Gemara resolves: there the impure produce had a time of fitness (שעת הכושר) when it could have been eaten, but here the leavened dough never had such a time.
The Gemara asks: what is the case without a time of fitness? It answers: when the dough leavened while still attached to the ground.
The Gemara asks: but if it leavened after being detached, is it indeed sanctified? Rav Huna bar Yehoshua answers: yes.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua confirms with an Aramaic dictum that this is the ruling in the study hall.

items.text: Transition to next topic
items.text_en: Transition to next topic
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that when Rav Huna bar Yehoshua arrived, he reported the ruling from the study hall, serving as a bridge to the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that when Rav Huna bar Yehoshua arrived, he reported the ruling from the study hall, serving as a bridge to the next discussion.

items.text: Opening statement: the verse 'first' requires recognizable remnants
items.text_en: Opening statement: the verse 'first' requires recognizable remnants
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'first' (Reishit) implies that the remnants of the offering must be recognizable to Israel, excluding a case where no remnants are visible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'first' (Reishit) implies that the remnants of the offering must be recognizable to Israel, excluding a case where no remnants are visible.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya's ruling in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya's ruling in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya cites Rabbi Yochanan: impure grapes may be pressed in less than egg-sized amounts, and the wine is fit for libations. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan holds liquids are separate (pekid) from the fruit, so they become impure only at pressing, when the quantity is insufficient. Rav Chisda objects that even an exact egg-sized amount should be pure per a mishnah, but the Gemara distinguishes between b'diavad (post-facto) and l'chatchilah (ab initio), adding a decree against pressing more than an egg.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya, sitting before Rav Chisda, states in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that impure grapes may be pressed in less than egg-sized amounts and the wine is fit for libations, explaining that liquids are separate (פקידי) from the fruit and only become impure at pressing when the quantity is insufficient.

The Gemara objects that even an exact egg-sized amount should be pure, citing a mishnah where a person impure from a corpse who presses olives or grapes exactly the size of an egg produces pure liquids.
The Gemara resolves that the mishnah refers to בדיעבד (after the fact), while Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is לכתחילה (ab initio), and adds a decree lest one come to press more than an egg-sized amount.

items.text: Rav Chisda's challenge: where did the impurity go?
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's challenge: where did the impurity go?
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rejects the ruling, arguing that if liquids are absorbed (b'lia) in the fruit, then the liquids become impure along with the fruit, so pressing cannot yield pure wine.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda objects: who will listen to you and your teacher Rabbi Yochanan? Where did the טומאה (impurity) go? He holds that liquids are absorbed into the fruit, so once the fruit became טמא, the liquids also became טמא.

items.text: Rav Acha's counter-argument from the mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Acha's counter-argument from the mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya challenges Rav Chisda by citing the mishnah that an exact egg-sized pressing of impure grapes yields pure liquids, which supports the view that liquids are separate (pekid), not absorbed.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya's counter-objection
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya's counter-objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya counters: don't you hold that liquids are separate? He cites the Mishnah about a person טמא מת squeezing exactly a כביצה producing טהור liquids, arguing that if liquids were absorbed, why would they be טהור?

items.text: Rav Chisda's resolution: grapes not yet made susceptible
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's resolution: grapes not yet made susceptible
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda answers that the case involves grapes that were never made susceptible to impurity (huchsh'ru). They become susceptible only at pressing, when the quantity is less than an egg. He supports this with a baraita about impure terumah of berries and grapes that has no permit for eating or burning, implying one could press them in small amounts.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda answers: we are dealing with grapes that were not made susceptible to טומאה (הכשר), so they only become susceptible when squeezed, at which point the quantity is below the threshold; he supports this with a baraita about תרומה (priestly portion) of berries and grapes that became טמא, which has no permit for eating or burning, implying one could tread them in less than a כביצה.

Rav Chisda explains that at pressing the quantity is less than an egg, and supports this with a baraita about impure terumah of berries and grapes that has no permit for eating or burning, implying one could press them in small amounts.

items.text: Rava's decree and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rava's decree and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the prohibition against pressing impure grapes is a decree lest one come to misuse them (takalah). Abaye objects, citing a baraita that allows lighting with impure terumah bread and oil, showing we do not fear misuse. Rava responds that bread is thrown among the wood and oil is placed in a repulsive vessel, preventing misuse.

sub.desc_en: Rava says it is a גזירה (decree) lest one come to a תקלה (stumbling block); Abaye objects citing a baraita that one may light with bread and oil of טמא תרומה, and Rava responds that bread is thrown among the wood and oil is placed in a repulsive vessel.
Abaye objects, citing a baraita that allows lighting with impure terumah bread and oil, showing we do not fear misuse.
Rava responds that bread is thrown among the wood and oil is placed in a repulsive vessel, preventing misuse.

items.text: Dispute about lighting with impure terumah grains
items.text_en: Dispute about lighting with impure terumah grains
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute: Abaye in the name of Chizkiyah and Rava citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Marta quoting Rav Huna say only bread may be used for lighting, not grains, lest one come to misuse them. Rabbi Yochanan permits even grains, as Rav Ashi explains that the concern is mitigated.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the baraita and dispute
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the baraita and dispute
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita itself: one may light with bread and oil of טמא תרומה; Abaye in the name of Chizkiya and Rava in the name of Rav Huna limit this to bread but not wheat, lest one come to a תקלה, while Rabbi Yochanan permits even wheat, and the Gemara asks why no concern for תקלה, introducing Rav Ashi's forthcoming answer.

sub.text: Abaye in the name of Chizkiyah
sub.text_en: Abaye in the name of Chizkiyah
sub.desc_en: Abaye citing Chizkiyah limits the leniency to bread, not grains, lest one come to misuse them.

sub.text: Rava citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Marta quoting Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rava citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Marta quoting Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rava citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Marta quoting Rav Huna agrees that only bread is permitted, not grains.
Rabbi Yochanan permits even grains for lighting.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yochanan is not concerned about misuse.
Rav Ashi explains that the concern is mitigated, as the Gemara will elaborate.

items.text: שימוש בחיטי תרומה טמאה ללישת עיסה בטהרה
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation of heating water with impure terumah wheat
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the case of Abba Shaul using impure terumah wheat to heat water for kneading pure dough is permitted because the wheat is boiled and repulsive, thus not fit for consumption.
items.desc: רב אשי מסביר שאבא שאול השתמש בחיטי תרומה טמאה רק לאחר שהן מבושלות ומאוסות, כך שאין חשש שיאכלו אותן בטעות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by stating that the wheat was boiled and repulsive, thus not fit for consumption.

items.text: קושיית רבא בר מתנה על שתילי תרומה שנטמאו
items.text_en: Rava bar Matna's question about planted impure terumah
items.desc_en: Rava bar Matna asks why planted impure terumah shoots are forbidden to eat if they are pure from imparting impurity. Rabbah answers that they are forbidden to non-priests, teaching that growths of terumah are terumah, even for things whose seed does not decay.
items.desc: רבא בר מתנה מקשה על המשנה בתרומות: שתילי תרומה שנטמאו ונטעו – טהורים מלטמא אך אסורים באכילה. הוא תוהה מדוע אסורים אם טהורים.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Matna encounters Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chananya bar Avin who were studying terumot in Rabbah's house, and asks what they say about terumot.
Rava bar Matna cites the Mishnah that shoots of impure terumah that were planted are pure from imparting impurity but forbidden to eat, and asks why they are forbidden if they are pure.
Rabbah explains that the Mishnah's 'forbidden' means forbidden to non-priests, teaching that growths of terumah are terumah, but this is already known from a Mishnah.
Rabbah clarifies that the novel teaching is about growths of growths in a thing whose seed does not decay, which are forbidden to eat, and the students fall silent.

items.text: תשובת רב ששת: איסור לכהנים מחמת היסח הדעת
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's alternative answer: forbidden to priests due to hesech hada'at
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains that the shoots are forbidden to priests because they became disqualified through hesech hada'at (mental diversion) while impure.
items.desc: רב ששת מסביר שהאיסור הוא לכהנים בלבד, משום שנפסלו בהיסח הדעת, ולכן גם גידוליהן אסורים לכהנים.

sub.text: Students' question to Rava bar Matna
sub.text_en: Students' question to Rava bar Matna
sub.desc_en: The students ask Rava bar Matna if he has heard anything regarding the shoots.
Rav Sheshet explains that the shoots are forbidden to priests because they became disqualified through היסח הדעת (mental diversion) while impure.

items.text: מחלוקת רבי יוחנן וריש לקיש בטיב היסח הדעת
items.text_en: Dispute over the nature of hesech hada'at: disqualification of impurity or body
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Sheshet's answer works only if hesech hada'at is a disqualification of the body. It then cites the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan (impurity disqualification) and Reish Lakish (body disqualification), each with their reasoning regarding Elijah's potential purification.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה מחלוקת: רבי יוחנן סובר שהיסח הדעת הוא פסול טומאה (ספק טומאה), וריש לקיש סובר שהוא פסול הגוף (גזירה עצמאית).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rav Sheshet's answer works according to the opinion that היסח הדעת (mental diversion) constitutes a physical disqualification.
The Gemara cites the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding the nature of היסח הדעת (mental diversion).
The Gemara elaborates the practical difference: according to Rabbi Yochanan, if Elijah comes and purifies it, we listen; according to Reish Lakish, we do not.

items.text: קושיית רבי יוחנן לריש לקיש ממעשה הלול
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish from the small channel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from a mishnah about disqualified bird sin-offerings placed in a small channel until their form decays before burning, arguing that if hesech hada'at were a body disqualification, there would be no need for form decay.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן מקשה לריש לקיש ממעשה הלול שבין כבש למזבח, שם ממתינים לעיבור צורה בפסולי חטאת העוף, דבר המוכיח שהיסח הדעת הוא פסול טומאה.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects to Reish Lakish by citing a baraita about a small channel where disqualified bird sin-offerings were left until their form decayed, then burned.

items.text: Opening statement and identification of the Tanna
items.text_en: Opening statement and identification of the Tanna
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anything invalidated due to a bodily defect is burned immediately, while items invalidated due to blood or owners require a formality before burning. The Gemara identifies this Tanna as the one from the school of Rabbah bar Avuh, who holds that even piggul requires a formality.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anything invalidated due to a bodily defect is burned immediately, while items invalidated due to blood or owners require a formality before burning.
The Gemara identifies this Tanna as the one from the school of Rabbah bar Avuh, who holds that even piggul requires a formality.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah about invalidated meat
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah about invalidated meat
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute whether to sprinkle blood when the meat becomes impure or invalidated. The Gemara questions what 'invalidated' means: if it is due to mental distraction (a bodily defect), why would the blood be accepted? This suggests it must be impurity, where the frontplate atones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute whether to sprinkle blood when the meat becomes impure or invalidated.
The Gemara questions what 'invalidated' means: if it is due to mental distraction (a bodily defect), why would the blood be accepted? This suggests it must be impurity, where the frontplate atones.

items.text: Resolution: 'invalidated' means by a tevul yom
items.text_en: Resolution: 'invalidated' means by a tevul yom
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that 'invalidated' refers to being invalidated by a tevul yom (one who immersed that day). The questioner objects that this is the same as 'impure', and the Gemara explains there are two types of impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that 'invalidated' in the baraita refers to being invalidated by a טבול יום (one who immersed that day and is still awaiting sunset).
The Gemara objects that a טבול יום is still considered impure, so 'invalidated' would be the same as 'impure'.
The Gemara resolves that there are two distinct types of impurity: full impurity (טומאה) and the lesser impurity of a טבול יום, so the baraita distinguishes them.

items.text: Ravin's report and Reish Lakish's teaching
items.text_en: Ravin's report and Reish Lakish's teaching
items.desc_en: When Ravin ascended, he presented this teaching before Rabbi Yirmeya, who criticized the Babylonians for saying dark teachings. He then cites a teaching from Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Oshaya: water of the Festival that became impure—if one touched it and then consecrated it, it is pure; if consecrated first, it remains impure.

sub.desc_en: When Ravin ascended, he presented his teaching before Rabbi Yirmeya, who criticized the Babylonians for saying dark teachings.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya citing Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Oshaya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya citing Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Oshaya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya cites Reish Lakish's teaching in the name of Rabbi Oshaya: water of the Festival that became impure—if one touched it and then consecrated it, it is pure; if consecrated first, it remains impure.

items.text: Inference: no 'sowing' for consecrated items
items.text_en: Inference: no 'sowing' for consecrated items
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from this that there is no concept of 'sowing' (transfer of purity through connection) for consecrated items, and similarly no 'sowing' for terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the status differs between consecration before or after mixing, given that both involve 'sowing' (connection).
The Gemara infers that there is no concept of 'sowing' (transfer of purity through connection) for consecrated items, and similarly no 'sowing' for terumah.

items.text: Abaye's question and Rav Dimi's response about consecration by mouth
items.text_en: Abaye's question and Rav Dimi's response about consecration by mouth
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi sat and stated this teaching. Abaye asked whether the consecration was in a vessel (implying a higher level) or by mouth, and whether the Sages instituted a higher level for mouth consecration. Rav Dimi responded with a parallel from Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan: grapes that became impure—if pressed and then consecrated, pure; if consecrated first, impure. Rav Yosef clarifies that those grapes were terumah, where mouth consecration is like vessel consecration, but for items requiring a vessel, mouth consecration does not have a higher level.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi sits and states the teaching of Rabbi Oshaya regarding the water libation.
Abaye asks Rav Dimi whether Rabbi Oshaya's ruling applies only when the water was consecrated in a vessel, or even when consecrated by mouth.

Rav Dimi says he did not hear that case, but he heard a similar one: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan that impure grapes pressed and then consecrated are pure, but consecrated first and then pressed are impure, proving that the Sages imposed a higher standard even for consecration by mouth.

Rav Yosef rejects the proof: those grapes were of תרומה (priestly portion), where consecration by mouth is like vessel consecration, but for items requiring a vessel, the Sages did not impose a higher standard for mouth consecration.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding pressing grapes
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding pressing grapes
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's statement: does he allow pressing even a large quantity? But he himself said that impure grapes should be pressed less than an egg-bulk at a time. Two answers are given: either here too it is less than an egg-bulk, or there the grapes touched a first-degree source (making them second-degree), while here they touched a second-degree source (making them third-degree).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's statement: does he allow pressing even a large quantity, given that he himself said impure grapes should be pressed less than an egg-bulk at a time?
The first answer suggests that here too the pressing is done less than an egg-bulk at a time.

The second answer distinguishes the cases: there the grapes touched a first-degree source (making them second-degree), while here they touched a second-degree source (making them third-degree), so the impurity levels differ.

items.text: Rava's support from a verse about living water
items.text_en: Rava's support from a verse about living water
items.desc_en: Rava brings support from a verse: 'And he shall put upon it living water into a vessel'—the water must be in a vessel, implying they are detached, yet they are attached (to the ground). This highlights the principle that consecration can affect the status.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita from the Mishnah (Parah 6:4) about living water in a vessel, showing that consecration can affect attached items, supporting the principle that consecration overrides the usual status of attached objects.

items.text: Continued discussion of the concept of "ma'alah"
items.text_en: Continued discussion of the concept of "ma'alah"
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings two additional proofs that the concept of "ma'alah" (a rabbinic elevation) applies even to a person who is fully pure, based on a baraita about one who immersed and ate terumah, and a verse about wood and frankincense.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that the concept of 'מעלה' (rabbinic elevation) applies here as well.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi cites a baraita about one who immersed and ate תרומה (priestly portion) to prove that 'מעלה' applies even to a pure person.
Rav Ashi cites a verse about wood and frankincense to further prove that 'מעלה' applies even to items that cannot become impure.

items.text: Mishnah: Grains and conditions for fulfilling the obligation of matzah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Grains and conditions for fulfilling the obligation of matzah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the five grains (wheat, barley, spelt, oats, and rye) with which one fulfills the obligation of matzah on Pesach, and specifies that one may use demai, properly tithed produce, and redeemed second tithe and consecrated items, but not tevel or improperly tithed produce. It also discusses the status of loaves of a thanks-offering and wafers of a nazirite.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the grains with which one fulfills the obligation of מצה (unleavened bread) on פסח (Passover).
The Mishnah lists items that are invalid for fulfilling the obligation, including טבל (untithed produce) and certain offerings.

items.text: Gemara: Identification of the grains and derivation from a verse
items.text_en: Gemara: Identification of the grains and derivation from a verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the specific types of spelt, oats, and rye, and then derives from the verse "You shall not eat leavened bread with it; seven days you shall eat matzot with it" that only items that can become leavened are valid for matzah, excluding rice and millet which spoil rather than leaven.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna identifies the species: spelt is a type of wheat, oats and rye are types of barley.
The Gemara provides the Aramaic names for spelt, rye, and oats.
The Gemara states that these grains are valid for matzah, but rice and millet are not.
The Gemara asks: from where are these matters derived?

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael, Tanna debei Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael, Tanna debei Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish and the Tannaim of the schools of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov derive from the verse 'You shall not eat leavened bread with it; seven days you shall eat matzot with it' that only items that can become leavened are valid for matzah, excluding rice and millet which spoil rather than leaven.

items.text: The Mishnah disagrees with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.text_en: The Mishnah disagrees with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's exclusion of rice and millet contradicts Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who considers rice a type of grain and liable for karet for its leavening.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah disagrees with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who considers rice a grain subject to כרת (excision) for leavening.
A baraita states that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri forbids rice and millet because they are close to leavening.

items.text: Inquiry about the meaning of "close to leavening"
items.text_en: Inquiry about the meaning of "close to leavening"
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's phrase "close to leavening" means it leavens quickly or that it becomes close to leavening but not fully leavened, and resolves this with a baraita where he explicitly states that rice is a grain and one is liable for karet for its leavening and fulfills the obligation with it on Pesach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's phrase 'close to leavening' means it leavens quickly or that it becomes close to leavening but not fully leavened.

The Gemara resolves the inquiry by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri explicitly states that rice is a grain, one is liable for karet for its leavening, and one fulfills the obligation with it on Pesach.

items.text: Additional statement of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri about karmit
items.text_en: Additional statement of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri about karmit
items.desc_en: The Gemara records that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri also said that karmit is liable for challah, and Abaye and Rav Papa identify it as a type of plant found among cabbage.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's additional statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's additional statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri also says that קרמית (a type of grain) is liable for חלה (dough offering).
The Gemara asks: what is קרמית?
Abaye identifies it as שיצניתא (a type of grain).
The Gemara asks: what is שיצניתא?
Rav Pappa explains that it is a type of grain found among כלניתא (a kind of plant).

items.text: Discussion of dough kneaded with fruit juice
items.text_en: Discussion of dough kneaded with fruit juice
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar bar Chanah quotes Reish Lakish that dough kneaded with wine, oil, or honey is not liable for karet for leavening. Rav Papa explains this is because one cannot fulfill the obligation of matzah with such dough (rich matzah). Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua objects from a baraita about swallowing a mixture that is liable for karet despite not being valid for matzah. Rav Idi bar Avin awakens and explains that Reish Lakish's reason is that fruit juices do not cause leavening.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that dough kneaded with wine, oil, or honey is not liable for karet for leavening.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua to Rav Papa
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua to Rav Papa
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua asks Rav Papa for the reason behind Reish Lakish's ruling.
Rav Papa explains that Reish Lakish derives from the verse that only items valid for matzah are liable for karet when leavened, and this dough is invalid because it is rich matzah (מצה עשירה).

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua objects by citing a baraita about swallowing a mixture that is liable for karet for leavening yet invalid for matzah, contradicting Rav Papa's reasoning.
Rav Idi bar Avin awakens and resolves that Reish Lakish's true reason is that fruit juices (מי פירות) do not cause leavening, not the matzah validity argument.

items.text: Opening Mishnah clause
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah clause
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that fruit juice does not cause leavening, establishing a basic principle for what liquids can be used for matzah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah establishes that fruit juice does not cause leavening, setting a basic principle for matzah preparation.

items.text: Gemara's question on demai and answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question on demai and answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why demai (doubtfully tithed produce) is permitted for matzah, since it might be untithed. It answers that a poor person may eat demai, and since the owner could renounce ownership and become poor, it is considered fit for him now.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can fulfill the obligation of matzah with demai (doubtfully tithed produce), since it may not be fit for him due to the prohibition of eating untithed produce.
The Gemara answers that since the owner could renounce ownership of his property and become poor, thereby permitting himself to eat demai, it is considered fit for him now as well.
The Gemara cites a baraita that states that poor people and guests may be fed demai, supporting the answer.
