Rav Huna adds that the baraita records a dispute: Beit Shammai say one does not feed demai to the poor, while Beit Hillel say one does, and the halakha follows Beit Hillel.

items.text: Gemara's question on first tithe and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question on first tithe and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to specify that first tithe whose terumah has been removed is permitted—it is obviously ordinary produce. It answers that the case is where the tithe was separated while still in sheaves, and only terumat ma'aser was removed, not terumah gedolah, following Rabbi Avahu's teaching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state that first tithe whose terumah has been removed is permitted, since it is obviously ordinary produce (חולין).

The Gemara answers that the case is where the tithe was separated while still in sheaves, and only תרומת מעשר (the priestly portion from the tithe) was removed, not תרומה גדולה (the main priestly portion).

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu cites Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish that first tithe separated in sheaves is exempt from תרומה גדולה, based on the verse 'מעשר מן המעשר' (a tithe from the tithe), not both portions.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye: if separating tithe in sheaves exempts from terumah gedolah, why not also when separated in a heap? Abaye answers that the verse specifies 'from all your gifts'—the produce must be fully processed (grain), not in sheaves.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye: if separating tithe in sheaves exempts from תרומה גדולה (the great priestly portion), why not also when separated in a heap (כרי)?
Abaye answers that the verse 'from all your gifts' requires the produce to be fully processed (grain), not in sheaves.
The Gemara clarifies the distinction: a heap (כרי) is already threshed (אידגן), while sheaves (שיבולים) are not yet threshed (לא אידגן).

items.text: Second tithe and consecrated produce redeemed without the fifth
items.text_en: Second tithe and consecrated produce redeemed without the fifth
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case of second tithe and consecrated produce that have been redeemed refers to paying the principal but not the added fifth, teaching that the fifth does not impede the redemption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions second tithe and consecrated property that were redeemed, and explains it refers to a case where the principal was paid but not the additional fifth, teaching that the fifth does not impede the redemption.
The Gemara answers that the case is where one paid the principal but not the added fifth, teaching that the fifth does not impede the redemption.

items.text: Priests using challah and terumah for matzah
items.text_en: Priests using challah and terumah for matzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's allowance for priests to use challah and terumah is obvious, but it is needed lest one think matzah must be equally available to all; the repetition of 'matzot' in the verse includes these.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah states that priests may use חלה (dough offering) and תרומה (priestly portion) for matzah, and explains that the repetition of 'מצות' (matzot) in the verse includes these.
The Gemara answers that the repetition of 'matzot' in the verse includes these priestly portions, teaching that they are valid for the מצוה (commandment).

items.text: Exclusion of tevel and first tithe without terumah
items.text_en: Exclusion of tevel and first tithe without terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's exclusion of tevel refers to rabbinically prohibited tevel grown in an unperforated pot, and the exclusion of first tithe without its terumah refers to tithe separated in a heap, countering Rav Pappa's earlier challenge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state that one cannot fulfill the obligation with tevel, since it is obvious.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to tevel that is only rabbinically prohibited, grown in an unperforated pot.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to exclude first tithe whose terumah has not been removed, since it is obvious.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to first tithe that was separated in a heap before the removal of terumah gedola.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah teaches that the halacha follows Abaye's answer to Rav Pappa, not Rav Pappa's objection.

items.text: Second tithe and consecrated produce improperly redeemed
items.text_en: Second tithe and consecrated produce improperly redeemed
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's exclusion of second tithe and consecrated produce that have not been redeemed actually refers to cases where redemption was invalid: second tithe redeemed with unminted metal, and consecrated property redeemed with land, contrary to Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's exclusion of second tithe and consecrated produce that have not been redeemed is necessary, since it is obvious that they are invalid for matzah.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah actually refers to produce that was redeemed, but improperly: second tithe redeemed with unminted metal (אסימון), which lacks the required 'צורה' (form) as per the verse 'וצרת הכסף'.
The Gemara adds that consecrated property was redeemed with land, contrary to Torah law which requires payment in silver ('ונתן הכסף וקם לו').

items.text: Baraita on tevel not fully prepared and Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Baraita on tevel not fully prepared and Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: A baraita clarifies that one cannot fulfill the obligation with tevel that has not been fully prepared—i.e., terumah gedolah removed but not terumat ma'aser, first tithe, second tithe, or poor tithe. The exclusion is based on the verse 'lo tochal alav chametz,' excluding items prohibited only by 'bal tochal tevel.' Rav Sheshet identifies this as Rabbi Shimon's view that one prohibition does not take effect on another.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by asking whether one can fulfill the obligation with tevel that has not been prepared, and the gemara immediately objects that all tevel is unprepared.

The baraita clarifies that it refers to tevel that has not been fully prepared—terumah gedolah removed but not terumat ma'aser, first tithe, second tithe, or even poor tithe—and asks for the scriptural source.

The baraita cites the verse 'לֹא תֹאכַל עָלָיו חָמֵץ' (you shall not eat leaven upon it) to exclude items prohibited only by 'בַּל תֹּאכַל טֶבֶל' (the prohibition of eating tevel), not by the prohibition of chametz.
The gemara asks: where did the prohibition of chametz go (since the tevel is also prohibited by chametz)?
Rav Sheshet answers that this baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one prohibition does not take effect on another (אֵין אִיסּוּר חָל עַל אִיסּוּר).

items.text: Gemara's question on Ravina's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Ravina's distinction
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that one who eats neveilah on Yom Kippur is exempt from karet because the prohibition is not solely due to chametz but also due to tevel. The Gemara challenges this, noting that the Torah does not write 'only,' and resolves it by citing Rav Sheishet's teaching.

sub.desc_en: Ravina distinguishes: one who eats neveila on Yom Kippur is exempt from karet because his prohibition includes both chametz and tevel, not solely chametz.
The Gemara objects: does the Torah actually write the word 'only' to support Ravina's inference?
The Gemara resolves the issue by explaining that Ravina's statement is actually a version of Rav Sheishet's teaching about multiple prohibitions.

items.text: Baraita on matzah from maaser sheni and the dispute between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Baraita on matzah from maaser sheni and the dispute between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one cannot fulfill the obligation of matzah with maaser sheni in Jerusalem because matzah must be 'lechem oni' (bread of affliction), which is eaten in mourning, not in joy. Rabbi Akiva derives from the plural 'matzot' that any matzah is valid, and interprets 'lechem oni' as excluding dough kneaded with wine, oil, or honey. The Gemara explains their scriptural reasoning and cites Shmuel's interpretation of 'oni' as bread over which many things are recited.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that one might think matzah from maaser sheni in Jerusalem fulfills the obligation, but the verse 'lechem oni' excludes it because it is eaten in joy, not in mourning — the position of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
Rabbi Akiva argues that the plural 'matzot' includes all matzah, and 'lechem oni' only excludes dough kneaded with wine, oil, or honey.
The Gemara asks what scriptural basis Rabbi Akiva has, noting that the verse reads 'עָנִי' (poor person) not 'עוֹנִי' (affliction).

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei HaGelili reads 'עוֹנִי' (affliction), while Rabbi Akiva reads 'עָנִי' (poor person) and interprets it via Shmuel's statement that 'lechem oni' is bread over which many things are recited.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's practice contradicts his ruling? Resolution via distinction between first and second Yom Tov
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's practice contradicts his ruling? Resolution via distinction between first and second Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Akiva's position that dough kneaded with wine, oil, or honey is invalid for matzah, citing a baraita where he himself kneaded such dough for Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua without objection. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between the first day of Yom Tov (when matzah must be eaten) and the second day (when it is optional). It supports this with Rabbi Yehoshua's instruction to his sons, and addresses a concern about milk by citing Ravina's principle of 'ke'ein tora' (like an ox).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Akiva's ruling that dough kneaded with wine, oil, or honey is invalid for matzah, citing a baraita where he himself kneaded such dough for Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua without objection.
The baraita continues with a dispute about whether one may form cakes from such dough, and a consensus that dough may not be kneaded with warm water.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the first day of Yom Tov (when matzah must be eaten) and the second day (when it is optional).

The Gemara supports the distinction with Rabbi Yehoshua's instruction to his sons not to knead with milk on the first day but to knead with honey on the second day, correcting a potential confusion about milk.

Alternatively, the Gemara resolves the milk concern by citing Ravina's principle that milk is permitted if it is only 'ke'ein tora' (like an ox, i.e., a small amount that does not create a meat-milk mixture).

items.text: Comparison with meal-offerings: kneading with warm water
items.text_en: Comparison with meal-offerings: kneading with warm water
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why dough for matzah may not be kneaded with warm water, while meal-offerings are kneaded with warm water. It answers that meal-offerings are handled by zealous priests, but matzah is not. The Gemara further distinguishes between kneading (which can be done by zealous people) and steeping (which cannot), citing a verse about pouring oil and mixing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why matzah dough may not be kneaded with warm water, while meal-offerings (מנחות) are kneaded with warm water, and suggests that if priests are zealous, perhaps ordinary people are not.

The Gemara objects that if the distinction is zeal, then steeping (לתיתה) of wheat for meal-offerings should also be permitted, but Rabbi Zeira citing Rabbah bar Yirmeyah citing Shmuel rules that wheat for meal-offerings is not steeped, showing that steeping is not done by zealous people.
The Gemara further objects that even kneading is not exclusively done by zealous priests, citing a verse that pouring oil and mixing (בלילה) are valid when performed by any person, not just priests.

The Gemara resolves that although kneading is not done exclusively by zealous priests, it is done in the place of zealous priests (the Temple courtyard), whereas steeping is neither done by zealous priests nor in their place.

items.text: Distinction from the omer offering
items.text_en: Distinction from the omer offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the omer offering is steeped, and answers that the omer is different because it is a communal offering (tzibbur).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the omer offering is treated differently, citing a baraita that the omer is steeped and piled.
The Gemara answers that the omer is different because it is a communal offering (ציבור).

items.text: Baraita on bikurim and Rabbi Akiva's a fortiori argument
items.text_en: Baraita on bikurim and Rabbi Akiva's a fortiori argument
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one cannot fulfill the obligation of matzah with bikurim (first fruits), since bikurim are only eaten in Jerusalem, not in all your dwellings. Rabbi Akiva argues from maror: just as maror is not bikurim, so too matzah is not bikurim, though the Gemara notes a potential flaw in the analogy.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by asking whether one can fulfill the obligation of matzah with bikurim (first fruits), and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili answers that the verse 'in all your dwellings' excludes bikurim, which are only eaten in Jerusalem.
Rabbi Akiva argues by analogy from maror: just as maror is not bikurim, so too matzah is not bikurim, though the Gemara notes a potential flaw in the analogy regarding the category of species.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's initial inclusion and retraction
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's initial inclusion and retraction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva initially thought that the repetition of 'matzot' includes first fruits, but he later retracted this view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Akiva initially included first fruits (ביכורים) via the repetition of 'matzot', but then retracted.

items.text: Baraita on first fruits and second tithe
items.text_en: Baraita on first fruits and second tithe
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that the verse 'in all your dwellings you shall eat matzot' excludes first fruits, which are only eaten in Jerusalem, but includes second tithe, which can be redeemed even in Jerusalem according to Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by considering whether one can fulfill the obligation of matzah with first fruits, and excludes them because they are only eaten in Jerusalem, not in all dwellings.
The baraita asks why second tithe is included while first fruits are excluded.
The baraita answers that second tithe is included because it has a permit to be eaten in all dwellings, unlike first fruits.
Rabbi Eliezer provides a proof that second tithe can be redeemed even in Jerusalem, supporting the baraita's claim that it has a permit in all dwellings.

items.text: Proof of Rabbi Akiva's retraction
items.text_en: Proof of Rabbi Akiva's retraction
items.desc_en: The Gemara deduces that since Rabbi Akiva excludes first fruits via 'in all your dwellings', he must have retracted his earlier position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deduces that since Rabbi Akiva excludes first fruits via 'in all your dwellings', he must have retracted his earlier position.

items.text: Rabbi Yose HaGelili's alternative exclusion
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose HaGelili's alternative exclusion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose HaGelili would exclude first fruits based on 'lechem oni' (bread of affliction), but the Gemara notes he follows Rabbi Shimon who permits first fruits to an onen (mourner).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yose HaGelili does not derive the exclusion of first fruits from the term 'לֶחֶם עוֹנִי' (bread of affliction), since first fruits are eaten only in joy.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yose HaGelili follows Rabbi Shimon, who permits first fruits to an אונן (mourner), so the joy requirement does not apply.

items.text: Debate on first fruits and mourning
items.text_en: Debate on first fruits and mourning
items.desc_en: The Rabbis derive that first fruits are forbidden to an onen via a hekesh to ma'aser, while Rabbi Shimon compares them to terumah which is permitted. The Gemara questions why Rabbi Shimon doesn't require joy, and answers that the joy verse refers to the time of bringing, not eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Rabbis who forbid first fruits to an onen, and explains that they derive a hekesh (analogy) from ma'aser.
Rabbi Shimon argues that the Torah calls first fruits 'תרומה' (terumah), so they are permitted to an onen like terumah.
The Gemara objects that even if Rabbi Shimon rejects the hekesh, the verse requiring joy (שמחה) should still forbid first fruits to an onen.
The Gemara resolves that the joy verse refers to the time of bringing the first fruits, not the time of eating them, so it does not apply to an onen.

items.text: Exclusion of rich dough and sweetened cakes
items.text_en: Exclusion of rich dough and sweetened cakes
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'lechem oni' excludes challah and ashisah (rich dough), but the repetition of 'matzot' includes even rich matzot like Solomon's. The Gemara explains the meaning of 'ashishah' with a debate between Rav Chanan bar Abba and Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the exclusion of challah (rich dough) and ashisah (sweetened cakes) from the definition of 'lechem oni'.
The baraita raises the possibility that only poor-quality bread (פת הדראה) fulfills the obligation.
The baraita answers that the repetition of 'matzot' includes even rich matzot like those of King Solomon.
The baraita resolves that 'lechem oni' excludes only challah and ashisah, not all rich matzot.
The Gemara asks how we know that 'ashishah' denotes a rich item.
The Gemara cites a verse from Chronicles where David distributes 'ashishah' as a gift, indicating its value.
Rav Chanan bar Abba explains that 'ashishah' is one-sixth of an ephah, a large and rich portion.
Shmuel objects and defines 'ashishah' as a wine-skin, citing the verse 'lovers of grape-ashishim'.

items.text: Beit Shammai's ruling on thick bread
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's ruling on thick bread
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Beit Shammai prohibits baking thick bread on Passover, introducing a new halakhic restriction.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that Beit Shammai prohibits baking thick bread on Passover.

items.text: Opening question on the definition of 'thick bread'
items.text_en: Opening question on the definition of 'thick bread'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how thick 'thick bread' (פת עבה) must be. Rav Huna answers that it is a handbreadth (טפח), based on the showbread (לחם הפנים) which was also a handbreadth thick.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how thick 'thick bread' (פת עבה) must be.
Rav Huna answers that it is a handbreadth (טפח), based on the showbread (לחם הפנים) which was also a handbreadth thick.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection to Rav Huna's analogy
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection to Rav Huna's analogy
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Rav Huna's comparison to the showbread, arguing that the showbread was made by diligent priests (זריזין), with kneaded dough (פת עמילה), dry wood, a hot oven, and a metal oven, none of which apply to ordinary Passover baking.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects that the analogy to the showbread is invalid because the showbread was made by zealous priests, with kneaded dough, dry wood, a hot oven, and a metal oven, unlike ordinary matzah.

items.text: Alternative explanation of 'thick bread'
items.text_en: Alternative explanation of 'thick bread'
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba reports that he asked Rabbi (either Rav or Rebbe) in private what 'thick bread' means, and was told it means 'abundant bread' (פת מרובה), called 'thick' because it requires much kneading, or because in that Tanna's locale, abundant bread is called thick.

sub.text: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba's alternative answer
sub.text_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba's alternative answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba reports that he asked Rabbi (either Rav or Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) in private, who explained that 'thick bread' (פת עבה) means 'abundant bread' (פת מרובה), called 'thick' because it requires much kneading.
An alternative explanation is offered: in the locale of this Tanna, 'abundant bread' (פת מרובה) is simply called 'thick bread' (פת עבה).
Rabbi answers that 'thick bread' means 'abundant bread' (פת מרובה).
The gemara explains that it is called 'thick' because it requires much kneading.
Alternatively, in that Tanna's locale, abundant bread is simply called 'thick bread'.

items.text: Clarifying the context: Yom Tov of Passover
items.text_en: Clarifying the context: Yom Tov of Passover
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the prohibition of thick bread is specific to Passover, as it should apply to any festival. It answers that the Tanna is discussing Yom Tov of Passover, and a baraita confirms that Beit Shammai prohibit and Beit Hillel permit baking thick bread on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the prohibition of thick bread is specific to Passover, arguing that if the reason is unnecessary labor, it should apply to any festival.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna is indeed discussing Yom Tov of Passover, and a baraita confirms that Beit Shammai prohibit and Beit Hillel permit baking thick bread on Yom Tov.

items.text: Discussion of figured cakes (סריקין המצויירין) on Passover
items.text_en: Discussion of figured cakes (סריקין המצויירין) on Passover
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one may fulfill the obligation with clean bread, but the Sages prohibited making figured cakes on Passover due to the woman tarrying and causing leavening. Baitytos ben Zonin questioned this, and the Sages responded that allowing an exception would lead to a slippery slope. Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok relates a story where Rabban Gamliel permitted them for professionals (נחתומין), while another version says the opposite.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one may fulfill the obligation with clean bread, but the Sages prohibited making figured cakes on Passover.
Baitytos ben Zonin asks the Sages why figured cakes are prohibited, and they answer that the woman tarries and causes leavening.
Baitytos ben Zonin objects that one could make the cake with a mold and set it immediately, avoiding delay.
The Sages reject the objection, arguing that allowing an exception would lead people to say all figured cakes are forbidden except Baitytos's.
Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok relates that Rabban Gamliel permitted figured cakes for professionals (נחתומין), implying the prohibition applies only to ordinary people.
An alternative version reverses the story: Rabban Gamliel said the prohibition applies to professionals, not ordinary people.

items.text: Rabbi Yosi's ruling on the shape of cakes
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosi's ruling on the shape of cakes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi rules that one may make cakes in the form of thin wafers (רקיקין) but not in the form of thick loaves (גלוסקאות).

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that the father said the opposite: the prohibition applies to all people, not just bakers. Rabbi Yosei adds that one may make cakes like thin wafers (רקיקין) but not like thick loaves (גלוסקאות).

items.text: Exemption from challah for certain baked goods and the dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Exemption from challah for certain baked goods and the dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: A baraita lists items exempt from challah, including sponge cakes (סופגנין) and others. Resh Lakish says these are made in a pan (אילפס) and thus exempt, while Rabbi Yochanan says pan-made items are obligated. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between boiling first and then adhering (הרתיח ולבסוף הדביק) versus adhering first and then boiling, with the latter being exempt.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists baked goods (sponge cakes, honey cakes, etc.) that are exempt from the obligation of חלה (priestly portion of dough).
The Gemara asks what 'חלת המסרת' (a type of baked good listed in the baraita) refers to.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that 'חלת המסרת' refers to a type of rolled dough (חלוט) made by householders.
Resh Lakish states that these items are made in a pan (אילפס) and therefore exempt from חלה.
Rabbi Yochanan objects that items made in a pan are obligated in חלה, contradicting Resh Lakish's exemption.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita's exemption applies only when these items are made in the sun (חמה), not in a pan.
A supporting baraita is cited that explicitly states: items made in a pan are obligated, and those made in the sun are exempt, contradicting Resh Lakish.

sub.text: Ulla's rejection on behalf of Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Ulla's rejection on behalf of Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: Ulla explains that Resh Lakish would distinguish: the baraita refers to a case where one first boiled the pan and then adhered the dough (הרתיח ולבסוף הדביק), which is obligated.
The Gemara asks what the ruling would be if one adhered the dough first and then boiled the pan (הדביק ולבסוף הרתיח).
The Gemara infers that in that case, the items would be exempt from חלה.
The Gemara objects: if the distinction is correct, the baraita should have stated it explicitly within its own text rather than only contrasting with sun-made items.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita is incomplete and should be read as: the exemption applies only when one boiled first and then adhered, but if one adhered first and then boiled, it is considered like sun-made and exempt.

items.text: Matzah made in a pan and the definition of 'matzah hina'
items.text_en: Matzah made in a pan and the definition of 'matzah hina'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that one may fulfill the obligation with matzah made in a pan (אילפס), but only if boiled first. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel defines 'matzah hina' as bread that can be broken without strings (חוטין) pulling. Rava extends this to the bread of thanksgiving (לחמי תודה), and the Gemara notes that both are called 'bread' (לחם).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that one may fulfill the obligation with 'matzah hina' and matzah made in a pan (אילפס), and explains that this refers to a case where one first boiled the pan and then attached the dough.
The Gemara asks for the definition of 'matzah hina'.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel defines 'matzah hina' as any bread that can be broken without strings (חוטין) pulling from it.
Rava extends the same definition to the bread of thanksgiving (לחמי תודה).
The Gemara objects that Rava's extension is obvious, since both matzah and the bread of thanksgiving are called 'bread' (לחם) in the Torah.

The Gemara resolves that Rava's statement was necessary to counter a possible assumption that the bread of thanksgiving might be excluded because the verse says 'and he shall offer from it' (והקריב ממנו), implying a different standard.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's requirement for a whole loaf is derived from the verse 'one from every offering,' teaching that one must not take a broken piece. Here, the dough is considered like a broken piece, so the Mishnah teaches us this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's requirement for a whole loaf is derived from the verse 'one from every offering,' teaching that one must not take a broken piece, and here the dough is considered like a broken piece, so the Mishnah teaches us this.

items.text: Baraita on me'isah and chalitah
items.text_en: Baraita on me'isah and chalitah
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Beit Shammai exempt me'isah from challah, while Beit Hillel obligate it; for chalitah, Beit Shammai obligate and Beit Hillel exempt. Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei says in his father's name that both are exempt, and some say both are obligated. The Sages rule that if made in a ilpas (a type of oven) they are exempt, but in a tanur (standard oven) they are obligated.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Beit Shammai exempt me'isah from challah, Beit Hillel obligate it; for chalitah the positions are reversed, and the two terms are defined.

Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei reports in his father's name that both are exempt; an alternate version says both are obligated; the Sages rule that if made in an ilpas they are exempt, but in a tanur they are obligated.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution of the Tanna Kamma's view
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution of the Tanna Kamma's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the Tanna Kamma, what is the difference between me'isah and chalitah? Rav Yehudah says in the name of Shmuel, and similarly Rav Yehudah or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: the dispute in one case is the same as in the other, and the Tanna who taught one did not teach the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the difference between me'isah and chalitah that causes Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel to reverse their rulings?

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, and some say Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, answers that the dispute in one case is the same as in the other, and the Tanna who taught one did not teach the other.

items.text: Refutation of Rabbi Yochanan and his response
items.text_en: Refutation of Rabbi Yochanan and his response
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita states the Sages' ruling that ilpas-made dough is exempt and tanur-made is obligated, which is a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan. Rabbi Yochanan responds that this is a dispute among Tannaim, citing a baraita that teaches that me'isah and chalutah might be obligated in challah, but the verse 'lechem' excludes them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the baraita states that the Sages rule that making them in an ilpas exempts and in a תנור (oven) obligates, which is a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan's position.

Rabbi Yochanan responds that it is a dispute among Tannaim, citing a baraita that one might think me'isah and chalutah are liable for חלה (dough offering), but the verse says 'לחם' (bread) to exclude them.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Yehudah's opinion and the dispute with Tanna Kamma
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Yehudah's opinion and the dispute with Tanna Kamma
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehudah says that 'lechem' refers only to what is baked in a tanur. The Gemara questions whether this is the same as the Tanna Kamma, and suggests the difference is about ilpas-made dough: Tanna Kamma obligates it, Rabbi Yehudah exempts. Alternatively, all agree ilpas-made dough is exempt, and they dispute about dough that was later baked in a tanur: Tanna Kamma considers it bread, Rabbi Yehudah does not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yehudah's statement that 'lechem' (bread) refers only to what is baked in a tanur (oven).
The Gemara asks: Is Rabbi Yehudah's opinion identical to that of the Tanna Kamma (first Tanna)?
The Gemara answers: The difference between them is regarding dough made in an ilpas (a shallow pan): the Tanna Kamma obligates it in חלה (the dough offering), while Rabbi Yehudah exempts it.

The Gemara rejects the previous answer and offers an alternative: all agree that ilpas-made dough is exempt, and they dispute about dough that was later baked in a tanur — the Tanna Kamma considers it bread, while Rabbi Yehudah does not.

items.text: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Yehudah's reasoning
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Yehudah's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rava explains Rabbi Yehudah's reasoning from the verse 'And ten women shall bake your bread in one oven' — only bread baked in one oven is called bread, not otherwise.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: the verse 'וְאָפוּ עֶשֶׂר נָשִׁים לַחְמְכֶם בְּתַנּוּר אֶחָד' (and ten women shall bake your bread in one oven) teaches that only bread baked in a single oven is called 'לחם' (bread), and what is not baked in an oven is not called bread.

items.text: Questions from Rabbah and Rav Yosef to Ulla via Rabbi Zeira
items.text_en: Questions from Rabbah and Rav Yosef to Ulla via Rabbi Zeira
items.desc_en: Rabbah asks Ulla via Rabbi Zeira: if one attached dough from inside and heated from outside, what is the law? Ulla responds that it is like ilpas-making. Rav Yosef asks: if one attached from inside and a flame is opposite it, what is the law? Ulla responds that most poor people do so, implying it is considered bread.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah, sitting behind Rabbi Zeira, asks Ulla via Rabbi Zeira: if one attached dough from inside and heated from outside, what is the law?
Ulla responds that the case is like ilpas-making (מעשה אילפס), implying it is not considered bread baked in a תנור (oven).

sub.text: Rav Yosef's question via Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's question via Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks Ulla via Rabbi Zeira: if one attached dough from inside and a flame is opposite it, what is the law?
Ulla responds that most poor people do so, implying it is considered bread.

items.text: Rav Asi's ruling on dough of second tithe
items.text_en: Rav Asi's ruling on dough of second tithe
items.desc_en: Rav Asi states: Dough made from second tithe, according to Rabbi Meir, is exempt from challah; according to the Sages, it is obligated.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi states: dough made from second tithe (מעשר שני) produce, according to Rabbi Meir, is exempt from חלה (dough offering), but according to the Sages, it is liable.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that according to Rabbi Meir, matzah of second tithe cannot fulfill one's obligation on Passover, while the Sages permit it. Similarly, an etrog of second tithe cannot fulfill one's obligation on Sukkot according to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages allow it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding matzah of second tithe on Passover and etrog of second tithe on Sukkot.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution via verbal analogy
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution via verbal analogy
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges the Mishnah: for dough and etrog, the Torah explicitly says "your dough" and "for yourselves," implying it must be yours, but for matzah, no such phrase exists. Rava (or Rav Yemar bar Shelemiah) answers with a verbal analogy: "bread" is used both for matzah ("bread of affliction") and for the land of Israel ("when you eat of the bread of the land"), teaching that just as there it must be yours, so too here.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges the Mishnah: for dough and etrog, the Torah explicitly says 'your dough' and 'for yourselves,' implying it must be yours, but for matzah, no such phrase exists.

sub.text: Rava (or Rav Yemar bar Shelemiah)'s answer
sub.text_en: Rava (or Rav Yemar bar Shelemiah)'s answer
sub.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Yemar bar Shelemiah) answers with a verbal analogy: 'bread' is used both for matzah ('bread of affliction') and for the land of Israel ('when you eat of the bread of the land'), teaching that just as there it must be yours, so too here.

items.text: Attempted support and clarification of the dispute
items.text_en: Attempted support and clarification of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether a baraita about challah of second tithe supports the Mishnah's dispute. It clarifies that the question is whether the dispute about dough extends to matzah and etrog, or whether the case of dough is unique because the verse "your dough" appears twice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a baraita about challah of second tithe supports the Mishnah's dispute.
The Gemara objects that the baraita is identical to the Mishnah's dispute, not a new support.
The Gemara clarifies that the question is whether the dispute about dough extends to matzah and etrog, or whether the case of dough is unique because the verse 'עֲרִיסֹתֵיכֶם' appears twice.

items.text: Resh Lakish's inquiry about challah of second tithe
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's inquiry about challah of second tithe
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish asks whether one can fulfill his obligation with challah of second tithe in Jerusalem. He sets aside the view of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who would not allow it even with non-sacred food. The question is according to Rabbi Akiva: since non-sacred food works because if it becomes impure it can be redeemed, but challah, if impure, has no redemption and is burned, perhaps it cannot fulfill the obligation. Alternatively, the principle of "ho'il" (since) might apply: if he had not designated it as challah and it became impure, it could be redeemed, so now too it fulfills the obligation.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish asks whether one can fulfill his obligation with challah of second tithe in Jerusalem, setting aside Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's view since he would not allow it even with non-sacred food.

Resh Lakish frames the question according to Rabbi Akiva: since non-sacred food works because if impure it can be redeemed, but challah, if impure, has no redemption and is burned, perhaps it cannot fulfill the obligation.

Resh Lakish proposes an alternative: the principle of 'הוֹאִיל' (since) might apply — if he had not designated it as challah and it became impure, it could be redeemed, so now too it fulfills the obligation.

items.text: Second version of the inquiry and the principle of double "ho'il"
items.text_en: Second version of the inquiry and the principle of double "ho'il"
items.desc_en: Some say the previous inquiry is settled in favor of "ho'il." The real question is about challah purchased with second-tithe money. According to the Rabbis, who say it can be redeemed, it is like regular tithe. The question is according to Rabbi Yehuda, who says it must be buried. The Gemara asks whether we apply a single "ho'il" (since if not purchased it could be redeemed) or a double "ho'il" (also considering if not designated). Rava concludes that the name of second tithe is one, implying the single "ho'il" applies.

sub.desc_en: Some say the previous inquiry is settled in favor of the principle of הוֹאִיל (since if it had not been designated, it could be redeemed).
The real question is about challah purchased with second-tithe money, specifically according to Rabbi Yehuda who says it must be buried.
A baraita is cited: produce purchased with second-tithe money that becomes impure is redeemed, but Rabbi Yehuda says it is buried.
The Gemara asks whether we apply a single הוֹאִיל (since if not purchased it could be redeemed) or a double הוֹאִיל (also considering if not designated).
Rava concludes that the name of second tithe is one, implying the single הוֹאִיל applies.

items.text: Introduction to the next Mishnah: Challah of a thanks-offering and nazirite wafers
items.text_en: Introduction to the next Mishnah: Challah of a thanks-offering and nazirite wafers
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to discuss the source for the rule about challah of a thanks-offering and nazirite wafers, quoting Rabba who cites a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source regarding the law of חלת תודה (loaves of the thanksgiving offering) and רקיקי נזיר (wafers of the nazirite), and Rabbah begins to answer by citing a verse.
Rabba cites a verse as the source for the rule.

items.text: Opening derivation from Rabba
items.text_en: Opening derivation from Rabba
items.desc_en: Rabba derives from the verse 'וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת הַמַּצּוֹת' that matzah must be guarded for the sake of matzah, excluding challot of a todah and wafers of a nazirite which are guarded for the sake of a sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: Rabba derives from the verse 'וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת הַמַּצּוֹת' that matzah must be guarded for the sake of matzah, excluding challot of a todah and wafers of a nazirite which are guarded for the sake of a sacrifice.

items.text: Alternative derivation from Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Alternative derivation from Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef derives from the verse 'שִׁבְעַת יָמִים מַצּוֹת תֹּאכֵלוּ' that matzah must be edible for seven days, excluding challot of a todah and wafers of a nazirite which are only edible for a day and a night.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef derives from the verse 'שִׁבְעַת יָמִים מַצּוֹת תֹּאכֵלוּ' that matzah must be eaten over seven days, excluding challot of a todah and wafers of a nazirite which are eaten only for a day and a night.

items.text: Baraitot supporting both derivations
items.text_en: Baraitot supporting both derivations
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of Rabba's view, and another baraita in support of Rav Yosef's view, each using the same verses to exclude challot of a todah and wafers of a nazirite.

sub.desc_en: The gemara announces that a baraita supports Rabba and another baraita supports Rav Yosef.
A baraita supports Rabba by citing the verse 'וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת הַמַּצּוֹת' to exclude challot of a todah and wafers of a nazirite, which are not guarded for matzah's sake.

A baraita supports Rav Yosef by citing the verse 'שִׁבְעַת יָמִים מַצּוֹת תֹּאכֵלוּ' to exclude challot of a todah and wafers of a nazirite, which are not eaten for seven days but only for a day and a night.

items.text: First objection and resolution
items.text_en: First objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one could derive the exclusion from 'לֶחֶם עֹנִי' (bread of affliction), which is eaten in mourning, unlike these which are eaten in joy. It resolves that the Tanna holds like Rabbi Akiva, who interprets 'עֹנִי' as 'עָנִי' (poor), not 'אֲנִינוּת' (mourning).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one could derive the exclusion from 'לֶחֶם עֹנִי' (bread of affliction), which is eaten in mourning, unlike these which are eaten in joy.
The Gemara resolves that the Tanna holds like Rabbi Akiva, who interprets 'עֹנִי' as 'עָנִי' (poor), not 'אֲנִינוּת' (mourning).

items.text: Second objection and resolution
items.text_en: Second objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that these are rich matzah (since they contain oil and wine). Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak answers that the measure is a quarter-log, which can be divided into many loaves, so they can be poor matzah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the loaves in question are rich matzah (מצה עשירה), which is not valid for the מצוה (commandment) of matzah.
Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak answers that the measure is only a quarter-log (רביעית), which can be divided into many loaves, so they can be considered poor matzah (מצה עניה).

items.text: Third objection and resolution
items.text_en: Third objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that these are not eaten in all settlements (only in Jerusalem). Resh Lakish answers that this implies challot of a todah and wafers of a nazirite were eaten in Nov and Givon (temporary sanctuaries), so the objection is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that challot of a todah and wafers of a nazirite cannot fulfill the matzah obligation because they are not eaten in all settlements, only in Jerusalem.
Resh Lakish answers that this implies challot of a todah and wafers of a nazirite were eaten in Nov and Givon (temporary sanctuaries), so the objection is invalid.

items.text: Tradition from Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Tradition from Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'ei reports asking Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua about this. Rabbi Yehoshua said that if one made them for himself, he does not fulfill his obligation, but if made for sale in the market, he does. Rabbi Eliezer affirmed this as a tradition from Sinai. The Gemara questions the need for a reason, and Rabba explains that when made for sale, one intends: if it sells, it sells; if not, I will use it myself.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'ei reports asking Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua whether one fulfills the obligation with challot of a thanksgiving offering and wafers of a nazirite; Rabbi Yehoshua rules that if made for oneself one does not fulfill the obligation, but if made for sale in the market one does.
When Rabbi Ila'ei later presented the matter to Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Eliezer affirmed that these are the very words spoken to Moses at Sinai.
The Gemara questions why a reason is needed if the ruling is a tradition from Sinai.
Rabba explains the reasoning: when one makes the loaves for the market, he deliberates, saying 'if it sells, it sells; if not, I will use them myself,' so they are guarded for the sake of matzah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: List of vegetables for maror
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: List of vegetables for maror
items.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates five vegetables with which one fulfills the obligation of maror at the Passover seder: lettuce, chicory, a certain plant, endives, and bitter herb. It adds that they may be eaten fresh or dry, but not pickled, stewed, or cooked; they combine to an olive's bulk; one may use the stalk; and they may be taken from demai, first tithe whose terumah was removed, and redeemed second tithe and consecrated produce.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the five vegetables with which one fulfills the obligation of maror at the Passover seder and specifies their conditions.

items.text: Gemara: Identification of the Mishnah's species
items.text_en: Gemara: Identification of the Mishnah's species
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies each vegetable from the Mishnah: חסא for חזרת, הינדבי for עולשין, תמכתא for תמכא, אצוותא דדיקלא for חרחבינא, and מרירתא for מרור. These are brief glosses attributed to named Amoraim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Aramaic names of the five vegetables listed in the Mishnah.

items.text: Bar Kappara's and Rabbi Meir's lists
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's and Rabbi Meir's lists
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara teaches a different list of vegetables, and Rabbi Yehuda adds field endives and garden endives and lettuce. The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yehuda means field endives are like garden endives and lettuce. Rabbi Meir adds עסווס and טורא and מר ירואר, but Rabbi Yosei objects that עסווס and טורא are the same, and מר is ירואר.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara teaches a list of vegetables for the Passover obligation: עולשין, תמכא, חרחלין, חרחבנין, and חזרין.
Rabbi Yehuda adds field endives, garden endives, and lettuce to the list.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehuda repeats garden endives and lettuce already listed in the baraita.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda means field endives are like garden endives and lettuce, not adding them separately.
Rabbi Meir adds עסווס, טורא, and מר ירואר to the list.
Rabbi Yosei objects that עסווס and טורא are the same plant.
Rabbi Yosei clarifies that מר is the same as ירואר, resolving the redundancy.

items.text: Additional lists from the school of Shmuel and Rabbi Ila'a
items.text_en: Additional lists from the school of Shmuel and Rabbi Ila'a
items.desc_en: The school of Shmuel teaches another list including חרבנין, חרגנין, and הרדופנין; Rabbi Yehuda adds lettuce of the sea and lettuce of the valleys. Rabbi Ila'a says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that ערקבאלין are also valid, and he reports that he searched among Rabbi Eliezer's students and found no companion, but Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov agreed with him.

sub.desc_en: The school of Shmuel teaches a baraita listing additional vegetables valid for the maror obligation: חרבנין, חרגנין, and הרדופנין.
Rabbi Yehuda adds lettuce of the sea and lettuce of the valleys as valid species.
Rabbi Ila'a reports in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that ערקבאלין are also valid, and that he searched among Rabbi Eliezer's students for a companion but found none.
Rabbi Ila'a concludes that when he came before Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, the latter agreed with his position.

items.text: Defining characteristics of maror
items.text_en: Defining characteristics of maror
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says any vegetable that has a milky sap; Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says any whose leaves whiten; Acheirim say any bitter vegetable that has a milky sap and whose leaves whiten. Rabbi Yochanan concludes from all of them that a bitter vegetable has a milky sap and its leaves whiten. Rav Huna rules the halakha follows Acheirim.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda defines maror as any plant that has a milky sap.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka defines maror as any plant whose leaves turn pale.
Acherim state that any bitter herb has both milky sap and pale leaves.
Rabbi Yochanan concludes from all opinions that a bitter herb must have both milky sap and pale leaves.
Rav Huna rules that the halacha follows Acherim.

items.text: Preference for lettuce and the symbolism of maror
items.text_en: Preference for lettuce and the symbolism of maror
items.desc_en: Ravina finds Rav Acha bar Rava seeking מרירתא (a very bitter herb). Ravina questions him, noting that the Mishnah lists חזרת (lettuce) first, and the school of Shmuel and Rabbi Oshaya say the mitzvah is specifically with lettuce. Rava explains that חסא (lettuce) is called so because God had mercy (חס) on us. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan explains that the Egyptians were compared to maror because, like maror, they started soft and ended hard. Rav Acha then says he will go back (to use lettuce).

sub.desc_en: Ravina finds Rav Acha bar Rava seeking a very bitter herb and questions why he prioritizes bitterness over the Mishnah's listing of lettuce.
Ravina cites the Mishnah and the school of Shmuel and Rabbi Oshaya that the mitzvah is specifically with lettuce.
Rava explains that lettuce (חסא) is called so because God had mercy (חס) on us.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan explains that the Egyptians were compared to maror because, like maror, they started soft and ended hard.
Rav Acha acknowledges the point and says he will go back to use lettuce.

items.text: Deriving the laws of maror from matzah
items.text_en: Deriving the laws of maror from matzah
items.desc_en: Rav Rechumi asks Abaye why maror must be a vegetable; perhaps it could be the sap of a palm tree? Abaye answers by analogy to matzah: just as matzah is a product of the ground, so maror must be. Further questions suggest other plants (הרדוף, הרזיפו), and Abaye answers with additional analogies: matzah is a type of grain, and maror must be a type of grain; matzah is purchased with ma'aser money, so maror must be. Rabba bar Rav Chanin asks Abaye why maror is not a single species, since the Torah says "מרורים" (plural). Abaye answers by analogy: just as matzah can be made from many grains, so maror can be from many species.

sub.desc_en: Rav Rechumi asks Abaye why maror must be a vegetable; perhaps it could be the sap of a palm tree.
Abaye answers by analogy to matzah: just as matzah is a product of the ground, so maror must be.
The gemara suggests another plant (הרדוף) as a possible candidate for maror.
Abaye answers with another analogy: matzah is a type of grain, so maror must be a type of grain.
The gemara suggests another plant (הרזיפו) as a possible candidate for maror.
Abaye answers with a third analogy: matzah is purchased with ma'aser money, so maror must be.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Chanin's question to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Chanin's question to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Chanin asks Abaye why maror is not a single species, since the Torah says 'מרורים' (plural).
Abaye answers by analogy: just as matzah can be made from many grains, so maror can be from many species.

items.text: Kilayim status of the maror vegetables
items.text_en: Kilayim status of the maror vegetables
items.desc_en: Rav says that all the vegetables listed for maror may be sown in a single bed, implying they are not kilayim with each other. Rava raises an objection from a baraita that lists pairs (e.g., lettuce and wild lettuce) that are not kilayim, but implies that lettuce and endives are kilayim. The Gemara questions whether Rav's statement means they are all sown together, but Rav himself said the baraita lists them in pairs. The Gemara resolves that Rav meant they are sown according to their halakhic requirements (i.e., each species in its own row, not intermingled).

sub.desc_en: Rav states that all the vegetables listed for maror may be sown in a single bed, implying they are not kilayim with each other.
The Gemara questions whether Rav's statement implies that these vegetables are not subject to the laws of kilayim (mixed species) with each other.

Rava raises an objection from a baraita that lists pairs of vegetables (e.g., lettuce and wild lettuce) that are not kilayim, but implies that lettuce and endives are kilayim, contradicting Rav's blanket statement.
The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that Rav himself said the baraita lists the vegetables in pairs, not all together, so the baraita does not contradict Rav's statement.

The Gemara resolves that Rav's statement 'sown together' means they are sown according to their halakhic requirements (each species in its own row), not intermingled, and then questions this interpretation by citing a baraita.

items.text: Garden bed size for maror
items.text_en: Garden bed size for maror
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's rule about planting five seeds in a six-by-six handbreadth bed applies to vegetables, specifically maror. It considers whether maror, being a vegetable that hardens, requires more space, but concludes that the Mishnah teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in a six-by-six handbreadth bed, five seeds may be planted, and Rava teaches that this applies to vegetables as well.
The Gemara questions whether vegetables are stricter than seeds, citing a Mishnah that seeds cannot be planted together but vegetables can, and answers that maror might be considered seeds.
The Gemara objects that maror is clearly a vegetable, but explains that the concern is about חסה (lettuce) which hardens, requiring more space.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's ruling about cabbage hardening to support the need for extra space, but concludes that the Mishnah teaches otherwise.

items.text: Rav Chisda's distinction between stalks and leaves
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's distinction between stalks and leaves
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda limits the Mishnah's ruling that one may fulfill the obligation with maror whether moist or dry to the stalk, but not to the leaves. The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's wording supports this distinction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda (רב חסדא) distinguishes between the stalk and leaves of bitter herbs: the Mishnah's ruling that one may fulfill the obligation whether moist or dry applies only to the stalk, but for leaves only moist ones are valid, not dry ones.
The Gemara objects: from the fact that the Mishnah's later clause mentions 'their stalks', it implies that the first clause refers to leaves, contradicting Rav Chisda's interpretation.
The Gemara resolves the objection: the Mishnah is explaining itself — when it taught 'whether moist or dry', it was referring specifically to the stalk, not the leaves.

items.text: Dispute about moist and dry maror
items.text_en: Dispute about moist and dry maror
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about whether one may fulfill the obligation with moist or dry maror, and whether one may use wilted maror. The Gemara explains that the dispute applies to the stalk.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states one may fulfill the obligation with the herbs or their stems, whether fresh or dried, according to Rabbi Meir.
The Sages disagree, ruling that fresh herbs are valid but dry ones are not.
Both agree that wilted herbs are valid, but pickled, over-boiled, or boiled ones are not.
The baraita concludes with a general principle: anything with the taste of bitter herbs is valid; without it, invalid.
The Gemara resolves the objection by interpreting the baraita's dispute as referring specifically to the stalk, not the leaves.

sub.text: Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok
sub.text_en: Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok
sub.desc_en: A separate baraita records that the Sages forbid wilted herbs, but Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok permits them.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question about second tithe maror
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question about second tithe maror
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether one may fulfill the obligation with maror of second tithe in Jerusalem. The Gemara distinguishes between the views of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, and Rava concludes that the question applies to both matzah and maror.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether one may fulfill the obligation with maror of second tithe in Jerusalem, and the Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Akiva the question is unnecessary since he permits it for matzah.
The Gemara reframes the question according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who prohibits matzah of second tithe, and asks whether maror, being rabbinic, might be permitted.
Rava concludes that since the Sages instituted maror in a manner similar to Torah law, the same restriction applies to both matzah and maror.

items.text: Laws of preventing leavening
items.text_en: Laws of preventing leavening
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists actions prohibited because they might cause leavening, such as soaking bran for chickens. The Gemara discusses which foods cannot become leavened, the case of flour that absorbs dripping water, and the practice of the pious regarding a certain dish.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists acts prohibited because they cause leavening: soaking bran for chickens, a woman taking wet bran to the bathhouse, and chewing wheat for a wound.
A baraita lists foods that cannot become leavened: baked, cooked, and scalded (חלוט) with boiling water.
The Gemara objects: 'cooked' — while being cooked, it undergoes leavening, so how can it be included?
Rav Pappa resolves the objection: the baraita means 'baked (אפוי) that was subsequently cooked' — the initial baking prevents leavening during the subsequent cooking.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's statement
sub.desc_en: A baraita quotes Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda: flour that absorbed dripping water all day long does not become leavened.
Rav Pappa qualifies the statement: this is only when the dripping is drop after drop, one at a time, which prevents continuous moisture.
Bei Rabbi Sheila reports: concerning the 'pious dish' (ותיקא), there is a tradition that it is permitted (known to the household of Rabbi Sheila).
The Gemara objects: a baraita explicitly states that the pious dish is forbidden.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one tradition permits when the dish is prepared with oil and salt, the other forbids when it is prepared with water and salt (which can cause leavening).
Mar Zutra rules: one should not wipe a pot with dried flour, lest it be insufficiently cooked and cause leavening.
Rav Yosef adds: one should not scalded (חלט) [dough] at all without proper roasting.

items.text: Concern about two wheat kernels together
items.text_en: Concern about two wheat kernels together
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that if two wheat kernels are roasted together, one might lodge in a crack of the other, preventing water from circulating and leading to leavening.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that if two wheat kernels are roasted together, one might lodge in a crack of the other, preventing water from circulating and leading to leavening.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on two stalks and Rava's objection
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on two stalks and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Abaye forbids roasting two stalks together due to moisture transfer, but Rava objects that even one stalk could have moisture transfer between its ends. Rava then rules that fruit juice does not cause leavening.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that one should not roast two stalks together, because moisture from one might be absorbed by the other and cause leavening.
Rava objects that by the same logic, even a single stalk could transfer moisture from one end to the other.
Rava resolves the issue by stating that fruit juice does not cause leavening, so the concern is moot.

items.text: Abaye retracts and discusses a dried gourd
items.text_en: Abaye retracts and discusses a dried gourd
items.desc_en: Abaye retracts his earlier statement, agreeing that moisture on the surface does not cause leavening. He then rules that a dried gourd placed upside down is permitted, but upright is forbidden; Rava permits even upright because fruit juice does not leaven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Abaye retracted his earlier statement, now agreeing that moisture on the surface of ears of grain does not cause leavening.

sub.text: Abaye's ruling on a dried gourd
sub.text_en: Abaye's ruling on a dried gourd
sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that a dried gourd placed upside down (סְחִיפָא) is permitted, but upright (זְקִיפָא) is forbidden, because moisture might collect and cause leavening.
Rava permits even the upright gourd, arguing that fruit juice (מֵי פֵירוֹת) does not cause leavening.

items.text: Baraita on soaking barley and the dispute over 'split'
items.text_en: Baraita on soaking barley and the dispute over 'split'
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one may not soak barley on Pesach; if soaked, if they split they are forbidden, if not split they are permitted. Rabbi Yosei permits soaking in vinegar, but Shmuel rules against him. Rav Chisda and Shmuel dispute the meaning of 'split' — Rav Chisda says it means they would split on their own, Shmuel says literally split, and he acted accordingly.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the general rule: one may not soak barley on Pesach, but if soaked, if they split they are forbidden, if not split they are permitted.
Rabbi Yosei permits soaking in vinegar, as vinegar 'צומת' them (prevents fermentation), but Shmuel rules against him, declaring the halacha does not follow Rabbi Yosei.

sub.text: Rav Chisda citing Mar Ukva vs Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda citing Mar Ukva vs Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda citing Mar Ukva interprets 'split' as 'would split of their own accord', while Shmuel insists on literal splitting, and Shmuel acted on his ruling in Dura deBei Bar Hashu.

items.text: Rabbah's ruling on soaking and the distinction between wheat and barley
items.text_en: Rabbah's ruling on soaking and the distinction between wheat and barley
items.desc_en: Rabbah says a scrupulous person should not soak even wheat, which is permitted. Rav Nachman criticizes this, citing that the households of Rav Huna and Rava bar Avin did soak. Rava then forbids soaking, but the Gemara explains the baraita permits wheat and forbids barley, with a clarification that the baraita is not needed for wheat but teaches that barley, which is smooth, might be thought permissible.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that a scrupulous person should not soak even wheat, which is permitted, and the Gemara clarifies that this is an extension beyond the baraita which only forbids barley.
Rav Nachman objects that following Rabbah's stringency leads to eating moldy bread, citing that the households of Rav Huna and Rava bar Avin did soak wheat.

The Gemara resolves the baraita by explaining that it is not needed for wheat, which has cracks and absorbs water, but teaches that barley, which is smooth, might be thought permissible and is forbidden.

items.text: Rava permits soaking, challenged by Rav Pappa
items.text_en: Rava permits soaking, challenged by Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: Rava reverses and permits soaking, citing a baraita that fine matzah requires soaking. Rav Pappa challenges from a mishna about gentiles' flour, implying that soaking is not done for fine flour. Rava initially answers that the mishna refers to coarse flour, but later realizes he could have cited Rabbi Zeira's ruling that wheat for meal-offerings is not soaked yet called fine flour.

sub.desc_en: Rava reverses his earlier position and permits soaking, citing a baraita that fine matzah requires soaking.
Rav Pappa challenges Rava from a mishna about gentiles' flour, implying that fine flour (סולת) is not soaked.
Rava initially answers that the mishna refers to coarse flour (קמחא), not fine flour.
Rava later realizes he could have cited Rabbi Zeira's ruling that wheat for meal-offerings is not soaked yet called fine flour (סולת).

items.text: Rava declares soaking a mitzvah and the requirement of guarding from the beginning
items.text_en: Rava declares soaking a mitzvah and the requirement of guarding from the beginning
items.desc_en: Rava declares soaking a mitzvah, derived from the verse 'guard the matzot', implying guarding from the start. He supports this with Rav Huna's ruling that one may fill up on gentiles' dough but must eat an olive's worth of matzah at the end, indicating that guarding from the beginning is essential. Despite a challenge that guarding from kneading might suffice, Rava does not retract, instructing those turning over clods to do so for the mitzvah, showing that guarding from the very beginning is required.

sub.desc_en: Rava declares that soaking grain is a mitzvah (מצוה), deriving it from the verse 'וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת הַמַּצּוֹת' (guard the matzot), arguing that guarding from kneading alone is insufficient.
Rava cites Rav Huna's ruling that one may fill up on gentiles' dough but must eat an olive's worth of matzah at the end, implying that guarding from the beginning is essential.
The Gemara questions why guarding from the beginning is needed, suggesting that guarding from baking onward might suffice, and concludes that guarding from the start is required.

The Gemara objects that the case of gentiles' dough is different because guarding was not performed at the time it was needed, but where guarding is done at the proper time, guarding from kneading might suffice.
Despite the objection, Rava does not retract, instructing those turning over clods to do so for the mitzvah (מצוה), showing that guarding from the very beginning is required.

items.text: Selling leavened grain to non-Jews
items.text_en: Selling leavened grain to non-Jews
items.desc_en: Rava initially permits selling a basket of wheat that became leavened to non-Jews, but Rabba bar Livai objects based on a baraita about a garment with forbidden mixtures. Rava then suggests selling it in small amounts to Jews so it is consumed before Passover.

items.text: Mixing flour with hot food on Passover
items.text_en: Mixing flour with hot food on Passover
items.desc_en: A baraita prohibits mixing flour with hot food on Passover, but allows it if flour is added before vinegar. The Gemara identifies the dissenting opinion as Rabbi Yehuda, and considers Rabbi Yossi's view that vinegar congeals, but limits it to when the item is intact, not through a mixture.

items.text: Ulla's strict ruling and a practical case
items.text_en: Ulla's strict ruling and a practical case
items.desc_en: Ulla prohibits both methods of mixing flour with hot food, citing a principle of keeping away from any potential transgression. The Gemara then recounts that Rav Papi permitted beating a pot with reeds, and Rava questions or approves this practice.

items.text: Placing flour into charoset or mustard
items.text_en: Placing flour into charoset or mustard
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not put flour into charoset or mustard, but if done, it must be eaten immediately; Rabbi Meir prohibits it entirely. The Gemara clarifies that for charoset, all agree it must be burned, while for mustard there is a dispute, and the halakha follows the Sages.

items.text: Question about the subject of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Question about the subject of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the earlier statement referred to חַרְדָּל (mustard) or חֲרוֹסֶת (charoset). The interlocutor asks what practical difference it makes, and Rav Kahana's ruling is cited: the dispute applies only to mustard, but for charoset all agree it must be burned immediately.

items.text: Rav Ashi's support for Rav Kahana
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's support for Rav Kahana
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that Rav Kahana's view is correct, based on Shmuel's ruling that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yosi. The Gemara infers that this implies the mixture does cause leavening, but the objection is raised that it might neither leaven nor cause leavening.

items.text: Derivation of prohibition for other liquids
items.text_en: Derivation of prohibition for other liquids
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Paschal lamb may not be cooked in water. A baraitha derives from a kal vachomer that other liquids are also prohibited, while Rabbi Eliezer (Rabbi) derives the same from the repetition of 'וּבָשֵׁל מְבֻשָּׁל'.

items.text: Difference between the opinions and the case of roasting in a pot
items.text_en: Difference between the opinions and the case of roasting in a pot
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the practical difference between the two opinions as 'צְלִי קֵדָר' (roasting in a pot). It then explains how the Rabbis interpret the extra phrase 'וּבָשֵׁל מְבֻשָּׁל' to include a case where one boiled then roasted or roasted then boiled. Rav Kahana attributes this to Rabbi Yosi, while Ulla says even Rabbi Meir would agree due to the verse.

items.text: Exemption for fully roasted lamb
items.text_en: Exemption for fully roasted lamb
items.desc_en: A baraitha teaches that one is not liable for eating the Paschal lamb if it was fully roasted, as the verse only prohibits 'נָא וּבָשֵׁל מְבֻשָּׁל'. Rav Ashi defines this as when it is 'חֲרוֹכָא' (scorched).

items.text: Exemption for raw meat and definition of 'נָא'
items.text_en: Exemption for raw meat and definition of 'נָא'
items.desc_en: Another baraitha exempts one who eats raw meat from liability, as the verse only prohibits 'נָא וּבָשֵׁל'. It then clarifies that raw meat is permitted only if roasted, and Rav defines 'נָא' as 'אֲבַרְנִים' (half-cooked).

items.text: Cooking in hot springs of Tiberias
items.text_en: Cooking in hot springs of Tiberias
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that one who cooks in the hot springs of Tiberias on Shabbat is exempt, but one who cooks the Paschal lamb in them is liable. Rava explains that 'liable' means he violates the prohibition of 'צְלִי אֵשׁ'. Rav Chiya bar Rav Natan teaches this explicitly, and Rava adds that eating it raw is also prohibited.

items.text: Opening statement on lashes for eating raw or boiled
items.text_en: Opening statement on lashes for eating raw or boiled
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who eats the Paschal lamb raw receives two sets of lashes, one for boiled receives two, and one who eats both raw and boiled receives three.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who eats the Paschal lamb raw receives two sets of lashes, one for boiled receives two, and one who eats both raw and boiled receives three.

items.text: Abaye's principle of לאו שבכללות and alternative views
items.text_en: Abaye's principle of לאו שבכללות and alternative views
items.desc_en: Abaye states that one does not receive lashes for a general prohibition (לאו שבכללות). Two alternative opinions are presented: one holds that one does not receive two lashes but does receive one, and another holds that one does not receive even one, as the prohibition is not distinct like that of muzzling an animal.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states the principle that one does not receive lashes for a general prohibition (לאו שבכללות).
An anonymous opinion holds that one does not receive two lashes for a general prohibition, but does receive one.
Another anonymous opinion holds that one does not receive even one lash, because the prohibition is not distinct like the prohibition of muzzling an animal.

items.text: Rava's parallel statement on eating grape pits and skins
items.text_en: Rava's parallel statement on eating grape pits and skins
items.desc_en: Rava states that one who eats grape pits receives two lashes, one who eats grape skins receives two, and one who eats both receives three. Abaye again applies his principle of לאו שבכללות, with the same alternative opinions repeated.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that eating grape pits incurs two lashes, eating grape skins incurs two, and eating both incurs three.
Abaye objects that one is not lashed for a לאו שבכללות (a general prohibition that includes multiple specifics).
Some say that for a לאו שבכללות, one is exempt from two lashes but still receives one.
Others say that one is exempt even from a single lash, because the prohibition is not uniquely designated, like the לאו (prohibition) of muzzling an animal.

items.text: Baraita on eating raw or roasted before nightfall
items.text_en: Baraita on eating raw or roasted before nightfall
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: one who eats an olive's bulk of raw meat before nightfall is exempt, but after nightfall is liable. One who eats an olive's bulk of roasted meat before nightfall does not disqualify himself from the group, but after nightfall does disqualify himself.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that eating raw meat before nightfall is exempt, but after nightfall is liable; eating roasted meat before nightfall does not disqualify one from the group, but after nightfall does disqualify.

items.text: Derivation that the prohibition of raw applies only when roasted is permitted
items.text_en: Derivation that the prohibition of raw applies only when roasted is permitted
items.desc_en: A second baraita presents a logical argument: one might think that eating raw before nightfall is prohibited, but the verse 'אַל תֹּאכְלוּ מִמֶּנּוּ נָא וּבָשֵׁל מְבֻשָּׁל בַּמָּיִם כִּי אִם צְלִי אֵשׁ' teaches that the prohibition of raw applies only when the commandment to eat roasted applies, i.e., after nightfall.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a logical argument: one might think that eating raw before nightfall is liable, using a קל וחומר (a fortiori inference) from the time when roasted is permitted.
The baraita presents an alternative: perhaps the prohibition of raw applies only when roasted is not permitted, and when roasted is permitted, raw is not prohibited.
The Gemara adds that one should not be surprised by this alternative, since the prohibition is relaxed in the context of roasted meat.

The baraita resolves the argument by citing the verse: the extra phrase 'כִּי אִם צְלִי אֵשׁ' teaches that the prohibition of raw applies only when the commandment to eat roasted applies, i.e., after nightfall.

items.text: Rabbi's derivation regarding boiled meat at any time
items.text_en: Rabbi's derivation regarding boiled meat at any time
items.desc_en: Rabbi expounds the verse 'בָּשֵׁל מְבֻשָּׁל' to include boiled meat even if cooked before nightfall. The Gemara notes that Rabbi uses this phrase to also include roasting in a pot and other liquids, and deduces that the double expression teaches two laws.

sub.desc_en: רבי (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) argues that the verse's double expression 'בָּשֵׁל מְבֻשָּׁל' (boiled in any way) teaches that the prohibition applies even if the meat was boiled before nightfall.
The Gemara objects that רבי (Rabbi) already used this same phrase 'בָּשֵׁל מְבֻשָּׁל' to derive the prohibition of roasting in a pot and cooking with other liquids.
The Gemara resolves that the varied wording 'בָּשֵׁל מְבֻשָּׁל' (rather than a repeated identical form) indicates that two separate laws are derived from it.

items.text: Baraita on liability for roasted meat before nightfall and derivation
items.text_en: Baraita on liability for roasted meat before nightfall and derivation
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who eats roasted meat before nightfall is liable, and one who eats raw after nightfall is liable. The Gemara explains that roasted is compared to raw: just as raw is prohibited by a negative commandment, so too roasted. The source for roasted is the verse 'וְאָכְלוּ אֶת הַבָּשָׂר בַּלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה', implying only at night, not by day. Rav Chisda identifies the Tanna of this baraita.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one who eats roasted meat before nightfall is liable, and one who eats raw meat after nightfall is liable.
The Gemara explains that the baraita compares roasted to raw: just as raw is prohibited by a negative commandment (לאו), so too roasted.
The Gemara asks: granted, raw meat has an explicit verse 'אַל תֹּאכְלוּ מִמֶּנּוּ נָא', but from where do we derive the prohibition for roasted meat?
The Gemara answers: it is derived from the verse 'וְאָכְלוּ אֶת הַבָּשָׂר בַּלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה', implying that eating is permitted only at night, not by day.
The Gemara objects: this is a negative commandment derived from a positive statement (לאו הבא מכלל עשה), and such a negative is treated as a positive commandment (עשה), not a full-fledged לאו.
Rav Chisda identifies the Tanna of this baraita, resolving the objection by attributing the baraita to a specific authority who holds that a לאו הבא מכלל עשה is a full לאו.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's derivation of a negative commandment for using unblemished animals
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's derivation of a negative commandment for using unblemished animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous mishnah as Rabbi Yehuda's view, citing a baraita that derives from the verse 'שׁוֹר וָשֶׂה שָׂרוּעַ וְקָלוּט נְדָבָה תַּעֲשֶׂה אֹתוֹ' that only blemished animals may be consecrated for Temple maintenance, not unblemished ones. Rabbi Yehuda then derives a negative commandment from the word 'לֵאמֹר', and Rabbi Levi bar Kappara questions the derivation, receiving an answer that 'לֵאמֹר' is not stated in the context of the matter. The school of Rav interprets 'לֵאמֹר' as 'לָאו אֱמוֹר' (say 'no').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous mishnah as Rabbi Yehuda's view and cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'שׁוֹר וָשֶׂה שָׂרוּעַ וְקָלוּט נְדָבָה תַּעֲשֶׂה אֹתוֹ' that only blemished animals may be consecrated for Temple maintenance, not unblemished ones, and one who does so violates a positive commandment.
Rabbi Yehuda asks: I have only a positive commandment; from where do I derive a negative commandment?
Rabbi Yehuda answers that the verse 'וַיְדַבֵּר ה׳ אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר' teaches that the entire section is subject to a negative commandment.
Rabbi Levi bar Kappara objects: What is the derivation?

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda's answer to Rabbi Levi bar Kappara
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's answer to Rabbi Levi bar Kappara
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda answers that the word 'לֵאמֹר' is not stated in the context of the matter, implying a negative commandment.
The school of Rav interprets 'לֵאמֹר' as 'לָאו אֱמוֹר' (say 'no'), supporting the derivation of a negative commandment.

items.text: Contradictory baraitot on where to pour water from a baker's trough
