items.text_en: Contradictory baraitot on where to pour water from a baker's trough
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites two conflicting baraitot: one says to pour water in a place of drainage, not in a cesspool; the other says to pour in a cesspool. The resolution is that the first refers to a large amount of water that pools, and the second to a small amount that does not pool.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that water from a baker's trough should be poured in a place of drainage, not in a cesspool.
The Gemara cites a second baraita that contradicts the first, stating that the water should be poured in a cesspool.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a large amount of water that pools (pour in a drainage place) and a small amount that does not pool (pour in a cesspool).

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on kneading with 'our water'
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on kneading with 'our water'
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that a woman should only knead dough with 'water that has rested' (overnight water). Rav Mattana taught this in Papponya, and the next day everyone brought their jugs to him, but he clarified he meant water that had rested in the house.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that a woman should only knead dough with 'our water' (water that has rested overnight).

sub.text: Rav Mattana's teaching and the people's misunderstanding
sub.text_en: Rav Mattana's teaching and the people's misunderstanding
sub.desc_en: Rav Mattana taught this in Papponya, and when the people brought their jugs the next day, he clarified that he meant water that had rested in the house (overnight water).

items.text: Rava's additional rulings on kneading
items.text_en: Rava's additional rulings on kneading
items.desc_en: Rava teaches that a woman should not knead with hot water, water heated by the sun, or water drawn from a boiler; she should not remove her hand from the oven until she finishes all the bread; and she needs two vessels—one for shaping and one for cooling her hands.

sub.desc_en: Rava teaches a series of restrictions for kneading matzah: not with hot water, sun-heated water, or boiler water; not removing hands from the oven until all bread is done; and requiring two vessels—one for shaping and one for cooling hands.

items.text: Dispute between Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi on retroactive validity of kneading
items.text_en: Dispute between Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi on retroactive validity of kneading
items.desc_en: A question is raised: if a woman violated the ruling and kneaded, what is the law? Mar Zutra permits it, citing a baraita about soaking barley for Passover where if they split they are forbidden, but if not they are permitted. Rav Ashi objects, arguing that the cases are not comparable, and the ruling stands only where stated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if a woman violated the ruling and kneaded with warm water, what is the law? It presents two positions: מָר זוּטְרָא (Mar Zutra) permits it, and רַב אָשֵׁי (Rav Ashi) forbids it.

Mar Zutra supports his position by citing a ברייתא (baraita): one may not soak barley on Passover, but if one did and the barley split, they are forbidden; if they did not split, they are permitted, implying that the product is forbidden only if actual leavening occurred.

Rav Ashi objects, arguing that the cases are not comparable: the ruling about soaking barley was stated only in that specific context, and it does not apply to kneading with warm water, where the Sages may have imposed a stricter penalty.
The Gemara concludes the discussion with the formulaic phrase 'הדרן עלך כל שעה' (we return to you, 'All Hour'), marking the end of the chapter.

items.text: Mishnah: Items that violate Passover and the general rule
items.text_en: Mishnah: Items that violate Passover and the general rule
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that are subject to the prohibition of chametz on Passover: Babylonian kutach, Median beer, Edomite vinegar, Egyptian zitom, dyer's paste, cook's starch, and scribe's glue. Rabbi Eliezer adds women's cosmetics. The general rule: anything from a grain species violates Passover; these are subject to a prohibition but not karet.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the items that violate Passover: Babylonian kutach, Median beer, Edomite vinegar, Egyptian zitom, dyer's paste, cook's starch, and scribe's glue.
רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer) adds women's cosmetics to the list of items that violate Passover.
The Mishnah states the general rule: anything from a grain species violates Passover; these items are subject to a prohibition but not karet.

items.text: Baraitot on the effects of Babylonian kutach and other foods
items.text_en: Baraitot on the effects of Babylonian kutach and other foods
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites baraitot: three things are said about Babylonian kutach—it dulls the heart, blinds the eyes, and weakens the body, each due to specific ingredients. Another baraita lists three things that increase waste, bend the stature, and impair eyesight: coarse bread, new beer, and raw vegetables. A third baraita lists three things that decrease waste, straighten the stature, and brighten the eyes: fine bread, fatty meat, and old wine.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states three harmful effects of Babylonian kutach: it dulls the heart, blinds the eyes, and weakens the body.
The baraita explains each effect: the whey (נסיובי דחלבא) dulls the heart, the salt (מילחא) blinds the eyes, and the moldy bran (קומניתא דאומא) weakens the body.
A second baraita lists three things that increase waste, bend the stature, and impair eyesight: coarse bread, new beer, and raw vegetables.
A third baraita lists three things that decrease waste, straighten the stature, and brighten the eyes: fine bread, fatty meat, and old wine.

items.text: Opening discussion on beneficial and harmful foods
items.text_en: Opening discussion on beneficial and harmful foods
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists items that are beneficial for one ailment but harmful for another, and those that are universally beneficial, such as fresh ginger, long pepper, fine bread, fatty meat, and aged wine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists foods that are universally beneficial, such as fine bread, fatty meat, and aged wine.

items.text: Definitions of Shekhar HaMadi and Chometz HaAdomi
items.text_en: Definitions of Shekhar HaMadi and Chometz HaAdomi
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'Shekhar HaMadi' is beer made with barley water, and 'Chometz HaAdomi' is vinegar made by adding barley to wine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara defines 'Shekhar HaMadi' as beer made with barley water and 'Chometz HaAdomi' as vinegar made by adding barley to wine.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's historical explanation of Chometz HaAdomi
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's historical explanation of Chometz HaAdomi
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that originally, Judean wine did not sour until barley was added, and it was called plain vinegar. Now, Edomite wine requires barley to sour, and it is called 'Chometz HaAdomi', fulfilling the verse about one nation's rise and another's fall.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that originally, Judean wine did not sour until barley was added, and it was called plain vinegar.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak concludes that now Edomite wine requires barley to sour, called 'Chometz HaAdomi', fulfilling the verse about one nation's rise and another's fall.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on vinegar from an am ha'aretz
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on vinegar from an am ha'aretz
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that in Judea, one who buys vinegar from an am ha'aretz need not tithe it, as it is assumed to come from temed (wine lees). Now, one must tithe, as it is assumed to come from wine. The Gemara questions this, citing a mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda obligates tithing temed, and resolves that the assumption is about suspicion, not halakhic status.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that in Judea, one who buys vinegar from an am ha'aretz (ignorant person) initially did not need to tithe it, as it was assumed to come from temed (wine lees), but now one must tithe, as it is assumed to come from wine.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's position, citing a mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda obligates tithing temed (wine lees mixed with water), implying he considers it subject to tithes.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling is not about the halakhic status of temed, but about the suspicion that amei ha'aretz (ignorant people) would use wine rather than temed for vinegar.
An alternative resolution: amei ha'aretz are indeed suspected, but the contradiction is resolved by distinguishing between vinegar from a barrel (דרווקא) and vinegar from a jug (דפורצני).

items.text: Definition and preparation of Zeitom HaMitzri
items.text_en: Definition and preparation of Zeitom HaMitzri
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Zeitom HaMitzri' is. Rav Yosef teaches it is three parts barley, three parts saffron, and three parts salt. Rav Papa substitutes barley with wheat. The mixture is roasted, ground, and drunk from the slaughter to the festival, with specific effects on the body.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Zeitom HaMitzri' is.
Rav Yosef teaches that it consists of three parts barley, three parts saffron, and three parts salt.
Rav Papa substitutes barley with wheat, with the mnemonic 'sisanei'.

sub.text: Gemara's statement on preparation and effects
sub.text_en: Gemara's statement on preparation and effects
sub.desc_en: The mixture is roasted, ground, and drunk from the slaughter to the festival, with specific effects on the body and danger for a sick person or pregnant woman.

items.text: Discussion on 'Zoman shel Tzaba'im' and 'Kolan shel Sofrim'
items.text_en: Discussion on 'Zoman shel Tzaba'im' and 'Kolan shel Sofrim'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'Zoman shel Tzaba'im' as water used by dyers for dyeing blue. 'Amilan shel Tabachim' is bread from unripe grain that absorbs fat. 'Kolan shel Sofrim' is interpreted as shoemakers' paste, but Rav Shimi says it is the leftover of rich girls given to poor girls. A challenge from a baraita leads to Rav Oshaya's resolution that scribes also use it for gluing paper.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'Zoman shel Tzaba'im' as water used by dyers for dyeing blue.
The Gemara explains 'Amilan shel Tabachim' as bread from unripe grain that absorbs fat.
The Gemara initially interprets 'Kolan shel Sofrim' as shoemakers' paste.
Rav Shimi offers an alternative interpretation: 'Kolan' is the leftover of rich girls given to poor girls.

The Gemara challenges Rav Shimi's interpretation by citing a baraita of Rabbi Chiyya that lists four types of country produce and three types of craftsmen's items, questioning how leftover cosmetics fits the latter category.
Rav Oshaya resolves the difficulty by affirming the original interpretation of shoemakers' paste and explaining that it is called 'Kolan shel Sofrim' because scribes also use it for gluing paper.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's addition of women's accessories
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's addition of women's accessories
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to discuss Rabbi Eliezer's statement about 'Tachshitei Nashim', correcting it to 'Tipulei Nashim' (women's cosmetics), citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Eliezer's statement from the Mishnah that includes 'תכשיטי נשים' (women's accessories) among forbidden items.
The Gemara objects: can it enter your mind that the Mishnah refers to actual 'תכשיטי נשים' (women's jewelry)?
The Gemara corrects the text: read instead 'אף טיפולי נשים' (also women's cosmetics).
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav provides a supporting tradition about 'בנות ישראל' (daughters of Israel) that clarifies the meaning of 'טיפולי נשים'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Anointing maidens with different substances
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Anointing maidens with different substances
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that maidens who have reached puberty but not yet a full year are anointed with various substances depending on their family's wealth: poor with lime, rich with fine flour, and princesses with oil of myrrh, citing Esther 2:12.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that maidens who have reached puberty but not a full year are anointed with lime, fine flour, or oil of myrrh depending on their family's wealth.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying 'oil of myrrh'
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying 'oil of myrrh'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'oil of myrrh' is. Rav Huna bar Yirmeya says it is stacte; Rav Yirmeya bar Abba says it is olive oil that has not reached a third of its growth. A baraita adds that Rabbi Yehuda calls it 'anpikinon' and explains it softens the skin and removes hair.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'oil of myrrh' (שמן המור) refers to.
Rav Huna bar Yirmeya identifies it as stacte (סטכת), a type of resin.
Rav Yirmeya bar Abba identifies it as olive oil from olives that have not reached a third of their growth.
A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda who calls it 'anpikinon' (אנפיקינין), explaining it is olive oil from unripe olives that softens the skin and removes hair.

items.text: The principle 'anything of grain' and the story of the Babylonian traveler
items.text_en: The principle 'anything of grain' and the story of the Babylonian traveler
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: anything of grain type is subject to Passover prohibition. Rabbi Yehoshua asks why the Sages enumerated specific items if the rule is general; the answer is to familiarize people with them and their names. A story illustrates this: a Westerner visiting Babylonia asked for 'matkhilta' (a dish), and when they brought him kutach (a leaven mixture), he realized it was forbidden and left.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: anything of grain type is subject to the Passover prohibition.
Rabbi Yehoshua asks: since the general rule is stated, why did the Sages enumerate specific items?
The Gemara answers: the enumeration is to familiarize people with the items and their names.
A story illustrates the principle: a Westerner visiting Babylonia asked for 'matkhilta' (a dish), and when they brought him kutach (a leaven mixture), he realized it was forbidden and left.

items.text: Mishnah: These are subject to a negative commandment
items.text_en: Mishnah: These are subject to a negative commandment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that these items (kutach, etc.) are subject to a negative commandment (לאו), not karet.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that these items (kutach, etc.) are subject to a negative commandment (לאו), not karet.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna: Rav Yehuda's view (Rabbi Meir)
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna: Rav Yehuda's view (Rabbi Meir)
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna that holds that fully leavened grain through mixtures is punishable by a negative commandment, and that 'nukasheh' (sour dough) itself is also punishable by a negative commandment. Rav Yehuda says it is Rabbi Meir, citing a baraita about 'si'ur' (sour dough) that must be burned and given to one's dog, and the eater is liable to forty lashes. The Gemara resolves an internal contradiction in the baraita by distinguishing between Rabbi Meir's view and Rabbi Yehuda's view. It concludes that Rabbi Meir holds that nukasheh itself is punishable by a negative commandment, and all the more so fully leavened grain through mixtures.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna who holds that fully leavened grain through mixtures and nukasheh itself are punishable by a negative commandment.
Rav Yehuda says it is Rabbi Meir, citing a baraita that si'ur must be burned and given to one's dog, and the eater is liable to forty lashes.
The Gemara objects that the baraita contradicts itself: it says si'ur must be burned (implying forbidden for benefit) yet also says give it to one's dog (implying permitted for benefit).

The Gemara resolves that the baraita is split: 'si'ur must be burned' is Rabbi Meir's view for Rabbi Meir, 'give it to one's dog' is Rabbi Meir's view for Rabbi Yehuda, and 'the eater is liable to forty' refers to Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Meir holds nukasheh itself is punishable by a negative commandment, and all the more so fully leavened grain through mixtures.

items.text: Rav Nachman's alternative view (Rabbi Eliezer)
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's alternative view (Rabbi Eliezer)
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says the Tanna is Rabbi Eliezer, citing a baraita: for fully leavened grain, karet; for its mixture, a negative commandment (Rabbi Eliezer's view); the Sages say mixture is nothing. Rabbi Eliezer holds that fully leavened grain through mixtures is punishable by a negative commandment, and all the more so nukasheh itself.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman identifies the Tanna of the Mishnah as Rabbi Eliezer.

A baraita is cited: for fully leavened grain, karet; for its mixture, a negative commandment (Rabbi Eliezer's view); the Sages say mixture is nothing; Rabbi Eliezer holds that fully leavened grain through mixtures is punishable by a negative commandment, and all the more so nukasheh itself.

items.text: Debate between Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Debate between Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav Nachman does not accept Rav Yehuda's view, and vice versa. Rav Nachman argues that Rabbi Meir only spoke about nukasheh itself, not about fully leavened grain through mixtures. Rav Yehuda argues that Rabbi Eliezer only spoke about fully leavened grain through mixtures, not about nukasheh itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav Nachman does not accept Rav Yehuda's view.
Rav Nachman explains that Rabbi Meir only spoke about nukasheh itself, not about fully leavened grain through mixtures.
The Gemara asks why Rav Yehuda does not accept Rav Nachman's view.
Rav Yehuda explains that Rabbi Eliezer only spoke about fully leavened grain through mixtures, not about nukasheh itself.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Yehuda: it derives from 'Kol machmetzet lo tochelu' that kutach, etc., are included, but only with a negative commandment, not karet. The Gemara notes that this baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer's view (who says mixture is a negative commandment), but he does not mention nukasheh, implying that for Rabbi Eliezer, nukasheh is not punishable at all.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Yehuda: it derives from 'Kol machmetzet lo tochelu' that kutach, etc., are included, but only with a negative commandment, not karet.

The Gemara notes that this baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer's view (who says mixture is a negative commandment), but he does not mention nukasheh, implying that for Rabbi Eliezer, nukasheh is not punishable at all.

items.text: Derivation of Rabbi Eliezer's view and resolution of verses
items.text_en: Derivation of Rabbi Eliezer's view and resolution of verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Eliezer derives the negative commandment for mixtures from 'Kol machmetzet'. It considers the possibility that 'Kol' could also imply karet, but resolves that the verse 'Ki kol ochel machmetzet' is needed to include leaven caused by another substance. The Gemara then questions whether the negative commandment also comes from 'Kol', and concludes that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is from 'Kol' itself. It then addresses the objection that 'Kol' is needed to include women, but resolves that women are already included from another verse (Rav Yehuda citing Rav). Finally, the Gemara notes that the verse is still necessary for other inclusions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Eliezer derives the negative commandment for mixtures, and answers that it is from the verse 'כל מחמצת לא תאכלו'.
The Gemara objects that if 'כל' includes mixtures for a negative commandment, it should also include them for karet, since the verse 'כי כל אוכל מחמצת ונכרתה' also uses 'כל'.
The Gemara answers that the 'כל' in the karet verse is needed to include leaven caused by another substance, as taught in a baraita.
The Gemara objects that if so, the 'כל' in the negative commandment verse should also be needed for the same inclusion, leaving no source for the negative commandment itself.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is from the word 'כל' itself in the negative commandment verse.
The Gemara objects that the 'כל' in the negative commandment verse is needed to include women.
The Gemara answers that women are already included from the teaching of Rav Yehuda citing Rav, and the Tanna de-bei Rabbi Yishmael, that the verse equates men and women for all punishments.
The Gemara concludes that the verse is still necessary for other inclusions.

items.text: Gemara's initial assumption and conclusion
items.text_en: Gemara's initial assumption and conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially thought that since women are exempt from the positive commandment of eating matzah (a time-bound positive mitzvah), they might also be exempt from the prohibition of eating chametz. The verse teaches that they are indeed obligated in the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that since women are exempt from the positive time-bound commandment of eating matzah (מצה), they might also be exempt from the prohibition of eating chametz (חמץ), but the verse teaches that they are obligated in the prohibition.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's derivation that women are obligated in matzah
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's derivation that women are obligated in matzah
items.desc_en: Now that women are included in the prohibition of chametz, they are also included in the commandment of eating matzah, according to Rabbi Eliezer. He derives this from the verse: whoever is included in the prohibition of chametz is included in the commandment of matzah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that since women are included in the prohibition of chametz, they are also included in the positive commandment of eating matzah, in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: Question: Why not include a mixture (עירובו)?
items.text_en: Question: Why not include a mixture (עירובו)?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the word "kol" is used to include women rather than to include a mixture of chametz and matzah (עירובו). It argues that since the verse deals with eaters (אוכלין), it is more logical to include other eaters (women) rather than things that are eaten (a mixture).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the word 'כל' (all) is used to include women rather than to include a mixture (עירובו) of chametz and matzah.
The Gemara answers that it is logical to include eaters (women) rather than things that are eaten (a mixture), since the verse deals with eaters.

items.text: Objection by Rav Nathan: A counterexample from the prohibition of chelev
items.text_en: Objection by Rav Nathan: A counterexample from the prohibition of chelev
items.desc_en: Rav Nathan objects: Is it always true that when the verse deals with eaters it does not include things eaten? A baraita shows that regarding the prohibition of chelev, the word "kol" includes chelev of blemished animals and chelev of non-sacred animals, even though the verse deals with eaters.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nathan objects to the gemara's reasoning by citing a baraita: regarding the prohibition of chelev, the word 'כל' (all) includes chelev of blemished animals and non-sacred animals, even though the verse deals with eaters, showing that 'כל' can include things eaten.

items.text: Resolution: Distinction between cases with and without eaters
items.text_en: Resolution: Distinction between cases with and without eaters
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: In the case of chelev, there are no other eaters to include, so the verse includes things eaten. Here, there are eaters (women) to include, so the verse does not leave them aside to include a mixture.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing: in the case of chelev, there are no other eaters to include, so the verse includes things eaten; here, there are eaters (women) to include, so the verse does not leave them aside to include a mixture.

items.text: The Rabbis' view: They do not expound "kol"
items.text_en: The Rabbis' view: They do not expound "kol"
items.desc_en: The Rabbis, who do not accept the inclusion of a mixture (עירובו), do not expound the word "kol" at all. However, they do expound the phrase "כי כל" (ki kol). So how do they derive that women are obligated? They derive it from "כי כל".

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Since the Rabbis do not accept the inclusion of a mixture (עירובו), and they do not expound the word "כל" (kol), how do they derive that women are obligated to avoid chametz?
The Gemara answers: The Rabbis do not expound the word "כל" (kol) alone, but they do expound the phrase "כי כל" (ki kol), and from that they derive the obligation for women.

items.text: Difficulty with Rabbi Eliezer's position
items.text_en: Difficulty with Rabbi Eliezer's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to Rabbi Eliezer, why not say that "kol" includes women and "כי כל" includes the mixture? But a baraita shows that Rabbi Eliezer does expound "כי כל" regarding the prohibition of leaven on the altar. This creates a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to Rabbi Eliezer, why not say that "כל" includes women and "כי כל" includes the mixture (עירובו)?
The Gemara objects: If you say Rabbi Eliezer does not expound "כי כל", a baraita shows he does expound it regarding the prohibition of leaven on the altar.
The Gemara concludes that the contradiction remains unresolved (קשיא).

items.text: Rabbi Avahu and Ze'iri: Principle of permitted substance combining with forbidden
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu and Ze'iri: Principle of permitted substance combining with forbidden
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states a general principle: For all prohibitions in the Torah, a permitted substance does not combine with a forbidden one, except for the prohibitions of a nazirite. Ze'iri adds: also the prohibition of leaven on the altar (שאור בל תקטירו). This is according to Rabbi Eliezer, who expounds "kol". The Gemara then questions this.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states a general principle: for all prohibitions in the Torah, a permitted substance does not combine with a forbidden one, except for the prohibitions of a nazirite, as the Torah said 'משרת' (soaking).
Ze'iri adds that the prohibition of leaven on the altar (שאור בל תקטירו) is also an exception.
The Gemara asks: according to whom does Ze'iri's addition apply?
The Gemara answers: it is according to Rabbi Eliezer, who expounds the word 'כל' (all).
The Gemara begins to question: if so, then what about the earlier derivation regarding women and leaven?

items.text: Application of the principle to chametz on Pesach
items.text_en: Application of the principle to chametz on Pesach
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the principle of 'heter mitztaref le'issur' applies to chametz on Pesach as well, and rejects Abaye's view that there is a concept of 'haktarah' for less than a kezayit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara affirms that the principle of 'היתר מצטרף לאיסור' (permitted combines with forbidden) applies to חמץ (leaven) on פסח (Passover) as well.
The Gemara rejects Abaye's view that there is a concept of 'הקטרה' (offering) for less than a כזית (olive's bulk), teaching that הקטרה does not apply to less than a כזית.

items.text: Abaye's challenge from the Mishnah of terumah and spices
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge from the Mishnah of terumah and spices
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Dimi's statement by citing a Mishnah where terumah spices mixed with hullin are nullified, yet a tevul yom invalidates the place of contact. The Gemara explains that this is because the permitted food combines with the forbidden food to form a kezayit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi sits and states the halachic teaching about the combination of permitted and forbidden food.
Abaye challenges Rav Dimi: do all Torah prohibitions combine permitted food with forbidden food to form a kezayit?
Abaye cites a Mishnah about terumah spices mixed with hullin, where a tevul yom invalidates only the place of contact, implying that permitted food combines with forbidden food.
The Gemara asks: why is the place of contact invalid, since the spices are nullified in the majority of hullin?
Rabbah bar bar Chanah explains that the reason is because a non-priest (זר) is liable for eating a kezayit of the mixture, implying that permitted food combines with forbidden food.

items.text: Reframing the kezayit as kezayit bikdei achilat pras
items.text_en: Reframing the kezayit as kezayit bikdei achilat pras
items.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the previous answer: the kezayit in question is actually a kezayit within the time it takes to eat a half-loaf (kdei achilat pras), not a simple kezayit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by reinterpreting the kezayit as a kezayit within the time it takes to eat a half-loaf (kdei achilat pras), not a simple kezayit.

items.text: Questioning the Torah status of kezayit bikdei achilat pras and the case of Babylonian kutach
items.text_en: Questioning the Torah status of kezayit bikdei achilat pras and the case of Babylonian kutach
items.desc_en: Abaye asks whether kezayit bikdei achilat pras is a Torah-level concept. Rav Dimi affirms it. The Gemara then questions why the Sages disagree with Rabbi Eliezer regarding Babylonian kutach, and resolves that kutach lacks a kezayit bikdei achilat pras, either because it is eaten alone (nullifying one's intent) or because it is eaten as a dip.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks whether the concept of a kezayit (olive's bulk) consumed within the time of a half-loaf (בכדי אכילת פרס) is a Torah-level principle.
Rav Dimi affirms that it is indeed a Torah-level concept.
The Gemara objects: If the principle is Torah-level, why do the Sages disagree with Rabbi Eliezer regarding Babylonian kutach (a dairy dip)?
The Gemara resolves that Babylonian kutach does not contain a kezayit within the time of a half-loaf, either because it is eaten alone (nullifying one's intent) or because it is eaten as a dip.

items.text: First objection from the Mishnah of two pots and mortars
items.text_en: First objection from the Mishnah of two pots and mortars
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a Mishnah where two pots (one hullin, one terumah) and two mortars are mixed, and we assume the terumah fell into terumah. If kezayit bikdei achilat pras were Torah law, why rely on this assumption? The answer is that terumah of spices is rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from a Mishnah about two pots (one hullin, one terumah) and two mortars, where we assume the terumah fell into terumah, implying that kezayit bikdei achilat pras is not Torah law.
The gemara asks: if kezayit bikdei achilat pras is Torah law, why do we rely on the assumption that terumah fell into terumah?
Rav Dimi answers that the Mishnah deals with terumah of spices, which is only rabbinic, so the assumption is valid.

items.text: Second objection from the Mishnah of two baskets and se'ah measures
items.text_en: Second objection from the Mishnah of two baskets and se'ah measures
items.desc_en: Another objection is raised from a Mishnah with two baskets and two se'ah measures, where we assume hullin fell into hullin. Again, if kezayit bikdei achilat pras were Torah law, why rely on this assumption? The answer is that terumah nowadays is rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from a Mishnah about two baskets and two se'ah measures, where we assume hullin fell into hullin and terumah into terumah, questioning why we rely on this assumption if kezayit bikdei achilat pras is Torah law.
Rav Dimi answers that terumah nowadays is rabbinic, so the Mishnah's leniency is not a proof against the Torah status of kezayit bikdei achilat pras.

items.text: The purpose of the word 'mishrat'
items.text_en: The purpose of the word 'mishrat'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the word 'mishrat' (in the verse) is only for this principle, and notes that it is needed for another teaching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the word 'מִשְׁרַת' (mishrat) in the verse is solely for the principle of היתר מצטרף לאיסור (permitted food combining with forbidden food), noting that it is needed for another teaching cited in a baraita.

items.text: Opening binyan av from nazir to all prohibitions
items.text_en: Opening binyan av from nazir to all prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that if one soaks grapes in water and they impart a wine flavor, the mixture is forbidden for a nazir. From this, a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument is made: if nazir, whose prohibition is not eternal and not for benefit, treats flavor as the substance, then kilayim (diverse kinds), whose prohibition is eternal and for benefit, certainly should.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating the principle of טעם כעיקר (flavor is like the substance itself) and gives the example of a nazir who soaks grapes in water and is liable if the water has a wine flavor.

The Gemara builds a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if nazir, whose prohibition is not eternal and not for benefit, treats flavor as the substance, then kilayim (diverse kinds), whose prohibition is eternal and for benefit, certainly should.

items.text: Identification of the mishnah's author and Rabbi Yochanan's view
items.text_en: Identification of the mishnah's author and Rabbi Yochanan's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the same logic applies to orlah (uncircumcised fruit) in a mixture of two types. It then identifies that the mishnah (which holds this principle) follows the Rabbis, and that Rabbi Yochanan says it aligns with Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara extends the principle of טעם כעיקר (taste is like the substance) to orlah (uncircumcised fruit) in a mixture of two types.
The Gemara identifies that the mishnah follows the Rabbis, and that Rabbi Yochanan says it aligns with Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Rejection of Rabbi Akiva from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rejection of Rabbi Akiva from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Rabbi Akiva is meant. If it is the one from the Mishnah (who says a nazir who soaks his bread in wine is liable only if there is a kezayit from the combination), the Gemara questions whether the liability is from the bread and wine together or just from the wine alone. It suggests that the Mishnah might be teaching that even a mixture is considered, but this is not a clear derivation of טעם כעיקר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Rabbi Akiva is meant, suggesting it might be the one from the Mishnah, and questions whether the liability is from the bread and wine together or just from the wine alone.
The Gemara responds that if the liability were only from the wine alone, there would be no novelty; rather, the Mishnah teaches that even a mixture is considered.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva from the Baraita and his derivation from meat in milk
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva from the Baraita and his derivation from meat in milk
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the reference is to Rabbi Akiva from a Baraita, where he explicitly says a nazir who eats a kezayit from bread and wine is liable. The Gemara then asks: from where does Rabbi Akiva derive the principle of טעם כעיקר? It answers that he learns it from meat in milk: just as there, mere flavor is forbidden, so too here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the reference is to Rabbi Akiva from a Baraita, citing the Baraita where Rabbi Akiva explicitly states that a nazir who soaks his bread in wine and eats a kezayit from both is liable.
The Gemara asks: from where does Rabbi Akiva derive the principle of טעם כעיקר (that mere flavor is considered like the substance itself)?
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva derives it from meat in milk: just as there, mere flavor is forbidden, so too here, flavor is treated as the substance.

items.text: Rabbis' rejection: meat in milk is a novelty
items.text_en: Rabbis' rejection: meat in milk is a novelty
items.desc_en: The Rabbis argue that one cannot derive from meat in milk because it is a novelty (חידוש). The Gemara explores what the novelty is: not that each alone is permitted and together forbidden (since kilayim is similar), but rather that if one roasts meat all day in milk it is permitted, but if cooked in a pot it is forbidden—a unique stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis reject deriving from meat in milk because it is a novelty (חידוש).
The Gemara asks what the novelty is, and suggests it is not that each alone is permitted and together forbidden, since kilayim is similar.
The Gemara explains the novelty: if one roasts meat all day in milk it is permitted, but if cooked in a pot it is forbidden—a unique stringency.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Akiva also agrees meat in milk is a novelty, so how can he derive from it?

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's alternative derivation from gentile libations
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's alternative derivation from gentile libations
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even Rabbi Akiva would agree meat in milk is a novelty. So it suggests he derives from gentile libation offerings (גיעולי גוים): just as there, mere flavor is forbidden, so too here. The Rabbis counter that gentile libations are also a novelty because normally a spoiled taste (נותן טעם לפגם) is permitted, but there it is forbidden. Rabbi Akiva, following Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna, holds that the Torah only forbids a pot used within the day, so it is not spoiled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Akiva derives the principle of טעם כעיקר (taste is like the substance) from the laws of גיעולי גוים (gentile libation offerings), where mere absorbed flavor is forbidden.
The Rabbis counter that גיעולי גוים (gentile libations) are also a novelty, because normally a spoiled taste (נותן טעם לפגם) is permitted, yet there it is forbidden.

sub.text: Rabbi Akiva's resolution via Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's resolution via Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva, following Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna, holds that the Torah only forbids a pot used within the day, so it is not a case of spoiled taste, and thus the derivation stands.

items.text: Rabbis' counter and Rav Acha's argument from the Rabbis to Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Rabbis' counter and Rav Acha's argument from the Rabbis to Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Rabbis argue that even a pot used within the day slightly spoils the taste. Then Rav Acha bar Rav Avya says to Rav Ashi: from the Rabbis we can learn for Rabbi Akiva—just as the Rabbis derive from the word 'משרת' that flavor is like the substance for all prohibitions, so too Rabbi Akiva should derive from 'משרת' that the permitted combines with the forbidden for all prohibitions. The Gemara cuts off with 'אמר ליה'.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis reject Rabbi Akiva's derivation from the pot used on the same day, arguing that even such a pot slightly spoils the taste, so the case of gentile vessels remains a novelty.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya's argument
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya's argument
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya argues to Rav Ashi that from the Rabbis' position one can infer for Rabbi Akiva: just as the Rabbis derive from 'משרת' that taste is like substance for all prohibitions, so too Rabbi Akiva should derive from 'משרת' that the permitted joins the forbidden for all prohibitions.
The Gemara begins Rav Ashi's response but cuts off, leaving the argument incomplete.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis on whether nazir and chatat are two verses that come as one
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis on whether nazir and chatat are two verses that come as one
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva holds nazir and chatat are two verses that come as one and therefore cannot teach other laws, while the Rabbis argue they are needed for specific teachings. The Rabbis claim each verse teaches a different principle: chatat teaches that permitted food combines with forbidden food, and nazir teaches that taste is like the substance itself. Rabbi Akiva counters that both verses teach the same principle of permitted combining with forbidden, making them two verses that come as one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that Rabbi Akiva holds nazir and chatat are two verses that come as one and therefore cannot teach other laws.

The Gemara cites a baraita explaining the verse regarding chatat: 'כל אשר יגע בבשרה יקדש' teaches that the meat must be absorbed into the flesh, and 'יקדש' means it becomes like the chatat — if it is invalid, it becomes invalid; if it is fit, it is eaten with the stringency of the chatat.
The Gemara asks: according to the Rabbis, should nazir and chatat also be considered two verses that come as one, and thus not teach other laws?
The Rabbis answer that those two verses are needed for specific teachings and therefore are not superfluous.

Rabbi Akiva questions why the verses are needed, arguing that if the Torah had written only about chatat, nazir could not learn from it because חולין (non-sacred) cannot learn from קדשים (sacred), but if it had written only about nazir, chatat could learn from it since all other prohibitions in the Torah learn from nazir.

The Rabbis respond that both verses are necessary: chatat teaches that permitted food combines with forbidden food (since חולין cannot learn from קדשים), and nazir teaches that taste is like the substance itself (ומשרת), and from nazir one can derive for all prohibitions in the Torah.
Rabbi Akiva counters that both verses teach the same principle — that permitted food combines with forbidden food — making them two verses that come as one, which cannot teach other laws.

items.text: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana about nazir prohibitions combining
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana about nazir prohibitions combining
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks Rav Kahana: according to Rabbi Akiva, if permitted and forbidden combine, then surely forbidden with forbidden should combine? Rav Kahana answers that the case of permitted and forbidden is simultaneous, while forbidden with forbidden is sequential, so the verse is needed for the latter.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks Rav Kahana: according to Rabbi Akiva, if a permitted substance combines with a forbidden one, then surely forbidden with forbidden should also combine, so why does the verse teach this?
Rav Kahana answers: the case of permitted and forbidden is simultaneous, while forbidden with forbidden is sequential, so the verse is needed for the latter.

items.text: Mishnah: Dough in the cracks of a kneading trough
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dough in the cracks of a kneading trough
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if there is an olive's bulk of dough in one place in the cracks of a trough, one must remove it for chametz; otherwise it is nullified. Similarly for impurity: if one is particular about it, it interposes; if one wants it to remain, it is considered part of the trough.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that dough in the cracks of a trough must be removed if it is an olive's bulk in one place, otherwise it is nullified.
The Mishnah applies a parallel rule for impurity: if one is particular about the dough it interposes, if one wants it to remain it is considered part of the trough.

items.text: Gemara: Two versions of Rav Yehuda's statement about the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Two versions of Rav Yehuda's statement about the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two versions of a statement by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel. One version applies to the first clause: only in a place not made to strengthen is one obligated to remove an olive's bulk; in a place made to strengthen, one is not obligated. The other version applies to the second clause: only in a place made to strengthen is less than an olive's bulk nullified; in a place not made to strengthen, one is obligated to remove even less than an olive's bulk.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's statement that the Mishnah's obligation to remove an olive's bulk applies only where the dough is not placed to strengthen the vessel, but where it is placed to strengthen, one is not obligated.
The Gemara infers from Shmuel's statement that less than an olive's bulk is never obligated for removal, even in a place not made to strengthen.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Yehuda's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Yehuda's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version applies Rav Yehuda's statement to the Mishnah's second clause: only in a place made to strengthen is less than an olive's bulk nullified, but in a place not made to strengthen one is obligated to remove even less than an olive's bulk, implying that an olive's bulk is always obligated.

items.text: Baraitot supporting both versions
items.text_en: Baraitot supporting both versions
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites two baraitot that support each version of Rav Yehuda's statement. The first baraita rules that in a place made to strengthen, dough does not interpose for impurity and one does not violate chametz; in a place not made to strengthen, it interposes and one violates, but only for an olive's bulk. The second baraita (partially cited) supports the other version.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara announces that two baraitot support the two versions of Rav Yehuda's statement.
The first baraita rules that dough in cracks of a kneading bowl in a place made to strengthen does not interpose for impurity and does not violate chametz.
The first baraita continues: in a place not made to strengthen, the dough interposes and one violates the chametz prohibition.
The first baraita qualifies: these rules apply only to an olive's bulk; less than that, even in a place not made to strengthen, it does not interpose and one does not violate.
The second baraita begins to cite the other version, supporting the latter version of Rav Yehuda's statement.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a piece of leavened bread smaller than an olive's bulk does not interpose or pass over, but if it is an olive's bulk it interposes and passes over even in a place made to strengthen.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a piece of leavened bread smaller than an olive's bulk does not interpose or pass over, but if it is an olive's bulk it interposes and passes over even in a place made to strengthen.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Huna's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Huna's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the Mishnah's statements. Rav Huna resolves it by distinguishing between a place made for strengthening and a place not made for strengthening. Rav Yosef challenges this and suggests the Mishnah is a dispute between Tannaim, citing a baraita about moldy bread.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out that the two parts of the Mishnah contradict each other regarding the halachot of ḥametz with respect to being a barrier and being nullified.

Rav Huna resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah is referring to a regular kilta (a container for kneading), not a khamirta (a trough for soaking bread), distinguishing between a place made for strengthening and a place not made for strengthening.
Rav Yosef rejects Rav Huna's answer and asserts that the Mishnah actually reflects a dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, citing a baraita about moldy bread.

The Gemara cites a baraita about moldy bread that is liable for removal, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's opinion that if the bread is designated for sitting, it is nullified; this is contrasted with Tanna Kamma's view that a k'zayit is never nullified.

From Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling that the bread is nullified, Rav Yosef infers that Tanna Kamma holds that a k'zayit (olive-sized) piece of ḥametz is never nullified even when it is intended for a different use, thus resolving the contradiction as a dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

items.text: Abaye's resolution and Rav Ashi's refinement
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution and Rav Ashi's refinement
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by attributing both statements to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, distinguishing between a place of kneading and not a place of kneading. Rav Ashi refines this to mean the rim of the kneading trough, not the trough itself, and the Gemara explains why this is necessary.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by attributing both statements to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, distinguishing between a place of kneading and not a place of kneading.
Rav Ashi refines Abaye's distinction, specifying that 'not a place of kneading' refers to the rim of the kneading trough, not the trough itself.
The Gemara explains why Rav Ashi's refinement is necessary, lest one think that the dough might extend from the rim into the trough.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and the dispute about Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and the dispute about Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. However, a contradiction arises from Rav Yitzchak bar Ashi's statement that only if one smears the bread with clay is it nullified. The Gemara resolves this by suggesting two different versions of Rav's teaching.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports in the name of Rav that the halakha (הלכה) follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

The Gemara objects: Rav Yitzchak bar Ashi said in Rav's name that only if one smears the bread with clay (טיט) is it nullified, implying that without smearing it is not nullified, contradicting the blanket ruling.
The Gemara resolves that the two statements come from different transmitters: one who transmits Rav's ruling does not transmit the other, so there is no contradiction.
An alternative version states that Rav Nachman actually said in Rav's name that the halakha does NOT follow Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, consistent with Rav Yitzchak bar Ashi's statement.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling about two half-olives and a dough thread
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling about two half-olives and a dough thread
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel rules that if there are two half-olive-sized pieces of leavened bread connected by a dough thread, one must remove them if the thread would carry them together. Ulla limits this to a kneading trough, and the Gemara discusses other cases like a house and attic, concluding with 'teiku'.

sub.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports Shmuel's ruling that two half-olive pieces of leavened bread connected by a dough thread must be removed if the thread would carry them together.
Ulla limits Shmuel's ruling to a kneading trough, but in a house one is obligated to remove the pieces.
The Gemara explains the reason for Ulla's distinction: in a house, one might gather the pieces and they would fall together.
Ulla reports that the sages in the West asked about analogous cases: a house and attic, a house and portico, and two inner rooms.
The Gemara concludes with 'תֵּיקוּ' (let it stand unresolved), indicating no definitive answer was found.

items.text: Baraita about moldy bread and impurity
items.text_en: Baraita about moldy bread and impurity
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that moldy bread unfit for humans but edible by dogs is susceptible to food impurity and is burned with impure food on Passover. Rabbi Nathan disagrees, and the Gemara notes that a general rule about purity follows the first opinion.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that moldy bread unfit for humans but edible by dogs is susceptible to food impurity and is burned with impure food on Passover.
Rabbi Nathan objects that such bread is not susceptible to impurity.
The Gemara notes that a general rule about purity follows the first opinion, not Rabbi Nathan's.

items.text: Baraita about the kneading trough of tanners and Rava's ruling
items.text_en: Baraita about the kneading trough of tanners and Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a kneading trough of tanners: if flour was added within three days, one must remove it; before three days, not. Rabbi Nathan adds that if hides were added, even within three days it is not required. Rava rules like Rabbi Nathan even for one day. The Gemara then discusses an analogy to impurity, with Abaye correcting the wording.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a tanner's kneading trough — if flour was added within three days, one must remove it; before three days, not. Rabbi Nathan adds that if hides were added, even within three days it is not required.
Rava rules like Rabbi Nathan, even for one day or one hour.
The Gemara extends the principle to impurity: if one is particular about the dough, it interposes; if one wants it to remain, it is like the kneading trough.
The Gemara objects: the cases are not comparable — there the matter depends on a measure (time), here on intent (being particular).
Rav Yehuda says the text should read: 'Regarding impurity, it is not so.'
Abaye rejects Rav Yehuda's correction, noting the text explicitly says 'and similarly regarding impurity,' and explains the intended meaning.

items.text: Initial statement about dough and impurity
items.text_en: Initial statement about dough and impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a distinction: on Pesach, dough is considered significant for combining impurity, while during the rest of the year it depends on whether one is particular about it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a distinction: on Pesach, dough is considered significant for combining impurity, while during the rest of the year it depends on whether one is particular about it.

items.text: Rava's objection and reinterpretation
items.text_en: Rava's objection and reinterpretation
items.desc_en: Rava objects that the Mishnah says 'interposes' (חוֹצֵץ) not 'combines' (מִצְטָרֵף), and reinterprets the case as regarding raising purity to a vessel.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that the Mishnah teaches 'חוֹצֵץ' (interposes) not 'מִצְטָרֵף' (combines), and reinterprets the rule as applying to raising purity to the kneading trough.
Rava reinterprets the Mishnah as referring to raising purity to a vessel (immersion), not combining impurity.

items.text: Explanation of Rava's case
items.text_en: Explanation of Rava's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rava's case: a vessel became impure and needs immersion; on Pesach the dough interposes, while during the rest of the year it depends on whether one is particular.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rava's scenario: if the trough is impure and one wants to immerse it, on Pesach the dough interposes and prevents immersion, while during the rest of the year it depends on one's concern.

items.text: Rav Pappa's objection and reinterpretation
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection and reinterpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects that the Mishnah says 'regarding impurity' not 'regarding purity', and reinterprets the case as regarding bringing impurity down to a vessel.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects that the Mishnah teaches about impurity, not purity, and reinterprets the rule as applying to lowering impurity to the trough.

items.text: Explanation of Rav Pappa's case
items.text_en: Explanation of Rav Pappa's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rav Pappa's case: a creeping animal touched the dough; on Pesach the dough interposes and prevents impurity from reaching the vessel, while during the rest of the year it depends on whether one is particular.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Pappa's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Pappa's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rav Pappa's scenario: if a creeping animal touches the dough, on Pesach the dough interposes and prevents impurity from reaching the trough, while during the rest of the year it depends on one's concern.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on deaf dough
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on deaf dough
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that deaf dough (that did not rise) is forbidden if there is similar dough that leavened. The Gemara asks about the measure of time for leavening, and Rabbi Avahu in the name of Reish Lakish answers: the time to walk from Migdal Nunaya to Tiberias, which is a mil.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that deaf dough (which did not rise) is forbidden if there is similar dough that leavened.
The Gemara asks what the measure of time for leavening is when there is no similar dough for comparison.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Reish Lakish answers: the time to walk from Migdal Nunaya to Tiberias, which is a mil.
The Gemara clarifies that the teaching is not merely that the measure is a mil, but that the measure of a mil is defined as the distance from Migdal Nunaya to Tiberias.

items.text: Distances for various halakhot
items.text_en: Distances for various halakhot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Reish Lakish states that for kneading, prayer, and hand-washing the distance is four mil. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that Ayvu said this, and one of the four is for the process of tanning, as taught in a Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Reish Lakish states that for kneading, prayer, and hand-washing the distance is four mil.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that Ayvu said this, and one of the four distances is for the process of tanning, as taught in a Mishnah citing Rabbi Inyiai in the name of Rabbi Yannai.

items.text: Distinction between before and after prayer
items.text_en: Distinction between before and after prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina says that the four-mil distance applies only before prayer, but after prayer one does not return even for a mil. Rav Acha adds that a mil is the threshold: less than a mil one returns.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina and Rav Acha
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina and Rav Acha
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina limits the rule to before the traveler, but after he has passed, even a mil he does not return; Rav Acha adds that less than a mil he does return.
Rav Acha clarifies that a mil is the threshold: less than a mil one returns, but a mil or more one does not return.

items.text: Mishnah on separating challah in impurity on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah on separating challah in impurity on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says not to name the challah until it is baked; Ben Beteira says to cast it into cold water; Rabbi Yehoshua begins his opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks how one separates challah in impurity on Yom Tov, and begins to present the opinions of Rabbi Eliezer, Ben Beteira, and Rabbi Yehoshua.
Rabbi Eliezer rules that one should not designate the challah by name until it is baked.
Ben Beteira rules that one should cast the challah into cold water.
Rabbi Yehoshua begins his opinion, which continues beyond the section boundary.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one separates terumah from a dough that might become chametz, it is not considered chametz subject to bal yera'eh; rather, one sets it aside until evening, and if it leavens, it leavens.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that dough designated for terumah is not subject to the prohibitions of chametz; one sets it aside until evening, and if it leavens, it leavens.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara first suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua is about whether טובת הנאה (the right to designate the priest) is considered money. It then rejects this and explains that both agree it is not money, and the dispute is about the principle of "ho'il": Rabbi Eliezer holds we say "ho'il" (since he could revoke the designation, it is considered his money), while Rabbi Yehoshua holds we do not say "ho'il".

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua is about whether טובת הנאה (the right to designate the priest) is considered money.

The Gemara rejects the suggestion, explaining that both agree טובת הנאה is not money, and the dispute is about the principle of הוֹאִיל (since he could revoke the designation, it is considered his money).

items.text: Dispute about baking on Yom Tov for a weekday
items.text_en: Dispute about baking on Yom Tov for a weekday
items.desc_en: An explicit dispute is cited: Rav Chisda says one who bakes on Yom Tov for a weekday is lashed, because we do not say "ho'il" (since guests might come, it is fit for them). Rabbah says he is not lashed, because we do say "ho'il".

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites an explicit dispute: Rav Chisda says one who bakes on Yom Tov for a weekday is lashed, Rabbah says he is not lashed.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Chisda's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Chisda's position
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda holds he is lashed because we do not invoke the principle of הוֹאִיל (since guests might come, it is fit for them).
Rabbah holds he is not lashed because we do invoke the principle of הוֹאִיל.

items.text: Rabbah's challenge and Rav Chisda's response
items.text_en: Rabbah's challenge and Rav Chisda's response
items.desc_en: Rabbah challenges Rav Chisda: according to you who does not say "ho'il", how can we bake on Yom Tov for Shabbat? Rav Chisda answers: through an eruv tavshilin. Rabbah objects: do we permit a Torah prohibition through an eruv tavshilin? Rav Chisda explains that baking for Shabbat is permitted by Torah law, and the rabbis only decreed a prohibition lest one bake for a weekday; the eruv tavshilin serves as a reminder.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah challenges Rav Chisda: according to your view that we do not invoke the principle of הוֹאִיל (since it could be used for guests), how can we bake on Yom Tov for Shabbat?
Rav Chisda answers: baking for Shabbat is permitted through an עירוב תבשילין (eruv tavshilin).
Rabbah objects: do we permit a Torah prohibition through an eruv tavshilin?
Rav Chisda resolves: by Torah law, Shabbat needs may be prepared on Yom Tov; the rabbis only decreed a prohibition lest one bake for a weekday, and the eruv tavshilin serves as a reminder (היכרא).

items.text: Objection from the case of a dangerously ill animal
items.text_en: Objection from the case of a dangerously ill animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a dangerously ill animal: one may slaughter it only if there is enough time to eat an olive's worth from it before Yom Tov, even if one does not intend to eat it. This supports Rabbah's view ("ho'il") but challenges Rav Chisda. Rav Chisda answers that it is due to financial loss, and the Gemara objects that financial loss does not permit a Torah prohibition. Rav Chisda explains that due to financial loss, one resolves in his heart to eat an olive's worth, and an olive's worth of meat requires slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a dangerously ill animal, which permits slaughter only if one could eat an olive's worth from it before Yom Tov, even if one does not intend to eat; this supports Rabbah's view ("ho'il") but challenges Rav Chisda.
Rav Chisda answers that the permission is due to financial loss, and the Gemara objects that financial loss does not permit a Torah prohibition.
Rav Chisda resolves that due to financial loss, one resolves in his heart to eat an olive's worth, and an olive's worth of meat requires slaughter.

items.text: Beginning of next sugya: Lechem HaPanim
items.text_en: Beginning of next sugya: Lechem HaPanim
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new topic, citing a baraita about Lechem HaPanim (the showbread), which will be discussed further.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens a new sugya by citing a baraita about Lechem HaPanim (the showbread), which will be discussed further.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Passover offering is eaten by nine, ten, or eleven people depending on the calendar, and concludes that it does not override Shabbat or Yom Tov. The Gemara questions why Yom Tov is not overridden if Yom Tov needs for Shabbat are permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for how many people eat the Passover offering depending on the calendar, and concludes that it does not override Shabbat or Yom Tov.
The Gemara questions why the Passover offering does not override Yom Tov, given that Shabbat needs may be performed on Yom Tov.

items.text: First answer: Distant vs. near shevut
items.text_en: First answer: Distant vs. near shevut
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that a near shevut (Shabbat-related work) is permitted on Yom Tov, but a distant shevut (work for after Shabbat) is not permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that a nearby שבות (prohibition of rabbinic rest) was permitted, but a distant one was not.

items.text: Challenge from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says the offering overrides Yom Tov but not a fast day, what can be said? The Gemara explains that they disagree: one holds that near shevut is permitted but distant is not, and the other holds that even distant shevut is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says the offering overrides Yom Tov but not a fast day, what can be said to explain the Mishnah's ruling?
The Gemara resolves that the two positions disagree: one holds that near shevut is permitted but distant is not, and the other holds that even distant shevut is permitted.

items.text: Objection from the Two Loaves and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the Two Loaves and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Mari objects from the Two Loaves, which are not eaten less than two or more than three, and questions why if Yom Tov needs for Shabbat are permitted, the Two Loaves baked on Yom Tov for after Shabbat should be permitted. The Gemara answers that the Two Loaves are different because the verse says 'for you' and not for the Most High.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari objects from the Two Loaves (שתי הלחם), which are not eaten less than two or more than three, arguing that if Yom Tov needs for Shabbat are permitted, then baking the Two Loaves on Yom Tov for after Shabbat should also be permitted, yet the mishnah shows it is not.
The Gemara resolves that the Two Loaves are different because the verse says 'לָכֶם' (for you) and not for the Most High (לגבוה), so the permission for human needs does not apply to Temple offerings.

items.text: Challenge from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on Two Loaves
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on Two Loaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says the offering overrides Yom Tov, would say about the Two Loaves. It answers that he holds like Abba Shaul, who interprets 'for you' as excluding non-Jews.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what can be said according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that the Passover offering overrides Yom Tov.
The Gemara answers that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds like Abba Shaul, who interprets 'לָכֶם' as excluding non-Jews, not the Most High.

items.text: Question about the principle of 'Ho'il'
items.text_en: Question about the principle of 'Ho'il'
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda sends a message to Rabbah via Rav Acha bar Rav Huna asking whether we say the principle of 'Ho'il' (since if one is permitted to do something for one purpose, it is permitted for another), citing a baraita about plowing a single furrow that incurs eight prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda sends a message to Rabbah via Rav Acha bar Rav Huna, questioning whether the principle of 'הוֹאִיל' (since) is applied, citing a baraita about plowing a single furrow that incurs eight prohibitions.

items.text: Initial objection to "Ho'il" from plowing on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Initial objection to "Ho'il" from plowing on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if we apply the principle of "Ho'il" (since plowing could be used for covering the blood of a bird, it should be permitted on Yom Tov), then one should not be liable for plowing on Yom Tov. This challenges the Mishnah's ruling that plowing is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if the principle of הוֹאִיל (since plowing could be used for covering the blood of a bird) applies, then one should not be liable for plowing on Yom Tov, challenging the Mishnah's ruling.

items.text: First resolution: plowing with sharp stones
items.text_en: First resolution: plowing with sharp stones
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel answers that the Mishnah refers to plowing with sharp stones ("avanim mekurzalot"), which are not fit for covering blood. The Gemara objects that they are fit for pounding, but pounding is permitted on Yom Tov if done indirectly. The Gemara then suggests "tzunma" (a type of soil), but notes that it is a seedbed and the underlying loose dirt would be fit for covering. Mar bar Rav Ashi finally suggests "tina" (mud), which is not fit for covering, and the Gemara clarifies it is "metuneta" (soft mud).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel answers that the Mishnah's case of plowing on Yom Tov involves sharp stones (אבנים מקורזלות), which are not fit for covering blood.
The Gemara objects that these stones are fit for pounding, which is a permitted use on Yom Tov.
The Gemara answers that pounding on Yom Tov is permitted only if done indirectly (כלאחר יד), so the stones are not fully fit for that use.
The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah refers to plowing with 'צונמא' (hard soil), which is not fit for covering blood.
The Gemara objects that 'צונמא' is a seedbed, meaning it is fit for planting.
The Gemara answers that the 'צונמא' is on top, with loose soil (עפר תיחוח) underneath.
The Gemara objects that the underlying loose soil would itself be fit for covering blood, undermining the exemption.
Mar bar Rav Ashi resolves that the Mishnah refers to plowing with 'טינא' (mud), which is not fit for covering blood.
The Gemara objects that mud is also a seedbed, fit for planting.
The Gemara clarifies that it is 'מתונתא' (soft mud), which is not fit for planting or covering blood.

items.text: Second objection: cooking the sciatic nerve in milk on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Second objection: cooking the sciatic nerve in milk on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Abaye raises an objection from a baraita: one who cooks the sciatic nerve (gid hanasheh) in milk on Yom Tov and eats it incurs five lashes, including one for the prohibited act of kindling (hav'arah). If we apply "Ho'il," the kindling should be permitted since the fire could be used for his own needs, so he should not be liable for that lash.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects from a baraita: one who cooks the sciatic nerve in milk on Yom Tov and eats it is liable for five lashes, but if הוֹאִיל applied, he should not be liable for the burning, since the fire is needed for his own purposes.

items.text: First answer to Abaye: replace kindling with sciatic nerve of a neveilah
items.text_en: First answer to Abaye: replace kindling with sciatic nerve of a neveilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers: remove the case of kindling and instead include the sciatic nerve of a neveilah (carcass), which is prohibited by itself, thus maintaining five lashes without relying on "Ho'il."

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the baraita should be emended: remove the liability for burning and insert the sciatic nerve of a neveila (carcass) instead.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Chiya's baraita
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Chiya's baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi Chiya taught that one incurs two lashes for eating and three for cooking. If the answer were correct, there should be three lashes for eating (including the neveilah prohibition), but the baraita states only two.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Chiya's baraita states one is liable for two lashes for eating and three for cooking, but if the emendation were correct, it should be three for eating as well.

items.text: Second answer: replace kindling with muktzeh wood
items.text_en: Second answer: replace kindling with muktzeh wood
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers a new answer: remove the case of kindling and instead include muktzeh wood (wood set aside, prohibited on Yom Tov). The Gemara questions whether muktzeh is a Torah prohibition, and answers yes, based on the verse "And on the sixth day they shall prepare that which they bring" and the prohibition "You shall do no work."

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a new answer: remove the case of kindling (הבערה) from the list of lashes and instead include wood that is מוקצה (set aside, prohibited on Yom Tov).
The Gemara questions whether מוקצה (set-aside) is a Torah prohibition, since the list of lashes requires Torah-level prohibitions.

The Gemara answers that מוקצה is indeed a Torah prohibition, citing the verse 'וְהָיָה בַּיּוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי וְהֵכִינוּ' (And on the sixth day they shall prepare) and deriving the warning from 'לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה כׇל מְלָאכָה' (You shall do no work).

items.text: Challenge from Rav Chisda's ruling on a sheep from the fold
items.text_en: Challenge from Rav Chisda's ruling on a sheep from the fold
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous answer by citing a ruling from Rav Chisda (or Rav Huna) about bringing a sheep from the fold (afar) and slaughtering it as the daily offering (tamid) on Yom Tov. The ruling states that only a regular sheep is permitted, not a firstborn, tithe, or hybrid (palgas), implying that muktzeh is not a Torah prohibition. This undermines the answer that muktzeh wood is a Torah prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous answer by citing a question asked of Rav Chisda (or Rav Huna) about bringing a sheep from the fold (אפר) and slaughtering it as the daily offering (תמיד) on Yom Tov.
The ruling states that only a regular sheep (שה) is permitted, excluding a firstborn (בכור).
The ruling further excludes the animal tithe (מעשר).
The ruling also excludes a hybrid animal (פלגס), implying that muktzeh is not a Torah prohibition, which undermines the previous answer.

items.text: Derivation of the prohibition of libations from untithed produce
items.text_en: Derivation of the prohibition of libations from untithed produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the biblical source for the prohibition of bringing libations from untithed produce, deriving it from the phrase "from the drink of Israel" meaning from what is permitted to Israel. It also derives the principle that orlah is nullified in 200 parts from the phrase "from the two hundred".

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the phrase 'מִן הַמָּאתַיִם' (from the two hundred) that orlah (fruit of a tree in its first three years) is nullified in a mixture of one part in two hundred.
The Gemara derives from the phrase 'מִמַּשְׁקֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל' (from the drink of Israel) that libations may only be brought from produce permitted to Israel, thus excluding untithed produce (טֶבֶל).

items.text: Distinguishing between prohibition due to the object itself and due to another factor
items.text_en: Distinguishing between prohibition due to the object itself and due to another factor
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether one might think that libations from set-aside produce are also prohibited, but distinguishes: tevel is prohibited due to its own essence, while set-aside produce is prohibited due to another factor. It then proposes an alternative: exclude burning and include wood of an asherah, with the warning from the verse "and nothing of the banned item shall cling to your hand".

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possibility: one might think that libations may not be brought from set-aside produce (מוקצה).
The Gemara distinguishes: tevel is prohibited due to its own essence (איסור גופו), while set-aside produce is prohibited due to another factor (איסור דבר אחר).
The Gemara objects: if set-aside prohibition is biblical, why distinguish between intrinsic and extrinsic prohibition?
The Gemara further rejects the distinction, citing the principle that there is division of labors for Shabbat but not for Yom Tov.
The Gemara resolves: exclude burning (הבערה) and include wood of an asherah (עצי אשירה), with a warning from the verse 'וְלֹא יִדְבַּק בְּיָדְךָ מְאוּמָה מִן הַחֵרֶם'.

items.text: Alternative derivation: wood of an asherah or consecrated wood
items.text_en: Alternative derivation: wood of an asherah or consecrated wood
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava suggests that one should also be liable for bringing an asherah into one's house. The Gemara then proposes another alternative: exclude burning and include consecrated wood, with the warning from the verse "and their asherahs you shall burn with fire... you shall not do so to the Lord your God".

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Abaye why one should not also be liable for bringing an asherah into one's house, citing the verse prohibiting bringing an abomination into one's home.
The Gemara rejects the proposal and instead suggests excluding burning and including consecrated wood, with the warning derived from the verse prohibiting doing to God what is done to asherahs.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the principle of "ho'il"
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the principle of "ho'il"
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asserts that the dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbah is actually the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the principle of "ho'il" (since it is permitted, it is considered as if it were done). Rav Pappa and Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi each qualify the positions, suggesting that the dispute may be limited to specific cases.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asserts that the dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbah corresponds to the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the principle of הוֹאִיל (since it is permitted, it is considered as if it were done).
Rav Pappa qualifies that Rabbi Eliezer's application of הוֹאִיל may be limited to cases where each loaf is fit for the owner himself, not where it is only fit for guests.
Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi qualifies that Rabbi Yehoshua's rejection of הוֹאִיל may be limited to cases where no loaf is fit for anyone, not where it is fit for guests.
