items.text: Discussion between Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zeira about accepting the tradition
items.text_en: Discussion between Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zeira about accepting the tradition
items.desc_en: The rabbis stated the tradition before Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zeira. Rabbi Yirmeya accepted it, but Rabbi Zeira did not. Rabbi Yirmeya argued that since it was stated in the name of a great man, it should be accepted. Rabbi Zeira countered with a baraita where Rabbi Yehoshua remained silent, implying he did not rely on "ho'il". Rabbi Yirmeya responded that Rabbi Eliezer also remained silent in a baraita but responded in a Mishnah, so silence is not conclusive.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis stated the tradition before Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zeira; Rabbi Yirmeya accepted it, but Rabbi Zeira did not.
Rabbi Yirmeya argued that since the tradition was stated in the name of a great man (גברא רבה), it should be accepted.
Rabbi Zeira objected, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehoshua remained silent instead of invoking the principle of 'הואיל' (since it is permitted), implying he did not rely on it.
Rabbi Yirmeya countered that Rabbi Eliezer also remained silent in a baraita but responded in a Mishnah, so silence is not conclusive; the same could apply to Rabbi Yehoshua.

items.text: The measure of dough for Passover and the dispute about quantities
items.text_en: The measure of dough for Passover and the dispute about quantities
items.desc_en: A baraita records that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules like Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Yitzchak rules like ben Beteira. The Gemara then discusses the measure of dough: Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says for wheat it is two kav, for barley three kav; Rabbi Natan says the reverse. A contradiction is resolved by distinguishing between poor and good quality grain. Rav Pappa notes that poor wheat is worse relative to good wheat than poor barley is to good barley. Rav states that a kav of logna is for Passover and for challah.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules like Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Yitzchak rules like ben Beteira.
The Gemara asks what is the measure of dough, and cites the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Natan.
The Gemara objects with a contradictory baraita that gives different measures, and resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between poor and good quality grain.
Rav Pappa notes that poor wheat is worse relative to good wheat than poor barley is to good barley.
Rav states that a kav of logna is the measure for Passover and for challah.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's measure for challah
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's measure for challah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'five quarters and more' refers to a specific measure, and that even a kav of mulyagnai (a type of measure) is subject to the same threshold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's measure 'five quarters and more' for challah liability also applies to a kav of mulyagnai (a specific type of measure).

items.text: Women's practice of baking small loaves for Passover and the dispute about combining them
items.text_en: Women's practice of baking small loaves for Passover and the dispute about combining them
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef notes that women bake small loaves (kefiza) for Passover, but Abaye objects that this leniency might lead to a stringency by exempting them from challah. Rav Yosef defends the practice as following Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that a basket combines loaves for challah. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi limits this to Babylonian loaves that touch, but Rabbi Chanina extends it even to cakes.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef observes that the women in his locale customarily bake small loaves (קְפִיזָא) for Passover.
Abaye objects that this practice, though intended as a leniency (לחומרא), actually leads to a stringency by exempting the dough from the obligation of חלה (priestly portion).
Rav Yosef defends the practice by citing Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that a basket (סל) combines loaves for חלה, and Rav Yehuda's report that Shmuel ruled the הלכה follows Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.text: Abaye's further objection via Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Abaye's further objection via Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Abaye counters that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi limited Rabbi Eliezer's ruling to Babylonian loaves that touch each other, but not to cakes (עכין) like these small loaves.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's resolution via Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's resolution via Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the objection by citing Rabbi Chanina, who extends Rabbi Eliezer's ruling even to cakes (עכין).

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about a flat board without rims
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about a flat board without rims
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether a flat board without rims (tavla she'ein lah levizbizin) can combine dough for challah, questioning whether the interior of a vessel is required or just the airspace of a vessel. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks about a flat board without rims (לְבִזְבְּזִין) whether it combines dough for challah, questioning if the interior of a vessel is required or just the airspace of a vessel.
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved with 'תֵּיקוּ' (let it stand).

items.text: Baraita: Dispute about what combines dough for challah
items.text_en: Baraita: Dispute about what combines dough for challah
items.desc_en: A baraita records the opinions of Rabbi Eliezer (a basket combines), Rabbi Yehoshua (an oven combines), and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (only Babylonian loaves that touch each other combine).

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites three positions: Rabbi Eliezer says the basket combines, Rabbi Yehoshua says the oven combines, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says only touching Babylonian loaves combine.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that only Babylonian loaves that touch each other combine for the חלה (challah) obligation.

items.text: Mishnah: Three women baking together and Rabbi Akiva's rule
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three women baking together and Rabbi Akiva's rule
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabban Gamliel's view that three women may knead and bake one after another in one oven, while the Sages say they should work simultaneously (one kneads, one rolls, one bakes). Rabbi Akiva adds that not all women, wood, or ovens are equal; the rule is: if the dough rises, cool it with cold water.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel rules that three women may knead and bake one after another in a single oven.
The Sages require the three women to work simultaneously—one kneads, one rolls, one bakes—to prevent the dough from leavening.
Rabbi Akiva states that not all women, wood, or ovens are equal; the general rule is: if the dough rises, cool it with cold water.

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of the women's work sequence
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of the women's work sequence
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the Sages' method: one woman kneads while another cuts, then they rotate roles, and as long as they are busy with the dough, it does not become leavened.

sub.desc_en: A baraita elaborates the Sages' method: one woman kneads while another cuts the dough, and as long as they are occupied with the dough, it does not become leavened.
The Gemara concludes that as long as the women are continuously occupied with the dough, it does not become leavened.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's dispute with Rabban Gamliel
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's dispute with Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Rabbi Akiva asked Rabban Gamliel whether the rule applies to diligent or non-diligent women, moist or dry wood, hot or cold ovens. Rabban Gamliel replied that only the general rule applies: if the dough rises, cool it with cold water.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Rabbi Akiva asked Rabban Gamliel whether the rule depends on the type of women, wood, or oven, and Rabban Gamliel replied that only the general rule applies: if the dough rises, knead it with cold water.

items.text: Mishnah: Definitions of si'ur and siduk
items.text_en: Mishnah: Definitions of si'ur and siduk
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that si'ur (incipient leavening) must be burned, but one who eats it is exempt; siduk (cracked leavening) must be burned, and one who eats it is liable to karet. Rabbi Yehuda defines si'ur as like locust horns, siduk as cracks that intermingle. The Sages say both are liable to karet, and si'ur is when the dough's face pales like a person whose hair stands on end.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the basic rule: si'ur (incipient leavening) is burned and the eater is exempt, while siduk (cracked leavening) is burned and the eater is liable to karet.
Rabbi Yehuda defines si'ur as like locust horns and siduk as cracks that intermingle.
The Sages argue that both si'ur and siduk render the eater liable to karet, and define si'ur as when the dough's face pales like a person whose hair stands on end.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages on si'ur and siduk
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages on si'ur and siduk
items.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Meir's definitions (si'ur: pale face; siduk: locust horns) and the Sages' definitions (si'ur: locust horns; siduk: intermingled cracks). The Gemara notes that our Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who exempts for si'ur, but for Rabbi Meir both are liable to karet. Rava explains Rabbi Meir's reasoning: every crack on top has many cracks underneath.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Meir's definitions: si'ur is a pale face like a person whose hair stands on end, and siduk is like locust horns.
The baraita then records the Sages' opposing definitions: si'ur is like locust horns, and siduk is when cracks are intermingled.
The baraita concludes that according to Rabbi Meir, one who eats either si'ur or siduk is liable to karet.
The Gemara notes a contradiction: our Mishnah rules that one who eats si'ur is exempt, following Rabbi Yehuda, whereas Rabbi Meir holds both are liable.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's exemption applies only according to Rabbi Yehuda, but for Rabbi Meir both si'ur and siduk incur karet.
Rava explains Rabbi Meir's reasoning: every visible crack on the surface has many cracks underneath, so si'ur is already a form of siduk.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Removing chametz on Shabbat eve
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Removing chametz on Shabbat eve
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute about when to remove chametz when the 14th of Nisan falls on Shabbat. Rabbi Meir says to remove it before Shabbat, the Sages say at its proper time (the 14th), and Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok distinguishes between terumah (before Shabbat) and chullin (at its proper time).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of the 14th of Nisan falling on Shabbat and presents Rabbi Meir's position that one must remove all chametz before Shabbat.
The Sages counter that chametz is removed at its proper time, i.e., on the 14th itself.
Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok distinguishes between terumah (removed before Shabbat) and chullin (removed at its proper time).

items.text: Gemara: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok
items.text_en: Gemara: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok's father acted according to his view: when the 14th fell on Shabbat, they removed chametz before Shabbat, following the instruction of Zunin, the appointee of Rabban Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok's father acted according to his view: when the 14th fell on Shabbat, they removed chametz before Shabbat, following the instruction of Zunin, the appointee of Rabban Gamliel.

items.text: Mishnah: One who remembers chametz while going to perform a mitzvah
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who remembers chametz while going to perform a mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one is on the way to perform a mitzvah (slaughter the Pesach, circumcise his son, eat a betrothal meal) and remembers chametz at home, he should return if possible; otherwise, he nullifies it in his heart. It also discusses cases of rescue from danger and returning from Jerusalem with sacred meat, with a dispute about the minimum measure for returning.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for one going to perform a mitzvah who remembers chametz at home: if possible, return and remove it; otherwise, nullify it in his heart.
The Mishnah adds that for rescue from danger or for a voluntary Shabbat rest, one nullifies in his heart or returns immediately.
The Mishnah gives a parallel case of one who left Jerusalem with sacred meat and remembers it: if past the lookout point, burn it in place; otherwise, return and burn it before the Temple.

The Mishnah records a dispute about the minimum measure for returning: Rabbi Meir says both sacred meat and chametz require a כביצה (egg-sized) amount, Rabbi Yehuda says both require a כזית (olive-sized) amount, and the Sages distinguish: sacred meat requires a כזית and chametz requires a כביצה.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction about the betrothal meal and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction about the betrothal meal and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says one who goes to eat a betrothal meal may return if he remembers chametz, but another source says he must return immediately. Rabbi Yochanan resolves this by attributing the views to Rabbi Yehuda (who considers it reshus) and Rabbi Yosei (who considers it a mitzvah). Rav Chisda adds that the dispute is only about the second meal, but the first meal is a mitzvah for all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says one going to a betrothal meal may return only if possible, but another source says he must return immediately.

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah's lenient view to Rabbi Yehuda (who considers the meal רשות (optional)) and the strict view to Rabbi Yosei (who considers it a מצוה (commandment)).

Rav Chisda adds that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei applies only to the second betrothal meal, while the first meal is a מצוה (commandment) for all, allowing even Rabbi Yehuda's view to be reconciled with both sources.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei on betrothal vs. gifts
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei on betrothal vs. gifts
items.desc_en: A baraita records that Rabbi Yehuda only heard of a betrothal meal (as a mitzvah), not a gift meal, while Rabbi Yosei heard both are included.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that he only heard of a betrothal meal (סעודת אירוסין) as a mitzvah, not a gift meal (סיבלונות).
Rabbi Yosei responds that he heard both the betrothal meal and the gift meal are included as mitzvot.

items.text: Aggadic teachings: Meals of reshus and marrying into Torah families
items.text_en: Aggadic teachings: Meals of reshus and marrying into Torah families
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that a Torah scholar should not benefit from a meal that is not a mitzvah. Rabbi Yochanan gives examples (e.g., a kohen's daughter marrying an Israelite). The Gemara discusses the consequences of such marriages and the importance of marrying into Torah scholar families, with stories about Rabbi Yehoshua, Rav Idi bar Avin, and others. It concludes with warnings about excessive feasting and the disgraceful names given to those who indulge.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon's ruling that a Torah scholar may not benefit from any meal that is not a mitzvah meal.
The Gemara asks for examples of such non-mitzvah meals.
Rabbi Yochanan gives examples: a kohen's daughter marrying an Israelite, or a Torah scholar's daughter marrying an ignoramus.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that the match of a kohen's daughter to an Israelite does not succeed.
The Gemara asks what the bad outcome of such a match is.
Rav Chisda says the woman becomes either a widow, a divorcee, or childless.
A baraita adds that the match leads to one burying the other or bringing the husband to poverty.
The Gemara objects: Rabbi Yochanan himself said that one who wants wealth should attach to Aaron's descendants, as Torah and priesthood enrich.
The Gemara resolves: the negative outcome applies when the husband is an ignoramus, but when he is a Torah scholar, the match is beneficial.
A story: Rabbi Yehoshua married a kohen's daughter and fell ill, saying Aaron would not be pleased to have such a son-in-law.

sub.text: Story about Rav Idi bar Avin
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Idi bar Avin
sub.desc_en: A story: Rav Idi bar Avin married a kohen's daughter and produced two ordained sons; Rav Pappa says he would not have become wealthy without marrying a kohen's daughter.
Rav Kahana says he would not have gone into exile without marrying a kohen's daughter, though the Gemara notes he did go to a place of Torah, just not a full exile.
Rabbi Yitzchak states that anyone who benefits from a voluntary meal will eventually go into exile, citing the verse about feasting leading to exile.

A baraita warns that a Torah scholar who overindulges in feasting will destroy his home, widow his wife, orphan his children, forget his learning, cause disputes, and bring a bad name for generations.
The Gemara asks what disgraceful name such a scholar is called.
Abaye, Rava, Rav Pappa, and Rav Shemayah each give a different derogatory nickname for such a scholar, such as 'son of the oven-heater' or 'son of the kneader of bowls'.

items.text: Baraitot: Marrying into Torah scholar families
items.text_en: Baraitot: Marrying into Torah scholar families
items.desc_en: Two baraitot teach that one should sell everything to marry a daughter of a Torah scholar or marry his daughter to a Torah scholar, using the metaphor of grapes on a vine versus grapes on a thornbush. The opposite is discouraged.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita teaches that one should sell everything to marry a daughter of a Torah scholar, ensuring his children become scholars, and avoid marrying an ignoramus's daughter.

The second baraita repeats the advice and adds a metaphor: marrying a Torah scholar's daughter is like grapes on a vine (beautiful and accepted), while marrying an ignoramus's daughter is like grapes on a thornbush (ugly).

items.text: Opening Tosefta on marrying into Torah scholars
items.text_en: Opening Tosefta on marrying into Torah scholars
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that a person should sell everything to marry the daughter of a Torah scholar, and if not possible, progressively lower standards, but never marry the daughter of an am ha'aretz, who are described as abominable.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches the hierarchy of desirable marriage partners, culminating in the prohibition against marrying the daughter of an am ha'aretz, who are compared to abominable creatures.

items.text: Rabbi's statement: am ha'aretz forbidden to eat meat
items.text_en: Rabbi's statement: am ha'aretz forbidden to eat meat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi states that an am ha'aretz is forbidden to eat meat of an animal or bird, based on the verse 'This is the Torah of the beast and the bird', implying only those who engage in Torah may eat meat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules that an am ha'aretz (ignoramus) is forbidden to eat meat of a beast or bird, based on the verse 'This is the Torah of the beast and the bird' — only one who engages in Torah may eat meat.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar: am ha'aretz may be stabbed on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar: am ha'aretz may be stabbed on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says an am ha'aretz may be stabbed on Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat; his students suggest slaughtering, but he explains the difference in blessing requirements.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that an am ha'aretz (ignoramus) may be stabbed on Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat.
Rabbi Elazar's students object, suggesting he should say 'slaughter him' rather than 'stab him'.
Rabbi Elazar explains that slaughter requires a blessing (ברכה) while stabbing does not, so stabbing is preferable for an am ha'aretz.

items.text: Further harsh statements about amei ha'aretz
items.text_en: Further harsh statements about amei ha'aretz
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says one should not travel with an am ha'aretz, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says it is permitted to tear him open like a fish, with Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak adding 'from his back'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that it is forbidden to travel with an am ha'aretz, citing the verse about Torah being one's life.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that it is permitted to tear an am ha'aretz open like a fish.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak adds that the tearing should be done from the back.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's past hatred for Torah scholars
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's past hatred for Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva recalls that when he was an am ha'aretz, he wished to bite a Torah scholar like a donkey; his students suggest 'like a dog', but he explains the difference in bone-breaking.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva recalls that when he was an am ha'aretz, he wished to bite a Torah scholar like a donkey.
Rabbi Akiva's students object, suggesting he should have said 'like a dog' rather than 'like a donkey'.
Rabbi Akiva explains the difference: a donkey bites and breaks bone, while a dog bites without breaking bone.

items.text: More tannaitic statements on amei ha'aretz
items.text_en: More tannaitic statements on amei ha'aretz
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir compares marrying a daughter to an am ha'aretz to throwing her before a lion; Rabbi Eliezer says without business dealings they would kill us; Rabbi Chiya says engaging in Torah before an am ha'aretz is like violating his betrothed; and a baraita states the hatred of amei ha'aretz for Torah scholars exceeds that of nations for Israel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir compares marrying a daughter to an am ha'aretz to throwing her before a lion, as both tear and eat without shame.
Rabbi Eliezer states that without business dealings with amei ha'aretz, they would kill the scholars.
Rabbi Chiya compares engaging in Torah before an am ha'aretz to violating his betrothed, based on a homiletic reading of 'מוֹרָשָׁה' (inheritance) as 'מְאוֹרָסָה' (betrothed).
A baraita states that the hatred of amei ha'aretz for Torah scholars exceeds that of nations for Israel, and their wives' hatred is even greater.

items.text: Six things said about amei ha'aretz
items.text_en: Six things said about amei ha'aretz
items.desc_en: A baraita lists six restrictions regarding amei ha'aretz: no testimony, no secrets, no guardianship, no traveling together, and some add no announcement of lost items. The Gemara explains the first Tanna's view: perhaps a worthy child will emerge and eat it.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists six restrictions regarding amei ha'aretz (ignoramuses): no testimony, no secrets, no guardianship, no traveling together, and some add no announcement of lost items.

The Gemara explains why the first Tanna omitted the restriction about lost items: perhaps a worthy child will emerge from the am ha'aretz and eat it, citing the verse 'יָכִין וְצַדִּיק יִלְבַּשׁ' (the righteous will wear what the wicked prepared).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on returning lost items
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on returning lost items
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a dispute about the measure for returning lost items: Rabbi Meir holds it is a ke'beitzah (egg-sized), Rabbi Yehuda holds it is a ke'zayit (olive-sized). Rabbi Yochanan says the positions are reversed from another dispute. Abaye explains that in the other case they argue over verses, here over reasoning: Rabbi Meir compares return to impurity (ke'beitzah), Rabbi Yehuda does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that Rabbi Meir considers a ke'beitzah (egg-sized) measure significant and Rabbi Yehuda considers a ke'zayit (olive-sized) measure significant, then raises a contradiction from a baraita where their positions are reversed regarding zimmun.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by stating that the positions are reversed between the two disputes.
Abaye rejects the reversal and explains that in the zimmun dispute they argue over verses (ke'zayit vs. ke'beitzah), while here they argue over reasoning.
Abaye concludes that here they argue over reasoning: Rabbi Meir compares the return of lost items to impurity (ke'beitzah), while Rabbi Yehuda does not make that comparison.

items.text: Gemara's opening question on the measure of return
items.text_en: Gemara's opening question on the measure of return
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that just as the prohibition of eating the Pesach offering is measured by an olive's bulk, so too its return (if lost) must be measured by an olive's bulk. A baraita cites Rabbi Nathan who says the measure is two egg-bulks, but the Sages disagree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that just as the prohibition of eating the Pesach offering is measured by an olive's bulk, so too its return (if lost) must be measured by an olive's bulk.
A baraita cites Rabbi Nathan who says the measure is two egg-bulks, but the Sages disagree.

items.text: Interpretations of 'light precious and congealed'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'light precious and congealed'
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse from Zechariah about light that is precious in this world but congealed in the next. Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi offer different explanations, with the latter relating a story about his son's near-death vision of the World to Come, where the righteous are reversed in status and Torah scholars are privileged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the verse 'light precious and congealed' from Zechariah.
Rabbi Elazar explains that the verse refers to light that is precious in this world but congealed (unavailable) in the World to Come.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse as referring to the laws of negaim (skin afflictions) and ohalot (tent impurity), which are precious in this world but congealed in the next.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets the verse as referring to people who are precious in this world but congealed in the next, and relates a story about his son's near-death vision of the World to Come where the righteous are reversed in status.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's son's report
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's son's report
sub.desc_en: The son reports hearing that one who comes to the World to Come with his Torah learning in hand is fortunate, and that those killed by the kingdom (martyrs) have a unique status.
The Gemara questions who these martyrs are, rejecting Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues as the sole example, and concludes they are the martyrs of Lod (the Lydda martyrs).

items.text: Interpretation of 'bells of the horse' and related verses
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'bells of the horse' and related verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse about the bells of the horse being holy to God. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Yochanan offer different interpretations. The Gemara then reconciles these with other verses about vessels in the Temple and the absence of a Canaanite, concluding that 'Canaanite' means merchant, supported by prooftexts from Genesis and Hosea.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the verse about the bells of the horse being holy to God and asks what 'bells of the horse' means.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets that the Holy One will expand Jerusalem so much that a horse runs and perspires.
Rabbi Elazar interprets that all bells hung on a horse between its eyes will be holy to God.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets that all spoils Israel plunders until a horse runs and perspires will be holy to God.

The Gemara reconciles Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation with the verse about vessels in the Temple, and explains that for the other two interpretations the verse about vessels refers to a different matter of Israel's wealth.
The Gemara reconciles Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation with the verse about no Canaanite in the Temple, and Rabbi Yirmeya explains that 'Canaanite' means there will be no poor person.
The Gemara proves that 'Canaanite' means merchant, citing a verse from Genesis and a verse from Hosea, with Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish providing the proof.

items.text: The oneness of God and His Name in the World to Come
items.text_en: The oneness of God and His Name in the World to Come
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how God is not already one. Rabbi Acha bar Chanina explains that in this world, blessings differ for good and bad news, but in the World to Come, all blessings will be 'the Good and the Beneficent'. Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that God's Name is written with Yod-Hei but pronounced with Alef-Dalet in this world, but in the World to Come it will be pronounced as written.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the verse 'God will be one' by asking whether God is not already one in this world.
Rabbi Acha bar Chanina explains that in this world, blessings differ for good and bad news, but in the World to Come, all blessings will be 'the Good and the Beneficent'.
The Gemara questions the phrase 'His Name will be one' by asking whether His Name is not already one in this world.
Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that in this world, God's Name is written with Yod-Hei but pronounced with Alef-Dalet, but in the World to Come it will be pronounced as written.

items.text: Rava's attempt and Rabbi Avina's resolution on God's Name
items.text_en: Rava's attempt and Rabbi Avina's resolution on God's Name
items.desc_en: Rava intended to expound the verse in public, but an old man told him it is written 'le-olam' (with a vav) meaning hidden. Rabbi Avina resolves a contradiction between verses: God says He is written with Yod-Hei but read with Alef-Dalet, indicating a distinction between His written and spoken Name in this world.

sub.desc_en: Rava intended to expound the verse about God's Name being one in a public lecture.
An old man objected that the verse is written 'לעלם' (with a vav), meaning hidden, so the exposition should not be publicized.
Rabbi Avina resolves a contradiction between verses: God says His Name is written with Yod-Hei but read with Alef-Dalet, indicating a distinction between His written and spoken Name in this world.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter and opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter and opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter with 'Hadran alach Elu Ovrin' and begins the new Mishnah, which discusses the local custom regarding work on Passover eve until noon, and the rule for one traveling between places with different customs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter with 'Hadran alach' and begins the new Mishnah about local customs regarding work on Passover eve and the rule for one traveling between places with different customs.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one should not change from the custom of not working on the eve of Passover after midday, even to avoid dispute. It gives a parallel example regarding seventh-year produce.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one must not deviate from local custom regarding work on the eve of Passover, and gives a parallel example of seventh-year produce.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that the same principle applies in the reverse direction as well.

items.text: Gemara's question and distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question and distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies the eve of Passover, as working on other eves is also problematic. It distinguishes the eve of Passover by the stricter prohibition starting from midday and the imposition of a ban.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifically mentions the eve of Passover, since a baraita prohibits work on the eves of Shabbat and festivals from the afternoon onward.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's prohibition begins at midday, stricter than the baraita's afternoon cutoff, and also includes excommunication, not just loss of blessing.
The Gemara gives a second answer: on other eves one merely does not see a sign of blessing, but no ban is imposed, whereas on Passover eve a ban is also imposed.

items.text: Baraita on working on eves
items.text_en: Baraita on working on eves
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that one who works on the eve of Shabbat or festivals from mincha onwards will never see a sign of blessing. It also includes other times of potential sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the full baraita about one who works on the eves of Shabbat and festivals from the afternoon onward, and on other occasions involving sin, never seeing a sign of blessing.

items.text: Four types of workers
items.text_en: Four types of workers
items.desc_en: The Sages teach about four types: the diligent who is rewarded, the diligent who is penalized, the lazy who is rewarded, and the lazy who is penalized. Rava applies this to the women of Mehoza.

sub.desc_en: A baraita classifies four types of people regarding work on Shabbat and its eve: the diligent who gain, the diligent who lose, the lazy who gain, and the lazy who lose.
Rava comments that the women of Meḥoza, who do not work on the eve of Shabbat due to indulgence, are still classified as 'lazy who gain'.

items.text: Rava's resolution of verses on God's kindness
items.text_en: Rava's resolution of verses on God's kindness
items.desc_en: Rava resolves a contradiction between two verses about God's kindness, explaining that one refers to those who act for the sake of heaven and the other to those who act not for its sake. He cites Rav Yehuda that one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, as this leads to doing them for their own sake.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises a contradiction between two verses about the greatness of God's kindness, resolving that one refers to those who act for its own sake (לִשְׁמָהּ) and the other to those who act not for its own sake.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav teaches that one should always engage in Torah and commandments even not for their own sake, because from not for their own sake one comes to do them for their own sake.

Rava supports his resolution with Rav Yehuda's teaching in the name of Rav: one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, because from doing them not for their own sake one comes to do them for their own sake.

items.text: On the reward of one's wife and mill
items.text_en: On the reward of one's wife and mill
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that one who anticipates the reward of his wife or his mill will never see a sign of blessing. However, if the wife works and sells, the verse praises her.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one who expects payment from his wife's work or from a mill never sees a sign of blessing.
The Gemara explains that 'payment of his wife' refers to her weaving, and 'mill' to its rental fee, but if she works and sells, Scripture praises her.
The baraita concludes that if the wife works and sells her product, Scripture praises her, citing the verse 'סָדִין עָשְׂתָה וַתִּמְכֹּר' (she made a garment and sold it).

items.text: On merchants of reeds and jars
items.text_en: On merchants of reeds and jars
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that one who profits from reeds and jars will never see a sign of blessing because their abundance attracts the evil eye. Similarly, certain other traders are also not blessed.

sub.desc_en: A baraita says that one who profits from reeds and jugs never sees a sign of blessing.
The Gemara explains the reason: because their containers are numerous, the evil eye prevails over them.
Another baraita lists market traders, raisers of small cattle, cutters of good trees, and those who set their eyes on a beautiful portion as never seeing a sign of blessing.
The Gemara explains the reason: because people gaze at them (with envy).

items.text: Four items without a sign of blessing
items.text_en: Four items without a sign of blessing
items.desc_en: The Sages list four items that never have a sign of blessing: wages of scribes, translators, orphans, and money from overseas. The Gemara explains each reason, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that the Great Assembly decreed fasts so that scribes of sacred texts would not become wealthy, lest they stop writing.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists four types of wages that never receive a sign of blessing: scribes, translators, orphans, and money from overseas.
The Gemara explains the reasons for three of the four items: translator's wages appear like Shabbat wages, orphans' money cannot be forgiven, and overseas money depends on a rare miracle.
The Gemara asks why scribes' wages are included in the list.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that the Great Assembly decreed fasts so that scribes of sacred texts would not become wealthy and stop writing.
A baraita adds that scribes, their dealers, and all who engage in heavenly work never see a sign of blessing unless they act לִשְׁמָהּ (for its own sake).

items.text: Custom of the people of Beyshan
items.text_en: Custom of the people of Beyshan
items.desc_en: The people of Beyshan had a custom not to travel from Tyre to Sidon on the eve of Shabbat. Their children asked Rabbi Yochanan to permit them, but he refused, citing the verse about not forsaking the tradition of one's parents.

sub.desc_en: The people of Beishan had a custom not to travel from Tyre to Sidon on the eve of Shabbat; their children came before Rabbi Yochanan and asked to be released from this custom.

Rabbi Yochanan responds that the ancestors already accepted the custom upon themselves, citing the verse 'Listen, my son, to the discipline of your father, and do not forsake the Torah of your mother.'
Rabbi Yochanan refuses to permit them, citing the verse 'Listen, my son, to the discipline of your father, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother' to justify upholding ancestral custom.

items.text: Custom of the people of Chozai regarding challah
items.text_en: Custom of the people of Chozai regarding challah
items.desc_en: The people of Chozai had a custom to separate challah from rice. They asked Rav Yosef, who said to let a non-Jew eat it in their presence. Abaye objected, citing the principle that if something is permitted but others treat it as forbidden, one should not act leniently in public.

sub.desc_en: The people of Chozai had a custom to separate חלה (the priestly portion of dough) from rice; they came before Rav Yosef, who said to let a non-priest eat it in their presence.
Abaye objects by citing the principle that regarding matters which are permitted but others have adopted as forbidden, one may not permit them in their presence.
Rav Yosef rules that a non-Jew should eat the challah in their presence, allowing them to circumvent the custom without violating it publicly.
Abaye objects by citing the principle that if something is permitted but others treat it as forbidden, one should not act leniently in public.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the earlier dispute about Samaritans
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the earlier dispute about Samaritans
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that Rav Chisda's statement about Samaritans applies to all who are stringent, but Rav Ashi distinguishes based on whether the majority eat rice or grain, determining whether a priest may eat challah in their presence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Chisda's statement about Samaritans applies to all who are stringent, suggesting that the same reasoning of 'they are accustomed to the stringency' applies to others as well.

Rav Ashi distinguishes based on whether the majority of the local population eats rice or grain, determining whether a priest may eat challah in their presence to avoid confusion between חיוב (obligation) and פטור (exemption).

items.text: Proofs from baraitot about local customs
items.text_en: Proofs from baraitot about local customs
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings three baraitot about bathing, wearing sandals, and sitting on benches, where people refrained from permitting what was customarily forbidden, and concludes that the principle applies even to non-Samaritans in places where rabbis are not common.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the core principle: things that are permitted but others treat as forbidden, you may not permit in their presence.
Rav Chisda restricts the principle to Samaritans (כותים), who are known to be strict.
The Gemara objects: does the principle apply only to Samaritans? It cites a baraita about two brothers bathing together in Kabul, where the townspeople rebuked them.
The baraita recounts that Judah and Hillel, sons of Rabban Gamliel, bathed together in Kabul, and the entire province rebuked them; Hillel slipped away rather than tell them it was permitted.

A second baraita: wearing sandals (קורדקיסון) on Shabbat is permitted generally but forbidden in Beiri; Judah and Hillel wore them there, were rebuked, and gave them to their slaves rather than permit it.

A third baraita: sitting on benches of gentiles on Shabbat is permitted generally but forbidden in Akko; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel sat on one there, was rebuked, and slid to the ground rather than permit it.
The Gemara concludes that the principle applies even to non-Samaritans in places where rabbis are not commonly found, as they are like Samaritans in their stringency.

items.text: Explanation of the prohibitions in the baraitot
items.text_en: Explanation of the prohibitions in the baraitot
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasons for the stringencies: sitting on benches of gentiles appears like business, wearing sandals might lead to carrying in public domain, and bathing together is forbidden due to the decree against bathing with one's wife's brother, with an exception for a student who needs his teacher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why sitting on gentiles' benches and wearing sandals are forbidden: the former appears like business, the latter might lead to carrying in the public domain.

The Gemara asks why bathing together is forbidden, and cites a baraita that prohibits bathing with one's father, father-in-law, mother's husband, and sister's husband, with Rabbi Yehuda permitting the father.

The Gemara resolves that the people of the place decreed against two brothers bathing together due to the concern about bathing with a sister's husband, and adds a baraita that a student may not bathe with his teacher unless the teacher needs him.

items.text: Story of Rabbah bar bar Chanah and the principle of local customs
items.text_en: Story of Rabbah bar bar Chanah and the principle of local customs
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah ate a permitted food in a place where it was forbidden, and when confronted, Abaye ruled that the visitors were treated like Samaritans. The Gemara questions whether Rabbah violated the rule of adopting the stringencies of both the place he left and the place he went to, and Abaye distinguishes between traveling from Babylonia to Israel and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah came and ate a permitted food (דְּאַיִּיתְרָא), and when Rav Avira Saba and Rabbah bar Rav Huna visited, he covered it from them.

sub.text: Rav Avira Saba and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's report to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Avira Saba and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's report to Abaye
sub.desc_en: They reported the incident to Abaye, who ruled that they are treated like Samaritans (כותים) regarding the prohibition of permitting the food in their presence.
The Gemara asks: Does Rabbah bar bar Chanah not accept the rule that one must adopt the stringencies of both the place he left and the place he went to?

Abaye answers: That rule applies only when traveling from Babylonia to Babylonia, from Israel to Israel, or from Babylonia to Israel, but not from Israel to Babylonia, because we (in Babylonia) are subordinate to them (the sages of Israel) and follow their customs.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation and Rabbah bar bar Chanah's ruling to his sons
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation and Rabbah bar bar Chanah's ruling to his sons
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the rule applies only when one does not intend to return, but Rabbah intended to return. Rabbah bar bar Chanah then instructs his sons not to eat the food in his presence or absence, relying on Rabbi Yochanan's authority only for himself, and the Gemara notes a contradiction in his own practice.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that even when traveling from Eretz Yisrael to Bavel, the rule of חומרי המקום (stringencies of the place) applies only when one does not intend to return, but Rabbah bar bar Chanah intended to return.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's instruction to his sons
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's instruction to his sons
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah instructs his sons not to eat the food in his presence or absence, relying on Rabbi Yochanan's authority only for himself.
The Gemara notes a contradiction in Rabbah bar bar Chanah's own practice, as he himself once relied on a local custom.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah recounts a story where he followed Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Yosi ben Lakonya into a garden, showing his own reliance on local practice.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's leniency on cabbage sefichin and the dispute with the Sages
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's leniency on cabbage sefichin and the dispute with the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts an incident where Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai ate cabbage sefichin and permitted his son to eat only in his presence. It then cites the Tosefta where Rabbi Shimon permits all sefichin except cabbage, while the Sages forbid all sefichin. Both opinions are based on Rabbi Akiva's derivation from a verse. The dispute is whether we decree against cabbage sefichin because of other sefichin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts an incident where Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai ate cabbage sefichin (ספיחי כרוב) and permitted his son to eat only in his presence, citing his own authority.
The Gemara cites a Tosefta where Rabbi Shimon permits all sefichin (ספיחים) except cabbage, while the Sages forbid all sefichin.

The Gemara explains that both opinions are based on Rabbi Akiva's derivation from the verse 'הֵן לֹא נִזְרָע וְלֹא נֶאֱסֹף' (they are not sown and we will not gather), which implies that sefichin (ספיחים) are forbidden.

The Gemara resolves the dispute: the Sages decree against cabbage sefichin (ספיחי כרוב) because of other sefichin, while Rabbi Shimon does not decree against cabbage sefichin because of other sefichin.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling for one traveling from a place that does work to a place that does not
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling for one traveling from a place that does work to a place that does not
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling: if one goes from a place that does work to a place that does not, he must take on the stringencies of the destination and not change due to dispute. But if he goes from a place that does not do work to a place that does, why not change and do work? The Mishnah already said he must take on the stringencies of both places.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one goes from a place that does work to a place that does not, the Mishnah's ruling that he must take on the stringencies of the destination and not change due to dispute is understandable.

The Gemara objects: but if one goes from a place that does not do work to a place that does, why does the Mishnah say not to change due to dispute? It already requires taking on the stringencies of both places, so doing work would violate the stringency of the origin.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's resolution of the Mishnah's apparent contradiction
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's resolution of the Mishnah's apparent contradiction
items.desc_en: Abaye says the Mishnah's second clause refers to the first case (going from a place that does work to one that does not). Rava says it always refers to the second case (going from a place that does not do work to one that does), and the Mishnah means there is no concern for changing due to dispute because onlookers will say there are many idle people in the market.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the Mishnah's contradiction by saying the second clause refers to the first case (going from a place that does work to one that does not).

Rava resolves the contradiction by saying the second clause always refers to the second case (going from a place that does not do work to one that does), and the Mishnah means there is no concern for changing due to dispute because onlookers will say there are many idle people in the market.

items.text: Rav Safra's question to Rabbi Abba about those who know the fixed month
items.text_en: Rav Safra's question to Rabbi Abba about those who know the fixed month
items.desc_en: Rav Safra asks Rabbi Abba about people like themselves who know the fixed month (i.e., the calendar), implying a question about the applicability of the Mishnah's rule to those who are knowledgeable.

sub.text: Rav Safra's question to Rabbi Abba
sub.text_en: Rav Safra's question to Rabbi Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav Safra asks Rabbi Abba about people like themselves who know the fixed month (i.e., the calendar), implying a question about the applicability of the Mishnah's rule to those who are knowledgeable.

items.text: Travel on the second festival day and the dispute about lashes vs. excommunication
items.text_en: Travel on the second festival day and the dispute about lashes vs. excommunication
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one may travel from a settled area to the desert on the second day of a festival. Rav Ami rules it is prohibited in settled areas but permitted in the desert. The story of Rav Nathan bar Asya traveling on Shavuot leads to a dispute between Rav Yosef and Abaye about whether lashes or excommunication is the appropriate penalty for a scholar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one may perform labor in the desert on the second festival day, given that in settled areas it is prohibited due to avoiding dispute.
Rav Ammi rules that in a settled area it is prohibited, but in the desert it is permitted.

The Gemara recounts that Rav Natan bar Asya traveled on the second day of Shavuot, and Rav Yosef excommunicated him; Abaye suggested flogging instead, but Rav Yosef explained that excommunication is more severe, as in Eretz Yisrael they vote to flog a Torah scholar but not to excommunicate him.

An alternative version states that Rav Yosef flogged him; Abaye then suggested excommunication, citing Rav and Shmuel's ruling, but Rav Yosef responded that the ruling applies to ordinary people, not to a Torah scholar, and flogging is more appropriate for a scholar.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's statement on seventh-year produce
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's statement on seventh-year produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah about one who brings seventh-year produce from a place where it has not perished to a place where it has perished. It questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's ruling contradicts the principle that one must observe the stringencies of both the place he left and the place he went to. Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi explains that Rabbi Yehuda is discussing a different case: moving produce between two places where it has not perished, but hearing that it perished in his own place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's ruling in the mishnah contradicts the established principle that one must observe the stringencies of both the place he left and the place he went to.

Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi explains that Rabbi Yehuda is discussing a different case: moving produce between two places where it has not perished, but hearing that it perished in his own place, and Rabbi Yehuda rules leniently because the produce has not perished in the current location.

items.text: Is Rabbi Yehuda lenient or stringent?
items.text_en: Is Rabbi Yehuda lenient or stringent?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's statement is lenient, given that Rabbi Elazar said he only spoke stringently. It therefore reverses the mishnah's text: the first clause says he is not obligated to remove, and Rabbi Yehuda says to bring from where he brought them, implying they have perished there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's statement is lenient, given that Rabbi Elazar said he only spoke stringently.
The Gemara resolves by reversing the mishnah's text: the first clause says he is not obligated to remove, and Rabbi Yehuda says to bring from where he brought them, implying they have perished there.

items.text: Abaye's explanation: returning produce to its original place
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation: returning produce to its original place
items.desc_en: Abaye insists the mishnah is as originally taught, but explains the case: one moves produce from a place where it has not perished to a place where it has perished, then returns it to its original place where it still has not perished. In that case, he is not obligated to remove, but Rabbi Yehuda says to bring from where he brought them, implying they have perished there.

sub.desc_en: Abaye insists the mishnah is as originally taught, explaining that one moves produce from a place where it has not perished to a place where it has perished, then returns it to its original place where it still has not perished; in that case he is not obligated to remove, but Rabbi Yehuda says to bring from where he brought them, implying they have perished there.

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects to Abaye's explanation: does Rabbi Yehuda think the produce absorbed the prohibition from the air of the place? He instead connects the dispute to a Tannaitic debate about pickling three vegetables in one jar, where Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabban Gamliel disagree on when to remove each type.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects to Abaye's explanation, asking whether according to Rabbi Yehuda the produce absorbed the prohibition from the back of the donkey.
Rav Ashi instead connects the dispute to a Tannaitic debate about pickling three vegetables in one jar, citing the mishna where Rabbi Elazar says one may eat based on the first.
The mishna continues: Rabbi Yehoshua says one may eat based on the last, and Rabban Gamliel says each type is removed when its kind ceases from the field, with the halakha following Rabban Gamliel.

items.text: Ravina's alternative explanation and the final Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative explanation and the final Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Ravina connects the dispute to another Tannaitic debate about eating dates until the last ones in Zoar are gone, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel offering a different opinion. The daf ends mid-sentence.

sub.desc_en: Ravina introduces an alternative explanation, linking the dispute to a Tannaitic debate about eating dates until the last ones in Tzoar are gone.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel begins to state his differing opinion, but the daf ends mid-sentence.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may eat from the produce that grows on the stems between the dates (between the branches) but not from the produce that grows between the shoots (the stumps).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may eat produce from the stems between the dates (בין הכיפין) but not from the shoots between the stumps (בין השיצין).

items.text: Gemara's question and the source for the three lands
items.text_en: Gemara's question and the source for the three lands
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that there are three lands for biur: Judea, Transjordan, and Galilee, each subdivided into three. It asks for the scriptural source, and Rav Chama bar Ukva quoting Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina derives it from the verse 'and for your cattle and for the beast that is in your land' – as long as a wild animal eats from the field, feed the domesticated animal in the house; when the wild animal's food is gone, remove the domesticated animal's food. The Gemara adds that it is a tradition that the wild animals of one region do not feed on the produce of another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that there are three lands for biur: Judea, Transjordan, and Galilee, each subdivided into three, so that one may eat in each until the last produce in that region is gone.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of this rule.

sub.text: Rav Chama bar Ukva quoting Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Chama bar Ukva quoting Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Ukva in the name of Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina derives the rule from the verse 'וְלִבְהֶמְתְּךָ וְלַחַיָּה אֲשֶׁר בְּאַרְצֶךָ' (and for your cattle and for the beast that is in your land): as long as a wild animal eats from the field, feed the domesticated animal in the house; when the wild animal's food is gone, remove the domesticated animal's food.
The Gemara adds a tradition that the wild animals of one region do not feed on the produce of another, justifying the division into three lands.

items.text: Dispute about produce that left Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Dispute about produce that left Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that produce that left Eretz Yisrael for outside the land is biur wherever it is. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says it must return to its place for biur, because the verse says 'in your land'. The Gemara questions this, and resolves it by reading the verse as 'in the land' and 'in your land', or alternatively 'from that which is in your land'.

sub.desc_en: The Sages taught that produce that left Eretz Yisrael for outside the land is biur wherever it is.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says the produce must return to its place for biur, because the verse says 'in your land'.
The Gemara questions: but the verse already excluded it (from the land)?
The Gemara resolves by reading the verse as 'in the land' and 'in your land', or alternatively 'from that which is in your land'.

items.text: Rav Safra's incident and the ruling
items.text_en: Rav Safra's incident and the ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Safra left Eretz Yisrael with a skin of seventh-year wine. Rav Huna bar Rav Ika and Rav Kahana accompanied him. Rav Safra asked if they heard from Rabbi Avahu whether the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. Rav Kahana said Rabbi Avahu ruled in favor, while Rav Huna bar Rav Ika said he ruled against. Rav Safra advised to hold Rav Huna's version, as he was precise in learning from his teacher, citing an example about the Temple Mount.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra left Eretz Yisrael with a skin of seventh-year wine, accompanied by Rav Huna bar Rav Ika and Rav Kahana.
Rav Safra asked if anyone had heard from Rabbi Avahu whether the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
Rav Kahana reported that Rabbi Avahu ruled in favor of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Ika reported that Rabbi Avahu ruled against Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
Rav Safra advised to hold Rav Huna's version, as he was precise in learning from his teacher, citing an example about the Temple Mount and Rav Yosef's critique.

items.text: Rabbi Ila'i's action and the dispute about orlah
items.text_en: Rabbi Ila'i's action and the dispute about orlah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'i cut down palm branches of the seventh year. The Gemara questions this, as the Torah said 'for eating' not for destruction. It considers whether this applies only when fruit has set, but then cites Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha that the buds of orlah are forbidden because they are a guard for the fruit. The Gemara objects that guards become fruit only when the fruit is small, yet they are called fruit. Rav Nachman follows Rabbi Yossi, who says the blossom is forbidden as fruit, though the Sages disagree. Rav Shimi from Nehardea challenges whether the Sages disagree with Rabbi Yossi regarding all trees, citing a Mishnah about when not to cut trees in the seventh year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rabbi Ila'i cut down palm branches of the seventh year.
The Gemara objects: how could he do this, since the Torah said 'for eating' (לאכלה) and not for destruction?
The Gemara suggests that the prohibition applies only when fruit has already set, but not when it has not yet set.
The Gemara objects by citing Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha that the buds of ערלה (orlah) are forbidden because they become a guard for the fruit.
The Gemara questions: when do the buds become a guard? Only when the fruit is small, yet the baraita calls them 'fruit'.
The Gemara answers that Rav Nachman follows Rabbi Yossi, who rules that the blossom (סמדר) is forbidden as fruit, though the Sages disagree.
Rav Shimi from Nehardea challenges: do the Sages actually disagree with Rabbi Yossi regarding all trees?
Rav Shimi cites a Mishnah about when not to cut trees in the seventh year, where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree, implying the Sages do not universally reject Rabbi Yossi's view.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's terms for fruit stages
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's terms for fruit stages
items.desc_en: Rav Asi clarifies that 'boser' (unripe grapes) is the same as 'gerua' (the stage when grapes begin to ripen) and 'pol ha'lavan' (white beans). The Gemara questions the comparison to white beans and corrects that the measure is like a white bean. It then identifies that Rabbi Ila'i's version of the Mishnah resolves a contradiction about when trees produce fruit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi equates the terms 'boser' (unripe grapes), 'gerua' (the stage when grapes begin to ripen), and 'pol ha'lavan' (white beans).
The Gemara objects: how can 'boser' be literally 'pol ha'lavan' (white beans)?
The Gemara corrects: the measure of 'boser' is like the size of a white bean, not that it is a white bean.
The Gemara asks: who holds that 'boser' (unripe grapes) is the relevant stage but 'semadar' (blossom) is not? It answers: the Rabbis.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Ila'i's version of the Mishnah cuts off the clause about 'other trees', resolving the contradiction.

items.text: Baraita on the times for eating fruits
items.text_en: Baraita on the times for eating fruits
items.desc_en: A baraita lists the latest times for eating grapes, olives, figs, and dates based on their availability. Rabbi Eliezer adds a condition for olives to ensure the poor can find them. Rabbi Yehuda notes that the mention of 'paggei beit hinei' (early figs of Beit Hinei) is only relevant for tithing. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between dates from different locations.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating the latest time for eating grapes: until the last clusters are gone, and if later ones appear, one may eat them.
The baraita gives the time for olives until the last of Gush Chalav, with Rabbi Eliezer adding a condition to ensure the poor can find a quarter-log of oil.
The baraita states the time for figs (dried figs) until the early figs of Beit Hinei are gone.
Rabbi Yehuda clarifies that the mention of 'paggei beit hinei' (early figs of Beit Hinei) is only relevant for tithing, citing a mishnah that they are obligated in מעשר (tithe).
The baraita gives the time for dates until the last of Tzo'ar, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between dates from different locations (between the capers vs. between the thorns).

items.text: Reconciliation of conflicting baraitot on fruit seasons
items.text_en: Reconciliation of conflicting baraitot on fruit seasons
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the previous baraita and another that gives different deadlines for fruits (grapes until Passover, olives until Shavuot, etc.). Rav Bibi says Rabbi Yochanan would swap the last two. The Gemara offers two resolutions: either both deadlines are the same, or the second baraita explicitly allows eating if later fruits remain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the previous baraita and another baraita that gives different deadlines for fruits (grapes until Passover, olives until Shavuot, etc.).
Rav Bibi says Rabbi Yochanan would swap the last two items (grogrot and dates) in the second baraita to align with the first.
The Gemara offers a first resolution: both deadlines are actually the same measure (the festivals align with the fruit seasons).
The Gemara offers a second resolution: the first baraita explicitly allows eating if later fruits remain, so the deadlines are not absolute.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's signs for geographical features
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's signs for geographical features
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel provides signs: mountains have mails (a type of tree), valleys have palm trees, streams have reeds, and lowlands have sycamores. The Gemara derives practical halakhot from these signs: for first fruits (bikkurim) from the seven species, for the 'nachal eitan' (hard stream) in the red heifer ceremony, and for sales of land.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel provides signs for identifying geographical features: mountains have mails (a type of tree), valleys have palm trees, streams have reeds, and lowlands have sycamores, with a biblical support.
The Gemara derives a halakha for first fruits (ביכורים): one does not bring bikkurim from palm trees in the mountains or from fruits in valleys.
The Gemara derives a halakha for the 'nachal eitan' (hard stream) in the red heifer ceremony: reeds indicate a stream.
The Gemara derives a halakha for sales of land: sycamores indicate lowlands, and now that this is established, all these signs apply to sales.

items.text: Mishnah: Selling animals to non-Jews and eating roasted meat on Passover eve
items.text_en: Mishnah: Selling animals to non-Jews and eating roasted meat on Passover eve
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that selling small animals to non-Jews depends on local custom, but large animals may never be sold. Rabbi Yehuda permits selling broken animals, and Ben Betera permits selling horses. It also states that eating roasted meat on Passover eve depends on local custom.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that selling small animals to non-Jews depends on local custom, but large animals may never be sold.
Rabbi Yehuda permits selling broken large animals to non-Jews.
Ben Betera permits selling horses to non-Jews.
The Mishnah concludes with the rule that eating roasted meat on Passover eve depends on local custom.

items.text: Gemara: Prohibition against declaring meat for Passover
items.text_en: Gemara: Prohibition against declaring meat for Passover
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav forbids saying 'this meat is for Passover' because it appears as if one is consecrating his animal and eating sacrifices outside. Rav Pappa clarifies that this applies only to meat, not to wheat. The Gemara challenges this with a story about Todos of Rome who fed roasted kids on Passover eve, and the Sages threatened him with excommunication for causing Israel to eat sacrifices outside.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav forbids saying 'this meat is for Passover' because it appears as if one is consecrating his animal and eating sacrifices outside.
Rav Pappa clarifies that the prohibition applies specifically to meat, not to wheat, since wheat is merely being set aside for Passover use.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita about Todos of Rome, who fed roasted kids on Passover eve and was threatened with excommunication for causing Israel to eat sacrifices outside.
The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that the term 'קָדָשִׁים' (sacrifices) is problematic, and suggests a corrected reading.

items.text: Opening Mishnah discussion on vows
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah discussion on vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling about one who vows to bring a sacrifice outside the Temple, distinguishing between a praised and unpraised person. It clarifies that if the person is praised, the vow is valid regardless of specification; if unpraised, it depends on explicit mention.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling: if the person is praised (מקולס), the vow is valid; if not praised, it is invalid — but this seems to contradict the principle that a vow depends on explicit mention.
The Gemara answers: for a praised person, the vow is valid whether or not he specified; for an unpraised person, it is valid only if he specified explicitly.

items.text: Debate over the Mishnah's attribution: Rabbi Shimon or Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Debate over the Mishnah's attribution: Rabbi Shimon or Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rav Acha teaches the Mishnah according to Rabbi Shimon, but Rav Sheshet objects, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon exempts one who did not donate in the usual manner. Ravina challenges Rav Ashi, noting that Rava said Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Yosei's view that a person is bound by the completion of his words. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shimon holds like Rabbi Yosei, but not vice versa.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha teaches the Mishnah according to Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Sheshet objects: for one who teaches the Mishnah as Rabbi Yosei it is fine, but for one who teaches it as Rabbi Shimon, is it fine?
Rav Sheshet cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon exempts one who did not donate in the usual manner, contradicting the Mishnah's attribution.
Ravina challenges Rav Ashi: even for one who teaches it as Rabbi Yosei, is it fine? Rava said that Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Yosei's view that a person is bound by the completion of his words.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shimon holds like Rabbi Yosei, but not vice versa.

items.text: Story of Todos of Rome and the kal vachomer from frogs
items.text_en: Story of Todos of Rome and the kal vachomer from frogs
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether Todos of Rome was a great man or a violent one. It brings a teaching where Todos derived a kal vachomer from frogs: if frogs, which are not commanded about sanctifying God's name, entered ovens, then Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, who are commanded, should certainly do so. Rabbi Yosei bar Avin explains that Todos was a philanthropist who supported Torah scholars, citing Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that such a person merits a place in the heavenly academy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Todos of Rome was a great man or a violent one.
The Gemara brings a teaching where Todos derived a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from frogs to justify Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah entering the furnace.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin explains that Todos was a philanthropist who supported Torah scholars, citing Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that such a person merits a place in the heavenly academy.

items.text: Mishnah: Lighting candles on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Mishnah: Lighting candles on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in places where it is customary to light candles on the night of Yom Kippur, one lights; where not, one does not. However, candles are lit in synagogues, study halls, dark alleys, and for the sick.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: in a place where it is customary to light a lamp on Yom Kippur nights, one lights; where not, one does not; but one lights in synagogues, study halls, dark alleys, and for the sick.

items.text: Gemara: Both customs intend the same thing
items.text_en: Gemara: Both customs intend the same thing
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught that both those who say to light and those who say not to light intended the same thing. Rava expounded the verse 'Your people are all righteous' to show that both customs are for a single purpose.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught: both those who said to light and those who said not to light intended the same thing; Rava expounded the verse 'Your people are all righteous' to support this.
Rav Yehoshua reports that Rava expounded the verse 'Your people are all righteous' to show that both customs are for a single purpose.

items.text: Debate on blessing fire only at Havdalah and Yom Kippur candle lighting
items.text_en: Debate on blessing fire only at Havdalah and Yom Kippur candle lighting
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that one only blesses fire at the conclusion of Shabbat because that is when it was first created. An elder (or Rabbah bar bar Chanah) confirmed this from Rabbi Yochanan. Ulla, while riding, discussed with Rabbi Abba and Rabbah bar bar Chanah, clarifying that the ruling applies to Havdalah. He then cited a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar permits lighting on Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat for the honor of Shabbat, and Rabbi Yochanan agreed with the Sages who forbid it. Rav Yosef applied a verse about deep waters.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that one only blesses fire at the conclusion of Shabbat because that is when fire was first created.

sub.text: Elder (or Rabbah bar bar Chanah) citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Elder (or Rabbah bar bar Chanah) citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: An elder (or Rabbah bar bar Chanah) affirms Shmuel's ruling and adds that Rabbi Yochanan said the same.

sub.text: Ulla, Rabbi Abba, and Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.text_en: Ulla, Rabbi Abba, and Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.desc_en: Ulla, while riding, is accompanied by Rabbi Abba on his right and Rabbah bar bar Chanah on his left, and Rabbi Abba asks Ulla to confirm the ruling about blessing fire only at the conclusion of Shabbat.
Ulla turns and sees Rabbah bar bar Chanah looking displeased, so he clarifies that his statement was not directed at him but at another matter.

sub.text: Baraita citing Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Baraita citing Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: Ulla cites a baraita taught before Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar permits lighting a candle on Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat for the honor of Shabbat.
Rabbi Yochanan responds that the Sages forbid it, and Ulla concludes that the matter is settled.
Rav Yosef applies a verse about deep waters to the preceding discussion.

items.text: Opening statement: Ulla and Rabbah bar bar Chanah as 'deep waters' and 'man of understanding'
items.text_en: Opening statement: Ulla and Rabbah bar bar Chanah as 'deep waters' and 'man of understanding'
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets Proverbs 20:5, identifying 'deep waters' as Ulla and 'man of understanding' as Rabbah bar bar Chanah. It then cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one recites a blessing over fire both on Saturday night and on Yom Kippur night, and the people followed this practice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets Proverbs 20:5, identifying 'deep waters' as Ulla and 'man of understanding' as Rabbah bar bar Chanah.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one recites a blessing over fire both on Saturday night and on Yom Kippur night, and the people followed this practice.

items.text: Objection from a baraita: blessing over fire only on Saturday night
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita: blessing over fire only on Saturday night
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that one only blesses over fire on Saturday night because that is when fire was first created, and one blesses immediately upon seeing it. Rabbi Yehuda says to recite the blessings in order over the cup, and Rabbi Yochanan rules in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states one only blesses over fire on Saturday night because that is when fire was first created, and one blesses immediately upon seeing it.
Rabbi Yehuda states that one recites the blessings in order over the cup of wine.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.

items.text: Resolution: distinction between fire that rested and fire from wood/stone
items.text_en: Resolution: distinction between fire that rested and fire from wood/stone
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the baraita that restricts blessing to Saturday night refers to fire that rested (i.e., was kindled before the Sabbath), while the earlier statement allowing blessing on Yom Kippur night refers to fire produced from wood and stones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between fire that rested (kindled before the Sabbath) and fire produced from wood and stones.

items.text: Contradiction between baraitot on fire from wood/stone
items.text_en: Contradiction between baraitot on fire from wood/stone
items.desc_en: Two baraitot conflict: one says one blesses over fire from wood/stone, the other says one does not. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between Saturday night (where one blesses) and Yom Kippur night (where one does not).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a contradiction between two baraitot: one says one blesses over fire from wood/stone, the other says one does not.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between Saturday night (where one blesses) and Yom Kippur night (where one does not).

items.text: Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya: scattering and gathering blessings
items.text_en: Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya: scattering and gathering blessings
items.desc_en: Rabbi would scatter the blessings (not reciting them in order), while Rabbi Chiyya would gather them. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi says that even though Rabbi scattered them, he would later recite them in order over the cup to fulfill the obligation for his household.

sub.desc_en: The stam reports that Rabbi would scatter the blessings (not reciting them in order), while Rabbi Chiyya would gather them (reciting them in order).
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi resolves the apparent contradiction: even though Rabbi scattered the blessings, he would later recite them in order over the cup to fulfill the obligation for his household.

items.text: Challenge: was fire created on Saturday night? The ten things created at twilight
items.text_en: Challenge: was fire created on Saturday night? The ten things created at twilight
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether fire was created on Saturday night, citing a baraita listing ten things created at twilight on the eve of the first Sabbath, which does not include fire. Rabbi Nechemya adds fire and the mule, Rabbi Yoshiya adds the ram and the shamir, and Rabbi Yehuda adds the tongs, arguing that tongs must have been created by Heaven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether fire was created on Saturday night, citing a baraita listing ten things created at twilight on the eve of the first Sabbath, which does not include fire.
