Rabbi Nechemya adds fire and the mule to the list of ten things created at twilight.
Rabbi Yoshiya adds the ram and the shamir to the list.
Rabbi Yehuda adds the tongs, arguing that tongs must have been created by Heaven since they require tongs to make.
The Gemara objects that tongs could be made by a mold, so they are a human creation, not necessarily heavenly.

items.text: Resolution: our fire vs. Gehinnom fire; Gehinnom created before the world
items.text_en: Resolution: our fire vs. Gehinnom fire; Gehinnom created before the world
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that 'our fire' was created on Saturday night, while Gehinnom's fire was created on Friday. But a baraita says seven things were created before the world, including Gehinnom. The Gemara answers that Gehinnom itself was created before the world, but its fire was created on Friday.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between 'our fire' (created on Saturday night) and Gehinnom's fire (created on Friday).
The Gemara objects that a baraita lists Gehinnom among seven things created before the world, contradicting its creation on Friday.
The Gemara answers that Gehinnom itself was created before the world, but its fire was created on Friday.

items.text: Challenge: Gehinnom's fire created on Monday?
items.text_en: Challenge: Gehinnom's fire created on Monday?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Gehinnom's fire was created on Monday, citing Rabbi Yosei that fire created on Monday has no quenching, and Rabbi Bena'ah that 'ki tov' was not said on Monday because Gehinnom's fire was created then. Rabbi Elazar says it was included in the general 'good' on the sixth day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the claim that Gehinnom's fire was created on the eve of Shabbat.
Rabbi Yosei states that the fire created on Monday (the second day) has no quenching, citing a verse.
Rabbi Bena'ah explains that 'ki tov' was not said on Monday because Gehinnom's fire was created then.
Rabbi Elazar resolves that although 'ki tov' was not said on Monday, it was included in the general 'good' on the sixth day.

items.text: Final resolution: Gehinnom before the world, its fire on Monday, our fire on Saturday night
items.text_en: Final resolution: Gehinnom before the world, its fire on Monday, our fire on Saturday night
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes: Gehinnom itself was created before the world, its fire on Monday, and our fire was contemplated for creation on Friday but only created on Saturday night. Rabbi Yosei describes how Adam brought two stones and produced fire, and two animals to produce a mule. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the mule existed in the days of Anah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Gehinnom's space was created before the world, its fire on Monday, and our fire was contemplated for creation on Friday eve but only created at the end of Shabbat.

Rabbi Yosei cites a baraita that two things were contemplated for creation on Friday eve but only created at the end of Shabbat: Adam brought two stones and produced fire, and two animals to produce a mule.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel argues that the mule already existed in the days of Anah, citing the verse 'הוּא עֲנָה אֲשֶׁר מָצָא אֶת הַיֵּמִם בַּמִּדְבָּר' (he is Anah who found the mules in the wilderness).

items.text: Darshei Chamurot: Anah was a bastard
items.text_en: Darshei Chamurot: Anah was a bastard
items.desc_en: The 'Darshei Chamurot' say Anah was a bastard, as his father Tziv'on had relations with his mother. Rava (or Rav Pappa) refutes the possibility of two Anahs by citing the verse 'hu Anah' (he is the same Anah).

sub.desc_en: The Darshei Chamurot claim that Anah was a bastard, because his father Tziv'on had relations with his mother, as derived from the verses listing Tziv'on's sons.
The gemara objects: perhaps there were two different individuals named Anah, so the inference of bastardy is not necessary.
Rava (or according to some, Rav Pappa) refutes the objection by citing the verse 'הוּא עֲנָה' (he is the same Anah), proving there was only one Anah.

items.text: Baraita: ten things created at twilight (repeated with additions)
items.text_en: Baraita: ten things created at twilight (repeated with additions)
items.desc_en: The baraita listing the ten things created at twilight is repeated, with some adding Aaron's staff, demons, and the ram of Abraham.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma lists the ten things created at twilight on the eve of Shabbat.
Some add Aaron's staff with its almonds and blossoms to the list.
Some add demons to the list of things created at twilight.
Some add the ram of Abraham to the list, though the text is cut off.

items.text: Opening statement about Adam's garment
items.text_en: Opening statement about Adam's garment
items.desc_en: The daf begins with a brief statement about the garment of Adam, likely a continuation from the previous page.

sub.desc_en: The daf opens with a brief statement about the garment of Adam, likely continuing from the previous page.

items.text: Seven and three hidden things
items.text_en: Seven and three hidden things
items.desc_en: Two baraitot list things hidden from people (seven items) and things that were created or should have been created (three items).

sub.desc_en: The first baraita lists seven things hidden from people: day of death, day of consolation, depth of judgment, what is in a friend's heart, one's profit, when the Davidic kingdom will return, and when the oppressive kingdom will end.

The second baraita lists three things that arose in thought to be created, and if they had not been created it would be fitting that they be created: that a corpse should decompose, that a corpse should be forgotten from the heart, and that produce should rot.
Some say that a fourth item should have been created: that coinage should go out of circulation.

items.text: Mishnah: Work on Tisha b'Av
items.text_en: Mishnah: Work on Tisha b'Av
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the custom regarding work on Tisha b'Av varies by location, and Torah scholars are always idle. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says one should always act like a Torah scholar.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the custom regarding work on Tisha b'Av varies by location.
The Mishnah adds that Torah scholars are always idle on Tisha b'Av.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says one should always act like a Torah scholar and refrain from work.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on Tisha b'Av in Babylonia
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on Tisha b'Av in Babylonia
items.desc_en: Shmuel says there is only one public fast in Babylonia: Tisha b'Av. The Gemara questions this based on Shmuel's own view that twilight on Tisha b'Av is permitted, and resolves it by distinguishing between twilight and nightfall.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that the only public fast in Babylonia is Tisha b'Av.
The Gemara questions whether Shmuel's ruling implies that twilight on Tisha b'Av is forbidden, given his own statement that it is permitted.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between twilight (בֵּין הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת) and nightfall (מִשֶּׁחָשֵׁיכָה), explaining that the Mishnah's phrase 'from while it is still day' excludes nightfall, not twilight.

items.text: Support for Shmuel from a baraita
items.text_en: Support for Shmuel from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the only difference between Tisha b'Av and Yom Kippur is that the former's uncertainty is permitted. The Gemara initially thinks this refers to twilight, but Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi explains it refers to the uncertainty of the new moon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that a baraita supports Shmuel's position, as it states that the only difference between Tisha b'Av and Yom Kippur is that the former's uncertainty is permitted.
The Gemara asks whether the permitted uncertainty refers to twilight (בין השמשות), which would support Shmuel's ruling.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi explains that the permitted uncertainty refers to the uncertainty of the new moon's establishment (whether the previous month was full or deficient), not to twilight.

items.text: Rava's ruling on pregnant and nursing women
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on pregnant and nursing women
items.desc_en: Rava rules that pregnant and nursing women fast and complete the fast on Tisha b'Av like Yom Kippur, and twilight is forbidden. The Gemara questions this from Rabbi Yochanan's statement that Tisha b'Av is not like a public fast, and resolves it by saying the difference is regarding work.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that pregnant and nursing women fast and complete the fast on Tisha b'Av like Yom Kippur, and twilight is forbidden.
The Gemara notes that the same ruling was stated in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan actually said this, given his statement that Tisha b'Av is not like a public fast.
The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Yochanan's statement that Tisha b'Av is not like a public fast.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that Rabbi Yochanan's statement refers to work, not to twilight.

items.text: Further analysis of Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.text_en: Further analysis of Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the explanation that Rabbi Yochanan meant work, citing the Mishnah. It then offers alternative explanations: regarding Ne'ilah prayer, regarding 24 hours, and Rav Pappa says it means Tisha b'Av is like the later fasts (which are stricter).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the explanation that Rabbi Yochanan meant work, citing the Mishnah that work on Tisha b'Av depends on local custom and even Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel does not prohibit it.
The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Yochanan meant Tisha b'Av is not like a public fast regarding Ne'ilah prayer, but then objects with Rabbi Yochanan's own statement that one should pray all day.

The Gemara resolves that regarding Ne'ilah, on Yom Kippur it is an obligation while on Tisha b'Av it is optional, and alternatively suggests Rabbi Yochanan meant Tisha b'Av is not like a public fast regarding the 24-hour duration.
Rav Pappa says that Rabbi Yochanan meant Tisha b'Av is not like the earlier fasts (which are lenient) but like the later fasts (which are strict), and thus it is prohibited.

items.text: Challenges and support for Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Challenges and support for Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that seems to support Shmuel, but Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi explains it refers to the new moon. This supports Rabbi Elazar who says one may not put a finger in water on Tisha b'Av like Yom Kippur. Another baraita compares Tisha b'Av to a public fast, but Rav Pappa notes a difference regarding washing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita that distinguishes Tisha b'Av from Yom Kippur only regarding the status of doubtful time, implying a difference in בין השמשות (twilight).

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi explains that the baraita's distinction refers to the uncertainty of the new moon's declaration, not to twilight, and for all other matters Tisha b'Av and Yom Kippur are equal.
The Gemara notes that this explanation supports Rabbi Elazar's ruling that one may not put a finger in water on Tisha b'Av, just as on Yom Kippur.
The Gemara raises another baraita that compares Tisha b'Av to a public fast, noting a difference regarding washing, which seems to contradict Rabbi Elazar's strict position.
Rav Pappa begins to resolve the contradiction, but his full statement is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Opening statement on the Mishnah's style
items.text_en: Opening statement on the Mishnah's style
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Tanna teaches leniencies in the Mishnah, implying a pattern of ruling leniently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara observes that the Tanna teaches leniencies (קוּלֵּי) in the Mishnah, implying a pattern of ruling leniently.

items.text: Contradiction between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages regarding יוהרא
items.text_en: Contradiction between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages regarding יוהרא
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages are consistent in their concern for יוהרא (haughtiness), citing a Mishnah about a groom reciting Shema. Rabbi Yochanan suggests the positions are reversed, while Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between work and recitation, and between the need for intention.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages are consistent in their concern for יוהרא (haughtiness), citing a Mishnah about a groom reciting Shema.
Rabbi Yochanan suggests that the positions of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages are reversed.
Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between work and recitation, and between the need for intention.

Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi further explains that the groom's case involves intention, so refraining from recitation appears haughty, while in the Mishnah about work, refraining appears as a lack of work, not haughtiness.

items.text: Mishnah: Work on Erev Pesach in Judah and Galilee
items.text_en: Mishnah: Work on Erev Pesach in Judah and Galilee
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in Judah work was done until noon on Erev Pesach, but in Galilee not at all. At night, Beit Shammai prohibit work while Beit Hillel permit it until dawn.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that in Judah work was done until noon on Erev Pesach, in Galilee not at all, and at night Beit Shammai prohibit work while Beit Hillel permit it until dawn.

items.text: Contradiction between custom and prohibition in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Contradiction between custom and prohibition in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah first describes a custom (minhag) but later implies a prohibition. Rabbi Yochanan resolves this by attributing the first view to Rabbi Meir (who sees it as custom) and the second to Rabbi Yehuda (who sees it as prohibition), citing a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Mishnah can first describe a custom (minhag) and then imply a prohibition.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by attributing the first view to Rabbi Meir (custom) and the second to Rabbi Yehuda (prohibition).
A baraita is cited showing Rabbi Yehuda's position that the practice in Judah and Galilee is a prohibition, while Rabbi Meir treats it as a custom.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yehuda's view from a baraita on planting
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yehuda's view from a baraita on planting
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehuda's view that work is prohibited on the fourteenth, citing a baraita where he permits planting on the thirteenth but not the fourteenth. Rava answers that the baraita was taught in Galilee, where work is prohibited entirely. Rav Sheishet and Rav Ashi offer alternative resolutions, and Ravina introduces the principle of 'a portion of the day is like the whole day' (מקצת היום ככולו).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehuda's view that work is permitted on the fourteenth, citing a baraita where he allows planting only on the thirteenth but not the fourteenth.
The Gemara elaborates the contradiction: if the fourteenth were permitted, why limit planting to the thirteenth, given Rabbi Yehuda's rule that grafting takes three days to take root?
Rava answers that the baraita was taught in Galilee, where work is prohibited entirely on the fourteenth.
The Gemara objects that even in Galilee, the night of the fourteenth is permitted according to Beit Hillel, so the baraita's prohibition of planting on the fourteenth remains problematic.
Rav Sheishet answers that the baraita follows Beit Shammai, who prohibit work on the night of the fourteenth.
Rav Ashi answers that the baraita can even follow Beit Hillel, because people do not normally weed at night, so the prohibition on the fourteenth effectively covers the day only.

Ravina answers that the baraita is in Judea, and the principle of מקצת היום ככולו (a portion of the day is like the whole day) applies only once, not twice, so planting on the fourteenth would require two such applications and is therefore prohibited.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Meir and the Sages on work on the fourteenth
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Meir and the Sages on work on the fourteenth
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Meir's view that work begun before the fourteenth may be completed, but not started anew. The Sages permit three specific trades (tailors, barbers, launderers) to work until noon, and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds shoemakers.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Meir's view that work begun before the fourteenth may be completed but not started anew, the Sages permit three trades until noon, and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds shoemakers.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry: Work for the festival vs. not for the festival
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry: Work for the festival vs. not for the festival
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir's ruling applies only to work needed for the festival or also to unnecessary work. It attempts to resolve this from a baraita about small items like a bell or lattice, but the resolution is inconclusive, and the Gemara continues to analyze the distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about whether Rabbi Meir's ruling in the Mishnah applies only to work needed for the festival, or also to unnecessary work, and considers three possible interpretations.
The Gemara attempts to resolve the question by citing a baraita that mentions even a small bell or lattice, suggesting that only work for the festival may be completed, but not begun.

The Gemara rejects the resolution, explaining that the baraita's 'even' refers to small items whose beginning is their completion, and it teaches that one may not begin even those, but unnecessary work may still be completed.
The Gemara begins to cite another source to further investigate the question, but the citation is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's initial clarification
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's initial clarification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may complete work on the fourteenth if started earlier, but not begin new work even for small items. The Gemara clarifies that this applies only to work needed for the holiday, not unnecessary work, and that even for holiday needs, only completion is permitted, not beginning.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may complete work on the fourteenth if started earlier, but may not begin new work, even for small items like a small basket or a small lattice.

The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's leniency applies only to work needed for the holiday (לצורך המועד), not unnecessary work, and that even for holiday needs, only completion (מיגמר) is permitted, not beginning (אתוחולי).

items.text: Support from Rabbi Meir's statement
items.text_en: Support from Rabbi Meir's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Meir says that work needed for the holiday may be completed on the fourteenth, but unnecessary work is forbidden. The Gemara concludes that this supports the distinction between needed and unnecessary work.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir rules that any work needed for the holiday may be completed on the fourteenth, but work not needed for the holiday is forbidden.

The baraita adds that work is done on Passover eve until noon only where the custom permits, and the Gemara concludes that this supports the distinction between holiday-need and non-holiday-need work.

items.text: Dispute about three craftsmen and the principle of learning beginning from end
items.text_en: Dispute about three craftsmen and the principle of learning beginning from end
items.desc_en: The Sages list three craftsmen (tailors, barbers, launderers) who may work on the fourteenth, and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds shoemakers. The Gemara explains that they dispute whether one can learn the permissibility of beginning a craft from the permissibility of completing it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three craftsmen (tailors, barbers, launderers) who may work on the fourteenth, and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds shoemakers, each with a reason based on חול המועד (intermediate festival day) practice.
The Gemara asks what is the underlying dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.
The Gemara explains that the dispute is whether one can learn the permissibility of beginning a craft (תחילת מלאכה) from the permissibility of completing it (סוף מלאכה).

items.text: Mishnah: Permitted activities on the fourteenth
items.text_en: Mishnah: Permitted activities on the fourteenth
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists activities permitted on the fourteenth: setting up coops for chickens, returning a runaway hen, replacing a dead hen, removing dung from under animals, and bringing vessels from a craftsman even if not needed for the holiday.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may set up coops for chickens on the fourteenth, return a hen that fled to its place, and if it died, seat another in its place.
The Mishnah states that one may sweep manure from under an animal's feet on the fourteenth, and on חול המועד (the intermediate festival days) one may only move it to the sides.
The Mishnah permits bringing and taking vessels from the craftsman's house, even if they are not needed for the holiday.

items.text: Gemara on returning a runaway hen
items.text_en: Gemara on returning a runaway hen
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions returning a hen if setting up a coop is already permitted. Abaye explains that the latter clause refers to Chol Hamoed. Rav Huna and Rabbi Ami dispute the time limits for returning a hen, based on whether the loss is significant or minor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah permits returning a runaway hen if setting up a coop is already permitted, implying the latter is more lenient.
Abaye explains that the latter clause of the Mishnah refers to חול המועד (the intermediate festival days), not to the fourteenth of Nisan.

Rav Huna limits the permission to return a hen to cases of significant loss: within three days of its flight (when feathers haven't settled) or after three days of sitting (when eggs are lost), but not otherwise.
Rabbi Ami permits returning the hen even within three days of its sitting, where the loss is minor.
The Gemara explains that Rav Huna and Rabbi Ami dispute whether the Sages were concerned only for significant loss (הפסד מרובה) or also for minor loss (הפסד מועט).

items.text: Gemara on removing dung
items.text_en: Gemara on removing dung
items.desc_en: A baraita states that dung in a courtyard may be moved to the sides, but dung in a stable or courtyard may be taken to the dump. The Gemara notes a contradiction and Abaye resolves it by distinguishing between the fourteenth and Chol Hamoed. Rava resolves it by saying if the courtyard becomes like a stable, it may be taken to the dump.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that dung in a courtyard may be moved to the sides, but dung in a stable or courtyard may be taken to the dump.
The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita: it first says dung in a courtyard may only be moved to the sides, then says dung in a stable or courtyard may be taken to the dump.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the fourteenth of Nisan (where taking to the dump is permitted) and Chol Hamoed (where only moving to the sides is allowed).
Rava resolves the contradiction differently: both cases refer to Chol Hamoed, but if the courtyard becomes as filthy as a stable, one may take the dung to the dump.

items.text: Gemara on bringing vessels from a craftsman
items.text_en: Gemara on bringing vessels from a craftsman
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports that Rava examined a contradiction between the Mishnah (permitting bringing vessels) and a baraita (forbidding it). The Gemara resolves it by distinguishing between the fourteenth and Chol Hamoed, or between trusting and not trusting the craftsman. A further baraita is cited and reconciled, and the Gemara concludes that the original resolution stands.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports that Rava examined a contradiction between the Mishnah (permitting bringing vessels) and a baraita (forbidding it).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the fourteenth of Nisan and Chol Hamoed, or between trusting and not trusting the craftsman.
A baraita is cited that details which vessels may be brought from a craftsman and which may not, with exceptions for trust and theft concerns.

The Gemara rejects the alternative answer because the baraita forbids both bringing and taking, and concludes that the original resolution (distinguishing between the fourteenth and Chol Hamoed) stands.

items.text: Mishnah: Six practices of the people of Jericho
items.text_en: Mishnah: Six practices of the people of Jericho
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists six practices of the people of Jericho: three they were rebuked for (grafting palm trees all day, reciting Shema without interruption, reaping and stacking before the Omer) and three they were not rebuked for (permitting hekdesh branches, etc.).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces that the people of Jericho did six things: for three the Sages protested, and for three they did not protest.
The Mishnah lists the three unprotested practices: grafting palm trees all day, reciting the Shema (קריאת שמע) without interruption, and reaping and stacking before the omer offering.
The Mishnah begins listing the three protested practices: permitting the use of consecrated branches (גמזיות של הקדש).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists practices of the people of Jericho: grafting palm trees all day, reciting the Shema without interruption, and giving pe'ah to vegetables, which the Sages prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three practices of the people of Jericho—grafting palm trees all day, reciting the Shema without interruption, and giving pe'ah to vegetables—and states that the Sages prohibited them.

items.text: Six Actions of Hezekiah
items.text_en: Six Actions of Hezekiah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing six actions of King Hezekiah: three were approved (concealing his father's bones, destroying the copper serpent, and hiding the book of remedies) and three were not (cutting the doors of the Temple, stopping the Gihon spring, and intercalating Nisan in Nisan).

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces King Hezekiah's six actions, three approved and three not approved.
The baraita lists the three approved actions: dragging his father's bones on a rope bed, destroying the copper serpent, and hiding the book of remedies.
The baraita lists the three disapproved actions: cutting Temple doors, stopping the Gihon spring, and intercalating Nisan in Nisan.

items.text: Method of Grafting Palm Trees
items.text_en: Method of Grafting Palm Trees
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how the people of Jericho grafted palm trees: Rav Yehuda describes a mixture of old myrtle, beer, and barley flour, while Rav Acha bar Rava suggests placing a male palm branch into a female tree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the people of Jericho performed the grafting of palm trees all day.
Rav Yehuda describes a method using old myrtle, beer, and barley flour boiled and poured into the palm tree.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava's alternative answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava's alternative answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava offers an alternative method: placing a male palm branch into a female tree.

items.text: How They Recited the Shema
items.text_en: How They Recited the Shema
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how the people of Jericho recited the Shema: Rav Yehuda says they said 'Shema Yisrael' without interruption, Rava says they paused but said 'today on your heart', and a baraita records a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about whether they said 'Baruch shem kevod malchuto le'olam va'ed'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the people of Jericho performed the practice of 'wrapping' the Shema.
Rav Yehuda answers that they recited the Shema without any interruption between the first verse and the rest.
Rava answers that they did pause, but they said 'today on your heart' to emphasize immediacy.
A baraita records the dispute between Rabbi Meir (no pause) and Rabbi Yehuda (pause, but no 'Baruch shem kevod malchuto').

items.text: Origin of 'Baruch Shem'
items.text_en: Origin of 'Baruch Shem'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why we say 'Baruch shem kevod malchuto le'olam va'ed' quietly: based on a midrash of Reish Lakish about Jacob and his sons, the Sages instituted it quietly, but Rabbi Avahu later instituted it aloud due to heretics, except in Nehardea where there were no heretics.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why we recite 'ברוך שם כבוד מלכותו לעולם ועד' (Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever) during the Shema.
Reish Lakish recounts the midrash: Jacob sought to reveal the end of days, the Divine Presence departed, his sons declared the Shema, and Jacob responded with 'ברוך שם כבוד מלכותו לעולם ועד'.
The Sages instituted reciting 'ברוך שם' quietly, using a parable of a princess who smelled a pottage, to resolve the dilemma that Jacob said it but Moses did not.
Rabbi Avahu later instituted saying 'ברוך שם' aloud due to heretics, except in Nehardea where there were no heretics and they still say it quietly.

items.text: Six Practices of Jericho
items.text_en: Six Practices of Jericho
items.desc_en: A baraita lists six practices of the people of Jericho: three approved by the Sages (grafting, reciting Shema, reaping before the omer) and three not approved (piling before the omer, making breaches for eagles, and allowing carob and sycamore trees). Rabbi Yehuda disputes, saying all were not approved, but the Sages only protested three.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists six practices of the people of Jericho, three approved by the Sages (grafting, reciting Shema, reaping before the omer) and three not approved (piling before the omer, making breaches for eagles, allowing carob and sycamore trees), attributed to Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda objects, arguing that all six practices were not approved by the Sages; the Sages only protested three of them, not the other three.

Rabbi Yehuda specifies the three unprotested practices (grafting, reciting Shema, reaping and piling before the omer) and the three protested ones (allowing carob and sycamore trees, making breaches for eagles, giving peah to vegetables).

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehuda's view that reaping before the omer was not approved, citing a Mishnah that explicitly states it was approved, and that only piling was not approved but not protested.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehuda's position by citing a Mishnah that explicitly states reaping before the omer was done with rabbinic approval, and that only piling was without approval yet not protested.

items.text: Gemara's question on the first leniency
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the first leniency
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions who holds the opinion of 'miḥu' and 'lo miḥu' that would allow harvesting with the consent of the Sages, and resolves that the fourth leniency is actually a subset of the first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who holds the opinion of 'miḥu' and 'lo miḥu' that would allow harvesting with the consent of the Sages, and identifies it as Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Yehuda holds this view, the Mishnah's statement 'they harvest with the consent of the Sages' would contradict the count of four leniencies.
The Gemara resolves that the fourth leniency (harvesting) is actually a subset of the first (permitting the storehouse), so the count remains four.

items.text: Second leniency: permitting sacred branches
items.text_en: Second leniency: permitting sacred branches
items.desc_en: The people of Jericho permitted the use of sacred branches of carob and sycamore, arguing that their ancestors only dedicated the trunks, and they deal with later growths, following the opinion that there is no misuse of sacred property for growths. The Sages hold that while there is no misuse, there is still prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the people of Jericho permitted the use of branches of consecrated carob and sycamore trees.
The people of Jericho argued that their ancestors only consecrated the main beams, not the branches, so they permit the branches.

The Gemara explains that the dispute concerns secondary growths that appear after the consecration, and the people of Jericho follow the opinion that there is no מעילה (misuse of consecrated property) regarding such growths.
The Sages hold that even though there is no מעילה (misuse), there is still a prohibition against using consecrated property.

items.text: Third leniency: breaking fences
items.text_en: Third leniency: breaking fences
items.desc_en: Ulla cites Resh Lakish that the dispute about breaking fences is only for those of the 'makhbedot' type, where the Sages fear one might climb and uproot, while the people of Jericho do not. For fences between pillars, all agree it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the people of Jericho would breach fences to allow the public to enter their gardens and orchards.

sub.text: Ulla citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.text_en: Ulla citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.desc_en: Ulla reports in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish that the dispute between the Sages and the people of Jericho is specifically about fences made of bundled branches, where the Sages decree a prohibition lest one come to uproot plants, while the people of Jericho do not.
Ulla concludes that regarding fences made of palm branches, everyone agrees it is permitted.

items.text: Rava's objection and resolution on set-aside
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution on set-aside
items.desc_en: Rava objects that the branches are set-aside (muktzeh), and questions whether preparedness for ravens constitutes preparedness for humans. The Gemara answers that preparedness for humans does not make something prepared for dogs, but preparedness for ravens does make it prepared for humans, since humans have their mind on it.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that the branches are set-aside (מוקצה), and questions whether preparedness for ravens constitutes preparedness for humans, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules that a carcass not prepared before Shabbat is forbidden for dogs.
The Gemara answers that preparedness for humans does not constitute preparedness for dogs, but preparedness for ravens does constitute preparedness for humans, since humans have their mind on it.

items.text: Alternate version of the dispute by Ravin
items.text_en: Alternate version of the dispute by Ravin
items.desc_en: Ravin reports Resh Lakish's alternative version: the dispute is about fences between pillars, where the Sages hold that preparedness for ravens does not constitute preparedness for humans, while the people of Jericho hold it does. For 'makhbedot' fences, all agree it is forbidden due to the concern of climbing and uprooting.

sub.text: Ravin citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.text_en: Ravin citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.desc_en: Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish that the dispute is specifically about fences made of palm branches, where the Sages hold that being prepared for ravens does not make it prepared for humans, while the people of Jericho hold the opposite.
Ravin concludes that regarding fences made of bundled branches, everyone agrees it is forbidden due to the decree lest one come to uproot plants.

items.text: Fourth leniency: giving pe'ah to vegetables
items.text_en: Fourth leniency: giving pe'ah to vegetables
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the people of Jericho could give pe'ah to vegetables, given the rule that pe'ah applies only to things that are stored. Rav Yehuda explains that they deal with the heads of leaves, and they dispute whether preserving through another means is considered preservation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the people of Jericho could give pe'ah to vegetables, given the Mishnah's rule that pe'ah applies only to things that are stored, which excludes vegetables.
The Gemara cites the baraita that elaborates the Mishnah's rule, explicitly excluding vegetables from pe'ah because they are not stored.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that the people of Jericho deal with the heads of leaves, and they dispute whether preserving through another means (על ידי דבר אחר) is considered preservation (קיום).

items.text: Baraita on earlier practices of pe'ah
items.text_en: Baraita on earlier practices of pe'ah
items.desc_en: A baraita records that initially pe'ah was given to turnip and cabbage, with Rabbi Yosei adding kafilot, and another baraita records turnip and kafilot, with Rabbi Shimon adding cabbage.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that initially they would give פיאה (the corner of the field) to turnips and cabbage, and Rabbi Yosei adds orach.
Another baraita states that they would give פיאה (the corner of the field) to turnips and orach, and Rabbi Shimon adds cabbage.
Another baraita records that pe'ah was given to turnip and kafilot.
Rabbi Shimon adds that cabbage was also included.

items.text: Clarification of the Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Clarification of the Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that there are only two Tannaim in the Mishnah, not three, by identifying the first Tanna of Rabbi Shimon as Rabbi Yosei and the first Tanna of Rabbi Yosei as Rabbi Shimon, and explains that the word 'af' refers to the first clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah implies three Tannaim are involved.

The Gemara answers that there are only two Tannaim, identifying the first Tanna of Rabbi Shimon as Rabbi Yosei and the first Tanna of Rabbi Yosei as Rabbi Shimon, and explains that the word 'af' refers to the first clause.

items.text: The story of Ben Buhyan and pe'ah for vegetables
items.text_en: The story of Ben Buhyan and pe'ah for vegetables
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Ben Buhyan gave pe'ah to vegetables, and his father told the poor to discard them, promising double in tithed produce, not out of stinginess but because the Sages ruled that pe'ah is not given to vegetables. The Gemara explains why the father added that he was not stingy: to avoid the poor thinking he was merely putting them off.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts that Ben Buhyan gave pe'ah to vegetables, and his father told the poor to discard them, promising double in tithed produce, because the Sages ruled that pe'ah is not given to vegetables.
The Gemara asks why the father added the statement that he was not stingy.
The Gemara answers that the father said this so the poor would not think he was merely putting them off.

items.text: Reforms regarding the distribution of sacred hides
items.text_en: Reforms regarding the distribution of sacred hides
items.desc_en: A baraita describes how hides of sacred offerings were initially distributed daily in the Parvah Chamber, but the powerful would take them by force. A reform was instituted to distribute them only on Shabbat eves so all watches could come together. Still, the powerful took them by force, so the owners (the Temple treasurers) consecrated them to Heaven. The Gemara adds that soon the entire Heichal was plated with gold tablets, which were displayed for pilgrims.

sub.desc_en: The baraita describes the initial practice of storing sacred hides in the Parvah Chamber and distributing them daily, and the reform to distribute them on Shabbat eves so all watches could participate.
The baraita reports that despite the reform, the powerful priests still took the hides by force, so the Temple treasurers consecrated them to Heaven.
The Gemara adds that soon the entire Heichal was plated with gold tablets, which were displayed for pilgrims to see the beauty of their work.

items.text: Abba Shaul's tradition about sycamore beams in Jericho
items.text_en: Abba Shaul's tradition about sycamore beams in Jericho
items.desc_en: Abba Shaul teaches that there were sycamore beams in Jericho which the powerful would take by force, so the owners consecrated them to Heaven.

sub.desc_en: Abba Shaul adds that sycamore beams in Jericho were similarly taken by force, and their owners consecrated them to Heaven.

items.text: Abba Shaul ben Botnit's lament over the high priestly families
items.text_en: Abba Shaul ben Botnit's lament over the high priestly families
items.desc_en: Abba Shaul ben Botnit, citing Abba Yosef ben Chanin, laments the oppressive high priestly families: Beit Baitos, Beit Chanin, Beit Katros, and Beit Yishmael ben Pi'aki, whose sons were treasurers, sons-in-law were administrators, and servants beat the people with clubs.

sub.text: Abba Shaul ben Batnit citing Abba Yosef ben Chanin
sub.text_en: Abba Shaul ben Batnit citing Abba Yosef ben Chanin
sub.desc_en: Abba Shaul ben Batnit, citing Abba Yosef ben Chanin, laments the oppressive priestly families (Beit Baytos, Beit Chanin, Beit Katros, Beit Yishmael ben Piaki) who abused their power.

items.text: The four cries of the Temple courtyard and the story of Yissakhar of Kefar Barkai
items.text_en: The four cries of the Temple courtyard and the story of Yissakhar of Kefar Barkai
items.desc_en: A baraita lists four cries of the Temple courtyard: against the sons of Eli, against Yissakhar of Kefar Barkai who wrapped his hands in silk and performed service, a welcome for Yishmael ben Pi'aki, and a welcome for Yochanan ben Narbai. The Gemara elaborates on Yochanan's gluttony and then recounts the story of Yissakhar of Kefar Barkai, who was asked by the king and queen to decide whether a goat or a lamb is better, and he signaled with a gesture.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing the first two cries of the Temple courtyard: against the sons of Eli for defiling the sanctuary, and against Yissakhar of Kefar Barkai who wrapped his hands in silk and performed service.
The baraita continues with the third and fourth cries: a welcome for Yishmael ben Pi'aki to serve as High Priest, and a welcome for Yochanan ben Narbai to fill his belly from the sacred offerings.

sub.text: Gemara's elaboration on Yochanan ben Narbai
sub.text_en: Gemara's elaboration on Yochanan ben Narbai
sub.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on Yochanan ben Narbai's gluttony, describing his consumption of three hundred calves, three hundred barrels of wine, and forty se'ah of pigeons, and that no leftover sacrificial meat (נוֹתָר) was ever found in the Temple during his tenure.
The Gemara asks what ultimately happened to Yissakhar of Kefar Barkai, and recounts that the king and queen debated whether a goat or a lamb is better, and they sought the High Priest's opinion.
The Gemara answers that the High Priest was brought to decide, and Yissakhar signaled with a gesture, leading to his downfall.

items.text: Story of Yissakhar of Kfar Barkai
items.text_en: Story of Yissakhar of Kfar Barkai
items.desc_en: Yissakhar signals that a goat should be brought for the daily sacrifice. The king, angered by his lack of fear of the monarchy, orders his right hand cut off. Yissakhar bribes the executioner to cut off his left hand instead, but the king finds out and has his right hand cut off as well. Rav Yosef blesses God for punishing Yissakhar in this world.

sub.desc_en: Yissakhar signals that a goat is suitable for the daily sacrifice; the king orders his right hand cut off for lacking fear of the monarchy, and after a bribe and discovery, both hands are severed.
Rav Yosef blesses God for punishing Yissakhar in this world for his transgression.

items.text: Rav Ashi and Ravina dispute Yissakhar's status
items.text_en: Rav Ashi and Ravina dispute Yissakhar's status
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that Yissakhar of Kfar Barkai was not a teacher of Mishnah, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says that lambs precede goats everywhere, but the verse 'If he brings a lamb as his offering' shows they are equal. Ravina adds that Yissakhar did not even read the Bible, as the verses 'If a lamb' and 'If a goat' indicate that either may be brought.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asserts that Yissakhar of Kfar Barkai did not study Mishnah, implying his ignorance of the law.
Rabbi Shimon teaches that lambs and goats are equal in priority for sacrifices, as derived from the verse 'if a lamb' and 'if a goat'.
Ravina argues that Yissakhar did not even read the verse, which states 'if a lamb' and 'if a goat', indicating either is acceptable.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: זמני התמיד בערב פסח
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the times for slaughtering and offering the daily Tamid on a regular day, on Erev Pesach, and on Erev Pesach that falls on Erev Shabbat.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שתמיד של בין הערביים נשחט בשמונה ומחצה וקרב בתשע ומחצה. בערבי פסחים מקדימים לשבע ומחצה ושומנה ומחצה, ובשבת ערב פסח מקדימים לשש ומחצה ושבע ומחצה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the times for slaughtering and offering the daily Tamid on a regular day, on Erev Pesach, and on Erev Pesach that falls on Erev Shabbat.
sub.desc: המשנה קובעת את זמני השחיטה והקרבה של תמיד של בין הערביים בימים רגילים, בערבי פסחים ובשבת ערב פסח.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source of the times. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives from the verse that the day is divided into two halves of two and a half hours each, with one hour for the actual offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source of the times stated in the Mishnah for the daily offering (תמיד).

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives from the verse 'את הכבש אחד תעשה בבקר ואת הכבש השני תעשה בין הערבים' that the day is divided into two halves of two and a half hours each, with one hour for the actual offering.

items.text: Rava's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava objects: if the Torah-mandated time is eight and a half, how can the Mishnah schedule the Tamid earlier on Erev Pesach? He instead explains that the Torah only requires the Tamid to be offered when shadows lengthen, i.e., from the sixth hour onward.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects: if the Torah-mandated time for the Tamid is eight and a half hours, how can the Mishnah schedule it earlier on Erev Pesach?
Rava explains that the Torah only requires the Tamid to be offered when shadows lengthen, i.e., from the sixth hour onward, so the Mishnah's earlier time is valid.

items.text: Explanation of the Mishnah's times based on practical considerations
items.text_en: Explanation of the Mishnah's times based on practical considerations
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that on regular days, the Tamid is delayed to eight and a half to allow for additional offerings (nedarim and nedavot). On Erev Pesach, it is moved earlier to seven and a half to accommodate the Pesach offering. On Erev Pesach that is Erev Shabbat, it is moved even earlier to six and a half because the Pesach cannot be roasted on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by explaining that on regular days, the Tamid is delayed because there are additional offerings (nedarim and nedavot), citing the verse 'עליה חלבי השלמים' (upon it the fats of the peace offerings).
Mar interprets the verse to mean that all offerings are completed upon the Tamid, so the Tamid is delayed by two hours and performed at eight and a half.

The Gemara concludes that on Erev Pesach the Tamid is moved one hour earlier to seven and a half, and on Erev Pesach that is Erev Shabbat it is moved to six and a half because the Pesach cannot be roasted on Shabbat.

items.text: First version of the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: First version of the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Yishmael says the order on Shabbat Erev Pesach is like the order on a weekday Erev Pesach; Rabbi Akiva says it is like the order on Erev Pesach that falls on Erev Shabbat. Abaye explains that the Mishnah's ruling that the times are the same on Shabbat as on weekdays follows Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael says the order on Shabbat Erev Pesach is like the weekday order; Rabbi Akiva says it is like the order on Erev Pesach.
The Gemara asks what the baraita means, since the phrasing is ambiguous.

Abaye explains that Rabbi Yishmael means the order on Shabbat Erev Pesach is like the weekday Erev Pesach, and Rabbi Akiva means it is like Erev Pesach that falls on Erev Shabbat; the Mishnah's ruling that the times are the same on Shabbat as on weekdays follows Rabbi Yishmael.

items.text: Explanation of the first version's dispute: Mussaf vs. Bazikhin
items.text_en: Explanation of the first version's dispute: Mussaf vs. Bazikhin
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute is about whether the Mussaf offering or the Bazikhin (the frankincense for the showbread) takes precedence. Rabbi Yishmael holds Mussaf precedes Bazikhin, leading to a later Tamid; Rabbi Akiva holds Bazikhin precede Mussaf, leading to an earlier Tamid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Over what principle do they disagree?

The Gemara explains: They disagree about whether the additional offerings (מוספין) precede the frankincense bowls (בזיכין); Rabbi Yishmael holds מוספין precede בזיכין, leading to the Tamid at 7.5, while Rabbi Akiva holds בזיכין precede מוספין, leading to the Tamid at 6.5.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yishmael's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yishmael's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yishmael holds Mussaf precedes Bazikhin, so the Mussaf is at six, Bazikhin at seven, and the Tamid at seven and a half.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva holds Bazikhin precede Mussaf, so the Bazikhin are at five, Mussaf at six, and the Tamid at six and a half.

items.text: התקפת רבא וביאור חדש למחלוקת
items.text_en: Rava's objection and second version of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rava objects to Abaye's interpretation, noting that Rabbi Akiva's statement does not specify 'Erev Shabbat'. He offers a different explanation: Rabbi Yishmael says the order on Shabbat Erev Pesach is like a regular weekday; Rabbi Akiva says it is like a regular Erev Pesach. The Mishnah then follows Rabbi Akiva. The dispute is about whether we are concerned about the meat becoming congealed (מכמר בשרא).
items.desc: רבא מקשה על פירוש אביי, שכן רבי עקיבא לא אמר 'כסדרו בערב פסח שחל בערב שבת' אלא סתם 'כסדרו בערב פסח'. רבא מבאר את הברייתא באופן אחר: רבי ישמעאל סובר שבשבת בערב פסח התמיד כשמונה ומחצה (כחול), ורבי עקיבא סובר שבשבת בערב פסח התמיד כשבע ומחצה (כערב פסח בחול). המחלוקת תלויה בחשש שמא יתחמם בשר הפסח ויסריח: רבי ישמעאל חושש, ורבי עקיבא אינו חושש.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Abaye's interpretation, pointing out that Rabbi Akiva's statement does not specify 'Erev Shabbat' but simply says 'like the order of Erev Pesach'.
sub.desc: רבא מקשה על פירוש אביי, שכן רבי עקיבא לא אמר 'כסדרו בערב פסח שחל בערב שבת' אלא סתם 'כסדרו בערב פסח'.

sub.desc_en: Rava offers his own interpretation: Rabbi Yishmael says the order on Shabbat Erev Pesach is like a regular weekday; Rabbi Akiva says it is like a regular Erev Pesach, and the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva.
sub.desc: רבא מקשה על פירוש אביי, שכן רבי עקיבא לא אמר 'כסדרו בערב פסח שחל בערב שבת' אלא סתם 'כסדרו בערב פסח'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute is about whether we are concerned about the meat becoming congealed (מכמר בשרא): Rabbi Yishmael is concerned, Rabbi Akiva is not.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבארת את שורש המחלוקת: רבי ישמעאל חושש שמא יתחמם בשר הפסח ויסריח, ורבי עקיבא אינו חושש לכך.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about the tamid time
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about the tamid time
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the tamid cannot be offered at six and a half hours if we do not worry about a decree, and answers that the additional offerings (musafin) precede the frankincense pans (bazikhin), so the schedule is adjusted accordingly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if we do not worry about a decree, why not perform the tamid at six and a half hours?
The Gemara answers: the additional offerings (מוספין) precede the frankincense pans (בזיכין), so the schedule is adjusted to perform the tamid at seven and a half.

items.text: Rabba bar Ulla's objection and correction
items.text_en: Rabba bar Ulla's objection and correction
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Ulla objects that the mishnah does not specify 'on Shabbat eve of Passover' but says 'on Shabbat' in general. He then corrects the mishnah's reading: the order on a regular Shabbat is like the order on a regular weekday, according to Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Ulla objects that the mishnah's phrase 'like its order on a weekday, so its order on Shabbat' is stated generally, not specifically for Shabbat eve of Passover.
Rabba bar Ulla corrects the mishnah's reading: the order on a regular Shabbat is like the order on a regular weekday, according to Rabbi Yishmael.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's opinion and the dispute's basis
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's opinion and the dispute's basis
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva says the order on Shabbat is like the order on a regular Passover eve, and the mishnah that mentions both weekday and Shabbat is accepted by all. The dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is about whether we decree regarding Shabbat due to weekday concerns for voluntary offerings and vows.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva states that the order on Shabbat is like the order on a regular Passover eve, and the mishnah that mentions both weekday and Shabbat is accepted by all.
The Gemara asks: On what basis do Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva dispute?
The Gemara explains: Rabbi Yishmael decrees regarding Shabbat due to weekday concerns for voluntary offerings and vows, while Rabbi Akiva does not decree.

items.text: Repeated question and answer about the tamid time
items.text_en: Repeated question and answer about the tamid time
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats the question: if we do not decree, why not offer the tamid at six and a half? The same answer is given: the additional offerings precede the frankincense pans, so the tamid is at seven and a half.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if we do not decree, why not perform the tamid at six and a half?
The Gemara answers: the additional offerings precede the frankincense pans, so the schedule is adjusted.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that on Passover eve, the tamid is slaughtered at seven and a half and offered at eight and a half, and if it falls on Shabbat, it is like a Monday according to Rabbi Yishmael. This poses a difficulty for Rava's view. Rava resolves it by reinterpreting 'like Monday' to mean 'like a regular Monday' (not a weekday in general).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that on Passover eve the tamid is slaughtered at seven and a half and offered at eight and a half, and if it falls on Shabbat it is like Monday according to Rabbi Yishmael, which contradicts Rava's view.
Rava resolves the objection by reinterpreting the baraita to mean 'like a regular Monday' (a weekday), not a Monday that fell on Passover eve.

items.text: Another objection and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Another objection and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Another baraita states that if Passover eve falls on Shabbat, the order is like the whole year according to Rabbi Yishmael, which is difficult for Abaye. Abaye resolves it by reinterpreting 'like the whole year' to mean 'like all years' (i.e., a regular Passover eve that falls on a Friday), and Rabbi Akiva says it is like a Passover eve that falls on Shabbat eve.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that if Passover eve falls on Shabbat, the order is like the whole year according to Rabbi Yishmael, which poses a difficulty for Abaye's position.

Abaye resolves the difficulty by reinterpreting 'like the whole year' to mean 'like all years' (i.e., a regular Passover eve that falls on a Friday), and Rabbi Akiva says it is like a Passover eve that falls on Shabbat eve.

items.text: Derashot about the tamid's precedence
items.text_en: Derashot about the tamid's precedence
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that nothing precedes the morning tamid, derived from 'and he shall arrange the burnt offering' (the first offering). Nothing comes after the afternoon tamid, derived from 'and he shall burn upon it the fat of the peace offerings'. Rava objects that this might only exclude peace offerings, not burnt offerings, so he reinterprets: 'the peace offerings' means 'complete all offerings upon it'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing a verse to prove that nothing precedes the morning tamid, and Rava explains the derivation: 'העולה' (the burnt offering) implies it is the first offering.
The baraita continues with a second derivation for the afternoon tamid, and Abaye explains that the verse 'עליה' (upon it) teaches that only peace offerings are offered on it, not on its counterpart.
Rava objects that Abaye's derivation might only exclude peace offerings, but burnt offerings could still be brought after the tamid.
Rava resolves the objection by reinterpreting 'השלמים' (the peace offerings) as a play on words: 'עליה השלם' — complete all offerings upon it.

items.text: Order of precedence among offerings
items.text_en: Order of precedence among offerings
items.desc_en: A baraita states the order: the tamid precedes the paschal offering, the paschal offering precedes the incense, and the incense precedes the candelabrum.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is taught: the tamid precedes the pesach, the pesach precedes the incense, the incense precedes the lamps.

items.text: Opening principle: delaying the Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Opening principle: delaying the Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a principle: a matter stated with both 'ba'erev' and 'bein ha'arbayim' (the tamid) is delayed for a matter stated only with 'bein ha'arbayim' (the Pesach). This establishes the Pesach's place after the tamid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a principle: a matter stated with both 'ba'erev' and 'bein ha'arbayim' (the tamid) is delayed for a matter stated only with 'bein ha'arbayim' (the Pesach).

items.text: Challenge: incense and lamps should precede the Pesach
items.text_en: Challenge: incense and lamps should precede the Pesach
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that incense and lamps, which are also stated only with 'bein ha'arbayim', should precede the Pesach. It answers that the Torah excludes them with the word 'oto' regarding the lamps, and the incense is linked to the lamps. A baraita confirms the order: tamid, incense, lamps, Pesach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the rule is based on the phrase 'בין הערבים' (in the afternoon), then incense and lamps, which also use only that phrase, should precede the Pesach.
The Gemara answers that the case of lamps is different because the Torah excludes them with the word 'אותו' (it), as taught in a baraita about the lamps burning from evening to morning.
The baraita further explains that the word 'אותו' (it) teaches that only the lamp-lighting is valid from evening to morning, excluding other rites.
The Gemara notes that incense is juxtaposed to lamps in the verse, so the same exclusion applies to incense.
A baraita confirms the order: the daily afternoon offering precedes incense, incense precedes lamps, and lamps precede the Pesach.

items.text: Refining the exclusion: 'oto' applies to inner service
items.text_en: Refining the exclusion: 'oto' applies to inner service
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the word 'oto' excludes the inner service, specifically the incense. It resolves a potential contradiction: the verse 'bein ha'arbayim yaktirenna' teaches that the incense is offered at the time of lighting the lamps, not before.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the word 'אותו' (it) is written, which should exclude the incense from being after the lamps, and explains that 'אותו' actually excludes the inner service (incense) from being performed after the lamps, resolving the potential contradiction that one might think to light the lamps first.

The Gemara asks why the verse 'בין הערבים יקטירנה' (in the afternoon he shall burn it) is needed, and answers that it teaches that at the time you light the lamps, the incense should already be burning.

items.text: Baraita: order of the morning and afternoon services
items.text_en: Baraita: order of the morning and afternoon services
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that only incense precedes the morning tamid, and after the afternoon tamid come incense, lamps, the Pesach, and a mechusar kippurim on Pesach eve. Rabbi Yishmael adds that a mechusar kippurim also eats sacrifices in the evening on other days.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that only incense precedes the morning tamid, and after the afternoon tamid come incense, lamps, the Pesach, and a mechusar kippurim on Pesach eve.

sub.text: Baraita (Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka)
sub.text_en: Baraita (Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael adds that a mechusar kippurim also eats sacrifices in the evening on other days of the year.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yishmael's ruling is justified, since both the positive commandment of the Pesach and the positive commandment of completion carry the same weight.

items.text: Question: why does the Pesach override the completion offering?
items.text_en: Question: why does the Pesach override the completion offering?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the positive commandment of the Pesach, which carries karet, overrides the positive commandment of completion (the mechusar kippurim's offering) which has no karet. This is understandable for the first tanna, but for Rabbi Yishmael, what is the strength of one positive commandment over another?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the first Tanna, the positive commandment of Pesach (with karet) overrides the positive commandment of completion (without karet), but for Rabbi Yishmael, what strength does this positive commandment have over that one?

items.text: Answers: the mechusar kippurim's offering is a bird chatat or already offered
items.text_en: Answers: the mechusar kippurim's offering is a bird chatat or already offered
items.desc_en: Ravina citing Rav Chisda says the case involves a bird chatat, which has only its blood for the altar. Rav Papa says even a beast chatat can be left overnight on the altar. The Gemara then addresses challenges about asham and olah, concluding that the olah of a metzora is different because the Torah says so.

sub.desc_en: Ravina in the name of Rav Chisda answers that the case involves a bird chatat, which has only its blood for the altar.
Rav Papa offers an alternative answer: even a beast chatat can be left overnight on the top of the altar.
The Gemara objects: what about the asham offering? It answers that the asham had already been offered.
The Gemara objects further: what about the olah, which according to Rabbi Yishmael also delays the mechusar kippurim?
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the olah was already offered, citing a baraita that the chatat always precedes the olah.
Rava resolves the difficulty by distinguishing the olah of a metzora, which the Torah treats differently.

items.text: Gemara's question about delaying the offering
items.text_en: Gemara's question about delaying the offering
items.desc_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba challenges Rav Pappa's view that one can place the offering on top of the altar and leave it overnight, arguing that priests might mistakenly think it is still the same day and come to offer it. Rav Pappa responds that priests are vigilant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'וְהֶעֱלָה הַכֹּהֵן אֶת הָעוֹלָה' and explains it means he has already brought it up.

Rav Shemen bar Abba objects to Rav Pappa's view that one can place the offering on top of the altar and leave it overnight, arguing that priests might mistakenly think it is still the same day and come to offer it.
Rav Pappa responds that priests are vigilant and will not err.

items.text: The necessity of offering the fats for priestly consumption
items.text_en: The necessity of offering the fats for priestly consumption
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi questions Rav Pappa: if the fats are not offered, priests cannot eat the meat, and without priestly consumption, the owners are not atoned. Rav Pappa answers that since it is impossible, the fats are treated as if they were lost or defiled, citing a baraita that priests still receive the breast and thigh.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi questions Rav Pappa: if the fats are not offered, the priests cannot eat the meat, as a baraita teaches that the breast and thigh are only permitted after the fats are burned.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's continuation of the question
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's continuation of the question
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi adds that without priestly consumption, the owners are not atoned, citing a baraita that priests eat and owners are atoned.
Rav Pappa answers that since it is impossible to burn the fats, the fats are treated as if they were lost or defiled, citing a baraita that the priests still receive the breast and thigh regardless.

items.text: Contradiction between verses on overnight storage
items.text_en: Contradiction between verses on overnight storage
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana raises a contradiction: one verse says the fat of the festival may not remain until morning, implying it can remain all night, while another verse says to offer all the fats on the altar. He resolves it by saying the contradiction applies when the fats are leftover.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana raises a contradiction between the verse 'לֹא יָלִין חֵלֶב חַגִּי עַד בֹּקֶר' (implying overnight storage is permitted) and the verse 'וְהִקְטִיר עָלֶיהָ חֶלְבֵי הַשְּׁלָמִים' (requiring immediate offering of all fats).
Rav Kahana resolves the contradiction by explaining that the verse permitting overnight storage applies only when the fats are leftover (נִתּוֹתְרוּ) and cannot be offered that night.

items.text: Another contradiction and resolution regarding the Passover
items.text_en: Another contradiction and resolution regarding the Passover
items.desc_en: Rav Safra raises a contradiction: one verse says the Passover sacrifice may remain all night, but another verse implies only the Sabbath offering may be offered on a festival. Rav answers that the verse deals with the 14th of Nisan falling on Shabbat, where the fats of Shabbat are offered on the festival. Rav Safra questions this forced interpretation, but Rav says to let the verse be forced.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra raises a contradiction: one verse permits the Passover sacrifice to remain all night, but another verse implies only the Sabbath offering may be offered on a festival.
Rav answers that the verse deals with the 14th of Nisan falling on Shabbat, where the fats of Shabbat are offered on the festival.
Rav Safra questions the forced interpretation, but Rav says to let the verse be forced.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on mixed intentions in the Passover sacrifice
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on mixed intentions in the Passover sacrifice
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a Passover sacrifice slaughtered not for its name, or with mixed intentions, is invalid. The Gemara questions whether this refers to a single act or multiple acts, and suggests it follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that a person is bound by the final intention, not Rabbi Meir who holds by the first.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a Passover sacrifice slaughtered not for its name, or with mixed intentions (for its name and not for its name, or vice versa), is invalid.
The Mishnah clarifies the mixed intentions: 'for its name and not for its name' means for the sake of a Passover offering and for the sake of a peace offering, and vice versa.
Rav Pappa asks whether the Mishnah's case of mixed intentions refers to a single sacrificial act or to two separate acts.
The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah refers to a single act and follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that a person is bound by the final intention (גמר דבריו).
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that one is bound by the first intention (תפוס לשון ראשון), implying the Mishnah must align with Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Gemara's question: one service vs. two services
items.text_en: Gemara's question: one service vs. two services
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's case of 'not for its sake and for its sake' refers to one service (where Rabbi Meir holds one is bound by the first expression) or two services (where even Rabbi Meir agrees it is invalid). It then clarifies that the dilemma is specifically about 'for its sake and not for its sake', since 'not for its sake and for its sake' would be invalid even for Rabbi Yosi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does the Mishnah's case of 'not for its sake and for its sake' refer to one service (where Rabbi Meir holds one is bound by the first expression) or two services (where even Rabbi Meir agrees it is invalid)?
The Gemara clarifies that the dilemma is specifically about 'for its sake and not for its sake', since 'not for its sake and for its sake' would be invalid even for Rabbi Yosi.

items.text: First attempt to resolve: Mishnah's case of 'not for its sake'
items.text_en: First attempt to resolve: Mishnah's case of 'not for its sake'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a Paschal lamb slaughtered not for its sake, and then receiving, walking, and sprinkling not for its sake. It argues that if all services were invalid, why mention them all? Rather, it must be that the Mishnah describes a case where some services are for its sake and some not, involving two services.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a Paschal lamb slaughtered not for its sake, and then receiving, walking, and sprinkling not for its sake, and questions why all services are listed if the first already invalidates.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah describes a case where some services are for its sake and some not, involving two services, so the listing is necessary.

items.text: Second attempt: Mishnah's case of 'for its sake and not for its sake'
items.text_en: Second attempt: Mishnah's case of 'for its sake and not for its sake'
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the Mishnah's case of 'for its sake and not for its sake'. If it involves two services, it would be identical to the first case. Therefore, it must be one service and follow Rabbi Yosi, who holds that one is bound by the final expression.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the Mishnah's case of 'for its sake and not for its sake': if it involves two services, it would be identical to the first case.
The Gemara concludes that the case must involve one service and follows Rabbi Yosi, who holds that one is bound by the final expression.

items.text: Rejection and resolution: thinking from one service to another
items.text_en: Rejection and resolution: thinking from one service to another
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous attempt, explaining that both cases involve two services: the first case is thinking during slaughter about slaughter, the second case is thinking during slaughter about sprinkling (e.g., 'I slaughter for its sake to sprinkle not for its sake'). This teaches that intention can transfer from one service to another, resolving Rav Papa's dilemma.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous attempt, explaining that both cases involve two services: the first case is thinking during slaughter about slaughter, the second case is thinking during sprinkling about sprinkling.
The Gemara resolves Rav Papa's dilemma by showing that the Mishnah teaches that intention can transfer from one service to another, as in the case of thinking during slaughter about sprinkling.

items.text: Third attempt: Mishnah's 'not for its sake and for its sake'
items.text_en: Third attempt: Mishnah's 'not for its sake and for its sake'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that 'not for its sake and for its sake' is invalid. If it involved two services, the case of 'for its sake and not for its sake' would already imply it. Thus, it must be one service, and the same applies to the first case. The Gemara rejects this, arguing that the Mishnah simply includes both formulations for completeness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that rules 'not for its sake and for its sake' is invalid, and argues that if it involved two services, the case of 'for its sake and not for its sake' would already imply it, so it must be one service.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's case must be a single service, and therefore the first case of the Mishnah also involves a single service.

The Gemara rejects the conclusion, arguing that the Mishnah always refers to two services, and the formulation 'not for its sake and for its sake' is included merely for completeness alongside 'for its sake and not for its sake'.

items.text: Fourth attempt: Mishnah about eaters and uncircumcised
items.text_en: Fourth attempt: Mishnah about eaters and uncircumcised
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about slaughtering not for its eaters, not for its members, for uncircumcised or impure persons, which is invalid. It argues that this is clearly one service, so the first case must also be one service. The Gemara rejects this, stating that the cases are different: the latter is one service, the former could be either one or two services.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that slaughtering the Paschal lamb not for its eaters, not for its members, for uncircumcised or impure persons is invalid.
The Gemara argues that this Mishnah is clearly about one service, so the first case (slaughter not for its name) must also be about one service.
The Gemara rejects the inference, stating that the cases are different: the latter is one service, the former could be either one or two services.

items.text: Fifth attempt: Mishnah about eaters and non-eaters
items.text_en: Fifth attempt: Mishnah about eaters and non-eaters
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that slaughtering 'for its eaters and not for its eaters' is valid. If this involved two services (e.g., thinking about eaters during sprinkling, where such thought is ineffective), then in one service (slaughter, where thought about eaters is effective) it would be invalid. But we know that partial thought about eaters does not invalidate. This suggests the case is one service, but the Gemara does not resolve the dilemma.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that slaughtering 'for its eaters and not for its eaters' is valid, and argues that if this involved two services (e.g., thought about eaters during sprinkling, where such thought is ineffective), then in one service (slaughter, where thought about eaters is effective) it would be invalid, but we know that partial thought about eaters does not invalidate, so the case must be one service, yet the dilemma remains unresolved.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's first clause might be in one act (avodah achat) like the latter clause, but resolves that the latter clause is definitely one act while the first clause could be either one or two acts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the latter clause of the Mishnah is performed in one act (עבודה אחת), then the first clause must also be in one act.
The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that the latter clause is definitely one act, while the first clause could be either one or two acts.

items.text: Question: Pesach slaughtered with lishmah and shelo lishmah
items.text_en: Question: Pesach slaughtered with lishmah and shelo lishmah
items.desc_en: A question is raised: if one slaughters a pesach during the rest of the year with both lishmah and shelo lishmah intent, does the shelo lishmah remove it from lishmah and make it valid?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if one slaughters a pesach offering during the rest of the year with both לִשְׁמוֹ (for its own sake) and שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמוֹ (not for its own sake) intent, does the שֶׁלֹּא לִשְמוֹ intent remove it from its לִשְׁמוֹ status and render it valid, or not?

sub.text: Rav Dimi's report in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi's report in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that he stated before Rabbi Yirmeya a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: just as לִשְׁמוֹ (for its own sake) which validates the offering in its proper time does not remove it from the status of שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמוֹ, so too שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמוֹ which validates it outside its proper time does not remove it from the status of לִשְׁמוֹ, and the offering is invalid.

Rabbi Yirmeya rejects the kal vachomer: the case of שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמוֹ is different because it applies to all offerings, whereas לִשְׁמוֹ applies only to the pesach offering, so the argument does not hold.

Rava rules that the offering is valid, reasoning that since even when one slaughters it only with שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמוֹ intent, the default presumption is that it stands for לִשְׁמוֹ, yet it is valid, so here too the שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמוֹ intent removes it from its לִשְׁמוֹ status.

Rav Adda bar Ahava objects by drawing an analogy to the case of slaughtering for those who will eat it and those who will not eat it: there, when one slaughters only for those who will not eat it, it is invalid despite the default presumption, showing that explicit intent differs from implicit default.

Rava rejects the objection: in the case of לִשְׁמוֹ, the default is indeed certain, but in the case of those who will eat it, the default is not certain because people may withdraw and appoint others, as per the mishnah that one can withdraw until the slaughter.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeyah's attempted proof and rejection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah's attempted proof and rejection
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports an attempted proof by Rabbi Yirmeyah that since lishmah qualifies it in its time and shelo lishmah qualifies it out of its time, neither removes the other, making it invalid. Rabbi Yirmeyah rejects this, arguing that shelo lishmah applies to all sacrifices while lishmah applies only to pesach.
