sub.text: Rav Dimi reporting Rabbi Yirmeyah's attempted proof
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi reporting Rabbi Yirmeyah's attempted proof
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah attempts to prove that a pesach sacrificed with both lishmah and shelo lishmah is invalid, arguing by analogy that just as lishmah does not remove shelo lishmah, so shelo lishmah does not remove lishmah.
Rabbi Yirmeyah rejects his own proof, arguing that shelo lishmah applies to all sacrifices while lishmah applies only to the pesach, so the analogy fails.

items.text: Rava's ruling: it is valid
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: it is valid
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a pesach slaughtered during the rest of the year with both lishmah and shelo lishmah is valid, because shelo lishmah removes it from lishmah, just as when one slaughters it with only shelo lishmah it is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a pesach slaughtered during the rest of the year with both לִשְׁמוֹ (for its sake) and שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמוֹ (not for its sake) is valid, because the שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמוֹ intention removes it from the category of לִשְׁמוֹ, just as when one slaughters it with only שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמוֹ it is valid.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's objection and Rava's response
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's objection and Rava's response
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah objects by analogy to the case of 'for its eaters' and 'not for its eaters', where the latter alone is invalid but combined with the former it is valid, showing that stated intent differs from unstated. Rava responds that the cases are different: in the pesach case, the default is lishmah, but for eaters, the default is not for its eaters because people may withdraw.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah objects to Rava's ruling by drawing an analogy to the case of 'for its eaters' and 'not for its eaters', where stated intent differs from unstated intent.

Rava rejects the analogy, explaining that in the pesach case the default is לִשְׁמוֹ (for its sake), whereas regarding eaters the default is not for its eaters because people may withdraw from the offering until the moment of slaughter.

items.text: Question and discussion on change of owners
items.text_en: Question and discussion on change of owners
items.desc_en: A new question is raised: does a change of owners (shinui ba'alim) during the rest of the year render the pesach valid like a change of sanctity (shinui kodesh)? Rav Pappa presents a proof that it does, but Rava rejects it because shinui kodesh is a bodily defect and applies to four acts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does a change of owners (שינוי בעלים) during the rest of the year render the pesach valid, analogous to a change of sanctity (שינוי קודש), or not?

Rav Pappa presents a proof before Rava: just as a change of sanctity (שינוי קודש) disqualifies the pesach in its time and validates it after its time, so too a change of owners (שינוי בעלים) disqualifies it in its time and should validate it after its time.

Rava rejects the analogy: a change of sanctity (שינוי קודש) is a bodily defect (פסולו בגופו) and applies to four acts, whereas a change of owners (שינוי בעלים) is not a bodily defect, so the comparison fails.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to the distinction between change of owner and change of sanctity
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to the distinction between change of owner and change of sanctity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier distinction between change of owner and change of sanctity, noting that both involve a mere mental intention (מחשבה בעלמא) and thus should be similar. It also raises a difficulty from Rav Pinchas's opinion that change of owner applies after death, which would undermine one of the differentiating criteria.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier distinction between change of owner and change of sanctity, arguing that both involve mere mental intention (מחשבה בעלמא) and thus should be similar.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Rav Pinchas bar Rav Ami
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rav Pinchas bar Rav Ami
sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a further difficulty from Rav Pinchas's opinion that change of owner applies after death, which would undermine one of the differentiating criteria.

items.text: Rava's resolution: Pesach slaughtered with change of owner becomes ownerless
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: Pesach slaughtered with change of owner becomes ownerless
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by explaining that a Pesach slaughtered during the rest of the year with a change of owner is considered like an animal without owners at its proper time, and is therefore invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by redefining the case: a פסח (Passover offering) slaughtered during the rest of the year with a change of owner is treated like an ownerless offering at its proper time and is invalid.

items.text: Mishnah: Invalid and valid intentions for slaughtering the Pesach
items.text_en: Mishnah: Invalid and valid intentions for slaughtering the Pesach
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases: slaughtering not for its eaters or not for its registered members, or for uncircumcised or impure people, is invalid. But slaughtering for both eaters and non-eaters, for both its members and others, or for both circumcised and uncircumcised, or for both impure and pure, is valid. It also rules that slaughtering before noon is invalid, but slaughtering before the daily tamid offering is valid if someone stirs the blood until the tamid is offered.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for a פסח (Passover offering) slaughtered with improper intentions: for non-eaters or non-members it is invalid, but for mixed intentions it is valid, and it gives rules about timing relative to midday and the daily offering.
The Mishnah then lists valid cases: slaughtering for both eaters and non-eaters, for both its members and others, for both circumcised and uncircumcised, or for both impure and pure.
The Mishnah rules that slaughtering before noon is invalid because the verse specifies 'between the evenings'.
The Mishnah rules that slaughtering before the daily tamid offering is valid provided someone stirs the blood until the tamid is offered, and if the blood was sprinkled it is valid.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's cases
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's examples: 'not for its eaters' means slaughtering for a sick or elderly person; 'not for its registered members' means slaughtering for a different group than the one registered.

sub.desc_en: A baraita clarifies the Mishnah: 'not for its eaters' means for a sick or elderly person, and 'not for its members' means slaughtering for a different group.

items.text: Derivation of the law for slaughtering not for its registered members
items.text_en: Derivation of the law for slaughtering not for its registered members
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita deriving from the verse 'בְּמִכְסַת' that the Pesach may only be slaughtered for its registered members, and the repetition 'תָּכֹסּוּ' teaches that doing otherwise invalidates it. Rabbi offers an alternative explanation using Syriac idiom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source that the Pesach may only be slaughtered for its registered members.
A baraita is cited: the verse 'בְּמִכְסַת' teaches that the Pesach is only slaughtered for its registered members, and the repetition 'תָּכֹסּוּ' indicates that doing otherwise invalidates it.
Rabbi offers an alternative explanation: the word 'תָּכֹסּוּ' is Syriac idiom, like one saying 'count me this lamb'.

items.text: Derivation of the law for slaughtering not for its eaters
items.text_en: Derivation of the law for slaughtering not for its eaters
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the law regarding slaughtering not for its eaters, and answers that the verse 'אִישׁ לְפִי אׇכְלוֹ תָּכֹסּוּ' links eaters to registered members, implying the same invalidation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found the source for 'not for its members,' but from where do we derive the rule for 'not for its eaters'?
The Gemara answers that the verse 'איש לפי אכלו תכסו' (each according to his eating you shall count) links eaters to members, implying the same rule applies.

items.text: Opening dispute: Rav Chisda vs. Rabbah on intent of foreskin in sprinkling
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rav Chisda vs. Rabbah on intent of foreskin in sprinkling
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda holds that intent of foreskin invalidates the sprinkling, while Rabbah holds it does not. The dispute is framed around whether there is 'machshevet arelim' (intent of foreskin) in sprinkling.

sub.desc_en: Presents the case: one slaughtered the Pesach offering for those who are circumcised, intending that uncircumcised men achieve atonement through the sprinkling.
Rav Chisda rules the offering is invalid (פסול), because there is intent of foreskin (מחשבת ערלים) in the sprinkling.
Rabbah rules the offering is valid (כשר), because there is no intent of foreskin in the sprinkling.

items.text: Rabbah's proof from a baraita: analogy to impurity and time
items.text_en: Rabbah's proof from a baraita: analogy to impurity and time
items.desc_en: Rabbah cites a baraita that compares foreskin to impurity and time, concluding that partial foreskin does not invalidate. The baraita uses logical arguments (kal vachomer and hekesh) to show that only complete foreskin invalidates, and this applies to slaughter, not sprinkling.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah introduces his proof by asking what his source is.
The baraita begins with a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from impurity to foreskin, concluding that partial foreskin does not invalidate.
The baraita presents an alternative argument by analogy to time, which would treat partial foreskin as fully invalidating.
The baraita resolves the conflict by preferring the analogy to impurity over time, since both foreskin and impurity do not apply to all offerings.
The baraita adds another argument: foreskin is like impurity in that neither was ever permitted in general, unlike time which was permitted in some cases.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: Derivation from 'זאת' and 'וכל ערל'
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Derivation from 'זאת' and 'וכל ערל'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the baraita's conclusion: the verse 'זאת' teaches that only complete foreskin invalidates in slaughter, but in sprinkling even complete foreskin does not invalidate. The reason is that there is no 'machshevet ochlin' (intent of eaters) in sprinkling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's use of 'זאת' (this), noting that if it teaches that complete foreskin invalidates in slaughter but partial does not, this is already derived from 'וכל ערל' (and every uncircumcised person).

The Gemara reinterprets the baraita: 'וכל ערל' teaches that complete foreskin invalidates in slaughter but partial does not; 'זאת' then teaches that in sprinkling, even complete foreskin does not invalidate.
The Gemara explains the leniency of sprinkling: there is no מחשבת אוכלין (intent of eaters) in sprinkling, so the foreskin status of the eaters is irrelevant.

items.text: Rav Chisda's counter-interpretation: Sprinkling is stricter
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's counter-interpretation: Sprinkling is stricter
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda argues oppositely: the verse 'וכל ערל' implies any foreskin invalidates, but 'זאת' limits it to slaughter only for partial foreskin; in sprinkling, even partial foreskin invalidates. The stringency of sprinkling is because piggul (improper intent) is established only through sprinkling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda reverses the interpretation: the verse 'וכל ערל' teaches that only complete foreskin invalidates slaughter, but 'זאת' limits this leniency to slaughter alone, while in sprinkling even partial foreskin invalidates.

sub.text: Rav Chisda's anticipated objection and response
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda's anticipated objection and response
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda anticipates the objection that the same rule might apply to sprinkling, and counters that 'זאת' explicitly restricts the leniency to slaughter, while sprinkling invalidates even with partial foreskin.

sub.text: Rav Chisda's explanation of sprinkling's stringency
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda's explanation of sprinkling's stringency
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains the stringency of sprinkling: piggul (improper intent) is established only through sprinkling, making it a more critical act.

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection: Alternative reading of 'וכל ערל'
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection: Alternative reading of 'וכל ערל'
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges both interpretations: 'וכל ערל' might mean any amount of foreskin, and 'זאת' teaches that only complete foreskin invalidates, equally in slaughter and sprinkling. The dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbah remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that the phrase 'וכל ערל' might mean any amount of foreskin, and 'זאת' teaches that only complete foreskin invalidates, equally in slaughter and sprinkling, leaving the dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbah unresolved.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Chisda regarding the uncircumcised person
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Chisda regarding the uncircumcised person
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Chisda argue over the exclusion of an uncircumcised person from the Paschal offering based on the verse 'וְנִרְצָה לוֹ לְכַפֵּר עָלָיו'. Rabbah holds that the uncircumcised is excluded because he is not a 'bar kapara' (subject to atonement), while Rav Chisda argues that since he can rectify himself, he is a 'bar kapara'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Chisda regarding the exclusion of an uncircumcised person from the Paschal lamb, based on the verse 'וְנִרְצָה לוֹ לְכַפֵּר עָלָיו' (and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him), and presents Rabbah's position that the uncircumcised is excluded because he is not a 'בר כפרה' (subject to atonement).

Rav Chisda argues that the uncircumcised person is also considered a 'בר כפרה' (subject to atonement) because he is obligated to bring the Paschal lamb, since he can rectify himself through circumcision.

items.text: Contradiction in Rav Chisda's position on 'הואיל'
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rav Chisda's position on 'הואיל'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Chisda accepts the principle of 'הואיל' (since), citing a contradiction: regarding baking on Yom Tov for a weekday, Rav Chisda says one is liable, while Rabbah says he is not liable due to 'הואיל'. The Gemara resolves that Rav Chisda rejects 'הואיל' for leniency but accepts it for stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Chisda accepts the principle of 'הואיל' (since), citing a contradiction: regarding baking on Yom Tov for a weekday, Rav Chisda says one is liable, while Rabbah says he is not liable.
The Gemara explains that Rabbah invokes 'הואיל' (since) to exempt the baker, while Rav Chisda rejects 'הואיל' (since) and holds him liable.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: Rav Chisda rejects 'הואיל' (since) for leniency but accepts it for stringency.

items.text: Mar Zutra's question: comparing foreskin and impurity
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's question: comparing foreskin and impurity
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra asks Ravina about a teaching that compares foreskin (ערלה) and impurity (טומאה) regarding partial disqualification. He suggests that just as partial impurity does not disqualify (e.g., some men being impure among pure ones), partial foreskin also does not disqualify, as per a mishnah that mixed circumcised and uncircumcised is valid. He questions why impurity is clear but foreskin is uncertain.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra asks Ravina about a teaching comparing foreskin (ערלה) and impurity (טומאה), suggesting that just as partial impurity among men does not disqualify, partial foreskin also does not disqualify, citing a mishnah that mixed circumcised and uncircumcised is valid.
Mar Zutra questions why the case of impurity is clear to him while the case of foreskin is uncertain, given the parallel.

items.text: Attempt to interpret impurity as impurity of the meat
items.text_en: Attempt to interpret impurity as impurity of the meat
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the impurity in the comparison is impurity of the meat (טומאת בשר), where partial impurity means only the impure limb is burned. But then the continuation of the teaching (about 'אינו נוהג בכל הזבחים') contradicts this, as impurity of the meat applies to all offerings. The Gemara concludes that the beginning refers to impurity of the meat and the end to impurity of people, creating a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the impurity in the comparison is טומאת בשר (impurity of the meat), where partial impurity means only the impure limb is burned.

The Gemara objects that if the impurity is טומאת בשר (impurity of the meat), the continuation of the teaching (about 'אינו נוהג בכל הזבחים') contradicts this, as impurity of the meat applies to all offerings.
The Gemara concludes that the beginning refers to טומאת בשר (impurity of the meat) and the end to טומאת גברי (impurity of people), creating a difficulty.

items.text: Ravina's response: the term 'טומאה' is problematic
items.text_en: Ravina's response: the term 'טומאה' is problematic
items.desc_en: Ravina responds that the term 'טומאה' is being challenged (קָא פָרֵיךְ), implying that the inconsistency is due to the word 'טומאה' being used in different senses.

sub.desc_en: Ravina responds that the term 'טומאה' (ritual impurity) is being challenged (קָא פָרֵיךְ), meaning the inconsistency arises from the word 'טומאה' being used in different senses.

items.text: Alternative interpretation: both parts refer to impurity of the meat
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation: both parts refer to impurity of the meat
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: the entire teaching refers to impurity of the meat. The phrase 'אינו נוהג בכל הזבחים' means that for other offerings, whether fat or meat is impure, the blood is sprinkled, but for the Paschal offering, if the meat is impure, the blood is not sprinkled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative interpretation: the entire teaching refers to impurity of the meat, explaining that for other offerings the blood is sprinkled regardless of which part is impure.
The Gemara concludes the alternative explanation: for the Paschal offering, if the meat is impure the blood is not sprinkled, unlike other offerings.

items.text: Further challenge: the teaching about 'לא הותר מכללו'
items.text_en: Further challenge: the teaching about 'לא הותר מכללו'
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to challenge this interpretation by citing another part of the teaching that compares foreskin to impurity regarding 'דבר שלא הותר מכללו' (something not permitted in general), questioning whether impurity was permitted in general.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the interpretation that the teaching refers to impurity of the meat (טומאת בשר), by citing the continuation of the teaching about 'דבר שלא הותר מכללו' (something not permitted in general), and asks what type of impurity is meant.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's reference to impurity
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's reference to impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah refers to impurity of the flesh or impurity of the person, and resolves that the first clause deals with flesh impurity while the latter deals with person impurity, or alternatively that the entire Mishnah deals with flesh impurity but in the context of the Pesach offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's reference to impurity being permitted in the community refers to impurity of the flesh or impurity of the person, and suggests it must be person impurity.
The Gemara answers that the first clause of the Mishnah deals with flesh impurity while the latter deals with person impurity, as the term 'impurity' is contrasted.
Alternatively, the entire Mishnah deals with flesh impurity, but the permission is in the context of the Pesach offering brought in impurity, which is eaten in impurity.

items.text: Rav Huna's objection and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Huna's objection and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua objects based on a baraita about a Pesach that passed its year, where Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies and Rabbi Yehoshua validates. The Gemara questions why the same logic doesn't apply outside its time, and Rav Pappa resolves by citing a verse that establishes the rule for its proper time.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua objects by citing a baraita about a Pesach that passed its year, where Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies and Rabbi Yehoshua validates when slaughtered in its proper time for its own sake.

The Gemara questions why the baraita implies that outside its proper time the offering is valid, given the logic that if it is invalid for other purposes in its time, it should also be invalid outside its time.

Rav Pappa resolves by citing the verse 'וַאֲמַרְתֶּם זֶבַח פֶּסַח הוּא' (and you shall say, it is a Pesach sacrifice), teaching that only in its proper time does the rule apply that a Pesach-offering cannot be designated for other purposes and other offerings cannot be designated for it.

items.text: Rabbi Simlai's request to study the Book of Genealogies
items.text_en: Rabbi Simlai's request to study the Book of Genealogies
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai comes before Rabbi Yochanan to study the Book of Genealogies, but Rabbi Yochanan rebukes him for being from Lod and residing in Nehardea, and then criticizes his request to learn it in three months by comparing it to Berurya who studied 300 traditions daily yet took three years.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai comes before Rabbi Yochanan to study the Book of Genealogies, and after being questioned about his origin and residence, Rabbi Yochanan rebukes him and forces him to accept the rebuke.
Rabbi Simlai asks to study the Book of Genealogies in three months.
Rabbi Yochanan rebukes Rabbi Simlai by comparing his request to Berurya, who studied 300 traditions daily yet took three years to fulfill her obligation.

items.text: Distinction between 'for its sake' and 'for its eaters'
items.text_en: Distinction between 'for its sake' and 'for its eaters'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai asks Rabbi Yochanan about the difference between offering for its own sake versus not for its own sake, and for its eaters versus not for its eaters. Rabbi Yochanan explains that the former is a disqualification in the body, cannot be clarified, applies to four services, and applies to the community as to an individual, while the latter does not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai asks Rabbi Yochanan to explain the difference between offering for its own sake versus not for its own sake, and for its eaters versus not for its eaters.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the disqualification for 'for its sake' versus 'not for its sake' is in the body of the offering, while for 'for its eaters' versus 'not for its eaters' it is not.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the prohibition for 'for its sake' versus 'not for its sake' cannot be clarified, while for 'for its eaters' versus 'not for its eaters' it can.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's third and fourth distinctions
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's third and fourth distinctions
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that 'for its sake' applies to four services and to the community as to an individual, while 'for its eaters' does not.

items.text: Rav Ashi's consolidation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's consolidation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that the disqualification in the body and the inability to clarify its prohibition are one and the same, because the reason for disqualification in the body is precisely that its prohibition cannot be clarified.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves that the disqualification in the body and the inability to clarify its prohibition are one and the same, because the reason for disqualification in the body is precisely that its prohibition cannot be clarified.

items.text: The loss of the Book of Genealogies
items.text_en: The loss of the Book of Genealogies
items.desc_en: Rami bar Rav Yuda quotes Rav that since the Book of Genealogies was hidden, the strength of the sages weakened and their eyes dimmed. Mar Zutra adds that between the words 'atzel' and 'atzal' there was a load of four hundred camels of exposition.

sub.text: Rami bar Rav Yuda quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rami bar Rav Yuda quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rami bar Rav Yuda quotes Rav that since the Book of Genealogies was hidden, the sages' strength weakened and their eyes dimmed.
Mar Zutra adds that between the words 'atzel' and 'atzal' there was a load of four hundred camels of exposition.

items.text: Acherim's ruling on circumcised and uncircumcised
items.text_en: Acherim's ruling on circumcised and uncircumcised
items.desc_en: Acherim teach that if one brings circumcised before uncircumcised it is valid, but uncircumcised before circumcised is invalid. The Gemara questions why the reverse is not also valid, since in both cases the requirement of complete foreskin is not met.

sub.desc_en: Acherim teach that if one brings circumcised before uncircumcised it is valid, but uncircumcised before circumcised is invalid.
The Gemara questions why the reverse case is not also valid, since in both cases the requirement of complete foreskin is not met.

items.text: Initial proposal: Others hold slaughter is only at the end
items.text_en: Initial proposal: Others hold slaughter is only at the end
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the 'Others' (Acherim) hold that slaughter is valid only at the end, following Rava's view. This leads to a ruling: if one designated the slaughter for the circumcised before the uncircumcised, the circumcised count, but if the order was reversed, the uncircumcised count.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the 'Others' (Acherim) hold that slaughter is valid only at the end, consistent with Rava's view that the dispute remains unresolved.
The Gemara derives a ruling: if one designated the circumcised before the uncircumcised, the circumcised count; if the order was reversed, the uncircumcised count.

items.text: Rabba's rejection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rabba's rejection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rabba rejects the initial proposal, asserting that the Others hold slaughter is valid from beginning to end. He explains the case as one where the slaughterer intended both groups in his heart but only verbalized 'for the uncircumcised' before the slaughter was completed. The dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis is whether we require his mouth and heart to be consistent.

sub.desc_en: Rabba rejects the initial proposal, asserting that the Others hold slaughter is valid from beginning to end, and explains the case as one where the slaughterer intended both groups in his heart but only verbalized 'for the uncircumcised' before the slaughter was completed.
Rabba resolves that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis is whether we require his mouth and heart to be consistent (פיו ולבו שוים).

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Meir's position from a baraita
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Meir's position from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the attribution to Rabbi Meir that he does not require mouth and heart to be consistent, citing a baraita where one who intends to say 'terumah' but says 'maaser' has said nothing until his mouth and heart are consistent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Meir's position by citing a baraita that requires mouth and heart to be consistent for a valid utterance.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: distinction between first and second signs
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: distinction between first and second signs
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the first and second signs. In the first case, where the first sign was for the circumcised and the second also for the uncircumcised, the circumcised are included in the second sign. In the second case, where the first sign was for the uncircumcised and the second for the circumcised, the circumcised are not included in the first sign. This aligns with Rabbi Meir's view that one can achieve piggul with half a permitting factor, and the Rabbis' view that one cannot.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the first and second signs: in the first case, circumcised are included in the second sign; in the second case, they are not included in the first sign.
Abaye's resolution aligns with Rabbi Meir's view that one can achieve piggul with half a permitting factor, and the Rabbis' view that one cannot.

items.text: Mishnah: Slaughtering the Pesach while leaven is present
items.text_en: Mishnah: Slaughtering the Pesach while leaven is present
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who slaughters the Pesach offering while leaven is in his possession violates a negative commandment. Rabbi Yehuda extends this to the daily offering. Rabbi Shimon distinguishes: on the 14th, slaughtering the Pesach for its own name is liable, not for its own name is exempt; other offerings are exempt. During the festival, slaughtering the Pesach for its own name is exempt, not for its own name is liable; other offerings are liable, except for a sin-offering slaughtered not for its own name.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one who slaughters the Pesach offering while leaven is in his possession violates a negative commandment.
Rabbi Yehuda extends the prohibition to the daily offering (תמיד).
Rabbi Shimon distinguishes: on the 14th, slaughtering the Pesach for its own name is liable, not for its own name is exempt; other offerings are exempt.

Rabbi Shimon continues: during the festival, slaughtering the Pesach for its own name is exempt, not for its own name is liable; other offerings are liable, except for a sin-offering slaughtered not for its own name.

items.text: Gemara: Resh Lakish's condition for liability
items.text_en: Gemara: Resh Lakish's condition for liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with Resh Lakish stating that one is never liable unless the leaven belongs to the slaughterer or the one who throws the blood.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that one is never liable for slaughtering the pesach (Passover offering) on chametz (leaven) unless the chametz belongs to the slaughterer or the one who throws the blood.

items.text: Opening dispute: Rabbi Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish on 'על' בסמוך
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rabbi Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish on 'על' בסמוך
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding whether the prohibition of slaughtering the paschal lamb while having leaven requires the leaven to be nearby ('על' בסמוך). Rabbi Yochanan holds it is not required, while Reish Lakish holds it is. The Gemara questions whether they already argued about this elsewhere.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule that the prohibition applies when the leaven belongs to the slaughterer or a group member, requiring proximity in the courtyard.
Rabbi Yochanan states that the prohibition applies even if the leaven is not with him in the courtyard.
The Gemara asks: over what principle do they disagree?
The Gemara suggests they disagree about whether the word 'על' (upon) requires proximity ('בסמוך').
The Gemara objects: but they already argued about this elsewhere, so why repeat it here?

items.text: Proof from the thanksgiving offering dispute
items.text_en: Proof from the thanksgiving offering dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about slaughtering a thanksgiving offering inside the Temple while its bread is outside the wall, and notes that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish already argued about 'על' בסמוך in that context. Rabbi Yochanan holds that the bread is sanctified even if outside the Temple courtyard, while Reish Lakish requires the bread to be nearby.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: one who slaughters a thanksgiving offering inside the Temple and its bread outside the wall — the bread is not sanctified.

The Gemara asks: what does 'outside the wall' mean? Rabbi Yochanan explains: outside the wall of Beit Pagei, but outside the Temple courtyard wall — the bread is sanctified, and we do not require 'על' (upon) in proximity.
Reish Lakish says: even outside the Temple courtyard wall, the bread is not sanctified, indicating that 'על' (upon) requires proximity.

items.text: Alternative explanation: dispute about התראת ספק
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: dispute about התראת ספק
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute might be about whether a doubtful warning (התראת ספק) is considered a valid warning. It cites a case of a vow to eat a loaf today, where Rabbi Yochanan holds that one is not lashed because it is a prohibition without an action, while Reish Lakish holds that one is not lashed because it is a doubtful warning. This shows they already argued about this as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish is about whether a doubtful warning (התראת ספק) is considered a valid warning, but immediately notes that they have already argued about this as well.

The Gemara cites a case of a vow to eat a loaf today, where Rabbi Yochanan holds that one is not lashed because it is a prohibition without an action, while Reish Lakish holds that one is not lashed because it is a doubtful warning, showing they already argued about this.
Reish Lakish states that one is not lashed because it is a doubtful warning (התראת ספק), but for a prohibition without an action, one is lashed.

items.text: Resolution: both disputes are necessary
items.text_en: Resolution: both disputes are necessary
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the dispute is indeed about 'על' בסמוך, and both cases are necessary. If only the leaven case were taught, one might think Rabbi Yochanan's leniency applies only there because leaven is a prohibition that exists wherever it is. If only the bread case were taught, one might think Reish Lakish's strictness applies only there because sanctification requires proximity. Thus both are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: they indeed disagree about 'על' (upon) requiring proximity, and both disputes are necessary.
The Gemara explains: if they had only argued about leaven, one might think Rabbi Yochanan's leniency is because the prohibition is inherent wherever the leaven is.

The Gemara continues: but regarding sanctification of bread, one might think Reish Lakish's stringency applies because the bread is sanctified only inside, requiring proximity — thus both disputes are necessary.

The Gemara adds: conversely, if only the sanctification case were taught, one might think Reish Lakish's stringency is limited to that context, but regarding leaven he would agree with Rabbi Yochanan — thus both are necessary.

items.text: Rav Oshaya's inquiry: leaven belonging to another member of the group
items.text_en: Rav Oshaya's inquiry: leaven belonging to another member of the group
items.desc_en: Rav Oshaya asks Rabbi Ami whether the prohibition applies when the leaven belongs to another member of the group but not to the slaughterer. Rabbi Ami answers that the verse says 'על חמץ' not 'על חמצך', implying it applies to any leaven. Rav Oshaya then asks if it applies even to someone at the end of the world, and Rabbi Ami limits it to those who are subject to the prohibition of 'לא ילין' (not leaving the meat overnight).

sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya asks Rabbi Ami: if the leaven does not belong to the slaughterer but to a group member, what is the law?
Rabbi Ami answers: the verse says 'על חמץ' (upon leaven), not 'על חמצך' (upon your leaven), so the prohibition applies regardless of ownership.
Rav Oshaya objects: if so, even if the leaven belongs to someone at the end of the world, the prohibition would apply?

Rabbi Ami answers: the verse juxtaposes 'לא תשחט' (do not slaughter) with 'לא ילין' (do not leave overnight), limiting the prohibition to those who are subject to the law of 'לא ילין' (i.e., those who can bring the meat to the altar).

items.text: Rav Papa's ruling: the priest who burns the fats also transgresses
items.text_en: Rav Papa's ruling: the priest who burns the fats also transgresses
items.desc_en: Rav Papa rules that the priest who burns the fats (מקטיר את החלב) also transgresses the prohibition, because he is included in the category of those who might cause the fats to be left overnight (הלנת אימורין).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules: therefore, a priest who burns the fats (אימורים) on the altar violates the prohibition, since he is included in the law of 'לא ילין' (not leaving overnight).

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Papa and resolution of contradiction
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Papa and resolution of contradiction
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Papa, stating that the slaughterer, the one who throws the blood, and the one who burns the fats are all liable. However, another baraita includes the one who pinches the bird (מולק) and the one who sprinkles (מזה) but excludes the one who burns the fats. The Gemara notes the contradiction and implies that the second baraita is from Rabbi Yehuda who adds the daily offering, but the Sages disagree.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Papa, listing the slaughterer, the one who throws the blood, and the one who burns the fats as liable, but the one who pinches the bird (מולק) is exempt.
The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing another baraita that includes the one who pinches (מולק) and the one who sprinkles (מזה) but excludes the one who burns the fats.
The Gemara implies that the second baraita is from Rabbi Yehuda, who adds the daily offering, but the Sages disagree, thereby resolving the contradiction.

items.text: Resolving contradictions in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Resolving contradictions in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two Mishnayot regarding melikah and haqtarah on Pesach versus Chol HaMoed. It resolves the melikah contradiction by attributing both statements to Rabbi Shimon, distinguishing between the 14th of Nisan and Chol HaMoed. The haqtarah contradiction is resolved by noting a dispute among Tanna'im whether haqtarah is compared to shechitah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two Mishnayot regarding melikah (pinching the neck) and haqtarah (burning) on Pesach versus Chol HaMoed.
The Gemara resolves the melikah contradiction by attributing both statements to Rabbi Shimon, distinguishing between the 14th of Nisan and Chol HaMoed.
The Gemara resolves the haqtarah contradiction by noting a dispute among Tanna'im whether haqtarah is compared to shechitah.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon on 'zivchi'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon on 'zivchi'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasoning of Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon regarding the verse 'zivchi'. Rabbi Yehudah interprets 'zivchi' as 'my unique sacrifice', referring to the daily offering (Tamid). Rabbi Shimon reads the double occurrence of 'zivchi' as 'zebach' and 'zevachai', implying that when there is a 'zebach' (Pesach), one is not liable for 'zevachai' (other sacrifices), but when there is no 'zebach', one is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Yehudah's reasoning and explains that he interprets 'zivchi' as 'my unique sacrifice', referring to the daily offering (Tamid).
The Gemara explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: the double occurrence of 'zivchi' is read as 'zebach' and 'zevachai', distinguishing between the Pesach and other sacrifices.
The Gemara resolves the halachic implication: when there is a 'zebach' (Pesach), one is not liable for 'zevachai' (other sacrifices), but when there is no 'zebach', one is liable.

items.text: Implication of the Mishnah regarding Pesach in the rest of the year
items.text_en: Implication of the Mishnah regarding Pesach in the rest of the year
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if one slaughters a Pesach offering for its own sake during the rest of the year, it is valid, but if not for its own sake, it is invalid. This implies that a Pesach offering in the rest of the year requires a designation (aqirah). Rabbi Chiyya bar Gamda clarifies that this refers to a case where the owners were impure and deferred to the second Pesach, so the animal is presumed to be for Pesach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if one slaughters a Pesach offering for its own sake during the rest of the year, it is exempt, but if not for its own sake, it is invalid; this implies that an unspecified slaughter is exempt.

The Gemara questions why an unspecified slaughter is exempt, since a Pesach offering in the rest of the year is considered a peace-offering (שלמים), and concludes that this implies a Pesach offering in the rest of the year requires a designation (עקירה).
Rabbi Chiyya bar Gamda clarifies that the case involves owners who were impure from a corpse and deferred to the second Pesach, so the animal is presumed to be for Pesach (פסח).

items.text: Mishnah: The three-group slaughter of the Pesach
items.text_en: Mishnah: The three-group slaughter of the Pesach
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for slaughtering the Pesach offering in three groups, based on the verse 'kol kehal adat Yisrael'. It details the entry of each group, the arrangement of the priests with silver and gold bowls, the passing of the blood, and the sprinkling. It also discusses the recitation of Hallel, the procedure on Shabbat, and the method of hanging and flaying the animal.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the Pesach offering is slaughtered in three groups, based on the verse 'כל קהל עדת ישראל' (the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel), interpreting the three terms קהל, עדה, and ישראל.

The Mishnah describes the entry of the first group, the locking of the courtyard gates, the blasts of the shofar, and the arrangement of the priests with silver and gold bowls without bases to prevent the blood from congealing.
The Mishnah details the slaughter by an Israelite, the passing of the blood from priest to priest, and the final sprinkling by the priest nearest the altar in a single throw against the base.

The Mishnah describes the exit of each group and the entry of the next, the recitation of Hallel (which may be repeated or tripled), and Rabbi Yehudah's statement that the third group never reached 'אהבתי כי ישמע ה׳' because the people were few.

The Mishnah states that the procedure on Shabbat is the same as on a weekday, except that the priests wash the courtyard against the sages' will; Rabbi Yehudah adds that a cup of mixed blood was sprinkled in one throw, but the sages disagreed.

The Mishnah concludes by describing how the animals were hung and flayed using iron hooks fixed in walls and pillars, or with thin smooth poles placed on shoulders, and Rabbi Eliezer adds that there were fourteen such hooks.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for slaughtering the Pesach when it falls on Shabbat, including how the animal is hung and skinned, and the removal of the sacrificial parts. It then describes the three groups of people involved and when they leave to roast their Pesach.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for slaughtering the Pesach when it falls on Shabbat, including hanging, skinning, removing sacrificial parts, and the three groups leaving to roast their Pesach.

items.text: Gemara's derivation of three groups
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation of three groups
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that the Pesach must be slaughtered by three groups of thirty people each, derived from the words 'kahal', 'edah', and 'yisrael'. The Gemara explains that this covers both possibilities: whether the groups come simultaneously or sequentially, and notes that fifty would suffice if they rotate.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that the Pesach is slaughtered only by three groups of thirty people each.
The Gemara asks the reason, and Rabbi Yitzchak answers that it derives from the three terms 'קהל', 'עדה', and 'ישראל'.
The Gemara resolves the doubt whether the groups enter simultaneously or sequentially by requiring three groups of thirty, and notes that fifty would also suffice with sequential entry.

items.text: Dispute about locking the courtyard
items.text_en: Dispute about locking the courtyard
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava dispute the correct reading of the Mishnah: Abaye says 'were locked' (נִנְעֲלוּ), implying reliance on a miracle, while Rava says 'they lock' (נוֹעֲלִין), implying no reliance on a miracle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute between Abaye and Rava about the correct version of the Mishnah: 'נִנְעֲלוּ' (were locked) or 'נוֹעֲלִין' (they lock).
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two versions.
The Gemara explains that the difference is whether one may rely on a miracle: Abaye's version allows relying on a miracle, while Rava's does not.

items.text: Support from a baraita about Akavya ben Mahalalel
items.text_en: Support from a baraita about Akavya ben Mahalalel
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says the courtyard was never locked for anyone as wise and God-fearing as Akavya ben Mahalalel. Abaye and Rava each reconcile this with their respective readings of the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited about Akavya ben Mahalalel, stating that the Temple courtyard was never locked on a person of his wisdom and fear of sin.
Abaye and Rava each reconcile the baraita with their own version of the Mishnah: Abaye reads 'נִנְעֲלָה' (was locked) and Rava reads 'נוֹעֲלִין' (they lock).
Rava reconciles the baraita with his reading that they would lock (נוֹעֲלִין) the courtyard, explaining that it was never locked for anyone as wise and God-fearing as Akavya.

items.text: Stories about crowding in the courtyard
items.text_en: Stories about crowding in the courtyard
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one about a Pesach called 'Pesach Me'uchin' where an old man was crushed, and another about King Agrippas who counted the kidneys of the Pesach offerings, finding 600,000 pairs, with each Pesach having at least ten people.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts that no one was ever crushed in the courtyard except during one Pesach in Hillel's time, when an old man was crushed, and that Pesach was called 'Pesach Me'uchin' (the crushed Pesach).

A second baraita relates that King Agrippas counted the kidneys of the Pesach offerings, finding 600,000 pairs, with each Pesach having at least ten people, and that Pesach was called 'Pesach Me'ubbin' (the crowded Pesach).

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution about the kidneys
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution about the kidneys
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that taking the kidneys would interfere with their burning, but resolves that Agrippas only took a token piece until they gave him something else.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that taking a kidney would prevent its burning, and cites a verse requiring each animal's fats to be offered separately.
The Gemara initially suggests that the kidneys were burned one by one, but then objects that a verse requires all fats to be burned together.
The Gemara resolves that Agrippas merely took a token from each, until they gave him something else.
The Gemara resolves that Agrippas only took a token piece (תְּפִיסָה בְּעָלְמָא) from each animal, holding it until they gave him something else, without actually removing the kidney for burning.

items.text: Reason for priests standing in rows
items.text_en: Reason for priests standing in rows
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the priests stood in rows: not to prevent theft of gold for silver, but because it is more proper.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the priests stand in rows, and after considering a concern about swapping gold and silver vessels, concludes that it is simply more proper.

The Gemara suggests the rows were to prevent priests from secretly substituting gold vessels for silver ones, but rejects this because the same concern would apply to substituting a 200-shekel vessel for a 100-shekel one.
The Gemara concludes that the rows were simply for the sake of proper order and dignity.

items.text: Basins without bases
items.text_en: Basins without bases
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that all basins in the Temple had no bases except those for the frankincense of the showbread, to prevent the bread from breaking.

sub.desc_en: A baraita explains that all Temple bowls had no bases, except for the frankincense bowls of the showbread, to prevent the bread from being set down and broken.
A baraita explains that all Temple basins lacked bases except those for the frankincense of the showbread, to prevent the bread from breaking when placed down.

items.text: Slaughter by a non-priest and reception by a priest
items.text_en: Slaughter by a non-priest and reception by a priest
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that slaughter is valid by a non-priest, and from reception onward it is a priestly mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies that an Israelite slaughters, and answers that it teaches that slaughter by a non-priest is valid, and that from reception onward it is a priestly duty.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches two points: slaughter is valid by a non-priest (זר), and from reception onward it is a priestly mitzvah (מצות כהונה).

items.text: Carrying without walking is valid
items.text_en: Carrying without walking is valid
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that carrying without moving the feet is considered valid 'holakhah', and also that it teaches 'be'rov am hadrat melekh'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether passing the blood to another priest constitutes valid 'הולכה' (carrying) without walking, and concludes that it teaches the principle of 'ברב עם הדרת מלך' (in a multitude of people is the king's glory).
The Gemara rejects the inference, suggesting the Mishnah may involve slight movement, and instead teaches the principle of 'be'rov am hadrat melekh'.

items.text: Support for Resh Lakish about not passing over mitzvot
items.text_en: Support for Resh Lakish about not passing over mitzvot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's rule that one receives a full vessel and returns an empty one supports Resh Lakish's principle that one does not pass over mitzvot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's rule of receiving a full bowl and returning an empty one supports Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's principle that one does not pass over mitzvot.

items.text: Source for Pesach requiring sprinkling and foundation
items.text_en: Source for Pesach requiring sprinkling and foundation
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Tanna who holds that Pesach requires sprinkling as Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who derives from the verse that bechor, ma'aser, and Pesach require blood and sacrificial parts on the altar. Rabbi Elazar then derives from a gezeirah shavah that they also require the foundation of the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that the Pesach offering requires sprinkling of blood.
Rav Chisda answers that the Tanna is Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
A baraita is cited in which Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives from the verse that bechor, ma'aser, and Pesach require blood and sacrificial parts on the altar.
The Gemara asks from where it is derived that these offerings also require the foundation of the altar.
Rabbi Elazar derives via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'זריקה' (sprinkling) used in the Pesach verse and in the olah verse that Pesach also requires the foundation of the altar.

items.text: Source for olah requiring the foundation
items.text_en: Source for olah requiring the foundation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where we derive that an olah requires the foundation of the altar, and answers from the verse 'el yesod mizbach ha'olah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that an olah itself requires the foundation of the altar.
The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'אֶל יְסוֹד מִזְבַּח הָעוֹלָה' (to the foundation of the altar of the olah), proving that an olah requires the foundation.

items.text: The first group called lazy
items.text_en: The first group called lazy
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the first group left, and a beraita calls them the lazy group. The Gemara questions what else they could have done, and answers that they should have hurried themselves, citing Rabbi's analogy about the necessity of perfumers and tanners.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states that the first group is called the lazy group.
The Gemara questions what else they could have done, since it was unavoidable.
The Gemara answers that even so, they should have hurried themselves.
Rabbi provides an analogy: just as the world needs both perfumers and tanners, one should strive to be in the better profession, so too the group should have hurried.

items.text: Dispute about shevut in the Temple
items.text_en: Dispute about shevut in the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion the Mishnah refers to when it says 'ke'ma'asehu bechol' (like its weekday practice). Rav Chisda says it is against Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that certain labors are prohibited by Torah law, while the Sages say they are only shevut, which is permitted in the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion the Mishnah's phrase 'ke'ma'asehu bechol' (like its weekday practice) opposes.
Rav Chisda answers that the Mishnah opposes Rabbi Eliezer, because the Sages hold that these labors are only shevut (rabbinic prohibition), which is permitted in the Temple.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Eliezer holds that these labors are Torah-prohibited (liable to a sin-offering or lashes), while the Sages say they are only shevut.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi suggests that the Mishnah could even be against the Sages, according to Rabbi Natan, who distinguishes between necessary and unnecessary shevut.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi proposes that the Mishnah's phrase 'שלא ברצון חכמים' (not with the Sages' approval) could even refer to the Sages themselves, and the Mishnah follows Rabbi Natan's distinction.
Rav Ashi cites a baraita where Rabbi Natan rules that a shevut (rabbinic prohibition) that is necessary for the Temple service was permitted, but one that is unnecessary was not permitted.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's cup of mixed blood
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's cup of mixed blood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Yehuda would fill a cup from the mixture of bloods. A beraita explains that this was to enable a sacrifice if one animal's blood spilled. The Sages question how one knows the blood was received in a vessel, and the Gemara answers that priests are diligent, though their diligence can cause spillage.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Yehuda would fill a cup from the mixture of bloods.
A beraita explains that Rabbi Yehuda's cup was to enable a sacrifice if one animal's blood spilled.
The Sages object that one cannot know whether the blood was received in a vessel.
Rabbi Yehuda responds that he only spoke of a case where the blood was received in a vessel.
The Gemara asks how one knows the blood was received in a vessel.
The Gemara answers that priests are diligent and would ensure proper reception.
The Gemara objects that if priests are diligent, why would blood spill?
The Gemara resolves that due to their haste, spillage can occur.

items.text: Issue of dam hatamtzit and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Issue of dam hatamtzit and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the problem that the blood of the tamtzit (the blood that oozes after the initial flow) is mixed in. It explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds that dam hatamtzit is considered valid blood, though Rabbi Elazar notes that he concedes it does not effect atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the objection that the blood of the tamtzit (the blood that oozes after the initial flow) is mixed into the cup of mixed bloods.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda follows his own consistent view that dam hatamtzit (the oozing blood) is considered valid blood (דם מעליא).
A baraita is cited: regarding dam hatamtzit, the Sages say it is subject to a negative prohibition (אזהרה), while Rabbi Yehuda says it is subject to karet (הכרת).
Rabbi Elazar objects that Rabbi Yehuda concedes that dam hatamtzit does not effect atonement (כפרה).
The Gemara cites the verse 'כי הדם הוא בנפש יכפר' (For the blood itself atones through the life) to support that only the lifeblood, not the oozing blood, effects atonement.

items.text: Blood that atones vs. blood that does not
items.text_en: Blood that atones vs. blood that does not
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that blood from which the soul departs atones, while blood from which the soul does not depart does not atone, and attributes Rabbi Yehuda's view to his principle that blood does not nullify blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that blood from which the soul departs atones, while blood from which the soul does not depart does not atone, and attributes Rabbi Yehuda's view to his principle that blood does not nullify blood.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's response to the Sages about blood in the courtyard
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's response to the Sages about blood in the courtyard
items.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Yehuda asking the Sages why they block the courtyard if blood does not nullify blood. The Sages reply that it is praiseworthy for the sons of Aaron to walk in blood up to their ankles. The Gemara questions whether this blood interposes, and answers that wet blood does not interpose, citing a baraita.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda's question to the Sages
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's question to the Sages
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda asks the Sages why they block the courtyard if blood does not nullify blood.
The Sages reply that it is praiseworthy for the sons of Aaron to walk in blood up to their ankles.
The Gemara objects that the blood interposes between the priests' feet and the ground.
The Gemara answers that wet blood does not interpose.
A baraita is cited that dry substances interpose but wet ones do not.

items.text: Concern about priests' garments and the solution of carrying organs on the ramp
items.text_en: Concern about priests' garments and the solution of carrying organs on the ramp
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a problem: if the priests' garments become soiled with blood, their service is invalid. It suggests they lift their garments, but that would violate the requirement that the priest's garments be of exact measure. The Gemara resolves that carrying organs to the ramp is not considered service, so the garments may be lifted. It then clarifies that carrying organs to the ramp is indeed service, so the solution is carrying wood to the pyre, which is not service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the priests' garments become soiled with blood, their service is invalid, citing the mishna that soiled garments disqualify the service.
The Gemara rejects the possible solution that the priests lifted their garments, citing the baraita that the priestly garments must be of exact measure, not shortened or lengthened.
The Gemara initially resolves that the priests walked in blood while carrying limbs to the ramp, which is not considered service, so the garments may be lifted.
The Gemara objects that carrying limbs to the ramp is indeed service, as it requires priesthood, citing the baraita that the verse 'וְהִקְרִיב הַכֹּהֵן' refers to this carrying.

The Gemara resolves that the priests walked in blood while carrying wood to the pyre, which is not considered service, so the garments may be lifted without violating the requirement of exact measure.

items.text: How priests walk with organs and blood
items.text_en: How priests walk with organs and blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when carrying organs to the ramp and blood, the priests walk on planks (אִיצְטְבֵי) to avoid the blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by stating that when carrying the limbs to the ramp and the blood, the priests walk on planks (אִיצְטְבֵי) to avoid soiling their garments.

items.text: How to hang and flay the Pesach offering
items.text_en: How to hang and flay the Pesach offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the process of hanging, flaying, and removing the sacrificial parts. The Gemara clarifies that the phrase 'to burn them' means to burn them on the altar, not that the priest himself burns them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for hanging, flaying, and removing the sacrificial parts of the Pesach offering.
The Gemara questions whether the priest himself burns the parts, given the Mishnah's phrasing.
The Gemara clarifies that the phrase 'to burn them' means to burn them on the altar, not that the priest himself performs the burning.

items.text: The first group leaves and each carries his Pesach
items.text_en: The first group leaves and each carries his Pesach
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that each person places his Pesach in its skin and slings it over his shoulder. Rav Ilish comments that this is like the practice of Tayya'ei (Arabs).

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that each person places his Pesach in its skin and slings it over his shoulder.
Rav Ilish comments that this practice is like that of the Tayya'ei (Arabs).

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that we have concluded the chapter 'Tamid Nishchat'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara formally concludes the chapter 'Tamid Nishchat' with the standard closing formula.

items.text: Mishnah: Which Pesach activities override Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Which Pesach activities override Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists activities that override Shabbat for the Pesach: slaughter, blood sprinkling, removal of innards, and burning of fats. Roasting and washing innards do not override. Carrying, bringing from outside the techum, and cutting a blemish do not override, but Rabbi Eliezer says they do.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists which Pesach activities override Shabbat and which do not, concluding with Rabbi Eliezer's dissenting opinion that carrying, bringing from outside the techum, and cutting a blemish do override.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Akiva about overriding Shabbat
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Akiva about overriding Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that if slaughter, which is a melacha, overrides Shabbat, then activities that are only shevut should certainly override. Rabbi Yehoshua counters that Yom Tov proves otherwise, as melacha is permitted but shevut is not. Rabbi Akiva adds that sprinkling (haza'ah) is a mitzvah but shevut and does not override Shabbat. Rabbi Eliezer then argues that sprinkling itself should override Shabbat by a kal vachomer from slaughter.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer opens with a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if slaughter, which is a melacha (forbidden labor), overrides Shabbat, then these activities, which are only shevut (rabbinic prohibitions), should certainly override Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects that Yom Tov proves the opposite: melacha is permitted but shevut is forbidden, so the kal vachomer is invalid.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer's rejection of the analogy
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's rejection of the analogy
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rejects the analogy, arguing that Yom Tov is a case of a permitted activity (רשות) while the Pesach sacrifice is a mitzvah (commandment), so the comparison is invalid.
Rabbi Akiva objects that sprinkling (haza'ah) proves the opposite: it is a mitzvah but only shevut, yet it does not override Shabbat, so the kal vachomer fails.
Rabbi Eliezer responds with a new kal vachomer: if slaughter, a melacha, overrides Shabbat, then sprinkling, which is only shevut, should certainly override Shabbat.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer dispute whether the Paschal lamb overrides Shabbat
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer dispute whether the Paschal lamb overrides Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva argues by kal vachomer that if sprinkling (a shevut) does not override Shabbat, then slaughter (a melachah) certainly should not. Rabbi Eliezer counters with the verse 'bemo'ado' (in its appointed time), which includes Shabbat. Rabbi Akiva then states his principle: any labor that can be done before Shabbat does not override Shabbat, but slaughter, which cannot be done before Shabbat, does override it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva argues by kal vachomer (a fortiori) that if sprinkling (הזאה), a shevut (rabbinic prohibition), does not override Shabbat, then slaughter (שחיטה), a melachah (Torah labor), certainly should not override Shabbat.
Rabbi Eliezer objects that Rabbi Akiva's argument uproots the Torah verse 'במועדו' (in its appointed time), which includes Shabbat as a valid time for the Paschal lamb.

Rabbi Akiva responds by stating his general principle: any labor that can be performed before Shabbat does not override Shabbat, but slaughter, which cannot be done before Shabbat, does override Shabbat.

items.text: The Bnei Beteira forget the law and summon Hillel
items.text_en: The Bnei Beteira forget the law and summon Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story: the Bnei Beteira forgot whether the Paschal lamb overrides Shabbat when the 14th of Nisan falls on Shabbat. They recall Hillel, who studied under Shemayah and Avtalyon, and summon him to ask.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the story: the Bnei Beteira forgot the law of whether the Paschal lamb overrides Shabbat, and they recall Hillel as someone who might know.
The Bnei Beteira summon Hillel and ask him whether the Paschal lamb overrides Shabbat.
Hillel responds rhetorically, noting that there are many more than two hundred Paschal lambs each year that override Shabbat, implying the question is trivial.

items.text: Hillel's proofs: gezerah shavah and kal vachomer
items.text_en: Hillel's proofs: gezerah shavah and kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Hillel first argues by gezerah shavah: the word 'mo'ado' is used for both the Paschal lamb and the daily tamid offering, just as the tamid overrides Shabbat, so does the Paschal lamb. He then adds a kal vachomer: if the tamid, which is not punishable by karet, overrides Shabbat, then the Paschal lamb, which is punishable by karet, certainly should.

sub.desc_en: The Bnei Beteira ask Hillel for the source of his claim that the Paschal lamb overrides Shabbat.

Hillel argues by גזירה שווה (verbal analogy): the word 'מועדו' (its appointed time) is used for both the Paschal lamb and the daily tamid offering, so just as the tamid overrides Shabbat, so does the Paschal lamb.
Hillel adds a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: if the tamid, which is not punishable by כרת (karet), overrides Shabbat, then the Paschal lamb, which is punishable by karet, certainly should.

items.text: Hillel appointed Nasi, rebukes them, and recalls a halakhah from practice
items.text_en: Hillel appointed Nasi, rebukes them, and recalls a halakhah from practice
items.desc_en: The Bnei Beteira immediately appoint Hillel as Nasi. He lectures all day and rebukes them for their laziness in not serving Shemayah and Avtalyon. When asked about a forgotten halakhah regarding bringing a knife on Shabbat, Hillel says he forgot but trusts Israel's intuition. The next day, observing the people's practice, he recalls the halakhah from Shemayah and Avtalyon.

sub.desc_en: The Bnei Beteira immediately appoint Hillel as Nasi, and he lectures all day on the laws of the Paschal offering.
Hillel rebukes the Bnei Beteira, attributing his rise to their laziness in not serving Shemayah and Avtalyon.
The Bnei Beteira ask Hillel about the law for one who forgot to bring a knife on Shabbat eve.
Hillel admits he forgot the halakhah but trusts Israel's intuition, saying they are sons of prophets.
The next day, observing the people's practice, Hillel recalls the halakhah from Shemayah and Avtalyon.

items.text: Gemara questions the gezerah shavah and provides the source for tamid overriding Shabbat
items.text_en: Gemara questions the gezerah shavah and provides the source for tamid overriding Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: how do we know the tamid itself overrides Shabbat? If from the word 'bemo'ado', the same word applies to the Paschal lamb, so it would be circular. Rather, the source is the verse 'olat Shabbat b'Shabbato al olat hatamid', which implies the tamid is offered even on Shabbat.

sub.text: Gemara's question on the source for tamid
sub.text_en: Gemara's question on the source for tamid
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the master said the verbal analogy from 'מועדו' in the tamid; but how do we know that the tamid itself overrides Shabbat? If from the same word 'מועדו', the Paschal lamb also has that word, so it would be circular.

The Gemara answers: the word 'מועדו' alone does not teach that it overrides Shabbat; rather, the verse 'עולת שבת בשבתו על עולת התמיד' (the Shabbat burnt-offering in addition to the daily burnt-offering) implies that the daily tamid offering is brought even on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara analyzes the kal vachomer and the order of Hillel's arguments
items.text_en: Gemara analyzes the kal vachomer and the order of Hillel's arguments
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the kal vachomer is refutable because the tamid is frequent (tadir) and wholly burnt (kalil). It explains that Hillel first presented the kal vachomer, which they refuted, and then the gezerah shavah. Since they could not derive a gezerah shavah on their own, Hillel rebuked them for not deriving the kal vachomer themselves, but they replied it was refutable.

sub.text: Gemara's question on the kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Gemara's question on the kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes the kal vachomer argument but points out it is refutable: the tamid is תדיר (frequent) and כליל (wholly burnt), so the Paschal lamb is not comparable; therefore Hillel first presented the kal vachomer, they refuted it, and then he presented the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy).

The Gemara asks: since the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) is sufficient, why did Hillel also present the kal vachomer? It answers: Hillel was addressing them, saying that since they could not derive a גזירה שווה on their own, they should have derived the kal vachomer themselves; they replied that the kal vachomer was refutable.
The Gemara asks why Hillel needed the kal vachomer if he already had the gezerah shavah.
The Gemara answers that Hillel was rebuking Bnei Beteira: since a gezerah shavah cannot be derived independently, they should have at least derived the kal vachomer themselves.
Bnei Beteira reply that the kal vachomer is refutable, so they could not derive it.

items.text: Gemara repeats the story of the next day's practice
items.text_en: Gemara repeats the story of the next day's practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara reiterates the detail: the next day, those with a lamb tucked it in its wool, and those with a goat tucked it between its horns.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara repeats the baraita's conclusion: the next day, those with a lamb stuck the knife in its wool, those with a goat between its horns.

items.text: Hillel's practice of bringing a voluntary burnt offering
items.text_en: Hillel's practice of bringing a voluntary burnt offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Hillel could bring a voluntary burnt offering on a festival, given the prohibition of performing labor on sacred animals. It cites a baraita that Hillel would bring the animal as unconsecrated to the Temple courtyard, then consecrate it, lean on it, and slaughter it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Hillel could perform labor (עבודה) with sacred animals on a festival.
A baraita is cited describing Hillel's practice: he would bring the animal unconsecrated (חולין) to the Temple courtyard, then consecrate it, lean on it, and slaughter it.

items.text: Sanctification on Shabbat for time-bound offerings
items.text_en: Sanctification on Shabbat for time-bound offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one cannot consecrate a Paschal lamb on Shabbat, citing a mishnah that prohibits consecration on festivals, let alone Shabbat. It resolves that this prohibition applies only to non-time-bound obligations, but for time-bound obligations like the Paschal lamb, consecration is permitted, as stated by Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one cannot consecrate a Paschal lamb on Shabbat, citing a mishnah that prohibits consecration on festivals, let alone Shabbat.
The Gemara resolves that the prohibition applies only to non-time-bound obligations, but for time-bound obligations like the Paschal lamb, consecration is permitted, citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.

items.text: The issue of digging (a rabbinic prohibition) for the Paschal lamb
items.text_en: The issue of digging (a rabbinic prohibition) for the Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the problem of digging (to find the knife) which is a rabbinic prohibition. It clarifies that the question was about a matter permitted by Torah law but with a rabbinic prohibition standing in the way, and whether one may override it for the sake of a mitzvah. Hillel responded that he had forgotten the halakhah but told them to leave it to Israel, for if they are not prophets, they are the children of prophets.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Hillel's action involved digging (a rabbinic prohibition), and clarifies that the digging was performed כלאחר יד (in an indirect manner).
The Gemara concedes that even indirect digging involves a rabbinic prohibition, though no Torah prohibition.
The Gemara explains that the Bnei Bathyra asked Hillel: when a Torah-permitted act is blocked only by a rabbinic prohibition, may one override it for the sake of a מצוה (commandment)?
Hillel responds that he had forgotten the halakhah, but tells them to leave the matter to Israel, for if they are not prophets, they are the children of prophets.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's teaching on arrogance causing loss of wisdom and prophecy
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's teaching on arrogance causing loss of wisdom and prophecy
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that anyone who is arrogant, if wise, loses his wisdom, and if a prophet, loses his prophecy. He proves this from Hillel (who forgot the halakhah after being arrogant) and from Deborah (whose prophecy was delayed due to arrogance).

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states the general principle: anyone who is arrogant loses their wisdom or prophecy.
The principle regarding a wise man is proven from Hillel, who forgot the halakhah after being arrogant.
The principle regarding a prophet is proven from Deborah, whose prophecy was delayed due to arrogance, as indicated by the verse 'עוּרִי עוּרִי דְּבוֹרָה' (Awake, awake, Deborah).

items.text: Reish Lakish's teaching on anger causing loss of wisdom and prophecy
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's teaching on anger causing loss of wisdom and prophecy
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that anyone who becomes angry, if wise, loses his wisdom, and if a prophet, loses his prophecy. He proves this from Moses (who forgot the halakhah of purification after anger) and from Elisha (who needed a musician to receive prophecy after anger).

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that anyone who becomes angry loses his wisdom if wise, and his prophecy if a prophet.
Reish Lakish proves the loss of wisdom from Moses, who forgot the law after becoming angry, as shown by the verse where Eleazar teaches the law that Moses had received.

Reish Lakish proves the loss of prophecy from Elisha, who after anger needed a musician to receive prophecy, as shown by the verses describing his anger at the king of Israel and the subsequent need for a musician.

items.text: Rabbi Mani bar Pattish on anger causing loss of greatness
items.text_en: Rabbi Mani bar Pattish on anger causing loss of greatness
items.desc_en: Rabbi Mani bar Pattish teaches that anyone who becomes angry, even if greatness was decreed for him from heaven, is brought down. He proves this from Eliab, who was rejected from kingship due to his anger at David.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Mani bar Pattish states that anyone who becomes angry, even if greatness was decreed from heaven, is brought down.
He proves this from Eliab, who was rejected from kingship due to his anger at David, as shown by the verses.

items.text: Deriving that the daily offering and Paschal lamb override impurity
items.text_en: Deriving that the daily offering and Paschal lamb override impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source that the daily offering (Tamid) and Paschal lamb override impurity. It first suggests a reciprocal derivation: as the Paschal lamb overrides Shabbat, so the daily offering overrides impurity. Then it questions the source for the Paschal lamb itself. Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse that an individual is deferred to the second Pesach, but the community is not deferred and instead offers in impurity. Reish Lakish objects and derives instead from the verse about sending out impure people from the camp, using a kal vachomer argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found that the daily offering (תמיד) and the Paschal lamb (פסח) override Shabbat, but from where do we derive that they override impurity (טומאה)?
The Gemara proposes a reciprocal derivation: just as the Paschal lamb learns from the daily offering regarding Shabbat, so too the daily offering learns from the Paschal lamb regarding impurity.
The Gemara asks: but the Paschal lamb itself — from where do we derive that it overrides impurity?

Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse 'אִישׁ אִישׁ כִּי יִהְיֶה טָמֵא לָנֶפֶשׁ' that an individual is deferred to the second Pesach, but the community is not deferred and instead offers the Paschal lamb in impurity.

Reish Lakish objects to Rabbi Yochanan's derivation: one could say that an individual is deferred to the second Pesach, but the community has no remedy at all — neither in the first nor the second Pesach.

Reish Lakish offers an alternative derivation from the verse 'וִישַׁלְּחוּ מִן הַמַּחֲנֶה' using a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: if those impure from a corpse are sent out of the camp, then those with a discharge (זבים) and lepers (מצורעים) — who are more stringent — are certainly sent out, implying that the community offers the Paschal lamb in impurity.

items.text: Redefining the kal va-chomer
items.text_en: Redefining the kal va-chomer
