items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the Mishnah's kal va-chomer actually proves the opposite: there is a time when zavim and metzoraim are sent away but tamei mei-tim are not—namely, Pesach brought in impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's kal va-chomer is flawed because there is a time when zavim and metzoraim are sent away but tamei mei-tim are not—namely, Pesach brought in impurity.

items.text: Abaye's initial challenge and the Mishnah's refutation
items.text_en: Abaye's initial challenge and the Mishnah's refutation
items.desc_en: Abaye proposes an alternative kal va-chomer to exclude metzora, but the Gemara notes that a Mishnah states that zavim and others may not eat from the Pesach brought in impurity, showing that the situation is not as he assumed.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes a kal va-chomer argument: if a zav is sent away from the Pesach brought in impurity, a metzora should certainly be sent away, so the verse should have omitted metzora.
The Gemara objects by citing a Mishnah that states that zavim and others may not eat from the Pesach brought in impurity, showing that Abaye's assumption is incorrect.

items.text: The superfluous phrase לָנֶפֶשׁ
items.text_en: The superfluous phrase לָנֶפֶשׁ
items.desc_en: Abaye reverts to the original verse and asks why the Torah wrote 'lanefesh' if it only excludes tamei met. A baraita shows that other impure individuals also make a second Pesach, so the phrase must teach something else.

sub.desc_en: Abaye reverts to the original verse and asks why the Torah wrote 'לָנֶפֶשׁ' (for a soul) if the exclusion of other impure individuals is already derived.
The Gemara anticipates an objection: perhaps 'לָנֶפֶשׁ' teaches that only a טמא מת (one impure from a corpse) is deferred to the second Pesach, but other impure individuals are not.
A baraita is cited showing that other impure individuals (zavin, metzoraim, etc.) also make a second Pesach, so the phrase 'לָנֶפֶשׁ' must teach something else.

items.text: The true teaching: individual vs. community
items.text_en: The true teaching: individual vs. community
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the verse teaches that an individual is deferred to the second Pesach, but the community does the first Pesach in impurity, and only for tamei met, not other impurities.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the verse teaches an individual is deferred to the second Pesach, but the community does the first Pesach in impurity, and only for טמא מת (impurity from a corpse), not other impurities.

items.text: Exemption for a metzora who enters the Temple
items.text_en: Exemption for a metzora who enters the Temple
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a metzora who enters beyond his designated limit is exempt from lashes, because the verse 'badad yashev' gives a positive commandment and overrides the negative prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a metzora who enters beyond his designated limit is exempt from lashes, citing the verse 'בדד ישב מחוץ למחנה מושבו'.
The Gemara explains that the phrase 'בדד ישב' means he dwells alone, and the verse transforms the prohibition into a positive commandment, exempting him from lashes.

items.text: Objection from a baraita on lashes
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita on lashes
items.desc_en: A baraita contradicts Rav Chisda: a metzora who enters inside his partition is liable for lashes, and similarly zavim, but a tamei met is allowed into the Levite camp, and even a corpse may be brought in.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav Chisda by citing a baraita that a metzora who enters inside his partition is liable for lashes.
The baraita adds that zavim who enter inside their partition are also liable, while a tamei met is permitted to enter the Levite camp.
The baraita further states that not only a tamei met but even a corpse itself may be brought into the Levite camp, citing the verse about Moses taking Joseph's bones.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The baraita is revealed as a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Yehuda learns three distinct camps from the verses, while Rabbi Shimon deduces a second camp for zavim and a third for metzoraim, and that the metzora's exclusion is a positive commandment.

sub.desc_en: The gemara identifies the dispute as a Tannaitic baraita, and presents Rabbi Yehuda's position that three distinct camps are derived from the verses.
Rabbi Shimon argues that the verse already implies the exclusion of zavim, so the explicit mention of 'zav' comes only to assign a second camp.
Rabbi Shimon continues that the mention of 'metzora' assigns a third camp, and the verse 'בדד ישב' (he shall dwell alone) makes the metzora's exclusion a positive commandment.

items.text: Comparing severities of impurities
items.text_en: Comparing severities of impurities
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates the relative severity of zav and tamei met, and also compares zav to tamei sheretz, concluding with the statement that zav is more stringent than tamei sheretz, though the objection about oness is raised.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what stringency the zav has over the tamei met, and answers that the zav's impurity emanates from his own body.
The Gemara objects that the tamei met is more stringent because it requires sprinkling on the third and seventh days.
The Gemara cites the verse 'טָמֵא' and 'וְכֹל טָמֵא' to include the tamei sheretz, and asserts that the zav is more stringent than the tamei sheretz.
The Gemara asks what the stringency of the zav over the tamei sheretz is, and answers as previously stated.
The Gemara objects that the sheretz is more stringent because it imparts impurity even when one is compelled (אונס).
The Gemara records that they said (אָמְרִי), indicating a transition or unresolved conclusion.

items.text: Gemara's first argument: zav also transmits under duress
items.text_en: Gemara's first argument: zav also transmits under duress
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that a zav also transmits impurity under duress, citing Rav Huna that the first sighting of a zav transmits impurity even under duress.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that a zav also transmits impurity under duress, citing Rav Huna that the first sighting of a zav transmits impurity even under duress.

items.text: Question: What is the stringency of a metzora over a zav?
items.text_en: Question: What is the stringency of a metzora over a zav?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what stringency a metzora has over a zav, and answers that a metzora requires unkempt hair and torn garments and is forbidden in marital relations. The Gemara counters that a zav is more stringent because he transmits impurity through lying and sitting and through moving a clay vessel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what stringency the metzora has over the zav, answering that the metzora requires unbound hair and torn garments and is forbidden from marital relations.
The Gemara objects that the zav is more stringent because he transmits impurity through a bed and seat and through moving a clay vessel.
The Gemara counters that a zav is more stringent because he transmits impurity through lying and sitting and through moving a clay vessel.

items.text: Resolution: The verse includes ba'al keri, and metzora is more stringent than ba'al keri
items.text_en: Resolution: The verse includes ba'al keri, and metzora is more stringent than ba'al keri
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'zav' and 'every zav' to include a ba'al keri. It then argues that a metzora is more stringent than a ba'al keri, but the Gemara counters that a ba'al keri is more stringent because he transmits impurity with any amount. The Gemara resolves that the Tanna holds like Rabbi Natan, who says a zav requires a quantity like the seal of a penis, and the Sages did not agree, and ba'al keri is compared to zav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'zav' and 'every zav' to include a ba'al keri, and asserts that a metzora is more stringent than a ba'al keri.
The Gemara asks what the stringency of the metzora is, and counters that a ba'al keri is more stringent because he transmits impurity with any amount.
The Gemara resolves that the Tanna holds like Rabbi Natan, who says a zav requires a quantity like the seal of a penis, and the Sages did not agree, and ba'al keri is compared to zav.

items.text: Question: Why is 'every leper' written?
items.text_en: Question: Why is 'every leper' written?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse says 'every leper' and answers that since it wrote 'every zav', it also wrote 'every leper'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'every metzora' is needed, and answers that since 'every zav' is written, 'every metzora' is also written.
The Gemara answers that since the verse wrote 'every zav' (כׇּל זָב), it also wrote 'every leper' (כׇּל צָרוּעַ) for symmetry.

items.text: Objection: Rabbi Yehuda says Rabbi Shimon spoke well?
items.text_en: Objection: Rabbi Yehuda says Rabbi Shimon spoke well?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda said Rabbi Shimon spoke well, and explains that the verse is needed for a teaching of Rabbi Eliezer: that zavim and metzoraim are sent out only when tamei meitim are sent out.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: does Rabbi Yehuda really mean that Rabbi Shimon spoke well (implying the verse is superfluous)?
The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for a teaching of Rabbi Eliezer: zavim and metzoraim are sent out only when tamei meitim are sent out.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yochanan: ba'al keri is sent out to two camps
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yochanan: ba'al keri is sent out to two camps
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the teaching that 'zav' and 'every zav' includes ba'al keri supports Rabbi Yochanan, who said that the underground chambers were not sanctified and a ba'al keri is sent out to two camps.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports Rabbi Yochanan, who says that the chambers were not sanctified and a ba'al keri is sent outside two camps.

items.text: Challenge and resolution: ba'al keri is like a sheretz
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution: ba'al keri is like a sheretz
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that a ba'al keri is like a sheretz, and asks if this refers to camps or impurity. It concludes that it refers to impurity, teaching that just as a sheretz transmits impurity under duress, so does a ba'al keri.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges by citing a baraita that compares a ba'al keri to a sheretz, and asks whether this comparison refers to the laws of camps.
The Gemara initially answers that the comparison refers to the laws of impurity, not camps.
The Gemara objects that both a ba'al keri and a sheretz have the same impurity duration of one day, so the comparison must be about camps.
The Gemara resolves that the comparison indeed refers to impurity, teaching that just as a sheretz transmits impurity under duress (באונס), so does a ba'al keri transmit impurity under duress.

items.text: Further challenge introduced
items.text_en: Further challenge introduced
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces another challenge with the word 'meitiv' (we raise an objection), but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces another objection.

items.text: Gemara's question on the comparison of a ba'al keri to a tamei met
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the comparison of a ba'al keri to a tamei met
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the purpose of comparing a ba'al keri (one who had a seminal emission) to a tamei met (one impure from a corpse). It suggests that if the comparison is for impurity status, both have seven-day impurity, so it must be for the camp system. The Gemara then clarifies that the first clause and the latter clause refer to different aspects.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the comparison of a ba'al keri to a tamei met teaches, rejecting the possibility that it is about impurity status since both have seven-day impurity.
The Gemara concludes that the comparison must be about the camp system, and clarifies that the first clause and latter clause refer to different aspects.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about the severity of impurity levels
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about the severity of impurity levels
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that ranks impurities: a metzora is more severe than a zav, a zav more severe than a tamei met, and a ba'al keri is excluded. The Gemara debates the meaning of 'excluded': whether it means the ba'al keri is permitted in the Levite camp (like a tamei met) or that he is excluded from the tamei met camp and included in the zav camp, despite tamei met being more severe.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that ranks impurity levels, stating that a ba'al keri is the least severe, implying he is excluded from the category of zav and included with tamei met.
The Gemara interprets the baraita as saying that a ba'al keri is excluded from the zav's camp restriction and permitted in the Levite camp, since tamei met is more severe.
The Gemara rejects the interpretation, explaining that the ba'al keri is excluded from the tamei met camp and enters the zav camp, because he is compared to what he resembles.

items.text: Tanna's teaching before Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi and the correction
items.text_en: Tanna's teaching before Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi and the correction
items.desc_en: A tanna taught before Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi that the verse 'וְיָצָא אֶל מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה' refers to the camp of the Divine Presence, and 'לֹא יָבֹא אֶל תּוֹךְ הַמַּחֲנֶה' refers to the Levite camp, deriving that a ba'al keri must leave both camps. Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi corrects him, saying that the verse should be interpreted oppositely: the first phrase refers to the Levite camp and the second to the camp of the Divine Presence.

sub.desc_en: A tanna teaches before רב יצחק בר אבדימי (Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi) that the verse 'וְיָצָא אֶל מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה' refers to the camp of the Divine Presence, and 'לֹא יָבֹא אֶל תּוֹךְ הַמַּחֲנֶה' refers to the Levite camp, deriving that a בעל קרי (one who experienced a seminal emission) must leave both camps.

רב יצחק בר אבדימי (Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi) objects that the tanna's interpretation is logically flawed: he has not yet brought the בעל קרי (ba'al keri) into the Levite camp before sending him out. He corrects the teaching, stating that 'מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה' refers to the Levite camp and 'לֹא יָבֹא אֶל תּוֹךְ הַמַּחֲנֶה' refers to the camp of the Divine Presence.

items.text: Ravina's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Ravina's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges the interpretation, suggesting that both phrases could refer to the camp of the Divine Presence, with the double language creating both a positive and negative commandment. The Gemara rejects this, arguing that if so, the word 'הַמַּחֲנֶה' would be unnecessary; thus, it must be that the verse gives a separate camp (the Levite camp).

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects that both phrases could refer to the camp of the Divine Presence, with the repetition creating both a positive and negative commandment.
The Gemara rejects Ravina's suggestion, arguing that if so, the word 'הַמַּחֲנֶה' would be unnecessary; thus, the verse must give a separate camp (the Levite camp).

items.text: Dispute about the meaning of 'מיחוי קרביו'
items.text_en: Dispute about the meaning of 'מיחוי קרביו'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions 'מיחוי קרביו'. Rav Huna says it means piercing the entrails with a knife. Rav Chiyya bar Rav says it is the membrane of the intestines that comes out due to the pressure of the knife. Rabbi Eliezer explains Rav Chiyya bar Rav's reasoning from a verse, with Rav Yosef's Aramaic translation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's term 'מיחוי קרביו' (piercing of the entrails) means.
Rav Huna explains that מיחוי קרביו means piercing the entrails with a knife.
Rav Chiyya bar Rav explains that מיחוי קרביו refers to the membrane of the intestines that protrudes due to the pressure of the knife.
Rabbi Eliezer explains Rav Chiyya bar Rav's reasoning by citing a verse and Rav Yosef's Aramaic translation, linking the term 'מחים' (entrails) to the inheritance of the wicked by the righteous.

items.text: Interpretation of 'וְרָעוּ כְבָשִׂים כְּדׇבְרָם' and the resurrection of the dead
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'וְרָעוּ כְבָשִׂים כְּדׇבְרָם' and the resurrection of the dead
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the verse 'וְרָעוּ כְבָשִׂים כְּדׇבְרָם'. Menashya bar Yirmeya quotes Rav that it means 'as spoken about them'. Abaye connects it to the previous verse about the wicked, but Rava objects. Rava then explains it according to Rav Chananel quoting Rav, that the righteous will resurrect the dead, linking the verse to Elisha and Elijah. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yonatan that the righteous will resurrect the dead, citing verses about old age and Elisha's staff.

sub.desc_en: Menashya bar Yirmeya quotes Rav that the verse 'וְרָעוּ כְבָשִׂים כְּדׇבְרָם' means 'as spoken about them'.
The Gemara asks what 'as spoken about them' refers to.
Abaye answers that it refers to the verse 'וְחׇרְבוֹת מֵחִים גָּרִים יֹאכֵלוּ' (the desolate ruins of the fat ones shall strangers eat).
Rava objects that if the verse read 'חׇרְבוֹת' (desolate ruins) it would support Abaye, but since it reads 'וְחׇרְבוֹת' (and the desolate ruins) it indicates something else.

sub.text: Rava's answer quoting Rav Chananel quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rava's answer quoting Rav Chananel quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the verse refers to the future resurrection of the dead by the righteous, citing a tradition from Rav Chananel quoting Rav and linking the verse to 'יִרְעוּ בָשָׁן וְגִלְעָד כִּימֵי עוֹלָם'.
The Gemara identifies 'בָּשָׁן' as Elisha and 'גִּלְעָד' as Elijah, supporting the connection to resurrection.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yonatan that the righteous will resurrect the dead, citing verses about old age and Elisha's staff.

items.text: Contradictions about death in the future and their resolutions
items.text_en: Contradictions about death in the future and their resolutions
items.desc_en: Ulla raises a contradiction: one verse says death will be swallowed up forever, another says a youth will die at 100. Resolution: for Israel, death is abolished; for gentiles, death remains. Rav Chisda raises a contradiction about the moon and sun: one verse says the moon will be ashamed, another says its light will be like the sun. Resolution: one refers to the World to Come, the other to the days of the Messiah. For Shmuel who says there is no difference except subjugation, the resolution is that both refer to the World to Come, but one is in the camp of the Divine Presence and the other in the camp of the righteous.

sub.desc_en: Ulla raises a contradiction between the verse 'בִּלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח' (death will be swallowed up forever) and the verse 'כִּי הַנַּעַר בֶּן מֵאָה שָׁנָה יָמוּת' (a youth will die at 100).
The gemara resolves: for Israel death is abolished, for gentiles it remains, citing the verse that gentiles will serve Israel in the future.
Rav Chisda raises a contradiction between the verse that the moon will be ashamed and the verse that the moon's light will be like the sun's.
The gemara resolves: one verse refers to the World to Come, the other to the days of the Messiah.
The gemara asks: according to Shmuel who says there is no difference between this world and the days of the Messiah except subjugation to kingdoms, what can be said?
The gemara resolves: both verses refer to the World to Come, but one describes the camp of the Divine Presence and the other the camp of the righteous.

items.text: Rava's contradiction and the baraita on resurrection
items.text_en: Rava's contradiction and the baraita on resurrection
items.desc_en: Rava raises a contradiction: one verse says 'I kill and I make alive', another says 'I wound and I heal'. The resolution is that God kills and then revives, just as He wounds and then heals. A baraita then teaches that from the juxtaposition of 'I kill and I make alive' with 'I wound and I heal', we learn that death and life can occur simultaneously, providing a proof for resurrection from the Torah. An alternative interpretation: first He kills and revives, then He wounds and heals.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises a contradiction between the verse 'I kill and I make alive' and the verse 'I wound and I heal', arguing that if He revives, surely He heals.
The gemara resolves that God kills and revives simultaneously, just as He wounds and heals simultaneously.

A baraita teaches that from the juxtaposition of 'I kill and I make alive' with 'I wound and I heal', we learn that death and life occur simultaneously, providing a proof for resurrection from the Torah.
An alternative interpretation: first He kills and revives, then He wounds and heals.

items.text: Opening baraita: Rabbi Shimon on performing a mitzvah at its proper time
items.text_en: Opening baraita: Rabbi Shimon on performing a mitzvah at its proper time
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon emphasizes the importance of performing a mitzvah at its proper time, using the example of burning fats and limbs which are valid all night but are not delayed until nightfall.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon teaches that performing a mitzvah at its proper time is beloved, as the burning of fats and limbs is valid all night but is not delayed until nightfall.

items.text: Contradiction about cutting a wart in the Temple
items.text_en: Contradiction about cutting a wart in the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: one may cut a wart in the Temple but not in the provinces, and if done with a tool, it is forbidden everywhere. This sets up the need for resolution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: one may cut a wart in the Temple but not in the provinces, and if done with a tool, it is forbidden everywhere.

items.text: Two Amoraim resolve the contradiction
items.text_en: Two Amoraim resolve the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina offer two resolutions: one distinguishes between a moist wart (cut by hand) and a dry one (cut with a tool), the other distinguishes between using the hand (permitted) and a tool (forbidden).

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: One of the two sages resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a moist wart (permitted by hand) and a dry wart (forbidden by hand).

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: The other sage resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between cutting by hand (permitted in the Temple) and cutting with a tool (forbidden everywhere).

items.text: Gemara challenges each opinion
items.text_en: Gemara challenges each opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks each Amora why they did not adopt the other's resolution. The first explains that a dry wart crumbles by hand, so the distinction must be by tool. The second explains that the mishnah already states that using a tool is forbidden everywhere, so the distinction must be by moisture.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the Amora who distinguished by tool why he did not adopt the distinction by moisture.
The first Amora explains that a dry wart crumbles by hand, so the distinction must be by tool.
The Gemara asks the second Amora why he did not adopt the distinction by tool.
The second Amora explains that the mishnah already states that using a tool is forbidden everywhere, so the distinction must be by moisture.
The Gemara resolves that the mention of a tool in the mishnah comes to teach the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.

items.text: Gemara explains the purpose of the tool clause
items.text_en: Gemara explains the purpose of the tool clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the mention of a tool in the mishnah comes to teach the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the other sage does not accept the tool distinction, and answers that the mention of a tool here comes to teach the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that Yom Tov is either entirely for God or entirely for oneself, while Rabbi Yehoshua says to divide it between eating/drinking and study. Rabbi Yochanan explains they derive this from the verses 'Atzeret for Hashem' and 'Atzeret for you'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that if shechita (slaughter) is permitted on Yom Tov, then other acts should be permitted; Rabbi Yehoshua responds that simchat Yom Tov (joy of the festival) is also a mitzvah.

sub.text: Supporting baraita: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer saying one should either eat and drink or sit and study on Yom Tov, and Rabbi Yehoshua saying one should divide the day between eating and study.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that both derive their views from the same verses: 'עֲצֶרֶת לַה׳' (a solemn assembly for God) and 'עֲצֶרֶת תִּהְיֶה לָכֶם' (a solemn assembly for you), with Rabbi Eliezer taking it as all for God or all for you, and Rabbi Yehoshua as half for God and half for you.

items.text: Agreement on Shavuot, Shabbat, and Purim requiring 'for you'
items.text_en: Agreement on Shavuot, Shabbat, and Purim requiring 'for you'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar, Rabbah, and Rav Yosef each state that everyone agrees Shavuot (day Torah was given), Shabbat (called 'oneg'), and Purim ('days of feasting') require a component for oneself.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that everyone agrees on Shavuot (עֲצֶרֶת) that we need an element 'for you' because it is the day the Torah was given.
Rabbah adds that everyone agrees on Shabbat we need an element 'for you' because the verse says 'וְקָרָאתָ לַשַּׁבָּת עוֹנֶג' (call the Shabbat a delight).
Rav Yosef adds that everyone agrees on Purim we need an element 'for you' because the verse describes it as 'יְמֵי מִשְׁתֶּה וְשִׂמְחָה' (days of feasting and joy).

items.text: Mar bar Ravina's practice of fasting except on special days
items.text_en: Mar bar Ravina's practice of fasting except on special days
items.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina fasted all year except on Shavuot, Purim, and the eve of Yom Kippur, citing the reasons: Shavuot is when the Torah was given, Purim is for feasting, and the eve of Yom Kippur is for eating as if fasting on the 9th and 10th.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina fasted all year except for Shavuot, Purim, and the day before Yom Kippur.
The Gemara explains: Shavuot because the Torah was given, Purim because of feasting and joy, and the day before Yom Kippur because eating then is credited as if fasting on both the ninth and tenth.
The Gemara explains the eve of Yom Kippur based on a teaching of Chiya bar Rav Midifti: one who eats and drinks on the ninth is credited as if fasting on both the ninth and tenth.

items.text: Rav Yosef's appreciation for Shavuot
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's appreciation for Shavuot
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef would have a three-year-old calf prepared on Shavuot, saying that without this day (when the Torah was given), there would be many Yosefs in the market (i.e., he would be insignificant).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef would order a third-born calf for Shavuot, saying that without this day there would be many Yosefs in the market.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's joy in reviewing Torah and the principle of intent
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's joy in reviewing Torah and the principle of intent
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet would review his studies every thirty days, rejoicing in his learning. The Gemara questions this, citing Rabbi Elazar that without Torah the world would not exist. It resolves that initially one studies for oneself, but the Torah sustains the world.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet would review his learning every thirty days and exclaim joyfully to his soul that it was for its sake he studied.
The Gemara objects: Rabbi Elazar said that without Torah, heaven and earth would not endure, implying Torah is for the world's sake, not for personal joy.
The Gemara resolves that initially a person studies for his own sake, but ultimately it benefits the world.

items.text: Rav Ashi's challenge to Rabbi Eliezer's view on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge to Rabbi Eliezer's view on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues against Rabbi Eliezer's position that Yom Tov is optional: if Yom Tov, which permits optional labor, does not permit accompanying שבות (rabbinic prohibitions), then Shabbat, which only permits mitzvah labor, certainly should not permit such שבות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises a challenge: if Rabbi Eliezer holds that Yom Tov is optional, then a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument would forbid even permitted labor on Shabbat, contradicting the allowance for mitzvah-related work.

items.text: Opening statement of Rabbi Eliezer's principle
items.text_en: Opening statement of Rabbi Eliezer's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Eliezer holds that a shevut (rabbinic prohibition) performed for a mitzvah is preferable and overrides Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that Rabbi Eliezer holds that a shevut (rabbinic prohibition) performed for a mitzvah is preferable and overrides Shabbat.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's argument and Rabbi Akiva's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's argument and Rabbi Akiva's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that if preparatory acts after slaughter override Shabbat, then those before slaughter should also override it. Rabbi Akiva counters that slaughter itself overrides Shabbat, so post-slaughter acts are justified, but pre-slaughter acts are not, and adds a concern that the offering might be found invalid, retroactively desecrating Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori): if post-slaughter preparatory acts override Shabbat, then pre-slaughter acts should also override it.
Rabbi Akiva counters that the analogy fails because slaughter itself overrides Shabbat, justifying post-slaughter acts, but pre-slaughter acts lack that justification.
Rabbi Akiva adds a second reason: pre-slaughter acts risk that the offering might be found invalid, retroactively desecrating Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Akiva's argument
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Akiva's argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Akiva's logic: if invalidation is a concern, then slaughter itself should not be allowed. It explains that Rabbi Akiva first stated a different argument and then later gave the kal vachomer reasoning.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of Rabbi Akiva's second objection
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of Rabbi Akiva's second objection
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the second objection: if that concern were valid, one could never slaughter on Shabbat due to the same retroactive risk.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Akiva first stated his main objection and then added the second point as a separate argument.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's second argument: haza'ah proves the point
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's second argument: haza'ah proves the point
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva responds that the sprinkling (haza'ah) of a zav on the seventh day proves that a shevut does not override Shabbat even for a mitzvah. Rabbi Eliezer rebukes him, and Rabbi Akiva clarifies that he received this tradition from Rabbi Eliezer himself.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Rabbi Akiva brought a proof from the sprinkling of purification water, which is a shevut and does not override Shabbat, and Rabbi Eliezer rebuked him, but Rabbi Akiva insisted he received this tradition from Rabbi Eliezer himself.
Rabbi Eliezer rebukes Rabbi Akiva, saying that since he answered with the slaughter argument, he should die by slaughter.
Rabbi Akiva clarifies that he received this tradition about haza'ah being a shevut that does not override Shabbat from Rabbi Eliezer himself.

items.text: Ulla's explanation of the haza'ah tradition
items.text_en: Ulla's explanation of the haza'ah tradition
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that Rabbi Eliezer's tradition about haza'ah referred to terumah, which itself does not override Shabbat. Rabbi Akiva mistakenly thought it referred to the Pesach offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Since Rabbi Eliezer himself taught Rabbi Akiva the tradition, why did he later retract it?
Ulla answers: When Rabbi Eliezer taught the tradition, he taught it regarding the haza'ah (sprinkling) of תרומה (priestly portion), which itself does not override Shabbat.

The Gemara explains: Rabbi Akiva, when he cited the objection, also thought the tradition was about the haza'ah of the Pesach offering, but Rabbi Eliezer had actually taught it about תרומה (priestly portion).

items.text: Rabba's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rabba's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabba objects that the baraita explicitly mentions haza'ah of a zav on the seventh day in the context of Pesach. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Eliezer indeed taught about Pesach haza'ah, but he forgot his tradition, and Rabbi Akiva reminded him indirectly out of respect.

sub.desc_en: Rabba objects that the baraita explicitly mentions haza'ah of a zav on the seventh day in the context of Pesach, proving that Rabbi Akiva's challenge was about Pesach haza'ah.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Eliezer indeed taught about Pesach haza'ah, but he forgot his tradition, and Rabbi Akiva reminded him indirectly out of respect.

items.text: Reason why haza'ah does not override Shabbat
items.text_en: Reason why haza'ah does not override Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabba explains that haza'ah is merely carrying, and a decree was made lest one carry it four cubits in the public domain. The Gemara questions why Rabbi Eliezer would not allow it, and answers that his principle applies only when the person is fit for the mitzvah, but here the person is not fit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why haza'ah (sprinkling) does not override Shabbat, given that it is merely carrying and should be permitted for the sake of the Pesach offering.
Rabba answers that a decree was made lest one carry the water four cubits in the public domain.
The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that preparations for a mitzvah override Shabbat, the decree should not apply.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Eliezer's principle applies only when the person is fit for the mitzvah, but here the person is not fit (טמא מת), so no obligation rests upon him.

items.text: Rabba and Rava on heating water for circumcision
items.text_en: Rabba and Rava on heating water for circumcision
items.desc_en: Rabba rules that according to Rabbi Eliezer, one may heat water for a healthy infant's circumcision but not for a sick one. Rava disagrees, stating that all infants are considered sick regarding circumcision, so one may never heat water for it on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rabba rules that according to Rabbi Eliezer, one may heat water for a healthy infant's circumcision on Shabbat but not for a sick one.
Rava objects that a healthy infant does not need hot water to strengthen him, and concludes that all infants are considered sick regarding circumcision, so one may never heat water for it on Shabbat.

items.text: Abaye's objection and Rabba's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and Rabba's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects from a baraita that an uncircumcised man who fails to circumcise himself is liable to karet, implying obligation even when unfit. Rabba resolves that Rabbi Eliezer holds that one does not slaughter or sprinkle for one impure with a sheretz.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects from a baraita that an uncircumcised man who fails to circumcise himself is liable to karet, implying obligation even when unfit.
Rabba resolves that Rabbi Eliezer holds that one does not slaughter or sprinkle for one impure with a sheretz.

items.text: Principle of communal vs. individual sacrifice in impurity
items.text_en: Principle of communal vs. individual sacrifice in impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a principle: anything that is deferred for an individual is performed in impurity for the community. Anything that applies to the community applies to the individual, and anything that does not apply to the community does not apply to the individual. It then applies this to the cases of orlah (uncircumcision) and tumah (impurity): for the community, if all are uncircumcised, they are told to circumcise themselves; for an individual, the same applies. For impurity, if the entire community is impure, they perform the Pesach in impurity; an individual is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a principle: anything deferred for an individual is performed in impurity for the community, and applies this to orlah (uncircumcision) and tumah (impurity).

items.text: Challenge from the second Pesach
items.text_en: Challenge from the second Pesach
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua challenges Rava: the second Pesach (Pesach Sheni) is not observed by the community but is observed by an individual, contradicting the principle. Rava responds that the second Pesach is different because the community already performed the first Pesach.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's challenge to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's challenge to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua challenges Rava by pointing out that the second Pesach (Pesach Sheni) is not observed by the community but is observed by an individual, contradicting the general principle.
Rava responds that the second Pesach is different because the community already performed the first Pesach.

items.text: Proof from a baraita about the uncircumcised and impure
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about the uncircumcised and impure
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one might think that only a pure person not on a distant journey is liable for karet, but from where do we derive that an uncircumcised person, one impure from a creeping creature, and all other impure persons are liable? The verse says 'and the man.' The Gemara infers from the fact that the baraita seeks a source for one impure from a creeping creature that it holds that we do not slaughter and sprinkle on behalf of one impure from a creeping creature; otherwise, he would be considered pure. This shows that even though such a person is not fit to eat, he is still liable, and even though the community does not observe it, the individual does.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one might think only a pure person not on a distant journey is liable for karet, but the verse 'וְהָאִישׁ' (and the man) includes the uncircumcised, one impure from a creeping creature, and all other impure persons.

The Gemara infers from the baraita's search for a source for one impure from a creeping creature that it holds we do not slaughter and sprinkle on behalf of such a person, proving that even though he is not fit to eat, he is still liable, and even though the community does not observe it, the individual does.

items.text: Rava's resolution: Rabbi Eliezer's view
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: Rabbi Eliezer's view
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Eliezer holds that we do slaughter and sprinkle on behalf of one impure from a creeping creature, and the same applies to one impure from a corpse on his seventh day. The sprinkling is only for eating, and eating the Pesach is not a prerequisite. Rav Adda bar Abba objects: if so, the Pesach would be slaughtered not for its eaters. Rava responds that 'not for its eaters' applies to a sick or elderly person who cannot eat, but this person can eat; he just lacks the proper preparation.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves that Rabbi Eliezer holds we slaughter and sprinkle on behalf of one impure from a creeping creature, and the same applies to one impure from a corpse on his seventh day, because eating the Pesach is not a prerequisite.
Rav Adda bar Abba objects that if so, the Pesach would be slaughtered not for its eaters.
Rava responds that 'not for its eaters' applies to a sick or elderly person who cannot eat, but this person can eat; he just lacks the proper preparation.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's rule and its application to Pesach and circumcision
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's rule and its application to Pesach and circumcision
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states a rule of Rabbi Akiva. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva. A similar rule is taught regarding circumcision: any work that can be done before Shabbat does not override Shabbat, but circumcision, which cannot be done before Shabbat, does override Shabbat. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva there as well. The Gemara explains why both rulings are necessary: for Pesach, one might think that preparatory acts for a mitzvah do not override Shabbat because no covenant of thirteen covenants was made for it, but for circumcision, which has thirteen covenants, it might override; and for circumcision, one might think that preparatory acts do not override Shabbat because there is no karet, but for Pesach, which has karet, it might override. Therefore, both are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Akiva's rule that any work which can be done before Shabbat does not override Shabbat, but circumcision, which cannot be done before Shabbat, does override Shabbat.
Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Rav that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Akiva regarding both Pesach and circumcision.

The Gemara explains why both rulings are necessary: for Pesach, one might think preparatory acts do not override Shabbat because no thirteen covenants were made for it, but for circumcision, which has thirteen covenants, it might override; and for circumcision, one might think preparatory acts do not override Shabbat because there is no כרת (karet), but for Pesach, which has כרת, it might override.

items.text: Mishnah: When to bring the chagigah with the Pesach
items.text_en: Mishnah: When to bring the chagigah with the Pesach
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: When does one bring the chagigah (festival offering) with the Pesach? When the Pesach comes on a weekday, in purity, and with a small number of people. But when it comes on Shabbat, with a large number, or in impurity, one does not bring the chagigah with it. The chagigah could be from the flock or the herd, from sheep or goats, from males or females, and is eaten for two days and one night.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for when the chagigah (festival offering) is brought with the Pesach: on a weekday, in purity, and with a small number; it may come from various animals and is eaten for two days and one night.

items.text: Gemara: The tannaitic source and Rav Ashi's inference
items.text_en: Gemara: The tannaitic source and Rav Ashi's inference
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the tannaitic source that teaches about the chagigah? It teaches that the bringing of the Pesach does not override Shabbat, and it also teaches that the chagigah does not override Shabbat. Rav Ashi says: Learn from this that the chagigah of the fourteenth (of Nisan) is not brought when the Pesach is brought on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the tannaitic source that teaches about the chagigah? It answers that the source teaches that the bringing of the Pesach does not override Shabbat, and it also teaches that the chagigah does not override Shabbat.
Rav Ashi infers from the Mishnah that the chagigah of the fourteenth (of Nisan) is not brought when the Pesach is brought on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara's initial question about the nature of the festival offering
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question about the nature of the festival offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the festival offering brought on the fourteenth is obligatory or optional, arguing that if it were obligatory it would override Shabbat, be brought in large numbers, and be brought in impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the festival offering brought on the fourteenth is obligatory or optional, arguing that if it were obligatory it would override Shabbat, be brought in large numbers, and be brought in impurity.

items.text: Reason for the festival offering even in small numbers
items.text_en: Reason for the festival offering even in small numbers
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the festival offering is brought even when the Paschal lamb is few in number, citing a baraita that it is eaten first so that the Paschal lamb is eaten on a full stomach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the festival offering is brought even when the Paschal lamb is few in number.
The Gemara answers with a baraita: the festival offering that comes with the Paschal lamb is eaten first, so that the Paschal lamb is eaten on a full stomach.

items.text: Ben Teima's opinion on the festival offering
items.text_en: Ben Teima's opinion on the festival offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's ruling that the festival offering is eaten for two days contradicts Ben Teima, who holds it is like the Paschal lamb and eaten only for one day and night. The Gemara explains his reasoning from a verse equating the festival offering with the Paschal lamb regarding the prohibition of leaving leftovers overnight.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the festival offering is eaten for two days.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah disagrees with Ben Teima, who holds the festival offering is eaten only for one day and night.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Ben Teima's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Ben Teima's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Ben Teima's reasoning from a verse equating the festival offering with the Paschal lamb regarding the prohibition of leaving leftovers overnight.

items.text: First unresolved question: must the festival offering be roasted?
items.text_en: First unresolved question: must the festival offering be roasted?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question whether Ben Teima's equation to the Paschal lamb extends to the requirement of roasting. It resolves from a statement by Rav Chisda that the festival offering must be roasted, confirming Ben Teima's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question whether according to Ben Teima the festival offering must be roasted like the Paschal lamb, or whether the equation applies only to the prohibition of leaving overnight (לִינָה).
The Gemara cites a baraita where the night is described as entirely roasted, and Rav Chisda attributes this statement to Ben Teima, thereby resolving that the festival offering must be roasted.

items.text: Second unresolved question: types of animals allowed
items.text_en: Second unresolved question: types of animals allowed
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the festival offering can come from cattle, females, or two-year-old animals. It resolves from a baraita that it must be from sheep, males, and yearlings, confirming all these restrictions apply according to Ben Teima.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question regarding Ben Teima's view: whether the festival offering (חגיגה) brought with the Paschal lamb can come from cattle, females, or two-year-old animals, or whether the analogy to the Paschal lamb is limited to matters of eating but not to all details.

The Gemara cites a baraita that explicitly states the festival offering brought with the Paschal lamb is like the Paschal lamb: it comes from sheep, males, yearlings, and is eaten roasted, within one day and night, and only by its registered group.
The Gemara concludes that since the baraita aligns with Ben Teima's position, all these restrictions (from sheep, males, yearlings) are indeed required according to Ben Teima, resolving the question.

items.text: Third unresolved question: prohibition of breaking bones
items.text_en: Third unresolved question: prohibition of breaking bones
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the festival offering is subject to the prohibition of breaking bones, like the Paschal lamb. It attempts to resolve from a Mishnah about a knife found on the fourteenth, suggesting that a hatchet requires immersion because it is used for the festival offering, implying bone-breaking is prohibited. This is attributed to Ben Teima.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question for Ben Teima: whether the festival offering brought with the Paschal lamb is subject to the prohibition of breaking bones, given the verse's limitation 'בּוֹ' (in it) to the Paschal lamb alone, or whether that limitation applies only to a fit lamb, not a disqualified one.

The Gemara cites a baraita about a knife found on the fourteenth requiring immediate slaughter, while a hatchet (קופיץ) always requires immersion, suggesting it is used for the festival offering where bone-breaking is prohibited.

The Gemara objects: if the baraita follows the Rabbis (who do not equate the festival offering with the Paschal lamb), why would a hatchet require immersion? It is fit for the festival offering, which they permit to break bones.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita must follow Ben Teima, and thus proves that the festival offering is subject to the prohibition of breaking bones.

items.text: Rejection of the resolution and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rejection of the resolution and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the attribution to Ben Teima, suggesting the Mishnah could be according to the Rabbis in a case where the fourteenth falls on Shabbat. However, the continuation of the Mishnah indicates the first clause does not deal with Shabbat, leaving the question unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the attribution to Ben Teima, suggesting the Mishnah could be according to the Rabbis in a case where the fourteenth falls on Shabbat.
The Gemara objects that the continuation of the Mishnah indicates the first clause does not deal with Shabbat.
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved, as the text breaks off.

items.text: Gemara's question about knowing when the Paschal lamb is brought in a state of impurity
items.text_en: Gemara's question about knowing when the Paschal lamb is brought in a state of impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one knows if the Paschal lamb is brought in a state of impurity (due to a deceased Nasi). It considers scenarios where the Nasi dies on the 13th or 14th of Nisan, and distinguishes between a knife (single uncertainty) and a hatchet (double uncertainty) regarding immersion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the public knows whether the Paschal lamb is brought in a state of impurity (due to a deceased Nasi).
The Gemara refines the question: ultimately, how do they know that the lamb is brought in impurity?
The Gemara considers the timing of the Nasi's death: if on the 13th, why immerse the knife? If on the 14th, why distinguish between a knife (immersed) and a hatchet (not immersed)?
The Gemara resolves: the Nasi was dying on the 13th; the knife (single uncertainty) is immersed, but the hatchet (double uncertainty) is not.

items.text: Baraita about Yehuda ben Dortai and the festival offering overriding Shabbat
items.text_en: Baraita about Yehuda ben Dortai and the festival offering overriding Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Yehuda ben Dortai and his son moved to the south, criticizing the great sages Shemaya and Avtalyon for not teaching that the festival offering (חגיגה) overrides Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Yehuda ben Dortai and his son moved south, criticizing Shemaya and Avtalyon for not teaching that the festival offering (חגיגה) overrides Shabbat.

items.text: Rav's explanation of ben Dortai's reasoning
items.text_en: Rav's explanation of ben Dortai's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rav explains ben Dortai's reasoning: the verse "and you shall sacrifice the Pesach to the Lord your God, sheep and cattle" implies that the Pesach (sheep) and the festival offering (cattle) are both to be sacrificed, and the Torah says "and you shall sacrifice the Pesach" — meaning the festival offering is included.

sub.desc_en: Rav explains ben Dortai's reasoning: the verse 'וְזָבַחְתָּ פֶּסַח לַה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ צֹאן וּבָקָר' (and you shall sacrifice the Pesach to the Lord your God, sheep and cattle) implies that the Pesach (sheep) and the festival offering (cattle) are both to be sacrificed, and the Torah says 'וְזָבַחְתָּ פֶּסַח' (and you shall sacrifice the Pesach) — meaning the festival offering is included.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative interpretation and Rav Nachman's derivation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative interpretation and Rav Nachman's derivation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi questions the need to explain ben Dortai's reasoning, suggesting the verse is actually for Rav Nachman's teaching: that the surplus of the Paschal lamb is offered as a peace-offering (שלמים), as derived from the same verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi questions the need to explain the reasoning of the separatists (ben Dortai), suggesting it is unnecessary.

Rav Ashi asserts that the verse actually serves Rav Nachman's teaching, citing Rav Nachman's statement in the name of Rabba bar Avuh that the surplus of the Paschal lamb is offered as a peace-offering (שלמים).

The gemara cites the verse 'וְזָבַחְתָּ פֶּסַח לַה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ צֹאן וּבָקָר' and explains that since the Paschal lamb cannot come from cattle, the surplus must be used for an offering that comes from both flock and cattle, namely a peace-offering (שלמים).

items.text: The Sages' reason why the festival offering does not override Shabbat
items.text_en: The Sages' reason why the festival offering does not override Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages hold that the festival offering does not override Shabbat, given it is a public offering. Rabbi Ila'a in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Safra derives from the verse "and you shall celebrate it as a festival to the Lord for seven days in the year" — implying seven days, not eight, teaching that the festival offering does not override Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages hold that the festival offering does not override Shabbat, given it is a public offering.

sub.text: Rabbi Ila'a in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Safra
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Safra
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Safra derives from the verse 'וְחַגֹּתֶם אֹתוֹ חַג לַה׳ שִׁבְעַת יָמִים בַּשָּׁנָה' (and you shall celebrate it as a festival to the Lord for seven days in the year) — implying seven days, not eight, teaching that the festival offering does not override Shabbat.

items.text: Ravin's challenge and Abaye's response
items.text_en: Ravin's challenge and Abaye's response
items.desc_en: Ravin notes that sometimes there are only six days of the festival (when the first day falls on Shabbat), so the verse's seven days are not always literal. Abaye dismisses this, saying that eight days never occur, while seven days occur in most years.

sub.desc_en: Ravin challenges the proof from the verse 'שִׁבְעַת יָמִים' (seven days) that the festival offering (חגיגה) does not override Shabbat, noting that sometimes only six days are available when the first day falls on Shabbat.
Abaye dismisses Ravin's objection, arguing that eight days never occur, while seven days occur in most years, so the verse's reference to seven days is valid for the majority of cases.

items.text: Ulla's ruling on peace-offerings slaughtered before the festival
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling on peace-offerings slaughtered before the festival
items.desc_en: Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar rules that peace-offerings (שלמים) slaughtered on the eve of a festival do not fulfill the obligation of joy (שמחה) or the festival offering (חגיגה), as the verse requires slaughtering and rejoicing on the same day.

sub.desc_en: Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar rules that peace-offerings (שלמים) slaughtered on the eve of a festival do not fulfill the obligation of joy (שמחה) or the festival offering (חגיגה), as the verse requires slaughtering and rejoicing on the same day.

items.text: Gemara's initial question about Chagigah and simcha
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question about Chagigah and simcha
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Chagigah offering requires slaughter during the time of joy, noting that it is an obligatory offering which must come from non-sacred animals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Chagigah offering requires slaughter during the time of joy, noting that it is an obligatory offering which must come from non-sacred animals.

items.text: Supporting baraita on the last night of Yom Tov
items.text_en: Supporting baraita on the last night of Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that derives from the verse 'וְהָיִיתָ אַךְ שָׂמֵחַ' that the last night of Yom Tov is included in the obligation of joy, and explains that the reason is because there is joy before it (the day), unlike the first night which has no preceding joy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'וְהָיִיתָ אַךְ שָׂמֵחַ' that the last night of Yom Tov is included in the obligation of joy, and the word 'אַךְ' divides the nights.
The Gemara asks why the last night is included and not the first, suggesting it is because there is nothing with which to rejoice on the first night.
The Gemara rejects that reasoning and explains that the baraita's own rationale is that the last night has preceding joy (the day), while the first night does not.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection and Rav Idi bar Avin's answer
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection and Rav Idi bar Avin's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects from a mishnah that the Chagigah of the 14th is valid for simcha but not for Chagigah, implying that slaughter during the time of joy is not required. Rav Idi bar Avin answers that the animal was delayed and slaughtered on the 14th itself.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects from a mishnah that the Chagigah of the 14th is valid for simcha but not for Chagigah, implying that slaughter during the time of joy is not required.
Rav Idi bar Avin answers that the animal was delayed and slaughtered on the 14th itself.
Rav Ashi supports this interpretation by noting that otherwise the mishnah would align with Ben Teima, who disqualifies the animal due to לִינָה (overnight stay).

items.text: Rava's objection and resolution regarding the days of simcha
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution regarding the days of simcha
items.desc_en: Rava objects that the mishnah says Hallel and simcha are eight days, but if slaughter during simcha were required, when the first day of Yom Tov falls on Shabbat there would only be seven days. Rav Huna bar Yehuda answers that one can rejoice with the goat-offerings of the festivals, but Rava refutes this because the goats are eaten raw and not roasted, and the priests eat them while Israelites have nothing. Rav Pappa suggests rejoicing with clean clothes and aged wine.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects from the mishnah that Hallel and simcha are eight days, arguing that if slaughter during simcha were required, when the first day of Yom Tov falls on Shabbat there would only be seven days.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda answers that one can rejoice with the goat-offerings of the festivals.
Rava refutes that the goats are eaten raw and not roasted, and the priests eat them while Israelites have nothing.
Rav Pappa resolves that one can rejoice with clean clothes and aged wine.

items.text: Ravin's statement in the name of Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Ravin's statement in the name of Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: Ravin reports that Rabbi Elazar ruled that peace-offerings slaughtered on the eve of Yom Tov are valid for simcha but not for Chagigah, because simcha does not require slaughter during the time of joy, while Chagigah is an obligatory offering that must come from non-sacred animals.

sub.text: Ravin in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Ravin in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Ravin reports Rabbi Elazar's ruling that peace-offerings slaughtered on the eve of Yom Tov are valid for simcha but not for Chagigah, because simcha does not require slaughter during the time of joy, while Chagigah is an obligatory offering that must come from non-sacred animals.

items.text: Objection from the baraita on the last night of Yom Tov
items.text_en: Objection from the baraita on the last night of Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the same baraita about the last night of Yom Tov, questioning whether the reason is because there is no animal to slaughter. The answer is that the reason is because there is no preceding joy, not because of a lack of slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that includes the last night of Yom Tov in the joy of the festival, implying a reason related to the availability of an animal to slaughter.
The Gemara asks whether the reason for including the last night is because there is no animal to slaughter for joy.
The baraita answers that the reason is because the last night has preceding joy (the day of Yom Tov), while the first night does not, not because of a lack of slaughter.

items.text: Discussion on the fats of the Chagigah of the 15th and the verse 'Reishit'
items.text_en: Discussion on the fats of the Chagigah of the 15th and the verse 'Reishit'
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana derives from the verse that the fats of the Chagigah of the 15th are invalidated by overnight stay (linah) because the verse says 'עַד בֹּקֶר' and is juxtaposed to 'רֵאשִׁית', meaning the first morning. Rav Yosef objects that without 'רֵאשִׁית' one might think it means the second morning, but that would be absurd since the meat is already invalidated from the night. Abaye counters with the example of the Paschal lamb according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, where meat is invalidated from midnight but fats until morning. Rava clarifies that Rav Yosef's difficulty is that the tanna does not require 'רֵאשִׁית' for meat, while Rav Kahana requires it for fats.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana derives from the verse that the fats of the Chagigah of the 15th are invalidated by overnight stay (לינה), because the verse says 'עַד בֹּקֶר' and is juxtaposed to 'רֵאשִׁית', meaning the first morning.

Rav Yosef objects that without 'רֵאשִׁית' one might think it means the second morning, but that would be absurd since the meat is already invalidated from the night while the fats would remain until morning.
Abaye counters with the example of the Paschal lamb according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, where meat is invalidated from midnight but fats remain valid until morning.
Rava clarifies that Rav Yosef's difficulty is that the tanna does not require 'רֵאשִׁית' for meat, while Rav Kahana requires it for fats.
The gemara cites a baraita that the meat of the Chagigah is invalidated by overnight stay without needing the word 'רֵאשִׁית', supporting Rav Yosef's difficulty.

items.text: Initial exposition of the verse for chagigah of the 14th
items.text_en: Initial exposition of the verse for chagigah of the 14th
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by stating that the verse teaches that the chagigah of the 14th is eaten for two days and one night. It then raises an alternative possibility that it might be only for one day and one night, but rejects this by citing the phrase 'on the first day in the morning' which implies a second morning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the verse teaches the חגיגה (Festival peace-offering) of the 14th is eaten for two days and one night, then raises the alternative that it might be only one day and night, and rejects this by citing the phrase 'on the first day in the morning' which implies a second morning.

The Gemara considers the possibility that the verse refers only to the first morning, and then explains that the phrase 'if a vow or a free-will offering' teaches that the חגיגה (Festival peace-offering) of the 14th is indeed eaten for two days and one night.

items.text: Clarification of the alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Clarification of the alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the alternative interpretation was not about a single morning but about two distinct chagigot—one for the 14th and one for the 15th—each with its own morning. This is a correction of the initial reading.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's phrasing: if it already established that 'morning' means the second morning, why does it need to propose an alternative interpretation about the first morning?
The Gemara explains that the baraita's alternative interpretation was not about a single morning but about two distinct chagigot—one for the 14th and one for the 15th—each with its own morning.

items.text: Resolution of the chagigah's eating period
items.text_en: Resolution of the chagigah's eating period
items.desc_en: The Gemara then notes that it is established that the chagigah is eaten for two days and one night. It questions the purpose of the phrase 'if a vow or a freewill offering' and concludes that one part of the verse applies to the chagigah of the 15th and the other to the chagigah of the 14th, teaching that the latter is eaten for two days and one night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that it is established that the chagigah is eaten for two days and one night, and then questions the purpose of the phrase 'if a vow or a freewill offering' by noting that both the chagigah of the 14th and the 15th are written as being eaten for only a day and a night.
The Gemara resolves that one part of the verse applies to the chagigah of the 15th and the other to the chagigah of the 14th, teaching that the latter is eaten for two days and one night.

items.text: Inference about the term 'morning'
items.text_en: Inference about the term 'morning'
items.desc_en: The Gemara deduces that only because the verse specifies 'on the first day in the morning' does it refer to a second morning; otherwise, a plain 'morning' would mean the first morning, even without the word 'first'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that only because the verse specifies 'on the first day in the morning' does it refer to a second morning; otherwise, a plain 'morning' would mean the first morning, even without the word 'first'.

items.text: Mishnah: Liability for slaughtering a pesach not for its sake on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for slaughtering a pesach not for its sake on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one slaughters the pesach offering not for its sake on Shabbat, he is liable for a sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: one who slaughters the pesach offering not for its own sake on Shabbat is liable to bring a sin-offering.

items.text: Mishnah: Other offerings slaughtered for the sake of pesach
items.text_en: Mishnah: Other offerings slaughtered for the sake of pesach
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues: For other offerings slaughtered for the sake of pesach, if they are not fit for pesach, one is liable; if they are fit, Rabbi Eliezer holds him liable for a sin-offering, and Rabbi Yehoshua exempts him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah continues: for other offerings slaughtered as a pesach, if they are not fit for a pesach, one is liable; if they are fit, Rabbi Eliezer holds one liable for a sin-offering, and Rabbi Yehoshua exempts.
Rabbi Eliezer holds that if the offerings are fit for pesach, one is liable for a sin-offering.
Rabbi Yehoshua exempts one from liability in that case.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues a fortiori: if the pesach, which is permitted for its own sake, incurs liability when its name is changed, then offerings that are forbidden for their own name should certainly incur liability. Rabbi Yehoshua counters that the pesach was changed to a forbidden matter, whereas these offerings are changed to a permitted matter. Rabbi Eliezer then cites communal emurim as a proof, but Rabbi Yehoshua distinguishes them because they have a fixed limit, unlike the pesach.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues a fortiori (קל וחומר): if the pesach, which is permitted for its own name, incurs liability when its name is changed, then other offerings, which are forbidden for their own name, should certainly incur liability when changed.

Rabbi Yehoshua objects that the analogy fails: the pesach was changed to a forbidden matter (חמץ), whereas other offerings are changed to a permitted matter (the pesach itself), so the a fortiori argument does not apply.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer's counter-proof from communal emurim
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's counter-proof from communal emurim
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer counters by citing communal emurim (אֵימוּרֵי צִיבּוּר), which are permitted for their own name yet one who slaughters them for their name is liable, proving that the a fortiori argument can hold.
Rabbi Yehoshua rejects the proof by distinguishing that communal emurim have a fixed limit (קִצְבָה), whereas the pesach has no fixed limit, so the analogy is not parallel.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's opinion
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's opinion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir says that even one who slaughters for the sake of communal emurim is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir adds: even one who slaughters for the sake of communal offerings is exempt.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of slaughtering for improper participants
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of slaughtering for improper participants
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details: If one slaughters the pesach not for its eaters or not for its counted members, for uncircumcised or impure people, he is liable. But if for its eaters and not for its eaters, for its members and not for its members, for circumcised and uncircumcised, for impure and pure, he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules: if one slaughters the pesach not for its eaters or not for its registered members, for uncircumcised or impure people, he is liable; but if for both eaters and non-eaters, members and non-members, circumcised and uncircumcised, impure and pure, he is exempt.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of blemished or terefah animals
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of blemished or terefah animals
items.desc_en: If one slaughtered the pesach and it was found to have a blemish, he is liable; if it was found to be a terefah in a hidden place, he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules: if one slaughters the pesach and it is found to have a blemish, he is liable; if it is found to be a treifah internally, he is exempt.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases where owners withdrew or died
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases where owners withdrew or died
items.desc_en: If one slaughtered the pesach and it became known that the owners had withdrawn their hand, or died, or became impure, he is exempt because he slaughtered with permission.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules: if one slaughters the pesach and it becomes known that the owners withdrew their hands, died, or became impure, he is exempt, because he slaughtered with permission.

items.text: Gemara's initial question: Is the Mishnah discussing a טועה or an עוקר?
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question: Is the Mishnah discussing a טועה or an עוקר?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's first clause deals with one who mistakenly intends to slaughter a different sacrifice (טועה) or one who explicitly uproots the Paschal lamb (עוקר). It concludes that if it were a טועה, the act of uprooting would be unintentional, so the case must be an עוקר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah deals with a טועה (one who mistakenly intends a different sacrifice) or an עוקר (one who explicitly uproots the Paschal lamb), concluding it must be an עוקר.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah's second clause
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah's second clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that the first clause deals with an עוקר by citing the second clause, where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute liability for slaughtering other sacrifices for the Paschal lamb. If the case is an עוקר, why would there be a difference between sacrifices that are fit or unfit for the Paschal lamb?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that the first clause deals with an עוקר (one who intends to abandon the original sacrifice) by citing the second clause, where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute liability for slaughtering other sacrifices for the Paschal lamb; if the case is an עוקר, why would there be a difference between sacrifices that are fit or unfit for the Paschal lamb?

items.text: Resolution: The Mishnah's first clause is an עוקר, the second is a טועה
items.text_en: Resolution: The Mishnah's first clause is an עוקר, the second is a טועה
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the first clause deals with an עוקר and the second with a טועה, as stated by Rabbi Avin. This explains the distinction between the two clauses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the first clause of the Mishnah deals with an עוקר (one who uproots the sacrifice) and the second with a טועה (one who errs), as stated by Rabbi Avin.
Rabbi Avin confirms the Gemara's resolution, stating explicitly that the first clause is about an עוקר and the second about a טועה.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef's encounter with Rabbi Avahu
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef's encounter with Rabbi Avahu
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef found Rabbi Avahu in a crowd and asked him about the Mishnah. Rabbi Avahu confirmed that the first clause is an עוקר and the second a טועה. Rabbi Yitzchak repeated this teaching forty times until it was as clear as if it were placed in his pocket.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef finds Rabbi Avahu in a crowd, asks about the Mishnah, receives the explanation that the first clause is an עוקר (one who uproots the sacrifice) and the second a טועה (one who errs), and repeats the teaching forty times until it is clear.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's kal vachomer argument challenged
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's kal vachomer argument challenged
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Eliezer's kal vachomer: if the Paschal lamb, which is permitted for its own sake, makes one liable when he changes its name, then other sacrifices, which are forbidden for their own sake, should certainly make one liable when he changes their name. The Gemara objects that this comparison fails because the first clause is an עוקר and the second a טועה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer's kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) is cited: if the Paschal lamb, which is permitted for its own sake, makes one liable when he changes its name, then other sacrifices, which are forbidden for their own sake, should certainly make one liable when he changes their name.

The Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer's kal vachomer fails because the first clause (the Paschal lamb) is an עוקר (one who intentionally uproots the sacrifice's designation) and the second clause (other sacrifices) is a טועה (one who errs), so the cases are not comparable.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's distinction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for Rabbi Eliezer, the distinction between עוקר and טועה does not matter, but for Rabbi Yehoshua, who distinguishes between them, the kal vachomer should be answered differently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that for Rabbi Eliezer, the distinction between עוקר (one who uproots the sacrifice) and טועה (one who errs) does not matter.
The Gemara asks that for Rabbi Yehoshua, who does distinguish between them, the kal vachomer argument should be answered differently.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's response to Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's response to Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua responds that for him, the cases are not comparable because the first clause is an עוקר and the second a טועה. He then argues that Rabbi Eliezer's kal vachomer is flawed: the Paschal lamb involves changing its name to a forbidden sacrifice, while other sacrifices involve changing their name to a permitted one (the Paschal lamb).

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's response to Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's response to Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua responds that for him, the cases are not comparable because the first clause is an עוקר (one who uproots the sacrifice) and the second a טועה (one who errs); he then argues that Rabbi Eliezer's kal vachomer is flawed: the Paschal lamb involves changing its name to a forbidden sacrifice, while other sacrifices involve changing their name to a permitted one (the Paschal lamb).

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's counter-argument: Emurei Tzibur
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's counter-argument: Emurei Tzibur
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer counters with the example of Emurei Tzibur (communal offerings), which are permitted for their own sake, yet one who slaughters them for their own name is liable. Rabbi Yehoshua responds that Emurei Tzibur have a fixed quantity (קצבה), unlike the Paschal lamb.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer objects to Rabbi Yehoshua's distinction by citing the case of Emurei Tzibur (communal offerings), which are permitted for their own sake, yet one who slaughters them for their own name is liable.
Rabbi Yehoshua responds that Emurei Tzibur have a fixed quantity (קצבה), unlike the Paschal lamb, so the analogy fails.

items.text: Challenge from the case of two infants (milah)
items.text_en: Challenge from the case of two infants (milah)
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehoshua's principle that fixed quantity (קצבה) determines liability, citing the case of two infants for circumcision: one due after Shabbat and one on Shabbat. If one mistakenly circumcises the wrong infant on Shabbat, Rabbi Eliezer holds him liable, but Rabbi Yehoshua exempts him, even though there is a fixed quantity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehoshua's principle that fixed quantity (קצבה) determines liability, asking whether he indeed always holds liable where there is a fixed quantity.

The Gemara cites a baraita about two infants for circumcision (מילה) where one is due after Shabbat and one on Shabbat, and mistakenly circumcising the wrong one on Shabbat is liable, showing a case with fixed quantity.

The baraita continues with a second case: one infant due before Shabbat and one on Shabbat, where mistakenly circumcising the earlier one on Shabbat leads to Rabbi Eliezer holding liable and Rabbi Yehoshua exempting, despite fixed quantity.

items.text: Rabbi Ami's resolution: The case of Emurei Tzibur involves prior action
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami's resolution: The case of Emurei Tzibur involves prior action
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami explains that the case of Emurei Tzibur is different because one first slaughtered the communal offerings (which have a fixed quantity) before the Paschal lamb, so the person is not distracted.
