In the circumcision case, the infant due on Shabbat was already circumcised earlier, so the person is preoccupied with that infant.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami resolves the contradiction by explaining that the circumcision case involves a prior action (the Shabbat infant was already circumcised earlier), so the person is preoccupied with that infant, whereas the case of Emurei Tzibur involves prior slaughter of the communal offerings, so the person is not distracted.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's opinion and the baraita's clarification
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's opinion and the baraita's clarification
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Meir, who says that one who slaughters for the sake of Emurei Tzibur is exempt, even if he slaughtered them first. A baraita from Rabbi Chiya clarifies that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua agree that if one circumcises the infant due on Shabbat on Friday, he is liable; they only dispute the case where one circumcises the infant due after Shabbat on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Meir's opinion that one who slaughters for the sake of Emurei Tzibur is exempt, even if he slaughtered them first.

A baraita from Rabbi Chiya clarifies that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua agree that one who circumcises the infant due on Shabbat on Friday is liable; they only dispute the case where one circumcises the infant due after Shabbat on Shabbat.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Meir's position
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Meir's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Meir's position: if in the circumcision case where no mitzvah is performed (circumcising the wrong infant), Rabbi Yehoshua exempts, then in a case where a mitzvah is performed (circumcising the correct infant), he should certainly exempt? This seems inconsistent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Meir's position: if in the circumcision case where no mitzvah is performed (circumcising the wrong infant), Rabbi Yehoshua exempts, then in a case where a mitzvah is performed (circumcising the correct infant), he should certainly exempt? This seems inconsistent.

items.text: Answer from the school of Rabbi Yannai
items.text_en: Answer from the school of Rabbi Yannai
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yannai explains that the first case (where Rabbi Yehoshua exempts) is where one circumcised the infant due on Shabbat on Friday, thereby performing a mitzvah, but the action was done at the wrong time, so he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yannai explains that the first case (where Rabbi Yehoshua exempts) is where one circumcised the infant due on Shabbat on Friday, thereby performing a mitzvah, but the action was done at the wrong time, so he is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's question on Shabbat being set aside for the Pesach
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Shabbat being set aside for the Pesach
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling about Shabbat being set aside for the Pesach, noting that Shabbat is already set aside for communal offerings. Rav Ashi challenges Rav Kahana that Shabbat is also set aside for any child's circumcision, but Rav Kahana responds that for this particular person, Shabbat was not set aside.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling by noting that Shabbat was not given to be set aside for the Pesach.
The Gemara answers that here, Shabbat was already set aside for communal offerings.
Rav Ashi objects to Rav Kahana that Shabbat is also set aside for any child's circumcision.
Rav Kahana responds that for this particular person, Shabbat was not set aside.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna behind the Mishnah's distinction between fit and unfit animals
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna behind the Mishnah's distinction between fit and unfit animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna that distinguishes between fit and unfit animals for the Pesach. It answers that it is Rabbi Shimon, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir exempts for all, and Rabbi Shimon states that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua only disagree on fit animals, while agreeing that unfit animals incur liability.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for other offerings slaughtered for the sake of Pesach, if unfit, one is liable; if fit, Rabbi Eliezer (רבי אליעזר) holds liable and Rabbi Yehoshua (רבי יהושע) exempts.
The Gemara asks: Who is the Tanna that distinguishes between fit and unfit animals?

The Gemara answers: It is Rabbi Shimon (רבי שמעון), citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר) exempts for all, and Rabbi Shimon (רבי שמעון) states that Rabbi Eliezer (רבי אליעזר) and Rabbi Yehoshua (רבי יהושע) only disagree on fit animals, while agreeing that unfit animals incur liability.

items.text: Rav Bibi's statement on Rabbi Meir's exemption for a calf of peace-offerings
items.text_en: Rav Bibi's statement on Rabbi Meir's exemption for a calf of peace-offerings
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi reports that Rabbi Elazar said Rabbi Meir would exempt even a calf of peace-offerings slaughtered for the Pesach. Rabbi Zeira objects based on Rabbi Yochanan's statement that Rabbi Meir admits liability for blemished animals, and Rav Bibi explains that blemished animals are not a concern for confusion, but this calf is a concern.

sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi reports in the name of Rabbi Elazar that Rabbi Meir would exempt even a calf of peace-offerings slaughtered for the purpose of the Paschal offering.
Rabbi Zeira objects to Rav Bibi, citing Rabbi Yochanan's statement that Rabbi Meir concedes liability for blemished animals.
Rav Bibi answers that blemished animals are not a concern for preoccupation, but this calf is a concern for preoccupation.

items.text: Rava's inquiry about non-sacred animals for the Pesach
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry about non-sacred animals for the Pesach
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about Rabbi Meir's view on non-sacred animals slaughtered for the Pesach. Rav Nachman says Rabbi Meir exempts even for non-sacred animals. The Gemara raises the objection from Rabbi Yochanan about blemished animals, and answers that blemished animals are not confused with the Pesach, but non-sacred animals are.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman what Rabbi Meir's ruling is regarding non-sacred animals (חולין) slaughtered for the sake of the Pesach.
Rav Nachman answers that Rabbi Meir would exempt even non-sacred animals slaughtered for the Pesach.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan said Rabbi Meir concedes liability for blemished animals, implying that the exemption is not absolute.
The Gemara resolves that blemished animals are not confused with the Pesach offering, but non-sacred animals are, so Rabbi Meir exempts only the latter.

items.text: Clarifying Rabbi Meir's rationale: confusion vs. preoccupation
items.text_en: Clarifying Rabbi Meir's rationale: confusion vs. preoccupation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir's reason is due to confusion or preoccupation, citing Rav Bibi's statement about a calf of peace-offerings which implies preoccupation. The answer is that both factors apply: preoccupation even without confusion, and confusion even without preoccupation, to exclude blemished animals which have neither.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir's rationale is due to confusion (איחלופי) or not.
The Gemara objects by citing Rav Bibi's statement that Rabbi Meir exempts even a calf of peace-offerings slaughtered for the Pesach, implying the reason is preoccupation (טריד), not confusion.
The Gemara concludes that Rav Bibi's statement shows Rabbi Meir's reason is preoccupation (טריד), not confusion.
The Gemara resolves that both factors apply: preoccupation even without confusion, and confusion even without preoccupation, to exclude blemished animals which have neither.

items.text: Debate between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on liability for mistaken action
items.text_en: Debate between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on liability for mistaken action
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says one who mistakenly eats leftover sacrifice from a spit is liable, while Rabbi Yochanan says one who mistakenly has relations with his wife thinking she is a menstruant is liable, but with his yevamah he is exempt. Two versions explain the difference: one says all the more so he is liable since he did not perform a mitzvah, the other says he is exempt because he should have inquired, unlike the case of the spit where inquiry was not possible.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak sit and discuss a statement of Resh Lakish.
Resh Lakish rules that one who mistakenly eats leftover sacrifice (נותר) from a spit is liable for a sin-offering.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who mistakenly has relations with his wife thinking she is a menstruant is liable, but with his yevamah (sister-in-law for levirate marriage) he is exempt.
One version says that in the yevamah case, all the more so he is liable because he did not perform a mitzvah (unlike the wife case where he performed the mitzvah of marital relations).
Another version says that in the yevamah case he is exempt because he should have inquired (whether she was a menstruant), unlike the spit case where inquiry was not possible.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Yochanan's distinction between wife and yevamah
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Yochanan's distinction between wife and yevamah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes between one's wife and yevamah, since both involve a mitzvah. It answers that the case is with a pregnant wife, where there is no mitzvah of procreation, but there is still the mitzvah of marital joy. It then specifies that it is not during her time for joy, and even though Rava says one must gladden his wife, it is close to her period. The difference is that with a yevamah he is wary, but with his wife he is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes between a yevamah (sister-in-law) and one's wife, since both involve a mitzvah (commandment).
The Gemara answers that the case is with a pregnant wife, where there is no mitzvah of procreation.
The Gemara objects that there is still the mitzvah of marital joy (שמחת עונה).
The Gemara answers that it is not during her time for joy (עונה).
The Gemara objects citing Rava's statement that one must gladden his wife with a mitzvah matter.
The Gemara answers that it is close to her menstrual period (וסתה), so the joy is diminished.
The Gemara objects that if so, even with a yevamah (sister-in-law) the same reasoning should apply.
The Gemara resolves that with a yevamah he is wary (בזיז), but with his wife he is not, so the distinction stands.

items.text: Attempts to align Rabbi Yochanan with a Tanna
items.text_en: Attempts to align Rabbi Yochanan with a Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to match Rabbi Yochanan's view with various Tannaitic opinions: Rabbi Yosei (lulav on Shabbat), Rabbi Yehoshua (sacrifices), Rabbi Yehoshua (children), and Rabbi Yehoshua (terumah). Each is rejected because of the factor of being rushed (zmano bahul) or because terumah is called 'avodah' and the Torah validates it. The Gemara concludes with a story about Rabbi Tarfon who called eating terumah 'avodah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna Rabbi Yochanan's view aligns with.
The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Yochanan follows Rabbi Yosei's ruling about lulav on Shabbat.
The Gemara rejects the proposal because the case of lulav involves being rushed (זמנו בהול).
The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Yochanan follows Rabbi Yehoshua's view regarding sacrifices.
The Gemara rejects this proposal because the case of sacrifices also involves being rushed.
The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Yochanan follows Rabbi Yehoshua's view regarding children.
The Gemara rejects this proposal because the case of children also involves being rushed.
The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Yochanan follows Rabbi Yehoshua's view regarding terumah.

The Gemara rejects this proposal, offering two alternatives: either the case involves being rushed on Passover eve, or terumah is called 'avodah' and the Torah validates it, as illustrated by the story of Rabbi Tarfon.

items.text: Opening statement: Comparison of eating terumah to Temple service
items.text_en: Opening statement: Comparison of eating terumah to Temple service
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse equating eating terumah in the border regions to Temple service, establishing a framework for liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse equating eating terumah in the border regions to Temple service, establishing a framework for liability.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about slaughtering not for its eaters
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about slaughtering not for its eaters
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that slaughtering the Paschal lamb not for its eaters is liable, since it parallels the case of slaughtering not for its name which is invalid. It explains that the Tanna included it because of the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state that slaughtering the Paschal lamb not for its eaters is liable, since it is obvious from the parallel case of slaughtering not for its name.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna included the case because the later clause teaches exemption, so the earlier clause teaches liability.
The Gemara objects that the exemption case is also obvious, since the parallel case of slaughtering for its name is valid.
The Gemara explains that since the Tanna taught the case of slaughtering not for its name on Shabbat, he also taught the case of not for its eaters.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to teach the case of slaughtering not for its name on Shabbat at all.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah includes this case because it establishes the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Chinana's inquiry about 'one who damages' and slaughter not for eaters
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana's inquiry about 'one who damages' and slaughter not for eaters
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana instructs his son to ask Rabbi Zerika whether, according to the opinion that one who damages through a wound is exempt, slaughtering not for its eaters is liable. The answer is that it is a tikun (constructive act) because if the offering ascended, it does not descend.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Chinana's instruction to his son
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana's instruction to his son
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana instructs his son to ask Rabbi Zerika whether, according to the opinion that one who damages through a wound is exempt, slaughtering not for its eaters is liable, and what constructive act (תיקון) it accomplishes.
The Gemara answers that the constructive act (תיקון) is that if the offering ascended the altar, it does not descend.

items.text: Case of slaughtering a blemished animal: liable
items.text_en: Case of slaughtering a blemished animal: liable
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses slaughtering a blemished animal on Shabbat, which is liable. The tikun is that it is considered a blemish of the eye, according to Rabbi Akiva who says if it ascended, it does not descend.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: regarding the case of slaughtering a blemished animal on Shabbat for which one is liable, what is the tikun (rectification) that makes the slaughter a constructive act?

The Gemara answers: the tikun is that the blemish is considered a defect of the eye (a blemish that does not disqualify the animal from the altar once it has ascended), in accordance with Rabbi Akiva who holds that if such an animal ascended the altar it does not descend.

items.text: Case of slaughtering a tereifah in a hidden place: exempt
items.text_en: Case of slaughtering a tereifah in a hidden place: exempt
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that slaughtering a tereifah in a hidden place is exempt, but in a revealed place it is liable. The tikun is to remove it from the status of neveilah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that slaughtering a tereifah in a hidden place is exempt, and the Gemara explains that the tikun is to remove it from the status of neveilah.

items.text: Ravina's objection: case of slaughtering a chatat on Shabbat outside for idolatry
items.text_en: Ravina's objection: case of slaughtering a chatat on Shabbat outside for idolatry
items.desc_en: Ravina objects with a baraita that one who slaughters a chatat on Shabbat outside for idolatry is liable for three chatat offerings. Rav Avira answers that the tikun is to remove it from the status of a limb from a living animal.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects by citing a baraita that one who slaughters a chatat on Shabbat outside for idolatry is liable for three chatat offerings, and asks what tikun (remedy) applies.
Rav Avira answers that the tikun is to remove it from the status of אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי (a limb from a living animal).

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling about an asham sent to pasture and slaughtered
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling about an asham sent to pasture and slaughtered
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says that an asham that was sent to pasture and then slaughtered without specification is valid for an olah, implying no need for a verbal designation. The Gemara questions why it wouldn't be valid even without being sent to pasture, and answers that it is a decree after atonement lest one do so before atonement. A proof is brought from a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehoshua allows selling the animal and bringing an olah with its money, but not the animal itself, due to the same decree.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states in the name of Rav that an asham (guilt-offering) that was sent to pasture and then slaughtered without specification is valid as an olah (burnt-offering), implying no need for a verbal designation (עקירה).
The Gemara questions why the animal would not be valid even without being sent to pasture, since the ruling seems to apply universally.
The Gemara answers that it is a decree (גזירה) after atonement lest one do so before atonement, restricting the rule to cases where the animal was sent to pasture.

The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute the fate of an asham whose owners died or achieved atonement, with Rabbi Yehoshua allowing sale and bringing an olah with the proceeds.
The Gemara infers from Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling that only the money, not the animal itself, may be used for an olah, due to the same decree after atonement, thus supporting Rav Huna's position.

items.text: Rav Chisda's objection to Rav Huna
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's objection to Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda objects to Rav Huna from a Mishnah about slaughtering and discovering that the owners had withdrawn their hands, challenging the previous ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda objects to Rav Huna by citing a Mishnah about slaughtering and discovering that the owners had withdrawn their hands, challenging the previous ruling.

items.text: Gemara's initial question: Does a Paschal lamb require עקירה?
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question: Does a Paschal lamb require עקירה?
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that a Paschal lamb slaughtered after the daily afternoon offering on a weekday must be burned immediately. It argues: if עקירה is required, the lamb is invalid because its owners died (פסולו בגופו), hence immediate burning. But if no עקירה is needed, it was always a peace-offering, and its invalidation is due to being slaughtered after the daily offering, which requires waiting for 'עיבור צורה' (disfigurement) before burning, as per the rule in the baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that a Paschal lamb slaughtered on a weekday after the owners died is burned immediately, and argues that if עקירה (uprooting) is required, the lamb's disqualification is in its body (פסולו בגופו), justifying immediate burning.

The Gemara raises the alternative: if no עקירה (uprooting) is needed, the lamb was always a peace-offering, and its disqualification is due to being slaughtered after the daily afternoon offering, which requires waiting for עיבור צורה (disfigurement) before burning.

The Gemara cites a baraita stating the principle: an offering with disqualification in its body is burned immediately, but if the disqualification is in the blood or owners, it requires עיבור צורה (disfigurement) before burning.

items.text: Resolution: The baraita refers to slaughtering for the sake of a burnt-offering
items.text_en: Resolution: The baraita refers to slaughtering for the sake of a burnt-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the baraita: it does not say 'slaughtered it without specification' but rather 'slaughtered it for the sake of a burnt-offering', which is valid. This implies that עקירה is required, as the lamb must be explicitly designated for another sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the baraita: it does not say 'slaughtered it without specification' but rather 'slaughtered it for the sake of a burnt-offering', which is valid, implying that עקירה (uprooting) is required.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda's view
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the conclusion that עקירה is always required, citing Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda who says that only in a specific case (where the blood was sprinkled on behalf of a group and the owners were impure with corpse impurity, deferred to the second Pesach) does עקירה apply. Otherwise, no עקירה is needed. This contradicts the previous resolution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous conclusion by citing Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda, who holds that עקירה (mental redirection) is only required in the specific case of owners who were טמאי מתים (impure from corpse impurity) and deferred to the second Pesach, implying that otherwise no עקירה is needed.

items.text: Answer of Rav Huna bar Yehoshua: The case involves a lamb set aside before noon with owners dying after noon
items.text_en: Answer of Rav Huna bar Yehoshua: The case involves a lamb set aside before noon with owners dying after noon
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua explains that the baraita deals with a lamb consecrated before noon, whose owners died after noon. Since the lamb was 'seen' (fit) at noon and then 'rejected' (due to owners' death), it cannot return to fitness. This explains why it requires immediate burning, without needing to invoke the issue of עקירה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua answers that the baraita deals with a lamb consecrated before noon whose owners died after noon, making it a case of נראה ונדחה (seen and rejected), which cannot return to fitness, so it requires immediate burning without invoking עקירה.

items.text: Objection from Rav's principle: Living animals are not subject to rejection
items.text_en: Objection from Rav's principle: Living animals are not subject to rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav holds living animals are not subject to the principle of 'נראה ונדחה' (seen and rejected), so Rav Huna's explanation cannot stand according to Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav Huna's explanation cannot stand according to Rav, because Rav holds that living animals are not subject to the principle of נראה ונדחה (seen and rejected).

items.text: Answer of Rav Papa: The baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Answer of Rav Papa: The baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Rav Papa suggests that the baraita is in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that one who slaughters other sacrifices for the sake of a Paschal lamb is invalid, and such invalidation is 'פסולו בגופו' (inherent), requiring immediate burning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that slaughtering other sacrifices for the sake of a Paschal lamb renders them invalid with an inherent invalidity (פסולו בגופו), requiring immediate burning.

items.text: Challenge: If it's Rabbi Eliezer, why is the slaughterer exempt from a sin-offering?
items.text_en: Challenge: If it's Rabbi Eliezer, why is the slaughterer exempt from a sin-offering?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Papa's suggestion: if the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer, who does not exempt one who errs in a mitzvah (טועה בדבר מצוה), then the slaughterer should be liable for a sin-offering. But the baraita implies exemption, as it only discusses the sacrifice's status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Papa's suggestion: if the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer, who does not exempt a טועה בדבר מצוה (one who errs in a mitzvah), then the slaughterer should be liable for a sin-offering, but the baraita implies exemption.

items.text: Answer of Rav Yosef bar Rav Salla: The baraita follows Yosef ben Chonai
items.text_en: Answer of Rav Yosef bar Rav Salla: The baraita follows Yosef ben Chonai
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Rav Salla explains before Rav Papa that the baraita follows Yosef ben Chonai, who holds that animals slaughtered for the sake of a Paschal lamb or a sin-offering are invalid (פסולו בגופו), and he agrees with Rabbi Yehoshua regarding exemption from a sin-offering.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Rav Salla's answer before Rav Papa
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Rav Salla's answer before Rav Papa
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Rav Salla explains that the baraita follows Yosef ben Chonai, who holds that animals slaughtered for the sake of a Paschal lamb or a sin-offering are invalid (פסולו בגופו), and he agrees with Rabbi Yehoshua regarding exemption from a sin-offering.

items.text: Alternative answer of Rav Ashi: Rav follows Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
items.text_en: Alternative answer of Rav Ashi: Rav follows Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi offers another explanation: Rav holds like Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who says that if there is time to check whether the owners withdrew, died, or became impure, the slaughterer is liable, and the animal requires 'עיבור צורה' before burning. This implies that no עקירה is needed, as the animal's status is not immediately determined.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that Rav follows Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds that if there is time to check whether the owners withdrew, died, or became impure, the slaughterer is liable and the animal requires עיבור צורה (a change in form) before burning, implying that no עקירה (mental withdrawal) is needed.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Ashi: Perhaps it follows the Tanna of Bei Rabba bar Avuha who requires עיבור צורה even for piggul
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Ashi: Perhaps it follows the Tanna of Bei Rabba bar Avuha who requires עיבור צורה even for piggul
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Ashi's proof: perhaps Rabbi Yishmael's view is because he holds like the Tanna of Bei Rabba bar Avuha, who requires 'עיבור צורה' even for piggul (by a gezeirah shava from notar). This would mean that even if עקירה is required, the animal still needs עיבור צורה, so the case of owners becoming impure (which certainly requires עקירה) would also require עיבור צורה, undermining the proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Ashi's proof: perhaps Rabbi Yishmael's ruling is because he follows the Tanna of Bei Rabba bar Avuha, who requires עיבור צורה (form-change) even for piggul via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from notar.

The Gemara supports the challenge: if not for this explanation, the case of owners becoming impure (which certainly requires עקירה (intentional designation)) would also require עיבור צורה, as per Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda's ruling that such owners are deferred to the second Pesach.

items.text: Conclusion: The original explanation (Yosef ben Chonai) is preferred
items.text_en: Conclusion: The original explanation (Yosef ben Chonai) is preferred
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the straightforward explanation (מחוורתא) is as originally revised: the baraita follows Yosef ben Chonai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the straightforward explanation (מחוורתא) is as originally revised: the baraita follows Yosef ben Chonai.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes how to roast the Paschal lamb: using a pomegranate-wood spit inserted through the mouth to the anus, with the legs and innards placed inside (Rabbi Yosei HaGelili). Rabbi Akiva objects that this is like cooking, and instead they should be hung outside. It also rules that the lamb may not be roasted on a metal spit or on a grill, citing a story of Rabban Gamliel who instructed his servant to roast on a grill.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry about the spit material
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry about the spit material
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a metal spit is not used, explaining that metal heats throughout and would cook the meat from the spit's heat, violating the requirement of 'roasting by fire' (צלי אש). It then considers a palm-wood spit, which has fibers that release water and cause steaming, and a fig-wood spit, which is porous and also releases water. Finally, it addresses oak, carob, and sycamore spits, which have knots that release water, and explains that pomegranate wood is used because its knots are smooth, or alternatively, a young branch without knots is used, with the ends removed.

items.text: Mishnah's dispute with Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Mishnah's dispute with Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling (allowing only a wooden spit) disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a metal spit does not cause the meat to boil because it does not heat throughout, whereas a wooden spit does not burn. The Sages argue that a metal spit heats throughout, while a wooden spit does not.

items.text: Names for the stuffed lamb
items.text_en: Names for the stuffed lamb
items.desc_en: A baraita records that Rabbi Yishmael calls the stuffed lamb 'תּוֹךְ תּוֹךְ' (inner parts), and Rabbi Tarfon calls it 'גְּדִי מְקוּלָּס' (a roasted kid).

items.text: Definition of 'גדי מקולס'
items.text_en: Definition of 'גדי מקולס'
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that a 'גדי מקולס' (roasted kid) forbidden on Passover eve is one roasted whole. If a limb was cut off or parboiled, it is not considered a 'גדי מקולס'. The Gemara questions why a cut-off limb is not considered, even if roasted together, and Rav Sheshet explains that the baraita refers to a limb that was parboiled while still attached.

items.text: Discussion of the 'mulayta' (stuffed dish) and support from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Discussion of the 'mulayta' (stuffed dish) and support from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbah permits eating a 'mulayta' (a stuffed dish), and Abaye objects that it absorbs blood. Rabbah responds that as it absorbs, so it expels. The Gemara suggests support from the Mishnah where the legs and innards are placed inside the lamb, implying that the innards absorb and then expel blood. The Gemara deflects, saying that the case of the Mishnah is different because the neck opening allows blood to escape.

items.text: Opening statement about dripping blood
items.text_en: Opening statement about dripping blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a brief statement about blood that drips (מֵידָב דָּיְיבִי), setting the context for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a brief statement about blood that drips (מֵידָב דָּיְיבִי), setting the context for the discussion.

items.text: Support for the principle of "as it absorbs, so it expels"
items.text_en: Support for the principle of "as it absorbs, so it expels"
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests a support from the law of the heart: one must tear it and remove its blood; if not done before cooking, it is permitted after cooking because we say "as it absorbs, so it expels." The Gemara rejects this proof because the heart is smooth (שיע) and thus different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests a support for the principle of "as it absorbs, so it expels" from the law of the heart: one must tear it and remove its blood; if not done before cooking, it is permitted after cooking because we say "as it absorbs, so it expels."
The Gemara rejects the proof because the heart is smooth (שיע) and thus different from other organs.

items.text: Challenges from the cases of Ravin and Rava
items.text_en: Challenges from the cases of Ravin and Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings two challenges: Ravin the Elder fed a young bird to Rav and asked for it if it was well-roasted, and Rava was fed a goose and only ate it if it was singed like a white zuz. These challenge the principle, but the Gemara distinguishes: the first case was with fine flour (סמידא) that crumbles, and the second with a white spot (חיוורתא) that is firm.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle by citing Ravin the Elder, who fed a young bird to Rav and asked to eat it only if it was well-roasted.
The Gemara distinguishes that the case involved fine flour (סמידא) which crumbles, so the roasting test was necessary.
The Gemara challenges further with Rava, who was fed a goose and only ate it if it was singed like a white zuz.
The Gemara objects that if the principle 'as it absorbs so it expels' applies, the singeing should be irrelevant.
The Gemara distinguishes that the case involved a white spot (חיוורתא) that is firm, requiring the singeing test.

items.text: Halachic ruling for different types of flour
items.text_en: Halachic ruling for different types of flour
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes with a ruling: for fine flour (סמידא), whether it reddened or not, it is permitted; for a white spot (חיוורתא), if it is singed like a white zuz, it is permitted, otherwise forbidden; for other flours, if reddened, forbidden, if not, permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Stam issues a final halachic ruling distinguishing between fine flour (סמידא), white spot (חיוורתא), and other flours regarding the permissibility after roasting.

items.text: Ruling on mulayta (a type of dish)
items.text_en: Ruling on mulayta (a type of dish)
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses mulayta: one who forbids does so even with the mouth downward, and one who permits does so even with the mouth upward. The halacha is that mulayta is permitted even with the mouth upward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute about mulayta: one who forbids does so even with the mouth downward, and one who permits does so even with the mouth upward.
The Gemara rules that mulayta is permitted even with the mouth upward.

items.text: General principle regarding Rav Acha and Ravina
items.text_en: General principle regarding Rav Acha and Ravina
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a general rule: in the entire Torah, Rav Acha is stringent and Ravina is lenient, and the halacha follows Ravina's leniency, except for three cases where Rav Acha is lenient and Ravina is stringent, and the halacha follows Rav Acha's leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a general rule: in the entire Torah, Rav Acha is stringent and Ravina is lenient, and the halacha follows Ravina's leniency, except for three cases where Rav Acha is lenient and Ravina is stringent, and the halacha follows Rav Acha's leniency.

items.text: Detailed laws of congealed blood (אומצא, ביעי, מיזרקי)
items.text_en: Detailed laws of congealed blood (אומצא, ביעי, מיזרקי)
items.desc_en: The Gemara details the laws for three types of congealed blood: if cut and salted, they are permitted even for a pot; if hung on a spit, they are permitted because the blood drips; if placed on coals, Rav Acha and Ravina dispute whether it is forbidden (because it congeals) or permitted (because it absorbs). The halacha follows that it absorbs (מישאב שאיב).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with the law of congealed blood (אומצא): if cut and salted, it is permitted even for a pot; if hung on a spit, it is permitted because the blood drips out.

The Gemara presents the dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina regarding congealed blood placed on coals: one forbids because it congeals (מצמת צמית), the other permits because it absorbs (מישאב שאיב), and the halacha follows that it absorbs.
The Gemara applies the same three-case pattern to eggs (ביעי) and to mizrakim (מיזרקי), each with the same dispute and ruling.

items.text: Dispute about the spleen and its ruling
items.text_en: Dispute about the spleen and its ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the spleen (חליא): if it reddened, it is forbidden; if not, it is permitted. Ravina says even if not reddened it is forbidden because there are blood vessels. Mar bar Ameimar and Rav Ashi practice swallowing it whole. Then Mar bar Ameimar asks Rav Ashi about a spleen that has been boiled once and cannot be boiled again, comparing it to a regular spleen.

sub.desc_en: The Stam states the basic rule: a spleen (אומצא) whose spleen (חליא) reddened is forbidden, but if not reddened it is permitted.
Ravina objects that even if the spleen did not redden, it is forbidden because it inevitably contains blood vessels (שורייקא דמא).

sub.text: Mar bar Ameimar and Rav Ashi's practice
sub.text_en: Mar bar Ameimar and Rav Ashi's practice
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ameimar reports that his father (or Rav Ashi himself) swallows the spleen whole (מגמע ליה גמועי) to avoid the blood issue.

sub.text: Mar bar Ameimar's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Mar bar Ameimar's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ameimar asks Rav Ashi about a spleen (חליא) that has been boiled once and cannot be boiled again, comparing it to a regular spleen.
Mar bar Ameimar asks what distinguishes this spleen from a regular spleen (חלא מתמהא) that we boil, implying the same rule should apply.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah and the story of Rabban Gamliel
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah and the story of Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction in the Mishnah by explaining that it is missing a clause: if the spit is perforated, it is permitted. It then cites the story of Rabban Gamliel instructing his servant to roast the Paschal lamb on a perforated spit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the spit's presence (which retains the juice) and its absence.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is missing a clause: if the spit is perforated, it is permitted, and cites the story of Rabban Gamliel instructing his servant to roast the Paschal lamb on a perforated spit.

items.text: Inquiry about an oven heated with orlah peels and then swept
items.text_en: Inquiry about an oven heated with orlah peels and then swept
items.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Idi asks Rav Adda bar Ahava about bread baked in an oven heated with orlah peels that was then swept out. Rav Adda rules the bread is permitted. Rav Chinana objects based on Rav Yochanan's teaching that roasting in a swept oven is not 'roasting over fire' for the Paschal lamb, but the Gemara distinguishes between the two cases: for the Paschal lamb, the Torah requires direct fire, while here the prohibition is about the forbidden wood, which is no longer present.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Idi asks Rav Adda bar Ahava about bread baked in an oven heated with orlah peels and then swept out, inquiring about its status according to the one who prohibits.
Rav Adda bar Ahava rules that the bread is permitted.
Rav Chinana bar Idi objects by citing Rav Yochanan's teaching that roasting in a swept oven is not considered 'roasting over fire' for the Paschal lamb.
The Gemara distinguishes: for the Paschal lamb, the Torah explicitly requires direct fire by repeating 'צלי אש' twice, but without that, a swept oven would be considered direct fire.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: for the Paschal lamb, the Torah requires direct fire, but here the prohibition is about the forbidden wood, which is no longer present after sweeping.

items.text: Rabbi's opinion on coals and the derivation from 'כויה'
items.text_en: Rabbi's opinion on coals and the derivation from 'כויה'
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi considers placing meat on coals to be 'roasting over fire'. Rav Achadvoi bar Ami challenges Rav Chisda: does Rabbi consider coals to be fire? He cites a derivation from the word 'כויה' repeated in the Torah to include coals. Rav Chisda answers that the verse is only needed for metal coals, not wood coals.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi rules that placing meat on coals is considered roasting over fire.

sub.text: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami's challenge to Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami's challenge to Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami challenges Rav Chisda: does Rabbi consider coals to be fire?
A baraita is cited: the Torah repeats the word 'מִכְוָה' (burn) to include coals, embers, and other fire-derived sources.
Rav Achadvoi bar Ami infers: if not for the repetition of 'מִכְוָה', coals would not be considered fire, contradicting Rabbi's view.
Rav Chisda answers: the verse is only needed to include metal coals, not wood coals, which are inherently fire.

items.text: Digression: metal coals and the burning of a priest's daughter
items.text_en: Digression: metal coals and the burning of a priest's daughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether metal coals are not fire, citing the case of a priest's daughter where a lead wick is used for burning. The Gemara explains that the verse 'בָּאֵשׁ תִּשָּׂרֵף' includes all forms of burning from fire, but the preferred method is a gentle death. The Gemara then clarifies the need for both the gezeirah shavah and Rav Nachman's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether metal coals are not considered fire, citing the case of a priest's daughter where a lead wick is used for burning.
The Gemara distinguishes that there the verse 'בָּאֵשׁ תִּשָּׂרֵף' includes all forms of burning from fire.

The Gemara objects that if so, one could surround her with bundles of twigs and burn her, but the gezeirah shavah from the sons of Aaron teaches that the burning must be of the soul while the body remains intact.
The Gemara asks why not use hot water from fire, and answers due to Rav Nachman's principle of choosing a gentle death.

The Gemara questions why both the gezeirah shavah and Rav Nachman's principle are needed, and explains that without the gezeirah shavah one might think soul-burning with body intact is not burning, and without Rav Nachman one might use many twigs for a quick death.
The Gemara resolves that the word 'בָּאֵשׁ' serves to exclude lead from the primary burning method.

items.text: Challenge from the burnt bulls and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the burnt bulls and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya challenges Rabbi Zeira: regarding the burnt bulls, the verse says 'בָּאֵשׁ' and a baraita excludes boiling lime and gypsum, implying only fire is valid. Rabbi Zeira resolves that there the verse structure is different: 'בָּאֵשׁ' is followed by 'תִּשָּׂרֵף' to include all fire-based burnings, while for the bulls the verse ends with 'בָּאֵשׁ', excluding other substances.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's challenge to Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's challenge to Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya challenges Rabbi Zeira: wherever the verse says 'בָּאֵשׁ תִּשָּׂרֵף', does it include all fire-based burnings? He cites the burnt bulls where the verse ends with 'בָּאֵשׁ' and a baraita excludes boiling lime and gypsum.

Rabbi Zeira resolves: there the verse structure is different — 'בָּאֵשׁ' is followed by 'תִּשָּׂרֵף' to include all fire-based burnings, while for the bulls the verse ends with 'בָּאֵשׁ', excluding other substances.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects: there too a burning is written at the end, as it is written — implying the same exclusion might apply.

items.text: Interpretation of "יִשָּׂרֵף"
items.text_en: Interpretation of "יִשָּׂרֵף"
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for the word "יִשָּׂרֵף" in the verse about the red heifer, and explains that it teaches that the heifer is burned even without ash present, and even if most of it is already ignited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse uses the word 'יִשָּׂרֵף' (it shall be burned) regarding the red heifer, implying it is superfluous.
The Tanna explains that the word 'יִשָּׂרֵף' teaches two laws: the heifer is burned even without ash present, and even if most of it is already ignited.

items.text: Ravina's teaching on "מִכְוַת אֵשׁ"
items.text_en: Ravina's teaching on "מִכְוַת אֵשׁ"
items.desc_en: Ravina teaches that the verse "מִכְוַת אֵשׁ" includes not only burns from fire and coal, but also from hot embers, lime, gypsum, and any substance heated by fire, derived from the repetition of "מִכְוָה".

sub.desc_en: Ravina teaches that the verse "מִכְוַת אֵשׁ" includes burns from hot embers, lime, gypsum, and any substance heated by fire, derived from the repetition of "מִכְוָה".

items.text: Rava's contradiction and resolution regarding coals
items.text_en: Rava's contradiction and resolution regarding coals
items.desc_en: Rava raises a contradiction: Rabbi Yehuda considers coals as fire, but a baraita distinguishes between coals and fire, requiring both. The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to smoldering coals, while Rabbi Yehuda refers to glowing coals. Rav Sheishes offers a different version of the baraita, but the contradiction with Rabbi Yehuda remains.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises a contradiction: Rabbi Yehuda considers coals as fire, but a baraita distinguishes between coals and fire, requiring both.
The Gemara objects that the baraita itself is internally contradictory: the first clause implies glowing coals are fire, the second implies even glowing coals are not fire.
Rav Sheishes offers a different version of the baraita that resolves the internal contradiction, but the contradiction with Rabbi Yehuda remains.

items.text: Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita means: smoldering coals are excluded by "אֵשׁ", but one might think he can bring either a flame or a coal; therefore "גַּחֲלֵי" teaches that he brings glowing coals.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the baraita: 'גַּחֲלֵי' excludes smoldering coals, 'אֵשׁ' excludes a flame, and the result is that one brings glowing coals (לוחשות).

items.text: Rabbah's objection and alternative
items.text_en: Rabbah's objection and alternative
items.desc_en: Rabbah objects that one could bring either a coal or a flame, but a flame without a coal is impossible; he suggests a case of oil in a vessel, but then argues that such a disrespectful act is unthinkable before God.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah objects that the verse should allow bringing either a coal or a flame, but a flame without a coal is impossible.
Rabbah suggests a case of oil in a vessel to produce a flame without a coal, but then argues that such a disrespectful act is unthinkable before God.

items.text: Rava's final resolution
items.text_en: Rava's final resolution
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the issue by explaining that the verse "וְלָקַח מְלֹא הַמַּחְתָּה גַּחֲלֵי אֵשׁ" teaches that at the time of taking, it must be coals, not a mixture of coal and flame.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that the verse 'וְלָקַח מְלֹא הַמַּחְתָּה גַּחֲלֵי אֵשׁ' teaches that at the time of taking, it must be coals, not a mixture of coal and flame.

items.text: Query about the spelling of "עוֹמְמוֹת"
items.text_en: Query about the spelling of "עוֹמְמוֹת"
items.desc_en: A question is raised whether the word is spelled "אוֹמְמוֹת" or "עוֹמְמוֹת". Rabbi Yitzchak cites a verse to support the spelling with an 'ayin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a query whether the word in the baraita is spelled with an aleph (אוֹמְמוֹת) or an ayin (עוֹמְמוֹת).
Rabbi Yitzchak cites the verse 'אֲרָזִים לֹא עֲמָמֻהוּ' (Ezekiel 31:8) to prove that the word is spelled with an ayin (עוֹמְמוֹת), as the verse uses the root עמם.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of a paschal lamb that touched a hot surface
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of a paschal lamb that touched a hot surface
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where the paschal lamb touched a hot potsherd, had gravy drip onto it, or was anointed with oil, and the remedies required. It also discusses the status of the oil used.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of the paschal lamb touching a hot potsherd, requiring peeling the affected area.
The Mishnah presents a second case: gravy drips onto a potsherd and returns to the lamb, requiring removal of the affected spot.
The Mishnah presents a third case: gravy drips onto flour, requiring removal of the affected area by pinching off.
The Mishnah discusses anointing with תרומה (priestly portion) oil: if the owners are priests, they may eat it; if Israelites, they must wash it off if raw.
The Mishnah adds: if the lamb is roasted, one peels off the outer layer.
The Mishnah concludes: anointing with second tithe oil cannot be redeemed for money for the group, because second tithe is not redeemed in Jerusalem.

items.text: Gemara: Beginning of discussion on "חַם לְתוֹךְ חַם"
items.text_en: Gemara: Beginning of discussion on "חַם לְתוֹךְ חַם"
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins its analysis with a statement about the case of hot into hot, which is agreed upon by all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement that the case of hot into hot is agreed upon by all.

items.text: Opening dispute: Rav vs. Shmuel on hot and cold mixtures
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rav vs. Shmuel on hot and cold mixtures
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that hot into hot is forbidden, cold into cold is permitted. Rav and Shmuel disagree on hot into cold and cold into hot: Rav says the upper element prevails, Shmuel says the lower element prevails.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that hot into hot is forbidden, cold into cold is permitted by all.
Rav and Shmuel disagree on hot into cold and cold into hot: Rav says the upper element prevails, Shmuel says the lower element prevails.

items.text: First challenge: Mishnah about gravy on a potsherd
items.text_en: First challenge: Mishnah about gravy on a potsherd
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel's view from a Mishnah where gravy drips onto a cold potsherd and returns to the Pesach, requiring removal of the spot. According to Shmuel, the cold potsherd should cool the gravy, so why is it forbidden? Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the potsherd was hot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel's view from a Mishnah where gravy drips onto a cold potsherd and returns to the Pesach, requiring removal of the spot; according to Shmuel, the cold potsherd should cool the gravy, so why is it forbidden?
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the Mishnah refers to a hot potsherd, not a cold one, thus resolving the challenge to Shmuel.

items.text: Second challenge: Mishnah about gravy on flour
items.text_en: Second challenge: Mishnah about gravy on flour
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel from a Mishnah where gravy drips onto flour, requiring removal of the spot. According to Shmuel, cold flour should cool the gravy, so why is removal needed? Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the flour was hot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel from a Mishnah where gravy drips onto flour and requires removal of the spot, arguing that according to Shmuel's principle that the lower element dominates, cold flour should cool the gravy, making removal unnecessary.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers in Shmuel's name that the Mishnah's case involves hot flour, not cold, so Shmuel's principle does not apply.

items.text: Third challenge: Mishnah about anointing with terumah oil
items.text_en: Third challenge: Mishnah about anointing with terumah oil
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel from a Mishnah where anointing a roasted Pesach with terumah oil only requires peeling the outer layer. According to Shmuel, the hot oil should be absorbed entirely. The Gemara answers that anointing is only a minimal amount.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel from a Mishnah where anointing a roasted Pesach with terumah oil only requires peeling the outer layer, arguing that according to Shmuel's principle that the lower (hot) element dominates, the hot meat should absorb all the oil and be entirely forbidden.
The Gemara answers that anointing is different because only a minimal amount of oil is applied, so absorption is negligible and peeling suffices.

items.text: Baraita supporting Shmuel
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Shmuel
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Shmuel's view: hot into cold requires rinsing. The Gemara questions why only rinsing is needed, since some absorption occurs, and suggests the text should say 'peeling' for hot into cold.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Shmuel's view: hot into hot is forbidden, cold into hot is forbidden, hot into cold and cold into cold require only rinsing.
The Gemara objects: since hot into cold inevitably absorbs a little before cooling, why does the baraita say only rinsing is needed? It should require peeling.
The Gemara corrects the baraita: hot into cold requires peeling, while cold into cold requires only rinsing.

items.text: Second baraita on meat and milk
items.text_en: Second baraita on meat and milk
items.desc_en: Another baraita is cited about hot meat falling into hot milk, and cold into hot, all forbidden. Hot into cold and cold into cold require rinsing. The Gemara again questions the rinsing for hot into cold and corrects to 'peeling'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that hot meat into hot milk and cold into hot are forbidden, while hot into cold and cold into cold require only rinsing.
The Gemara objects that since the hot meat is hot, it must absorb some forbidden milk before cooling, so rinsing is insufficient and peeling should be required.
The Gemara corrects the baraita: hot into cold requires peeling, while cold into cold requires only rinsing.

items.text: Rav Huna's distinction: salted foods are like hot
items.text_en: Rav Huna's distinction: salted foods are like hot
items.desc_en: Rav Huna qualifies that cold into cold is only permitted if the food is not salted, because salted food is considered hot. Rava adds that this applies only if the saltiness makes it inedible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Mar's statement that cold into cold requires only rinsing.
Rav Huna qualifies that the leniency of rinsing applies only if the food was not salted, because salted food is considered hot.

sub.text: Shmuel's principle cited by Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Shmuel's principle cited by Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna supports his qualification by citing Shmuel's principle that a salted item is like a hot one, and a pickled item is like a cooked one.
Rava further qualifies that Shmuel's principle applies only when the saltiness makes the food inedible, but not when it remains edible despite the salt.

items.text: Case of a young bird in a pot of salt
items.text_en: Case of a young bird in a pot of salt
items.desc_en: A young bird fell into a pot of salt. Rav Chinana bar Rava permitted it because the salt was edible. Rava praises him, and adds that for a roasted bird, peeling is required, and if there are cracks or spices, it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a young bird fell into a pot of salt, and Rav Chinana bar Rava permitted it.
Rava praises Rav Chinana bar Rava and explains that Shmuel's principle of 'salt is like boiling' applies only when the salt is inedible, but here the salt is edible, so it is permitted.
Rava adds that for a roasted bird, peeling is required, and if there are cracks or spices, it is forbidden.

items.text: Rav's statement (unfinished)
items.text_en: Rav's statement (unfinished)
items.desc_en: The daf ends with Rav beginning to speak, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rava praises Rav Ḥinnana bar Rava of Pashronya for his wisdom in permitting the bird that fell into kutaḥ.
Rava explains that Rav Ḥinnana applied Shmuel's principle that a salted food is like boiling only when it is inedible due to salt, but this kutaḥ is still edible despite its salt.
The Gemara adds that this leniency applies only to raw bird, but if roasted it requires peeling the outer layer.
The Gemara further qualifies that the bird is permitted only if it has no cracks; if it has cracks or is spiced, it is forbidden.
The daf ends with Rav beginning to speak, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Rav and Levi dispute roasting meat together
items.text_en: Rav and Levi dispute roasting meat together
items.desc_en: Rav forbids roasting fat kosher meat with lean neveila because they fatten each other; Levi permits even lean kosher meat with fat neveila because smell is insignificant. Levi acted on his ruling in the Exilarch's house with a kid and something else.

sub.desc_en: Rav forbids roasting fat kosher meat with lean neveila because they fatten each other.
Levi permits even lean kosher meat with fat neveila because smell is insignificant.
Levi acted on his ruling in the Exilarch's house with a kid and something else.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah of two Paschal lambs
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah of two Paschal lambs
items.desc_en: A baraita forbids roasting two Paschal lambs together due to תערובת. The Gemara initially assumes this means mixture of tastes, challenging Levi, but then explains it means mixture of bodies, supported by the clause 'even a kid and a lamb' which makes sense only for physical mixing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that forbids roasting two Paschal lambs together due to תערובת (mixing), initially assuming this means mixture of tastes, which challenges Levi's position.
The Gemara rejects the objection by reinterpreting the baraita's תערובת as referring to physical mixing of the bodies, not mixture of tastes.

items.text: Resolution: Rav's position and the case of two pots
items.text_en: Resolution: Rav's position and the case of two pots
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the baraita forbids only physical mixture, but taste mixture is permitted, which would be a refutation of Rav. Rabbi Yirmeya explains the baraita deals with two pots (or similar), where even without taste mixture it is forbidden due to physical mixture, and even a kid and a lamb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the baraita forbids only physical mixture (תערובת גופין), not taste mixture, which would be a refutation of Rav.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the baraita deals with a case like two pots, where even without taste mixture it is forbidden due to physical mixture.
The Gemara objects that two actual pots cannot be meant, and rephrases to 'like two pots'.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita forbids even a case like two pots due to physical mixture, and even a kid and a lamb.

items.text: Rav Mari connects to a Tannaitic dispute about bread and wine
items.text_en: Rav Mari connects to a Tannaitic dispute about bread and wine
items.desc_en: Rav Mari says the dispute between Rav and Levi parallels a Tannaic dispute about hot bread placed on a wine barrel: Rabbi Meir forbids, Rabbi Yehuda permits, and Rabbi Yosei distinguishes. The Gemara notes that for Levi it is clearly a Tannaic dispute, but asks whether Rav also holds it is a Tannaic dispute.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari introduces a Tannaitic dispute about hot bread on a wine barrel as a parallel to the dispute between Rav and Levi.
The Gemara asks whether the Tannaitic dispute is indeed about whether רֵיחָא (smell) is considered a significant substance (מִילְּתָא) or not.
The Gemara resolves that for Levi the dispute is clearly Tannaitic, but questions whether Rav also holds it is a Tannaitic dispute.

items.text: Resh Lakish's resolution of the Tannaic dispute
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's resolution of the Tannaic dispute
items.desc_en: Rav (via Rabba bar bar Hana citing Resh Lakish) explains that all agree smell is significant in the case of hot bread and an open barrel; the dispute is only about hot bread with a sealed barrel or cold bread with an open barrel. The case of roasting meat is like hot bread and an open barrel, so all forbid.

sub.text: Rav's answer (via Rabba bar bar Hana citing Resh Lakish)
sub.text_en: Rav's answer (via Rabba bar bar Hana citing Resh Lakish)
sub.desc_en: Rav resolves the Tannaic dispute by explaining that all agree smell is significant (רֵיחָא מִילְּתָא הִיא) in the case of hot bread and an open barrel, and the roasting meat case is analogous to that, so all forbid it.

items.text: Practical ruling: bread baked with roast is forbidden with kutach
items.text_en: Practical ruling: bread baked with roast is forbidden with kutach
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana taught that bread baked with roast in an oven is forbidden to eat with kutach. Rava of Parzikya forbade a fish roasted with meat from being eaten with kutach, and Mar bar Rav Ashi even forbade it with salt because it is harmful for smell and other things.

sub.text: Rav Kahana bar Rav Chinana Saba
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana bar Rav Chinana Saba
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana taught that bread baked with roast in an oven is forbidden to eat with kutach (a dairy dip).
Rava of Parzikya forbade a fish roasted with meat from being eaten with kutach.
Mar bar Rav Ashi forbade it even with salt, because it is harmful for smell and other things.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Five offerings brought in impurity
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Five offerings brought in impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five offerings that are brought in impurity but not eaten in impurity, except the Paschal lamb which is eaten in impurity. The Gemara explains that the list excludes the Chagigah of the 15th because it has make-up days and does not override Shabbat or impurity, and questions why goat-offerings of festivals are not listed separately.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five offerings that are brought in impurity but not eaten in impurity, except the Paschal lamb which is eaten in impurity because it was brought only for eating.
The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's list of five excludes.
The Gemara answers that the list excludes the Chagigah of the 15th of Nisan.

The Gemara explains that one might have thought the Chagigah overrides impurity because it is a communal offering with a fixed time, but it does not because it has make-up days and does not override Shabbat, so it does not override impurity.
The Gemara asks why the goat-offerings of festivals are not listed separately.
The Gemara answers that they are already included in the category of 'communal peace-offerings' (זִבְחֵי שַׁלְמֵי צִבּוּר).
The Gemara objects that if so, the goat-offerings of New Moons should also not be listed separately, since they too are included in 'communal peace-offerings'.
The Gemara begins to resolve the objection, but the text cuts off; the resolution is implied to follow.

items.text: Inclusion of goat offerings of new moons from "moed"
items.text_en: Inclusion of goat offerings of new moons from "moed"
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the goat offerings of new moons needed to be included in the rule that communal offerings override Shabbat and impurity, because one might think that since "moed" is not written in their verse, they are excluded. The verse teaches that the new moon is called a "moed," as per Abaye's proof from Lamentations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the goat offerings of new moons needed to be included in the rule that communal offerings override Shabbat and impurity, because one might think that since 'moed' is not written in their verse, they are excluded; the verse teaches that the new moon is called a 'moed'.
Abaye supports this by citing a verse from Lamentations where the new moon of Tammuz is called a 'moed'.

items.text: Derivation of all communal offerings from "moed"
items.text_en: Derivation of all communal offerings from "moed"
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that all communal offerings override Shabbat and impurity. It cites a baraita that derives from the verse "And Moses spoke the appointed times of the Lord" that just as the daily offering and the Paschal lamb, which have "in its appointed time" written, override Shabbat and impurity, so too do all other communal offerings. The baraita further includes the omer and the two loaves and their accompanying offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that all communal offerings are derived from the word 'moed' (appointed time).

The baraita cites the verse 'And Moses spoke the appointed times of the Lord' to teach that the daily offering and the Paschal lamb, which have 'in its appointed time' written, override Shabbat and impurity.
The baraita derives other communal offerings from the verse 'These you shall do for the Lord on your appointed times'.

The baraita includes the omer and the two loaves and their accompanying offerings by the verse 'And Moses spoke the appointed times of the Lord to the children of Israel', establishing one appointed time for all.

items.text: Why all these verses are necessary
items.text_en: Why all these verses are necessary
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why multiple verses are needed: each verse addresses a potential exclusion. The daily offering might be excluded because it is frequent and wholly burnt; the Paschal lamb because it carries the penalty of karet; other communal offerings because they come for atonement; and the omer and two loaves because they only permit consumption. Each verse teaches that all are included.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why all these verses are necessary, implying they seem redundant.
The Gemara explains that the verse for the daily offering (תמיד) is needed, because without it one might exclude the Paschal lamb, which is less frequent and not wholly burnt.
The Gemara explains that the verse for the Paschal lamb is needed, because without it one might exclude the daily offering, which lacks the penalty of karet.

The Gemara explains that the verse for other communal offerings (אֵלֶּה תַּעֲשׂוּ לַה׳ בְּמוֹעֲדֵיכֶם) is needed, because without it one might exclude them, as they lack the stringent features of the daily offering and the Paschal lamb.
The Gemara explains that the verse for the omer and two loaves is needed, because without it one might exclude them, as they do not come for atonement but only to permit consumption.

The Gemara explains that the verse for the daily offering and Paschal lamb is needed, because without it one might exclude them, thinking only the omer and two loaves, which are powerful in permitting consumption, are included.

items.text: Impurity is pushed aside in public offerings
items.text_en: Impurity is pushed aside in public offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that everyone agrees impurity is pushed aside (dechuyah) in public offerings and requires the tzitz to appease. It notes that only Rabbi Yehuda holds that impurity is permitted (hutterah) in public offerings, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says the tzitz appeases whether on the forehead or not, while Rabbi Yehuda says it only appeases when on the forehead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that everyone agrees impurity is pushed aside (דחויה) in public offerings and requires the ציץ (frontplate) to appease.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon holds the ציץ appeases whether on the forehead or not, while Rabbi Yehuda holds it only appeases when on the forehead, proving only Rabbi Yehuda permits impurity in public offerings.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's proof and Rabbi Yehuda's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's proof and Rabbi Yehuda's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon argues that the High Priest on Yom Kippur proves that the tzitz appeases even when not on the forehead. Rabbi Yehuda responds that Yom Kippur is different because impurity is permitted in public offerings. This implies that Rabbi Shimon holds impurity is pushed aside.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon argues that the High Priest on Yom Kippur proves that the ציץ (frontlet) appeases even when not on the forehead.
Rabbi Yehuda rejects the proof, arguing that Yom Kippur is different because impurity is permitted in public offerings, implying that Rabbi Shimon holds impurity is pushed aside.

items.text: The tzitz does not appease for eating
items.text_en: The tzitz does not appease for eating
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that everyone agrees the tzitz does not appease for eating (the consumption of offerings), except for Rabbi Eliezer. A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer saying the tzitz appeases for eating, and Rabbi Yosei saying it does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that everyone agrees the ציץ (frontplate) does not appease for eating, except for Rabbi Eliezer.
A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer saying the ציץ appeases for eating, and Rabbi Yosei saying it does not.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer on blood and meat
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer on blood and meat
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah might not follow Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds that if there is no blood there is no meat, and vice versa. Rabbi Eliezer argues that blood can be sprinkled even without meat, citing the verse "and the blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out." The Gemara explains that there is a small hole between the ramp and the altar, and addresses Rabbi Yehoshua's interpretation of the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah might not align with Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds that blood and meat are interdependent.

Rabbi Eliezer argues that blood can be sprinkled even without meat, citing the verse 'וְדַם זְבָחֶיךָ יִשָּׁפֵךְ' and interpreting 'וְעָשִׂיתָ עֹלֹתֶיךָ הַבָּשָׂר וְהַדָּם' to require both blood and meat to be brought to the altar.
The Gemara explains that there is a small hole between the ramp and the altar, resolving the dispute by showing how blood can be sprinkled without the meat being present.
The Gemara addresses Rabbi Yehoshua's interpretation of the verse, noting that the verse continues 'וְהַבָּשָׂר תֹּאכֵל', implying that the blood is poured out only when the meat is eaten.

items.text: Gemara's question on the two verses
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the two verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why two verses are needed (one for burnt offerings and one for peace offerings) and explains that each is necessary to counter a potential logical inference about the stringency of the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why two verses are needed (one for burnt offerings and one for peace offerings) and explains that each is necessary to counter a potential logical inference about the stringency of the other.
The Gemara answers that if only the verse for peace offerings were written, one might think the opposite stringency applies, so both verses are needed.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation of the verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation of the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that the verse 'and the flesh you shall eat' teaches that flesh is not permitted for eating until blood is sprinkled. The Gemara questions if this is the sole purpose, and Rabbi Eliezer responds that the order of the verses implies both that blood is valid even without flesh and that flesh requires blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to Rabbi Eliezer as well, isn't it written 'and the flesh you shall eat'? Rabbi Eliezer answers that this verse teaches that flesh is not permitted for eating until the blood is sprinkled.
The Gemara objects: If so, say the entire verse comes for this purpose; from where do we derive that blood is valid even without flesh?

Rabbi Eliezer answers: If the verse were only for that purpose, it would have written 'the flesh you shall eat' first; the fact that it precedes 'the blood of your offerings' teaches both that blood is valid without flesh and that flesh requires blood.

items.text: Rabbi Joshua's kal vachomer and the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Joshua's kal vachomer and the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Joshua derives from a kal vachomer that flesh is not permitted without blood. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer nevertheless wrote a verse for something that could be derived logically, while Rabbi Joshua prefers to expound the verse when possible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Joshua derives the halakha that meat is not permitted for eating until the blood is sprinkled through a קל וחומר (a fortiori inference) from the sacrificial portions.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer holds the Torah wrote a verse even for something derivable by קל וחומר (a fortiori inference), while Rabbi Joshua holds that wherever a verse can be expounded, we expound it.

items.text: Attempt to identify the Mishnah with Rabbi Joshua
items.text_en: Attempt to identify the Mishnah with Rabbi Joshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah might not follow Rabbi Joshua, since he requires both blood and flesh, and the frontplate does not atone for eating. It then resolves that Rabbi Joshua holds the frontplate atones for items that ascend (עולין).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah can follow Rabbi Joshua, since he requires both blood and flesh, and the frontplate does not atone for eating, so how can the Mishnah permit offering in impurity?
The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Joshua, the frontplate (ציץ) atones for items that ascend (עולין), allowing the Mishnah's ruling.

items.text: Challenge from the Omer and two loaves
items.text_en: Challenge from the Omer and two loaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that for the Omer and two loaves there are no items that ascend, so how can the frontplate help? It answers that Rabbi Joshua only requires both for animal offerings, not for meal offerings. But a Mishnah about meal offerings seems to require both, so the Gemara distinguishes between the Tanna's view and Rabbi Joshua's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that while the frontplate can help for animal offerings which have items that ascend, for the Omer and two loaves there are no ascending items, so how can the frontplate help?
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Joshua only requires both blood and flesh for animal offerings, not for meal offerings.

The Gemara objects by citing a Mishnah where, according to Rabbi Joshua's measure, a meal offering whose remnants were lost or impure is invalid, implying he applies the requirement to meal offerings as well.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Joshua's measure in requiring both, but not his full view, since he only required both for animal offerings, while this Tanna applies it even to meal offerings.

items.text: Rabbi Yose's ruling on meal offerings
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose's ruling on meal offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yose says he sees Rabbi Eliezer's view for meal offerings and animal offerings, and Rabbi Joshua's view for both. It elaborates on their respective positions regarding blood and flesh, and the handful and remnants.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: who is the Tanna who holds like Rabbi Joshua but is more stringent than him?
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yose states he sees Rabbi Eliezer's view for meal offerings and animal offerings, and Rabbi Joshua's view for both.

The baraita elaborates: Rabbi Eliezer's view for animal offerings is that blood is valid even without flesh, and for meal offerings that the handful is valid even without remnants; Rabbi Joshua's view for both is that each requires the other.

items.text: Revisiting the frontplate's atonement
items.text_en: Revisiting the frontplate's atonement
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Joshua holds the frontplate atones for both ascending items and eating. But then why is the Mishnah's case of impurity ruled invalid? It answers that it refers to lost or burned remnants. A baraita shows Rabbi Joshua rules that if either flesh or fat remains, the blood is sprinkled, but if both are impure, not, indicating the frontplate does not atone for either.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Joshua holds the frontplate (ציץ) atones for both ascending items (עולין) and eating (אכילות).
The Gemara asks: if so, why is the Mishnah's case ruled invalid according to Rabbi Joshua? It answers that it refers to lost or burned remnants.
The Gemara objects: the Mishnah's case of impurity (נטמא) is obvious for Rabbi Eliezer, so it must be for Rabbi Joshua, yet it rules invalid, contradicting the suggestion.
A baraita shows Rabbi Joshua rules that if either flesh or fat remains, the blood is sprinkled, but if both are impure, not, indicating the frontplate does not atone for either.

items.text: Distinction between lechatchila and b'dieved
items.text_en: Distinction between lechatchila and b'dieved
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Joshua, but distinguishes between initial intent (לכתחילה) and after the fact (דיעבד). Rabbi Joshua's requirement for both is only lechatchila; b'dieved the blood is accepted. Proof is brought from a baraita where Rabbi Joshua agrees that if blood was sprinkled, it is accepted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by asserting that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Joshua, but distinguishes between לכתחילה (the ideal standard) and בדיעבד (after the fact); Rabbi Joshua's requirement for both blood and flesh applies only לכתחילה, not בדיעבד.

The Gemara brings a baraita as proof that Rabbi Joshua distinguishes between לכתחילה and בדיעבד: in the baraita, Rabbi Joshua says one should not sprinkle the blood if the flesh is impure, but he concedes that if one did sprinkle, it is accepted (הורצה).
The Gemara adds two linguistic proofs: the Mishnah's term 'פסולה' (invalid) implies בדיעבד, and the phrase 'חמשה דברים באין' (five things come) implies לכתחילה.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction regarding the frontplate's atonement
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction regarding the frontplate's atonement
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a previous contradiction by distinguishing between an individual and the community: in one case it refers to an individual, in the other to the community.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between an individual case and a community case.

items.text: Attempt to prove the Mishnah is not like Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Attempt to prove the Mishnah is not like Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah might not follow Rabbi Yosei, who holds that the frontplate does not atone for impure sacrificial meat. It initially assumes Rabbi Yosei agrees with Rabbi Yehoshua that both blood and meat are required, which would contradict the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah might not follow Rabbi Yosei, who holds that the frontplate does not atone for impure sacrificial meat.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Eliezer says the frontplate atones for impure sacrificial meat, while Rabbi Yosei says it does not.
The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Yosei follows Rabbi Yehoshua, who requires both blood and meat, then the Mishnah would indeed not align with Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Rejection: Rabbi Yosei follows Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Rejection: Rabbi Yosei follows Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous assumption, stating that Rabbi Yosei actually follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that blood alone suffices even without meat.
