sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the assumption that Rabbi Yosei follows Rabbi Yehoshua, asserting that Rabbi Yosei actually follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that blood alone suffices even without meat.

items.text: Clarification of the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Clarification of the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the practical difference between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei regarding the frontplate's atonement for impure meat. It explains that they dispute whether the frontplate renders the meat as pure for the purposes of establishing piggul (sacrificial invalidation) and removing the prohibition of me'ilah (misuse of consecrated property).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if Rabbi Yosei agrees with Rabbi Eliezer's principle, what practical difference does his ruling that the frontplate does not atone for eating have?

The Gemara explains that the dispute concerns whether the frontplate renders the meat as pure for the purposes of establishing piggul (sacrificial invalidation) and removing the prohibition of me'ilah (misuse of consecrated property).
Rabbi Yosei holds that the frontplate does not atone for the meat, so it does not establish piggul nor remove the prohibition of me'ilah.

items.text: Rav Mari's objection regarding the two loaves
items.text_en: Rav Mari's objection regarding the two loaves
items.desc_en: Rav Mari objects: even if Rabbi Yosei follows Rabbi Eliezer, for sacrifices there is blood, for the omer there is the handful, for the showbread there are the frankincense bowls, but for the two loaves, what is there? If one suggests they are offered with the communal peace-offerings, that would make four loaves, but the Mishnah teaches five.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari objects: even if Rabbi Yosei follows Rabbi Eliezer, for sacrifices there is blood, for the omer there is the handful, for the showbread there are the frankincense bowls.
Rav Mari asks: but for the two loaves, what is there to say?
Rav Mari rejects the suggestion that the two loaves are offered with the communal peace-offerings, because that would yield only four loaves, but the Mishnah teaches five.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's view that impurity is permitted in the community
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's view that impurity is permitted in the community
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yosei holds that impurity is permitted for communal offerings, but then cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei requires sprinkling on the third and seventh days, contradicting that view. The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah is not like Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yosei holds that טומאה (ritual impurity) is permitted for communal offerings.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yosei requires sprinkling on the third and seventh days, contradicting the view that impurity is permitted for communal offerings.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah is not like Rabbi Yosei, since his requirement for sprinkling shows he does not hold that impurity is permitted for communal offerings.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's statement and its interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's statement and its interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye about Rabbi Yosei's statement that he sees the words of Rabbi Eliezer in sacrifices and in meal-offerings, and similarly for Rabbi Yehoshua. Abaye explains that Rabbi Yosei means it is reasonable that the dispute applies in both areas. The Gemara then revises the statement to refer to cases of impurity and loss or burning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether Rabbi Yosei's statement that he sees the words of both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua in both sacrifices and meal-offerings means he endorses both positions simultaneously.
Abaye explains that Rabbi Yosei means it is reasonable that the dispute applies in both areas, depending on which context he is discussing.
Rav Pappa objects that the analogy from meal-offerings to sacrifices is problematic because the primary verses are written regarding sacrifices, not meal-offerings.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by revising Rabbi Yosei's statement: he sees Rabbi Eliezer's words in cases of impurity and Rabbi Yehoshua's words in cases of loss or burning.

items.text: Final resolution: Rabbi Yosei's view on impurity in the community
items.text_en: Final resolution: Rabbi Yosei's view on impurity in the community
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the revised statement, noting that Rabbi Yosei holds the frontplate does not atone for impure meat, so impurity cannot be the basis. It then resolves that Rabbi Yosei's statement refers to communal offerings (where impurity is permitted) versus individual offerings, but raises a difficulty: Rabbi Yosei holds impurity is merely pushed aside, not permitted, and questions whether Rabbi Eliezer would permit in communal cases while Rabbi Yehoshua would not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Yosei's statement 'I see Rabbi Eliezer's words in a case of impurity' is because the frontplate (ציץ) atones, then this contradicts Rabbi Yosei's known position that the frontplate does not atone for eating.
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yosei's statement means he sees Rabbi Eliezer's view in communal offerings (where impurity is permitted) and Rabbi Yehoshua's view in individual offerings.

The Gemara objects: if the basis for Rabbi Yosei's view in communal offerings is that impurity is permitted in the community, this contradicts Rabbi Yosei's known position that impurity is merely pushed aside (דחויה), not permitted; moreover, if it were about communal offerings, Rabbi Eliezer would permit and Rabbi Yehoshua would not, but Rabbi Yosei's statement attributes both views to different cases.

items.text: Resolution of the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Resolution of the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yosei's statement 'I see the words of Rabbi Eliezer after the fact' applies specifically to a case where the meat was lost or burned, but for impurity, Rabbi Yehoshua concedes even after the fact. The distinction is made between impurity and loss/burning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If you say that in a communal case even Rabbi Yehoshua concedes, then what does Rabbi Yosei's statement mean?

The Gemara answers: Rabbi Yosei's statement 'I see the words of Rabbi Eliezer after the fact' applies to a case where the meat was lost or burned, but for impurity Rabbi Yehoshua concedes even after the fact.
The Gemara resolves: The case of impurity is separate from the case of loss or burning; Rabbi Yosei's leniency applies only to loss or burning.

items.text: Mishnah: Sprinkling blood when fat remains but meat is impure
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sprinkling blood when fat remains but meat is impure
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if the meat becomes impure but the fat remains, one does not sprinkle the blood; if the fat becomes impure but the meat remains, one does sprinkle. For consecrated offerings, the rule is different: even if the meat is impure and the fat remains, one sprinkles.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: if the meat is impure but the fat remains, one does not sprinkle the blood; if the fat is impure but the meat remains, one does sprinkle; for consecrated offerings, even if the meat is impure and the fat remains, one sprinkles.

items.text: Gemara: Rav's ruling and the necessity of eating
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav's ruling and the necessity of eating
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel said in the name of Rav that if one sprinkled the blood after the meat was impure, it is accepted. The Gemara questions this, citing the requirement of eating from the Paschal lamb. It resolves that eating is not essential for atonement, and Rav follows Rabbi Natan who holds that eating does not impede.

sub.text: Rav Giddel in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Giddel in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel reports Rav's ruling that if one sprinkled the blood after the meat became impure, it is accepted.
The Gemara objects that the Paschal lamb requires eating, yet here the meat is impure and cannot be eaten.
The Gemara responds that eating does not impede the atonement; the blood alone effects acceptance.
The Gemara objects citing the verse 'אִישׁ לְפִי אׇכְלוֹ' (each according to his eating), which seems to make eating essential.
The Gemara explains that the verse is only for the מצוה (commandment) of eating, not to impede the sacrifice.

The Gemara objects further, citing a baraita that derives from 'בְּמִכְסַת' (by number) that the Paschal lamb must be slaughtered for its designated participants, and the verse 'אִישׁ לְפִי אׇכְלוֹ' teaches that this requirement is essential (מעכב).
The Gemara adds that eaters are linked (היקש) to the participants, implying that eating is essential.
The Gemara resolves that Rav follows Rabbi Natan, who holds that eating the Paschal lamb does not impede the sacrifice.

items.text: Identifying Rabbi Natan's source
items.text_en: Identifying Rabbi Natan's source
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks to identify which statement of Rabbi Natan supports Rav's view. It first considers a source about all Israel going out with one Paschal lamb, but rejects it because the meat could be shared. It then finds a source where Rabbi Natan says that even those without a k'zayit are exempt from the second Passover because the blood was already sprinkled, proving that eating is not essential.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which statement of Rabbi Natan supports Rav, and proposes the baraita where Rabbi Natan says all Israel can fulfill their obligation with one Paschal lamb.
The Gemara objects that the case is different because the meat could be shared among the groups, so it does not prove that eating is non-essential.

The Gemara cites another baraita where Rabbi Natan rules that both earlier and later groups are exempt from the second Passover because the blood was already sprinkled, showing that eating is not essential.
The Gemara resolves the objection by noting that the baraita explicitly says 'since the blood was already sprinkled,' proving that the matter depends on the blood, not on eating.

items.text: Rav's reasoning from the Mishnah's language
items.text_en: Rav's reasoning from the Mishnah's language
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Rav interprets the Mishnah as applying only initially, not after the fact: the Mishnah says 'does not sprinkle' rather than 'it is invalid', implying that if done, it is valid. Rav thus holds that even after the fact it is acceptable, aligning with Rabbi Natan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what forces Rav to interpret the Mishnah as applying only לכתחילה (the ideal standard) and to align with Rabbi Natan.

The Gemara explains that Rav was pressed by the Mishnah's language: it says 'אֵין זוֹרֵק' (does not sprinkle) rather than 'פָּסוּל' (invalid), implying that if done, it is valid, so Rav holds that even after the fact it is acceptable, aligning with Rabbi Natan.

items.text: The verse 'according to his eating' and other tannaitic sources
items.text_en: The verse 'according to his eating' and other tannaitic sources
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Natan does with the verse 'according to his eating', and answers that it requires a person fit to eat. It then examines three baraitot to determine whether they follow Rabbi Natan or the Rabbis, concluding that they can be reconciled with either view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what purpose the verse 'איש לפי אכלו' (a man according to his eating) serves according to Rabbi Natan, who holds that eating does not impede the sacrifice.
The Gemara answers that the verse requires a person fit to eat (i.e., the participant must be capable of eating, even if actual eating is not required).
The Gemara asks which Tanna authored the baraita stating that if they slaughtered for its eaters but sprinkled the blood not for its eaters, the paschal lamb is valid and one fulfills his obligation.
The Gemara suggests that this baraita follows Rabbi Natan's view, not the Rabbis, since it validates the sacrifice despite the mismatch between eaters and blood sprinkling.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion, saying that even according to the Rabbis, the intention of eaters is not relevant at the time of blood sprinkling, so the baraita can be reconciled with their view.
The Gemara asks which Tanna authored the baraita about a person who was sick at slaughter time and healthy at sprinkling time, or vice versa, requiring health from slaughter through sprinkling.
The Gemara suggests that this baraita follows the Rabbis, not Rabbi Natan, since it requires the person to be fit for eating at the time of both slaughter and sprinkling.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion, saying that even according to Rabbi Natan, we require a person fit for eating, so the baraita can be reconciled with his view as well.

items.text: Dispute about sprinkling blood when owners become impure
items.text_en: Dispute about sprinkling blood when owners become impure
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if the Paschal lamb was slaughtered in purity and the owners later became impure, the blood is sprinkled in purity but the meat is not eaten in impurity. Rabbi Eliezer says this follows the dispute and is Rabbi Natan's view, while Rabbi Yochanan says it can be the Rabbis' view, dealing with a public offering where impurity is permitted. The Gemara then questions why the meat is not eaten, and explains it is a decree to prevent confusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the baraita that rules that if the Paschal lamb was slaughtered in purity and the owners later became impure, the blood is sprinkled in purity but the meat is not eaten in impurity.
Rabbi Eliezer says the baraita is taught in a dispute and follows Rabbi Natan's view.
Rabbi Yochanan says the baraita can even follow the Rabbis, because it deals with a public offering where impurity is permitted.
The Gemara questions why the meat is not eaten in impurity if it is a public offering where impurity is permitted.

The Gemara explains it is a decree to prevent confusion: people might mistakenly think they can eat the meat even if they become impure after the sprinkling, not realizing the difference in their status at the time of sprinkling.

items.text: Rav's view aligned with Rabbi Yehoshua on sprinkling blood when fat remains
items.text_en: Rav's view aligned with Rabbi Yehoshua on sprinkling blood when fat remains
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative explanation that Rav holds like Rabbi Yehoshua, who rules that for all sacrifices, if the meat is impure but the fat remains, one may sprinkle the blood. For a Nazirite and the Paschal lamb, if the fat is impure but the meat remains, one may sprinkle; if the meat is impure and the fat remains, one may not sprinkle, but if he did, it is accepted. If the owners are impure from a corpse, one may not sprinkle, and if he did, it is not accepted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation that Rav holds like Rabbi Yehoshua, who rules that for all sacrifices, if either the meat or the fat remains, one may sprinkle the blood.

Rabbi Yehoshua specifies that for a Nazirite and the Paschal lamb, if the fat is impure but the meat remains, one may sprinkle; if the meat is impure but the fat remains, one may not sprinkle, but if he did, it is accepted.
Rabbi Yehoshua rules that if the owners are impure from a corpse, one may not sprinkle the blood, and if he did, it is not accepted.

items.text: Identifying the Mishnah as Rabbi Yehoshua's view on minimal meat or fat
items.text_en: Identifying the Mishnah as Rabbi Yehoshua's view on minimal meat or fat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose view the Mishnah follows, and answers it is Rabbi Yehoshua, who taught that for all sacrifices, if an olive's bulk of meat or fat remains, one may sprinkle the blood. If there is half an olive of meat and half of fat, one may not sprinkle. For a burnt offering, even half and half is allowed because it is entirely consumed. For a meal offering, even if entirely intact, one may not sprinkle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose view the Mishnah follows, given its ruling about consecrated offerings.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehoshua, citing a baraita where he rules that for all sacrifices, an olive's bulk of meat or fat permits blood sprinkling, but half and half does not, except for a burnt offering, and a meal offering is never permitted.

items.text: Clarifying the meal offering in question
items.text_en: Clarifying the meal offering in question
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what meal offering is being discussed, and Rav Papa answers it is the meal offering of libations, which comes by virtue of a sacrifice. One might think it is like the sacrifice itself, but the Mishnah teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what meal offering (מנחה) is being discussed in the Mishnah's ruling.
Rav Papa answers that it is the meal offering of libations (מנחת נסכים), which comes by virtue of a sacrifice; one might think it is like the sacrifice itself, but the Mishnah teaches otherwise.

items.text: Deriving that fat alone permits blood sprinkling, and including other parts
items.text_en: Deriving that fat alone permits blood sprinkling, and including other parts
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that fat alone suffices for sprinkling. Rabbi Yochanan cites a verse that the fat is offered for a pleasing aroma even without meat. It then asks about the diaphragm and kidneys, and derives from the phrase 'for a pleasing aroma' that anything offered for a pleasing aroma is included. Both the explicit mention of fat and the general phrase are necessary to exclude meal offerings and include other parts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that fat alone permits the blood to be sprinkled?

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a verse: 'And the priest shall burn the fat for a pleasing aroma to the Lord' — fat alone suffices even without meat.
The Gemara asks: We have found the source for fat; from where do we derive that the diaphragm and two kidneys also permit the blood?
The Gemara asks: Where do we say that we sprinkle? From the mishnah's exclusion of meal offering, we infer that diaphragm and kidneys are valid; but from where do we derive this?
Rabbi Yochanan himself says: The verse says 'for a pleasing aroma' — anything that you offer for a pleasing aroma is included.

The Gemara explains that both the explicit mention of fat and the general phrase 'for a pleasing aroma' are necessary: fat alone excludes meal offerings, and the general phrase includes diaphragm and kidneys.

items.text: Mishnah: When the Paschal lamb is offered in impurity
items.text_en: Mishnah: When the Paschal lamb is offered in impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the majority of the community or the priests are impure, the Paschal lamb is offered in impurity. If a minority is impure, the pure ones offer the first Paschal lamb and the impure ones offer the second.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if the majority of the community or the priests are impure, the Paschal lamb is offered in impurity; if a minority is impure, the pure offer the first lamb and the impure offer the second.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute over impurity of vessels and the principle of pushed-off impurity
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute over impurity of vessels and the principle of pushed-off impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that if Israelites are impure but priests and vessels are pure, or vice versa, the Paschal lamb is offered in impurity because the public sacrifice is not divided. Rav Chisda limits this to a knife impure from a corpse, which conveys impurity to a person, but if impure from a creeping thing, only the meat becomes impure, so the pure should offer rather than eat meat with impurity of the body which carries karet. This shows Rav Chisda holds impurity is pushed off for the public. Rava argues that even impure people may offer, based on a verse: where the verse 'meat that touches any impure thing shall not be eaten' does not apply, the verse 'all pure persons may eat meat' does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that if Israelites are impure but priests and vessels are pure, or vice versa, the Paschal lamb is offered in impurity because the public sacrifice is not divided.

Rav Chisda limits the baraita to a knife impure from a corpse, which conveys impurity to a person, but if impure from a creeping thing, only the meat becomes impure, so the pure should offer rather than eat meat with impurity of the body which carries karet.
The Gemara infers that Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yitzchak hold that impurity is pushed off (דחויה) for the public.

Rava argues that even impure people may offer, based on a verse: where the verse 'meat that touches any impure thing shall not be eaten' does not apply, the verse 'all pure persons may eat meat' does not apply.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rav Kahana on half-pure, half-impure community
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rav Kahana on half-pure, half-impure community
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where half the Israelites are pure and half impure. Rav says half is considered a majority, so each group offers for itself. Rav Kahana says half is not a majority, so the pure offer the first Paschal lamb and the impure offer the second. A second version states Rav Kahana's view similarly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: in a case where half the Israelites are pure and half impure, Rav says half is like a majority, and Rav Kahana says half is not like a majority.
Rav explains his position: since half is considered a majority, each group (pure and impure) performs the Paschal lamb for itself.
Rav Kahana explains his position: since half is not a majority, the pure perform the first Paschal lamb and the impure perform the second.
An alternative version reports that Rav Kahana said: half is not a majority, so the pure perform the first Paschal lamb.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that impure people do not perform either the first or second Pesach: in the first because they are not a majority, in the second because they are not a minority.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that impure people do not perform either the first or second Pesach: in the first because they are not a majority, in the second because they are not a minority.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rav
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rav
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: if the majority of the congregation is impure, the Pesach is done in impurity, implying that if it is exactly half, it is not done in the first Pesach. This challenges Rav's view that half-and-half each do for themselves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that if the majority of the congregation is impure, the Pesach is done in impurity, implying that if it is exactly half, it is not done in the first Pesach, challenging Rav's view.
Rav responds that when the majority is impure, everyone does it in impurity, but when it is half-and-half, each group does it for themselves.

items.text: Support for Rav from the seifa
items.text_en: Support for Rav from the seifa
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the seifa supports Rav: if a minority is impure, the pure do the first and the impure do the second, implying that half-and-half do not do the second but each do for themselves in the first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the seifa supports Rav: if a minority is impure, the pure do the first and the impure do the second, implying that half-and-half do not do the second but each do for themselves in the first.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Kahana
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Kahana
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Kahana: the seifa implies that half-and-half pure do the first, but impure do neither, contradicting Rav Kahana's view that impure do the second.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Kahana: the seifa of the Mishnah implies that when the congregation is half pure and half impure, the pure do the first Pesach and the impure do neither, contradicting Rav Kahana's view that the impure do the second Pesach.

items.text: Rav Kahana's two versions
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's two versions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Kahana has two versions: one where impure do the second, and another where they do neither. For the latter, the Mishnah's wording is just a stylistic parallel to the reisha.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's wording fits the second version of Rav Kahana.
The Gemara asks what can be said for the first version of Rav Kahana, where impure do the second Pesach.
Rav Kahana explains that the same law applies even for half-and-half, and the Mishnah's wording 'minority' is merely a stylistic parallel to the reisha's 'majority'.

items.text: Tannaitic support for both views
items.text_en: Tannaitic support for both views
items.desc_en: Three baraitot are cited: one supports Rav (each half does for themselves), one supports Rav Kahana's first version (pure do first, impure do second), and one supports his second version (pure do first, impure do neither).

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited supporting Rav's position that when half the Israelites are pure and half impure, each half performs the Pesach (פסח) offering for themselves.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rav Kahana's first version
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rav Kahana's first version
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited supporting Rav Kahana's first version that the pure perform the first Pesach (פסח) and the impure perform the second.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rav Kahana's second version
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rav Kahana's second version
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited supporting Rav Kahana's second version that the pure perform the first Pesach (פסח) and the impure perform neither the first nor the second.

items.text: Reconciling the baraita for Rav and Rav Kahana's second version
items.text_en: Reconciling the baraita for Rav and Rav Kahana's second version
items.desc_en: For Rav and Rav Kahana's second version, the baraita where pure do first and impure do second is explained as a case where women supplement the impure, making them a minority, and women are optional for the first Pesach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rav and Rav Kahana's second version reconcile the baraita that says pure people perform the first Pesach and impure people perform the second.
The Gemara explains that the case involves half pure and half impure Israelites, with women supplementing the impure group.
The Gemara adds that women's participation in the first Pesach is optional (רשות), so when women are removed from the impure group, the impure become a minority and are deferred to the second Pesach.

items.text: Reconciling the baraita for Rav
items.text_en: Reconciling the baraita for Rav
items.desc_en: For Rav, the baraita where pure do first and impure do neither is explained as a case where women outnumber the pure, making the impure a minority (so they don't do first) and after removing women, half-and-half (so they don't do second).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rav and the first version of Rav Kahana reconcile the baraita that states pure people do the first Pesach and impure do neither.

Rav explains the baraita as a case where women outnumber the pure, making the impure a minority (so they don't do the first), and after removing women, the groups are half-and-half (so they don't do the second).

items.text: Reconciling the baraita for Rav Kahana's first version
items.text_en: Reconciling the baraita for Rav Kahana's first version
items.desc_en: For Rav Kahana's first version, the baraita is explained as a case where women supplement the pure, making the impure a majority (so they don't do second), and half-and-half don't do first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the need to reconcile the baraita for Rav Kahana's first version, where half-and-half do perform the second Pesach.
The Gemara explains that the baraita refers to a case where women supplement the pure group, making the impure a majority, so the impure do not perform the second Pesach.

items.text: Rav Kahana's resolution for the baraita of each doing for themselves
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's resolution for the baraita of each doing for themselves
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana explains the baraita where each half does for themselves as a dispute among Tannaim: some consider half as a majority, others do not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rav Kahana how he resolves the baraita that says each half does for themselves.
Rav Kahana answers that the baraita reflects a dispute among Tannaim: some consider a half-half split as a majority, others do not.

items.text: Baraita on majority impurity and Rabbi Elazar ben Matya's objection
items.text_en: Baraita on majority impurity and Rabbi Elazar ben Matya's objection
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if the impure outnumber the pure by even one, they do the Pesach in impurity because the communal sacrifice is not divided. Rabbi Elazar ben Matya argues that an individual does not tip the community to impurity, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that when the impure outnumber the pure by even one, the Pesach is performed in impurity because the communal sacrifice is not divided.
Rabbi Elazar ben Matya objects, arguing that an individual does not tip the community to impurity, citing a verse.

items.text: Opening dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Opening dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Shimon says that if one tribe is impure and the rest pure, each group offers its own Paschal lamb, because a single tribe is called a 'congregation'. Rabbi Yehuda says that even if one tribe is impure, all offer in impurity, because a public offering cannot be divided, and a single tribe is also called a 'congregation'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the verse 'You may not slaughter the Paschal lamb in any of your gates' as the basis for the dispute.
Rabbi Shimon states that even if one tribe is impure and the rest pure, each group offers its own Paschal lamb, because a single tribe is called a 'congregation'.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that even if one tribe is impure, all offer in impurity, because a public offering cannot be divided, and a single tribe is also called a 'congregation'.

items.text: Rav's ruling on half pure, half impure
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on half pure, half impure
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where half of Israel is pure and half impure. Rav says they make one of the impure people impure with a sheretz (crawling creature). The Gemara questions this, given Rav's own view that each group can offer separately. The resolution is that the impure outnumber the pure by one, and Rav follows Rabbi Elazar ben Matya that an individual does not tip the community to impurity, but then the question returns. Finally, the Gemara explains that Rav's ruling combines the first Tanna's view (that half and half do not all offer in impurity) with Rabbi Yehuda's view (that a public offering cannot be divided).

sub.desc_en: The Stam introduces a case where half of Israel is pure and half impure, and reports Rav's ruling: they render one of the pure people impure with a sheretz (crawling creature).
The Gemara questions Rav's ruling, asking why the pure and impure cannot each offer separately, citing Rav's own statement that each group may do so.
The Gemara answers that the case is where the impure outnumber the pure by one.
The Gemara objects that if the impure are a majority, they should all offer in impurity.
The Gemara answers that Rav follows Rabbi Elazar ben Matya, who holds that an individual does not tip the community to impurity.
The Gemara objects that the original question returns: why not let each group offer separately?

The Gemara resolves that Rav's ruling combines the first Tanna's view (that half and half do not all offer in impurity) with Rabbi Yehuda's view (that a public offering cannot be divided), so they render one pure person impure with a sheretz.

items.text: Ulla's alternative: send one on a distant journey
items.text_en: Ulla's alternative: send one on a distant journey
items.desc_en: Ulla suggests sending one of the impure people on a distant journey instead of making him impure with a sheretz. The Gemara questions why not make him impure with a sheretz, and Ulla holds that one may slaughter and sprinkle on behalf of one impure from a sheretz. The Gemara then asks why not make him impure with a corpse, and Ulla responds that would exempt him from the Chagigah offering. The Gemara counters that he is already exempt from the Paschal lamb, but Ulla says he can offer it in the second Pesach. The Gemara further argues that with corpse impurity he could also offer in the second Pesach, but Ulla holds that all Pesach offerings are make-up for the first, and one who is unfit for the first is unfit for all.

sub.desc_en: Ulla proposes sending one of the pure people on a distant journey instead of rendering him impure with a שֶׁרֶץ (creeping animal).
The Gemara asks why not simply render him impure with a שֶׁרֶץ (creeping animal) as Rav suggested.
Ulla holds that one may slaughter and sprinkle the blood on behalf of one impure from a שֶׁרֶץ (creeping animal), so rendering him impure would not disqualify him from the Paschal lamb.
The Gemara objects: why not render him impure with a corpse, which would cause seven-day impurity and effectively remove him from the group?
Ulla responds that rendering him impure with a corpse would exempt him from the חגיגה (Festival peace-offering), which is undesirable.
The Gemara counters that sending him on a distant journey also exempts him from the Paschal lamb, so why is that acceptable?
Ulla answers that the person sent on a distant journey can still offer the Paschal lamb on the second Pesach, so he is not entirely exempt.
The Gemara argues that with corpse impurity, he could also offer the חגיגה (Festival peace-offering) on the seventh day of Passover, which is his eighth day of impurity.

Ulla holds that all days of the Festival are make-up for the first day, so one unfit on the first day is unfit for all, thus corpse impurity would prevent the חגיגה (Festival peace-offering) entirely.

items.text: Rav Nachman's dismissal of Ulla
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's dismissal of Ulla
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman tells his students to go tell Ulla that only a fool would uproot his stake and run (i.e., Ulla's reasoning is flawed).

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman dismisses Ulla's reasoning by calling him a fool who uproots his stake and runs.

items.text: Rav's ruling on majority zavim, minority corpse-impure
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on majority zavim, minority corpse-impure
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where the majority are zavim (with a discharge) and the minority are corpse-impure. Rav says the corpse-impure do not offer either on the first or second Pesach. The Gemara explains: they do not offer on the first because they are a minority, and a minority does not offer on the first; they do not offer on the second because wherever the community offers on the first, an individual offers on the second, but where the community does not offer on the first, an individual does not offer on the second. Shmuel challenges Rav with a verse, and Rav responds that when all are zavim, it is impossible, so they offer in impurity; here too it is impossible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that when the majority are zavim and the minority are corpse-impure, Rav rules that the corpse-impure do not offer the Pesach on either the first or second Pesach.
The Gemara explains Rav's reasoning: the minority does not offer on the first Pesach, and since the community does not offer on the first, the individual does not offer on the second.

Shmuel challenges Rav by citing the verse 'וְיַעֲשׂוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת הַפָּסַח בְּמוֹעֲדוֹ' (and the children of Israel shall make the Pesach in its appointed time), implying that even the minority should offer.

Rav responds that when all are zavim, it is impossible to offer in purity, so they offer in impurity; here too, since the minority cannot offer on the first, it is impossible for them to offer on the second.

items.text: Dispute on make-up for Pesach offered in impurity
items.text_en: Dispute on make-up for Pesach offered in impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where the majority are corpse-impure and the minority are zavim. Rav Huna says there is no make-up (second Pesach) for a Pesach offered in impurity, while Rav Adda bar Ahavah says there is. The Gemara suggests they disagree on whether impurity is pushed aside or permitted for the community, but then rejects this, saying all agree impurity is pushed aside, and the dispute is about something else (the text cuts off).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute about a case where the majority are corpse-impure and the minority are zavim.
Rav Huna states that there is no make-up (second Pesach) for a Pesach offered in impurity.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah states that there is a make-up (second Pesach) for a Pesach offered in impurity.
The Gemara suggests that the dispute hinges on whether impurity is pushed aside (דחויה) or permitted (הותרה) for the community.
The Gemara rejects this, stating that all agree impurity is pushed aside, and the real dispute is about something else (the text cuts off).

items.text: Gemara's opening dispute on purity and impurity
items.text_en: Gemara's opening dispute on purity and impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts two views: one holds that purity pushes off the first Pesach but impurity does not, while another holds that even impurity pushes it off. Rabbi Mani bar Pattish then discusses a case where a third of the people are zavim, a third are pure, and a third are impure from a corpse, concluding that the impure do not participate in either the first or second Pesach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by contrasting two views: one holds that purity (טהרה) pushes off the first Pesach but impurity (טומאה) does not, while another holds that even impurity pushes it off.

Rabbi Mani bar Pattish discusses a case where a third of the people are zavim, a third are pure, and a third are impure from a corpse, concluding that the impure do not participate in either the first or second Pesach.

The Gemara explains the reasoning: in the first Pesach the zavim outnumber the pure, making the impure a minority who do not participate; in the second Pesach the zavim join the impure to form a majority who are not pushed off to the second Pesach.

items.text: Mishnah: The frontplate atones for blood impurity but not body impurity
items.text_en: Mishnah: The frontplate atones for blood impurity but not body impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the Pesach's blood was thrown and then it became known that the offering was impure, the frontplate atones. However, if the body became impure, the frontplate does not atone. It also says that for impurity of the deep, the frontplate atones.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if the blood of the Paschal lamb was sprinkled and then its impurity became known, the frontplate atones; but if the body of the person became impure, the frontplate does not atone, because the frontplate atones for blood impurity but not for body impurity.
The Mishnah adds that if one became impure with impurity of the deep, the frontplate atones.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's condition and a contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's condition and a contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that if the impurity was known before the blood was thrown, the frontplate does not atone. It then raises a contradiction from a baraita that says the frontplate atones for blood, flesh, and fat that became impure, whether unintentionally or intentionally. Ravina and Rabbi Sheila offer different resolutions: Ravina distinguishes between the impurity (always atones) and the throwing (only if unintentional), while Rabbi Sheila reverses the distinction. The Gemara ultimately explains that the Mishnah's phrasing is for stylistic symmetry with the latter clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that the frontplate atones only if the blood was sprinkled before the impurity was discovered, but not if the impurity was known beforehand.

The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that states the frontplate atones for impure blood, flesh, and fat regardless of whether the impurity was known or unknown, and whether the act was intentional or unintentional.
Ravina resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the impurity itself (atonement always applies) and the sprinkling (atonement only if done unintentionally).
Rabbi Sheila offers an alternative resolution: the sprinkling always atones, but the impurity itself atones only if it occurred unintentionally.

The Gemara explains that the baraita's phrase 'whether unintentionally or intentionally' refers to the impurity occurring unintentionally, while the sprinkling can be either intentional or unintentional and still be accepted.
The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's condition (sprinkling before discovery) is not exclusive; even if the impurity was known before sprinkling, the frontplate still atones.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrasing ('sprinkled and then discovered') is for stylistic symmetry with the latter clause about bodily impurity, where even that order does not atone.

items.text: Debate on טומאת התהום for the priest
items.text_en: Debate on טומאת התהום for the priest
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether the priest who officiates is also permitted טומאת התהום (unknown impurity) like the owner. Rava brings a baraita from Rabbi Chiya that limits טומאת התהום to a corpse, excluding a creeping creature. The Gemara analyzes whether this applies to the owner or the priest, concluding that it refers to the priest, thus permitting טומאת התהום for the priest. Rav Yosef objects, arguing it refers to the owner in the context of Pesach, excluding טומאת התהום of a zav, and cites a baraita about a woman who is a שומרת יום כנגד יום.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether the priest who officiates is also permitted טומאת התהום (unknown impurity) like the owner, or whether the tradition applies only to the owner.

sub.text: Rava's citation of a baraita from Rabbi Chiya
sub.text_en: Rava's citation of a baraita from Rabbi Chiya
sub.desc_en: Rava brings a baraita from Rabbi Chiya that limits טומאת התהום (unknown impurity) to a corpse, excluding a creeping creature, to resolve the question.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis rejecting the owner interpretation
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis rejecting the owner interpretation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes that if the baraita referred to the owner (a nazirite or Pesach participant), it would be redundant or illogical, thus it must refer to the priest.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita refers to the priest, thus permitting טומאת התהום (unknown impurity) for the priest.
Rav Yosef objects, arguing that the baraita refers to the owner in the context of Pesach, excluding טומאת התהום (unknown impurity) of a zav (gonorrhea sufferer).

sub.text: Rav Yosef's supporting baraita from Rabbi Yosi
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's supporting baraita from Rabbi Yosi
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosi rules that a woman who is a שומרת יום כנגד יום (one who observes a day for a day) is not permitted טומאת התהום (unknown impurity) of a zav, supporting his interpretation.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who sees blood on the second day after immersion is exempt from Pesach Sheni and does not eat the Pesach.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who sees blood on the second day after immersion is exempt from Pesach Sheni and does not eat the Pesach.

items.text: Gemara's question and initial answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and initial answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling is because the tzitz effects atonement, and answers that Rabbi Yosei holds that impurity is only from now onward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the reason for the exemption? Is it not because the ציץ (high priest's forehead plate) effects atonement for her?
The Gemara answers: no, it is because Rabbi Yosei holds that she imparts טומאה (ritual impurity) only from now onward (מכאן ולהבא), not retroactively.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yosei's view
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yosei's view
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Yosei rules that a zav or shomeret who sees after slaughter are exempt from Pesach Sheni but retroactively defile, and the Gemara explains that this retroactive defilement is only rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in which Rabbi Yosei rules that a zav with two emissions or a shomeret yom keneged yom who see after slaughter are exempt from Pesach Sheni but retroactively defile.
The Gemara resolves that the retroactive defilement mentioned in the baraita is only rabbinic (מדרבנן), not biblical.

items.text: Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya holds that a zav who sees on the seventh day retroactively defiles, but Rabbi Yochanan argues, and the Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yosei agrees with Rabbi Yochanan that retroactive defilement is rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that Rabbi Oshaya also holds that retroactive defilement is rabbinic, citing a baraita.
The Gemara objects: from either perspective (retroactive or onward defilement), Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that the zav only negates his day is inconsistent.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yosei agrees with Rabbi Yochanan that retroactive defilement is rabbinic, concluding with 'שמע מינה' (learn from this).

items.text: Question about the scope of Rabbi Yosei's leniency
items.text_en: Question about the scope of Rabbi Yosei's leniency
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the leniency of tum'at hatehom excludes according to Rabbi Yosei, and suggests it applies to a kohen and the Pesach offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: now that Rabbi Yosei holds that tum'ah only defiles from now onward (for the case of a corpse), what does his leniency of טומאת התהום (tum'at hatehom, a hidden impurity) exclude?
The Gemara suggests that the leniency applies to a kohen (priest) and the Pesach offering, permitting him to bring it despite טומאת התהום (tum'at hatehom).

items.text: Alternative explanation and case of a complete zavah
items.text_en: Alternative explanation and case of a complete zavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative that the leniency applies to owners and the Pesach, and then discusses how to find a case of a complete zavah according to Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation that the leniency of טומאת התהום (unresolvable impurity) applies to owners and the Pesach, and that Rabbi Yosei holds one does not slaughter or sprinkle on behalf of those impure from a creeping creature, necessitating the exclusion.
The Gemara asks how, according to Rabbi Yosei, one can find a case of a complete zavah (זבה גמורה) who is fully impure.
The Gemara answers that a complete zavah can be found either in a case of continuous discharge (שופעת) or in a case where she saw during all the twilight periods (בין השמשות) of two consecutive days.

items.text: Rav Yosef's inquiry about the daily offering
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's inquiry about the daily offering
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether a kohen serving in the daily offering is also permitted tum'at hatehom, and Rabba attempts to prove it via a kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether a kohen serving in the daily offering (תמיד) is also permitted טומאת התהום (an unknown corpse impurity), or whether this leniency is limited to the Paschal offering.
Rabba attempts to prove by a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) that the kohen serving in the daily offering is permitted טומאת התהום, reasoning from the case where known impurity is not permitted.

items.text: Initial a fortiori argument for tum'at hatehom
items.text_en: Initial a fortiori argument for tum'at hatehom
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal va-chomer (a fortiori) argument: if a nazirite is permitted tum'at hatehom, then a Passover offerant should also be permitted, since the Passover is more lenient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal va-chomer (a fortiori) argument: if a nazirite is permitted tum'at hatehom, then a Passover offerant should also be permitted, since the Passover is more lenient.

items.text: Objection: No kal va-chomer from halakha
items.text_en: Objection: No kal va-chomer from halakha
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one cannot derive a kal va-chomer from a halakha (tradition), citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer tells Rabbi Akiva that a bone the size of a barley is a halakha, but a quarter-log of blood is a kal va-chomer, and one does not derive a kal va-chomer from a halakha.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: we do not derive a kal va-chomer from a halacha (received tradition), citing the baraita where Rabbi Eliezer rebukes Rabbi Akiva for doing so.

items.text: Rava's derivation via gezerah shavah
items.text_en: Rava's derivation via gezerah shavah
items.desc_en: Rava instead derives the permission for the Passover offerant from a gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) between the word 'mo'ado' (its appointed time) in the context of the nazirite and the Passover.

sub.desc_en: Rava derives the permission for a nazirite from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of the word 'מועדו' (its appointed time) from the Passover offering.

items.text: Three opinions on the source of tum'at hatehom
items.text_en: Three opinions on the source of tum'at hatehom
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where tum'at hatehom is written. Rabbi Elazar says it is derived from 've-chi yamut met alav' referring to a hidden corpse. For the Passover, Rabbi Yochanan derives from 'be-derech rechokah lachem' meaning hidden from you. Reish Lakish says it is like a road: just as a road is exposed, so too the impurity must be exposed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the concept of טומאת התהום (hidden corpse impurity) is written in the Torah.
Rabbi Elazar derives טומאת התהום from the verse 'וְכִי יָמוּת מֵת עָלָיו' (and if a corpse falls upon him), interpreting it as a hidden corpse.
Rabbi Yochanan derives טומאת התהום for the Passover from the verse 'בְּדֶרֶךְ רְחוֹקָה לָכֶם' (a distant way for you), interpreting it as hidden from you.
Reish Lakish says טומאת התהום is like a road: just as a road is exposed, so too the impurity must be exposed.

items.text: Challenge from the baraita and resolution as halakha
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita and resolution as halakha
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the three opinions with a baraita defining tum'at hatehom as impurity unknown to anyone in the world. For Rabbi Elazar, it is unknown to him; for Rabbi Yochanan, unknown to two; for Reish Lakish, unknown to all. The Gemara concludes that tum'at hatehom is actually a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai, and the verses are mere support.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the three opinions by citing a baraita that defines טומאת התהום (unknown grave impurity) as impurity unknown to anyone in the world.
The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Elazar, who derives the law from the verse 'עליו' (upon him), the impurity is considered unknown only if the nazirite himself did not know of it.
The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yochanan, who derives from the plural 'לכם' (to you), the impurity is unknown only if two people do not know of it.
The Gemara concludes that the definition of טומאת התהום is actually a הלכה למשה מסיני (halakha transmitted to Moses at Sinai), and the verses are merely support (אסמכתא).

items.text: Mar bar Rav Ashi's distinction about when impurity is discovered
items.text_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi's distinction about when impurity is discovered
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi initially says that tum'at hatehom only appeases if discovered after the blood is sprinkled, but not before. A challenge is raised from a baraita about a corpse found on a road. The Gemara then retracts: even if discovered before sprinkling, it appeases.

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Ashi's initial statement
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi's initial statement
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi initially distinguishes that the leniency of טומאת התהום (undiscovered corpse impurity) only applies if the impurity was discovered after the blood was sprinkled, but not before.

The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a corpse found lying across a road, which rules that for a nazirite and a Passover-offering bringer the person is pure, implying that even before sprinkling the impurity is appeased.

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Ashi's revised statement
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi's revised statement
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi retracts his initial distinction and clarifies that even if the impurity is discovered before the blood is sprinkled, the offering still appeases.

items.text: Detailed laws of a corpse found on a road
items.text_en: Detailed laws of a corpse found on a road
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the baraita about finding a corpse lying across a road. It explains the conditions: if there is no alternative path, the corpse is considered tum'at hatehom for a nazirite and Passover offerant; if the corpse is broken or dismembered, it is pure; if the person is carrying a load or riding, they are impure; and the definition of tum'at hatehom is reiterated.

sub.desc_en: The baraita is cited: one who finds a corpse lying across the road is impure for תרומה (priestly portion) but pure for a nazirite and Passover offerant.
The baraita qualifies: this applies only when there is no alternative path; if there is, even for תרומה (priestly portion) the person is pure.
The baraita qualifies further: the corpse must be intact; if broken or dismembered, it is pure, unless in a grave which joins the pieces.
The baraita qualifies: the leniency applies only to a pedestrian; one carrying a load or riding is impure because contact or overshadowing is inevitable.
The baraita qualifies: the purity ruling applies only to טומאת התהום (unknown impurity); for known impurity, the person is impure.
The baraita defines טומאת התהום (unknown impurity) as impurity that no one at the end of the world knew about; if anyone knew, it is not טומאת התהום.
The baraita concludes with examples: a corpse hidden in straw, earth, or pebbles is טומאת התהום; in water, darkness, or crevices it is not; and the rule applies only to a corpse.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on burning impure or leftover Passover
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on burning impure or leftover Passover
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if most of the Passover lamb becomes impure, it is burned before the Temple with wood from the arrangement; if only a minority is impure or it is leftover, it is burned in their courtyards with their own wood. The Gemara explains the reason: to shame those who caused the impurity, and raises a contradiction with a baraita about one who left Jerusalem with sacred meat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if most of the Passover lamb becomes impure, it is burned before the Temple with wood from the arrangement.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind the Mishnah's distinction.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina answers that the purpose is to shame those who caused the impurity.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about one who left Jerusalem with sacred meat, which implies a different rule.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a paschal lamb that left its boundaries or became impure is burned before the Temple with wood from the arrangement.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a paschal lamb that left its boundaries or became impure is burned before the Temple with wood from the arrangement.

items.text: Amoraic dispute on the ruling's applicability
items.text_en: Amoraic dispute on the ruling's applicability
items.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Ukva, Rav Pappa, and Rav Zevid debate whether the Mishnah applies to a guest or a homeowner, and whether the guest had already set out on the road, with Rav Zevid citing a Tosefta about the 'ציקינין' (those who have no wood).

sub.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Ukva resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a guest (אכסנאי) and a homeowner (בעל הבית).
Rav Pappa offers an alternative resolution: both cases involve a guest, but one had already set out on the road (החזיק בדרך) and the other had not.

Rav Zevid supports Rav Chama bar Ukva's distinction, adding that even if the guest has not set out, he is treated like a 'ציקינין' (one without wood) based on a Tosefta that allows such people to burn the leftover meat at the Temple courtyard.

items.text: Baraita on burning locations and fuel
items.text_en: Baraita on burning locations and fuel
items.desc_en: A Baraita teaches that if people want to burn the lamb in their courtyards with wood from the arrangement, we do not listen to them; likewise, if they want to burn it before the Temple with their own wood, we do not listen.

sub.desc_en: The Baraita rules that burning the lamb in courtyards with Temple wood or before the Temple with private wood is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why burning with one's own wood before the Temple is forbidden, and Rav Yosef and Rava offer reasons: to avoid shaming those without wood, and to avoid suspicion. The difference between them is whether one brings reeds and twigs unsuitable for the arrangement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why burning with one's own wood before the Temple is forbidden, given that the reason for forbidding burning with Temple wood in one's courtyard (fear of leftover coals causing a mishap) does not apply.
Rav Yosef answers that the prohibition is to avoid shaming those who have no wood of their own and cannot afford to bring their own.
Rava answers that the prohibition is to avoid suspicion that one is using Temple wood for personal benefit.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rav Yosef's and Rava's explanations.

The Gemara resolves that the difference is in a case where one brings reeds and twigs unsuitable for the Temple arrangement: according to Rav Yosef, bringing them would still shame those without wood, while according to Rava, there is no suspicion since they are not fit for the arrangement.

items.text: Parallel discussion on the head of the watch
items.text_en: Parallel discussion on the head of the watch
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about the head of the watch placing impure people at the eastern gate, and Rav Yosef and Rava again debate the reason: to shame them or due to suspicion, with the difference being a pampered person or one raised in luxury.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about the head of the watch placing impure people at the eastern gate.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind this practice.
Rav Yosef explains that the purpose is to shame them.
Rava explains that the purpose is due to suspicion.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two explanations.
The Gemara resolves that the difference lies in the case of a pampered person or one raised in luxury.

items.text: Mishnah: When to burn the paschal lamb
items.text_en: Mishnah: When to burn the paschal lamb
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a paschal lamb that left its boundaries or became impure is burned immediately; if the owners became impure or died, it is kept until the sixteenth and then burned. Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says it is burned immediately because it has no eaters.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a paschal lamb that left its boundaries or became impure is burned immediately.
The Mishnah rules that if the owners became impure or died, the lamb is kept until the sixteenth and then burned.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka argues that even this case is burned immediately because it has no eaters.

items.text: Gemara: Source for burning an impure or out-of-bounds sacrifice
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for burning an impure or out-of-bounds sacrifice
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the law for an impure sacrifice from a verse, and for one that left its boundaries from Moses' dialogue with Aaron about the sin-offering, implying that if it went out or its blood entered the inner sanctum, it would be burned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for an impure sacrifice the source is clear from the verse, but from where do we derive that a sacrifice that left its boundaries must be burned?
The Gemara cites the verse about the sin-offering and Moses' dialogue with Aaron, where Moses asks whether the blood entered the inner sanctum and Aaron denies it.

Moses then asks whether the sacrifice went outside its boundary, and Aaron denies that too; the Gemara concludes that if it had gone out or its blood entered the inner sanctum, it would be subject to burning.

items.text: Gemara: Extending the law to lesser sacrifices
items.text_en: Gemara: Extending the law to lesser sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the law for an out-of-bounds sacrifice applies to lesser holy things, and notes a Baraita about blood that remained overnight, beginning a new discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the law of an out-of-bounds sacrifice (יוצא) applies to lesser holy things (קדשים קלים), since the Torah explicitly addresses only impurity for lesser holy things and only the out-of-bounds case for most holy things.
The Gemara introduces a Baraita about blood that remained overnight (לן דמה), which will serve as a basis for further discussion on the extension of the law.

items.text: Derivation that all disqualified sacrifices are burned
items.text_en: Derivation that all disqualified sacrifices are burned
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that a sacrifice whose blood was spilled or taken outside the courtyard is burned. It cites Rabbi Shimon's teaching that the verse 'in the sanctuary it shall be burned with fire' applies to all disqualified most holy sacrifices and holy offerings, and concludes that this is a tradition, with Aaron's sin-offering being a special case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that a sacrifice whose blood was spilled or taken outside the courtyard is burned.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Shimon's teaching that the verse 'בַּקֹּדֶשׁ בָּאֵשׁ תִּשָּׂרֵף' teaches that a sin-offering is burned in the sanctuary.
The baraita extends the verse to include all disqualified most holy sacrifices and holy offerings.
The Gemara concludes that the rule that all disqualified sacrifices are burned is a tradition (גְּמָרָא גְּמִירִי לַהּ), and Aaron's sin-offering was a special case due to the event.

items.text: Derivation that piggul requires disfigurement
items.text_en: Derivation that piggul requires disfigurement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the school of Rabbah bar Avuh knows that piggul requires disfigurement. It derives it via a verbal analogy of 'avon' from notar. An objection is raised to derive it from Aaron's sin-offering, but the Gemara answers that Aaron's sin-offering also required disfigurement for future generations, but that case was a temporary ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the Tanna of the school of Rabbah bar Avuh, who says that even piggul requires disfigurement (עיבור צורה), from where does he derive this?
The Gemara answers: he derives it via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of the word 'עָוֹן' (iniquity) from notar (leftover sacrificial meat).
An objection is raised: why not derive the verbal analogy from Aaron's sin-offering (which also involved 'עָוֹן') instead?
The Gemara answers: Aaron's sin-offering also requires disfigurement for future generations, but that case was a temporary ruling (הוראת שעה), so it cannot serve as a source.
The Gemara resolves the objection by clarifying that Aaron's sin-offering was a temporary ruling, not a precedent for permanent law.

items.text: Clarifying the need for the verse and the case of impurity
items.text_en: Clarifying the need for the verse and the case of impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse 'in the sanctuary it shall be burned with fire' is needed if the rule is a tradition. It answers that it teaches that the burning must be in the sanctuary. It then asks why the verse 'and the flesh that touches any unclean thing shall not be eaten, it shall be burned with fire' is needed, and explains that it teaches that even impurity, which also disqualifies unconsecrated food, requires burning and not burial.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: now that we have a tradition that all disqualified consecrated items are burned, why is the verse 'in the sanctuary it shall be burned with fire' needed?
The Gemara answers: that verse is needed to teach that the burning must take place in the sanctuary.
The Gemara asks: why is the verse 'and the flesh that touches any unclean thing shall not be eaten, it shall be burned with fire' needed?
The Gemara answers: that verse is needed for itself, to teach that even impurity, which also disqualifies unconsecrated food, requires burning and not burial.

items.text: Rav Yosef's distinction regarding impurity of owners
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's distinction regarding impurity of owners
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that the dispute about whether the flesh requires disfigurement applies only when the owners became impure after sprinkling, when the flesh was fit for eating. But if they became impure before sprinkling, all agree it is burned immediately. An objection is raised from a baraita that compares owners to blood, implying that owners before sprinkling require disfigurement.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef distinguishes the dispute: it applies only when owners became impure after sprinkling, but before sprinkling all agree the flesh is burned immediately.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states a general rule: anything disqualified in its body is burned immediately, but blood and owners require disfigurement.
The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that the baraita compares owners to blood, implying that owners before sprinkling also require disfigurement, contradicting Rav Yosef's distinction.

items.text: Revised version of Rav Yosef's statement and Rabbi Yochanan's view
items.text_en: Revised version of Rav Yosef's statement and Rabbi Yochanan's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara revises Rav Yosef's statement: the dispute is when owners became impure before sprinkling, but after sprinkling all agree it requires disfigurement. Rabbi Yochanan says the dispute applies even after sprinkling, and he aligns himself with Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Nechemya, who said a similar thing. The Gemara explains that the case of aninut (mourning) occurred after sprinkling, and if they were combined, they would be burned immediately.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara revises Rav Yosef's statement: the dispute is when owners became impure before sprinkling, but after sprinkling all agree it requires disfigurement.
Rabbi Yochanan says the dispute applies even after sprinkling, and he aligns himself with Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Nechemya who said a similar thing.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Nechemya's statement that the case of aninut (mourning) occurred after sprinkling, and if they were combined, they would be burned immediately.
The Gemara explains that the case of aninut occurred after sprinkling, and if they were combined, they would be burned immediately.

items.text: Rabba's addition and Rabbi Yose HaGelili's view
items.text_en: Rabba's addition and Rabbi Yose HaGelili's view
items.desc_en: Rabba adds that Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds that the entire biblical passage deals only with bulls and goats that are burned, requiring their invalid parts to be burned in the Temple courtyard and prohibiting their consumption. The Sages ask about a sin-offering whose blood entered the inner sanctuary, and Rabbi Yose HaGelili derives from a verse that if the blood entered, the meat is burned. Rabbi Yochanan holds that blood and meat are one matter, but the owners are a separate matter.

sub.desc_en: Rabba adds that Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds the entire passage deals only with bulls and goats that are burned, requiring burning their invalid parts in the Temple courtyard and prohibiting their consumption.
The Sages ask Rabbi Yose HaGelili: from where do we derive that a sin-offering whose blood entered the inner sanctuary is burned?

Rabbi Yose HaGelili answers from the verse 'הֵן לֹא הוּבָא אֶת דָּמָהּ אֶל הַקֹּדֶשׁ פְּנִימָה' (if its blood was not brought inside the sanctuary), implying that if the blood entered, the meat is burned.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that blood and meat are one matter, but the owners are a separate matter.

items.text: Mishnah: Bones, sinews, and leftover meat are burned on the sixteenth
items.text_en: Mishnah: Bones, sinews, and leftover meat are burned on the sixteenth
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that bones, sinews, and leftover meat (נותר) of the Paschal lamb are burned on the sixteenth of Nisan. If the sixteenth falls on Shabbat, they are burned on the seventeenth, because these do not override Shabbat or Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that bones, sinews, and leftover meat of the Paschal lamb are burned on the sixteenth of Nisan, and if the sixteenth falls on Shabbat, they are burned on the seventeenth, because these do not override Shabbat or Yom Tov.

items.text: Gemara: Rav Mari bar Avuha's statement and proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav Mari bar Avuha's statement and proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Avuha says in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak that bones of consecrated animals that have served as a base for leftover meat (שימוש נותר) impart impurity to hands, because they became a base for a forbidden item. The Gemara attempts to prove this from the Mishnah, analyzing that the bones must contain marrow, and if שימוש נותר is significant, they require burning; otherwise, they could be broken to extract the marrow. The proof is that the Mishnah requires burning, implying שימוש נותר is significant.

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Avuha citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Avuha citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Avuha states in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak that bones of consecrated animals that served as a base for leftover meat (שימוש נותר) impart impurity to hands, because they became a base for a forbidden item.
The Gemara proposes to bring support for Rav Mari bar Avuha from the Mishnah, which states that bones, sinews, and leftover meat are burned on the sixteenth.
The Gemara analyzes the bones in the Mishnah, concluding they must contain marrow, otherwise they would not require burning.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's requirement to burn the bones proves that שימוש נותר (serving as a base for leftover meat) is significant.

items.text: Rejection and alternative explanation: the verse 'בו' in a fit state
items.text_en: Rejection and alternative explanation: the verse 'בו' in a fit state
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, suggesting that שימוש נותר is not significant, and the Mishnah's requirement to burn the bones is because the verse 'בו' (in it) applies to a fit state, and even to an invalid state if it had a period of fitness. This view is attributed to Rabbi Yaakov, who distinguishes between a sacrifice that had a period of fitness and one that did not. Rabbi Shimon holds that neither case involves the prohibition of breaking a bone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, asserting that the principle of שימוש נותר (use of leftover sacrificial meat) is not significant.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's requirement to burn the bones is because the verse 'בּוֹ' (in it) applies to a fit state, and even to an invalid state if it had a period of fitness.

sub.text: Supporting baraita with Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita with Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attributes this view to Rabbi Yaakov, who distinguishes between a sacrifice that had a period of fitness and one that did not, while Rabbi Shimon holds that neither case involves the prohibition of breaking a bone.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that all bones of consecrated animals do not require burning, except for bones of the Paschal lamb due to the concern of stumbling. The Gemara challenges that if שימוש נותר is significant, why don't other consecrated bones require burning? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the case is where the bones were found already hollowed out: for other consecrated animals, the marrow was removed before they became leftover, so there was no שימוש נותר; for the Paschal lamb, the marrow was removed only after it became leftover, so the bones served as a base and require burning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges from a baraita that all consecrated animal bones do not require burning except for Paschal lamb bones, and argues that if שימוש נותר (use of leftover) is significant, why don't other consecrated bones require burning?

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the case involves bones found already hollowed out: for other consecrated animals, the marrow was removed before they became leftover, so there was no שימוש נותר; for the Paschal lamb, the marrow was removed only after it became leftover, so the bones served as a base and require burning.

items.text: Rav Zevid's alternative explanation (incomplete)
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's alternative explanation (incomplete)
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid begins to offer an alternative explanation for the baraita, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid offers an alternative explanation for the baraita, beginning to describe a case where the bones were found already hollowed out.

items.text: Distinction between bones of consecrated animals and bones of the Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Distinction between bones of consecrated animals and bones of the Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between bones of consecrated animals, which have no prohibition of breaking the bone and can be completely hollowed out and eaten, and bones of the Paschal lamb, which have a prohibition of breaking the bone, so it is uncertain whether they were hollowed out, and they require burning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between bones of consecrated animals, which have no prohibition of breaking the bone and can be completely hollowed out and eaten, and bones of the Paschal lamb, which have a prohibition of breaking the bone, so it is uncertain whether they were hollowed out, and they require burning.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on sinews
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on sinews
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that all sinews are considered meat except for the sinews of the neck.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that all sinews are considered meat except for the neck sinews.

items.text: Question on the Mishnah's sinews and Rav Chisda's answer
items.text_en: Question on the Mishnah's sinews and Rav Chisda's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which sinews the Mishnah refers to when it says sinews must be burned. If they are meat-sinews, they could be eaten; if they are leftover, that is already notar. It must be neck-sinews. Rav Chisda answers that the Mishnah refers to the sciatic nerve according to Rabbi Yehuda, who is uncertain which side is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions which sinews the Mishnah refers to, concluding they must be neck-sinews (גידי צואר).
Rav Chisda answers that the Mishnah refers to the sciatic nerve (גיד הנשה) according to Rabbi Yehuda's view.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's uncertainty and the need for burning
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's uncertainty and the need for burning
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says the sciatic nerve applies only to one side, and reason inclines to the right. The Gemara then asks: if Rabbi Yehuda is uncertain, then the permitted side could be eaten and the forbidden side discarded, so why require burning?

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda states that the sciatic nerve applies only to one side, and reason inclines to the right.
The Gemara asks: if Rabbi Yehuda is uncertain about which side is forbidden, then the permitted side could be eaten and the forbidden side discarded, so why require burning?

items.text: Rav Ika bar Chinana's answer: they were recognizable and then mixed
items.text_en: Rav Ika bar Chinana's answer: they were recognizable and then mixed
items.desc_en: Rav Ika bar Chinana answers that the case is where the sinews were initially recognizable (which side is forbidden) but later became mixed, so both require burning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ika bar Chinana answers that the case is where the two sides were initially distinguishable but later became mixed together.

items.text: Rav Ashi's answer: the fat of the sciatic nerve
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer: the fat of the sciatic nerve
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that the Mishnah refers to the fat of the sciatic nerve, which is permitted by Torah law but prohibited by custom, and thus requires burning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that the Mishnah refers to the fat of the sciatic nerve, which is permitted by Torah law but treated as forbidden by pious practice.

items.text: Ravina's answer: the outer sinew according to Shmuel
items.text_en: Ravina's answer: the outer sinew according to Shmuel
items.desc_en: Ravina answers that the Mishnah refers to the outer sinew, which is forbidden but not punishable by lashes, as per Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: Ravina answers that the Mishnah refers to the outer sciatic nerve, which is forbidden but does not incur liability, as per Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel.

items.text: Why the burning does not override the festival prohibition
items.text_en: Why the burning does not override the festival prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the burning of notar on the sixteenth does not override the negative commandment of performing labor on a festival. Chizkiya answers that the verse gives a second morning for burning. Abaye answers that the verse 'olah of Shabbat on its Shabbat' excludes a weekday offering on Shabbat or Yom Tov. Rava answers that the verse 'it alone shall be done for you' excludes its accessories.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the burning of notar on the sixteenth does not override the negative commandment of performing labor on a festival.
