Chizkiya answers that the verse gives a second morning for burning, implying it is not limited to the festival day.
Abaye answers that the verse 'עולת שבת בשבתו' (the burnt-offering of Shabbat on its Shabbat) excludes a weekday offering from being offered on Shabbat or Yom Tov.
Rava answers that the verse 'הוא לבדו יעשה לכם' (it alone shall be done for you) excludes its accessories from being performed on Yom Tov.

items.text: Opening Gemara: Circumcision and the positive commandment of Yom Tov
items.text_en: Opening Gemara: Circumcision and the positive commandment of Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues a prior discussion about whether a positive commandment overrides a negative one. Rav Ashi explains that the word 'Shabbaton' for Yom Tov is a positive commandment, and a positive commandment does not override a negative and positive commandment combined.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of circumcision not at its proper time, derived by a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument.
Rav Ashi explains that the word 'שַׁבָּתוֹן' for Yom Tov is a positive commandment, and a positive commandment does not override a negative and positive commandment combined.

items.text: Mishnah: What is eaten in a large ox is eaten in a young goat
items.text_en: Mishnah: What is eaten in a large ox is eaten in a young goat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that whatever parts of a large ox are edible are also edible in a young goat for the Paschal lamb, listing the wing tips and cartilage.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that whatever parts of a large ox are edible are also edible in a young goat for the Paschal lamb, listing the wing tips and cartilage.

items.text: Gemara: Resolving a contradiction in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Resolving a contradiction in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbah raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says only what is eaten in a large ox is eaten in a young goat, but then lists wing tips and cartilage which are not eaten in a large ox. Rava resolves that the Mishnah means 'what are they?' and lists those items as examples of what is eaten in a large ox when boiled, and in a young goat when roasted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah raises a contradiction: the Mishnah states that only what is eaten in a large ox is eaten in a young goat, but the end of the Mishnah lists wing tips and cartilage, which are not eaten in a large ox.
The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah reflects a dispute between Tannaic traditions: one tradition limits the rule to what is eaten in a large ox, while another adds wing tips and cartilage.

Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah means 'what are they?' and lists wing tips and cartilage as examples of what is eaten in a large ox when boiled and in a young goat when roasted.

items.text: Supporting baraita for Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava's interpretation, adding that soft sinews are considered as meat.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rava's interpretation, adding that soft sinews are treated as meat.

items.text: Dispute about sinews that will harden
items.text_en: Dispute about sinews that will harden
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish dispute whether sinews that will eventually harden are counted for the Paschal lamb. Rabbi Yochanan follows the present state, Reish Lakish follows the future state. Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan from the Mishnah, and Rabbi Yochanan deflects. Rabbi Yirmeya raises a contradiction from a different ruling, but Rabbi Avin dismisses it, saying Rabbi Yochanan retracted.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says sinews that will harden are counted for the Paschal lamb, following the present state; Reish Lakish says they are not counted, following the future state.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's objection to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's objection to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan from the Mishnah, which lists only wing tips and cartilage, implying sinews that will harden are excluded.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's answer to Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's answer to Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan deflects the objection, arguing that the Mishnah mentions these examples but the same rule applies to sinews that will harden, since they too are edible in a large ox when boiled.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's challenge to Rabbi Avin
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's challenge to Rabbi Avin
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya raises a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan ruled that the soft calf's head skin does not transmit impurity, following the future state, contradicting his own position on sinews.
Rabbi Avin dismisses the contradiction, explaining that Rabbi Yochanan retracted his position toward Reish Lakish, saying he taught that ruling as an individual opinion.

items.text: Mishnah: Breaking a bone in the Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Mishnah: Breaking a bone in the Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who breaks a bone in a pure Paschal lamb is lashed, but one who leaves over meat in a pure offering or breaks a bone in an impure offering is not lashed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who breaks a bone of a pure Paschal lamb receives lashes, but one who leaves over meat of a pure lamb or breaks a bone of an impure lamb does not receive lashes.

items.text: Gemara: Sources for the exceptions
items.text_en: Gemara: Sources for the exceptions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the source for leaving over in a pure offering (a positive commandment after a negative) and for breaking a bone in an impure offering (the word 'bo' excludes unfit offerings). A dispute between Rabbi and the Sages about the criterion for the prohibition is resolved by Rabbi Yirmeya: the difference is a Paschal lamb brought in impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of leaving over in a pure offering, citing a baraita that the verse gives a positive commandment after a negative to exempt from lashes, according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yaakov argues that the exemption is not from the positive commandment but because the prohibition involves no action, and one is not lashed for such a prohibition.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the exemption for breaking a bone in an impure offering?
The Gemara answers that the verse 'ועצם לא תשברו בו' (do not break a bone in it) uses the word 'בו' (in it) to limit the prohibition to a fit offering, excluding an unfit one.

A baraita is cited: the Sages derive from 'בו' that the prohibition applies only to a fit offering; Rabbi derives from the context of eating that only a bone fit for eating is subject to the prohibition.
The Gemara asks: what is the practical difference between the two positions (the Sages' and Rabbi's)?
Rabbi Yirmeya resolves the dispute: the difference is a Paschal lamb brought in impurity — according to the one who says 'fit' (the Sages) it is excluded, while according to Rabbi it may be included.

items.text: Opening dispute: invalid bone vs. bone that was once fit
items.text_en: Opening dispute: invalid bone vs. bone that was once fit
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the core disagreement: according to the one who says 'fit for consumption' (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi), a bone that is invalid is not subject to the prohibition of breaking a bone; according to the one who says 'valid' (the Sages), even an invalid bone is subject if it was once fit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens the dispute: according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi who requires 'fit for consumption', an invalid bone is exempt from the prohibition of breaking a bone; according to the Sages who require 'valid', even an invalid bone that was once fit is subject.

items.text: Rav Yosef's explanation: all agree there is no bone-breaking here
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's explanation: all agree there is no bone-breaking here
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef argues that in this specific case (a bone that was never fit), everyone agrees there is no bone-breaking prohibition, because Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi came to be lenient, and this bone is already invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the dispute by stating that in this case of a bone that was never fit, everyone agrees there is no bone-breaking prohibition, since Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi came to be lenient and this bone is already invalid.

items.text: Rav Yosef's real dispute: a bone that was fit and then became invalid
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's real dispute: a bone that was fit and then became invalid
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef clarifies that the actual dispute is about a bone that had a time of fitness and then became invalid: the one who says 'valid' holds it is still subject to bone-breaking, while the one who says 'fit for consumption' holds it is not, since it is no longer fit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the dispute: the bone that had a time of fitness and then became invalid is the real point of contention, with one opinion deeming it valid for bone-breaking and the other deeming it invalid because it is no longer fit for consumption.

items.text: Abaye's explanation: all agree there is no bone-breaking here; dispute is about breaking the bone before nightfall
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation: all agree there is no bone-breaking here; dispute is about breaking the bone before nightfall
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that in this case everyone agrees there is no bone-breaking prohibition because the bone is currently invalid. The real dispute is about breaking the bone before nightfall (while it is still fit): the one who says 'valid' holds it is subject, while the one who says 'fit for consumption' holds it is not, since it is not yet fit for consumption.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by stating that everyone agrees there is no bone-breaking prohibition here because the bone is currently invalid.

Abaye resolves that the real dispute is about breaking the bone before nightfall: the one who says 'valid' holds it is subject, while the one who says 'fit for consumption' holds it is not yet fit for consumption.

items.text: Objection to Abaye from a baraita about marrow in the skull vs. in a leg bone
items.text_en: Objection to Abaye from a baraita about marrow in the skull vs. in a leg bone
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection against Abaye from a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says one may count on marrow in the skull (because it can be scraped out) but not on marrow in a leg bone. If breaking the bone before nightfall were permitted, one could break the leg bone before nightfall and count on the marrow. This challenges Abaye's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection against Abaye from a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi distinguishes between marrow in the skull (countable) and marrow in a leg bone (not countable), implying that if breaking the bone before nightfall were permitted, one could break the leg bone and count on its marrow.

items.text: Abaye's response: the objection is invalid because one could also use fire after nightfall
items.text_en: Abaye's response: the objection is invalid because one could also use fire after nightfall
items.desc_en: Abaye deflects the objection by pointing out that the same logic would apply after nightfall: one could bring a coal and roast the bone to extract the marrow, since a baraita states that burning bones or cutting sinews does not violate the bone-breaking prohibition. So the objection is not specific to his view.

sub.desc_en: Abaye deflects the objection by arguing that the same logic would apply after nightfall, where one could use fire to extract marrow without violating the bone-breaking prohibition, citing a baraita that burning bones or cutting sinews is exempt.

items.text: Alternative explanations: Abaye says due to 'peka' (splitting), Rava says due to loss of sanctity
items.text_en: Alternative explanations: Abaye says due to 'peka' (splitting), Rava says due to loss of sanctity
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the real reason one cannot break the bone before nightfall is either because of 'peka' (splitting the bone into pieces, which is a form of bone-breaking) or because of loss of sanctity (the fire might damage the marrow). And there is a decree that breaking before nightfall is forbidden lest one come to break after nightfall.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the prohibition against breaking the bone before nightfall is due to 'peka' (splitting the bone into pieces, which is a form of bone-breaking).
Rava explains that the prohibition is due to loss of sanctity (הפסד קדשים), as the fire might damage the marrow, causing a loss of consecrated food.
The Gemara adds that there is a decree forbidding breaking the bone before nightfall lest one come to break it after nightfall.

items.text: Rav Pappa's explanation: all agree there is bone-breaking here; dispute is about a limb that partially emerged
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation: all agree there is bone-breaking here; dispute is about a limb that partially emerged
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that in this case everyone agrees there is a bone-breaking prohibition because the bone is fit for consumption at night. The real dispute is about a limb that partially emerged from the boundary: the one who says 'valid' holds it is subject, while the one who says 'fit for consumption' holds it is not, since it is not fit. A baraita supports this: Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says a limb that partially emerged and was broken has no bone-breaking prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asserts that in this case everyone agrees there is a bone-breaking prohibition because the bone is fit for consumption at night.

Rav Pappa explains that the real dispute is about a limb that partially emerged: the one who says 'valid' holds it is subject, while the one who says 'fit for consumption' holds it is not, since it is not fit.

A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka states that a limb that partially emerged and was broken has no bone-breaking prohibition, supporting Rav Pappa's position.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's explanation: all agree there is no bone-breaking; dispute is about breaking a bone while it is still raw
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's explanation: all agree there is no bone-breaking; dispute is about breaking a bone while it is still raw
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet argues that in this case everyone agrees there is no bone-breaking prohibition because the limb is invalid. The real dispute is about breaking a bone while it is still raw (before roasting): the one who says 'valid' holds it is subject, while the one who says 'fit for consumption' holds it is not, since it is not yet fit for consumption.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet asserts that in this case everyone agrees there is no bone-breaking prohibition because the limb is invalid; the dispute is about breaking a bone while it is still raw, where the one who says 'valid' holds it is subject, while the one who says 'fit for consumption' holds it is not, since it is not yet fit for consumption.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation: all agree there is bone-breaking; dispute is about breaking the tail
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation: all agree there is bone-breaking; dispute is about breaking the tail
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak argues that in this case everyone agrees there is a bone-breaking prohibition because the bone is fit for consumption (one can roast and eat it). The real dispute is about breaking the tail (which is offered on the altar): the one who says 'valid' holds it is subject, while the one who says 'fit for consumption' holds it is not, since the tail goes up to the altar and is not for human consumption.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the dispute: all agree there is a bone-breaking prohibition for a bone fit for consumption; the dispute is about the tail, which goes up to the altar and is not for human consumption.

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation: all agree there is no bone-breaking; dispute is about a limb without an olive's bulk of meat
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation: all agree there is no bone-breaking; dispute is about a limb without an olive's bulk of meat
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that in this case everyone agrees there is no bone-breaking prohibition because the bone is certainly not fit for consumption at all. The real dispute is about a limb that does not have an olive's bulk of meat on it: the one who says 'valid' holds it is subject, while the one who says 'fit for consumption' holds it is not, since we require a measure of consumption and there is none.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the dispute: all agree there is no bone-breaking here since the bone is certainly unfit; the real dispute is about a limb without an olive's bulk of meat, where one opinion requires a measure of consumption and the other does not.

items.text: Ravina's explanation: all agree there is no bone-breaking; dispute is about a limb with an olive's bulk elsewhere
items.text_en: Ravina's explanation: all agree there is no bone-breaking; dispute is about a limb with an olive's bulk elsewhere
items.desc_en: Ravina argues that in this case everyone agrees there is no bone-breaking prohibition because we require a measure of consumption. The real dispute is about a limb that does not have an olive's bulk of meat in this place but has an olive's bulk in another place: the one who says 'valid' holds it is subject, while the one who says 'fit for consumption' holds it is not, since we require a measure of consumption at the place of breaking and there is none.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the dispute: all agree there is no bone-breaking prohibition here because we require a measure of consumption; the real dispute is about a limb that lacks an olive's bulk of meat in this place but has it elsewhere.

items.text: Baraita supporting the four Amoraim: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's position
items.text_en: Baraita supporting the four Amoraim: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's position
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports the views of the four Amoraim (Rav Yosef, Abaye, Rav Pappa, etc.). It states: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says that the verse 'in one house it shall be eaten... and you shall not break a bone in it' implies liability only for a valid bone, not an invalid one. It then lists several cases: a bone that was fit and became invalid has no bone-breaking; if there is a measure of consumption there is bone-breaking, if not there is none; a bone fit for the altar has no bone-breaking; during the time of eating there is bone-breaking, not at other times.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a baraita that supports the four Amoraim (Rav Yosef, Abaye, Rav Pappa, etc.).

The baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's exposition of the verse 'בבית אחד יאכל... ועצם לא תשברו בו' (in one house it shall be eaten... and you shall not break a bone in it), deriving liability only for a valid bone, not an invalid one.
The baraita states that a bone which had a time of fitness but became invalid at the time of eating has no bone-breaking prohibition.
The baraita rules that if there is a measure of consumption (כזית) there is bone-breaking liability; if not, there is none.
The baraita states that a bone fit for the altar has no bone-breaking prohibition.
The baraita concludes that during the time of eating there is bone-breaking liability; at other times there is none.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about a limb with an olive's bulk elsewhere
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about a limb with an olive's bulk elsewhere
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute about a limb that does not have an olive's bulk of meat in this place but has an olive's bulk in another place: Rabbi Yochanan says there is a bone-breaking prohibition, while Reish Lakish says there is not. Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from a baraita that seems to include such a case as subject to bone-breaking. The Gemara cuts off with 'He said to him...'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding a limb that lacks an olive's bulk of meat in one place but has it elsewhere: Rabbi Yochanan holds there is a bone-breaking prohibition, while Reish Lakish holds there is not.
Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from a baraita that seems to include a limb with an olive's bulk elsewhere as subject to the bone-breaking prohibition.
The Gemara cuts off the discussion with 'He said to him...', indicating that the response is not recorded here.

items.text: Clarification of the bone-breaking prohibition
items.text_en: Clarification of the bone-breaking prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the prohibition applies both to a bone with an olive's bulk of meat on the outside and to a bone with an olive's bulk of meat inside at the place of breaking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the bone-breaking prohibition applies both to a bone with an olive's bulk of meat on the outside and to a bone with an olive's bulk of meat inside at the breaking point.

items.text: Derivation from verses about bones with and without marrow
items.text_en: Derivation from verses about bones with and without marrow
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that derives from the verse 'and you shall eat the flesh' that the meat referred to is on the bone, not inside. Another verse teaches that the prohibition of breaking a bone applies to all bones, whether they have marrow or not, as the redundant verse in the Second Passover indicates.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'and you shall eat the flesh' that the meat referred to is on the bone, not inside.

The baraita raises a possible alternative interpretation: the meat might be inside the bone, and the prohibition of breaking a bone would then apply only to bones without marrow, with the positive commandment overriding the prohibition for bones with marrow.
The baraita resolves the ambiguity by citing the redundant verse about the Second Passover, teaching that the prohibition applies to all bones, whether they have marrow or not.

items.text: Objection from the law of a limb that partially left
items.text_en: Objection from the law of a limb that partially left
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita about a limb that partially left its boundary: one cuts until the bone, peels until the joint, and cuts. If the prohibition only applies when there is an olive's bulk of meat, why peel? One could just break the bone directly.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a limb that partially left its boundary, which requires cutting, peeling to the joint, and cutting again.
The gemara challenges: if the prohibition of breaking the bone applies only when there is an olive's bulk of meat, why peel to the joint? One could just peel a little and break the bone directly.

items.text: Answers of Abaye and Ravina
items.text_en: Answers of Abaye and Ravina
items.desc_en: Abaye answers that the peeling is due to the tendon (פקע), and Ravina says it is because of the shinbone (קולית).

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that the peeling is due to the tendon (פקע) that must be removed to avoid breaking the bone.
Ravina answers that the peeling is due to the shinbone (קולית) that requires careful handling.

items.text: Dispute about why piggul and notar impart impurity to hands
items.text_en: Dispute about why piggul and notar impart impurity to hands
items.desc_en: A dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda: one says it is due to suspicion of the priesthood, the other due to lazy priests. They also disagree whether the measure is an olive's bulk (like the prohibition) or an egg's bulk (like impurity).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that piggul and notar impart impurity to hands.
The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda about the reason for the decree: one says due to suspicion of the priesthood, the other due to lazy priests.

The Gemara resolves the dispute: one master applies the decree to piggul due to suspicion, the other to notar due to lazy priests; they also disagree on the measure — one says an olive's bulk (like the prohibition), the other an egg's bulk (like impurity).

items.text: Inquiry about impurity of meat that left its boundary
items.text_en: Inquiry about impurity of meat that left its boundary
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires: did the rabbis decree impurity on meat that left its boundary? Perhaps not, since one would not take it out with hands, or perhaps it is no different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the rabbis decreed impurity on meat that left its boundary, considering whether one would not take it out with hands or if it is no different.

items.text: Attempted resolution from the limb that partially left
items.text_en: Attempted resolution from the limb that partially left
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the inquiry from the baraita about a limb that partially left: if impurity was decreed, cutting would cause impurity. The answer is that it is hidden impurity, which does not impart impurity. For Ravina, who holds that food connections are not connections, the answer is that there is less than an olive's bulk or less than an egg's bulk.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita about a limb that partially left the boundary, which requires cutting until the bone and peeling until the joint, to resolve the inquiry about whether the Sages decreed impurity on יוֹצֵא (that which left the boundary).
The Gemara answers that the cutting involves טומאת סתרים (hidden impurity), which does not impart impurity, so the baraita does not prove that impurity was decreed.
The Gemara objects that according to Ravina, who holds that food connections are not connections, the pieces are separate and the cut piece would still be impure, so the baraita remains problematic.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a case where the limb lacks a כזית (olive's bulk) of meat, according to the version that sets the threshold at a כזית, or lacks a כביצה (egg's bulk), according to the version that sets the threshold at a כביצה, so there is no impurity to transmit.

items.text: Resolution from the case of meat taken from one group to another
items.text_en: Resolution from the case of meat taken from one group to another
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: one who takes meat of the Paschal offering from one group to another is tahor. This suggests no impurity was decreed. The Gemara concludes that for the Paschal offering, no impurity was decreed because the group members are vigilant, but the question remains for other sacrifices, left unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: one who takes meat of the Paschal offering from one group to another is tahor, suggesting no impurity was decreed.
The Gemara infers that the baraita means 'tahor and forbidden', implying that even though the meat is invalid as יוֹצֵא (an excluded case), no rabbinic impurity was decreed.

The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the baraita means 'tahor and permitted', because taking meat from one group to another is not considered יוֹצֵא (an excluded case) and does not invalidate the offering.

The Gemara objects: the baraita's continuation states that eating it is a negative commandment, which contradicts the 'tahor and permitted' interpretation, and questions how this fits with the opinion that the minimum size is a כְּזַיִת (olive's bulk).
The Gemara resolves that for the Paschal offering, no impurity was decreed because the group members are vigilant, but the question remains unresolved (תיקו) for other sacrifices.

items.text: Continuation of the baraita
items.text_en: Continuation of the baraita
items.desc_en: The baraita continues with the case of one who takes out meat of the Paschal offering.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the case of one who takes out meat of the Paschal offering from one group to another.

items.text: Source for prohibition from group to group
items.text_en: Source for prohibition from group to group
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a verse that removing meat from one group to another is prohibited, based on the word 'חוּצָה' meaning outside the eating area.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is it derived that removing meat from one group to another is prohibited?

A baraita is cited: the verse 'לֹא תוֹצִיא מִן הַבַּיִת מִן הַבָּשָׂר חוּצָה' (do not take meat outside the house) is interpreted to include removal from group to group, based on the word 'חוּצָה' meaning outside the eating area.

items.text: Rabbi Ammi's ruling on liability
items.text_en: Rabbi Ammi's ruling on liability
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi states that one is not liable for carrying out paschal meat from one group to another unless he performs both lifting and placing, analogous to Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi rules that one is liable for carrying paschal meat from one group to another only after performing both lifting and placing, analogous to Shabbat.

items.text: Objection from baraita about carrying with poles
items.text_en: Objection from baraita about carrying with poles
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects from a baraita where those carrying the paschal lamb on poles who exit the Temple courtyard are impure, even though they did not place the meat down. He resolves it by explaining the case involved dragging, not carrying.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects from a baraita where those carrying the paschal lamb on poles who exit the Temple courtyard are impure, even though they did not place the meat down.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel resolves the objection by explaining the case involved dragging, not carrying.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of a limb that partially exits
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of a limb that partially exits
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a limb of the paschal lamb partially exits, one cuts until the bone, peels to the joint, and cuts. For consecrated offerings, one uses a chopper. It also defines the status of the threshold, windows, and wall thickness as inside.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a limb of the paschal lamb partially exits, one cuts until the bone, peels to the joint, and cuts.
The Mishnah adds that for consecrated offerings, one uses a chopper, as there is no concern about breaking the bone.
The Mishnah defines the threshold area, windows, and wall thickness as inside for the purpose of the paschal lamb.

items.text: Gemara: Rav's analogy to prayer and dispute with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav's analogy to prayer and dispute with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav applies the same rule to prayer, but Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagrees, stating that no partition separates Israel from their Father in heaven.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports from Rav that the same rule of chambers applying to the paschal offering also applies to prayer.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagrees, asserting that no partition, not even an iron wall, separates Israel from their Father in heaven.

items.text: Contradiction in the Mishnah regarding the threshold
items.text_en: Contradiction in the Mishnah regarding the threshold
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes an internal contradiction in the Mishnah about the status of the threshold itself. It resolves by distinguishing between the gates of the Temple courtyard and the gates of Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the Mishnah: the first clause implies the threshold itself is like the outside, while the second clause implies it is like the inside.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the gates of the Temple courtyard (עזרה), where the threshold is treated as inside, and the gates of Jerusalem, where the threshold is treated as outside.

items.text: Reason gates of Jerusalem and Nikanor Gate were not sanctified
items.text_en: Reason gates of Jerusalem and Nikanor Gate were not sanctified
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak explains that the gates of Jerusalem were not sanctified to provide shelter for lepers, and the Nikanor Gate was not sanctified so lepers could insert their fingers for inspection.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's question
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak asks why the gates of Jerusalem were not sanctified, and answers that it was to provide shelter for lepers from sun and rain.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's second statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's second statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak further explains that the Nikanor Gate was not sanctified so that lepers could stand there and insert their fingers for inspection.

items.text: Rav's statement on roofs and upper chambers
items.text_en: Rav's statement on roofs and upper chambers
items.desc_en: Rav states that roofs and upper chambers were not sanctified, but a contradiction is raised from a statement by Rav in the name of Rabbi Chiya about the paschal lamb being eaten on the roof.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that roofs and upper chambers were not sanctified with the sanctity of Jerusalem.
The Gemara objects: Did Rav not himself say in the name of Rabbi Chiya that the paschal lamb was eaten on the roof, implying roofs were sanctified?

items.text: Gemara's question about eating and saying in the upper chamber
items.text_en: Gemara's question about eating and saying in the upper chamber
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the earlier statement means they eat in the upper chamber and say the blessing there, and answers that they eat on the ground and say the blessing in the upper chamber.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the earlier statement means they eat in the upper chamber and say the blessing there.
The Gemara answers that they eat on the ground and say the blessing in the upper chamber.

items.text: Contradiction from the Mishnah about afikoman and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction from the Mishnah about afikoman and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from the Mishnah that one may not conclude after the Paschal lamb with afikoman, and Rav's explanation that one may not move from one group to another. It resolves by distinguishing between during the meal and after the meal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that one may not conclude the Passover meal with אפיקומן (afikoman), and Rav's explanation that this is to prevent people from moving from one group to another.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one case is during the time of eating, the other is not during the time of eating.

items.text: Baraita about the upper chamber of the Holy of Holies and Rav Yosef's objection
items.text_en: Baraita about the upper chamber of the Holy of Holies and Rav Yosef's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Abba Shaul's statement that the upper chamber of the Holy of Holies is more stringent than the Holy of Holies itself, as it is entered less frequently. Rav Yosef objects from the Temple, citing a verse that David gave Solomon the pattern of the upper chambers, implying they were holy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Abba Shaul states that the upper chamber of the Holy of Holies is more stringent than the Holy of Holies itself because it is entered less frequently.
Rav Yosef objects from the Temple, citing a verse that David gave Solomon the pattern of the upper chambers, implying they were holy, and questions how one can sit in the Sanctuary.

items.text: Baraita about chambers built in the sacred area and opened to the non-sacred area
items.text_en: Baraita about chambers built in the sacred area and opened to the non-sacred area
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about chambers built in the sacred area and opened to the non-sacred area: their interior is non-sacred and their roofs are sacred. Rav Chisda explains this refers to when the roofs are level with the floor of the Temple courtyard. The Gemara then raises a contradiction from the second clause about chambers built in the non-sacred area and opened to the sacred area, and resolves with Rabbi Yochanan's distinction between openings to the Temple Mount and openings to the courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about chambers built in the sacred area and opened to the non-sacred area: their interior is non-sacred and their roofs are sacred.
Rav Chisda explains that the baraita refers to when the roofs are level with the floor of the Temple courtyard.

The Gemara objects from the second clause about chambers built in the non-sacred area and opened to the sacred area, which would contradict Rav Chisda's explanation because the roofs would be chambers (מחילות) that Rabbi Yochanan said were not sanctified.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing: Rabbi Yochanan's statement about chambers (מחילות) not being sanctified refers to those opened to the Temple Mount, while the baraita refers to chambers opened to the courtyard.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda about chambers under the Temple
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda about chambers under the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says chambers under the Temple are non-sacred, and explains that this refers to chambers opened to the non-sacred area.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says underground chambers under the Heikhal are non-sacred, and resolves that this applies to chambers opening to the non-sacred area.

items.text: Contradiction about the roof being sacred and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction about the roof being sacred and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that says 'its roof is sacred' and then raises a contradiction from another baraita that says one may not eat most holy offerings or slaughter lesser holy offerings on these roofs. Rav Chama bar Gurya resolves that the roof is sacred only for the two cubits (the area of the Shushan Habirah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that states 'its roof is sacred' as evidence for the sanctity of the roof.
The Gemara objects: how can the roof be sacred, when another baraita explicitly forbids eating most holy offerings and slaughtering lesser holy offerings on these roofs?
Rav Chama bar Gurya resolves the contradiction: the roof is sacred only for the two cubits (the area of the Shushan Habirah).

items.text: Explanation of the two cubits of Shushan Habirah
items.text_en: Explanation of the two cubits of Shushan Habirah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah about the two cubits in Shushan Habirah, one larger and one smaller, used by artisans to avoid misuse of sacred property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah describing the two cubits in Shushan Habirah, one larger and one smaller, with specific measurements relative to Moses' cubit.
The Mishnah explains that one cubit was large and one small so that artisans would take with the small and return with the large, preventing misuse of sacred property (מעילה).
The Mishnah clarifies that two cubits were needed: one for silver and gold, and one for building materials.

items.text: Baraita about windows and the thickness of the wall
items.text_en: Baraita about windows and the thickness of the wall
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that windows and the thickness of the wall are considered inside. It questions how the thickness of the wall can be level with the courtyard floor, and answers that it refers to the outer wall (bar shura), citing a verse and Rabbi Acha or Rabbi Chanina.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita that windows and the thickness of the wall are considered inside, and then questions how the thickness of the wall can be level with the courtyard floor.
The Gemara answers that the thickness of the wall refers to the outer wall (בר שורא), citing a verse and the statement of Rabbi Acha or Rabbi Chanina.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara about two groups eating in one house
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara about two groups eating in one house
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that two groups may eat the Paschal lamb in one house by turning their faces away, with the kettle in the middle. The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as Rabbi Yehuda's opinion, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda derives from verses that the Paschal lamb is eaten in two groups but not in two places, while Rabbi Shimon holds that one may eat in two places.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that two groups may eat the Paschal lamb in one house by turning their faces away, with the kettle in the middle, and describes the attendant's conduct.
The Gemara asks whose opinion the Mishnah follows and answers that it is Rabbi Yehuda's.
A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's derivation from verses that the Paschal lamb is eaten in two groups but not in two places.
The baraita continues with Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about the attendant who ate near the oven and the option for the group to join him.
Rabbi Shimon holds that the verse teaches that the eater may eat in two places.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on eating the paschal lamb in two groups
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on eating the paschal lamb in two groups
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds that the verse 'in one house it shall be eaten' is interpreted by tradition (yesh em la-masoret), while Rabbi Shimon holds that the verse itself is the primary source (yesh em la-mikra). This determines whether the paschal lamb may be eaten in two groups.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the possibility that the paschal lamb might be eaten in two groups, and cites the verse 'in one house it shall be eaten' to reject this.

The Gemara explains the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds that the tradition (yesh em la-masoret) interprets the verse, while Rabbi Shimon holds that the verse itself (yesh em la-mikra) is the primary source.

items.text: Effect of a partition that appears or disappears between diners
items.text_en: Effect of a partition that appears or disappears between diners
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses two cases: if a partition arises between diners, those who allow eating in two groups permit continued eating, while those who forbid it do not. If a partition is removed, those who allow eating in two places permit it, while those who forbid it do not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the first case: a partition arises between diners, and the ruling depends on whether one permits eating in two groups.
The first opinion permits continued eating if the partition arises, while the second opinion forbids it.
The Gemara presents the second case: a partition is removed between diners, and the ruling depends on whether one permits eating in two places.
The first opinion permits continued eating if the partition is removed, while the second opinion forbids it.

items.text: Unresolved question about partition removal and creation
items.text_en: Unresolved question about partition removal and creation
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana was explaining the matter straightforwardly, but Rav Ashi challenged him: should we consider the removal or creation of a partition as equivalent to two places or two groups? The Gemara concludes with 'teiku' (let it stand unresolved).

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana was sitting and explaining the matter straightforwardly, as if it were absolutely clear.
Rav Ashi challenged Rav Kahana: should we raise a dilemma about whether removal or creation of a partition is considered like two places or two groups, or not?
The Gemara concludes with 'תיקו' (let it stand unresolved), indicating that the dilemma remains unanswered.

items.text: Reason the bride turns her face away
items.text_en: Reason the bride turns her face away
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's statement that the bride turns her face away: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that it is because she is embarrassed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the bride turns her face away (as stated in the Mishnah).

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the bride turns her face away because she is embarrassed.

items.text: Story of Rav Huna's conduct at Rav Nachman's house
items.text_en: Story of Rav Huna's conduct at Rav Nachman's house
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Nathan visited Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's house. He was invited to sit, accepted the cup in one go, drank it in two sips, and did not turn his face away. When questioned, he explained each action: he is a man of name, he does whatever the host says except 'leave', one may refuse a small person but not a great one, drinking in one gulp is greedy, two is proper, and the bride turns her face away as taught.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan, visited the house of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, was asked his name, offered a seat, given a cup which he accepted in one gulp and drank in two, and did not turn his face away.
The hosts ask Rav Huna why he calls himself Rav Huna, why he sat when told, and he answers that he is a man of name and that one should do whatever the host says except 'leave'.

The hosts ask why he accepted the cup in one gulp, drank in two, and did not turn his face; Rav Huna answers with the baraita on drinking styles and cites the Mishnah that the bride turns her face away.
Rav Huna explains that one may refuse a small person but not a great person, so he accepted the cup immediately.
Rav Huna cites a baraita that drinking in one gulp is greedy, two is proper, and three is arrogant, explaining why he drank in two sips.
Rav Huna explains that he did not turn his face away because the mishnah teaches that a bride turns her face away, implying that only a bride should do so.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Yishmael's drinking in one gulp
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yishmael's drinking in one gulp
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei visited Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Yosei ben Lakonya. He accepted and drank the cup in one go. When questioned about the rule that drinking in one gulp is greedy, he replied that the rule applies to a small cup, but his cup was small, his wine sweet, and his stomach wide.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Yishmael visited Rabbi Shimon ben Lakonya, accepted and drank a cup in one gulp, and when questioned about the baraita, he explained that it applies to a small cup of sweet wine and a narrow stomach.
The hosts ask Rabbi Yishmael: does the master not hold that one who drinks his cup in one gulp is a glutton?
Rabbi Yishmael answers: they only said that rule regarding a small cup, but my cup was small, my wine sweet, and my stomach wide.

items.text: Rules for entering and leaving a group for the paschal lamb
items.text_en: Rules for entering and leaving a group for the paschal lamb
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says members of a group may enter in threes and leave even one at a time. Rabba adds that this applies when one enters at the usual time and the doorkeeper is aware. Ravina adds that they pay the value of the meat, and the last must add money, but the halakha is not like him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that members of a group may enter the paschal lamb's consumption with three people, but may leave even with one.
Rabbah qualifies that this applies only when entering at the usual time and when the doorkeeper is aware of them.
Ravina adds that they pay the cost of the meat, and the last person must add money, but the halacha does not follow him.
The Gemara rules that the halakha (הלכה) is not like Ravina's opinion.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a woman is in her husband's house and both her husband and father slaughter a Pesach offering for her, she eats from her husband's. If she went to her father's house for the first festival, she eats where she wishes. It also discusses an orphan whose guardians slaughtered for him, a slave of two partners, and a half-slave.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a woman in her husband's house eats from her husband's Pesach offering; if she went to her father's house for the first festival, she eats where she wishes.
The Mishnah adds cases: an orphan eats where he wishes, a slave of two partners eats from neither, and a half-slave does not eat from his master.

items.text: Gemara's question about ברירה
items.text_en: Gemara's question about ברירה
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrase 'where she wishes' that retroactive clarification (ברירה) is valid, but immediately reinterprets 'wishes' to mean at the time of slaughter, not retroactively.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's phrase 'where she wishes' implies that retroactive clarification (ברירה) is valid.
The Gemara reinterprets 'wishes' to refer to the time of slaughter, not retroactive choice.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised from a baraita that says a woman eats from her father's offering on the first festival, but thereafter she may choose. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to a woman who is eager to go (to her father's house), while the baraita refers to one who is not eager.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that says a woman eats from her father's offering on the first festival, but thereafter she may choose between her father's and her husband's.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to a woman who is eager to go to her father's house, while the baraita refers to one who is not eager.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's allegorical interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's allegorical interpretation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'Then I was in his eyes as one who finds peace' as a bride who is complete in her father-in-law's house but eager to go tell her praise in her father's house, and another verse about calling God 'my husband' as a bride in her father-in-law's house, not in her father's house.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse about finding peace as a bride complete in her father-in-law's house, and the verse about calling God 'my husband' as a bride in her father-in-law's house, not her father's house.

items.text: Further allegories by Rabbi Yochanan and Rava
items.text_en: Further allegories by Rabbi Yochanan and Rava
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'A little sister' as Elam, which learned but did not teach. He then interprets 'I am a wall' as Torah and 'my breasts like towers' as Torah scholars. Rava offers an alternative: 'I am a wall' is the congregation of Israel, and 'my breasts like towers' are synagogues and study halls.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'A little sister with no breasts' as referring to Elam, which merited to learn but not to teach.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'I am a wall' as the Torah and 'my breasts like towers' as Torah scholars.
Rava offers an alternative interpretation: 'I am a wall' is the congregation of Israel, and 'my breasts like towers' are synagogues and study halls.

items.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviya's interpretation
items.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya's interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav interprets 'Our sons are like plants' as Israelite youths who never tasted sin, and 'our daughters like corner pillars' as Israelite virgins who open their entrances to their husbands. Both are considered as if the Temple was built in their days.

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav introduces a verse about children and daughters, setting up the interpretation.

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya interprets 'our sons like plants' as Israelite youths who never tasted sin, and 'our daughters like corner pillars' as virgins who open their entrances to their husbands, supporting with additional verses.

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya concludes that both groups are considered by Scripture as if the Temple was built in their days.

items.text: Hosea's prophecy and God's response
items.text_en: Hosea's prophecy and God's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses that four prophets prophesied in the same period, with Hosea being the first among them. God told Hosea that Israel sinned, but Hosea failed to plead for mercy and instead suggested replacing them with another nation. God then commanded Hosea to marry a harlot to teach him a lesson about His love for Israel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse introducing Hosea's prophecy and explains that four prophets prophesied in the same period, with Hosea being the first among them.
God tells Hosea that Israel sinned, but Hosea fails to plead for mercy and instead suggests replacing them with another nation.
God decides to teach Hosea a lesson by commanding him to marry a harlot, demonstrating His own enduring love for Israel.

items.text: Interpretations of Gomer's name
items.text_en: Interpretations of Gomer's name
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents three interpretations of the name 'Gomer' from Hosea 1:3. Samuel says it means sweet in everyone's mouth like a dried fig, Rabbi Yochanan says everyone treads upon her like a dried fig, and another view links it to the word 'dibbah' (evil report).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the first interpretation of the name 'Gomer bat Diblayim' as 'dibbah ra'ah' (evil report).
Samuel interprets 'Diblayim' as meaning sweet in everyone's mouth like a dried fig (דבלה).
Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'Diblayim' as meaning everyone treads upon her like a dried fig.

items.text: Interpretation of 'Gomer' as destruction
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'Gomer' as destruction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda interprets 'Gomer' as referring to the desire to finish off Israel's wealth, while Rabbi Yochanan says they plundered and finished, citing a verse about the king of Aram.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda interprets 'Gomer' as referring to the desire to finish off Israel's wealth in her days.
Rabbi Yochanan says they plundered and finished, citing a verse about the king of Aram destroying them like dust.

items.text: God's rebuke to Hosea and the four acquisitions
items.text_en: God's rebuke to Hosea and the four acquisitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the birth of Hosea's children with symbolic names (Jezreel, Lo-Ruhamah, Lo-Ammi). God rebukes Hosea for not learning from Moses to separate from his wife, comparing Israel to God's precious acquisitions: Torah, heaven and earth, the Temple, and Israel. Hosea's request to replace Israel with another nation is rejected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the biblical verses describing the birth of Hosea's children with symbolic names: Jezreel, Lo-Ruhamah, and Lo-Ammi.
God rebukes Hosea for not learning from Moses to separate from his wife, and Hosea responds that he cannot divorce her because of their children.
God compares Israel to His four precious acquisitions—Torah, heaven and earth, the Temple, and Israel—and rejects Hosea's request to replace them with another nation.

items.text: Prooftexts for the four acquisitions
items.text_en: Prooftexts for the four acquisitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides scriptural proof for each of the four acquisitions: Torah (Proverbs 8:22), heaven and earth (Genesis 14:19), the Temple (Exodus 15:17), and Israel (Exodus 15:16).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites four scriptural verses to prove that Torah, heaven and earth, the Temple, and Israel are each a unique acquisition of God.

items.text: Hosea's repentance and blessing
items.text_en: Hosea's repentance and blessing
items.desc_en: Hosea realizes his sin and prays for mercy. God instructs him to pray for Israel instead, as three decrees were issued because of him. Hosea prays, the decrees are annulled, and he blesses Israel with verses from Hosea 2:1-25.

sub.desc_en: Hosea realizes his sin and stands to pray for mercy for himself.
God instructs Hosea to pray for Israel instead, as three decrees were issued because of him.
Hosea prays, the decrees are annulled, and he blesses Israel with verses from Hosea 2:1-25.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on the burden of prophecy
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on the burden of prophecy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan laments that leadership buries its bearers, noting that every prophet outlasted four kings, citing Isaiah's vision in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan laments that leadership buries its bearers, noting that every prophet outlasted four kings, citing Isaiah's vision in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah.

items.text: Jeroboam ben Joash's merit for rejecting slander
items.text_en: Jeroboam ben Joash's merit for rejecting slander
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Jeroboam ben Joash was counted with the kings of Judah because he did not accept slander against Amos. The Gemara proves this from verses showing he dismissed the report that Amos prophesied his death by the sword.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by asking why Jeroboam ben Joash merited to be counted with the kings of Judah, and answers that it was because he did not accept slander against Amos.
The Gemara proves that Jeroboam was counted with the kings of Judah by citing the verse that lists him alongside the kings of Judah in the superscription of Hosea.
The Gemara proves that Jeroboam did not accept slander by citing the story where Amaziah reported Amos's prophecy against him, and Jeroboam dismissed it, attributing the prophecy to the Shechinah.

items.text: God's mercy in anger and the purpose of exile
items.text_en: God's mercy in anger and the purpose of exile
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yose bar Chanina show that God remembers mercy even in anger, citing verses from Hosea. Rabbi Elazar says Israel was exiled among the nations to increase converts, like sowing a se'ah to bring in many kor. Rabbi Yochanan derives this from 'I will have mercy on Lo-Ruhamah'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that even in God's anger, He remembers mercy, citing the verse 'כִּי לֹא אוֹסִיף עוֹד אֲרַחֵם' (I will no longer have mercy) and Rabbi Yose bar Chanina adds proof from 'כִּי נָשֹׂא אֶשָּׂא לָהֶם' (for I will surely lift them up).
Rabbi Elazar explains that God exiled Israel among the nations only to increase converts, comparing it to sowing a se'ah (סאה) to bring in many kor (כורין).
Rabbi Yochanan derives the same idea from the verse 'וְרִחַמְתִּי אֶת לֹא רֻחָמָה' (I will have mercy on Lo-Ruhamah).

items.text: The lesson from Hosea against slander
items.text_en: The lesson from Hosea against slander
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explains Proverbs 30:10: even in a generation that curses father and mother, one should not slander a servant to his master, as learned from Hosea who did not slander Israel.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, quoting Proverbs 30:10, 'Do not slander a servant to his master, lest he curse you and you be guilty.'
The Gemara questions the juxtaposition: because a generation curses father and mother, should one therefore not slander a servant to his master?
The Gemara resolves: even in a generation that curses father and mother, one should not slander a servant to his master, as learned from Hosea.

items.text: The righteousness of scattering Israel and a debate with a heretic
items.text_en: The righteousness of scattering Israel and a debate with a heretic
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya explains that God did a righteous act by scattering Israel among the nations. A heretic challenges Rabbi Chanina, saying the nations do not destroy Israel despite long exile. Rabbi Oshaya responds that the nations do not know how to destroy them completely, and that they call them a 'severed kingdom'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya opens by interpreting a verse, stating that God performed a righteous act (צדקה) by scattering Israel among the nations.
A heretic challenges Rabbi Chanina, arguing that the nations have not destroyed Israel despite their long exile, citing a verse about a short stay in Edom.
Rabbi Chanina responds by offering to have a student (Rabbi Oshaya) engage with the heretic.
Rabbi Oshaya explains that the nations do not know how to destroy Israel completely, and that they call them a 'severed kingdom' (מלכותא קטיעתא).
The heretic dismisses Rabbi Oshaya's answer with an insult ('Gappa d'Roma'i!'), and the discussion ends.

items.text: Reasons for exile to Babylonia and the return to origin
items.text_en: Reasons for exile to Babylonia and the return to origin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya, Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Chanina, and Rabbi Yochanan give reasons for exile to Babylonia: because Israel cannot bear Roman decrees, because it is deep as Sheol, because its language is close to Torah, and because it is like sending a wife to her mother's house. Rabbi Alexandri notes three things that returned to their origin: Israel, Egyptian silver, and the writing of the tablets.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya explains that God exiled Israel to Babylonia because they could not bear Roman decrees.
Rabbi Elazar gives a second reason: Babylonia is as deep as Sheol, as per the verse.
Rabbi Chanina gives a third reason: Babylonia's language is close to the language of the Torah.
Rabbi Yochanan gives a fourth reason: God sent Israel to Babylonia as a husband sends an angry wife to her mother's house.
Rabbi Alexandri notes three things that returned to their origin: Israel, Egyptian silver, and the writing of the tablets.

items.text: Ulla's reason for exile
items.text_en: Ulla's reason for exile
items.desc_en: Ulla states that Israel was exiled to Babylonia so that they would eat dates and engage in Torah study.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that Israel was exiled to Babylonia so that they would eat dates and engage in Torah study.

items.text: Ulla's story about dates and Torah study
items.text_en: Ulla's story about dates and Torah study
items.desc_en: Ulla visits Pumpedita and is offered dates. He comments on the cheapness of dates and the lack of Torah study among Babylonians. Later, he is pained at night and revises his statement, praising Babylonians for their Torah study despite the high cost of a basket of death.

sub.desc_en: Ulla visits Pumpedita, is offered dates, and comments that Babylonians do not engage in Torah study despite the low price of dates.
Ulla suffers from the dates at night and revises his statement, praising Babylonians for their Torah study despite the high cost of a basket of death.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's explanation of the verse 'to the house of the God of Jacob'
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's explanation of the verse 'to the house of the God of Jacob'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains why the verse says 'the God of Jacob' and not 'the God of Abraham and Isaac'. He explains that Abraham is associated with a mountain, Isaac with a field, but Jacob called it a house, so the Temple is called the house of Jacob.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks why the verse mentions 'the God of Jacob' and not 'the God of Abraham and Isaac'.
Rabbi Elazar explains that Abraham is associated with a mountain, Isaac with a field, but Jacob called the place a house, so the Temple is called the house of Jacob.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on the greatness of the ingathering of the exiles
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on the greatness of the ingathering of the exiles
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the ingathering of the exiles is as great as the day heaven and earth were created, citing a verse from Hosea and comparing it to the creation account.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan declares that the ingathering of the exiles is as great as the day heaven and earth were created, citing a verse from Hosea and comparing it to the creation account.

items.text: Gemara's inference about bereira from the Mishnah of an orphan
items.text_en: Gemara's inference about bereira from the Mishnah of an orphan
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah about an orphan for whom guardians slaughtered a Paschal lamb implies the principle of bereira (retroactive clarification). Rabbi Zeira explains that the verse 'seh labayit' (a lamb for the house) indicates that the lamb is designated for the household from any source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah about an orphan for whom guardians slaughtered a Paschal lamb and infers that this implies the principle of bereira (retroactive clarification).
Rabbi Zeira explains that the verse 'שֶׂה לַבָּיִת' (a lamb for the house) indicates that the lamb is designated for the household from any source, supporting the inference of bereira.

items.text: Baraita on slaughtering for minors and adults
items.text_en: Baraita on slaughtering for minors and adults
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one may slaughter a Paschal lamb on behalf of his minor children and Canaanite slaves whether or not they consent, but for his adult children, Hebrew slaves, and wife, only with their consent. Another baraita adds that if the master slaughtered for them, they fulfill their obligation with the master's lamb, except for a wife who can object.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that one slaughters the Paschal lamb for minors and Canaanite slaves regardless of consent, but for adult children, Hebrew slaves, and wife only with their consent.
A second baraita repeats the rule and adds that if the master slaughtered for them, they fulfill their obligation with the master's lamb, except for a wife who can object.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the exception for a wife
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the exception for a wife
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the exception for a wife applies to any similar case. The Gemara notes an internal contradiction: the first baraita says slaughtering for a wife requires consent, implying that without consent she does not fulfill her obligation, but the second baraita says she can object, implying that if she does not object she does fulfill it. Rava resolves that once they slaughtered, the act itself is the greatest objection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the wife is singled out as an exception in the baraita.
Rava answers that the exception applies to a wife and any similar case.
The Gemara points out an internal contradiction between the two baraitot regarding the wife's consent.
The Gemara suggests that 'from their consent' means only when they explicitly refuse, not that silence is insufficient.
The Gemara objects that the second baraita explicitly says the wife can object, implying that without objection she is included.
Rava resolves that once they slaughtered, the act itself is the greatest objection, so the wife's silence beforehand is irrelevant.

items.text: Contradiction regarding a slave of two partners
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding a slave of two partners
items.desc_en: Rav Eina Sava raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says a slave of two partners may not eat from either's Paschal lamb, but a baraita says he may eat from whichever he chooses. Rav Nachman resolves that the Mishnah refers to partners who are particular with each other, while the baraita refers to those who are not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Eina Sava raises a contradiction between the Mishnah, which says a slave of two partners may not eat from either's Paschal lamb, and a baraita, which says he may eat from whichever he chooses.
Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between partners who are particular with each other (Mishnah) and those who are not (baraita).

items.text: Contradiction regarding a half-slave half-free person
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding a half-slave half-free person
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a half-slave half-free person may not eat from his master's lamb but may eat from his own. A baraita says he may eat from neither. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows the earlier Mishnah (Beit Hillel's view that he works for his master one day and himself the next), while the baraita follows the later Mishnah (Beit Shammai's view).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah permits a half-slave half-free person to eat from his own lamb, but a baraita forbids him from eating from either his own or his master's.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows the earlier Mishnah (Beit Hillel's view that he works alternately for his master and himself), while the baraita follows the later Mishnah (Beit Shammai's view).

items.text: Opening Mishnah context: the half-slave case
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah context: the half-slave case
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous discussion about a half-slave, ruling that the court forces the master to free him for the sake of procreation, and Beit Hillel retracts to follow Beit Shammai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the court forces the master to free a half-slave for the sake of procreation, writing a document for half his value.
The Gemara notes that Beit Hillel retracted to rule like Beit Shammai.

items.text: Mishnah: slave who forgets his master's instruction
items.text_en: Mishnah: slave who forgets his master's instruction
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a slave told to slaughter a Paschal lamb; if he slaughters both a kid and a lamb, he eats from the first. If he forgets, he slaughters both and declares one his own. If the master forgets, both are burned and they are exempt from the second Passover.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a master telling his slave to slaughter a Paschal lamb, and rules that if the slave slaughters a kid or a lamb, he eats from it, and if he slaughters both, he eats from the first.
The Mishnah presents the case where the slave forgets his master's instruction, and prescribes that he slaughters both a lamb and a kid, declaring one as his own and the other as his master's.
The Mishnah concludes with the case where the master himself forgets, ruling that both animals are burned and they are exempt from the second Passover.

items.text: Gemara's first question: why state the obvious?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: why state the obvious?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah states that if the slave slaughters a kid or a lamb he eats, as it is obvious. It then raises a contradiction from a baraita that one cannot be counted on two Paschal lambs simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah states the obvious: if the slave slaughters a kid he eats, even if he is accustomed to a lamb, and vice versa.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's ruling that one eats from the first contradicts a baraita which states that one cannot be counted on two Paschal lambs simultaneously.

items.text: Answer: the case of a king and queen
items.text_en: Answer: the case of a king and queen
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with a king and queen, whose minds are light, so they eat from the first. It then recounts a story of Rabban Gamliel resolving a similar case and a lizard incident, showing the chain of authority.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's case deals with a king and queen, whose minds are light, so they eat from the first.

A baraita is cited recounting a story of a king and queen who sent their servants to slaughter two Passover offerings, and Rabban Gamliel ruled that the king and queen eat from the first, but the servants eat from neither.

The baraita continues with another incident where a lizard was found in the kitchen, and Rabban Gamliel ruled that the kitchen was hot, so a cold cup was poured on the lizard to test it, and he declared the entire meal pure.
The Gemara concludes that the king was dependent on the queen, the queen on Rabban Gamliel, and the entire meal on Rabban Gamliel, demonstrating the chain of authority.

items.text: Difficulty: the slave's declaration 'mine'
items.text_en: Difficulty: the slave's declaration 'mine'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the slave can say 'my lamb' since a slave's acquisitions belong to his master. Abaye resolves that the slave goes to a shepherd his master frequents and acquires one animal on condition that the master has no rights in it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the slave cannot claim 'my lamb' because a slave's acquisitions belong to his master.
Abaye resolves that the slave goes to a shepherd his master frequents and acquires one animal on condition that the master has no rights in it.

items.text: Abaye's distinction: forgetting before or after sprinkling
items.text_en: Abaye's distinction: forgetting before or after sprinkling
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Mishnah's exemption from the second Passover applies only if the master forgot after the blood was sprinkled, when the offering was fit. If before, they are liable. A baraita about mixed blemished offerings is similarly distinguished.

sub.desc_en: Abaye distinguishes the Mishnah's exemption from the second Passover: it applies only if the master forgot after the blood was sprinkled, when the offering was fit for eating; if before, they are liable.

sub.text: Alternative version of Abaye's statement on a baraita
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Abaye's statement on a baraita
sub.desc_en: Some teach Abaye's distinction on a baraita about five people whose Passover offerings' hides were mixed and one had a blemish, all going to the fire and exempt from the second Passover.

sub.text: Abaye's application of the distinction to the baraita
sub.text_en: Abaye's application of the distinction to the baraita
sub.desc_en: Abaye applies the same distinction to the baraita: the exemption applies only if the hides were mixed after the blood was sprinkled; if before, they are liable.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the two versions
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the two versions
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the version teaching the distinction on the Mishnah applies it all the more so to the baraita, while the version teaching it on the baraita does not apply it to the Mishnah, since the Mishnah's offerings were fit and only forgotten, which is known to Heaven.

items.text: Question: how can all be exempt if one is valid?
items.text_en: Question: how can all be exempt if one is valid?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how all five are exempt from the second Passover when one offering was valid. It considers various solutions but concludes it is impossible to resolve without bringing a non-sacred animal into the Temple or eating the Paschal lamb not by its registered members.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how all five are exempt from the second Passover when one of them did not fulfill the obligation because his offering was blemished.
The Gemara answers that it is impossible to resolve the situation properly.
The Gemara objects that if each brings his own offering, four would be bringing non-sacred animals into the Temple.
The Gemara objects that if they all bring one Paschal lamb together, it would be eaten by those not registered for it.
The Gemara objects that if each brings his own and stipulates conditionally, it is impossible to avoid bringing non-sacred animals into the Temple.
The Gemara concludes that it is truly impossible to resolve, so all are exempt from the second Passover.

items.text: Rejection of the priestly portion reason
items.text_en: Rejection of the priestly portion reason
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the earlier suggestion that the reason five cannot join for one Passover is because of the priestly portions (breast and thigh). It argues that each could bring a priest with them, but this leads to problems: if the priest already has his own Passover, the offering might be eaten by non-members; if he does not, it might be a peace-offering. Alternatively, they could bring one priest who has not yet performed his Passover and enroll the five offerings on him, but this is also problematic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the reason five cannot join for one Passover is because of the priestly portions (breast and thigh) that only priests may eat.
The Gemara suggests that each of the five could bring a priest along with them.
The Gemara objects that if the priest already has his own Passover, the offering might be eaten by non-members; if he does not, it might be a peace-offering.
The Gemara suggests that all five could bring one priest who has not yet performed his Passover and enroll the five offerings on him, but this is also problematic.

items.text: Reason: reduction of eating time for peace-offerings
items.text_en: Reason: reduction of eating time for peace-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the real reason is that by joining five people for one Passover, they would reduce the time available for eating peace-offerings (which can be eaten for two days and one night) compared to the Passover (which is only one day and one night).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the real reason is that joining five people for one Passover reduces the time available for eating peace-offerings (שלמים), which can be eaten for two days and one night, compared to the Passover which is only one day and one night.

items.text: Rejection of the eating time reason and proposal of leftover Passover
items.text_en: Rejection of the eating time reason and proposal of leftover Passover
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the eating time reason by proposing that they could bring the leftover of the Passover (a blemished animal) and stipulate: if my animal is blemished, this one is the Passover; if it is unblemished, this one is a peace-offering. However, this is rejected because one does not initially set aside an animal for leftovers, and it would be burdensome.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes bringing leftover Passover (מותר הפסח) with a stipulation: if one's animal is blemished, the leftover becomes the Passover; if unblemished, it becomes a peace-offering, thus solving the eating-time issue.
The Gemara objects that one does not initially set aside an animal for leftovers (מותרות), and it would be burdensome to bring such an animal.

items.text: Reason: semikhah (leaning on the sacrifice)
items.text_en: Reason: semikhah (leaning on the sacrifice)
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the reason is semikhah: the Passover does not require semikhah, but the leftover (which becomes a peace-offering) does require semikhah. However, this is problematic for women's offerings, which do not require semikhah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the reason is semikhah (leaning on the sacrifice): the Passover does not require semikhah, but the leftover (which becomes a peace-offering) does require semikhah.
The Gemara objects that this explanation works for men's offerings, but for women's offerings, which do not require semikhah, what can be said?

items.text: Reasons: blood applications and pouring vs. sprinkling
