items.text_en: Reasons: blood applications and pouring vs. sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers the difference in blood applications (one for Passover, four for peace-offerings) but notes that even one application suffices. Then it considers the difference between pouring (for Passover) and sprinkling (for peace-offerings), but notes that if one sprinkles instead of pouring, it is valid. The Gemara questions whether this distinction applies initially.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the difference between Passover and peace-offerings is due to the number of blood applications: one for Passover, four for peace-offerings.
The Gemara objects that even one application suffices for atonement, citing a Mishnah that all offerings placed on the outer altar with a single application achieve atonement.
The Gemara offers another distinction: Passover is poured (שפיכה) while peace-offerings are sprinkled (זריקה).
The Gemara objects that if one sprinkled instead of pouring, it is valid בדיעבד (after the fact), questioning whether this distinction applies לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

items.text: Mishnah: father promises Passover for first to reach Jerusalem
items.text_en: Mishnah: father promises Passover for first to reach Jerusalem
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a father says he will slaughter the Passover for whichever child first reaches Jerusalem, once the first child enters with his head and most of his body, he acquires his portion and enables his brothers to join. The Gemara infers that this supports the principle of bereirah (retroactive clarification). Rabbi Yochanan explains it is merely to encourage them in mitzvot. The Gemara supports this by noting that the Mishnah says 'enables his brothers with him,' implying they were enrolled from the start, as after slaughter they cannot enroll.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a father who promises to slaughter the פסח (Passover) for whichever child first reaches Jerusalem, and the first child acquires his portion and enables his brothers to join.
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that there is retroactive clarification (ברירה), meaning the child's identity is clarified retroactively.
רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) explains that the father's statement was only to encourage them in מצות (commandments), not to establish retroactive clarification.
The Gemara supports רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) by noting that the Mishnah says 'enables his brothers with him,' implying they were enrolled from the start, as after slaughter they cannot enroll.

items.text: Supporting baraita: daughters were quicker
items.text_en: Supporting baraita: daughters were quicker
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: it once happened that daughters were quicker than sons, and the daughters were found to be zealous and the sons sluggish.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited to support the idea that the father's statement was only to encourage alacrity, as it recounts an incident where daughters were quicker than sons, showing the daughters were zealous and the sons sluggish.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: enrolling and withdrawing from the Passover
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: enrolling and withdrawing from the Passover
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may always enroll on a Passover as long as there is an olive's bulk per person, and one may withdraw until slaughter. Rabbi Shimon says until the blood is sprinkled. The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that even if one group enrolled, another group may enroll. Abaye explains the dispute: for withdrawing, the Sages derive from 'from being a lamb' (while alive), and Rabbi Shimon from 'from its existence' (until the blood is sprinkled). For enrolling, all agree it is only until slaughter, based on the verse 'by the number of souls' and then 'you shall count.' A baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for enrolling and withdrawing from the Passover lamb: one may enroll as long as there is an olive's bulk per person, and withdraw until slaughter; Rabbi Shimon says until the blood is sprinkled.
The Gemara asks what novel point the Mishnah teaches, and answers that even if one group has already enrolled, another group may still enroll.

Abaye explains the dispute: for withdrawing, the Sages derive from 'מִהְיוֹת מִשֶּׂה' (from being a lamb, i.e., while alive) and Rabbi Shimon from 'מֵהֲוָיָיתֵיהּ דְּשֶׂה' (from its existence, i.e., until the blood is sprinkled); for enrolling, all agree it is only until slaughter, based on the verse 'בְּמִכְסַת נְפָשֹׁת' (by the number of souls) and then 'תָּכֹסּוּ' (you shall count).
A baraita supports Abaye's explanation, stating that one may enroll until slaughter and withdraw until slaughter, but Rabbi Shimon says withdraw until the blood is sprinkled.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one appoints another to share his portion of the Paschal lamb, the group may give him his portion, and he eats his own while they eat theirs.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that if one appoints another to share his portion of the Paschal lamb, the group may give him his portion and each eats separately.

items.text: Gemara's first question
items.text_en: Gemara's first question
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one member of the group has a large appetite (literally 'hands are good'), can the others say 'take your portion and leave'? Is it because they accepted him, or can they claim they only accepted him for the sake of the sacrifice, not for him to eat more?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if one member of a group has a larger appetite, can the others tell him to take his portion and leave, or can he claim they accepted him as is?

items.text: First attempted proof and rejection
items.text_en: First attempted proof and rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that they cannot force him out, but rejects this: the case of appointing another is different because the appointee is like an outsider, and the group can say they do not want a stranger among them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that one cannot be forced out, arguing that the case of appointing another is analogous to having skilled hands.
The Gemara rejects the proof, distinguishing the case because the appointee is a stranger whom the group can reject, unlike a member with skilled hands.

items.text: Second attempted proof and rejection
items.text_en: Second attempted proof and rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from a baraita about a servant eating by the oven: if the group wants, they can do him a favor and eat with him, implying they can refuse. But this is rejected: they accepted him only to serve them, not for them to serve him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a servant eating by the oven, where the group may choose to do him a favor and eat with him, implying they can refuse, and asks why they cannot be told 'you accepted him'.
The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the servant was accepted only to serve them, not for them to serve him.

items.text: Third proof and resolution
items.text_en: Third proof and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita explicitly states that if one member has a large appetite, the group may tell him to take his portion and leave, and even in a case of a mere association (like a bundle of grain), they can force him out. The Gemara concludes that this resolves the question.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that explicitly rules that members of a group may tell a member with a large appetite to take his portion and leave, and even in a case of a mere association (sibolet) they may do so, concluding that this resolves the dilemma.

The Gemara explains the baraita's phrasing: the expression 'and not only' means that the ruling applies a fortiori — if it applies to a Paschal lamb, where the group can claim they accepted him only for the preparation of the offering, it certainly applies to a mere association (sibolet), which is just for companionship.

items.text: Alternative version of the question
items.text_en: Alternative version of the question
items.desc_en: Some say the question was different: whether the group may divide the lamb among themselves. A baraita proves that if one has a large appetite they can force him out, but if not, they cannot, implying they may not divide arbitrarily.

sub.desc_en: Some say the previous question was not the real dilemma; rather, the real question is whether members of a group are permitted to divide the lamb among themselves or not.
The Gemara brings a baraita: if one has a large appetite they can force him out, but if not, they cannot, implying they may not divide arbitrarily; the Gemara concludes that this is the ruling.

items.text: Story of Rav Pappa and Rav Huna
items.text_en: Story of Rav Pappa and Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua shared bread; Rav Pappa ate four loaves for each one of Rav Huna. Rav Huna demanded a division, and Rav Pappa said 'you accepted'. Rav Huna brought all the previous objections, and Rav Pappa answered as before. Later, Rav Huna partnered with Ravina, who ate eight to his one, leading to a quip.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua shared bread, with Rav Pappa eating four loaves for each one of Rav Huna.
Rav Huna demanded a division of the bread, and Rav Pappa responded that Rav Huna had accepted the arrangement.
Rav Huna raised all the previous objections from the sugya, and Rav Pappa answered each as before.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's objection from the baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's objection from the baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna cited the baraita about partners in a group, and Rav Pappa distinguished it by saying the group accepted him only for the sake of the sacrifice.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's objection from the sheaf
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's objection from the sheaf
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna cited the baraita about the sheaf, and Rav Pappa was forced to divide with him.
Rav Huna later partnered with Ravina, who ate eight loaves to his one, leading to Rav Huna's quip that he prefers a hundred Rav Pappas over one Ravina.

items.text: Baraita on appointing others and selling offerings
items.text_en: Baraita on appointing others and selling offerings
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if one appoints others for his Paschal lamb or festive offering, the money in his hand is non-sacred. If one sells his burnt offering or peace offerings, he has done nothing, and any money falls to the Temple treasury as a donation. Rava explains this is a penalty. Ulla or Rabbi Oshaya questions how consecration can take effect on consecration.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches: one who appoints others for his Paschal lamb or festive offering — the money in his hand is non-sacred; one who sells his burnt offering or peace offerings — he has done nothing, and any money falls to the Temple treasury as a donation.
The Gemara questions: since the sale is void, why should the money fall to the Temple treasury?
Rava explains that this is a penalty (קנס) imposed by the rabbis, even on the extra money beyond the animal's value.

Ulla (or Rabbi Oshaya) asks: how can consecration take effect on consecration — one person set aside a lamb for his Paschal lamb, another set aside money for his Paschal lamb, yet the baraita says the money is non-sacred?

items.text: Abaye's initial analysis and rejection of Rabbi Oshaya's interpretation
items.text_en: Abaye's initial analysis and rejection of Rabbi Oshaya's interpretation
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that without Rabbi Oshaya's interpretation, he would have understood the Mishnah as referring to קדשים קלים according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, but not to Pesach. He argues that one does not leave over money from Pesach, but does leave over from other funds. He then notes that Rabbi Oshaya's interpretation is necessary because the Mishnah cannot be explained according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that without Rabbi Oshaya's interpretation, he would have explained the Mishnah as referring to קדשים קלים (lesser sanctities) according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who holds that such offerings are the owner's property.
Abaye argues that regarding Pesach one does not leave over money, but regarding other funds one certainly does, since from the outset one designates them with that intention.
Abaye concludes that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and therefore the leftover money is חולין (non-sacred), because one does not leave over from Pesach but does leave over from money.
Abaye explains that he would not have interpreted the Mishnah as Rabbi Oshaya did, because regarding Pesach one does not leave over, but regarding money one does.
Abaye cites a baraita that the Mishnah cannot be explained according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, because it states that one who sells his burnt offering or peace offerings has done nothing.

items.text: Conclusion that Rabbi holds one may leave over money from Pesach
items.text_en: Conclusion that Rabbi holds one may leave over money from Pesach
items.desc_en: Abaye concludes that since Rabbi Oshaya established the Mishnah as referring to one who designates a harlot for his Pesach and follows Rabbi, it follows that Rabbi holds one may leave over money even from his Pesach.

sub.desc_en: Abaye concludes that since Rabbi Oshaya established the Mishnah as referring to one who designates a harlot for his Pesach and follows Rabbi, it follows that Rabbi holds one may leave over money even from his Pesach.

items.text: Rabbi Oshaya's baraita and his interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya's baraita and his interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita of Rabbi Oshaya regarding the prohibition of a harlot's hire for consecrated animals. It presents a kal vachomer argument that would have applied the prohibition to consecrated animals, but the Torah excludes it with the word 'neder'. Rabbi Oshaya explains that the case involves one who designates a harlot for his Pesach, and it follows Rabbi's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Oshaya's baraita, which rules that consecrated animals given as a harlot's hire are permitted, but non-consecrated birds are forbidden, and derives this from the verse 'to every vow'.
The baraita presents a kal vachomer argument that would apply the prohibition to consecrated animals, but the Torah excludes it with the word 'neder'.
The Gemara objects: without the verse, one would think the prohibition applies to consecrated animals, but a person cannot prohibit what is not his own.
Rabbi Oshaya resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves one who designates a harlot for his Pesach, and it follows Rabbi's opinion.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi and Sages on leftover consecrated money
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi and Sages on leftover consecrated money
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between Rabbi and the Sages regarding the verse 'if the house be too little for a lamb'. The Sages say one may only use leftover money for the lamb itself, while Rabbi says one may use it for other needs, including a cloak or a talit. The Gemara presents two versions of the dispute: one about wood for roasting, and another about matzah and maror.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi's position is, citing a baraita that interprets the verse 'if the house be too little for a lamb' as limiting the use of leftover money to the lamb's needs, not for purchase.

Rabbi argues that leftover money may also be used for purchase, including appointing another partner for the paschal offering and its festive offering, with the money becoming חולין (non-sacred) because that was the original intent of the Israelites.

sub.text: Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira's first version
sub.text_en: Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira's first version
sub.desc_en: One of them (Rabbah or Rabbi Zeira) states that all agree leftover money may be used for wood for roasting, as it is integral to the paschal offering; the dispute is only about matzah and maror.

sub.text: Sages' position on matzah and maror
sub.text_en: Sages' position on matzah and maror
sub.desc_en: The Sages hold that matzah and maror are a separate consumption, not part of the paschal offering itself, while Rabbi considers them essential preparation and thus equivalent to the offering.

sub.text: Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira's second version
sub.text_en: Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira's second version
sub.desc_en: The other of them states that all agree matzah and maror are permitted, citing the verse 'עַל מַצּוֹת וּמְרֹרִים יֹאכְלֻהוּ'; the dispute is about purchasing a cloak or talit, where the Sages limit to the lamb's needs and Rabbi allows self-sustenance from the lamb.

items.text: Abaye's difficulty with the explicit Mishnah
items.text_en: Abaye's difficulty with the explicit Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty against Abaye: the Mishnah explicitly states that Israelites consecrated their Paschal lambs on the condition that leftover money is חולין. Abaye resolves this by explaining that the Mishnah refers to the money of the Paschal lamb, not the lamb itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty against Abaye: the Mishnah explicitly states that Israelites consecrated their Paschal lambs on the condition that leftover money is חולין, contradicting Abaye's view that one does not stipulate regarding the lamb itself.
Abaye resolves the difficulty by explaining that the Mishnah refers to the money of the Paschal lamb (מעות פסחיהן), not the lamb itself, so the stipulation applies only to the funds, not the animal.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on slaughtering for a zav or zava
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on slaughtering for a zav or zava
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a zav who saw two emissions may have the Paschal lamb slaughtered for him on the seventh day, while one who saw three on the eighth. A shomeret yom keneged yom may have it slaughtered on the second day, and a zava on the eighth. The Gemara cites Rav Yehudah who says that we may slaughter and sprinkle for a tevul yom and a mechusar kippurim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the rule for a zav (זב) who saw two or three emissions: slaughter for him on the seventh or eighth day respectively.
The Mishnah continues with the rule for a shomeret yom keneged yom (שומרת יום כנגד יום): slaughter for her on the second day, or on the third if she saw two days.
The Mishnah concludes with the rule for a zava (זבה): slaughter for her on the eighth day.
The Gemara cites Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav, stating that we may slaughter and sprinkle for a tevul yom (טבול יום) and a mechusar kippurim (מחוסר כפורים).

items.text: Opening dispute between Rav and Ulla
items.text_en: Opening dispute between Rav and Ulla
items.desc_en: Rav prohibits slaughtering and sprinkling for one impure from a sheretz, while Ulla permits it. This sets up the central question of the daf.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that one may not slaughter the Pesach offering nor sprinkle its blood on behalf of someone impure from a sheretz (carcass of a creeping creature).
Ulla disputes Rav, permitting slaughter and sprinkling even for one impure from a sheretz.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rav's position
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rav's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav's distinction between a tevul yom (who is permitted because he will be pure at night) and one impure from a sheretz (who also will be pure at night after immersion). The Gemara resolves that the latter lacks immersion, but then compares to a mechusar kapparah who lacks atonement. The Gemara answers that a mechusar kapparah is different if his offering is already with the court, as per Rav Shmaya's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rav: why distinguish between a tevul yom (טבול יום) and one impure from a sheretz (טמא שרץ), since both will be pure at nightfall?
The Gemara answers that the sheretz-impure person lacks immersion (טבילה), while the tevul yom lacks only sunset, which happens automatically.
The Gemara objects: a mechusar kapparah (מחוסר כפרה) also lacks atonement, yet Rav permits slaughter for him if his offering is in hand.
The Gemara rejects: the sheretz-impure person might neglect to immerse, unlike the mechusar kapparah whose offering is already deposited.
The Gemara invokes Rav Shmaya's principle that the court ensures offerings are brought promptly, so the mechusar kapparah is reliable.

items.text: Alternative explanation: Rav's ruling is rabbinic
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Rav's ruling is rabbinic
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav's prohibition might be rabbinic, but then argues that even biblically one impure from a sheretz is not fit, citing the verse about impurity from a corpse and Rabbi Yitzchak's interpretation that the paschal lamb was deferred for those who were impure from a corpse on the seventh day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rav's prohibition might be only rabbinic, since biblically the person impure from a sheretz is fit.

The Gemara rejects this, arguing that even biblically the person is not fit, citing the verse about impurity from a corpse and inferring that the paschal lamb is deferred for those impure on the seventh day.
The Gemara raises an objection: how do we know that the verse refers to impurity from a sheretz?
The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Rabbi Yitzchak's interpretation that those impure from a corpse on the seventh day were deferred, and the same logic applies to impurity from a sheretz.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah about a zav
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah about a zav
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that one may slaughter for a zav on the seventh day, implying it is permitted for one impure from a sheretz. The Gemara rejects this, explaining that the zav immersed, and the case teaches that even though he lacks sunset, sunset automatically occurs. The Gemara then analyzes the case of a zav who saw three emissions, concluding that the Mishnah's necessity is to teach that even a mechusar kapparah is eligible, relying on Rav Shmaya's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah about a zav who saw two emissions, suggesting that slaughtering for him on the seventh day proves that one may slaughter for one impure from a sheretz.
The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the zav had already immersed, and the Mishnah merely teaches that even though he lacks sunset, sunset automatically occurs.
The Gemara supports this interpretation by analyzing the Mishnah's second clause about a zav who saw three emissions, concluding that the case of two emissions must involve immersion.
The Gemara objects that if the zav did not immerse, the case of three emissions would be superfluous, and concludes that the zav must have immersed.

The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the zav did not immerse, but the Mishnah is necessary to teach that even a mechusar kapparah (one lacking atonement) is eligible, relying on Rav Shmaya's principle that the court ensures the offering.

items.text: Discussion of zavah
items.text_en: Discussion of zavah
items.desc_en: A tanna taught before Rav Adda bar Ahava that one may slaughter for a zavah on her seventh day. Rav Adda bar Ahava corrects this to the eighth day, because even according to Ulla, a zavah requires atonement. The Gemara notes that this is obvious but teaches Rav Shmaya's principle.

sub.text: Tanna's teaching before Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.text_en: Tanna's teaching before Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rav Adda bar Ahava that one may slaughter for a zavah on her seventh day.

Rav Adda bar Ahava objects that a zavah on her seventh day is not fit for slaughter, since even according to Ulla's leniency for a טמא שרץ (one impure from a creeping thing), she requires atonement which is not yet available.
Rav Adda bar Ahava emends the teaching to say that one slaughters for a zavah on the eighth day, after she has brought her atonement offering.
The Gemara asks why this correction is necessary, as it seems obvious that a zavah cannot be slaughtered on the seventh day.

The Gemara explains that the teaching is necessary to counter a possible assumption that a zavah lacking atonement is unfit, and it teaches the principle of Rav Shmaya that the court ensures the offering is brought.

items.text: Discussion of niddah
items.text_en: Discussion of niddah
items.desc_en: Ravina taught that one may slaughter for a niddah on the seventh day. The Gemara corrects this to the eighth day, because a niddah immerses at night and requires sunset. The Gemara explains that this teaches that a niddah immerses at night, unlike other impurities, as derived from the verse.

sub.desc_en: Ravina taught that a baraita states one may slaughter the Paschal lamb for a niddah on her seventh day.
Rav Adda bar Ahava objects that a niddah is not fit on the seventh day because she immerses at nightfall of the seventh and still needs sunset on the eighth.
Rav Adda bar Ahava corrects the baraita to read 'on the eighth day' instead of the seventh.
The Gemara asks: is this not obvious? If a zavah who needs atonement (כפרה) is slaughtered for on the eighth, a niddah who needs no atonement certainly is.
The Gemara answers: the baraita is needed to teach that a niddah may be slaughtered for only on the eighth, not the seventh, because her immersion is at night, as taught in a baraita.
A baraita derives from the verse 'שבעת ימים תהיה בנדתה' that a niddah must be in her impurity all seven days, immersing only at night, and a yoledet is analogized to a niddah.

items.text: Beginning of the next Mishnah
items.text_en: Beginning of the next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins discussing the onen (one whose close relative died and is not yet buried).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins discussing the onen (one whose close relative died and is not yet buried).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Conditions for slaughtering on behalf of others
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Conditions for slaughtering on behalf of others
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those for whom the Paschal lamb may be slaughtered (e.g., one clearing a mound, a prisoner promised release, a sick or elderly person who can eat an olive's bulk). It rules that for all these, the lamb is not slaughtered for them alone, lest it become invalid; if it becomes invalid, they are exempt from the second Passover, except for the one clearing a mound who was impure from the start.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those for whom the Paschal lamb may be slaughtered and rules that for all of them the lamb is not slaughtered alone, except the mound clearer who was impure from the start.

items.text: Gemara: Distinction between Jewish and gentile prisons
items.text_en: Gemara: Distinction between Jewish and gentile prisons
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Huna citing Rabbi Yochanan limits the Mishnah's leniency to gentile prisons; for Jewish prisons, since the promise is reliable (based on the verse 'the remnant of Israel will not do wrong'), the lamb may be slaughtered for him alone. Rav Chisda adds that even in a gentile prison, if it is within the wall of Beit Pagei, the lamb may be slaughtered for him alone, as he might be brought the meat.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Huna citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Huna citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Huna citing Rabbi Yochanan limits the Mishnah's leniency to gentile prisons, but for Jewish prisons the lamb may be slaughtered for him alone because the promise is reliable based on the verse 'the remnant of Israel will not do wrong'.
Rav Chisda adds that even in a gentile prison, if it is within the wall of Beit Pagei, the lamb may be slaughtered for him alone because he might be brought the meat.

items.text: Gemara: Distinction between round and long mounds
items.text_en: Gemara: Distinction between round and long mounds
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes between a round mound (where impurity is certain) and a long mound (where one can assume he was pure at slaughter). A baraita supports this with Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's ruling: one clearing a mound is sometimes exempt, sometimes liable—round mound with impurity underneath makes him liable, long mound makes him exempt.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes between a round mound (where impurity is certain, making him liable for second Pesaḥ) and a long mound (where one can assume he was pure at slaughter, exempting him).

A baraita supports this with Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's ruling: one clearing a mound is sometimes exempt, sometimes liable—round mound with impurity underneath makes him liable, long mound makes him exempt.

items.text: Mishnah: Slaughtering for an individual and group composition
items.text_en: Mishnah: Slaughtering for an individual and group composition
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Paschal lamb is not slaughtered for an individual according to Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Yosei permits it. Even a group of one hundred who cannot eat an olive's bulk may not have a lamb slaughtered for them. Additionally, one may not form a group of women, slaves, or minors alone.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei regarding slaughtering the Paschal lamb for an individual.
The Mishnah adds that even a group of one hundred who cannot eat an olive's bulk may not have a lamb slaughtered for them.
The Mishnah concludes that one may not form a group of women, slaves, or minors alone.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural sources for individual slaughter and Rabbi Shimon's derivation
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural sources for individual slaughter and Rabbi Shimon's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'You cannot slaughter the Passover in one of your gates' that it is not slaughtered for an individual; Rabbi Yosei holds that an individual who can eat it may have it slaughtered. Rabbi Yosei uses the verse for Rabbi Shimon's teaching about slaughtering at a private altar during the prohibition of high places. Rabbi Yehuda learns two things from the verse. The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei's interpretation is consistent, and he answers that 'each according to his eating' supports his view.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse 'לֹא תוּכַל לִזְבֹּחַ אֶת הַפָּסַח בְּאַחַד' that the Paschal lamb is not slaughtered for an individual, while Rabbi Yosei permits it for an individual who can eat it.
The Gemara asks: since Rabbi Yosei does not use the word 'בְּאַחַד' (in one) to prohibit individual slaughter, what does he do with that word?

The Gemara answers: Rabbi Yosei uses the word for Rabbi Shimon's teaching, which derives from the verse that one who slaughters the Paschal lamb at a private altar during the prohibition of high places violates a negative commandment, but not during the permitted period.
The Gemara asks: from where does Rabbi Yehuda derive Rabbi Shimon's teaching, since he uses the word 'בְּאַחַד' for the prohibition of individual slaughter?
The Gemara answers: Rabbi Yehuda learns two things from the verse — both the prohibition of individual slaughter and Rabbi Shimon's teaching.
The Gemara objects: how does Rabbi Yosei know that Rabbi Shimon's derivation is correct? Perhaps Rabbi Shimon actually agrees with Rabbi Yehuda's interpretation of the verse.

The Gemara resolves: it cannot enter your mind that Rabbi Shimon agrees with Rabbi Yehuda, because the verse 'אִישׁ לְפִי אׇכְלוֹ' (each according to his eating) supports Rabbi Yosei's view that an individual who can eat may slaughter.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction from women's status and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction from women's status and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ukva bar Chinana from Parshishna challenges Rava: Rabbi Yehuda says no slaughter for an individual, yet a baraita says for a woman in the first Passover, it is slaughtered for her alone according to Rabbi Yehuda. Rava resolves by reinterpreting 'for herself' as 'for themselves' (i.e., with others). Rav Ukva objects that a group of only women is not allowed, citing the Mishnah. Rava explains the Mishnah means women with slaves and minors, not women alone.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ukva bar Chinana challenges Rava by citing a contradiction: Rabbi Yehuda says no slaughter for an individual, yet a baraita says for a woman in the first Passover, it is slaughtered for her alone according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rava resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting 'for herself' (בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָהּ) as 'for themselves' (בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָן), meaning the woman slaughters with others.
Rav Ukva objects that a group consisting entirely of women is not allowed, citing the Mishnah that one does not form a group of women, slaves, or minors alone.

Rava explains that the Mishnah means women with slaves and minors, not women alone, and provides reasons: women with slaves due to promiscuity (תִּפְלוּת), and minors with slaves due to the minor's inability to eat.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about women and the Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about women and the Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three opinions: Rabbi Yehuda says a woman may slaughter for herself on the first Pesach but is secondary on the second; Rabbi Yosei says she may slaughter for herself on the second, and certainly on the first; Rabbi Shimon says she is secondary on the first and cannot slaughter at all on the second.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Yehuda's opinion: a woman may slaughter the Paschal lamb for herself on the first Pesach, but on the second she is secondary to others.
Rabbi Yosei states that a woman may slaughter for herself on the second Pesach, and certainly on the first.
Rabbi Shimon rules that a woman is secondary to others on the first Pesach, and on the second she cannot slaughter at all.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse "by number of souls" that women are included in the first Pesach, but from "that man shall bear his sin" that women are excluded from the second Pesach. However, the verse "according to all the statute of the Pesach" allows them to be secondary on the second.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what underlies the dispute, and explains that Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse 'בְּמִכְסַת נְפָשֹׁת' (by the count of souls) that women are included in the obligation on the first Pesach.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda limits the second Pesach to men only, based on the verse 'חֶטְאוֹ יִשָּׂא הָאִישׁ הַהוּא' (that man shall bear his sin), excluding women from obligation.

sub.text: Gemara's answer — Rabbi Yehuda's secondary status
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer — Rabbi Yehuda's secondary status
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'כְּכָל חֻקַּת הַפֶּסַח' (according to all the statute of the Pesach) that a woman can still be secondary on the second Pesach.
Rabbi Yehuda applies the verse 'כְּכׇל חֻקַּת הַפֶּסַח' (according to all the statute of the Pesach) to allow women to be secondary (טְפִילָה) on the second Pesach.

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi Yosei's reasoning
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi Yosei's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei derives from "by number of souls" that women are included in the first Pesach, and from "that soul shall be cut off" that women are included in the second. The verse "that man shall bear his sin" excludes a minor from karet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei derives from 'בְּמִכְסַת נְפָשֹׁת' on the first Pesach and 'וְנִכְרְתָה הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַהִוא' (that soul shall be cut off) on the second that women are fully obligated on both.

sub.text: Gemara's answer — Rabbi Yosei's exclusion of minors
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer — Rabbi Yosei's exclusion of minors
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei interprets 'חֶטְאוֹ יִשָּׂא הָאִישׁ הַהוּא' to exclude a minor from the punishment of כרת (spiritual excision), not to exclude women.

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon derives from "man" in the first Pesach that women are excluded, but "by number of souls" allows them to be secondary. For the second Pesach, "that man shall bear his sin" excludes women even from being secondary, since if they are exempt from obligation, they are certainly exempt from being secondary.

sub.text: Gemara's answer — Rabbi Shimon's reasoning on first Pesach
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer — Rabbi Shimon's reasoning on first Pesach
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon derives from 'אִישׁ' (a man) on the first Pesach that women are excluded from obligation, but 'בְּמִכְסַת נְפָשֹׁת' allows them to be secondary.

sub.text: Gemara's answer — Rabbi Shimon's reasoning on second Pesach
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer — Rabbi Shimon's reasoning on second Pesach
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon excludes women even from secondary status on the second Pesach, based on 'חֶטְאוֹ יִשָּׂא הָאִישׁ' (that man shall bear his sin).
The Gemara resolves that since women are exempt from obligation in the first Pesach, the exclusion in the second Pesach must apply to being secondary (טפילה).

items.text: Clarification of which verse 'man' refers to for Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Clarification of which verse 'man' refers to for Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which verse Rabbi Shimon uses for 'man'. It cannot be from the verse about taking a lamb, as that teaches that an adult acquires for the group, not a minor. It must be from 'according to a man's eating', which also teaches that the Paschal lamb is slaughtered for an individual. The Gemara concludes that the verse teaches both lessons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which verse Rabbi Shimon uses for 'איש', and rejects the possibility that it is from 'ויקחו להם איש שה לבית אבות' because that verse is needed for Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching that an adult acquires for the group, not a minor.

The Gemara suggests that the verse might be 'מאיש לפי אכלו', but notes that Rabbi Yosei holds like Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Shimon holds like Rabbi Yosei, and that verse is needed to teach that the Paschal lamb is slaughtered for an individual.

The Gemara resolves that since the Torah could have written 'לפי אכלו' but instead wrote 'איש', the extra word teaches both lessons: that the Paschal lamb is slaughtered for an individual and that an adult acquires for the group, not a minor.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's statement about women and the Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's statement about women and the Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says that a woman's obligation on the first Pesach is a duty and on the second is optional, but both override Shabbat. The Gemara clarifies that the second is optional, and this aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion Rabbi Elazar's statement follows: a woman on the first Pesach is obligated and on the second is optional, and it overrides Shabbat.
The Gemara objects: if the second Pesach is optional, why does it override Shabbat? It then corrects the statement to say the first is obligatory and the second optional.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Elazar's ruling aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.

items.text: Rule about a group of converts for the Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Rule about a group of converts for the Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov quoting Rabbi Yochanan states that one should not form a group entirely of converts for the Paschal lamb, lest they be overly meticulous and cause it to become invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that one should not form a group entirely of converts, lest they be overly meticulous and cause the Paschal lamb to become invalid.

items.text: Dispute about obligations for matzah and maror after the first night
items.text_en: Dispute about obligations for matzah and maror after the first night
items.desc_en: A baraisa states that Pesach, matzah, and maror are obligatory on the first night and optional thereafter, but Rabbi Shimon says Pesach is obligatory for men and optional for women. The Gemara questions this, citing Rabbi Elazar that women are obligated in matzah by Torah law. The Gemara resolves that the baraisa refers only to Pesach, not matzah and maror.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa states that Pesach, matzah, and maror are obligatory on the first night and optional thereafter, but Rabbi Shimon says they are obligatory for men and optional for women.
The Gemara asks which part of the baraisa Rabbi Shimon's statement refers to, noting that Pesach is not eaten all seven days, so it must refer to matzah and maror.

The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon cannot hold that matzah is optional for women, citing Rabbi Elazar's principle that women are obligated in eating matzah by Torah law because they are included in the prohibition against eating חמץ (leaven).
The Gemara resolves that the baraisa's dispute applies only to Pesach, not to matzah and maror, so Rabbi Shimon's statement refers solely to the Pesach offering.

items.text: Mishnah: An onen immerses and eats his Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Mishnah: An onen immerses and eats his Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins a new topic: an onen (one in acute mourning) immerses and eats his Paschal lamb in the evening, but not other sacrifices. It also mentions one who hears about his deceased relative.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins: an onen (one in acute mourning) immerses and eats his Paschal lamb in the evening, but not other sacrifices; also one who hears about his deceased relative.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who gathers bones for his deceased relative may immerse and eat sacred offerings. It then presents a dispute: Beit Shammai says a convert who converts on Passover eve may immerse and eat his Paschal lamb that evening, while Beit Hillel says one who separates from foreskin is like one who separates from a grave.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that one who gathers bones for his deceased relative may immerse and eat sacred offerings.

The Mishnah presents the dispute: Beit Shammai says a convert who converts on Passover eve may immerse and eat his Paschal lamb that evening, while Beit Hillel says one who separates from foreskin is like one who separates from a grave.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the reason for the Mishnah's ruling? It explains that the principle is that nighttime mourning (aninut) is a rabbinic decree, and regarding the Paschal lamb, the rabbis did not uphold their decree in the face of karet, but regarding other sacred offerings, they did uphold their decree in the face of a positive commandment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind the Mishnah's ruling.

The Gemara explains that nighttime mourning (אנינות) is a rabbinic decree; regarding the Paschal lamb the rabbis did not uphold their decree in the face of karet, but regarding other sacred offerings they upheld it in the face of a positive commandment.

items.text: Clarification on gathering bones
items.text_en: Clarification on gathering bones
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement about gathering bones: does it not require sprinkling on the third and seventh days? It resolves that the Mishnah refers to bones that were already gathered for him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can discuss gathering bones without requiring sprinkling on the third and seventh days.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to bones that were already gathered for him, not to the act of gathering.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: The dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is specifically regarding an uncircumcised gentile. Beit Hillel decrees lest he become impure the following year and mistakenly think he can immerse again, not realizing that as a gentile he was not susceptible to impurity. Beit Shammai does not make such a decree. But regarding an uncircumcised Israelite, all agree he immerses and eats his Paschal lamb that evening, and we do not decree about an uncircumcised Israelite because of an uncircumcised gentile.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is specifically regarding an uncircumcised gentile.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan explaining Beit Hillel's reasoning
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan explaining Beit Hillel's reasoning
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Beit Hillel decrees lest the convert become impure the following year and mistakenly think he can immerse again, not realizing that as a gentile he was not susceptible to impurity.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan explaining Beit Shammai's reasoning and the consensus
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan explaining Beit Shammai's reasoning and the consensus
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Beit Shammai does not make such a decree, and that regarding an uncircumcised Israelite all agree he immerses and eats his Paschal lamb that evening, without decreeing due to an uncircumcised gentile.

items.text: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.desc_en: A baraita supports this: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not disagree about an uncircumcised Israelite, who immerses and eats his Paschal lamb that evening. They only disagreed about an uncircumcised gentile, with Beit Shammai permitting and Beit Hillel prohibiting.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: A baraita supports the previous distinction: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel only disagreed about an uncircumcised gentile, not an uncircumcised Israelite.

items.text: Rava's principle and examples
items.text_en: Rava's principle and examples
items.desc_en: Rava states a principle: For an uncircumcised person, sprinkling, and a scalpel, the rabbis upheld their decrees in the face of karet. For an onen, a leper, and a beit hapras, they did not uphold their decrees. The Gemara then explains each case: the uncircumcised person is as stated; sprinkling is a rabbinic prohibition that does not override Shabbat; the scalpel is not brought even through private domains; the onen is as stated; the leper is illustrated by a baraita where a leper whose eighth day falls on Passover eve and who has a seminal emission immerses and eats; and beit hapras is referenced from a Mishnah where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree.

sub.desc_en: Rava states a principle: for an uncircumcised person, sprinkling, and a scalpel, the rabbis upheld their decrees in the face of karet; for an onen, a leper, and a beit hapras, they did not.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the uncircumcised case
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the uncircumcised case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the case of the uncircumcised person is as already stated in the earlier discussion.
The Gemara cites the principle that sprinkling is a rabbinic prohibition (שבות) and does not override Shabbat.
The Gemara cites a baraita that just as one may not bring the scalpel through a public domain, one may not bring it through roofs, courtyards, or enclosures.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the onen case
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the onen case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the case of the onen is as already stated in the earlier discussion.
The Gemara cites a baraita: a leper whose eighth day (of purification) falls on Passover eve and who had a seminal emission immerses and eats the Passover offering.

The Sages explain that although a טבול יום (one who immersed but awaits sunset) normally may not enter the Temple, this leper enters because the positive commandment with karet overrides the positive commandment without karet.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that by Torah law, even a positive commandment is not involved, citing a verse about the new courtyard where they innovated that a טבול יום may not enter the Levite camp.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree regarding beit hapras (a field with a plowed-over grave).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that we inspect for those who perform the Pesach but do not inspect for those who eat terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that we inspect for those who perform the Pesach but do not inspect for those who eat terumah.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of inspection
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of inspection
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains what inspection means: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that one sifts a beit hapras and proceeds, while Rav Yehuda bar Avyei said in the name of Rav Yehuda that a beit hapras that was trodden is pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the inspection mentioned in the Mishnah entails.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that one sifts a beit hapras (a field with a buried corpse) and proceeds.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda bar Avyei in the name of Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda bar Avyei in the name of Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Avyei in the name of Rav Yehuda gives an alternative answer: a beit hapras that was trodden is pure.

items.text: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter with the phrase 'Hadran alach ha'ishah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter with the standard concluding phrase 'הדרן עלך האשה' (we return to you, the chapter of 'The Woman').

items.text: New Mishnah: Pesach Sheni
items.text_en: New Mishnah: Pesach Sheni
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one who was impure or on a distant journey and did not perform the first Pesach performs the second; one who was negligent or forced performs the second; the difference is that the former are exempt from karet while the latter are liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who was impure or on a distant journey and did not perform the first Pesach performs the second; one who was negligent or forced also performs the second, but the former are exempt from karet while the latter are liable.

items.text: Dispute: distant journey and sacrifice offered on his behalf
items.text_en: Dispute: distant journey and sacrifice offered on his behalf
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: if one was on a distant journey and others slaughtered and sprinkled the blood for him, Rav Nachman says it is accepted, while Rav Sheshet says it is not accepted. Rav Nachman explains that the Merciful One merely exempted him, but if he did it, blessing comes upon him; Rav Sheshet says the Merciful One pushed him aside like an impure person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: if one was on a distant journey and others slaughtered and sprinkled the blood for him, Rav Nachman says it is accepted, while Rav Sheshet says it is not accepted.
Rav Nachman explains that the Merciful One merely exempted him, but if he performed it, blessing comes upon him.
Rav Sheshet argues that the Merciful One pushed him aside like an impure person, so the sacrifice is not accepted.

items.text: Rav Nachman's proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites the Mishnah: one who was impure or on a distant journey and did not perform the first performs the second, implying that if he wanted, he could have performed the first.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites the Mishnah to prove that one who was impure or on a distant journey could have performed the first Pesach if he wanted.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects: if so, the Mishnah's case of one who was negligent or forced also implies he could have done it, but that is not true. Rather, the Mishnah includes a willful sinner alongside them; similarly, here it includes an onen alongside them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects: if the Mishnah's first clause implies one could have done it, then the second clause about one who was negligent or forced would also imply he could have done it, which is absurd.
Rav Sheshet resolves: rather, the Mishnah includes a willful sinner alongside the negligent and forced; similarly, here it includes an onen alongside the tamei and distant traveler.

items.text: Rav Ashi's support for Rav Sheshet
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's support for Rav Sheshet
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says the Mishnah itself is precise: it says 'these are exempt from karet and these are liable to karet.' On whom? If on the negligent and forced, they are liable to karet? Rather, it must be on the willful sinner and the onen.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that the Mishnah's precise wording supports Rav Sheshet: the distinction between 'exempt from karet' and 'liable to karet' must refer to the willful sinner and the onen, not the negligent and forced.

items.text: Rav Nachman's response to Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's response to Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that the Mishnah refers only to the willful sinner, and the plural 'liable' is because the first clause used 'exempt' in plural.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman responds that the Mishnah's 'liable' refers only to the willful sinner, and the plural form is merely because the first clause used 'exempt' in plural.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's proof from a baraita
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's proof from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita where Rabbi Akiva says: it is stated 'impure' and it is stated 'distant journey'...

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet introduces his proof by citing a baraita.
Rabbi Akiva states that the Torah uses both the term 'טָמֵא' (impure) and 'בְּדֶרֶךְ רְחוֹקָה' (distant journey) in the context of the Pesach sacrifice.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rav Nachman's position
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rav Nachman's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Nachman's view that a person on a distant journey is like a tamei met (impure from a corpse) by drawing an analogy from a tamei sheretz (impure from a creeping creature). Rav Nachman responds that Rabbi Akiva holds that one does not slaughter or sprinkle the blood for a tamei sheretz, but he himself follows the opinion that one does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman by drawing an analogy: just as a tamei met (impure from a corpse) has the ability to purify but does not, so too a person on a distant journey has the ability to come but does not, so why should the latter be exempt?

Rav Nachman responds that Rabbi Akiva holds that one does not slaughter or sprinkle the blood for a tamei sheretz (impure from a creeping creature), but he himself follows the opinion that one does, so the analogy fails.

items.text: Baraita listing those who observe the second Passover
items.text_en: Baraita listing those who observe the second Passover
items.desc_en: A baraita lists those who observe the second Passover: zavim, zavot, metzoraim, metzoraot, niddot, those who engage in relations with niddot, women who gave birth, those who were unaware, forced, or intentional, and the tamei and one on a distant journey. The Gemara questions why 'tamei' is mentioned, since such a person would not be allowed to offer the first Passover, and explains that 'distant journey' is stated to exempt one from karet, according to the opinion that the second Passover is a rectification.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists those who observe the second Passover, including various impure individuals, those who were unaware, forced, or intentional, and the tamei and one on a distant journey.
The Gemara questions why 'tamei' is mentioned in the baraita, since such a person would not be allowed to offer the first Passover anyway.
The Gemara explains that 'distant journey' is stated to exempt one from karet, according to the opinion that the second Passover is a rectification.

items.text: Question about women's obligation in the second Passover
items.text_en: Question about women's obligation in the second Passover
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a woman is obligated in the second Passover, citing a baraita that only a tamei nefesh (impure from a corpse) and one on a distant journey are obligated, while zavim, metzoraim, and those who engage in relations with niddot are derived from 'ish ish'. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the first baraita to Rabbi Yosei and the second to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a woman is obligated in the second Passover, citing a baraita that only a tamei nefesh (impure from a corpse) and one on a distant journey are obligated, while zavim, metzoraim, and those who engage in relations with niddot are derived from 'איש איש' (each man).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the first baraita to Rabbi Yosei and the second to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Dispute about karet for the first and second Passover
items.text_en: Dispute about karet for the first and second Passover
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi says one is liable to karet for neglecting the first and the second; Rabbi Natan says liable for the first but exempt for the second; Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya says one is not liable for the first unless one also neglected the second.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi's position: one is liable to karet for neglecting the first Passover and also for neglecting the second.
Rabbi Natan states that one is liable to karet for the first but exempt for the second.
Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya holds that one is not liable to karet for the first unless one also neglected the second.

items.text: Explanation of the dispute through a baraita on a convert or minor
items.text_en: Explanation of the dispute through a baraita on a convert or minor
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the three Tannaim follow their reasoning in a baraita about a convert who converts between two Passovers or a minor who reaches majority between them: Rabbi says they are obligated in the second; Rabbi Natan says only one obligated in the first is obligated in the second; Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya holds the second is a rectification of the first. They all derive their views from the same verse, with Rabbi focusing on 'v'chadal la'asot haPesach' and 'Korban Hashem lo hikriv b'mo'ado' to include the second. The Gemara then questions whether 'chet'o yisa' implies karet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara announces that the three Tannaim in the dispute about karet follow their own reasoning from a baraita.

The Gemara cites a baraita about a convert who converts between two Passovers or a minor who reaches majority between them: Rabbi says they are obligated in the second; Rabbi Natan says only one obligated in the first is obligated in the second.
The Gemara asks what is the underlying principle of their dispute.
Rabbi holds that the second Pesach is an independent festival (רגל בפני עצמו), so one who was exempt from the first is obligated in the second.
Rabbi Natan holds that the second Pesach is a make-up (תשלומין) for the first, so one who was not obligated in the first cannot make it up.
Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya holds that the second Pesach is a rectification (תקנתא) of the first, so one who did not perform the first is only liable if he also neglects the second.

The Gemara explains that all three Tannaim derive their views from the same verse, with Rabbi focusing on 'וְחָדַל לַעֲשׂוֹת הַפֶּסַח' and 'קׇרְבַּן ה׳ לֹא הִקְרִיב בְּמוֹעֲדוֹ' to include the second.
The Gemara questions whether the phrase 'חֶטְאוֹ יִשָּׂא' (his sin shall be borne) implies karet.

items.text: Debate on the source of karet for neglecting the Pesach
items.text_en: Debate on the source of karet for neglecting the Pesach
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the positions of Rabbi, Rabbi Natan, and Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya regarding the derivation of karet for one who fails to bring the Pesach. Rabbi derives it from the blasphemer, Rabbi Natan from the phrase 'for he did not bring the offering of the Lord in its appointed time' referring to the first Pesach, and Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya applies that phrase to the second Pesach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi equates the blasphemer with one who curses God, and derives karet for neglecting the Pesach through a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) on the word 'חטאו' (his sin).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Natan's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Natan's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Natan interprets the verse 'כי קרבן ה׳ לא הקריב במועדו' (for he did not bring the offering of the Lord in its appointed time) as referring to the first Pesach, and uses the word 'חטאו' to derive karet for the blasphemer.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya applies the verse 'כי קרבן ה׳ לא הקריב במועדו' to the second Pesach, and handles the word 'חטאו' as previously stated.

The Gemara summarizes the halachic conclusions: one who intentionally neglects both Pesachs is liable by all opinions; one who errs in both is exempt; and the rulings for mixed cases depend on which sage's position is followed.

items.text: Practical ruling on intentional and unintentional neglect
items.text_en: Practical ruling on intentional and unintentional neglect
items.desc_en: The Gemara summarizes the halakhic conclusions based on the three opinions: if one intentionally neglected both Pesachs, all agree he is liable; if he unintentionally neglected both, all agree he is exempt. Disputes arise when one is intentional and the other unintentional, with each opinion yielding different results.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakhic conclusion: if one intentionally neglected both Pesachs, all agree he is liable; if he unintentionally neglected both, all agree he is exempt.
The Gemara rules that if one intentionally neglected the first Pesach and unintentionally neglected the second, Rabbi and Rabbi Natan hold him liable, while Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya exempts him.
The Gemara rules that if one unintentionally neglected the first Pesach and intentionally neglected the second, Rabbi holds him liable, while Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya exempt him.

items.text: Mishnah: Definition of 'distant journey'
items.text_en: Mishnah: Definition of 'distant journey'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer regarding the definition of 'distant journey' (derech rechoka) that exempts one from the Pesach. Rabbi Yosei notes a dotted 'heh' in the verse to indicate that the distance is not absolute but relative to the Temple courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines 'distant road' (דרך רחוקה) according to Rabbi Akiva as beyond Modi'im, and according to Rabbi Eliezer as beyond the Temple courtyard threshold, with Rabbi Yosei noting a dotted letter hei to indicate the distance is not absolute.
Rabbi Eliezer defines the distant journey as from the threshold of the Temple courtyard and outward.
Rabbi Yosei notes that a dot is placed on the 'heh' in the verse to indicate that the distance is not absolute but relative to the Temple courtyard.

items.text: Gemara: Ulla's calculation of the distance
items.text_en: Gemara: Ulla's calculation of the distance
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that Modi'im is 15 mil from Jerusalem, based on the calculation that a person walks 10 parsaot (40 mil) in a day. He supports this with a tradition from Rabbi Yochanan about the times of day. The Gemara then derives the 5 mil from dawn to sunrise from the verse about Lot's arrival in Zoar.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that the distance from Modi'im to Jerusalem is 15 mil, and supports this with Rabba bar bar Chana's tradition from Rabbi Yochanan about a person's daily walking distance of 10 parsaot (40 mil), broken into segments of 5 mil each.
The Gemara notes that Ulla's calculation aligns with his own definition of 'distant way' as any place from which one cannot enter the Temple at the time of slaughter.
The Gemara derives the 5 mil from dawn to sunrise from the verse about Lot's arrival in Zoar, citing Rabbi Chanina's testimony that the distance was 5 mil.

items.text: Dispute between Ulla and Rav Yehuda on 'distant journey'
items.text_en: Dispute between Ulla and Rav Yehuda on 'distant journey'
items.desc_en: Ulla defines 'distant journey' as one who cannot enter at the time of slaughter, while Rav Yehuda defines it as one who cannot enter at the time of eating. Rabba challenges both with the case of one impure from a creeping animal: Ulla's view is contradicted because such a person cannot enter at slaughter time yet the Pesach is offered for him, and Rav Yehuda's view is contradicted because such a person can enter at eating time yet the Pesach is not offered for him. Ulla resolves that 'distant journey' applies only to a pure person, not an impure one.

sub.desc_en: Ulla defines 'distant journey' as one who cannot enter the Temple at the time of slaughter.
Rav Yehuda defines 'distant journey' as one who cannot enter at the time of eating the Pesach offering.
Rabba challenges Ulla: his definition is contradicted by the case of one impure from a creeping animal, who cannot enter at slaughter time yet the Pesach is offered for him.
Rabba challenges Rav Yehuda: his definition is contradicted by the case of one impure from a creeping animal, who can enter at eating time yet the Pesach is not offered for him.
Ulla resolves the objections by clarifying that 'distant journey' applies only to a pure person, not an impure one.

items.text: Resolution of Rav Yehuda's difficulty
items.text_en: Resolution of Rav Yehuda's difficulty
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a potential difficulty for Rav Yehuda regarding a person who becomes impure from a creeping thing, whose seventh day of impurity falls on Passover eve, and who is still required to bring the Paschal lamb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rav Yehuda's difficulty by citing the verse about one impure from a corpse, showing that even if the seventh day falls on Passover eve, the Torah still requires the Paschal lamb to be deferred.

items.text: Baraita on being on the way
items.text_en: Baraita on being on the way
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one standing outside Modi'im who could enter with horses and mules is exempt because he was on the way, while one standing inside Modi'im who cannot enter due to camels and wagons is liable because he was not on the way.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that one standing outside Modi'im who could enter with horses and mules is exempt because he was on the way.
The baraita teaches that one standing inside Modi'im who cannot enter due to camels and wagons is liable because he was not on the way.

items.text: Rava's statement on the world's dimensions
items.text_en: Rava's statement on the world's dimensions
items.desc_en: Rava states that the world is 6,000 parasangs and the firmament's thickness is 1,000 parasangs, citing a tradition and reasoning. He supports this with Rabbi Yochanan's calculation that a person walks 10 parasangs per day, making the firmament's thickness one-sixth of a day's journey.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the world is 6,000 parasangs and the firmament's thickness is 1,000 parasangs, based on both tradition and reasoning.

sub.text: Rava's reasoning via Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rava's reasoning via Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rava supports his calculation with Rabbi Yochanan's tradition that an average person walks 10 parasangs per day, making the firmament's thickness one-sixth of a day's journey.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Yehuda's calculation
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Yehuda's calculation
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised from Rabbi Yehuda, who calculates the firmament's thickness as one-tenth of a day's journey, based on different travel times. This contradicts Rava and Ulla, and the Gemara declares it a refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from Rabbi Yehuda, who calculates the firmament's thickness as one-tenth of a day's journey based on different travel times, contradicting Rava and Ulla.
The Gemara declares that this is a refutation of both Rava and Ulla.

items.text: Defense of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina
items.text_en: Defense of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether Rabbi Yochanan is also refuted, but explains that he spoke of daytime only, and the rabbis erred in their calculation. It then considers Rabbi Chanina, but deflects by noting the case of the spies who hurried, which is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yochanan's position is also refuted by the baraita.

sub.text: Gemara's answer in defense of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer in defense of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara deflects the refutation by explaining that Rabbi Yochanan spoke only about daytime, and the rabbis erred in their calculation of dawn and dusk.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Chanina's position is also refuted.

sub.text: Gemara's answer in defense of Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer in defense of Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: The Gemara deflects the refutation by noting that the case of the spies who hurried (וַיָּאִיצוּ) is different from normal travel.

items.text: Tradition on the size of Egypt and Gehinnom
items.text_en: Tradition on the size of Egypt and Gehinnom
items.desc_en: A tradition is cited that Egypt was 400 parasangs, one-sixtieth of Kush, which is one-sixtieth of the world, which is one-sixtieth of the Garden, which is one-sixtieth of Eden, which is one-sixtieth of Gehinnom, making the whole world like a pot lid for Gehinnom. This is presented as a refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a tradition that Egypt was 400 parasangs, one-sixtieth of Kush, which is one-sixtieth of the world, which is one-sixtieth of the Garden, which is one-sixtieth of Eden, which is one-sixtieth of Gehinnom, making the whole world like a pot lid for Gehinnom, and presents this as a refutation.

items.text: Rabbi Natan on the inhabited world under one star
items.text_en: Rabbi Natan on the inhabited world under one star
items.desc_en: Rabbi Natan teaches that the entire inhabited world sits under one star, as evidenced by a person walking in any direction and the star remaining opposite him. This is presented as a refutation.

sub.text: Baraita of the school of Elijah
sub.text_en: Baraita of the school of Elijah
sub.desc_en: A baraita from the school of Elijah cites Rabbi Natan's teaching that the entire inhabited world sits under one star, proven by a star remaining opposite a person in all directions, presented as a refutation.

items.text: Astronomical tradition on the inhabited world
items.text_en: Astronomical tradition on the inhabited world
items.desc_en: A tradition states that the Wagon is in the north, the Scorpion in the south, and the entire inhabited world sits between them, receiving sunlight only one hour a day. This is supported by the position of the sun at different hours, and presented as a refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a tradition that the Wagon constellation is in the north, the Scorpion in the south, and the entire inhabited world sits between them, receiving sunlight only one hour a day.

The Gemara provides a supporting proof: at the fifth hour the sun is in the east, at the seventh in the west, and at half past six it stands directly overhead, concluding that this refutes the earlier position.

items.text: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai on the Bat Kol's response
items.text_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai on the Bat Kol's response
items.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai relates that a Bat Kol responded to the wicked one who said 'I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, I will be like the Most High', calling him a wicked son of a wicked man.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a statement of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai as a supporting source.

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai relates that a Bat Kol responded to the wicked one who said 'I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, I will be like the Most High', calling him a wicked son of a wicked man.

items.text: Opening aggadic statement and refutation
items.text_en: Opening aggadic statement and refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita describing the dimensions of the cosmos: the distance from earth to the firmament is a 500-year journey, the thickness of the firmament is 500 years, and similarly between each firmament. It concludes with a refutation (teyuvta) based on the verse 'But you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about Nimrod's grandson and the lifespan of man, citing the verse 'The days of our years are seventy years, and if by strength, eighty years.'
The baraita describes the cosmic dimensions: the distance from earth to the firmament is a 500-year journey, the firmament's thickness is 500 years, and similarly between each firmament.
The Gemara refutes the baraita's claim by citing the verse 'But you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit,' implying a contradiction.

items.text: Debate on the celestial sphere and zodiac
items.text_en: Debate on the celestial sphere and zodiac
items.desc_en: The Tannaim teach: Jewish sages say the celestial sphere is fixed and the constellations revolve; gentile sages say the sphere revolves and the constellations are fixed. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi offers a proof: we never find the Wagon (Ursa Major) in the south nor Scorpio in the north. Rav Acha bar Yaakov challenges this, suggesting the sphere might move like a millstone or a door hinge.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Jewish sages hold that the celestial sphere (גלגל) is fixed and the constellations (מזלות) revolve, while gentile sages hold the opposite.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi offers a proof for the Jewish sages' view: we never find the Wagon (Ursa Major) in the south nor Scorpio in the north, implying the constellations revolve around a fixed sphere.

Rav Acha bar Yaakov challenges Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's proof, suggesting the sphere might move like a millstone (בוצינא דריחיא) or a door hinge (צינורא דדשא), which would also keep the constellations in fixed positions relative to each other.

items.text: Debate on the sun's path at night
items.text_en: Debate on the sun's path at night
items.desc_en: Jewish sages say the sun travels below the firmament by day and above the firmament by night; gentile sages say it travels below the firmament by day and below the earth by night. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi comments that the gentile view seems more plausible because springs are cool by day and hot at night.

sub.desc_en: The Jewish sages state their view that the sun travels below the firmament by day and above the firmament by night.
The gentile sages present their opposing view that the sun travels below the firmament by day and below the earth by night.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi comments that the gentile view appears more plausible because springs are cool by day and hot at night.

items.text: Rabbi Natan's explanation of seasonal sun paths
items.text_en: Rabbi Natan's explanation of seasonal sun paths
items.desc_en: A baraita of Rabbi Natan explains: in summer the sun travels in the height of the firmament, so the world is hot and springs are cool; in winter the sun travels at the bottom of the firmament, so the world is cool and springs are hot.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Natan explains the sun's seasonal path: in summer it travels high in the firmament, making the world hot and springs cool; in winter it travels low, making the world cool and springs hot.

items.text: The sun's four seasonal paths
items.text_en: The sun's four seasonal paths
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the sun's path in four seasons: in Nisan, Iyar, Sivan it travels in the mountains to melt snow; in Tammuz, Av, Elul it travels in settled areas to ripen fruit; in Tishrei, Marcheshvan, Kislev it travels in the seas to dry rivers; in Tevet, Shevat, Adar it travels in the desert to avoid drying seeds.

sub.desc_en: A baraita describes the sun's four seasonal paths: in Nisan-Iyar-Sivan it travels in the mountains to melt snow; in Tammuz-Av-Elul in settled areas to ripen fruit; in Tishrei-Marḥeshvan-Kislev in the seas to dry rivers; in Tevet-Shevat-Adar in the desert to avoid drying seeds.

items.text: Transition to halakha: definition of 'derekh reḥokah'
items.text_en: Transition to halakha: definition of 'derekh reḥokah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins discussing the halakha of a person who becomes impure on a distant path (derekh reḥokah) regarding the Paschal lamb. It cites Rabbi Eliezer's view that an uncircumcised Jew is liable to karet. Abaye explains that 'distant path' applies to a pure person but not to an impure person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Eliezer's view that an uncircumcised Jew who fails to bring the Paschal lamb is liable to karet, and raises the question of whether he could have entered the Temple to offer it.
Abaye resolves the difficulty by distinguishing that the halakha of 'distant path' (דרך רחוקה) applies only to a pure person, not to an impure person, so the uncircumcised Jew is not exempted by it.

items.text: Dispute on the definition of 'derekh reḥokah'
items.text_en: Dispute on the definition of 'derekh reḥokah'
items.desc_en: Rava says the dispute is between Tannaim: Rabbi Eliezer compares 'distant place' in Pesach to that in Ma'aser, defining it as outside the place of eating; Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Eliezer defines it as outside the place of preparation. The Gemara then notes that Rabbi Yitzchak bar Rav Yosef's ruling follows Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda. Finally, Rabbi Yosei HaGelili explains that 'derekh' means from the threshold of the Temple courtyard outward.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by asserting that the dispute about 'derekh reḥokah' is between Tannaim.
