A baraita is cited: Rabbi Eliezer compares 'distant place' in Pesach to that in Ma'aser, defining it as outside the place of eating.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda cites Rabbi Eliezer's alternative definition: 'derekh reḥokah' means outside the place of preparation.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yitzchak bar Rav Yosef's ruling follows Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's position in the name of Rabbi Eliezer.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili explains that 'derekh' means from the threshold of the Temple courtyard outward.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the differences between the first and second Pesach: the first prohibits chametz under 'bal yera'eh' and 'bal yimatzei', while the second allows chametz and matzah together in the house; the first requires Hallel at its eating, the second does not; both require Hallel at their preparation, are eaten roasted with matzah and bitter herbs, and override Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates the differences between the first and second Pesach offerings regarding chametz, Hallel, and shared requirements.

items.text: First Baraita: Derivation of bodily commandments
items.text_en: First Baraita: Derivation of bodily commandments
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that interprets "כְּכׇל חוּקַּת הַפֶּסַח יַעֲשׂוּ אוֹתוֹ" as referring only to commandments that apply to the body of the offering. It derives this from the verse "עַל מַצּוֹת וּמְרוֹרִים יֹאכְלוּהוּ" and limits it further with "וְעֶצֶם לֹא יִשְׁבְּרוּ בוֹ" to exclude non-bodily commandments.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'כְּכׇל חוּקַּת הַפֶּסַח יַעֲשׂוּ אוֹתוֹ' and states that it speaks only of commandments that apply to the body of the offering.
The baraita derives that bodily commandments include eating matzah and maror, and limits the scope by a verbal analogy from 'וְעֶצֶם לֹא יִשְׁבְּרוּ בוֹ' to exclude non-bodily commandments.

items.text: Isi ben Yehuda's view and Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: Isi ben Yehuda's view and Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: Isi ben Yehuda agrees that the verse refers to bodily commandments. The Gemara questions the baraita's logic: if the verse already specifies bodily commandments, why mention "עֶצֶם"? It explains that the baraita initially thought "יַעֲשׂוּ אוֹתוֹ" was precise, but after "עַל מַצּוֹת וּמְרוֹרִים" it becomes a general principle that might include all commandments, so "עֶצֶם" limits it.

sub.desc_en: Isi ben Yehuda states that the verse 'יַעֲשׂוּ אוֹתוֹ' (they shall do it) refers to bodily commandments.
The Gemara questions the baraita's logic: if the verse already specifies bodily commandments, why mention 'עֶצֶם' (bone) as a limiting factor?

The Gemara explains that the baraita initially thought 'יַעֲשׂוּ אוֹתוֹ' was precise, but after 'עַל מַצּוֹת וּמְרוֹרִים' (on matzot and bitter herbs) it becomes a general principle that might include all commandments, so 'עֶצֶם' (bone) limits it.

items.text: Isi ben Yehuda and the Rabbis on the extra verses
items.text_en: Isi ben Yehuda and the Rabbis on the extra verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how Isi ben Yehuda uses the word "עֶצֶם" to include bones with and without marrow, and how the Rabbis use "יַעֲשׂוּ אֹתוֹ" to teach that the Pesach is not slaughtered for an individual, but rather we try to include as many as possible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Isi ben Yehuda interprets the word 'עֶצֶם' (bone) in the verse, and explains that he uses it to include both bones with marrow and bones without marrow.

The Gemara asks how the Rabbis interpret the phrase 'יַעֲשׂוּ אֹתוֹ' (they shall do it), and explains that it teaches that the Pesach is not slaughtered for an individual, but rather we try to include as many as possible.

items.text: Second Baraita: Derivation of all commandments for the second Pesach
items.text_en: Second Baraita: Derivation of all commandments for the second Pesach
items.desc_en: Another baraita derives that the second Pesach includes all commandments of the first: it excludes 'bal yera'eh' and 'bal yimatzei' via "עַל מַצּוֹת וּמְרוֹרִים", includes positive commandments via "לֹא יַשְׁאִירוּ", and includes negative commandments (both those that are broken to a positive and absolute ones) via "וְעֶצֶם לֹא יִשְׁבְּרוּ בוֹ", using a general principle from the specifics.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse "כְּכׇל חוּקַּת הַפֶּסַח יַעֲשׂוּ אוֹתוֹ" and immediately limits it: the verse speaks only of commandments that apply to the body of the Pesach offering, excluding the prohibitions of "בַּל יֵרָאֶה" and "בַּל יִמָּצֵא" (leaven not being seen or found), as derived from "עַל מַצּוֹת וּמְרוֹרִים יֹאכְלוּהוּ".

The baraita then derives that positive commandments (מצות עשה) are included for the second Pesach from the verse "לֹא יַשְׁאִירוּ מִמֶּנּוּ עַד בֹּקֶר" (they shall not leave any of it until morning), which is a negative commandment that is broken to a positive one.

The baraita further derives that absolute negative commandments (לא תעשה גמור) are included from the verse "וְעֶצֶם לֹא יִשְׁבְּרוּ בוֹ" (and they shall not break a bone in it), using a general principle (כלל ופרט) from the specifics of the three cited verses: a positive commandment, a negative commandment broken to a positive, and an absolute negative commandment.

items.text: Analysis of the general and specific clauses
items.text_en: Analysis of the general and specific clauses
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the baraita's general and specific clauses: from "מַצּוֹת וּמְרוֹרִים" it includes roasting over fire and excludes removing leaven; from "לֹא יַשְׁאִירוּ" it includes "לֹא תוֹצִיא" (similar in being invalidated by remaining/going out) and excludes "לֹא יֵרָאֶה" (similar in being a negative commandment broken to a positive). In both cases, the bodily commandment is preferred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the general clause 'מַצּוֹת וּמְרוֹרִים' (matzot and bitter herbs) includes.
The Gemara answers that it includes roasting over fire (צְלִי אֵשׁ).
The Gemara asks what the specific clause excludes.
The Gemara answers that it excludes the removal of leaven (הַשְׁבָּתַת שְׂאוֹר).
The Gemara objects that one could reverse the inclusion and exclusion.
The Gemara resolves that a bodily commandment (מִצְוָה דְגוּפֵיהּ) is preferred, so the inclusion of roasting over fire (a bodily act) and exclusion of removing leaven (not bodily) is correct.
The Gemara asks what the general clause 'לֹא יַשְׁאִירוּ' (do not leave over) includes.
The Gemara answers that it includes the prohibition 'לֹא תוֹצִיא' (do not take out), which is similar in being invalidated by remaining or going out.
The Gemara asks what the specific clause excludes.
The Gemara answers that it excludes the prohibitions 'לֹא יֵרָאֶה' and 'לֹא יִמָּצֵא' (do not see or find leaven), which are similar in being a negative commandment broken to a positive.
The Gemara objects that one could reverse the inclusion and exclusion.
The Gemara resolves that a bodily commandment (מִצְוָה דְגוּפֵיהּ) is preferred, so the inclusion of 'לֹא תוֹצִיא' (a bodily prohibition) and exclusion of 'לֹא יֵרָאֶה' (not bodily) is correct.

items.text: Incomplete analysis of the third clause
items.text_en: Incomplete analysis of the third clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to analyze the general clause of "עֶצֶם לֹא יִשְׁבְּרוּ בוֹ" but the text is cut off, indicating the discussion continues.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to analyze the general clause of 'עֶצֶם לֹא יִשְׁבְּרוּ בוֹ' (a bone shall not be broken in it), but the text is cut off, indicating the discussion continues.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's derivation
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's derivation of the prohibition of eating the Pesach raw or boiled, and the exclusion of the prohibition of slaughtering on chametz. It suggests reversing the derivations but concludes that the mitzvah of the body (the Pesach itself) is preferable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's general and particular clauses include and exclude, noting the derivation of the prohibition of eating the Pesach raw or boiled and the exclusion of slaughtering on chametz.
The Gemara considers reversing the derivations but concludes that the mitzvah of the body (the Pesach itself) is preferable.

items.text: Source for Hallel on the first Pesach
items.text_en: Source for Hallel on the first Pesach
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak derives from a verse that the night sanctified for the festival (the first night of Pesach) requires Hallel, while a night not sanctified (the second Pesach) does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the first Pesach requires Hallel when eaten.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a verse to show that only a night sanctified for the festival requires Hallel, not an ordinary night.

items.text: Reason for Hallel on both Pesachs during their performance
items.text_en: Reason for Hallel on both Pesachs during their performance
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both the first and second Pesach require Hallel during their performance (slaughter and offering). Two answers are given: the verse only excludes the night, not the day; and it is inconceivable that Israel would slaughter their Pesachs and take their lulavs without saying Hallel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason why both the first and second Pesach require Hallel when performed.
The Gemara offers one explanation: the verse excludes only the night, not the day, so the day requires Hallel.
The Gemara offers another explanation: it is impossible that Israelites slaughter their Pesach offerings and take their lulavs without reciting Hallel.

items.text: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda on Pesach overriding Shabbat and impurity
items.text_en: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda on Pesach overriding Shabbat and impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Pesach is eaten roasted, and it overrides Shabbat but not impurity. The Gemara notes this is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, who holds it also overrides impurity. The Tanna Kamma argues that since impurity pushed it off, it should not be done in impurity; Rabbi Yehuda argues that the Torah sought to have it done in purity, but if one did not merit, it is done in impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Pesach is eaten roasted, and it overrides Shabbat but not impurity.
The Gemara notes that this Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that Pesach also overrides impurity.
A baraita is cited: the Pesach overrides Shabbat but not impurity; Rabbi Yehuda says it also overrides impurity.
The Gemara asks the reasoning of the Tanna Kamma: since impurity pushed it off, should it be done in impurity?
Rabbi Yehuda argues that the Torah sought to have the Pesach done in purity, but if one did not merit, it is done in impurity.

items.text: Baraita on first and second Pesach regarding Shabbat, impurity, and lodging
items.text_en: Baraita on first and second Pesach regarding Shabbat, impurity, and lodging
items.desc_en: A baraita states that both the first and second Pesach override Shabbat and impurity, and require lodging (linah). The Gemara identifies the view on impurity as Rabbi Yehuda, but then questions whether Rabbi Yehuda requires lodging, citing a baraita where he exempts the second Pesach from lodging. The Gemara resolves that there are two tannaitic opinions in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that both the first and second Pesach override Shabbat and impurity, and require lodging (לִינָה).
The Gemara asks whose view the baraita follows regarding impurity overriding, and answers that it follows Rabbi Yehuda.

The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda himself exempts the second Pesach from lodging, citing a baraita where he derives this from the verse 'וּפָנִיתָ בַבֹּקֶר' and the principle that only what is eaten for six days requires lodging.
The Gemara resolves that there are two tannaitic opinions in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Mishnah: Impure individuals eating from a Pesach brought in impurity
items.text_en: Mishnah: Impure individuals eating from a Pesach brought in impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that zavim, zavot, niddot, and yoledot may not eat from a Pesach brought in impurity, but if they do, they are exempt from karet. Rabbi Eliezer also exempts them from liability for entering the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that zavim, zavot, niddot, and yoledot may not eat from a Pesach brought in impurity, but if they do, they are exempt from karet.
Rabbi Eliezer adds that such individuals are also exempt from liability for entering the Temple.

items.text: Gemara: Source for exemption of impure individuals from karet for eating the Pesach
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for exemption of impure individuals from karet for eating the Pesach
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from a verse that only a Pesach eaten by pure individuals incurs liability for impure eaters; one not eaten by pure individuals does not. Rabbi Eliezer adds that zavim who entered the Temple during a Pesach brought in impurity are exempt, based on a verse that only when impure people are sent out are zavim and lepers sent out.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites a verse to exempt impure individuals from liability for eating the Pesach brought in impurity, since it is not eaten by pure individuals.
Rabbi Eliezer adds that zavim who entered the Temple during a Pesach brought in impurity are exempt, based on a verse linking their expulsion to that of impure individuals.

items.text: Rav Yosef's query and Rava's answer on impure people entering the Heikhal
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's query and Rava's answer on impure people entering the Heikhal
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether impure people who entered the Heikhal (inner sanctuary) during a Pesach brought in impurity are liable. Rava answers with a verse that implies even part of the camp is included, or alternatively, that wherever the verse says 'send them outside the camp' it also says 'send from the camp'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether impure people who entered the Heikhal (inner sanctuary) during a Pesach brought in impurity are liable, given that the impurity of the courtyard was permitted.
Rava answers by citing a verse that implies even part of the camp is included, so the Heikhal is included.
An alternative version of Rava's answer: wherever the verse says 'send them outside the camp' it also says 'send from the camp', so the Heikhal is included.

items.text: Rav Yosef's query on impure people eating the sacrificial portions
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's query on impure people eating the sacrificial portions
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether impure people who ate the sacrificial portions (emurim) of a Pesach brought in impurity are liable.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether tamei metim who ate the sacrificial portions (emurim) of the Pesach brought in impurity are liable.

items.text: Gemara's question on impurity of fats
items.text_en: Gemara's question on impurity of fats
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the leniency allowing impurity to override the Passover extends to the fats (eimurim) as well. Rava resolves this by noting that the impurity of eimurim is derived from the impurity of the meat, so wherever meat impurity applies, eimurim impurity applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the leniency allowing impurity to override the Passover extends to the fats (eimurim) as well, or only to the meat.
Rava resolves the question by explaining that the impurity of eimurim is derived from the impurity of the meat via the verse, so wherever meat impurity applies, eimurim impurity applies.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's query on burning eimurim of Egyptian Passover
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's query on burning eimurim of Egyptian Passover
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks where the eimurim of the Egyptian Passover were burned, since there was no altar. Abaye responds that they were burned on the lintel and doorposts, citing a baraita of Rav Yosef that three altars existed there.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks where the fats of the Egyptian Passover were offered on the altar.
Abaye suggests that perhaps they made small spits (shviskei) to roast the fats.
Rav Yosef's baraita supports that there were three altars (lintel and two doorposts) and no other place for offering, implying the fats were not offered on a formal altar.

items.text: Mishnah: Differences between Egyptian and later Passovers
items.text_en: Mishnah: Differences between Egyptian and later Passovers
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the differences: the Egyptian Passover was taken on the tenth, required sprinkling with hyssop on the lintel and doorposts, was eaten in haste, and only one night, while the later Passover is observed for seven days.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the differences between the Egyptian Passover and the permanent Passover: the Egyptian was taken on the tenth, required sprinkling with hyssop on lintel and doorposts, was eaten in haste in one night, while the permanent Passover is observed for seven days.

items.text: Gemara's derivation of taking on the tenth
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation of taking on the tenth
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse that the Egyptian Passover was taken on the tenth, but not later Passovers. It then addresses a potential contradiction from a baraita of Ben Bag Bag that the daily offering requires inspection four days prior, and distinguishes using the word 'tishmeru'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the Mishnah's rule that the Egyptian Passover was taken on the tenth, and answers by citing the verse 'דברו אל כל עדת ישראל לאמר בעשור לחדש הזה ויקחו', deriving that only this Passover requires taking on the tenth.
The Gemara objects that if the verse 'והיה לכם למשמרת' is taken literally, it would imply that only the Egyptian Passover requires inspection four days before slaughter, but not later Passovers.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Ben Bag Bag
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Ben Bag Bag
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Ben Bag Bag that the daily offering (תמיד) requires inspection four days before slaughter, derived from a verbal analogy between 'תשמרו' and 'והיה לכם למשמרת', showing that the inspection requirement applies to other offerings as well.

The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing that the inspection requirement for the daily offering is derived from the word 'תשמרו', which is not present in the verse about the Egyptian Passover, so the inspection rule is not limited to the Egyptian Passover alone.

items.text: Deriving other laws from 'hazeh' and 'va'avadta'
items.text_en: Deriving other laws from 'hazeh' and 'va'avadta'
items.desc_en: The Gemara uses the verse 'va'avadta et ha'avodah hazot' to teach that all services of this month are like this one, applying to later Passovers. It then addresses a challenge from the verse 've'achlu et habasar balaylah hazeh', which might imply only the Egyptian Passover is eaten at night, but the Gemara deflects using 'va'avadta' and assigns 'hazeh' to the teaching of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah and Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'וְעָבַדְתָּ אֶת הָעֲבוֹדָה הַזֹּאת' to teach that all services of this month are like this one, applying to later Passovers.
The Gemara deflects the challenge by assigning the word 'הַזֶּה' to exclude the second Passover (פסח שני) which is similar to it.
The Gemara objects that the verse 'וְאָכְלוּ אֶת הַבָּשָׂר בַּלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה' might imply only the Egyptian Passover is eaten at night, not later Passovers.
The Gemara resolves by citing 'וְעָבַדְתָּ' to include later Passovers, and assigns 'הַזֶּה' to the teaching of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah and Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Series of challenges and resolutions using 'bo' and 'mimenu'
items.text_en: Series of challenges and resolutions using 'bo' and 'mimenu'
items.desc_en: The Gemara systematically challenges each restriction from the Egyptian Passover (e.g., uncircumcised, alien, sojourner, breaking bones, eating raw) by suggesting it might not apply to later Passovers, but each time deflects using 'va'avadta'. The extra words 'bo' and 'mimenu' are then explained for specific halakhot: apostasy disqualifies for Passover but not terumah, circumcision of males and slaves is required for Passover but not terumah, breaking bones only in a fit offering, and the prohibition of eating raw is for the teaching of Rabbah bar Rav Yitzchak.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if the word 'בּוֹ' (in it) restricts the Egyptian Passover, does it mean an uncircumcised person may eat the later Passover?
The Gemara deflects the challenge by invoking the verse 'וְעָבַדְתָּ' (and you shall serve) to equate all Passover services.
The Gemara explains that the word 'בּוֹ' teaches that apostasy disqualifies one from eating the Passover but not from eating תרומה (priestly portion).
The Gemara justifies why both 'עָרֵל' (uncircumcised) and 'בֶּן נֵכָר' (alien) are written, each covering a different reason for disqualification.
The Gemara challenges: does the restriction on a sojourner and hired hand apply only to the Egyptian Passover?
The Gemara again deflects with the verse 'וְעָבַדְתָּ'.
The Gemara explains that 'בּוֹ' teaches that circumcision of males and slaves is required for Passover but not for תרומה.
The Gemara challenges: does the prohibition of breaking bones apply only to the Egyptian Passover?
The Gemara deflects with the verse 'וְעָבַדְתָּ'.
The Gemara explains that 'בּוֹ' teaches that breaking bones is prohibited only in a fit (כשר) offering, not in a disqualified one.
The Gemara challenges: does the prohibition of eating raw apply only to the Egyptian Passover?
The Gemara deflects with the verse 'וְעָבַדְתָּ'.
The Gemara explains that 'מִמֶּנּוּ' (from it) is needed for the teaching of Rabbah bar Rav Yitzchak.

items.text: Derivation of eating in haste and duration of later Passover
items.text_en: Derivation of eating in haste and duration of later Passover
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse that only the Egyptian Passover is eaten in haste. It then questions the Mishnah's statement that the later Passover is observed for seven days, asking whether the Passover itself lasts seven days, implying it refers to the prohibition of chametz.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the rule that only the Egyptian Passover is eaten in haste, and answers with a verse derivation.
The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that the later Passover is observed for seven days, asking whether the Passover itself lasts seven days.

items.text: Clarification of the duration of chametz prohibition for the Paschal lamb in Egypt vs. later generations
items.text_en: Clarification of the duration of chametz prohibition for the Paschal lamb in Egypt vs. later generations
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Paschal lamb in Egypt was only one night, and cites Rabbi Yossi HaGelili's derivation that chametz was prohibited only one day. It then clarifies that the Mishnah means one night, and the same applies to later generations, but the prohibition of chametz lasts all day for the Egyptian Pesach, while for later generations it lasts seven days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Paschal lamb in Egypt was only one night, implying the chametz prohibition was only that night.

sub.text: Supporting baraita citing Rabbi Yossi HaGelili
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita citing Rabbi Yossi HaGelili
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yossi HaGelili derives from the verse that the chametz prohibition for the Egyptian Pesach was only one day.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah means one night, and the same applies to later generations, but the chametz prohibition for the Egyptian Pesach lasts all day, while for later generations it lasts seven days.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva on the substitute of a Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva on the substitute of a Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua states he heard that the substitute of a Paschal lamb is offered and also not offered, but he cannot explain. Rabbi Akiva explains: if the Paschal lamb was found before slaughter, it grazes until blemished, is sold, and with its money a peace-offering is brought; likewise its substitute. If found after slaughter, it is offered as a peace-offering; likewise its substitute.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua states he heard that the substitute of a Paschal lamb (תמורת פסח) is offered and also not offered, but he cannot explain the contradiction.

Rabbi Akiva explains: if the Paschal lamb was found before its slaughter, it grazes until blemished, is sold, and with its money a peace-offering (שלמים) is brought; likewise its substitute. If found after slaughter, it is offered as a peace-offering; likewise its substitute.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah says 'the substitute is offered and not offered' rather than 'the Paschal lamb is offered and not offered'. It answers that the Mishnah teaches that there is a substitute of the Paschal lamb that is not offered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah says 'the substitute is offered and not offered' rather than 'the Paschal lamb is offered and not offered'.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that there is a substitute of the Paschal lamb that is not offered.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira on the meaning of 'before slaughter' and 'after slaughter'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira on the meaning of 'before slaughter' and 'after slaughter'
items.desc_en: Rabbah says the Mishnah's distinction is before and after the actual slaughter. Rabbi Zeira says it is before and after midday (the time of slaughter). The Gemara then adjusts Rabbi Zeira's reading of the Mishnah to 'before the time of slaughter' and 'after the time of slaughter'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a dispute: Rabbah says the Mishnah's terms refer to before and after the actual slaughter, while Rabbi Zeira says they refer to before and after midday (the time of slaughter).
The Gemara objects to Rabbi Zeira's position: the Mishnah explicitly says 'before the slaughter of the Passover offering,' not 'before midday.'
The Gemara resolves the objection by adjusting Rabbi Zeira's reading: the Mishnah means 'before the time of the slaughter of the Passover offering,' i.e., before midday.

items.text: Support from a Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Support from a Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the dispute between Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira parallels a Tannaitic dispute: one Tanna says before slaughter it grazes, after slaughter it is offered; Rabbi Eliezer says before midday it grazes, after midday it is offered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaitic dispute that parallels the Amoraic dispute between Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira.
Rabbi Eliezer states that the criterion is before or after midday, not before or after slaughter.

items.text: Rava's distinction regarding the timing of the substitution
items.text_en: Rava's distinction regarding the timing of the substitution
items.desc_en: Rava says the Mishnah's ruling that the substitute is offered applies only when the animal was found after slaughter and the substitution was made after slaughter. But if found before slaughter and substituted after slaughter, the substitute comes from a rejected sanctity and is not offered.

sub.desc_en: Rava distinguishes that the Mishnah's ruling that the substitute is offered applies only when the animal was found after slaughter and the substitution was made after slaughter; but if found before slaughter and substituted after slaughter, the substitute comes from a rejected sanctity and is not offered.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution regarding the verse 'If a sheep'
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution regarding the verse 'If a sheep'
items.desc_en: Abaye objects from a verse that includes the substitute of the Paschal lamb after the Pesach as offered as peace-offerings. He argues this must refer to a case where the animal was found before slaughter and substituted after slaughter, otherwise the verse is unnecessary. The Gemara deflects by saying the verse is merely an asmakhta (support).

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects by citing a verse that includes the substitute of the Paschal lamb after Pesach as offered as peace-offerings.
Abaye argues that the verse must refer to a case where the animal was found before slaughter and substituted after slaughter, otherwise the verse would be superfluous.
The Gemara deflects by saying the verse is merely an אסמכתא (support) and does not indicate a new halachic case.

items.text: Alternative interpretation of the verse: including the Paschal lamb for the tail and other laws
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation of the verse: including the Paschal lamb for the tail and other laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'If a sheep' actually comes to include the Paschal lamb for the requirement of the tail (alya). And 'If a sheep' also includes a Paschal lamb that has passed its first year and peace-offerings that come from a Paschal lamb for all the laws of peace-offerings (semikha, libations, breast and thigh waving). 'And if a goat' teaches that a goat does not require the tail.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse 'If a sheep' actually comes to teach, since it was not needed for the previous interpretation.
A baraita teaches that the word 'כֶּשֶׂב' (sheep) comes to include the Paschal lamb for the requirement of the tail (אליה).

The baraita further teaches that the phrase 'אִם כֶּשֶׂב' includes a Paschal lamb that has passed its first year and peace-offerings that come from a Paschal lamb for all the laws of peace-offerings (semikha, libations, breast and thigh waving).
The baraita concludes that the phrase 'וְאִם עֵז' (and if a goat) interrupts the context, teaching that a goat does not require the tail.

items.text: Alternative version of Rava's statement and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rava's statement and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Some teach Rava's statement on the first clause of the Mishnah: if found before slaughter and substituted before slaughter, the substitute is offered; but if found before slaughter and substituted after slaughter, the substitute is offered because slaughter determines what is fit for it. Abaye objects with the same verse, but the Gemara does not resolve it here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative version of the Mishnah's first clause, stating that if a Paschal lamb is found before slaughter, it is left to graze, sold, and a peace-offering is brought with its proceeds, and the same applies to its substitute.

Rava explains that the Mishnah's ruling applies only when the animal was found before slaughter and the substitution was made before slaughter; but if found before slaughter and substituted after slaughter, the substitute is offered as a peace-offering because the slaughter determines what is fit for it.
Abaye objects by citing the verse 'אם כשב' (If a sheep), asking what it comes to teach, and answers that it includes the substitute of a Paschal lamb offered after Passover as a peace-offering.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rava's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava's earlier statement by analyzing the verse 'hu' which implies that only the Pesach itself is offered, not its temurah. It then clarifies the scenario: the animal was found before slaughter but the owner exchanged it after slaughter, leading to a refutation of Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the verse might include the case of an animal exchanged before Pesach.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'הוּא' (he) teaches that only the Pesach itself is offered, not its temurah (substitute).
The Gemara asks to clarify the scenario under discussion.
The Gemara objects that if the animal was found and exchanged before slaughter, the verse would be superfluous.
The Gemara resolves that the case is where the animal was found before slaughter but exchanged after slaughter, concluding that this refutes Rava's position.

items.text: Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute
items.text_en: Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that any Pesach which would cause a Chatat to die is offered as a peace-offering, and any that would cause a Chatat to graze also grazes. Rabbi Yochanan limits this to cases where the Pesach was found after slaughter, not before.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states a general rule: any Pesach that would cause a Chatat to die is offered as a peace-offering, and any that would cause a Chatat to graze also grazes.
Rabbi Yochanan limits Shmuel's rule, stating that the Pesach is offered as a peace-offering only if found after slaughter, but not before.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection from a year-old Pesach
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection from a year-old Pesach
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Shmuel's general rule by citing a Chatat that is over a year old, which is left to graze, yet a Pesach in a similar situation is offered as a peace-offering, as derived from the verse 'im kesev' which includes a year-old Pesach in all peace-offering requirements.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Shmuel's general rule by citing a Chatat that is over a year old, which is left to graze.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita that a Pesach over a year old is offered as a peace-offering, derived from the verse 'אִם כֶּשֶׂב' (if a lamb), which includes it in all peace-offering requirements.

items.text: Shmuel's response: distinction between lost and rejected
items.text_en: Shmuel's response: distinction between lost and rejected
items.desc_en: Shmuel responds that his rule applies only to lost animals (avudin), not to rejected ones (dechuyin), thus excluding the case of a year-old animal which is rejected.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel responds that his rule applies only to lost animals (אבודין), not to rejected ones (דחויין), thus excluding the case of a year-old animal which is rejected.

items.text: Gemara's challenge from a lost Chatat
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge from a lost Chatat
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a lost animal can be found, citing a Mishnah where a lost Chatat, according to the Rabbis, grazes if found before atonement, yet a lost Pesach found after midday before slaughter is offered as a peace-offering. It concludes that Shmuel follows Rabbi's opinion that a lost Chatat dies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a lost animal can be found, citing a Mishnah about a lost Chatat.
The Mishnah states that according to Rabbi, a lost Chatat found before atonement dies, but according to the Sages, it grazes.
The Gemara concludes that Shmuel follows Rabbi's opinion that a lost Chatat dies, explaining why a lost Pesach found after midday before slaughter is offered as a peace-offering.

items.text: Resolution: lost before midday is not considered lost
items.text_en: Resolution: lost before midday is not considered lost
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for Rabbi, all lost Chatat animals die, but a Pesach lost before midday and found before midday grazes. It resolves that a loss before midday is not considered a loss, as per Rava's principle that a nighttime loss is not a loss. The Gemara then asks how a grazing case exists for Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that for Rabbi, all lost Chatat animals die, yet a Pesach lost before midday and found before midday grazes.
The Gemara resolves that a loss before midday is not considered a loss, citing Rava's principle that a nighttime loss is not a loss.
The Gemara then asks how a grazing case exists for Rabbi at all.

items.text: Analogy to Rabbi Oshaya's law of chatat
items.text_en: Analogy to Rabbi Oshaya's law of chatat
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests Shmuel's ruling aligns with Rabbi Oshaya's principle that one who sets aside two chatat for liability may be atoned with one, and the other grazes. This is contrasted with Pesach, where a similar case would be offered as shelamim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Shmuel's ruling follows Rabbi Oshaya's principle regarding one who sets aside two chatat offerings for liability.

items.text: Rejection: Shmuel follows Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Rejection: Shmuel follows Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the analogy, noting that Shmuel actually holds like Rabbi Shimon, who says five chatat die. The Gemara then questions how this fits with the grazing law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that in the analogous case of a lost Pesach, the animal would be offered as a shelamim (peace offering), not graze.
The Gemara answers that Shmuel follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that five specific chatat (sin offerings) die, so the analogy to a lost Pesach does not apply.

items.text: Resolution: Shmuel's statement is limited
items.text_en: Resolution: Shmuel's statement is limited
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Shmuel only meant that whatever would die in the case of chatat is offered as shelamim in Pesach, not that all cases align.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon does not have a category of רועה (grazing) at all, so Shmuel's comparison seems flawed.

The Gemara resolves that Shmuel only meant that whatever would die in the case of a חטאת (sin-offering) is offered as a שלמים (peace-offering) in the case of a פסח (Paschal lamb), not that all cases align.

items.text: Implication: Shmuel disputes Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Implication: Shmuel disputes Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Shmuel's ruling teaches that midday (חצות) determines the status, contrary to Rabbi Yochanan who holds that slaughter determines it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novel point Shmuel is teaching by his ruling.
The Gemara explains that Shmuel's ruling rejects Rabbi Yochanan's view that slaughter (שחיטה) determines the status, and instead teaches that midday (חצות) determines it.

items.text: Alternative version: Shmuel follows Rabbah
items.text_en: Alternative version: Shmuel follows Rabbah
items.desc_en: An alternative version suggests Shmuel holds like Rabbah that slaughter determines the status, but the Gemara deduces from Rabbi Yochanan's comment that Shmuel actually holds midday determines it.

sub.desc_en: The alternative version presents the premise: if a Pesach offering is lost and found after midday but before slaughter, it should be brought as a שלמים (peace offering), implying Shmuel holds like Rabbah that slaughter determines the status.

The Gemara objects: from Rabbi Yochanan's comment that only a Pesach found after slaughter may be brought as a שלמים, it follows that Shmuel actually holds that midday (חצות) determines the status, not slaughter.

items.text: Final resolution: Shmuel follows Rabbi
items.text_en: Final resolution: Shmuel follows Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Shmuel holds like Rabbi, who says a lost animal goes to death. However, since a Pesach lost before midday is not considered lost, and midday determines its status, it grazes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Shmuel follows Rabbi's view that a lost animal goes to death, but since a Pesach lost before midday is not considered lost and midday determines its status, it grazes.

items.text: Mishnah: Invalid offerings for Pesach
items.text_en: Mishnah: Invalid offerings for Pesach
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one designates a female or a two-year-old male for his Pesach, the animal grazes until it becomes blemished, is sold, and its proceeds go to a nedavah for shelamim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one designates a female or a two-year-old male for his Pesach offering, the animal grazes until it becomes blemished, is sold, and its proceeds go to a nedavah (freewill offering) for shelamim.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one sets aside his Passover offering and dies, his son may not bring it as a Passover but as a peace offering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one sets aside his Passover offering and dies, his son may not bring it as a Passover but only as a peace offering.

items.text: Rav Huna's inference of three principles
items.text_en: Rav Huna's inference of three principles
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua derives three principles from the Mishnah: that living animals can be rejected (nidchin), that initial rejection is considered rejection, and that rejection applies to money (damim).

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua announces that he derives three principles from the Mishnah, beginning with the principle that living animals can be rejected (nidchin).
Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua states the second and third principles: that initial rejection is considered rejection, and that rejection applies to money (damim).

items.text: Baraita elaborating on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Baraita elaborating on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: A Baraita clarifies that if the son was appointed with the father, he brings it as a Passover; otherwise, he brings it as a peace offering on the sixteenth, because vows and free-will offerings are not brought on a festival.

sub.desc_en: The Baraita elaborates on the Mishnah's ruling: if the son was appointed with the father, he brings it as a Passover; otherwise, he brings it as a peace offering on the sixteenth, because vows and free-will offerings are not brought on a festival.

items.text: Gemara's question on timing of death
items.text_en: Gemara's question on timing of death
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Baraita: if the father died before noon, the son cannot bring it as a Passover because the father's mourning (aninut) already applied; if after noon, the Passover is already designated and cannot be changed to a peace offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks when the father died: if before noon, the son cannot bring it as a Passover because the father's mourning (אנינות) already applied from the start.
The Gemara asks alternatively: if the father died after noon, the son cannot bring it as a peace offering because noon already designated it as a Passover.

items.text: Rava's answer: death before noon, second Passover
items.text_en: Rava's answer: death before noon, second Passover
items.desc_en: Rava answers that the father died before noon, and 'bring it as a Passover' refers to the second Passover (Pesach Sheni).

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by asserting that the father died before noon, and the phrase 'bring it as a Passover' refers to the second Passover (Pesach Sheni).

items.text: Abaye's answer: conditional ruling
items.text_en: Abaye's answer: conditional ruling
items.desc_en: Abaye says the Baraita is stated conditionally: if death after noon, the son brings it as a Passover; if before noon, as a peace offering.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Baraita is stated conditionally: if the father died after noon, the son brings it as a Passover; if before noon, as a peace offering.

items.text: Rav Sherevya's answer: father was dying at noon
items.text_en: Rav Sherevya's answer: father was dying at noon
items.desc_en: Rav Sherevya explains that the father died after noon, but was in a dying state (goses) at noon, so the animal was not yet fully designated.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sherevya resolves the contradiction by explaining that the father died after noon but was in a dying state (גוסס) at noon, so the animal was not yet fully designated.

items.text: Rav Ashi's answer: Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer: Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says the Baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that living animals are not rejected (ein ba'alei chayim nidchin).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the baraita's difficulty by attributing it to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that living animals are not subject to rejection (אין בעלי חיים נדחין).

items.text: Ravina's answer: animal set aside after noon
items.text_en: Ravina's answer: animal set aside after noon
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the animal was set aside after noon and the owners died after noon, and the Baraita holds that noon designates the offering.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the Baraita's difficulty by positing that the animal was set aside after noon and the owners died after noon, and the Baraita holds that noon designates the offering.

items.text: Mishnah: Passover mixed with other offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Passover mixed with other offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a Passover that became mixed with other sacrifices: all must graze until blemished, sold, and the best of each type is brought, with the owner covering the loss.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a Passover offering mixed with other sacrifices: all graze until blemished, sold, and the owner brings the best of each type, covering any loss from his own funds.

items.text: Mishnah: Passover mixed with firstborns
items.text_en: Mishnah: Passover mixed with firstborns
items.desc_en: The Mishnah adds that if mixed with firstborns, Rabbi Shimon says a group of priests may eat them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a Passover offering is mixed with firstborn animals (בכורות), Rabbi Shimon permits a group of priests to eat them.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution regarding bringing sacrifices to a disqualifying place
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution regarding bringing sacrifices to a disqualifying place
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Shimon can allow bringing a paschal lamb to a place that disqualifies it, given his own ruling. It explains that Rabbi Shimon holds that one may bring sacrifices to a disqualifying place, citing a mishnah. The Sages disagree, and Rava proposes a solution: wait until the animal develops a blemish, then designate it as a firstborn and eat it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Shimon can allow bringing a paschal lamb to a place that disqualifies it, given his own ruling.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon holds that one may bring sacrifices to a disqualifying place, citing a mishnah where he rules that an asham mixed with a shelamim is slaughtered in the north and eaten under the stricter rules.
The Sages object to Rabbi Shimon, asserting that one does not bring sacrifices to a disqualifying place.
Rava proposes a solution: wait until the animal develops a blemish, then designate it as a firstborn and eat it.

items.text: Mishnah: Case of a lost paschal lamb with agency
items.text_en: Mishnah: Case of a lost paschal lamb with agency
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents a case where a group lost its paschal lamb and appointed an agent to find and slaughter it. If the agent's lamb was slaughtered first, he eats from his own and they eat with him. If theirs was slaughtered first, they eat from theirs and he eats from his own. If unknown or simultaneous, he eats from his own, they do not eat with him, and theirs is burned; they are exempt from the second Passover.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the case of a group that lost its paschal lamb and appointed an agent; if the agent's lamb was slaughtered first, he eats from his own and they eat with him.
The mishnah continues with the case where the group's lamb was slaughtered first, and then the case of unknown or simultaneous slaughter, concluding that the group is exempt from the second Passover.

items.text: Mishnah: Agent's conditional instruction
items.text_en: Mishnah: Agent's conditional instruction
items.desc_en: The mishnah continues with a case where the agent said, 'If I am delayed, go and slaughter for me.' If theirs was slaughtered first, they eat from theirs and he eats with them. If his was slaughtered first, he eats from his and they eat from theirs. If unknown or simultaneous, they eat from theirs, he does not eat with them, and his is burned; he is exempt from the second Passover.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah presents the case of an agent who gave conditional instructions, detailing the rules for eating and liability based on whose sacrifice was slaughtered first.

items.text: Mishnah: Mutual agency and no agency
items.text_en: Mishnah: Mutual agency and no agency
items.desc_en: The mishnah rules that if both parties appointed each other as agents, they all eat from the first slaughtered. If unknown which was first, both are burned. If neither appointed the other, they are not responsible for each other.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah rules that if both parties appointed each other as agents, they all eat from the first slaughtered.
The mishnah states that if unknown which was first, both are burned.
The mishnah concludes that if neither appointed the other, they are not responsible for each other.

items.text: Mishnah: Two or more groups with mixed paschal lambs
items.text_en: Mishnah: Two or more groups with mixed paschal lambs
items.desc_en: The mishnah describes a procedure for two groups whose paschal lambs were mixed: each group draws one lamb, and members from each group join the other, declaring conditional transfer of membership. The same applies to five groups of varying sizes.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the case of two groups whose paschal lambs were mixed, each group drawing one lamb.
The mishnah extends the same procedure to five groups of varying sizes.

items.text: Mishnah: Two individuals with mixed paschal lambs
items.text_en: Mishnah: Two individuals with mixed paschal lambs
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents a case of two individuals whose paschal lambs were mixed: each draws one lamb, appoints a stranger from the market, and they exchange with conditional declarations.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the case of two individuals whose paschal lambs were mixed, each drawing one lamb and appointing a stranger from the market.
The mishnah describes the conditional exchange declaration each individual makes, transferring membership to the other's lamb if the drawn lamb belongs to the other.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita summarizing the mishnah's rulings
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita summarizing the mishnah's rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that restates the mishnah's rulings: if they appointed each other, they eat from the first; if not, they are not responsible for each other.

sub.desc_en: The baraita restates the mishnah's two rulings: if they appointed each other, they eat from the first; if not, they are not responsible for each other.

items.text: Opening aphorism on silence
items.text_en: Opening aphorism on silence
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general statement praising silence for the wise and especially for fools, citing Proverbs 17:28.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general statement praising silence for the wise and especially for fools, citing Proverbs 17:28.

items.text: Challenge: Mishnah against Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Challenge: Mishnah against Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling about mixed offerings contradicts Rabbi Yehuda, who requires at least one original member to remain in the group, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yose disagrees.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the Mishnah's ruling about mixed Passover offerings contradicts Rabbi Yehuda's position.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda requires at least one original member to remain in the group, while Rabbi Yose disagrees.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's defense of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's defense of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that the Mishnah can align with Rabbi Yehuda, because Rabbi Yehuda holds that a paschal lamb is not slaughtered for an individual, so the original members intended to include others, making each participant like a member of the group.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan defends the Mishnah by arguing that it can align with Rabbi Yehuda, because Rabbi Yehuda holds that a paschal lamb is not slaughtered for an individual, so the original members intended to include others, making each participant like a member of the group.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi provides additional support by noting that the Mishnah specifies groups of five, implying that each group must have at least one member remaining, consistent with Rabbi Yehuda's requirement.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that the Mishnah itself supports Rabbi Yehuda's position, because it specifies groups of exactly five, implying that at least one member must remain with each group.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on the eve of Passover, close to minḥah time, one may not eat until nightfall. Even the poorest person in Israel must not eat until they recline, and they must be given no fewer than four cups of wine, even if from the charity plate.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that on the eve of Passover close to minḥah time, one may not eat until nightfall, and even the poorest must recline and receive at least four cups of wine.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why only Passover eve?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why only Passover eve?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies the eve of Passover; the same prohibition should apply on the eves of Shabbat and festivals, as taught in a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda prohibits eating from minḥah onward, while Rabbi Yosei permits eating until nightfall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies the eve of Passover, since the same prohibition should apply on the eves of Shabbat and festivals.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda prohibits eating from minḥah onward on eves of Shabbat and festivals, while Rabbi Yosei permits eating until nightfall.

items.text: Rav Huna's answer: Even according to Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Rav Huna's answer: Even according to Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that the Mishnah is necessary even according to Rabbi Yosei, who permits eating on other eves until dark, but on Passover eve he agrees it is prohibited due to the obligation of matzah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that the Mishnah is necessary even according to Rabbi Yosei, who permits eating on other eves until dark, but on Passover eve he agrees it is prohibited due to the obligation of matzah.

items.text: Rav Pappa's alternative answer: Even according to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's alternative answer: Even according to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa offers a different explanation: even according to Rabbi Yehuda, on other eves the prohibition begins only from minḥah, but close to minḥah it is permitted; on Passover eve, however, even close to minḥah it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa offers a different explanation: even according to Rabbi Yehuda, on other eves the prohibition begins only from minḥah, but close to minḥah it is permitted; on Passover eve, however, even close to minḥah it is forbidden.

items.text: Objection to Rav Pappa: A contradictory baraita
items.text_en: Objection to Rav Pappa: A contradictory baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav Pappa's claim that close to minḥah is permitted on Shabbat eve, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda prohibits eating from the ninth hour onward, which is close to minḥah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav Pappa's leniency for close to minḥah on Shabbat eve, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda prohibits eating from the ninth hour onward, which is close to minḥah.

items.text: Mar Zutra's question: Is the baraita reconciled?
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's question: Is the baraita reconciled?
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra asks who can tell us that the baraita is reconciled (with Rav Pappa's view), implying that the contradiction remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra questions whether the baraita is truly reconciled with Rav Pappa's view, implying the contradiction remains unresolved.

items.text: Gemara's initial doubt
items.text_en: Gemara's initial doubt
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a doubt about a previous statement, suggesting it might be a scribal error.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a doubt that the previous statement might be a scribal error (משבשתא).

items.text: Marimar's testimony and resolution
items.text_en: Marimar's testimony and resolution
items.desc_en: Marimar (or Rav Yeimar) testifies that he attended Rav Pinchas's lecture where a Tanna recited a baraita that was accepted, leading to the conclusion that the earlier text is a clarification like Rav Huna's.

sub.desc_en: Marimar (or Rav Yeimar) testifies that he attended Rav Pinchas's lecture where a Tanna recited a baraita before him and he accepted it.
The Gemara resolves that the earlier text is not a contradiction but a clarification (מחוורתא) like Rav Huna's position.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Yirmeya's tradition
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Yirmeya's tradition
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even according to Rav Huna, there is a difficulty because Rabbi Yirmeya cited Rabbi Yochanan (or Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina) that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda on Erev Pesach and Rabbi Yosei on Erev Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even according to Rav Huna, there is a difficulty because Rabbi Yirmeya cited Rabbi Yochanan (or Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina) that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda on Erev Pesach and Rabbi Yosei on Erev Shabbat.

items.text: Clarifying the dispute: interruption vs. no interruption
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute: interruption vs. no interruption
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the halakha that Rabbi Yosei must disagree in both cases, but then clarifies that the dispute is specifically about whether one interrupts the meal for Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the ruling that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda on Passover eve that Rabbi Yosei must disagree in both cases.
The Gemara rejects the inference and clarifies that the dispute is specifically about whether one interrupts the meal for Shabbat (הפסקה), not about the general rule.

items.text: Baraita on interruption for Shabbatot
items.text_en: Baraita on interruption for Shabbatot
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda says one interrupts for Shabbatot, Rabbi Yosei says one does not interrupt.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda rules that one interrupts the meal for Shabbatot (שבתות), while Rabbi Yosei rules that one does not interrupt.

items.text: Ma'aseh with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Ma'aseh with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: A story is told: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei were dining in Akko when Shabbat began. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel suggested interrupting for Rabbi Yehuda's view, but Rabbi Yosei objected, and they ultimately ruled like Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a story about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei dining in Akko when Shabbat began.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel asks Rabbi Yosei if they should interrupt their meal to heed Rabbi Yehuda's view.
Rabbi Yosei objects, accusing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel of favoring Rabbi Yehuda's words in his presence, citing a biblical verse.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel concedes not to interrupt, fearing the students will establish a permanent ruling.
The story concludes that they did not leave until they ruled in accordance with Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling: spread a cloth and recite Kiddush
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling: spread a cloth and recite Kiddush
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that the halakha follows neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Yosei, but rather one spreads a cloth and recites Kiddush. The Gemara then questions this with another statement from Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that the halakha follows neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Yosei, but rather one spreads a cloth and recites Kiddush.
The Gemara objects by citing a contradictory statement from Shmuel via Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi, that one interrupts for Kiddush.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'interrupting for Havdalah' means: does it refer to clearing the table (עקירת שולחן) or spreading a cloth (מפה)? It answers that it means spreading a cloth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'interrupting for Havdalah' means: does it refer to clearing the table (עקירת שולחן)?
The Gemara answers that it means spreading a cloth (מפה).

items.text: Supporting story and baraita
items.text_en: Supporting story and baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna visited the Exilarch's house, where they brought a table before him, he spread a cloth, and recited Kiddush. A baraita similarly states that one does not bring the table unless Kiddush has been recited, and if brought, one spreads a cloth and recites Kiddush.

sub.text: Story of Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna visited the Exilarch's house, where they brought a table before him, he spread a cloth, and recited Kiddush.
A baraita similarly states that one does not bring the table unless Kiddush has been recited, and if brought, one spreads a cloth and recites Kiddush.

items.text: Contradictory baraitot on beginning a meal
items.text_en: Contradictory baraitot on beginning a meal
items.desc_en: Two baraitot conflict: one says they agree that one does not begin, another says they agree that one begins. The Gemara resolves: the first applies to Passover eve, the second to Shabbat eve. The contradiction is further resolved by time: before the ninth hour (when the meal is early) vs. after the ninth hour.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that the schools agree one does not begin a meal on Passover eve.
Another baraita states that the schools agree one does begin a meal.
The Gemara explains that the first baraita applies to Passover eve, where the מצה (unleavened bread) obligation prevents starting a meal.
The Gemara asks when the second baraita applies, since on Shabbat eve the schools disagree.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by time: before the ninth hour (early meal) they agree one begins; after the ninth hour (late meal) they agree one does not begin.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel on Kiddush in the synagogue
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel on Kiddush in the synagogue
items.desc_en: Regarding those who recited Kiddush in the synagogue, Rav says they fulfilled the obligation of Kiddush but not of wine, while Shmuel begins his opinion (the rest is on the next amud).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of those who recited Kiddush in the synagogue.
Rav rules that they fulfilled the obligation of Kiddush but not the obligation of wine.
Shmuel begins his opinion, which continues on the next amud.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's reasons for reciting kiddush at home and in synagogue
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's reasons for reciting kiddush at home and in synagogue
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav recites kiddush at home to fulfill the obligation for his household, while Shmuel recites it in the synagogue to fulfill the obligation for guests who eat and sleep there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav needs to recite kiddush at home if the obligation was already fulfilled in the synagogue.
The Gemara explains that Rav recites kiddush at home to fulfill the obligation for his sons and household members who did not hear it in the synagogue.
The Gemara asks why Shmuel needs to recite kiddush in the synagogue if he already fulfills the obligation at home.
The Gemara explains that Shmuel recites kiddush in the synagogue to fulfill the obligation for guests who eat and sleep there.

items.text: Shmuel's principle: no kiddush except in the place of the meal
items.text_en: Shmuel's principle: no kiddush except in the place of the meal
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Shmuel holds that kiddush is only valid where one eats. It was thought this applies only when moving from house to house, but Rav Anan bar Tahlifa testifies that Shmuel would descend from the roof to the ground and then recite kiddush, indicating it applies even within the same building.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Shmuel's principle that קידוש (sanctification) is only valid in the place of the meal.
The Gemara initially assumes Shmuel's rule applies only when moving from house to house, not within the same building.
Rav Anan bar Tahlifa testifies that Shmuel would descend from the roof to the ground and then recite קידוש, proving the rule applies even within the same building.

items.text: Rav Huna and Rabbah also hold the same principle
items.text_en: Rav Huna and Rabbah also hold the same principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings evidence that Rav Huna and Rabbah also hold that kiddush must be in the place of the meal. Rav Huna, when his lamp was extinguished, moved to his son Rabbah's room to eat, and Rabbah would instruct his students to taste something immediately after kiddush to avoid missing the meal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rav Huna also holds the principle that kiddush must be in the place of the meal.
The Gemara recounts that when Rav Huna's lamp was extinguished after kiddush, he brought his belongings to his son Rabbah's room to eat there, demonstrating his adherence to the principle.

sub.text: Supporting story about Rabbah via Abaye
sub.text_en: Supporting story about Rabbah via Abaye
sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds that Rabbah also holds this principle, as Abaye reports that Rabbah instructed his students to taste something immediately after kiddush to avoid missing the meal if their lamp went out.

items.text: Objection: Rabbah usually followed Rav, not Shmuel
items.text_en: Objection: Rabbah usually followed Rav, not Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Abaye said Rabbah followed Rav in all matters except three where he followed Shmuel, implying he did not hold Shmuel's view on kiddush. The Gemara resolves that Rabbah followed Rav's stringencies but not his leniencies, so he could still hold Shmuel's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Abaye said Rabbah followed Rav in all matters except three where he followed Shmuel, implying he did not hold Shmuel's view on קידוש (sanctification).
The Gemara cites a ברייתא (baraita) where Rabbi Shimon permits dragging furniture on שבת (Sabbath) if one does not intend to make a furrow.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbah followed Rav's stringencies (חומרות) but not his leniencies (קולות), so he could still hold Shmuel's view on קידוש (sanctification).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's view: one fulfills obligation even with a different wine
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's view: one fulfills obligation even with a different wine
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds that one fulfills the obligation of kiddush even if the wine is changed, as stated by Rabbi Chanin bar Abaye in the name of Rabbi Pedat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one fulfills the obligation of kiddush even if the wine is changed, citing the tradition from Rabbi Chanin bar Abaye in the name of Rabbi Pedat.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that states changing location requires a blessing, while changing wine does not, which contradicts Rabbi Yochanan's earlier statement. The Gemara concludes that this is a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that changing location requires a blessing while changing wine does not, concluding that this refutes Rabbi Yochanan's earlier position.

items.text: Rav Huna's distinction and Rav Idi's comment
items.text_en: Rav Huna's distinction and Rav Idi's comment
items.desc_en: Rav Huna, cited by Rav Chisda, distinguishes between moving from house to house (requires blessing) and moving from place to place within the same house (does not). Rav Idi bar Avin notes that this matches a teaching from the school of Rav Heinak, and questions whether Rav Huna was merely teaching a known baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda, sitting before Rav Idi bar Avin, cites Rav Huna's distinction: the rule that changing location requires a new blessing applies only when moving from house to house, not within the same house.
Rav Idi bar Avin notes that this teaching matches a baraita from the school of Rav Heinak, and questions whether Rav Huna was merely teaching a known baraita.
The gemara resolves that Rav Huna had not heard the baraita, so he was not merely repeating it.

items.text: Rav Chisda's own distinction and Rav Sheshet's objection
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's own distinction and Rav Sheshet's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the requirement to bless upon changing location applies only to items that do not require a blessing after consumption in their place; for items that do require such a blessing, no new blessing is needed because one returns to the original place. Rav Sheshet disagrees and says that in both cases a blessing is required.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states his own distinction: the requirement to bless upon changing location applies only to items that do not require a blessing after consumption in their place, because for items that do require such a blessing, one returns to the original fixed place.
Rav Sheshet objects, asserting that in both cases — whether the item requires a blessing after consumption in its place or not — a new blessing is required upon changing location.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Chisda from a baraita
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Chisda from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita about a group that leaves to greet a bridegroom or bride is cited. It states that if they left a sick or elderly person behind, they do not bless upon leaving or returning; otherwise they do. The Gemara infers that this deals with items requiring a blessing after consumption, and the ruling contradicts Rav Chisda's position.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited describing a group drinking who leave to greet a bridegroom or bride, with rules about whether they need to bless upon leaving and returning depending on whether they left a sick or elderly person behind.

The Gemara infers from the baraita that it deals with items requiring a blessing after consumption in their place, and the ruling that one must bless upon leaving when no one is left behind contradicts Rav Chisda's position that such items do not require a blessing upon changing location.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's response
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's response
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak begins to offer a resolution, but the text cuts off. The daf ends with his name, indicating that the discussion continues on the next page.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak begins to speak, but the text cuts off at the end of the daf, leaving his response incomplete.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah's ruling about 'uprooting' (leaving the meal). It cites a Tosefta where Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between leaving some friends behind (no new blessing) and leaving none (new blessing required).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah's ruling about 'uprooting' (leaving the meal) and cites a Tosefta where Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between leaving some friends behind (no new blessing) and leaving none (new blessing required).

items.text: Gemara's inference and challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Gemara's inference and challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that the Tosefta's leniency applies only to foods requiring a blessing after them in their place, implying that for foods without such requirement, even the Sages would require new blessings. This challenges Rabbi Yochanan's view that no new blessing is ever needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Tosefta's leniency applies only to items requiring a blessing after them in their place, but for items not requiring such a blessing, even the Rabbis would require a blessing when leaving and returning.
The Gemara declares that this inference constitutes a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan's position, noting that it has already been challenged once before.

Rabbi Yochanan responds that the same leniency applies even to foods without a blessing after them in their place, and the Tosefta's specification is only to highlight the stringency of Rabbi Yehuda's position.

items.text: Repeated objection against Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Repeated objection against Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara exclaims that this is a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan, noting that he was already challenged once before, and now this is another difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that this constitutes a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan's position, noting that it has already been refuted once before.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's defense
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's defense
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Tosefta's ruling applies even to foods without an after-blessing, but the case of 'uprooting' was chosen to highlight Rabbi Yehuda's stringency: even for such foods, if no friends remain, new blessings are required.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that the same rule applies even to items not requiring a blessing after them in their place, and the Tosefta's mention of 'uprooting' is only to show the strength of Rabbi Yehuda's position.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan elaborates that even for foods requiring an after-blessing, Rabbi Yehuda's stringency applies only when no friends remain, requiring new blessings upon return.

items.text: Support for Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Support for Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: A Tosefta is cited that explicitly supports Rav Chisda: friends who leave and return to drink wine do not need to recite a new blessing.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of Rav Chisda's view: friends sitting to drink wine who leave and return do not need to recite a blessing.

items.text: Dispute about Kiddush and Birkat HaMazon
items.text_en: Dispute about Kiddush and Birkat HaMazon
items.desc_en: A Baraita presents a dispute: if a group is eating and the day becomes sanctified (Shabbat or Yom Tov), Rabbi Yehuda says they bring a cup of wine and recite Kiddush, then a second cup for Birkat HaMazon; Rabbi Yose says they may continue eating until nightfall.

sub.text: Tannaic dispute about Kiddush and Birkat HaMazon
sub.text_en: Tannaic dispute about Kiddush and Birkat HaMazon
sub.desc_en: The Sages taught: For members of a group who were reclining and the day became sanctified (Shabbat or Yom Tov began), Rabbi Yehuda says they bring him a cup of wine and he recites Kiddush over it, and another recites Birkat HaMazon over it; Rabbi Yosei says he may continue eating until nightfall.
Rabbi Yose states his dissenting position that the group may continue eating until nightfall without interruption.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's order
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's order
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah prescribes reciting Birkat HaMazon over the first cup and Kiddush over the second, asking why not combine both blessings over one cup.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah prescribes Birkat HaMazon on the first cup and Kiddush on the second, asking why not combine both blessings over one cup.

items.text: Rav Huna and Rav Sheishet's principle
items.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Sheishet's principle
items.desc_en: Rav Huna quoting Rav Sheishet states that one does not recite two sanctifications over one cup, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the reason: one does not bundle mitzvot together.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rav Sheishet states the principle that one does not recite two sanctifications over a single cup.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rav Sheishet's principle.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the reason is because one does not bundle mitzvot together (אין עושין מצות חבילות חבילות).

items.text: Challenge from the baraita on Motza'ei Shabbat
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita on Motza'ei Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle by citing a baraita where one entering home on Motza'ei Shabbat recites multiple blessings over one cup, and if only one cup is available, all blessings are deferred after the meal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where one entering home on Motza'ei Shabbat recites multiple blessings over one cup, and if only one cup is available, all blessings are deferred after the meal, implying that multiple sanctifications can be said over one cup.

items.text: Distinction for Yom Tov after Shabbat
items.text_en: Distinction for Yom Tov after Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that on Yom Tov after Shabbat, one does have wine, yet Rav said a specific order (Yakneh), implying a different rule. The answer suggests the case is the seventh day of Pesach when one has no wine left.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: on Yom Tov after Shabbat one does have wine, yet Rav said the order יקנה (wine, kiddush, candle, havdalah), implying a different rule.
The Gemara answers: since Rav did not include the blessing of זמן (shehecheyanu), the case is the seventh day of Pesach when one has no wine left.

items.text: Further challenge from the first day of Yom Tov
items.text_en: Further challenge from the first day of Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges again with the first day of Yom Tov when one does have wine, yet Abaye and Rava prescribe different orders (Yakzena and Yaknehaz), showing that the principle is not absolute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that on the first day of Yom Tov, when one does have wine, Abaye and Rava prescribe different orders (Yakzena and Yaknehaz), showing the principle is not absolute.

items.text: Resolution: Havdalah and Kiddush are one matter
items.text_en: Resolution: Havdalah and Kiddush are one matter
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Havdalah and Kiddush are considered one matter (both sanctifications), while Birkat HaMazon and Kiddush are two separate matters, hence the Mishnah's order.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Havdalah and Kiddush are considered one matter (both sanctifications), while Birkat HaMazon and Kiddush are two separate matters, hence the Mishnah's order.

items.text: Gufa: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on order
items.text_en: Gufa: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on order
