items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the core dispute: for Yom Tov after Shabbat, Rav says the order is Yakneh (wine, Kiddush, candle, Havdalah), while Shmuel says Yinhak (wine, candle, Havdalah, Kiddush).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the core dispute regarding the order of blessings for Yom Tov that falls after Shabbat.
Rav states the order as יקנה (wine, Kiddush, candle, Havdalah).
Shmuel states the order as ינהק (wine, candle, Havdalah, Kiddush).

items.text: Acronyms for Havdalah order
items.text_en: Acronyms for Havdalah order
items.desc_en: Various Amoraim propose different acronyms for the order of blessings in Havdalah: Rabba says יַהְנֵ״ק, Levi says קְנִיָּ״ה, the Rabbis say קִינָ״ה, Mar bar Ravna says נְקִיָּ״ה, and Marta in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua says נִיהָ״ק.

sub.desc_en: Rabba proposes the acronym יַהְנֵ״ק for the order of Havdalah blessings.
Levi proposes the acronym קְנִיָּ״ה for the order of Havdalah blessings.
The Rabbis propose the acronym קִינָ״ה for the order of Havdalah blessings.
Mar bar Ravna proposes the acronym נְקִיָּ״ה for the order of Havdalah blessings.
Marta in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua proposes the acronym נִיהָ״ק for the order of Havdalah blessings.

items.text: Rabbi's response and parable
items.text_en: Rabbi's response and parable
items.desc_en: Shmuel's father asks Rabbi about the order of Havdalah. Rabbi responds with a tradition from Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya: נְהִי״ק. Rabbi Chanina then offers a parable of a king and a governor to explain the order.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel's father sends a query to Rabbi asking about the proper order of Havdalah.
Rabbi responds with a tradition from Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya: the order is נְהִי״ק (ner, havadalah, yayin, kiddush).

items.text: Abaye and Rava's dispute
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the conclusion is. Abaye says יַקְזְנָ״ה, Rava says יַקְנְהָ״ז, and the halakha follows Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the conclusion is regarding the order of the Havdalah acrostic.
Abaye states the acrostic יַקְזְנָ״ה (wine, kiddush, candle, Havdalah, season).
Rava states the acrostic יַקְנְהָ״ז (wine, kiddush, candle, season, Havdalah).
The Gemara rules that the halakha follows Rava's acrostic.

items.text: Incident with Rava and Rav Huna bar Yehuda
items.text_en: Incident with Rava and Rav Huna bar Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda visited Rava's house, and they brought light and spices. Rava blessed over spices first, then light. Rav Huna bar Yehuda objects, citing the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel where light comes first. The Mishnah is cited: Beit Shammai says light, then food, then spices, then Havdalah; Beit Hillel says light, then spices, then food, then Havdalah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda visited Rava's house; they brought light and spices, and Rava blessed over spices first, then light.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda objects that both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that light comes before spices.
The gemara cites the Mishnah: Beit Shammai says light, then food, then spices, then Havdalah; Beit Hillel says light, then spices, then food, then Havdalah.

items.text: Rava's resolution and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.text_en: Rava's resolution and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.desc_en: Rava responds that the Mishnah is according to Rabbi Meir, but Rabbi Yehuda says Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that food comes first and Havdalah last; they only dispute about light and spices. Rabbi Yochanan says the people follow Beit Hillel according to Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: Rava responds that the Mishnah is according to Rabbi Meir, but Rabbi Yehuda says Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that food comes first and Havdalah last.
Rabbi Yehuda clarifies that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is only about the order of light and spices.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that the people follow Beit Hillel according to Rabbi Yehuda's version of the dispute.

items.text: Incident with Rav Yaakov bar Abba and Rava
items.text_en: Incident with Rav Yaakov bar Abba and Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Yaakov bar Abba visited Rava's house and saw Rava bless over the first cup of wine, then over the cup of blessing, and drink. Rav Yaakov questions why two blessings are needed. Rava explains he follows the practice of the Exilarch's house, where they are uncertain if more wine will come. Rav Yaakov objects that here the cup is before them and they intend to drink it. Rava responds that he acts like the students of Rav.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yaakov bar Abba visits Rava's house and observes Rava blessing over the first cup of wine, then over the cup of blessing, and drinking.
Rav Yaakov questions why Rava recites two blessings when one blessing on the first cup should suffice.
Rava explains that he follows the practice of the Exilarch's house, where they bless each cup separately due to uncertainty about additional wine.
Rav Yaakov objects that the Exilarch's practice is justified by uncertainty, but here the cup is before them and they intend to drink it, so one blessing should suffice.
Rava responds that he acts like the students of Rav, citing Rav Brona and Rav Chananel as precedent for blessing each cup separately.

items.text: Rav Yevai Sava's ruling on when drinking is forbidden
items.text_en: Rav Yevai Sava's ruling on when drinking is forbidden
items.desc_en: Rav Yevai Sava was asked to lead the blessing after a meal, and later to give wine for drinking. He ruled that once they asked for the blessing, they had diverted their minds from drinking and are forbidden to drink.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yevai Sava was present at their meal; they first asked for the blessing and later for a drink, and he ruled that once they asked for the blessing they are forbidden to drink.
The Gemara explains the reason: because they diverted their minds from drinking.

items.text: Three Amoraim's practices regarding blessing on each cup
items.text_en: Three Amoraim's practices regarding blessing on each cup
items.desc_en: Amemar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi were at a meal. Amemar blessed on each cup, Mar Zutra on the first and last, and Rav Ashi only on the first. Rav Acha bar Rava asked which practice to follow, and each defended his own.

sub.desc_en: The narrator describes the setting: Amemar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi were at a meal with Rav Acha bar Rava present, and each had a different practice regarding blessing on cups of wine.
Rav Acha bar Rava asks the three Amoraim which practice should be followed.
Amemar defends his practice of blessing on each cup, saying he consults his own reasoning.
Mar Zutra defends his practice of blessing on the first and last cups, claiming he follows the students of Rav.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof and the distinction
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof and the distinction
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argued that the halakha does not follow the students of Rav, citing a case of Yom Tov after Shabbat where Rav said 'Yakneh' (a short Havdalah). The Gemara distinguishes: there one diverts his mind from drinking, but here he does not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that the halakha does not follow the students of Rav, citing a case of Yom Tov after Shabbat where Rav said 'Yakneh' (a short Havdalah).
The Gemara distinguishes: there (in the Yom Tov case) one diverts his mind from drinking, but here (in the meal case) he does not divert his mind from drinking.

items.text: The servant's action and the principle of Avuka for Havdalah
items.text_en: The servant's action and the principle of Avuka for Havdalah
items.desc_en: When it came time for Havdalah, the servant lit a torch from a lamp. Rav Acha bar Rava questioned why, since a lamp was available. The servant said he acted on his own, but Rav Acha noted he wouldn't have done so without a master's teaching. The Gemara explains that a torch is the preferred way to fulfill the mitzvah of Havdalah.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: when it came time for Havdalah, the servant lit a torch from a lamp.
Rav Acha bar Rava questions why the servant went to the trouble of lighting a torch when a lamp was already available.
The servant claims he acted on his own initiative, not based on any teaching.
Rav Acha bar Rava objects that the servant would not have acted this way without having heard a teaching from his master.
The Gemara explains that a torch (אבוקה) is the preferred way (מצוה מן המובחר) to fulfill the Havdalah blessing, resolving the servant's action.

items.text: The text of Havdalah and the dispute about its length
items.text_en: The text of Havdalah and the dispute about its length
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava began a long Havdalah text, but was questioned because Rav Yehuda said Rav's Havdalah was just 'Who separates between holy and profane.' He replied that he follows Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Oshaya: one may not reduce below three blessings nor add beyond seven.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava began a lengthy Havdalah text, including multiple distinctions.
The listener questioned Rav Acha bar Rava's lengthy text, citing Rav Yehuda in Rav's name that the Havdalah of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi consisted only of 'Who separates between holy and profane.'
Rav Acha bar Rava justified his lengthy text by citing Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya: one may not reduce the Havdalah below three  ברכות (blessings) nor add beyond seven.

items.text: Dispute about 'me'ein chatimah' placement
items.text_en: Dispute about 'me'ein chatimah' placement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the earlier source did not mention three or seven blessings. It explains that the phrase 'between the seventh day and the six days of creation' is a 'me'ein chatimah' (a summary of the closing), and cites Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that one must say the 'me'ein chatimah' close to the closing. The Pumbeditans say it should be 'me'ein petichatan' (summary of the opening) close to the closing. The practical difference is when a festival occurs after Shabbat: according to the one who says 'me'ein petichatan', one does not need to say 'between the sanctity of Shabbat and the sanctity of the festival', while according to the other view, one must.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the earlier source did not mention three or seven blessings.

The Gemara explains that the phrase 'between the seventh day and the six days of creation' is a summary of the closing (מעין חתימה), and cites Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that one must say the summary close to the closing, while the Pumbeditans say it should be a summary of the opening (מעין פתיחתן) close to the closing.

The Gemara explains the practical difference between the two views: when a festival occurs after Shabbat, according to the one who says summary of the opening, one does not need to say 'between the sanctity of Shabbat and the sanctity of the festival', while according to the other view, one must.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on number of blessings
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on number of blessings
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a statement by Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya: one who reduces should not reduce below three, and one who adds should not add beyond seven.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Oshaya states that one who reduces should not reduce below three, and one who adds should not add beyond seven.

items.text: Baraita challenge and resolution with Tannaim
items.text_en: Baraita challenge and resolution with Tannaim
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that lists occasions for Havdalah and says a regular person says many, while an irregular one says one. This challenges the minimum of three. The Gemara resolves that it is a dispute among Tannaim: Rabbi Yochanan says the 'sons of the holy ones' (Rabbi Menachem bar Simai) says one, but the people practice three. A message from Rav Shmuel bar Idi says Chananya his brother says one, but the halakha is not like him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita listing occasions for Havdalah and stating that a regular person says many, while an irregular one says one, challenging the minimum of three.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita reflects a dispute among Tannaim, citing Rabbi Yochanan that the 'sons of the holy ones' (Rabbi Menachem bar Simai) says one, but the people practice three.
The Gemara identifies Rabbi Menachem bar Simai as the 'sons of the holy ones' and explains the epithet because he never gazed at the image on a coin.
Rav Shmuel bar Idi reports that Chananya his brother says one, but the halakha is not like him.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's requirement and baraita on order
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's requirement and baraita on order
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says one must say distinctions similar to those in the Torah. A baraita is cited listing the order of Havdalah, including 'between sea and dry land', and the closing formulas: 'Seder Bereishit', 'Yotzer Bereishit', or 'Mekadesh Yisrael'. The Gemara objects that 'between sea and dry land' is not written as a distinction in the Torah, and suggests removing it.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that lists the order of Havdalah, including 'between the sea and the dry land' and 'between the upper waters and the lower waters', which are not explicit separations in the Torah.
A baraita is cited that lists the order of Havdalah distinctions, including 'between sea and dry land' and other pairs, and presents the closing formulas of different authorities.
The baraita continues with the closing formula and the opinion of others, and the Gemara objects that 'between the sea and the dry land' is not written as a separation in the Torah.

The Gemara answers that 'between the sea and the dry land' is derived from a verse, and similarly explains that 'between priests and Levites and Israelites' includes two separations: between Levites and Israelites, and between priests and Levites, each supported by a verse.

items.text: Resolution of the count of seven distinctions
items.text_en: Resolution of the count of seven distinctions
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if so, 'between the seventh day and the six days of creation' is also a 'me'ein chatimah', so we lack one and there are not seven. They answer: 'priests, Levites, and Israelites' are two matters: between Levites and Israelites (from the verse about the tribe of Levi) and between priests and Levites (from the verse about Aaron).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if 'between the seventh day and the six days of creation' is only a 'me'ein chatimah' (echo of the closing), then the count of seven distinctions is missing one.

The Gemara resolves that 'priests, Levites, and Israelites' counts as two distinctions: between Levites and Israelites (from the verse about the tribe of Levi) and between priests and Levites (from the verse about Aaron).

items.text: Dispute about the closing formula and a blessing
items.text_en: Dispute about the closing formula and a blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: with what does one close? Rav says 'Mekadesh Yisrael', Shmuel says 'Hamavdil bein kodesh lechol'. Abaye (or Rav Yosef) curses the one who follows Rav. A Tanna taught in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya: whoever closes with 'Mekadesh Yisrael vehamavdil bein kodesh lechol' will have his days and years lengthened.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what closing formula one should recite in the Havdalah blessing.
Rav says the closing formula is 'מקדש ישראל' (Who sanctifies Israel).
Shmuel says the closing formula is 'המבדיל בין קודש לחול' (Who separates between sacred and profane).
Abaye (or Rav Yosef) curses the one who follows Rav's opinion.

sub.text: Supporting baraita in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya that whoever closes with both 'מקדש ישראל' and 'המבדיל בין קודש לחול' will have his days and years lengthened.

items.text: Conclusion of earlier dispute
items.text_en: Conclusion of earlier dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the law does not follow the earlier opinion (presumably that of Rabbi Meir or another Tanna) regarding Havdalah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that the law does not follow the earlier opinion regarding Havdalah.

items.text: Ulla's Havdalah practice and the ensuing incident
items.text_en: Ulla's Havdalah practice and the ensuing incident
items.desc_en: Ulla visits Pumbedita, and Rav Yehuda sends Abaye to observe how Ulla recites Havdalah. Ulla says only 'Baruch hamavdil bein kodesh lechol.' When Rav Yehuda hears this from Abaye, he criticizes his son Rav Yitzchak for not going himself, implying that the teaching would have been more authoritative if heard directly.

sub.desc_en: The gemara narrates that Ulla visited Pumbedita, Rav Yehuda sent Abaye to observe Ulla's Havdalah, and Abaye reported that Ulla recited only 'ברוך המבדיל בין קודש לחול' (Blessed is He who separates between sacred and profane).
Rav Yehuda criticizes his son Rav Yitzchak for not going himself to hear Ulla, implying that the teaching would have been more authoritative if heard directly from Ulla's mouth.

items.text: General rules of blessing structure
items.text_en: General rules of blessing structure
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that lists exceptions to the rule that all blessings open and close with 'Baruch': blessings over mitzvot, fruits, a blessing adjacent to another, and the final blessing of Shema. It notes that some open but do not close, and some close but do not open, and specifically mentions that 'Hatov vehametiv' opens with 'Baruch' but does not close with it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that lists exceptions to the rule that all blessings open and close with 'Baruch': blessings over mitzvot, fruits, a blessing adjacent to another, and the final blessing of Shema.

The baraita explains that some blessings open but do not close with 'Baruch', and some close but do not open, and specifically mentions that 'Hatov vehametiv' opens with 'Baruch' but does not close with it.

items.text: Ulla's defense of his position
items.text_en: Ulla's defense of his position
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty against Ulla's view, and Ulla responds that the blessing for havdalah is like a blessing over a commandment, which is an expression of praise, so it is appropriate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty against Ulla's position.
Ulla responds that the blessing for havdalah is like a blessing over a commandment, which is an expression of praise, so it is appropriate.

items.text: Shabbat establishes itself for kiddush
items.text_en: Shabbat establishes itself for kiddush
items.desc_en: Rav Hannanya bar Shelemaya and Rav's students were sitting at a meal, and Rav Hamnuna Saba told them they need not interrupt to declare Shabbat, because Shabbat establishes itself, as Rav said: just as Shabbat establishes for tithes, so it establishes for kiddush.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hannanya bar Shelemaya and Rav's students were eating, and Rav Hamnuna Saba told them they need not interrupt to declare Shabbat, because Shabbat establishes itself.
Rav is cited: just as Shabbat establishes itself for tithes, so it establishes itself for kiddush.

items.text: Havdalah is not established by Shabbat
items.text_en: Havdalah is not established by Shabbat
items.desc_en: They thought that just as Shabbat establishes for kiddush, so it establishes for havdalah, but Rav Amram said in the name of Rav: Shabbat establishes for kiddush, but not for havdalah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that just as Shabbat establishes for kiddush, so it establishes for havdalah.
Rav Amram reports in the name of Rav that Shabbat establishes for kiddush but not for havdalah.

items.text: Limitations on interrupting for Shabbat
items.text_en: Limitations on interrupting for Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the rule about not interrupting applies only to eating, not drinking, and only to wine or beer, not water.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the rule about not interrupting applies only to not interrupting an existing meal, but one should not begin a meal at all.
The Gemara clarifies that the prohibition of interrupting applies only to eating, not to drinking.
The Gemara further clarifies that the prohibition of drinking applies only to wine or beer, not to water.

items.text: Dispute about drinking water before havdalah
items.text_en: Dispute about drinking water before havdalah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna saw a man drinking water before havdalah and warned him about the danger of askara, citing Rabbi Akiva that one who tastes anything before havdalah dies of askara. However, the rabbis of Rav Ashi's house were not concerned about water.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute with Rav Huna, who saw a man drinking water before havdalah and warned him that anyone who tastes anything before havdalah dies of askara, citing Rabbi Akiva.
The gemara notes that the rabbis of Rav Ashi's house were not concerned about drinking water before havdalah, indicating a lenient position.

items.text: One who missed kiddush on Friday night
items.text_en: One who missed kiddush on Friday night
items.desc_en: Ravina asked Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak whether one who did not recite kiddush on Friday night can recite it throughout the day. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answered in the affirmative, based on a parallel with havdalah. An objection was raised from a baraita that distinguishes between night and day, but the Gemara resolves that the baraita does not say 'if' (דְאִי), implying it is not a conditional case.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak whether one who did not recite kiddush on Friday night can recite it throughout the day.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers in the affirmative, drawing a parallel from the ruling of the sons of Rabbi Chiyya regarding havdalah.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that distinguishes between night (which has קידוש על הכוס) and day (which does not).
The Gemara argues that if the ruling were as Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said, the baraita should have mentioned the possibility of reciting kiddush on the day after missing it at night.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the objection by noting that the baraita does not use the conditional term 'דְאִי' (if), so it is not addressing the case of one who missed kiddush at night.

items.text: Preference for day honor over night honor
items.text_en: Preference for day honor over night honor
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion: the honor of the day takes precedence over the honor of the night, and if one has only one cup, he recites the blessing over it for the day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita stating that the honor of the day takes precedence over the honor of the night, and if one has only one cup, he recites the blessing over it for the day.

items.text: The principle of cherishing a mitzvah at its time
items.text_en: The principle of cherishing a mitzvah at its time
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Kiddush of the day takes precedence over honor of the day (and honor of the night). It questions why one cannot postpone the cup until the next day and use it for both Kiddush and Havdalah. The answer is that a mitzvah is cherished at its proper time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that Kiddush of the day (קידוש היום) takes precedence over honor of the day (כבוד יום) and honor of the night (כבוד לילה).
The Gemara questions why one cannot postpone the cup until the next day and use it for both Kiddush and Havdalah.
The answer is given that a מצוה (commandment) is cherished at its proper time (חביבה מצוה בשעתה).

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about Havdalah
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about Havdalah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle by citing a baraita: one who enters his home at the conclusion of Shabbat recites blessings over wine, light, and spices, and then says Havdalah over the cup. If he has only one cup, he postpones it until after the meal and strings all the blessings after it, showing that we do not say a mitzvah is cherished at its time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by asking whether we indeed say 'a mitzvah is cherished at its time', citing a baraita about one entering his home on מוצאי שבת (Saturday night) who recites blessings over wine, light, and spices.
The baraita continues that if one has only one cup, he leaves it until after the meal and strings all the blessings after it, contradicting the principle of cherishing a mitzvah at its time.

items.text: Distinction between entering and leaving the day
items.text_en: Distinction between entering and leaving the day
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that there is a distinction between entering the day (Kiddush) and leaving the day (Havdalah): for entering, the earlier the better and we cherish it; for leaving, we delay it so it is not a burden upon us.

sub.desc_en: Rava responds humbly that he is not a sage, not a seer, not a unique individual, but a learner and arranger, and that they rule in the study hall (בית מדרש) like him.

Rava distinguishes between bringing in the day (עיולי יומא) and taking out the day (אפוקי יומא): for bringing in the day, the earlier the better and we cherish it; for taking out the day, we delay it so it is not a burden upon us.

items.text: Inferences from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Inferences from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives several halakhot from the Mishnah: one who recites Havdalah in prayer must also recite it over a cup; a blessing requires a cup; a cup of blessing requires a minimum measure; the one who blesses must taste; tasting it invalidates it; and if one tasted, he may still recite Havdalah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara announces that it will derive several halakhot from the Mishnah.
The Gemara infers that one who recites Havdalah in prayer must also recite it over a cup of wine.
The Gemara infers that a blessing requires a cup of wine.
The Gemara infers that a cup of blessing requires a minimum measure.
The Gemara infers that the one who recites the blessing must taste the wine.
The Gemara infers that tasting the wine invalidates it for the blessing.
The Gemara infers that if one tasted the wine, he may still recite Havdalah.

items.text: Gemara's inference about the cup of blessing
items.text_en: Gemara's inference about the cup of blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from a previous statement that one can say two sanctifications over one cup, and that this follows Beit Shammai according to Rabbi Yehuda. Rav Ashi explains that the statement 'tasting it invalidates it' and 'the cup of blessing requires a measure' are one and the same, with the latter being the reason for the former.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from a previous statement that one can say two sanctifications over one cup, and that this follows Beit Shammai according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Ashi explains that the statement 'tasting it invalidates it' and 'the cup of blessing requires a measure' are one and the same, with the latter being the reason for the former.

items.text: Amoraim's strictness about a chipped cup
items.text_en: Amoraim's strictness about a chipped cup
items.desc_en: Various Amoraim were particular about using a chipped vessel for Kiddush: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi was particular about a chipped jug, Rav Idi bar Shisha about a chipped cup, and Mar bar Rav Ashi even about a chipped barrel.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi was particular about a chipped jug, Rav Idi bar Shisha about a chipped cup, and Mar bar Rav Ashi even about a chipped barrel, demonstrating strictness regarding the Kiddush cup's perfection.

items.text: Source for Kiddush at night and day
items.text_en: Source for Kiddush at night and day
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from 'Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it' that one must recite Kiddush over wine. The Gemara questions the baraita's logic, since the primary Kiddush is at night, and the verse mentions 'day'. The baraita is reinterpreted: the verse teaches Kiddush at its entrance (night), and then asks about day, deriving it from the same verse.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it' and derives that one must recite קידוש (Kiddush) over wine, initially understanding the verse to refer to the day, and then asking about the night, deriving it from the same verse.
The Gemara objects that the primary קידוש (Kiddush) is at night, as one sanctifies the beginning of the day, and the baraita's logic is backwards: it seeks a source for night from a verse about day.
The Gemara reinterprets the baraita: the verse teaches קידוש (Kiddush) at the entrance of שבת (Shabbat), i.e., night, and then asks about the day, deriving it from the same verse.

items.text: What blessing is recited for Kiddush during the day
items.text_en: What blessing is recited for Kiddush during the day
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says that for daytime Kiddush one recites 'Borei pri hagafen'. Rav Ashi once visited Machoza and was asked to recite 'Kiddusha Rabba'. He mistakenly thought it required a long blessing, but an elder showed him that one simply bows and drinks, and Rav Ashi applied the verse 'The wise man's eyes are in his head' to himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what blessing is recited for קידוש (sanctification) during the day.
Rav Yehuda answers that one recites the blessing 'בורא פרי הגפן' (Who creates the fruit of the vine).

The Gemara relates that Rav Ashi visited Machoza and was asked to recite 'קידושא רבה' (the great Kiddush); he mistakenly thought it required a long blessing, but an elder showed him that one simply bows and drinks, and Rav Ashi applied the verse 'החכם עיניו בראשו' (The wise man's eyes are in his head) to himself.

items.text: Time limit for Havdalah after Shabbat
items.text_en: Time limit for Havdalah after Shabbat
items.desc_en: The children of Rabbi Chiya taught that one who did not recite Havdalah at the conclusion of Shabbat may do so throughout the entire Shabbat. Rabbi Zeira limits this until the fourth day of the week. A story illustrates this with a discussion about divorce documents, and Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi adds that one may not recite Havdalah over fire after this time.

sub.desc_en: The children of Rabbi Chiya teach that one who did not recite Havdalah at the conclusion of Shabbat may do so throughout the entire Shabbat.
The Gemara asks until when this extension applies.
Rabbi Zeira limits the time for Havdalah until the fourth day of the week.

sub.text: Story about Rabbi Zeira and Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbi Zeira and Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: A story illustrates Rabbi Zeira's ruling through a parallel discussion about divorce documents, where days are categorized relative to Shabbat.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi adds that after the fourth day, one may not recite the blessing over fire in Havdalah.

items.text: Opening statement and Rav Yitzchak's anecdote
items.text_en: Opening statement and Rav Yitzchak's anecdote
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with the rule that one who washes hands for a meal may not recite kiddush. Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta reports that Rav would sometimes recite kiddush on bread and sometimes on wine, depending on which was more beloved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with the rule that one who washes hands for a meal may not recite קידוש (sanctification over wine).

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta's anecdote
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta's anecdote
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta reports that Rav would sometimes recite קידוש on bread and sometimes on wine, depending on which was more beloved.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling and the inquiry about havdalah
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling and the inquiry about havdalah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna quotes Rav: one who has tasted food may not recite kiddush. Rav Chana bar Chinana asks Rav Huna whether one who has tasted may recite havdalah. Rav Huna permits it, but Rav Asi forbids it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna quotes Rav: one who has tasted food may not recite קידוש (sanctification of the day).
Rav Chana bar Chinana asks Rav Huna whether one who has tasted food may recite הבדלה (havdalah).
Rav Huna rules leniently: one who has tasted may recite הבדלה (havdalah).
Rav Asi objects and rules strictly: one who has tasted may not recite הבדלה (havdalah).

items.text: Rav Yirmiyah's incident with Rav Asi
items.text_en: Rav Yirmiyah's incident with Rav Asi
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba visited Rav Asi, accidentally tasted food, and was given a cup to recite havdalah. Rav Asi's wife objected, but Rav Asi explained that Rav Yirmiyah follows his own teacher's lenient view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba visited Rav Asi, accidentally tasted food, and was given a cup to recite havdalah.
Rav Asi's wife objected that Rav Asi himself does not act this way.
Rav Asi explained that Rav Yirmiyah follows his own teacher's lenient view.

items.text: Conflicting reports from Shmuel
items.text_en: Conflicting reports from Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef quotes Shmuel that one who has tasted may not recite kiddush or havdalah. Rabba quotes Rav Nachman quoting Shmuel that one who has tasted may recite both kiddush and havdalah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports Shmuel's position that one who has tasted food may not recite קידוש (sanctification) or הבדלה (havdalah).

sub.text: Rabba citing Rav Nachman citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabba citing Rav Nachman citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabba, citing Rav Nachman in Shmuel's name, contradicts the first report, asserting that one who has tasted may recite both קידוש and הבדלה.

items.text: Rava's ruling on making up missed Kiddush and Havdalah
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on making up missed Kiddush and Havdalah
items.desc_en: Rava states the halakha: if one tasted before Kiddush or Havdalah, they may still recite the blessing; if one missed Kiddush on Friday night, they may recite it all day Shabbat; if one missed Havdalah on Saturday night, they may recite it all day Sunday. Amemar transmits this ruling in a slightly different wording.

sub.desc_en: Rava states the halakha: one who tasted before Kiddush or Havdalah may still recite the blessing, and one who missed Kiddush on Friday night may recite it all day Shabbat, and one who missed Havdalah on Saturday night may recite it all day Sunday.
Amemar transmits Rava's ruling in a slightly different wording, omitting the repetition of 'טָעַם' and using 'כׇּל הַיּוֹם' for both cases.

items.text: Story of Amemar and beer for Havdalah
items.text_en: Story of Amemar and beer for Havdalah
items.desc_en: Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha, sons of Rav Chisda, relate to Rav Ashi that when Amemar visited them and had no wine, he did not recite Havdalah over beer and fasted. The next day, they brought wine, and he recited Havdalah and tasted. Another year, when again no wine was available, Amemar declared beer to be 'wine of the region' and recited Havdalah over it and tasted.

sub.text: Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha tell Rav Ashi that when Amemar visited and had no wine, he did not recite Havdalah over beer and fasted.

sub.text: Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha continue
sub.text_en: Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha continue
sub.desc_en: The next day they brought wine, and Amemar recited Havdalah and tasted.

sub.text: Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha conclude
sub.text_en: Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha conclude
sub.desc_en: Another year when no wine was available, Amemar declared beer to be 'wine of the region' and recited Havdalah over it and tasted.

items.text: Three inferences from Amemar's actions
items.text_en: Three inferences from Amemar's actions
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives three halakhot from Amemar's conduct: one who recites Havdalah in prayer must also recite it over a cup; it is forbidden to eat before Havdalah; and one who missed Havdalah on Saturday night may recite it all day Sunday.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara announces that three halakhot are inferred from Amemar's actions.
The Gemara infers that one who recites Havdalah in prayer must also recite it over a cup of wine.
The Gemara infers that it is forbidden to eat before Havdalah.
The Gemara infers that one who missed Havdalah on Saturday night may recite it all day Sunday.

items.text: Inquiry about Kiddush over beer and Rav Chisda's response
items.text_en: Inquiry about Kiddush over beer and Rav Chisda's response
items.desc_en: Rav Huna asks Rav Chisda whether one may recite Kiddush over beer. Rav Chisda responds that if even a question about פרזומא (a type of beer) and dates and figs was not resolved by the chain from Rav to Rabbi, then beer is certainly questionable. The Sages initially thought that while Kiddush may not be recited over beer, Havdalah may be. Rav Chisda then quotes Rav that just as one may not recite Kiddush over beer, so too one may not recite Havdalah over it. Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi cites Shmuel to the same effect.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna asks Rav Chisda whether one may recite Kiddush over beer.
Rav Chisda argues that if even the question about פרזומא (a type of beer) and dates and figs was unresolved through the chain from Rav to Rabbi, then beer is certainly questionable.
The Sages initially thought that while Kiddush may not be recited over beer, Havdalah may be.
Rav Chisda quotes Rav that just as one may not recite Kiddush over beer, so too one may not recite Havdalah over it.

sub.text: Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi cites Shmuel to the same effect, confirming that beer is invalid for both Kiddush and Havdalah.

items.text: Levi's beer and reactions to drinking beer
items.text_en: Levi's beer and reactions to drinking beer
items.desc_en: Levi sent Rabbi a beer that was very tasty, and Rabbi said it was worthy for Kiddush and all praises. But at night it caused him distress, and he said it both chastises and appeases. Rav Yosef swore publicly not to drink beer, and Rava said he would drink water from the dregs rather than beer.

sub.text: Narrative: Levi sends beer to Rabbi
sub.text_en: Narrative: Levi sends beer to Rabbi
sub.desc_en: Levi sent Rabbi a very tasty beer, and Rabbi praised it as worthy for Kiddush and all songs.
At night the beer caused Rabbi distress, and he said it both chastises and appeases.
Rav Yosef swore publicly not to drink beer.
Rava said he would drink water from the dregs rather than beer.

items.text: Rava's curse and Rav Huna finding Rav reciting Kiddush over beer
items.text_en: Rava's curse and Rav Huna finding Rav reciting Kiddush over beer
items.desc_en: Rava says that one who recites Kiddush over beer should have beer as his drink. Rav Huna found Rav reciting Kiddush over beer and asked him if he was acquiring a headache from beer.

sub.desc_en: Rava declares that one who recites Kiddush over beer should have beer as his drink (as a curse).
Rav Huna finds Rav reciting Kiddush over beer and asks him if he is acquiring a headache from beer.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on Kiddush over beer
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on Kiddush over beer
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that one may only recite Kiddush over wine and only bless over wine. Abaye clarifies that the meaning is that one only says 'bring a cup of blessing to bless' over wine. Another baraita states that one may not recite Kiddush over beer, but Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon permits it.

sub.desc_en: The Sages taught that one may only recite Kiddush over wine and only bless over wine.
The Gemara objects: surely one does bless over beer and water with the blessing 'שהכל נהיה בדברו' (by Whose word all things exist)?
Abaye explains that the baraita means one only says 'bring a cup of blessing to bless' over wine, not that one cannot bless over other beverages at all.
Another baraita states that one may not recite Kiddush over beer, but Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon permits it.

items.text: Amount of wine required for Kiddush
items.text_en: Amount of wine required for Kiddush
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one must taste a minimal amount of wine; Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda says a cheekful (מלוא לוגמא). Rav Huna citing Rav, and Rav Giddel from Naresh, teach that one who recites Kiddush and tastes a cheekful has fulfilled the obligation, otherwise not. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies that the tradition is from Rav Giddel without patronymic, to avoid contradiction.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states the required amount of wine for tasting: the Tanna Kamma says any amount, Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda says a cheekful (מלוא לוגמא).

sub.text: Rav Huna citing Rav, and Rav Giddel from Naresh
sub.text_en: Rav Huna citing Rav, and Rav Giddel from Naresh
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna citing Rav, and Rav Giddel from Naresh, teach that one who recites Kiddush and tastes a cheekful has fulfilled the obligation, otherwise not.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies that the tradition is from Rav Giddel without patronymic, to avoid contradiction with other statements of Rav Giddel.

items.text: Inquiry about 'close to mincha' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Inquiry about 'close to mincha' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether the Mishnah's phrase 'close to mincha' refers to the great mincha (early afternoon) or the small mincha (late afternoon). It suggests that if it means the great mincha, it is because of the Paschal lamb, lest one be drawn to continue eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's phrase 'close to mincha' refers to the great mincha (early afternoon) or the small mincha (late afternoon).
The Gemara suggests that it means the great mincha, and the reason is because of the Paschal lamb, lest one be drawn to continue eating.

items.text: Gemara's question about the timing of the prohibition
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the timing of the prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a doubt: does the Mishnah mean the prohibition begins near mincha ketana (the later afternoon) to prevent one from being prevented from eating the Passover offering, or near mincha gedola (the earlier afternoon) to prevent one from eating matzah in a gluttonous manner?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a doubt: does the Mishnah mean the prohibition begins near mincha ketana (the later afternoon) to prevent one from being prevented from eating the Passover offering, or near mincha gedola (the earlier afternoon) to prevent one from eating matzah in a gluttonous manner?

items.text: Proof from Agrippas the king
items.text_en: Proof from Agrippas the king
items.desc_en: Ravina brings a proof: the Mishnah says that even Agrippas the king, who usually eats at the ninth hour, may not eat on that day until dark. If the prohibition began near mincha gedola, this would be no novelty, as the prohibition would already apply. Therefore, it must be near mincha ketana. The Gemara then explains that the novelty is that Agrippas's ninth hour is like our fourth hour, so he might have thought he could eat earlier.

sub.desc_en: Ravina opens by citing the Mishnah's ruling that even King Agrippas, who normally eats at the ninth hour, may not eat on that day until dark.
The Gemara explains that if the Mishnah refers to near mincha ketana (the later time), then Agrippas's case is indeed a novelty, as he would normally eat before the prohibition begins.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah refers to near mincha gedola (the earlier time), then Agrippas's case is no novelty, since the prohibition would already apply at his usual eating time.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah must refer to near mincha ketana (the later time).
The Gemara questions what the novelty of Agrippas's case is even with the later time, since the prohibition would still apply at his eating hour.
The Gemara answers that the novelty is that Agrippas's ninth hour is like our fourth hour, so one might have thought he could eat earlier; the Mishnah teaches that he may not.

items.text: Permitted dipping before the meal
items.text_en: Permitted dipping before the meal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei says that one may dip in cooked dishes (מיני תרגימא) before the meal. Rabbi Yitzchak dips in vegetables. A baraita supports this: the attendant dips in innards and places them before the guests.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei permits dipping in cooked dishes, Rabbi Yitzchak dips in vegetables, and a baraita adds that the attendant dips innards and serves them to guests.
Rabbi Yitzchak practices dipping in vegetables, illustrating a lenient custom.
A baraita supports the practice: the attendant dips in innards and places them before the guests.

items.text: Scriptural support for the practice
items.text_en: Scriptural support for the practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that although there is no direct proof for this practice, there is a hint from the verse: 'Plow for yourselves a plowing, and do not sow among thorns.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse as a mere hint (not a proof) for the practice of dipping before the meal.

items.text: Rava's practice of drinking wine to stimulate appetite
items.text_en: Rava's practice of drinking wine to stimulate appetite
items.desc_en: Rava would drink wine all day on Passover eve to stimulate his appetite to eat more matzah at night. He cites a Mishnah as proof that wine stimulates the appetite.

sub.desc_en: Rava would drink wine all day on Passover eve to stimulate his appetite for eating matzah at night, citing a mishnah that wine whets the appetite.
Rava cites a Mishnah as proof that wine stimulates the appetite.

items.text: Drinking between the third and fourth cups
items.text_en: Drinking between the third and fourth cups
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that one may drink between the first two cups but not between the third and fourth. It suggests that if eating matzah after drinking would be a forbidden 'gross eating' (אכילה גסה), then drinking should be prohibited between all cups. The Gemara concludes that drinking does not interfere with the matzah obligation because it 'scrapes' (מגרר גריר) the palate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction: if wine satiates (מסעד סעיד), why is drinking between the first two cups permitted, since it would cause אכילה גסה (gross eating) of matzah?
The Gemara resolves that wine does not satiate but rather מגרר גריר (scrapes the palate), so it does not interfere with the matzah obligation.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's fast on Passover eve
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's fast on Passover eve
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rav Sheshet would fast on the eve of Passover. It suggests he holds that the Mishnah's prohibition of eating close to minchah applies to the large minchah (מנחה גדולה), and the reason is to avoid being prevented from eating the Paschal lamb. This is supported by a tradition from Rabbi Oshaya citing Rabbi Elazar about Ben Beteira's ruling. However, the Gemara rejects this, explaining that Rav Sheshet was a delicate eater (איסתניס) who could not eat in the morning and then eat at night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav Sheshet would fast on the entire eve of Passover.
The Gemara suggests that Rav Sheshet holds the Mishnah's prohibition applies to the large minchah (מנחה גדולה) and is due to concern about being prevented from eating the Paschal lamb.

Rabbi Oshaya in the name of Rabbi Elazar cites Ben Beteira's ruling that the Paschal lamb may be slaughtered in the morning on the fourteenth, supporting the view that the entire day is fit for the Paschal lamb.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that Rav Sheshet was a delicate eater (איסתניס) who could not eat in the morning and then benefit from eating at night.

items.text: Reclining for matzah, maror, and wine
items.text_en: Reclining for matzah, maror, and wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute regarding whether matzah requires reclining (הסיבה), maror does not, and wine is disputed in the name of Rav Nachman: one tradition says it requires reclining, another says it does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a tradition: matzah requires reclining (הסיבה), maror does not.

sub.text: First tradition in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: First tradition in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: One tradition reports that Rav Nachman said wine requires reclining.

sub.text: Second tradition in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Second tradition in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Another tradition reports that Rav Nachman said wine does not require reclining.

items.text: Reconciling the dispute about wine and reclining
items.text_en: Reconciling the dispute about wine and reclining
items.desc_en: The Gemara reconciles the two traditions about Rav Nachman: one refers to the first two cups (which require reclining because freedom begins), the other to the last two cups (which do not require reclining because the freedom is already established). An alternative explanation reverses the reasoning: the last two cups require reclining because freedom is then actualized, while the first two do not because we are still recounting servitude. The Gemara concludes that both opinions agree that all four cups require reclining.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the two contradictory traditions about Rav Nachman by assigning one to the first two cups and the other to the last two cups.
One version holds that the first two cups require reclining because freedom begins, while the last two do not because freedom is already established.
The alternative version reverses the reasoning: the last two cups require reclining because freedom is actualized then, while the first two do not because we are still recounting servitude.
The Gemara concludes that since both versions have been stated, all four cups require reclining.

items.text: Improper forms of reclining
items.text_en: Improper forms of reclining
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules that reclining on one's back (פרקדן) is not considered valid reclining, nor is reclining on the right side (הסיבת ימין), because it may cause the windpipe to precede the esophagus, leading to danger.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that reclining on one's back (פרקדן) or on the right side (הסיבת ימין) is not considered valid reclining.
The Gemara adds that reclining on the right side is dangerous because it may cause the windpipe to precede the esophagus, leading to choking.

items.text: Who is obligated to recline: women, sons, students, and servants
items.text_en: Who is obligated to recline: women, sons, students, and servants
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses who must recline: a wife by her husband does not need to, but an important woman does; a son by his father must recline. A dilemma is raised about a student by his teacher. Abaye testifies that when they were at the home of their master, they would recline on each other's knees, but when they came to Rav Yosef, he said they did not need to, out of reverence. A baraita is cited that a student may recline even by his teacher, but this is explained as referring to carpenters' apprentices. Another dilemma about a servant is resolved by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's statement that a servant who eats a kezayit of matzah while reclining fulfills his obligation, implying reclining is required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the basic rules of reclining: a wife by her husband does not need to recline, but an important woman does; a son by his father must recline; then raises a dilemma about a student by his teacher.

Abaye testifies that when they were at their master's home they would recline on each other's knees, but when they came to Rav Yosef, he told them they did not need to, out of reverence for the teacher.
A baraita is cited that a student may recline even by his teacher, which contradicts Abaye's testimony; the Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to carpenters' apprentices, not Torah students.

A dilemma about a servant is raised and resolved by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's statement that a servant who eats a kezayit of matzah while reclining fulfills his obligation, implying reclining is required.

items.text: Women's obligation in the four cups
items.text_en: Women's obligation in the four cups
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that women are obligated in the four cups of wine.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that women are obligated in the four cups of wine.

items.text: Opening statement: reason for four cups
items.text_en: Opening statement: reason for four cups
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides the reason for the four cups: because they correspond to the four expressions of redemption, and even the poor must drink them, as they were part of the miracle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the four cups of wine at the Seder correspond to the four expressions of redemption, and even the poor must drink them because they too were part of the miracle.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on the four cups
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on the four cups
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel stating that each of the four cups must contain enough wine to dilute a 'good cup' (a standard measure). He adds that if one drank them undiluted, in one gulp, or gave them to his household, he fulfills his obligation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda transmits Shmuel's ruling that each of the four cups must contain enough wine to dilute a 'good cup', and that drinking them undiluted, in one gulp, or giving them to one's household fulfills the obligation.

items.text: Rava's qualification on drinking undiluted wine
items.text_en: Rava's qualification on drinking undiluted wine
items.desc_en: Rava qualifies Shmuel's ruling: if one drank the cups undiluted, he fulfills the obligation of wine but not the obligation of freedom (cherut), which requires diluted wine.

sub.desc_en: Rava qualifies Shmuel's ruling: drinking undiluted wine fulfills the obligation of wine (יין) but not the obligation of freedom (חירות), which requires diluted wine.

items.text: Rav's qualification on drinking in one gulp
items.text_en: Rav's qualification on drinking in one gulp
items.desc_en: Rav qualifies Shmuel's ruling: if one drank the cups in one gulp, he fulfills the obligation of wine but not the obligation of four cups. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that giving the cups to one's household is valid only if the recipient drinks most of the cup.

sub.desc_en: Rav qualifies Shmuel's ruling: if one drank the four cups in one gulp, he fulfills the obligation of wine but not the obligation of the four cups.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that giving the cups to one's household is valid only if the recipient drinks most of the cup.

items.text: Objection from a baraita on the measure
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita on the measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states each cup must contain a revi'it (a specific volume), whether undiluted or diluted, new or old. Rabbi Yehuda adds that it must have the taste and appearance of wine. The baraita's requirement of a revi'it contradicts Shmuel's requirement of 'enough to dilute a good cup'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection by citing a baraita that requires each of the four cups to contain a revi'it (a specific volume), regardless of whether the wine is undiluted or diluted, new or old.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that the wine must have both the taste and appearance of wine.
The Gemara points out the contradiction: the baraita explicitly requires a revi'it, whereas Shmuel required 'enough to dilute a good cup'.

items.text: Resolution: both measures are the same
items.text_en: Resolution: both measures are the same
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that both measures are the same: 'enough to dilute a good cup' refers to the total for all four cups, which together equal a revi'it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that both measures are the same: 'enough to dilute a good cup' refers to the total for all four cups, which together equal a revi'it.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's requirement for taste and appearance
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's requirement for taste and appearance
items.desc_en: Rava explains Rabbi Yehuda's requirement that the wine must have taste and appearance, citing the verse 'Do not look at wine when it reddens' to show that redness is a sign of good wine.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that the wine for the four cups must have both taste and appearance of wine.
Rava explains Rabbi Yehuda's reason by citing the verse 'אַל תֵּרֶא יַיִן כִּי יִתְאַדָּם' (Do not look at wine when it reddens), indicating that redness (appearance) is a sign of good wine.

items.text: Baraita on obligation of all, including children
items.text_en: Baraita on obligation of all, including children
items.desc_en: A baraita states that all are obligated in the four cups: men, women, and children. Rabbi Yehuda questions the benefit of wine for children, and suggests that they should be given something else (like nuts or sweets) to keep them awake.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that all are obligated in the four cups: men, women, and children.
Rabbi Yehuda objects that children derive no benefit from wine, and proposes giving them nuts or sweets instead.

items.text: Practices to keep children awake on Passover eve
items.text_en: Practices to keep children awake on Passover eve
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that roasted grain and nuts are distributed to children on Passover eve to prevent them from sleeping and to encourage them to ask questions. A baraita adds that Rabbi Akiva would do this, and another baraita notes that he would leave the study hall early on Passover eve and Yom Kippur eve for this purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that roasted grain and nuts are distributed to children on Passover eve to prevent them from sleeping and to encourage them to ask questions.
A baraita reports that Rabbi Akiva would distribute roasted grain and nuts to children on Passover eve to keep them awake and asking questions.
A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer who says that matzot are snatched on Passover nights for the sake of children so they will not sleep.

sub.text: Baraita about Rabbi Akiva's study hall practice
sub.text_en: Baraita about Rabbi Akiva's study hall practice
sub.desc_en: A baraita adds that Rabbi Akiva never said it was time to leave the study hall except on Passover eve for the sake of children and on Yom Kippur eve so that they could feed their children.

items.text: The obligation to rejoice on festivals with wine
items.text_en: The obligation to rejoice on festivals with wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that one must make his children and household happy on the festival, and the Sages say this is done with wine. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between men (with wine) and women (with colored garments in Babylonia or pressed linen in Eretz Yisrael). Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira adds that when the Temple stood, joy was with meat, but now it is with wine.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating the obligation to rejoice with one's family on the festival, citing the verse 'וְשָׂמַחְתָּ בְּחַגֶּךָ', and the Sages rule that this joy is fulfilled with wine.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between men (with wine) and women (with colored garments in Babylonia or pressed linen in Eretz Yisrael), as taught by Rav Yosef.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira adds that when the Temple stood, joy was with meat (from שלמים), but now it is with wine, citing verses for each.

items.text: Measurement of the revi'it for Passover
items.text_en: Measurement of the revi'it for Passover
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak and Rabbi Yochanan describe historical measures used to determine the revi'it (quarter-log) for the four cups of wine. Rav Chisda then gives the Torah's measurement for a revi'it in fingerbreadths, citing a baraita about the minimum size of a mikveh.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that a certain jar of brine from Tzippori, which was about a log in size, was used to measure the revi'it (quarter-log) for Passover.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that an earlier eight-cup measure from Tiberias was larger by a quarter, and it too was used to measure the revi'it for Passover.
Rav Chisda gives the Torah's measurement for a revi'it in fingerbreadths: two by two fingers, with a height of two and a half fingers plus a fifth of a finger.

A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'וְרָחַץ בַּמַּיִם אֶת כׇּל בְּשָׂרוֹ' (and he shall wash all his flesh in water) the minimum size of a mikveh, which provides the basis for the revi'it measurement.

items.text: Mishnah: Measure of a mikveh
items.text_en: Mishnah: Measure of a mikveh
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a mikveh must contain 40 se'ah of water, based on a space of one cubit by one cubit by three cubits.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a mikveh must contain 40 se'ah of water, based on a space of one cubit by one cubit by three cubits.

items.text: Gemara's question about the Temple table
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the Temple table
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites Ravin bar Chinana that the Temple table was sectional, otherwise it could not be immersed in a mikveh. The Gemara objects that it could be immersed in Solomon's Sea, which held 150 mikva'ot.

sub.text: Rav Ashi citing Ravin bar Chinana
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi citing Ravin bar Chinana
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports Ravin bar Chinana's claim that the Temple table was sectional (של פרקים), because if it were solid, how could one immerse a one-amah-by-one-amah object in a mikveh?
The Gemara objects: why the difficulty? Perhaps the table was immersed in Solomon's Sea, which held 150 mikva'ot, as taught by Rabbi Chiya.

items.text: Question about danger in rabbinic decrees
items.text_en: Question about danger in rabbinic decrees
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the rabbis could institute four cups of wine, which might lead to danger, citing a baraita that one should not do things in pairs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the rabbis could institute four cups of wine, which might lead to danger, citing a baraita that one should not do things in pairs.

items.text: Answers: The night is protected
items.text_en: Answers: The night is protected
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman answers that the night of Passover is a 'night of protection' from harmful spirits. Rava adds that the cup of blessing combines for good, not for evil. Ravina says the four cups are for freedom, and each one is a separate mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman answers that the night of Passover is a 'ליל שמורים (night of protection)' from harmful spirits, so the concern about pairs does not apply.
Rava adds that the cup of blessing (כוס של ברכה) combines for good, not for evil, so it does not create a dangerous pair.
Ravina says the four cups were instituted as a way of freedom (דרך חירות), and each one is a separate mitzvah, so they are not counted as pairs.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the prohibition of pairs
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the prohibition of pairs
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the statement that one should not do his needs in pairs, suggesting it might be a mere advice. Abaye explains that the prohibition is against eating two and drinking two, or even doing his needs once, because of the danger of weakness and harm.

items.text: Baraita on drinking in pairs and Rav Yehuda's qualification
items.text_en: Baraita on drinking in pairs and Rav Yehuda's qualification
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who drinks in pairs is liable for his blood. Rav Yehuda qualifies that this applies only if he did not see the marketplace, but if he did, he is permitted. Rav Ashi testifies that Rav Chananya bar Bibi would go out and see the marketplace after each cup.

items.text: Exceptions for going out, sleeping, and bathroom; practices of Amoraim
items.text_en: Exceptions for going out, sleeping, and bathroom; practices of Amoraim
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the danger applies only to going out on the road, but not at home. Rabbi Zeira compares sleeping to going out, and Rav Papa compares going to the bathroom to going out. The Gemara questions this with Rava's practice of counting beams, and then recounts how Abaye and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak would have cups held for them, concluding that a distinguished person is different.

items.text: Ulla's statement on ten cups and the reasoning
items.text_en: Ulla's statement on ten cups and the reasoning
items.desc_en: Ulla states that ten cups are not subject to the concern of pairs, consistent with his view that the Sages instituted ten cups at a house of mourning, and they would not institute something dangerous. However, eight cups are subject to the concern.

items.text: Debate on how many cups are safe: from eight down to four
items.text_en: Debate on how many cups are safe: from eight down to four
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna say that 'Shalom' (the priestly blessing) can be counted for good but not for bad, so six cups are problematic. Rabbah and Rav Yosef say 'Vichuneka' can be counted for good, so four cups are problematic. Abaye and Rava say 'Veyishmerecha' can be counted for good. Rava acted on his view by taking the rabbis out with four cups, ignoring an incident with Rava bar Levi, attributing it to being seated in the study hall.

items.text: Rav Yosef's tradition about Ashmedai and pairs
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's tradition about Ashmedai and pairs
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports from Yosef the demon that Ashmedai, king of demons, is appointed over all pairs, and a king is not called a harmful spirit. An alternative version says that a king is wrathful and can do as he pleases, breaking fences.

items.text: Rav Papa's report on demonic harm and remedy for going out in pairs
items.text_en: Rav Papa's report on demonic harm and remedy for going out in pairs
items.desc_en: Rav Papa reports from Yosef the demon that demons kill with two, but not with four; with four they only harm. With two, whether intentional or accidental; with four, only intentional. If one inadvertently went out in pairs, the remedy is to hold his thumbs and say 'You and I are three', and if the demon says four, respond five, etc., up to a hundred and one, at which point the demon bursts.

items.text: Amemar's incantation against witches
items.text_en: Amemar's incantation against witches
items.desc_en: Amemar reports from the head of the sorceresses that if one encounters witches, he should say a specific incantation invoking hot excrement in a basket to their mouths, and that their baldness and spells should fly away.

items.text: Opening anecdote and general principle about pairs
items.text_en: Opening anecdote and general principle about pairs
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a story about a demonic threat related to pairs, then states that in the West they are not concerned about pairs. Rav Dimi from Nehardea was concerned even about the mark of a barrel, and when a barrel burst, the principle is established: whoever is concerned about pairs is affected, and whoever is not concerned is not, but one should still be cautious.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a story about a demonic threat related to pairs (זוגות), where a demon warns people about their wives' witchcraft.

The Gemara states that in the West they are not concerned about pairs, but Rav Dimi from Nehardea was concerned even about a barrel's mark; after a barrel burst, the principle is established: whoever is concerned is affected, whoever is not is not, but one should still be cautious.

items.text: Rav Dimi's tradition about pairs and the 'other thing'
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's tradition about pairs and the 'other thing'
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports a tradition that two eggs, two nuts, two cucumbers, and 'another thing' are a halakha from Sinai. The Sages were uncertain what the 'other thing' is, so they decreed concern for all pairs because of it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports a tradition that two eggs, two nuts, two cucumbers, and 'another thing' are a halakha from Sinai.
The Sages were uncertain what the 'other thing' is, so they decreed concern for all pairs because of it.

items.text: Distinction between pairs for demons and for sorcery
items.text_en: Distinction between pairs for demons and for sorcery
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the statement about ten, eight, six, four having no concern for pairs applies only regarding demons, but regarding sorcery, even many pairs are a concern.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the rule about even numbers (זוגות) not applying to ten, eight, six, four is only regarding demons (מזיקין), but regarding sorcery (כשפים), even many pairs are a concern.

items.text: Story of a man protected from sorcery by pairs
items.text_en: Story of a man protected from sorcery by pairs
items.desc_en: A story illustrates the danger: a man divorced his wife, who remarried a shopkeeper. The ex-wife tried to use sorcery against him, but he was protected by being careful about pairs. One day he drank too much and lost count, so she succeeded in harming him with a pair. A traveler later identified him as a dead man, and he was killed.

sub.desc_en: A story: a man divorced his wife, who remarried a shopkeeper. The ex-wife used sorcery against him, but he was protected by being careful about pairs. One day he drank too much and lost count, so she succeeded with a pair. A traveler later identified him as dead, and he was killed.

items.text: Rav Avira's rule: bowls and loaves exempt from pairs
items.text_en: Rav Avira's rule: bowls and loaves exempt from pairs
items.desc_en: Rav Avira states that bowls and loaves are not subject to the concern of pairs. The general rule: anything whose completion is in human hands has no concern for pairs; if its completion is in heaven's hands, we are concerned regarding food items.

sub.desc_en: The question: a shop has no pair concern; a borrowed item has no pair concern; a guest has no pair concern; a woman has no pair concern. But if a woman is important, we are concerned.
Rav Avira provides the general rule: anything whose completion is in human hands has no concern for pairs; if its completion is in heaven's hands, we are concerned regarding food items.

items.text: Exemptions: shop, reconsideration, guest, woman
items.text_en: Exemptions: shop, reconsideration, guest, woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists additional exemptions: a shop (where pairs are sold) has no concern; reconsidering a purchase has no concern; a guest has no concern; a woman has no concern, but if she is important, we are concerned.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Rabbi Yehoshua says: asparagus combines for good and does not combine for bad.

items.text: Rav Chinana: asparagus joins for good but not for bad
items.text_en: Rav Chinana: asparagus joins for good but not for bad
items.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Rabbi Yehoshua says that asparagus (a drink) combines with pairs for good (i.e., to make a pair that is beneficial) but does not combine for bad (i.e., to create a dangerous pair).

sub.desc_en: Ravina in the name of Rava: pairs are stringent. They said to him: pairs are lenient. Rav Yosef: two of wine and one of beer do not combine; two of beer and one of wine combine.

items.text: Ravina and Rav Yosef: combining different drinks
items.text_en: Ravina and Rav Yosef: combining different drinks
items.desc_en: Ravina reports in Rava's name that pairs are stringent (i.e., we are concerned), and some say pairs are lenient. Rav Yosef rules: two cups of wine and one of beer do not combine (to form a pair), but two of beer and one of wine do combine. A mnemonic is given from the laws of impurity.

sub.desc_en: Ravina reports in Rava's name that the rule of pairs (זוגי) is applied stringently (לחומרא).
An alternative version states that the rule of pairs is applied leniently (לקולא).
Rav Yosef rules that two cups of wine and one of beer do not combine to form a pair, but two of beer and one of wine do combine.
A mnemonic is provided from the laws of impurity: anything connected to something more stringent is impure, and to something lighter is pure.

items.text: Rav Nachman and Rav Mesharshiya: positioning relative to a table
items.text_en: Rav Nachman and Rav Mesharshiya: positioning relative to a table
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says in Rav's name: two cups before the table and one on the table combine; one before the table and two on the table do not combine. Rav Mesharshiya objects, arguing that we are not fixing the table but the person, and the person is already fixed. He then states that all agree: two on the table and one behind the table do not combine, citing the story of Rabbah bar Nachmani.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states in Rav's name the rule for combining cups: two before the table and one on the table combine, but one before the table and two on the table do not combine.
Rav Mesharshiya objects: we are not fixing the table but the person, and the person is already fixed, so the table's position is irrelevant.
Rav Mesharshiya resolves that all agree: two on the table and one behind the table do not combine, citing the story of Rabbah bar Nachmani.

items.text: Rav Yehuda: any mixed drink combines
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda: any mixed drink combines
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in Shmuel's name: any mixed drink (מזוג) combines to form a pair.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states in Shmuel's name that any mixed drink (מזוג) combines to form a pair.

items.text: Dispute about pouring water
items.text_en: Dispute about pouring water
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and an unnamed first opinion regarding the prohibition of pouring water. Rav Pappa qualifies that the prohibition applies only when pouring hot into cold or cold into hot, but not when the temperatures are the same.

items.text: Four life-threatening actions
items.text_en: Four life-threatening actions
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish lists four actions that put one's life at risk: relieving oneself between a palm tree and a wall, passing between two palm trees, drinking drawn water, and passing over spilled water.

items.text: Qualifications and exceptions for the four actions
items.text_en: Qualifications and exceptions for the four actions
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides detailed exceptions for each of the four actions: for relieving oneself between a palm and a wall, it is only dangerous if there is no four-cubit space and no alternative path; for passing between two palms, only if they are not separated by a public domain; for drinking drawn water, only if drawn by a child in the field; for passing over spilled water, only if not covered with earth or spit, not exposed to sun or sixty steps, and if one is not riding a donkey or wearing shoes.

items.text: Concern for sorcery overrides exceptions
items.text_en: Concern for sorcery overrides exceptions
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that all these exceptions apply only where there is no concern for sorcery; but where sorcery is a concern, one must be cautious even with all the mitigating factors. It then tells a story of a man who rode a donkey and wore shoes but still suffered harm.

items.text: Three things one should not walk between
items.text_en: Three things one should not walk between
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that one should not walk between a dog, a palm tree, or a woman, nor should they walk between you. Some add a pig or a snake. Rav Pappa advises that if one does walk between them, the remedy is to begin with 'El' and end with 'El', or begin with 'Lo' and end with 'Lo'.

items.text: Walking between two women who are menstruating
items.text_en: Walking between two women who are menstruating
items.desc_en: If two people have a menstruating woman pass between them, if it is the beginning of her period she kills one of them, if it is the end she causes a quarrel. The remedy is to begin with 'El' and end with 'El'.

items.text: Two women sitting at a crossroads
items.text_en: Two women sitting at a crossroads
items.desc_en: If two women sit at a crossroads facing each other, they are certainly engaged in sorcery. The remedy is to take an alternate path, or if none, to hold hands with another person and pass, or if alone, to recite a specific incantation.

items.text: Encountering a woman after her immersion
items.text_en: Encountering a woman after her immersion
items.desc_en: If a man encounters a woman returning from her ritual immersion and he initiates intercourse, a spirit of lewdness seizes him; if she initiates, it seizes her. The remedy is to recite a specific verse.

items.text: Sleeping under a lone palm tree or in the moonlight
items.text_en: Sleeping under a lone palm tree or in the moonlight
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak interprets a verse as referring to one who sleeps under a lone palm tree or in the moonlight, which is dangerous unless the shadow of another tree falls on him. The Gemara resolves a contradiction about sleeping in a courtyard, concluding that in a courtyard it is dangerous even with another shadow. For moonlight, it is only dangerous in the west.

items.text: Dangers of palm tree actions
items.text_en: Dangers of palm tree actions
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists three dangerous actions involving a palm tree: relieving oneself under a palm tree causes a spirit of half, sleeping under it causes a spirit of shivering, and stepping over it can lead to death or injury, unless one places a foot on it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists three dangerous actions involving a palm tree: relieving oneself under it causes a spirit of half, sleeping under it causes a spirit of shivering, and stepping over it can lead to death or injury unless one places a foot on it.

items.text: Five harmful shadows and Rav Ashi's practice
items.text_en: Five harmful shadows and Rav Ashi's practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara enumerates five types of shadows that are harmful: a single palm tree, a myrtle, a pomegranate, and a zardeta (a type of tree). Some add a willow and an arba tree. The rule is that a dense branch or a hard trunk makes a harmful shadow, except for the carob tree. Rav Ashi observed Rav Kahana avoiding all such shadows.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara enumerates five types of harmful shadows: a single palm tree, a myrtle, a pomegranate, and a zardeta tree.
Some add a willow and an arba tree to the list of harmful shadows.
The Gemara states the general rule: a dense branch or a hard trunk makes a harmful shadow, except for the carob tree.
A demoness told her son to flee from the carob tree, as it killed her husband and will kill him too, explaining why its shadow is not harmful.
Rav Ashi observed Rav Kahana avoiding all such harmful shadows.

items.text: Spirits associated with specific trees
items.text_en: Spirits associated with specific trees
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the spirits associated with different trees: pomegranate trees have spirits, zardeta trees have demons, and fig trees have sparks. The practical difference is for writing amulets.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists the spirits associated with three types of trees: pomegranate trees have spirits (רוחות), zardeta trees have demons (שידא), and fig trees have sparks (רישפי).
The Gemara asks what practical difference this classification makes.
