The Gemara answers that the practical difference is for writing amulets (קמיעא), as each type of spirit requires a different amulet.

items.text: The eyeless creature of the pomegranate tree
items.text_en: The eyeless creature of the pomegranate tree
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes a creature without eyes that resides in pomegranate trees, and the practical difference is for cutting it. A story is told of a scholar who went to relieve himself near a pomegranate tree, heard the creature coming, cut it, and it hugged a palm tree, causing it to scream and burst.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a creature without eyes that resides in pomegranate trees, and states the practical difference is for cutting it.
A story is told of a scholar who went to relieve himself near a pomegranate tree, heard the creature coming, cut it, and it hugged a palm tree, causing it to scream and burst.

items.text: The zardeta tree and sixty demons
items.text_en: The zardeta tree and sixty demons
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a zardeta tree near a town has no fewer than sixty demons, and this is relevant for writing amulets. A story is told of a bow-maker who stood near such a tree, was attacked by sixty demons, and fell ill. A rabbi who did not know this wrote an amulet for one demon, but the demons mocked him. Another rabbi who knew wrote an amulet for sixty demons, and they fled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a zardeta tree near a town has no fewer than sixty demons, and this is relevant for writing amulets.
A story is told of a bow-maker who stood near such a tree, was attacked by sixty demons, and fell ill.
A rabbi who did not know the tree's demon count wrote an amulet for one demon, and the demons mocked him.
Another rabbi who knew wrote an amulet for sixty demons, and they fled.

items.text: Two types of Keteiv Meriri
items.text_en: Two types of Keteiv Meriri
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes two types of the demon Keteiv Meriri: one before noon named 'Keteiv Meriri' that looks like a pot of camphor and turns into a bush, and one after noon named 'Keteiv Yashud Tzaharayim' that looks like a goat's horn and turns into a winnowing fan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that there are two types of the demon Keteiv Meriri, describing the appearance and transformation of each type before and after noon.

items.text: Abaye's encounter with Keteiv Meriri
items.text_en: Abaye's encounter with Keteiv Meriri
items.desc_en: Abaye was walking with Rav Pappa on his right and Rav Huna on his left. He saw Keteiv Meriri approaching from the left, so he switched them. Rav Pappa asked why he was not afraid, and Abaye replied that his hour (mazal) was favorable.

sub.desc_en: Abaye is walking with Rav Pappa on his right and Rav Huna on his left.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye why he is not afraid of the demon approaching from the left.
Abaye replies that Rav Pappa's hour (mazal) is favorable, so he is not at risk.

items.text: Times and places of Keteiv Meriri's presence
items.text_en: Times and places of Keteiv Meriri's presence
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Keteiv Meriri is definitely present from the first of Tammuz until the sixteenth, and uncertain thereafter. It is found in the shadow of a privy that is not a cubit high, in the shadows of morning and evening that are not a cubit, and primarily in the shadow of a bathroom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Keteiv Meriri is definitely present from the first of Tammuz until the sixteenth.
The Gemara states that after the sixteenth, its presence is uncertain.
The Gemara states that Keteiv Meriri is found in the shadow of a privy that is not a cubit high.
The Gemara states that Keteiv Meriri is found in the shadows of morning and evening that are not a cubit.
The Gemara concludes that Keteiv Meriri is primarily found in the shadow of a bathroom.

items.text: Three things that give power to a fever
items.text_en: Three things that give power to a fever
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef says three things give power to a fever: one who combs his hair dry, one who drinks drop by drop, and one who ties his shoes while sitting.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef lists three actions that give power to a fever: combing dry hair, drinking drop by drop, and tying shoes while sitting.

items.text: Omens of poverty and times of danger
items.text_en: Omens of poverty and times of danger
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that hanging bread in the house is bad for poverty, but only bread, not meat or fish. Also, hanging fruits, a sieve, or a broom in the house is bad for poverty. On Friday nights and Wednesday nights, harmful spirits are prevalent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that hanging bread in the house is bad for poverty, citing a folk saying that hanging a basket hangs one's sustenance.
The Gemara qualifies that the omen applies only to bread, not to meat or fish, which are normally hung.
The Gemara adds that hanging fruits and a sieve in the house are also bad omens for poverty.

sub.text: Gemara's statement about times of danger
sub.text_en: Gemara's statement about times of danger
sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that on Friday nights and Wednesday nights, harmful spirits are prevalent.

items.text: Various superstitions and their effects
items.text_en: Various superstitions and their effects
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses various superstitions: a coin for sustenance is called 'Nakid', a coin for poverty is called 'Naval'. A bowl placed on a jug's mouth is bad for poverty. Drinking water from a bowl is bad for a hernia. Eating leeks without washing hands causes fear for thirty days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists various superstitions: a coin for sustenance is called 'Nakid', a coin for poverty is called 'Naval', a bowl on a jug is bad for poverty, drinking from a bowl is bad for a hernia, and eating leeks without washing hands causes fear for thirty days.

items.text: Dangers of not washing hands after certain actions
items.text_en: Dangers of not washing hands after certain actions
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists the duration of fear caused by not washing hands after cutting hair, nails, or bloodletting, and notes that placing a hand on certain body parts invites fear or sleep.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists the durations of fear caused by not washing hands after bloodletting, haircutting, or nail-cutting, and notes that placing a hand on certain body parts invites fear or sleep.

items.text: Prohibition against drinking water on certain nights and remedies
items.text_en: Prohibition against drinking water on certain nights and remedies
items.desc_en: A baraita forbids drinking water on Wednesday and Saturday nights due to an evil spirit. If thirsty, one should recite the seven voices of David over water, or an incantation, or wake a companion, or clink a lid on a jug, or throw something into the water before drinking.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that food and drink placed under a bed are subject to an evil spirit, even if covered with an iron vessel.
A second baraita forbids drinking water on Wednesday and Saturday nights due to danger from an evil spirit.
The gemara asks: if one is thirsty on those nights, what is the remedy?
The first remedy: recite the seven voices of David over water before drinking, citing the full psalm.
The second remedy: if unable to recite the psalm, recite an incantation formula.
The third remedy: if a companion is present, wake him and announce one's thirst before drinking.
The fourth remedy: clink the lid on the jug before drinking.
The fifth remedy: throw something into the water before drinking.

items.text: Danger of drinking from rivers and lakes at night due to shabririri
items.text_en: Danger of drinking from rivers and lakes at night due to shabririri
items.desc_en: Another baraita warns against drinking from rivers or lakes at night due to the danger of shabririri (a demon). If thirsty, one should address a companion or recite a specific incantation to ward off the demon.

sub.desc_en: A baraita forbids drinking from rivers or lakes at night due to the danger of the demon shabririri.
The gemara asks what remedy exists if one is thirsty.
If a companion is present, one should address him by name and say 'I am thirsty for water'.
If alone, one should recite a specific incantation invoking the demon's name and then state 'I am thirsty for water in white cups'.

items.text: Even from a trough: necessity for publicity of the miracle
items.text_en: Even from a trough: necessity for publicity of the miracle
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the obviousness of a ruling and explains that even Rabbi Akiva, who says to make Shabbat like a weekday rather than rely on others, agrees here due to the need for publicizing the miracle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's ruling about even from a trough is necessary, as it seems obvious.

The Gemara answers that the ruling is needed even for Rabbi Akiva, who normally says to make Shabbat like a weekday rather than rely on others, but here he agrees due to the need for publicizing the miracle.

items.text: A small thing in one's house despite the principle
items.text_en: A small thing in one's house despite the principle
items.desc_en: A Tanna from the school of Elijah teaches that even though Rabbi Akiva said to make Shabbat like a weekday, one may still do a small thing in his house, identified by Rav Pappa as a cup of harasana, citing the mishnah about being bold as a leopard.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Elijah teaches that despite Rabbi Akiva's ruling to make Shabbat like a weekday, one may still do a small thing in his house.
Rav Pappa identifies the 'small thing' as a cup of harasana (a spiced drink).
The gemara supports this by citing the mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima exhorts one to be bold as a leopard to do the will of one's Father in Heaven.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's seven instructions to his son and Rav Pappa's elaboration
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's seven instructions to his son and Rav Pappa's elaboration
items.desc_en: A baraita lists seven things Rabbi Akiva commanded his son Yehoshua, including not sitting in a high place of the city to study, not entering one's home suddenly, and making Shabbat like a weekday. Rav Pappa explains the last instruction about associating with a lucky person, and Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak adds that even buying from or selling to such a person is fine, citing Job.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists seven instructions Rabbi Akiva gave his son Yehoshua, including not sitting in a high place of the city to study, not entering one's home suddenly, and making Shabbat like a weekday.
Rav Pappa explains that the instruction to associate with a lucky person means forming a partnership, not buying from or selling to him.
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak cites the verse about Job to support that even buying from or selling to a lucky person is beneficial.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's five instructions to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai in prison
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's five instructions to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai in prison
items.desc_en: While imprisoned, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai asks Rabbi Akiva to teach him Torah. Rabbi Akiva initially refuses, then instructs him with five things: hang on a great tree, teach your son from a corrected book, and do not cook in a pot used by your friend (interpreted as a divorced woman or even a widow).

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces that Rabbi Akiva gave five instructions to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai while imprisoned, and recounts their initial exchange where Rabbi Shimon asks to be taught Torah and Rabbi Akiva refuses, then Rabbi Shimon threatens to inform on him.

Rabbi Akiva instructs Rabbi Shimon: if you seek to be strangled, hang on a great tree (interpreted as rely on a great person), and when teaching your son, use a corrected book (explained by Rava or Rav Mesharshiya as a new book, since once a mistake enters an old book it remains).

sub.text: Rabbi Akiva's third instruction and its interpretation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's third instruction and its interpretation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva instructs: do not cook in a pot used by your friend, interpreted as a divorced woman during her husband's lifetime, citing Mar's statement that a divorcee who marries a divorcee brings four opinions to the bed, and alternatively even a widow.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Four things Rabbi commanded his sons
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Four things Rabbi commanded his sons
items.desc_en: Rabbi HaKadosh commands his sons: don't dwell in Shakhnatzib due to mockers, don't sit on an Aramean bed (interpreted as not reciting Shema or not marrying a convert), and don't avoid taxes lest they take all you have.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why not stand before a rising ox?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why not stand before a rising ox?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one should not stand before a rising ox, citing Rabbi Samuel's answer: because Satan dances between its horns, specifically for a black ox in Nissan.

items.text: Tanna's teaching: Distance from oxen
items.text_en: Tanna's teaching: Distance from oxen
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya teaches: distance from a tam ox is 50 amot, from a mu'ad ox is as far as the eye can see.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's teaching: Climb and throw ladder
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's teaching: Climb and throw ladder
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir says: if an ox is in a pit, climb out and throw the ladder down — don't let it climb up after you.

items.text: Rav's sayings: Names of dangerous animals
items.text_en: Rav's sayings: Names of dangerous animals
items.desc_en: Rav lists dangerous animals' names: ox's danger is 'hen hen', lion's is 'zeh zeh', camel's is 'da da', and elephant's is 'heileini hayya hila hul'ya'.

items.text: Abaye's list: Dangerous items
items.text_en: Abaye's list: Dangerous items
items.desc_en: Abaye lists: skin, fish, cup, hot water, eggs, and lice for children — all dangerous for different reasons.

items.text: Rav Papa's warning: Cat in house
items.text_en: Rav Papa's warning: Cat in house
items.desc_en: Rav Papa warns: don't enter a house with a cat without shoes, because a cat kills snakes and leaves dangerous bones.

items.text: Rabbi Ishmael's three commands
items.text_en: Rabbi Ishmael's three commands
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ishmael ben Rabbi Yosi commands: don't be a litigant with three (one plaintiff and two witnesses), don't stand on a purchase when you have no money, and don't enter a new bath lest you get crushed.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's addition: Duration of new bath danger
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's addition: Duration of new bath danger
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: the danger of a new bath lasts up to twelve months.

items.text: Tanna's teaching: Standing naked before a candle causes epilepsy
items.text_en: Tanna's teaching: Standing naked before a candle causes epilepsy
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches: standing naked before a candle causes epilepsy, and using the bed by candlelight gives epileptic children.

items.text: Rabbis' teaching: Sleeping on a child's bed causes epilepsy
items.text_en: Rabbis' teaching: Sleeping on a child's bed causes epilepsy
items.desc_en: Rabbis teach: sleeping on a bed where a child slept causes the child to become epileptic, unless the child is over a year old, sleeps on its side, or the man doesn't put his hand on it.

items.text: Gemara's rule: Don't go out alone at night
items.text_en: Gemara's rule: Don't go out alone at night
items.desc_en: The Gemara states: don't go out alone at night on specific nights (Wednesdays and Sabbaths) because the demon Agrat bat Machlat and 180,000 destroying angels roam.

items.text: Story: Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa and the demon
items.text_en: Story: Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa and the demon
items.desc_en: The demon Agrat bat Machlat initially frequented daily, but after Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa decreed she not pass through inhabited areas, she only appears on Shabbat and Wednesday eves.

items.text: Second story: Abaye and the demon
items.text_en: Second story: Abaye and the demon
items.desc_en: The demon later met Abaye, who threatened to decree she never pass through inhabited areas if she didn't heed the heavenly proclamation about him; she then only appears on Shabbat and Wednesday eves.

items.text: Rav's advice to Rav Asi on choosing a city and marriage
items.text_en: Rav's advice to Rav Asi on choosing a city and marriage
items.desc_en: Rav advises Rav Asi not to live in a city without a horse's neigh or a dog's bark, not to live in a city whose head is a doctor, and not to marry two women; if he does, he should marry a third.

items.text: Rav's advice to Rav Kahana on humility and work
items.text_en: Rav's advice to Rav Kahana on humility and work
items.desc_en: Rav tells Rav Kahana to engage in menial work rather than idle talk, and not to refuse work due to his status as a priest or great man.

items.text: Rav's advice to his son Chiyya and the Tanna on jealousy
items.text_en: Rav's advice to his son Chiyya and the Tanna on jealousy
items.desc_en: Rav advises his son Chiyya not to drink medicine, jump over a ditch, uproot a tooth, or provoke a snake or an Aramean. The Tanna adds that three should not be provoked: a small gentile, a small snake, and a small student, because their power is behind their ears.

items.text: Rav's advice to his son Aivu on commerce
items.text_en: Rav's advice to his son Aivu on commerce
items.desc_en: Rav advises his son Aivu that if he cannot succeed in Torah study, he should engage in worldly matters: sell everything except wine, and prefer a small amount from the ground over a large amount from the roof.

items.text: Advice on dates and the meaning of 'Sudana'
items.text_en: Advice on dates and the meaning of 'Sudana'
items.desc_en: The Gemara advises that if you have dates in your belt, run to a house of Sudana (a place of charity). Rava specifies up to three se'ah. Rav Papa and Rav Chisda discuss the source of their wealth, and Rav Chisda explains 'Sudana' as 'Sod Na'eh' (beautiful secret) and gemilut chasadim (acts of kindness).

items.text: Rav Papa on credit and collection
items.text_en: Rav Papa on credit and collection
items.desc_en: Rav Papa states that any sale on credit requires a guarantee, and any loan is uncertain whether it will be repaid; if repaid, the money is considered bad money.

items.text: Three things from Rabbi Yochanan in the name of the people of Jerusalem
items.text_en: Three things from Rabbi Yochanan in the name of the people of Jerusalem
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says in the name of the people of Jerusalem: when going to war, go last to come in first; treat your Shabbat as a weekday rather than need others; and associate with one whom fortune favors.

items.text: Three things from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of the people of Jerusalem
items.text_en: Three things from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of the people of Jerusalem
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says in the name of the people of Jerusalem: do not increase disgrace; if your daughter is mature, free your slave and give her to him; and be careful with your wife regarding her first husband. Rav Chisda and Rav Kahana debate the reason: due to immorality or money, and both reasons apply.

items.text: Three who inherit the World to Come
items.text_en: Three who inherit the World to Come
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan lists three who inherit the World to Come: one who lives in Eretz Yisrael, one who raises his sons for Torah study, and one who makes Havdalah over wine at the end of Shabbat. The Gemara explains this as leaving over from Kiddush for Havdalah.

items.text: Three whom God proclaims daily
items.text_en: Three whom God proclaims daily
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that God proclaims three daily: a bachelor living in a city who does not sin, a poor person who returns a lost item, and a rich person who tithes his fruits in secret. The Gemara notes that Rav Safra was a bachelor living in a city.

items.text: Opening story about Rav Safra's anger
items.text_en: Opening story about Rav Safra's anger
items.desc_en: A tanna recites a teaching before Rava and Rav Safra, causing Rav Safra to become angry. Rava rebukes him, citing the example of Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Oshaya who worked as shoemakers in the market of prostitutes but did not look at them.

items.text: Three whom God loves and three whom God hates
items.text_en: Three whom God loves and three whom God hates
items.desc_en: A baraita lists three types of people God loves: one who does not get angry, one who does not get drunk, and one who is not stubborn. It also lists three types God hates: one who speaks insincerely, one who knows testimony but does not testify, and one who sees something improper in another and testifies alone.

items.text: Story of Toviya and Ziggud
items.text_en: Story of Toviya and Ziggud
items.desc_en: The Gemara illustrates the third category with a story: Toviya sinned, and Ziggud testified alone against him before Rav Pappa. Rav Pappa had Ziggud flogged for giving Toviya a bad name by testifying alone, as per the verse 'One witness shall not rise up against a man.'

items.text: Permissibility of hating a sinner
items.text_en: Permissibility of hating a sinner
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak says in the name of Rav that it is permitted to hate such a person, citing the verse about one's enemy's donkey. The Gemara clarifies that this refers to a Jewish enemy, not a gentile, and questions how this is allowed given the prohibition against hating one's brother. It concludes that this applies when one sees the person commit a sin, as everyone hates a sinner.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's ruling and further discussion
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's ruling and further discussion
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says it is a mitzvah to hate such a person, citing the verse 'Fear of the Lord is hatred of evil.' Rav Acha the son of Rava asks Rav Ashi whether one may tell his teacher to hate such a person. Rav Ashi responds that if the teacher trusts him like two witnesses, he may tell him; otherwise, not.

items.text: Three whose lives are not lives
items.text_en: Three whose lives are not lives
items.desc_en: A baraita states that three types of people have no life: the overly merciful, the hot-tempered, and the fastidious. Rav Yosef says all these traits are found in him.

items.text: Three who hate each other
items.text_en: Three who hate each other
items.desc_en: A baraita lists three types that hate each other: dogs, roosters, and magicians. Some add prostitutes, and some add Babylonian Torah scholars.

items.text: Three who love each other
items.text_en: Three who love each other
items.desc_en: A baraita lists three types that love each other: converts, slaves, and ravens.

items.text: Four whom the mind cannot tolerate
items.text_en: Four whom the mind cannot tolerate
items.desc_en: A baraita lists four types: a poor person who is arrogant, a rich person who denies, an old adulterer, and a leader who lords over the community for nothing. Some add a man who divorces his wife and remarries her. The Gemara explains that the first tanna does not include this because sometimes the ketubah is large or he has children from her.

items.text: Canaan's five commands to his sons
items.text_en: Canaan's five commands to his sons
items.desc_en: A baraita lists five things Canaan commanded his sons: love each other, love robbery, love lewdness, hate your masters, and do not speak truth.

items.text: Six things said about a horse
items.text_en: Six things said about a horse
items.desc_en: A baraita lists six traits of a horse: loves lewdness, loves war, is haughty, despises sleep, eats much and excretes little. Some add that it seeks to kill its owner in war.

items.text: Seven excommunicated by Heaven
items.text_en: Seven excommunicated by Heaven
items.desc_en: A baraita lists seven types excommunicated by Heaven: one without a wife, one with a wife but no children, one who has children but does not raise them for Torah study, one without tefillin on head and arm, tzitzit on garment, and mezuzah on door, and one who withholds shoes from his feet. Some add one who does not recline in a mitzvah group.

items.text: Source for not consulting astrologers
items.text_en: Source for not consulting astrologers
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah says in the name of Rav Shmuel bar Marta quoting Rav from Rabbi Yosi of Hutza: The source that one should not consult astrologers is the verse 'You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God.'

items.text: Honoring one greater in any matter
items.text_en: Honoring one greater in any matter
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse about Daniel that one who knows another is greater even in one matter must honor him.

items.text: Law of a woman sitting on pure blood
items.text_en: Law of a woman sitting on pure blood
items.desc_en: A brief halakha: a woman who sits on pure blood (i.e., after her period) is forbidden to have relations. Rav says for one period (onah).

items.text: Identifying Yosef of Hutza
items.text_en: Identifying Yosef of Hutza
items.desc_en: A tanna states that Yosef of Hutza is the same as Yosef the Babylonian, Isi ben Gur Aryeh, Isi ben Yehuda, Isi ben Gamliel, Isi ben Mahalalel, and his real name is Isi ben Akavya. He is also Rabbi Yitzchak ben Tavla, Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chakla, Rabbi Yitzchak ben Il'a, and the text cuts off.

items.text: Opening aggadic sayings about frugality
items.text_en: Opening aggadic sayings about frugality
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak ben Acha is identified as the same person as Rav Yitzchak ben Pinchas of aggadah. Rava bar bar Chanah quotes Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yehudah bar Rabbi Il'ai advising to eat an onion and sit in the shade rather than eat rich foods that cause anxiety, and to spend less on food and drink to afford better housing. Ulla reports a Western proverb about the consequences of eating fatty tail versus cheap vegetables.

sub.desc_en: The gemara identifies Rav Yitzchak ben Acha of halachic tradition as the same person as Rav Yitzchak ben Pinchas of aggadah, with a mnemonic.

sub.text: Rava bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yehudah bar Rabbi Il'ai
sub.text_en: Rava bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yehudah bar Rabbi Il'ai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehudah bar Rabbi Il'ai advises frugality: eat an onion and sit in the shade rather than rich foods that cause anxiety, and spend less on food to afford better housing.

sub.text: Ulla's report of a Western proverb
sub.text_en: Ulla's report of a Western proverb
sub.desc_en: Ulla reports a Western proverb: one who eats fatty tail hides in the attic, but one who eats cheap vegetables sleeps at the city's thresholds.

items.text: Mishnah: dispute over blessing order for first cup
items.text_en: Mishnah: dispute over blessing order for first cup
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when they have mixed the first cup for him, Beit Shammai say: bless the day first, then bless the wine; Beit Hillel say: bless the wine first, then bless the day.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the dispute: when the first cup is mixed, Beit Shammai say to bless the day first, then the wine.
Beit Hillel state the opposing view: bless the wine first, then the day.

items.text: Gemara: Tosefta with reasons for both opinions and ruling
items.text_en: Gemara: Tosefta with reasons for both opinions and ruling
items.desc_en: The Tosefta elaborates: Beit Shammai argue that the day causes the wine to come, so the day is primary; Beit Hillel argue that the wine causes the kiddush to be recited, and also that the blessing over wine is more frequent, so the frequent precedes. The Gemara concludes that the halakha follows Beit Hillel.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta cites Beit Shammai's position: one blesses over the day first because the day causes the wine to come, and the day is already sanctified while the wine has not yet arrived.

The Tosefta cites Beit Hillel's position: one blesses over the wine first because the wine causes the kiddush to be recited, and also because the blessing over wine is more frequent (תדיר) and the frequent precedes.
The Gemara concludes that the הלכה (binding law) follows Beit Hillel.

items.text: Gemara: clarification of 'davar acher'
items.text_en: Gemara: clarification of 'davar acher'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what does 'davar acher' mean? It explains that if you think Beit Shammai's reason is two points and Beit Hillel's only one, here too Beit Hillel has two: the frequent and the non-frequent, and the frequent precedes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'דבר אחר' (another explanation) in the baraita means.
The Gemara answers that even according to Beit Hillel there are two reasons: the frequent (תדיר) and the non-frequent, and the frequent takes precedence.

items.text: Gemara: why state halakha explicitly?
items.text_en: Gemara: why state halakha explicitly?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why state that the halakha follows Beit Hillel? It is obvious, since a Bat Kol already ruled in their favor. Two answers are given: either this was stated before the Bat Kol, or after the Bat Kol, and it follows Rabbi Yehoshua who says we do not heed a Bat Kol.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah states the halakha follows Beit Hillel, since it is obvious given that a Bat Kol (heavenly voice) already ruled in their favor.
The first answer suggests that the Mishnah was stated before the Bat Kol was issued.
The second answer says the Mishnah was stated after the Bat Kol, and it follows Rabbi Yehoshua's view that we do not heed a Bat Kol.

items.text: Mishnah: order of dipping and items brought for the Seder
items.text_en: Mishnah: order of dipping and items brought for the Seder
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the Seder procedure: they bring before him, he dips the lettuce until he reaches the bread course. They bring before him matzah, lettuce, charoset, and two cooked dishes, even though charoset is not a mitzvah according to the first Tanna; Rabbi Eliezer ben Tzadok says it is a mitzvah. In the Temple they would bring the body of the Paschal lamb.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by describing the initial Seder procedure: they bring before him and he dips the lettuce until he reaches the bread course.
The Mishnah lists the items brought before him: matzah, lettuce, charoset, and two cooked dishes, noting that charoset is not a mitzvah according to the first Tanna.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Tzadok states that charoset is indeed a mitzvah.
The Mishnah concludes by noting that in the Temple they would bring before him the body of the Paschal lamb.

items.text: Reish Lakish's proof that mitzvot require intention
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's proof that mitzvot require intention
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish argues that the Mishnah's requirement for two dippings shows that mitzvot require intention, because otherwise one dipping would suffice for maror.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish argues that the Mishnah's requirement for two dippings proves that mitzvot require intention (כַּוּוֹנָה), because otherwise one dipping would suffice for maror.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the two dippings might be for the sake of child education, not intention. It then explains why the Mishnah specifically mentions lettuce rather than other vegetables.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the two dippings might be for child education, not for intention, and that מצות (commandments) may not require כוונה (intention).
The Gemara explains why the Mishnah specifically mentions lettuce: to teach that even with lettuce alone, two dippings are needed for child education.

items.text: Baraita supporting no intention needed
items.text_en: Baraita supporting no intention needed
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that one who ate maror without intention fulfills the obligation, supporting the view that mitzvot do not require intention.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that one who ate maror without intention fulfills the obligation, supporting the view that mitzvot do not require intention.
The baraita adds a condition that one must not pause between eating portions longer than the time it takes to eat a half-loaf (כדי אכילת פרס).

items.text: Tannaic dispute and Rabbi Yosei's view
items.text_en: Tannaic dispute and Rabbi Yosei's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the issue is a dispute among Tannaim, citing Rabbi Yosei who requires lettuce, charoset, and two dishes. The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei holds that mitzvot require intention.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the issue as a Tannaic dispute, citing Rabbi Yosei who requires lettuce, charoset, and two dishes even after the initial dipping.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei might hold that mitzvot do not require intention, and that the two dippings are merely for the children's recognition.
The Gemara objects: if so, why does Rabbi Yosei use the term 'מצוה' (commandment) regarding the second dipping, implying it is obligatory?

items.text: Discussion of the two dishes
items.text_en: Discussion of the two dishes
items.desc_en: Rav Huna identifies the two dishes as beets and rice. Rava seeks them based on Rav Huna's authority. Rav Ashi notes that Rav Huna ignores Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's view that rice is a grain. Other opinions include fish and egg, two types of meat, or bone and broth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the two cooked dishes (שני תבשילין) are that are placed on the Seder plate.
Rav Huna answers that the two dishes are beets (סילקא) and rice (ארוזא).
Rava would seek out beets and rice because they were the opinion of Rav Huna.
Rav Ashi notes that Rav Huna ignores Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's view that rice is a grain (מין דגן) and thus subject to the laws of חמץ (leaven) on Passover.
Chizkiyah says the two dishes can even be fish and the egg on top of it.
Rav Yosef says one needs two types of meat: one as a memorial for the Paschal lamb (פסח) and one for the festival offering (חגיגה).
Ravina says even a bone and its broth suffice for the two dishes.

items.text: Blessing order for maror
items.text_en: Blessing order for maror
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes with the practical ruling on the order of blessings when other vegetables are available versus when only lettuce is available.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the obvious case: when other vegetables are available, one recites the blessing 'בורא פרי האדמה' (Who creates the fruit of the ground) on them and eats, then recites 'על אכילת מרור' (on eating maror) and eats the maror.
The Gemara asks: when only lettuce (חסה) is available, what is the ruling?
Rav Huna rules: one first recites 'בורא פרי האדמה' on the maror and eats, and afterward recites 'על אכילת מרור' and eats again.

items.text: Rav Chisda's challenge and the practical ruling
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's challenge and the practical ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda challenges Rav Huna's view that one recites a blessing over maror after eating matzah, arguing that one cannot bless after being satisfied. He proposes instead that one recites both the blessing for matzah and maror at the start, eats maror, and then eats lettuce without a blessing. The Gemara notes that the halakha follows Rav Chisda, and Rav Acha bar Rava seeks other vegetables to avoid the dispute.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda objects to Rav Huna's view that one recites a blessing over maror after eating matzah, arguing that one cannot bless after being satisfied.
Rav Chisda proposes that one recites both the blessing for matzah and maror at the start, eats maror, and then eats lettuce without a blessing.

sub.text: Gemara's ruling and Rav Acha's practice
sub.text_en: Gemara's ruling and Rav Acha's practice
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the halakha follows Rav Chisda, and Rav Acha bar Rava seeks other vegetables to avoid the dispute.

items.text: The prohibition of eating matzah and maror together
items.text_en: The prohibition of eating matzah and maror together
items.desc_en: Ravina quotes Rav Mesharshiya citing Hillel that one should not eat matzah and maror together because matzah is biblical and maror is rabbinic, and the rabbinic maror would nullify the biblical matzah. This applies even to those who hold that mitzvot do not nullify each other, as that principle only applies when both are of the same level (biblical or rabbinic), not when one is biblical and the other rabbinic.

sub.text: Ravina quoting Rav Mesharshiya citing Hillel
sub.text_en: Ravina quoting Rav Mesharshiya citing Hillel
sub.desc_en: Ravina reports Hillel's ruling that one should not eat matzah and maror together because the rabbinic maror would nullify the biblical matzah.

The gemara clarifies that even for those who hold that mitzvot do not nullify each other, this principle only applies when both are on the same level (biblical or rabbinic), not when one is biblical and the other rabbinic.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna who holds mitzvot do not nullify each other
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna who holds mitzvot do not nullify each other
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies Hillel as the Tanna who holds that mitzvot do not nullify each other, based on a baraita that describes Hillel eating matzah and maror together, citing the verse 'on matzot and maror they shall eat it.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that mitzvot do not nullify each other.

The Gemara answers that it is Hillel, citing a baraita where Hillel would eat matzah and maror together, based on the verse 'עַל מַצּוֹת וּמְרוֹרִים יֹאכְלוּהוּ' (on matzot and maror they shall eat it).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge and Rav Ashi's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge and Rav Ashi's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Hillel's colleagues disagree with him, citing a baraita that interprets the verse to allow eating them separately. Rav Ashi challenges this, questioning the use of 'even' in the baraita, and then reinterprets the baraita to mean that one might think one must eat them together, but the verse teaches that even separately is valid.

sub.desc_en: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) states that Hillel's colleagues disagree with him, citing a baraita that interprets the verse 'על מצות ומרורים יאכלוהו' (they shall eat it with matzot and bitter herbs) to permit eating them separately, even without wrapping them together.
רב אשי (Rav Ashi) challenges the baraita's wording, questioning the use of 'אפילו' (even) if the Sages completely reject Hillel's practice.
רב אשי (Rav Ashi) reinterprets the baraita: it means that one might think one must eat them together like Hillel, but the verse teaches that even eating them separately fulfills the obligation.

items.text: The practical halakha for the Seder
items.text_en: The practical halakha for the Seder
items.desc_en: Since no definitive ruling was given for either Hillel or the Rabbis, the Gemara prescribes a practical procedure: recite the blessing for matzah and eat, then recite the blessing for maror and eat, and finally eat matzah and lettuce together without a blessing, as a remembrance of the Temple, following Hillel's practice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a practical procedure for the Seder: recite the blessing for מצה (unleavened bread) and eat, then recite the blessing for מרור (bitter herbs) and eat, and finally eat מצה and lettuce together without a blessing as a remembrance of the Temple, following Hillel's practice.

items.text: The requirement for hand-washing before dipping in liquid
items.text_en: The requirement for hand-washing before dipping in liquid
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar quoting Rav Oshaya states that anything dipped in liquid requires hand-washing. Rav Pappa infers from this that lettuce (chasa) requires hand-washing before being dipped.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says in the name of Rav Oshaya that anything dipped in liquid requires hand washing.
Rav Pappa infers from this that lettuce (חסה) requires hand washing before dipping.

items.text: טבילת מרור בחרוסת ונטילת ידיים
items.text_en: The necessity of dipping maror in charoset
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that maror must be dipped in charoset to neutralize the kapa (a harmful substance). It questions why hand-washing is needed if one does not touch the maror, and suggests that even without dipping, the kapa might be neutralized by smell, but hand-washing is still required in case one does dip.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בצורך לטבול את המרור בחרוסת מחמת סכנת 'קפא', ומסבירה מדוע יש ליטול ידיים אף אם לא נוגע בחרוסת, שמא יטבול.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that maror must be dipped in charoset to neutralize the harmful substance kapa.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בקביעה שיש לטבול את המרור בחרוסת מחמת סכנת 'קפא'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: if dipping is not required, why is hand-washing needed, since one does not touch the maror directly?
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בקביעה שיש לטבול את המרור בחרוסת מחמת סכנת 'קפא'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that even without dipping, the kapa might be neutralized by smell alone.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בקביעה שיש לטבול את המרור בחרוסת מחמת סכנת 'קפא'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that hand-washing is still required because one might dip the maror after all.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בקביעה שיש לטבול את המרור בחרוסת מחמת סכנת 'קפא'.

items.text: אי-שהיית מרור בחרוסת ונטילת ידיים בטיבול שני
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's warning about maror in charoset and Rav Chisda's ruling on hand-washing
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa warns not to leave maror in charoset too long, lest the sweetness of the spices nullify the bitter taste. Rav Chisda then teaches that one who washed hands for the first dipping must wash again for the second dipping.
items.desc: רב פפא אומר שאין להשהות מרור בחרוסת שמא תתבטל מרירותו, ורב חסדא מתיר ליטול ידיים גם בטיבול שני.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that one should not leave maror soaking in charoset, lest the sweetness of the spices nullify the required bitter taste.
sub.desc: רב פפא אוסר להשהות מרור בחרוסת שמא מתיקות התבלינים תבטל את טעם המרירות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda instructs Ravana Ukva that one who washed hands for the first dipping must wash again for the second dipping.
sub.desc: רב פפא אוסר להשהות מרור בחרוסת שמא מתיקות התבלינים תבטל את טעם המרירות.

items.text: מחלוקת אם נטילת ידיים נאמרה כאן או בעלמא
items.text_en: Debate on the context of Rav Chisda's ruling
items.desc_en: The rabbis question whether Rav Chisda's statement was said in this context (the seder) or elsewhere. Rav Pappa argues it was said here, as otherwise two dippings would be unnecessary. The Gemara resolves that two hand-washings are needed because one might become distracted by the Haggadah and touch food.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה אם דברי רב חסדא נאמרו על פסח או על טיבול כללי, ומסיקה שנאמרו על פסח, משום שבין הטיבולים אומרים הגדה והלל ועלולים להסיח דעת.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis challenge Rav Pappa, arguing that Rav Chisda's ruling was said in a general context, not at the seder, because if it were at the seder, one hand-washing would suffice for both dippings.
sub.desc: החכמים מקשים לפני רב פפא: דברי רב חסדא נאמרו בעלמא, ולא על פסח, שאם נאמרו על פסח, למה צריך נטילת ידיים פעמיים, הרי כבר נטל פעם אחת.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa counters that the ruling was indeed said here, because otherwise the two dippings would be unnecessary.
sub.desc: רב פפא דוחה את דבריהם: להיפך, הדברים נאמרו דווקא על פסח, שאם נאמרו בעלמא, למה צריך שני טיבולים? הרי בדרך כלל אין טובלים אלא פעם אחת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that two hand-washings are needed because one might become distracted by the Haggadah and touch food, reconciling the apparent redundancy.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם נאמרו על פסח, למה צריך נטילת ידיים פעמיים? ומתרצת: מכיוון שבין הטיבולים אומרים הגדה והלל, עלול להסיח דעתו ולגעת בטומאה, ולכן צריך נטילה שנית.

items.text: בליעת מצה ומרור
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on swallowing matzah and maror
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if one swallows matzah without chewing, he fulfills his obligation; but if he swallows maror, he does not. If he swallows both together, he fulfills matzah but not maror. If he wraps them in a fiber and swallows, he does not fulfill even matzah.
items.desc: רבא פוסק שבולע מצה יצא, אבל בולע מרור לא יצא, ואם כרכם בסיב ובלעם לא יצא אף ידי מצה.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that one who swallows matzah fulfills the obligation, but one who swallows maror does not; if he swallows both together, he fulfills matzah but not maror; if he wraps them in a fiber and swallows, he does not fulfill even matzah.
sub.desc: רבא פוסק שבולע מצה יצא ידי חובתו, אבל בולע מרור לא יצא, ואם כרכם בסיב ובלעם לא יצא אף ידי מצה.

sub.desc_en: Rava adds that if one swallows both together, he fulfills matzah but not maror.
sub.desc: רבא פוסק שבולע מצה יצא ידי חובתו, אבל בולע מרור לא יצא, ואם כרכם בסיב ובלעם לא יצא אף ידי מצה.

sub.desc_en: Rava concludes that if one wraps them in a fiber and swallows, he does not fulfill even matzah.
sub.desc: רבא פוסק שבולע מצה יצא ידי חובתו, אבל בולע מרור לא יצא, ואם כרכם בסיב ובלעם לא יצא אף ידי מצה.

items.text: הצגת מצה, מרור וחרוסת לפני כל אחד
items.text_en: Placement of matzah, maror, and charoset, and the removal of the table
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi states that matzah, maror, and charoset are placed before each person, and the table is removed only before the one reciting the Haggadah. Rav Huna disagrees, saying all items are placed before the one reciting, and the halakha follows Rav Huna.
items.desc: רב שמי בר אשי אומר שמצה, מרור וחרוסת מונחים לפני כל אחד, ורב הונא אומר שלפני מסדר ההגדה בלבד, והלכה כרב הונא.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi states that matzah, maror, and charoset are placed before each person, and the table is removed only before the one reciting the Haggadah.
sub.desc: רב שמי בר אשי קובע שמצה, מרור וחרוסת מונחים לפני כל אחד ואחד, ואין עוקרין את השולחן אלא לפני מי שאומר הגדה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna disagrees, saying all items are placed before the one reciting the Haggadah, and the halakha follows Rav Huna.
sub.desc: רב הונא חולק וסובר שכל המצות מונחות רק לפני מסדר ההגדה, וההלכה נפסקה כמותו.

items.text: טעם עיקירת השולחן
items.text_en: Reason for removing the table and Abaye's story
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the table is removed so that children will notice and ask questions. Abaye, seeing the table removed before eating, questions it, and Rabbah responds that this exempts them from reciting 'Ma Nishtanah'.
items.desc: הגמרא מסבירה שעוקרים את השולחן כדי שילדים ישאלו, ומספרת מעשה שאביי שאל ופטר את רבא מאמירת 'מה נשתנה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the table is removed.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה הטעם לעיקירת השולחן, ומשיבה בשם בית רבי ינאי שזה כדי שהילדים יכירו וישאלו.

sub.desc_en: Beit Rabbi Yannai answers that the table is removed so that children will notice and ask questions.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה הטעם לעיקירת השולחן, ומשיבה בשם בית רבי ינאי שזה כדי שהילדים יכירו וישאלו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that when Abaye saw the table being removed before eating, he questioned it, and Rabbah told him that he had exempted them from reciting 'Mah Nishtanah'.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה הטעם לעיקירת השולחן, ומשיבה בשם בית רבי ינאי שזה כדי שהילדים יכירו וישאלו.

items.text: פירוש 'לחם עוני'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'Lechem Oni'
items.desc_en: Shmuel interprets 'Lechem Oni' as bread over which one recites many things (the Haggadah). A baraitha supports this, and an alternative interpretation connects it to the word 'oni' (poverty), like a poor person's broken piece.
items.desc: שמואל וברייתא מפרשים 'לחם עוני' כלחם שעונים עליו דברים, ויש פירוש נוסף על פי כתיב 'עוני' – כלחם של עני שדרכו בפרוסה.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel interprets the verse 'lechem oni' as bread over which one recites many words (the Haggadah).
sub.desc: שמואל מפרש 'לחם עוני' כלחם שעונים עליו דברים, כלומר שמספרים עליו את סיפור יציאת מצרים.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Shmuel's interpretation, explaining 'lechem oni' as bread over which many things are recited.
sub.desc: שמואל מפרש 'לחם עוני' כלחם שעונים עליו דברים, כלומר שמספרים עליו את סיפור יציאת מצרים.

sub.desc_en: An alternative interpretation reads 'lechem oni' as 'lechem oni' (bread of poverty), comparing it to a poor person who eats a broken piece.
sub.desc: שמואל מפרש 'לחם עוני' כלחם שעונים עליו דברים, כלומר שמספרים עליו את סיפור יציאת מצרים.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's comparison to a poor person
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's comparison to a poor person
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's analogy that just as a poor person heats the oven and his wife bakes, so too here he heats and she bakes, applying it to the case of פרוסה (a piece of matzah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's analogy of a poor person heating the oven and his wife baking applies specifically to a piece of matzah (פרוסה).

items.text: The reason for bringing charoset despite it not being a commandment
items.text_en: The reason for bringing charoset despite it not being a commandment
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why charoset is brought if it is not a commandment, and Rabbi Ami answers it is for קפא (a type of dip). Rav Asi elaborates on the sequence of dips, and a folk saying is cited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Since חרוסת (charoset) is not a מצוה (commandment), why is it brought to the table?
Rabbi Ami answers that charoset is brought because of קפא (dip, to neutralize bitterness).
Rav Asi elaborates on the sequence of dipping: lettuce in ḥama (a type of dip), then ḥama in leeks, then leeks in hot water, and all dips ultimately in hot water.
The Gemara adds a folk incantation to be recited during the dipping: 'Dip, dip, I remember you and your seven daughters and your eight daughters-in-law.'

items.text: The symbolic reasons for charoset as a commandment
items.text_en: The symbolic reasons for charoset as a commandment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok says charoset is a commandment. Rabbi Levi says it is a reminder of the apple (תפוח), and Rabbi Yochanan says it is a reminder of the mud (טיט). Abaye concludes that one must both sour it (for the apple) and thicken it (for the mud).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the מצוה (commandment) associated with charoset according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok?
Rabbi Levi answers that charoset is a remembrance of the apple (תפוח) — the apple trees under which the Israelites conceived in Egypt.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that charoset is a remembrance of the טיט (mud) used by the Israelites in Egypt.
Abaye resolves the two opinions: charoset must be both thin (to recall the apple) and thick (to recall the mud).
Abaye resolves the two opinions: one must sour the charoset (for the apple) and thicken it (for the mud).

items.text: A beraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan's view
items.text_en: A beraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan's view
items.desc_en: A beraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan: spices are a reminder of straw, and charoset is a reminder of mud. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok recounts that the merchants of Charak in Jerusalem would say to take spices for the commandment.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's view: spices recall straw, and charoset recalls mud.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's testimony
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's testimony
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok testifies that the spice merchants of Jerusalem would call out: 'Come take spices for the מצוה (commandment).'

items.text: The Mishnah on the second cup and the son's questions
items.text_en: The Mishnah on the second cup and the son's questions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that after mixing the second cup, the son asks his father. If the son lacks understanding, the father teaches him. The questions of Mah Nishtanah are listed, and the father begins with disgrace and ends with praise, expounding from 'Arami oved avi' until the entire portion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that after mixing the second cup, the son asks his father, and if the son lacks understanding, the father teaches him.
The Mishnah lists the four questions of Mah Nishtanah regarding matzah, maror, roasted meat, and dipping twice.
The Mishnah concludes that the father teaches according to the son's understanding, beginning with disgrace and ending with praise, expounding from 'Arami oved avi' until the entire portion.

items.text: Gemara on who asks the questions
items.text_en: Gemara on who asks the questions
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a beraita: if the son is wise, he asks; if not, his wife asks; if not, he asks himself; even two scholars ask each other.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches: If the son is wise, he asks; if not, his wife asks; if not, he asks himself; even two Torah scholars who know the laws of Passover ask each other.

items.text: Rava and Rav Safra's emendations to the Mishnah's question about dipping
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Safra's emendations to the Mishnah's question about dipping
items.desc_en: Rava objects that the Mishnah's wording 'we dip once' is problematic because every day we dip at least once. He emends to 'we are not obligated to dip even once'. Rav Safra objects further that obligation does not apply to children, and emends to 'we do not dip even once'.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that the Mishnah's wording 'we dip once' is problematic because every day we dip at least once, and emends to 'we are not obligated to dip even once'.
Rav Safra objects that obligation does not apply to children, and emends to 'we do not dip even once'.

items.text: The dispute about what constitutes 'disgrace' in the Maggid
items.text_en: The dispute about what constitutes 'disgrace' in the Maggid
items.desc_en: Rav says the disgrace is 'originally our ancestors were idol worshippers', while Shmuel says it is 'we were slaves'. Rav Nachman tests his servant Daru, who says a freed slave should thank and praise, and Rav Nachman concludes that this exempts one from saying Mah Nishtanah, and he begins with 'Avadim Hayinu'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes the 'disgrace' with which the Maggid begins.
Rav answers that the disgrace is 'originally our ancestors were idol worshippers'.
Shmuel answers that the disgrace is 'we were slaves'.
Rav Nachman asks his servant Daru what a freed slave should say, and Daru responds that he should thank and praise.
Rav Nachman concludes that Daru's answer exempts one from saying Mah Nishtanah, and he begins with 'Avadim Hayinu'.

items.text: Beginning of the Mishnah about Rabban Gamliel's statement
items.text_en: Beginning of the Mishnah about Rabban Gamliel's statement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins Rabban Gamliel's statement that whoever did not say the three things (Pesach, Matzah, Maror) has not fulfilled his obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins Rabban Gamliel's statement: 'Anyone who did not say...' (the three things of Passover, matzah, and maror has not fulfilled his obligation).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The three items and the obligation to see oneself as redeemed
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The three items and the obligation to see oneself as redeemed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the three essential items of the Seder—Pesach, matzah, and maror—and explains their symbolic meanings. It then states that in every generation one must see oneself as personally having left Egypt, leading to the obligation to praise God.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute on how far to recite Hallel and the concluding blessing
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute on how far to recite Hallel and the concluding blessing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding how much of Hallel to recite at the Seder, and a dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva about the concluding blessing of the Haggadah.

items.text: Gemara: Rava's rulings on the Haggadah and lifting matzah and maror
items.text_en: Gemara: Rava's rulings on the Haggadah and lifting matzah and maror
items.desc_en: Rava states that one must say 'and He took us out from there' in the Haggadah, and that one must lift the matzah and maror when reciting their explanations, but not the meat, as it would appear to be eating consecrated food outside the Temple.

items.text: Gemara: Rav Acha bar Yaakov exempts a blind person from the Haggadah
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav Acha bar Yaakov exempts a blind person from the Haggadah
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov derives from a verbal analogy that a blind person is exempt from reciting the Haggadah, just as the Torah excludes a blind son from the law of the rebellious son.

items.text: Gemara: Challenge and resolution regarding the blind person's exemption
items.text_en: Gemara: Challenge and resolution regarding the blind person's exemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Acha bar Yaakov's ruling by citing that Rav Yosef and Rav Sheshet, who were blind, would recite the Haggadah, implying they held that matzah nowadays is rabbinic. The Gemara resolves that even those who hold matzah is rabbinic still require the Haggadah because rabbinic enactments follow the biblical model, but the verbal analogy for the blind person is rejected as the verse 'because of this' refers to matzah and maror, not to seeing.

items.text: Gemara: Conclusion with the phrase 'Therefore we are obligated'
items.text_en: Gemara: Conclusion with the phrase 'Therefore we are obligated'
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes by citing the Mishnah's phrase 'Therefore we are obligated,' which serves as a transition to the next part of the Haggadah.

items.text: Dispute over the meaning of 'Halleluyah' and similar words
items.text_en: Dispute over the meaning of 'Halleluyah' and similar words
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda cites Rabbi Yochanan that 'Halleluyah', 'Kesyah', and 'Yedidyah' are each one word. Rav says 'Kesyah' and 'Merchavyah' are one word. Rabbah says only 'Merchavyah' is one word.

items.text: Three unresolved inquiries about these words
items.text_en: Three unresolved inquiries about these words
items.desc_en: Three inquiries are raised: for Rav Chisda, what about 'Merchav Yah'? It remains unresolved. For Rav, what about 'Yedidyah'? Rav says it is divided into two: 'Yedid' is profane, 'Yah' is holy. For Rav, what about 'Halleluyah'? Rav saw scrolls where 'Hallelu' and 'Yah' were written on separate lines.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's view on 'Halleluyah' and the ten praises of Psalms
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's view on 'Halleluyah' and the ten praises of Psalms
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says 'Halleluyah' means 'praise Him with many praises'. He also states that Psalms was said with ten expressions of praise, and 'Halleluyah' is the greatest because it includes both the name and praise together.

items.text: Shmuel on the authorship of the Song at the Sea and Hallel
items.text_en: Shmuel on the authorship of the Song at the Sea and Hallel
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says Moses and Israel said the Song at the Sea. Hallel was instituted by the prophets for Israel to recite on every occasion and when they are redeemed.

items.text: Dispute over the author of Hallel: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yosei, and his colleagues
items.text_en: Dispute over the author of Hallel: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yosei, and his colleagues
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir says David said all praises in Psalms. Rabbi Yosei says his son Elazar said Moses and Israel said Hallel at the sea, but his colleagues say David said it. Rabbi Yosei's view seems more plausible: could Israel have slaughtered their Paschal lambs and taken their lulavs without reciting a song? Another objection: could they say Hallel while Micah's idol stood in Beit El?

items.text: Dispute over whether David's Psalms were for himself or the community
items.text_en: Dispute over whether David's Psalms were for himself or the community
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: Rabbi Eliezer says David said all Psalms for himself; Rabbi Yehoshua says for the community; the Sages say some for himself and some for the community, distinguished by singular or plural language.

items.text: Interpretations of Psalm headings and the requirement of joy for prophecy
items.text_en: Interpretations of Psalm headings and the requirement of joy for prophecy
items.desc_en: Various headings are interpreted: 'Nitzuach' and 'Niggunn' are for the future; 'Maskil' is through an interpreter; 'Ledavid Mizmor' means the Shekhina rested on him first; 'Mizmor Ledavid' means he sang first. This teaches that the Shekhina rests only through joy of a mitzva. Rav Yehuda says the same applies to halakha; Rav Nachman says to a good dream. A contradiction is raised from Rav Giddel about a student's lips dripping bitterness, resolved by distinguishing between before and after the teacher opens the lesson.

items.text: Multiple opinions on who said Hallel
items.text_en: Multiple opinions on who said Hallel
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: Rabbi Eliezer says Moses and Israel said it at the sea; Rabbi Yehuda says Joshua and Israel; Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i says Deborah and Barak; Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says Hezekiah and his company; Rabbi Akiva says Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah; Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says Mordechai and Esther. The Sages say the prophets instituted it for every occasion and redemption.

items.text: Dispute over whether 'Halleluyah' ends or begins a chapter
items.text_en: Dispute over whether 'Halleluyah' ends or begins a chapter
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says 'Halleluyah' ends a chapter; Rabbah bar Rav Huna says it begins one. Rav Chisda saw scrolls in Rav Chanin's house where 'Halleluyah' was written in the middle, indicating uncertainty. Rav Chanin bar Rava lists specific verses where the following 'Halleluyah' begins a chapter. Karaites add more examples.

items.text: Tannaic dispute on how far Hallel is recited
items.text_en: Tannaic dispute on how far Hallel is recited
items.desc_en: Beit Shammai says until 'Em HaBanim Semeichah'; Beit Hillel says until 'Chalamish Lema'yeno Mayim'. Another baraita: Beit Shammai says until 'B'tzeit Yisrael MiMitzrayim'; Beit Hillel says until 'Lo Lanu Hashem Lo Lanu'.

items.text: Dispute over the placement of 'Halleluyah' in Hallel
items.text_en: Dispute over the placement of 'Halleluyah' in Hallel
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes a dispute about whether 'Halleluyah' marks the end of a section or the beginning. Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna each offer a resolution, but both are challenged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute about the end of Hallel is about whether 'Halleluyah' marks the beginning or end of a section.
Rav Chisda resolves the dispute by asserting that everyone agrees 'Halleluyah' ends a section, and the disagreement is about whether 'עַד' includes the endpoint.
The Gemara objects that if 'Halleluyah' ends a section, the disputants could have simply said 'until Halleluyah' rather than specifying a psalm.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna resolves the dispute by asserting that everyone agrees 'Halleluyah' begins a section, and the disagreement is about whether 'עַד' excludes the endpoint.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if 'Halleluyah' begins a section, the disputants could have simply said 'until Halleluyah' rather than specifying a psalm.

items.text: Difference between prayer and Hallel in concluding blessing
items.text_en: Difference between prayer and Hallel in concluding blessing
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the blessing after Hallel concludes with 'Ga'al Yisrael' (past tense), while the prayer concludes with 'Go'el Yisrael' (present tense), because prayer is a request for mercy.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one concludes the blessing after Hallel with redemption.
Rava explains that the blessing after Shema and Hallel concludes with 'גאל ישראל' (past tense), while the prayer concludes with 'גואל ישראל' (present tense), because prayer is a request for mercy.

items.text: Difference between kiddush and prayer in sanctification blessing
items.text_en: Difference between kiddush and prayer in sanctification blessing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains that kiddush concludes with 'Asher Kiddeshanu' (past tense), while prayer concludes with 'Kaddeshenu' (request), because prayer is a request for mercy.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains that kiddush concludes with 'אשר קדשנו' (past tense) while prayer concludes with 'קדשנו' (request), because prayer is a request for mercy.

items.text: Requirement to mention the Exodus in kiddush
items.text_en: Requirement to mention the Exodus in kiddush
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov states that one must mention the Exodus from Egypt in the kiddush of the day, derived from a scriptural analogy.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov rules that one must mention the Exodus from Egypt in the kiddush of the day, deriving this from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between the verses 'לְמַעַן תִּזְכּוֹר אֶת יוֹם' and 'זָכוֹר אֶת יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת לְקַדְּשׁוֹ'.

items.text: Concluding blessings of prayer and haftarah, and the Patriarchs
items.text_en: Concluding blessings of prayer and haftarah, and the Patriarchs
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Sheila states that prayer concludes with 'Matsmiach Keren Yeshuah' and haftarah with 'Magen David'. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish connects the blessings of the Patriarchs to the Amidah, and a baraita teaches that only Abraham is used for the concluding seal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Sheila states that the prayer concludes with 'Matsmiach Keren Yeshuah' and the haftarah with 'Magen David'.
Rav Yosef teaches a baraita that the verse 'I will make you a great name' refers to the blessing 'Magen David'.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish connects the three blessings of the Patriarchs in the Amidah to the three promises made to Abraham.
The baraita concludes that one might think to seal with all three Patriarchs, but the verse 'and be a blessing' teaches that only Abraham is used for the concluding seal.

items.text: Dispute over the concluding blessing for Shabbat and Festivals
items.text_en: Dispute over the concluding blessing for Shabbat and Festivals
items.desc_en: Rava disputes the elders of Pumbedita about whether the prayer and kiddush for Shabbat and Festivals conclude with 'Mekadesh HaShabbat' or 'Mekadesh Yisrael VeHaZemanim'. After analysis and practical cases, the Gemara concludes that the halakha follows the elders of Pumbedita.

sub.desc_en: Rava reports the position of the elders of Pumbedita regarding the concluding blessing for Shabbat and Festivals, and then states his own opposing view.

Rava explains the reasoning behind the elders' position: Shabbat is fixed by God, so the blessing mentions Shabbat alone; Festivals depend on Israel's calendar-setting, so the blessing mentions both Israel and the seasons.
Rava explains his own reasoning: prayer is public, so it uses 'Mekadesh Yisrael'; kiddush is private, so for Shabbat it uses 'Mekadesh HaShabbat' and for Festivals 'Mekadesh Yisrael VeHaZemanim'.
The Gemara objects that Rava's distinction fails because prayer can be private and kiddush can be public, and notes that Rava himself ultimately follows the essential principle.

Two incidents show that Rava and Rav Pappa accepted the elders' position: Ulla bar Rav led prayer before Rava according to the elders' view without objection, and Rav Nathan led before Rav Pappa and was praised.
Ravina testifies that Marimar ruled in practice that the halakha follows the elders of Pumbedita, silencing those who objected.

items.text: The four cups at the Seder and the third and fourth cups
items.text_en: The four cups at the Seder and the third and fourth cups
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the third cup for Grace after Meals and the fourth cup for completing Hallel and the Blessing of Song. The Gemara discusses whether Grace after Meals requires a cup, and explains that each of the four cups is for a specific mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for the third and fourth cups at the Seder: the third cup is for Grace after Meals, the fourth for completing Hallel and the Blessing of Song, with a restriction on drinking between the third and fourth cups.
Rav Chanan asks Rava whether the Mishnah's rule that the third cup is for Grace after Meals proves that Grace after Meals requires a cup of wine.

Rava answers that the Sages instituted four cups as a symbol of freedom, and each cup is designated for a specific mitzvah, so the third cup does not prove that Grace after Meals independently requires a cup.
The Mishnah is cited again to confirm the rule for the fourth cup, completing Hallel and the Blessing of Song.

items.text: Opening dispute: What is Birkat HaShir?
items.text_en: Opening dispute: What is Birkat HaShir?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Birkat HaShir' refers to. Rav Yehuda says it is 'Yehallelucha', while Rabbi Yochanan says it is 'Nishmat Kol Chai'. A baraisa adds that on the fourth cup one completes Hallel and says Hallel HaGadol, according to Rabbi Tarfon, while others say 'Hashem Ro'i Lo Echsar'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Birkat HaShir' refers to.
Rav Yehuda says Birkat HaShir is the prayer 'Yehallelucha'.
Rabbi Yochanan says Birkat HaShir is the prayer 'Nishmat Kol Chai'.
A baraisa adds that on the fourth cup one completes Hallel and says Hallel HaGadol according to Rabbi Tarfon, while others say 'Hashem Ro'i Lo Echsar'.

items.text: Defining Hallel HaGadol and its name
items.text_en: Defining Hallel HaGadol and its name
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates the scope of Hallel HaGadol: Rabbi Yehuda says from 'Hodu' to 'Naharot Bavel', Rabbi Yochanan says from 'Shir HaMa'alot' to 'Naharot Bavel', and Rav Acha bar Yaakov says from 'Ki Yaakov Bachar Lo Yah' to 'Naharot Bavel'. Rabbi Yochanan explains it is called 'great' because God sits on high and distributes sustenance to all creatures.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where does Hallel HaGadol begin?
Rabbi Yehuda says Hallel HaGadol is from 'Hodu' (Psalm 136) until 'Naharot Bavel' (Psalm 137).
Rabbi Yochanan says Hallel HaGadol is from 'Shir HaMa'alot' (Psalm 126) until 'Naharot Bavel'.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov says Hallel HaGadol is from 'Ki Yaakov Bachar Lo Yah' (Psalm 135) until 'Naharot Bavel'.
The Gemara asks: Why is it called Hallel HaGadol (the Great Hallel)?
Rabbi Yochanan explains it is called 'great' because the Holy One sits on high and distributes sustenance to all creatures.

items.text: The twenty-six 'Hodu's correspond to generations
items.text_en: The twenty-six 'Hodu's correspond to generations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that the twenty-six instances of 'Hodu' in Hallel HaGadol correspond to the twenty-six generations that God created without giving them the Torah, yet He sustained them with His kindness.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that the twenty-six instances of 'Hodu' in Hallel HaGadol correspond to the twenty-six generations that God created without giving them the Torah, yet He sustained them with His kindness.

items.text: God collects debts through one's best possessions
items.text_en: God collects debts through one's best possessions
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains the verse 'Hodu LaHashem Ki Tov' as praising God for collecting a person's debt through his best possession: a rich person through his ox, a poor person through his sheep, an orphan through his egg, and a widow through her chicken.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains the verse 'Hodu LaHashem Ki Tov' as praising God for collecting a person's debt through his best possession: a rich person through his ox, a poor person through his sheep, an orphan through his egg, and a widow through her chicken.

items.text: Sustenance is harder than childbirth and redemption
items.text_en: Sustenance is harder than childbirth and redemption
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that a person's sustenance is twice as hard as childbirth, as childbirth uses 'etzev' while sustenance uses 'itzavon'. He further states that sustenance is harder than redemption, as redemption involved an angel while sustenance involves God directly.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by teaching that a person's sustenance is twice as hard as childbirth, based on the word 'עצב' (pain) used for childbirth versus 'עצבון' (greater pain) used for sustenance.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that sustenance is harder than redemption, as redemption involved an angel (מלאך) while sustenance involves God directly (האלהים הרועה אותי).

items.text: Adam's tears and Resh Lakish's comment
items.text_en: Adam's tears and Resh Lakish's comment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi relates that when God told Adam 'thorns and thistles shall it bring forth to you', Adam wept, thinking he would eat from a trough like an animal. When God said 'by the sweat of your brow you shall eat bread', he was calmed. Resh Lakish then remarks that we would be fortunate if we had remained at the first decree, yet we still eat desert herbs.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi relates that when God told Adam 'thorns and thistles shall it bring forth to you', Adam wept, thinking he would eat from a trough like an animal, but was calmed when God said 'by the sweat of your brow you shall eat bread'.
Resh Lakish remarks that we would be fortunate if we had remained at the first decree, yet we still eat desert herbs.

items.text: Sustenance and bodily functions compared to the splitting of the sea
items.text_en: Sustenance and bodily functions compared to the splitting of the sea
items.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya teaches that a person's sustenance is as difficult as the splitting of the Red Sea, citing verses. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya adds that a person's bodily functions are as difficult as the day of death and the splitting of the sea, citing further verses.

sub.text: Rav Sheizvi in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
sub.text_en: Rav Sheizvi in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi reports in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya that a person's sustenance is as difficult as the splitting of the Red Sea, citing the juxtaposition of verses.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya adds that a person's bodily functions are as difficult as the day of death and the splitting of the Red Sea, citing a verse sequence.

items.text: Desecrating festivals is like idolatry; slanderers deserve dogs
items.text_en: Desecrating festivals is like idolatry; slanderers deserve dogs
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya teaches that one who despises the festivals is as if he worships idolatry, citing verses. He further teaches that one who speaks slander, receives slander, or bears false witness deserves to be thrown to dogs, citing verses.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet citing Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet citing Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya teaches that one who despises the festivals is like an idolater, citing the verse about not making a molten god followed by the command to keep the Festival of Matzot.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet citing Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet citing Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet further teaches in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya that one who speaks slander, receives slander, or bears false witness deserves to be thrown to dogs, citing the verse about throwing to dogs followed by the prohibition against bearing false witness.

items.text: Why we recite the standard Hallel instead of Hallel HaGadol
items.text_en: Why we recite the standard Hallel instead of Hallel HaGadol
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why we recite the standard Hallel when Hallel HaGadol exists. The answer is that the standard Hallel contains five themes: the Exodus, the splitting of the sea, the giving of the Torah, the resurrection of the dead, and the birth pangs of the Messiah. Each is supported by verses, and Rabbi Yochanan offers two interpretations for the verse regarding the birth pangs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why we recite the standard Hallel (הלל) when Hallel HaGadol (הלל הגדול) exists.
The answer is that the standard Hallel contains five themes: the Exodus, the splitting of the sea, the giving of the Torah, the resurrection of the dead, and the birth pangs of the Messiah.
Each of the first four themes is supported by a verse from the standard Hallel.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'לֹא לָנוּ ה׳ לֹא לָנוּ' as referring to the subjugation of the kingdoms (שעבוד מלכיות), the birth pangs of the Messiah.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rabbi Yochanan interprets the same verse as referring to the war of Gog and Magog (מלחמת גוג ומגוג).

items.text: Additional reasons for Hallel: rescue of the righteous and the fiery furnace
items.text_en: Additional reasons for Hallel: rescue of the righteous and the fiery furnace
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says Hallel is recited because it contains the rescue of the righteous from Gehinnom. Chizkiyah says it contains the descent and ascent of the righteous from the fiery furnace. The Gemara elaborates on the verses recited by Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, and recounts the story of Gabriel and the angel Yorekmo regarding the rescue from the furnace, including the merit of Abraham.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that Hallel is recited because it contains the rescue of the righteous from Gehinnom, citing the verse 'אָנָּה ה׳ מַלְּטָה נַפְשִׁי'.
Chizkiyah offers an alternative reason: Hallel contains the descent and ascent of the righteous from the fiery furnace.
The Gemara elaborates on the descent: each of Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah recited a verse from Hallel as they entered the furnace.
The Gemara elaborates on the ascent: each of the three recited verses from Hallel upon their miraculous exit from the furnace.

An alternative tradition attributes the verse 'וֶאֱמֶת ה׳ לְעוֹלָם' to the angel Gabriel, recounting the story of Abraham in the furnace and Gabriel's request to save him, which God declined but promised Gabriel would save three of his descendants.

Rabbi Shimon HaShiloni teaches that when Nebuchadnezzar cast Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah into the furnace, the angel Yorekmo (prince of hail) offered to cool the fire, but Gabriel argued that water extinguishing fire is not a display of God's power, and instead Gabriel, as the prince of fire, would cool it from within.

items.text: Gabriel's declaration and the opening of the verse
items.text_en: Gabriel's declaration and the opening of the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that when God told Moses to descend from the sea, Gabriel opened and said 'And the truth of the Lord endures forever.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that when God told Moses to descend from the sea, Gabriel opened and said 'And the truth of the Lord endures forever.'

items.text: Rabbi Nathan's tradition: the fish said the verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Nathan's tradition: the fish said the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nathan says the fish of the sea said 'And the truth of the Lord endures forever,' based on Rav Huna's teaching that Israel in that generation were small of faith.
