The Gemara elaborates with the story of the sea's refusal to release the Egyptians, God's promise of one and a half, and the eventual fulfillment through the Kishon River.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nathan states that the fish of the sea recited the verse 'And the truth of the Lord endures forever.'
Rav Huna explains that the Israelites of that generation were small of faith, providing context for the fish's praise.
Rabbah bar Mari expounds the verse 'They rebelled at the sea, at the Sea of Reeds,' teaching that Israel said they and the Egyptians would both emerge from the sea.
God commands the angel of the sea to cast the Egyptians onto dry land; the angel objects that a slave does not return a gift, and God promises one and a half in return.
The sea further objects that a slave cannot sue his master; God appoints the Kishon River as guarantor, and the sea casts the Egyptians onto dry land.
The Gemara asks what is meant by 'one and a half' among them.
The Gemara answers: Pharaoh had 600 chosen chariots, while Sisera had 900 iron chariots, so Sisera's force was one and a half times that of Pharaoh.
When Sisera came with iron spikes, God sent stars from their courses to heat and soften the spikes, causing the Canaanites to descend to cool off in the Kishon River.
God commands the Kishon River to fulfill its guarantee; it sweeps the Canaanites into the sea, and at that moment the fish of the sea recite the verse 'And the truth of the Lord endures forever.'

items.text: Resh Lakish and Rava's homilies on Knesset Yisrael
items.text_en: Resh Lakish and Rava's homilies on Knesset Yisrael
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets 'He makes the barren woman dwell in a house' as Knesset Yisrael saying she is like a weasel dwelling in the foundations. Rava interprets 'I love that the Lord hears' as Knesset Yisrael saying she is beloved when He hears her supplications, and 'I was poor and He saved me' as despite being poor in mitzvot, she is His.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse 'He makes the barren woman dwell in a house' as Knesset Yisrael complaining that her children have made her like a weasel dwelling in the foundations of houses.

Rava interprets two verses: 'I love that the Lord hears' means Knesset Yisrael is beloved when He hears her supplications, and 'I was poor and He saved me' means despite being poor in mitzvot, she is His and it is fitting for Him to save her.

items.text: Rav Kahana's report: Rabbi Yishmael's message about Psalm 117
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's report: Rabbi Yishmael's message about Psalm 117
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports that when Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei was ill, Rabbi sent to ask him to say something in his father's name. He replied that 'Praise the Lord, all nations' refers to the nations praising God for His mighty deeds, and all the more so Israel, upon whom His kindness has prevailed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports that when Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei was ill, Rabbi sent to ask him to say something in his father's name.

Rabbi Yishmael replies in his father's name that 'Praise the Lord, all nations' refers to the nations praising God for His mighty deeds, and all the more so Israel, upon whom His kindness has prevailed.

items.text: Future tribute: Egypt, Cush, and wicked Rome
items.text_en: Future tribute: Egypt, Cush, and wicked Rome
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues the message: Egypt will bring a gift to the Messiah, and God commands acceptance because they hosted Israel. Cush argues a fortiori and is accepted. Wicked Rome argues a fortiori but is rejected; God tells Gabriel to 'rebuke the beast of the reed.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that in the future Egypt will bring a gift to the Messiah, and God commands acceptance because they hosted Israel in Egypt.
Cush argues a fortiori that if Egypt, which enslaved Israel, is accepted, then Cush, which did not enslave them, should certainly be accepted, and God commands acceptance.

sub.text: Wicked Rome's a fortiori argument and rejection
sub.text_en: Wicked Rome's a fortiori argument and rejection
sub.desc_en: Wicked Rome argues a fortiori that if Egypt and Cush, who are not brothers, are accepted, then Rome, which is a brother, should certainly be accepted, but God rejects them and tells Gabriel to 'rebuke the beast of the reed.'

items.text: Alternative interpretation and Rabbi Yochanan's exposition
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation and Rabbi Yochanan's exposition
items.desc_en: An alternative interpretation of 'rebuke the beast of the reed' refers to a beast dwelling among reeds. Rabbi Yochanan explains it as rebuking the beast whose deeds are written with one quill, and interprets the subsequent verses as referring to those who slaughter the mighty like calves, stretch out hands for money, and cause Israel's dispersion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation of the verse 'גְּעוֹר חַיַּת קָנֶה' (rebuke the beast of the reed), explaining it as referring to a beast that dwells among reeds, citing the verse 'יְכַרְסְמֶנָּה חֲזִיר מִיָּעַר וְזִיז שָׂדַי יִרְעֶנָּה' (the boar from the forest ravages it, and the creatures of the field feed on it).

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the verse rebukes the beast whose deeds are all written with a single quill (i.e., Rome, whose power is unified).

Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'עֲדַת אַבִּירִים בְּעֶגְלֵי עַמִּים' (the congregation of the mighty among the calves of the peoples) as referring to those who slaughtered the mighty (righteous) like calves that have no owners (i.e., without accountability).

Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'מִתְרַפֵּס בְּרַצֵּי כָסֶף' (trampling on pieces of silver) as referring to those who stretch out their hands to accept money but do not perform the will of the Owner (God).

Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'פִּיזַּר עַמִּים קְרָבוֹת יֶחְפָּצוּן' (he scattered peoples, they desire wars) as asking what caused Israel to be dispersed among the nations — the sacrifices (קְרִיבוֹת) that they desired (i.e., their improper attachment to offerings).

items.text: The markets of Rome and the fate of its wealth
items.text_en: The markets of Rome and the fate of its wealth
items.desc_en: The message continues: Rome has 365 markets, each with 365 towers, etc., sufficient to feed the whole world. Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi asks Rabbi to whom this wealth belongs, and answers it is for him, his colleagues, and their disciples, as per the verse 'its merchandise and its hire shall be holy to the Lord.' Rav Yosef and Rabbi Elazar explain the terms.

sub.text: Message from Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Message from Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: The message describes the vast markets of Rome, each with towers and steps sufficient to feed the entire world.
Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi asks Rabbi to whom this immense wealth belongs.
Rabbi answers that the wealth is for him, his colleagues, and their disciples, citing the verse 'its merchandise and its hire shall be holy to the Lord.'
Rav Yosef explains the terms 'לֹא יֵאָצֵר' and 'לֹא יֵחָסֵן' as referring to a storehouse and a treasury, respectively.
Rabbi Elazar begins to explain the phrase 'כִּי לַיּוֹשְׁבִים לִפְנֵי ה׳' (the continuation of the verse).

items.text: Interpretations of 'one who covers the ancient'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'one who covers the ancient'
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two interpretations of the phrase 'one who covers the ancient' from a verse. One opinion identifies it as one who covers matters that the Ancient of Days concealed, namely the secrets of the Torah. Another opinion identifies it as one who reveals matters that the Ancient of Days concealed, namely the reasons of the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces two interpretations of the phrase 'one who covers the ancient' from a verse, first citing an opinion that it refers to one who recognizes his fellow's place in the study hall.
Some say Rabbi Elazar identifies 'one who covers the ancient' as one who covers matters that the Ancient of Days concealed, namely the secrets of the Torah.
Others say 'one who covers the ancient' refers to one who reveals matters that the Ancient of Days concealed, namely the reasons of the Torah.

items.text: God rejoices when defeated
items.text_en: God rejoices when defeated
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana in the name of Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei explains a verse from Psalms, interpreting it as a call to sing to God, who is defeated and rejoices. This is contrasted with human nature, where being defeated causes sadness, while God rejoices, as evidenced by a verse about Moses standing in the breach.

sub.text: Rav Kahana in the name of Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana in the name of Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana cites Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei interpreting the verse 'לַמְנַצֵּחַ מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד' as a call to sing to God, who is defeated and rejoices.
The Gemara contrasts human nature, where defeat causes sadness, with God, who rejoices when defeated, citing the verse about Moses standing in the breach.

items.text: God's hand under the wings of the Chayot
items.text_en: God's hand under the wings of the Chayot
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana in the name of Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nasia, interprets a verse about 'hands of a man under their wings' as referring to God's hand, which is spread under the wings of the Chayot to receive penitents from the attribute of justice.

sub.text: Rav Kahana citing Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, citing Rabbi Yehuda Nasia
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana citing Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, citing Rabbi Yehuda Nasia
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana interprets the verse 'וידֵי אדם מתחת כנפיהם' (and hands of a man under their wings) as referring to God's hand spread under the wings of the Chayot (heavenly creatures) to receive penitents from the attribute of justice.

items.text: The journey of Joseph's wealth through history
items.text_en: The journey of Joseph's wealth through history
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that Joseph gathered all the silver and gold in the world and brought it to Egypt. This wealth was taken by the Israelites when they left Egypt, and then passed through a series of rulers: Rehoboam, Shishak, Zerah, Asa, Hadrimmon, the Ammonites, Jehoshaphat, Ahaz, Sennacherib, Hezekiah, Zedekiah, the Chaldeans, the Persians, the Greeks, and finally the Romans, where it remains.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that Joseph gathered all the silver and gold in the world and brought it to Egypt, citing a verse and expanding it to include all lands.

The gemara reports that when the Israelites left Egypt they took this wealth, with Rav Asi and Rabbi Shimon offering different interpretations of the verse 'וַיְנַצְּלוּ אֶת מִצְרָיִם' (they despoiled Egypt).
The gemara traces the wealth's journey from Rehoboam to Shishak and then to Zerah king of Cush.
The gemara continues the chain: Asa took it from Zerah and sent it to Hadrimmon, the Ammonites took it, Jehoshaphat recovered it, and it remained until Ahaz.

The gemara completes the chain: Sennacherib took it from Ahaz, Hezekiah from Sennacherib, then it passed through Zedekiah, the Chaldeans, the Persians, the Greeks, and finally the Romans, where it remains.

items.text: The three treasures of Joseph and Korach's wealth
items.text_en: The three treasures of Joseph and Korach's wealth
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina states that Joseph hid three treasures in Egypt: one was revealed to Korach, one to Antoninus ben Asverus, and one is hidden for the righteous in the future. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish identifies the verse 'wealth kept for its owner to his harm' as referring to Korach's wealth. Rabbi Elazar explains that a person's money stands them on their feet, and Rabbi Levi describes the immense size of Korach's treasure house keys.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina states that Joseph hid three treasures in Egypt: one was revealed to Korach, one to Antoninus ben Asverus, and one is hidden for the righteous in the future.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish identifies the verse 'wealth kept for its owner to his harm' as referring to Korach's wealth.
Rabbi Elazar explains that a person's money stands them on their feet, citing the verse 'and all the substance that was at their feet'.
Rabbi Levi describes the immense size of Korach's treasure house keys, which required a load of three hundred white mules.

items.text: Distribution of Psalm 118 verses among David's family
items.text_en: Distribution of Psalm 118 verses among David's family
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan assigns each verse of Psalm 118 to a different speaker: David, Jesse, David's brothers, and Samuel. The verses are distributed among them, with some verses spoken by all.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan assigns the first set of Psalm 118 verses to David, Jesse, David's brothers, and Samuel.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan (continued)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan (continued)
sub.desc_en: The same authority continues assigning the remaining verses of Psalm 118 to the same speakers, with some verses spoken by all.

items.text: Introduction of a Mishnah from elsewhere
items.text_en: Introduction of a Mishnah from elsewhere
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a Mishnah from another tractate, indicating a transition to a new topic, likely related to customs of work on the eve of Passover.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Mishnah from another tractate, signaling a transition to a new topic about local customs regarding work on the eve of Passover.

items.text: Blessing before and after eating
items.text_en: Blessing before and after eating
items.desc_en: Abaye distinguishes between blessing after eating (dependent on local custom) and before eating (a mitzvah). A proof is brought from Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that all mitzvot require a blessing before performance, and the meaning of 'over' is clarified with biblical verses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the practice of folding or spreading the matzah cover and whether to recite a blessing after eating depends on local custom.
Abaye distinguishes: the Mishnah's leniency applies only to the blessing after eating, but the blessing before eating is a מצוה (commandment) that must be performed.
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel's principle that one recites a blessing over all מצות (commandments) before performing them, supporting Abaye's ruling.
The Gemara questions how the word 'עוֹבֵר' (passes) implies 'before' (i.e., performing the blessing before the act).
Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak proves from the verse 'וַיַּעֲבוֹר אֶת הַכּוּשִׁי' (and he passed the Cushite) that 'עוֹבֵר' means 'preceding' or 'passing before'.
Abaye offers an alternative proof from the verse 'וְהוּא עָבַר לִפְנֵיהֶם' (and he passed before them).
An anonymous tradition cites the verse 'וַיַּעֲבוֹר מַלְכָּם לִפְנֵיהֶם' (their king passed before them) as further proof that 'עוֹבֵר' means 'before'.

items.text: Rabbi's and Rabbi Elazar ben Parta's additions
items.text_en: Rabbi's and Rabbi Elazar ben Parta's additions
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi would double words in the blessing, while Rabbi Elazar ben Parta would add words. Abaye explains that the addition is to double from 'Odekha' onward.

sub.desc_en: A baraita reports that Rabbi would double words in the blessing and Rabbi Elazar ben Parta would add words.
The gemara asks what Rabbi Elazar ben Parta would add.
Abaye explains that the addition is to double from the word 'אוֹדְךָ' (I will thank You) onward.

items.text: The future feast for the righteous
items.text_en: The future feast for the righteous
items.desc_en: Rav Avira expounds on the verse about the feast God will make for the righteous. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and Joshua each decline to lead the blessing over the cup, citing their shortcomings, but David accepts, citing his worthiness.

sub.text: Rav Avira (citing Rav Ami or Rav Asi)
sub.text_en: Rav Avira (citing Rav Ami or Rav Asi)
sub.desc_en: Rav Avira expounds that God will make a feast for the righteous, and after eating, they give Abraham the cup of blessing to lead the blessing.

Abraham declines to bless because Ishmael came from him; Isaac declines because Esau came from him; Jacob declines because he married two sisters while they were alive, which the Torah would later forbid.
Moses declines because he did not merit entering the Land of Israel; Joshua declines because he had no son, as the verse only mentions 'Joshua son of Nun' without further descendants.
David accepts the cup of blessing, declaring it fitting for him, citing the verse 'I will lift the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.'

items.text: Mishnah: No afikoman after the Passover
items.text_en: Mishnah: No afikoman after the Passover
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not conclude the Passover meal with afikoman, meaning no additional eating after the sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that one may not conclude the Passover meal with afikoman, meaning no additional eating after the sacrifice.

items.text: Gemara: Defining afikoman
items.text_en: Gemara: Defining afikoman
items.desc_en: Rav explains afikoman as not moving from one group to another. Shmuel defines it as dishes like ordeals and pigeons. Rabbi Yochanan defines it as dates, parched grain, and nuts, and a baraita supports him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'afikoman' means, and Rav answers that it means not moving from one group to another.
Shmuel defines afikoman as dishes like ordeals and pigeons.
Rabbi Yochanan defines afikoman as dates, parched grain, and nuts.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's definition, stating that one may not conclude the Passover meal with dates, parched grain, and nuts.

items.text: Afikoman after matzah vs. after the Passover
items.text_en: Afikoman after matzah vs. after the Passover
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says no afikoman after matzah either. The Gemara questions this from the Mishnah, which only prohibits after the Passover. The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's statement is a fortiori: if after matzah it is prohibited, after the Passover it is certainly prohibited.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that one may not conclude the meal with afikoman after matzah.
The Gemara challenges Shmuel from the Mishnah, which only prohibits afikoman after the Passover lamb, implying it is permitted after matzah.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's statement is a fortiori: if after matzah it is prohibited, after the Passover it is certainly prohibited.

items.text: Support from a baraita about sponges and honey cakes
items.text_en: Support from a baraita about sponges and honey cakes
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one may fill his stomach with sponges, honey cakes, and iskritin, provided he eats an olive's bulk of matzah at the end. The Gemara notes that this implies eating after matzah is permitted, but the discussion is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to bring a supporting baraita that allows filling one's stomach with sponges, honey cakes, and iskritin, provided he eats an olive's bulk of matzah at the end, implying that eating after matzah is permitted.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's first statement
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's first statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'at the first [cup] no' is not a qualification but a clarification: even at the first cup one may not eat, and certainly not at the last cup where one might eat a heavy meal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's phrase 'at the first cup no' is not a qualification but a clarification: even at the first cup one may not eat, and certainly not at the last cup where one might eat a heavy meal.

items.text: Mar Zutra's version and support for afikoman after matzah
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's version and support for afikoman after matzah
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra teaches that Rav Yosef said in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: one may conclude after matzah with afikoman. A baraita is cited that seems to support this, but the Gemara explains it is not a proof but a clarification.

sub.text: Mar Zutra's version of Rav Yosef's statement
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra's version of Rav Yosef's statement
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra teaches a version where Rav Yosef in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules that one may conclude the meal with matzah as afikoman, and a supporting baraita is cited.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita is not a proof but a clarification: after matzah one may certainly conclude, and after the pesach offering one might think not, so it teaches that one may.

The Gemara rejects the support, explaining that the baraita is not a proof but a clarification: it teaches that even after matzah, where the taste is less strong, one may not conclude with afikoman, and certainly not after the pesach sacrifice.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about sponge cakes and matzah
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about sponge cakes and matzah
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought as an objection: one may fill his stomach with sponge cakes, honey cakes, and iskritin, provided he eats an olive's bulk of matzah at the end. This implies that at the beginning one may not eat such items, contradicting the earlier teaching. The Gemara again explains that this is not a problem but a clarification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that permits filling one's stomach with various cakes only if one eats an olive's bulk of matzah at the end, implying that at the first cup one may not eat such cakes.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita is not a qualification but a clarification: at the first cup one certainly may not eat, and at the last cup one might think not, so it teaches that one may.

items.text: Rava's distinction between matzah and maror in the present era
items.text_en: Rava's distinction between matzah and maror in the present era
items.desc_en: Rava states that in the present era (without the Temple), matzah is a Torah obligation while maror is rabbinic. The Gemara questions this based on the verse 'upon matzot and marorim', and Rava explains that the Torah later reestablished matzah as an independent obligation. Rav Acha bar Yaakov argues both are rabbinic. The Gemara resolves the verses and supports Rava's view.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that matzah nowadays is a Torah obligation, while maror is rabbinic, and explains that maror is derived from the verse 'על מצות ומרורים' which only applies when the pesach offering exists.
The Gemara objects that matzah also appears in the same verse, and cites Rav Acha bar Yaakov who says both matzah and maror are rabbinic nowadays.

The Gemara objects further that the verse 'בערב תאכלו מצות' seems to mandate matzah, and explains that this verse is needed for a person who is impure or on a distant journey, lest one think they are exempt from matzah and maror as well.
Rava responds that the impure and distant traveler do not need a special verse, as they are no worse than an uncircumcised person or a gentile, who are permitted to eat matzah and maror.
The Gemara concludes that both verses are needed, as each teaches a different aspect.

sub.text: Gemara's answer on behalf of Rav Acha bar Yaakov
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer on behalf of Rav Acha bar Yaakov
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse is needed to teach that a person who is טמא (ritually impure) or on a distant journey, who cannot eat the Pesach sacrifice, must still eat matzah and maror.

sub.text: Rava's rejection of the alternative explanation
sub.text_en: Rava's rejection of the alternative explanation
sub.desc_en: Rava rejects this, arguing that the case of a טמא (ritually impure person) or distant traveler does not need a special verse, since they are no worse than an ערל (uncircumcised person) or בן נכר (alien), who are permitted to eat matzah and maror as taught in a baraita.
The Gemara resolves the dispute by stating that both verses are written and both are necessary, supporting Rava's view that matzah is a Torah obligation.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rava's view on matzah as a Torah obligation
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rava's view on matzah as a Torah obligation
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava: from the verse 'six days you shall eat matzot' it is derived that the six days are optional, but the first night is obligatory due to the verse 'upon matzot and marorim they shall eat it'. This applies both when the Temple stands and when it does not, as the verse 'in the evening you shall eat matzot' establishes it as a duty.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rava by citing a verse that compares the six days of matzah to the seventh day, which is a voluntary holiday, implying that matzah is voluntary except for the first night.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the hermeneutic principle
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the hermeneutic principle
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the hermeneutic principle that when something is included in a general rule and then excluded to teach, it teaches about the entire general rule.
The baraita continues that one might think even the first night is voluntary, but the verse 'על מצות ומרורים יאכלוהו' teaches that it is obligatory.
The baraita concludes that even when the Temple is not standing, the verse 'בערב תאכלו מצות' establishes matzah as an obligation.

items.text: Mishnah: sleeping during the Seder
items.text_en: Mishnah: sleeping during the Seder
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: if some of the participants fell asleep, they may eat; if all fell asleep, they may not eat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if some of the participants fell asleep, they may eat, but if all fell asleep, they may not eat.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between drowsiness (nimnum) and deep sleep (nirdam) regarding eating the paschal offering, and states that after midnight the paschal offering and piggul/notar impart impurity to hands.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei rules that drowsy participants may eat the paschal offering but deeply asleep ones may not, and states that after midnight the paschal offering, piggul, and notar impart impurity to hands.

items.text: Gemara's definition of nimnum
items.text_en: Gemara's definition of nimnum
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the definition of nimnum (drowsiness) through Rav Ashi's description and an anecdote about Abaye and Rabbah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definition of dozing (נתנמנם).
Rav Ashi defines dozing as a state where one is neither fully asleep nor fully awake, can respond but cannot reason coherently, and later remembers when reminded.
An anecdote illustrates the definition: Abaye sees Rabbah dozing and asks if he is sleeping; Rabbah responds that he is dozing, citing the mishna's distinction.

items.text: Source for midnight limit
items.text_en: Source for midnight limit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who the Tanna is that holds the paschal offering becomes notar after midnight, and Rav Yosef identifies it as Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, who derives from a gezerah shavah with the Exodus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the mishna that the Paschal lamb becomes notar after midnight and asks which tanna holds this view.
Rav Yosef identifies the tanna as Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya derives from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between 'בלילה הזה' here and in the Exodus passage that the Paschal lamb may be eaten only until midnight.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva objects based on the verse 'chippazon' (haste), and the Gemara explains that the word 'laylah' teaches that the paschal offering is eaten only at night, not during the day.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva objects to Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's derivation from 'בלילה הזה' (this night), citing the verse 'חיפזון' (haste) to argue that the paschal offering may be eaten until the time of haste (dawn).

The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the word 'בלילה' (at night) teaches that the paschal offering is eaten only at night, not during the day, while 'חיפזון' defines the end time as dawn.

items.text: Debate on 'hazeh' and alternative derivations
items.text_en: Debate on 'hazeh' and alternative derivations
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how Rabbi Akiva uses the word 'hazeh' to exclude eating the paschal offering over two nights, while Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya derives the same from 'lo totiru ad boker', and they debate the meaning of 'boker'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Akiva does with the word 'hazeh' (this), and explains that it excludes the possibility of eating the paschal offering over two nights, based on a comparison to peace offerings.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya argues that the same exclusion is derived from the verse 'lo totiru ad boker' (do not leave over until morning).
Rabbi Akiva objects that without 'hazeh', one might interpret 'boker' (morning) as the second morning, allowing two nights.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya responds that wherever 'boker' is written in the Torah, it always means the first morning, so no further exclusion is needed.

items.text: Rava's ruling on matzah after midnight
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on matzah after midnight
items.desc_en: Rava states that one who eats matzah after midnight nowadays, according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, does not fulfill his obligation, and the Gemara clarifies that the hekesh to the paschal offering is restored for this matter.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that one who eats matzah after midnight in the present era, according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, does not fulfill his obligation, because matzah is linked to the paschal offering and the verse that excluded it from the comparison only restored it for the original matter.
The Gemara asks: This is obvious, since matzah is linked (הוקש) to the paschal offering, so it should be like the paschal offering.

The Gemara explains that Rava's statement is necessary lest one think that the verse removed matzah from the hekesh (link) to the paschal offering; Rava teaches that the verse only restored the hekesh for the first matter (the time limit).

items.text: Reasons for impurity of piggul and notar
items.text_en: Reasons for impurity of piggul and notar
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda about whether the impurity of piggul and notar on hands is due to suspicion of priests or laziness of priests, and whether it applies to an olive's bulk or an egg's bulk.

sub.text: Gemara's question about the impurity of piggul and notar
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about the impurity of piggul and notar
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes the Mishnah's ruling that piggul and notar impart impurity to hands, and records a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda: one says it is due to suspicion of priests (חשדי כהונה) and the other due to lazy priests (עצלי כהונה).
A further dispute is recorded: one opinion holds that the impurity applies to an olive's bulk (כזית), while the other holds it applies to an egg's bulk (כביצה).

sub.text: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda's second dispute
sub.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda's second dispute
sub.desc_en: They also dispute the minimum measure that imparts impurity: one says an olive's bulk (כזית), the other says an egg's bulk (כביצה).

items.text: Dispute about the wording of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Dispute about the wording of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Two Tannaim differ on whether the Mishnah's phrase refers to piggul or notar, each offering a reason based on priestly concerns. A second dispute concerns the measure for liability: a kezayit or a ke'beitzah, each tied to different halakhic principles.

sub.desc_en: One Tanna teaches that the Mishnah's phrase refers to פיגול (piggul), while another teaches it refers to נותר (notar).
The Gemara explains that the one who says פיגול (piggul) is concerned about suspicion against priests, while the one who says נותר (notar) is concerned about lazy priests.

A second dispute: one Amora says the measure for liability is a כזית (olive's bulk) because it matches the prohibition's measure, while another says it is a כביצה (egg's bulk) because it matches the impurity's measure.

items.text: Mishnah: Blessing for Pesach exempts the blessing for the festival peace-offering
items.text_en: Mishnah: Blessing for Pesach exempts the blessing for the festival peace-offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yishmael holds that the blessing for the pesach sacrifice exempts the blessing for the festival peace-offering, but not vice versa. Rabbi Akiva holds that neither exempts the other.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the ruling that the blessing for the pesach sacrifice exempts the blessing for the festival peace-offering.
Rabbi Yishmael states that the blessing for the festival peace-offering does not exempt the blessing for the pesach sacrifice.
Rabbi Akiva holds that neither blessing exempts the other.

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of the underlying principles
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of the underlying principles
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yishmael, the rite of 'zerikah' (sprinkling) is included in the general category of 'shefikhah' (pouring), but not vice versa. According to Rabbi Akiva, neither rite is included in the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the underlying principle: according to Rabbi Yishmael, the rite of זריקה (sprinkling) is included in the general category of שפיכה (pouring), but not vice versa.
The Gemara completes the explanation: according to Rabbi Akiva, neither rite is included in the other.

items.text: Opening scenario
items.text_en: Opening scenario
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai arrives at a pidyon haben ceremony and asks a straightforward question: who recites the blessing 'who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the redemption of the son' — the father or the priest?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai arrives at a pidyon haben ceremony and asks who recites the blessing 'who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the redemption of the son' — the father or the priest.
Rabbi Simlai then asks who recites the blessing of shehecheyanu (who has kept us alive and sustained us) — the father or the priest.

items.text: Gemara's first question
items.text_en: Gemara's first question
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the dilemma: the priest receives the money (benefit) so he should bless, but the father performs the mitzvah so he should bless. Since neither is obvious, Rabbi Simlai asks the academy.

sub.desc_en: The gemara considers the reasoning: perhaps the priest recites the blessing because he receives the benefit (the five silver coins), or perhaps the father recites it because he performs the מצוה (commandment).
Rabbi Simlai did not know the answer, so he asked at the study hall, and they told him: the father recites both blessings.
The gemara concludes with the binding הלכה (law): the father recites both blessings.

items.text: Academy's answer
items.text_en: Academy's answer
items.desc_en: The academy answers: the father recites two blessings — both the redemption blessing and the 'shehecheyanu' blessing.

sub.desc_en: The gemara considers the reasoning: perhaps the priest recites the blessing because he receives the benefit (the five silver coins), or perhaps the father recites it because he performs the מצוה (commandment).
Rabbi Simlai did not know the answer, so he asked at the study hall, and they told him: the father recites both blessings.
The gemara concludes with the binding הלכה (law): the father recites both blessings.

items.text: Halakhic conclusion
items.text_en: Halakhic conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara records the final ruling: the father recites two blessings.

sub.desc_en: The gemara considers the reasoning: perhaps the priest recites the blessing because he receives the benefit (the five silver coins), or perhaps the father recites it because he performs the מצוה (commandment).
Rabbi Simlai did not know the answer, so he asked at the study hall, and they told him: the father recites both blessings.
The gemara concludes with the binding הלכה (law): the father recites both blessings.
